DIPHTHERIA

OVERVIEW OF THE DISEASE

- **Disease Nature**: An acute bacterial infectious disease caused by toxigenic strains of Corynebacterium diphtheriae.
- **Major clinical types**: Anterior nasal, faucial, and laryngeal. Skin, conjunctiva, and vulva may also be affected.
- **Characterized By The**: Characterized by the formation of a greyish/yellowish false membrane and signs of toxaemia.
- **Fatality rate**: 5-10%.

EPIDEMIOLOGICAL DETERMINANTS

- **Agent**: C. diphtheriae (gram-positive, non-motile organism). Four types: gravis, mitis, belfanti, intermedius. Produces a powerful exotoxin (beta phage dependent).
- **Source of infection**: Cases and carriers (temporary or chronic; nasal carriers are particularly dangerous due to frequent shedding).
- **Period of infectivity**: 14 to 28 days (longer in carriers).
- **Age**: Affects children aged 1 to 5 years predominantly.
- **Immunity**: Infants immune for first few months if mother is immune. 75% of children in developing countries have protective antibodies by age 6-8 years due to inapparent infections.
- **Transmission**: Droplet infection, direct contact with cutaneous lesions, or infected objects (cups, toys).
- **Incubation period**: 2 to 6 days.

CLINICAL FEATURES

- **Clinical Presentation**: Sore throat, difficulty swallowing, low-grade fever.
- **False membrane**: Greyish/yellowish patch over tonsils/pharynx. Extends to become thick and adherent. Bleeds on attempt to remove.
- **Bullneck Appearance Due**: "Bull-neck" appearance due to marked oedema of the submandibular area and lymphadenopathy.
- **Complications**: Myocarditis, nerve paralysis.

CONTROL AND PREVENTION

- **Cases & Carriers**: Isolation for at least 14 days (or until 2 consecutive negative swabs). Diphtheria antitoxin (20,000-100,000 units IV/IM) + Penicillin or Erythromycin (5-6 days). Carriers receive 10 days of oral erythromycin.
- **Contacts**: Throat swabbing. Booster dose of toxoid or prophylactic penicillin/erythromycin + 1000-2000 units of antitoxin.
- **Active Immunization**: DPT vaccine or Pentavalent vaccine. Contains 25 Lf of diphtheria toxoid per dose. Adsorbed on aluminium phosphate/hydroxide. Adult type (dT) contains <= 2 Lf per dose.
- **Efficacy**: Failures may occur if the toxin dose is extremely large, despite high antitoxin titres.

OUTBREAK INVESTIGATION AND CONTROL (SCHOOL / COMMUNITY)

1. Verify diagnosis: clinical membrane + toxigenicity testing / culture of C. diphtheriae when available; notify.
2. Case management: isolate; diphtheria antitoxin + antibiotics (penicillin or erythromycin); airway support for laryngeal disease.
3. Contact management: throat swabs of close contacts; prophylactic antibiotics; booster toxoid if immunization incomplete/outdated; surveillance for secondary cases.
4. Search for carriers and additional cases in the class/household.
5. Environmental: limit crowding; reinforce respiratory hygiene; no sharing of cups/utensils during outbreak.
6. Programmatic: review DPT/pentavalent and booster coverage; catch-up immunization of susceptibles.

FACTORS FOR REEMERGENCE OF DIPHTHERIA

- **Contributing Factor**: Incomplete primary immunization and missed boosters (waning antitoxin with age).
- **Pockets Of Low**: Pockets of low coverage, migration, and urban crowding.
- **Contributing Factor**: Delayed recognition of faucial/laryngeal disease and incomplete contact chemoprophylaxis.
- **Complacency After Long**: Complacency after long periods of low incidence.
- **Control**: sustain high coverage with primary series + boosters; early antitoxin; contact treatment; outbreak immunization.

> **EXAM TIP:** Case definition → isolation + antitoxin + antibiotic → contact swab/chemoprophylaxis/toxoid → coverage gap analysis. For reemergence: list 4–5 host–programme factors then control.

WHOOPING COUGH (PERTUSSIS)

OVERVIEW OF THE DISEASE

- **Disease Nature**: Acute infectious disease usually of young children, caused by B. pertussis.
- **Characterized By Insidious**: Characterized by insidious onset with mild fever, irritating cough becoming paroxysmal with a characteristic "whoop" (loud crowing inspiration), cyanosis, and vomiting.
- **Chinese Call It**: Chinese call it a "Hundred Day Cough".

EPIDEMIOLOGICAL DETERMINANTS

- **Agent**: Bordetella pertussis. B. parapertussis causes <5% of cases.
- **Source of infection**: Case of pertussis. No chronic carrier state exists.
- **Infective material**: Nasopharyngeal and bronchial secretions.
- **Period of infectivity**: Most infectious during catarrhal stage. Extends from 1 week after exposure to ~3 weeks after onset of paroxysmal stage.
- **Secondary attack rate**: 90% in unimmunized household contacts.
- **Age**: Infants and pre-school children. Highest incidence below 5 years. Median age of infection is 20-30 months in developing countries.
- **Sex**: Incidence and fatality are higher in females.
- **Transmission**: Droplet infection and direct contact.
- **Incubation period**: 7 to 14 days (not more than 3 weeks).

CLINICAL COURSE

- **Catarrhal stage (10 days)**: Insidious onset, lacrimation, sneezing, coryza, hacking night cough.
- **Paroxysmal stage**: Paroxysmal stage (2-4 weeks): Bursts of rapid consecutive coughs followed by a deep, high-pitched inspiration (whoop). Followed by vomiting.
- **Convalescent stage**: Convalescent stage (1-2 weeks): Recovery phase. Total illness lasts 6-8 weeks.
- **Complications**: Bronchopneumonia, bronchiectasis, subconjunctival haemorrhages, epistaxis. Encephalopathy is rare.

CONTROL AND PREVENTION

- **Treatment**: Erythromycin (drug of choice, 30-50 mg/kg/day in 4 divided doses for 10 days). Azithromycin, Clarithromycin.
- **Immunization**: DPT, DTwP, or DTaP vaccine. Administered at 6, 10, and 14 weeks with boosters. Both whole-cell and acellular vaccines provide ~85% protection. Immunity lasts 6-12 years.

[SN]Adverse Events Following Immunization (AEFI)[/SN]

[LAQ]Classification of AEFI and investigation of clustered deaths after vaccination[/LAQ]

ADVERSE EVENTS FOLLOWING IMMUNIZATION (AEFI)

DEFINITION

- **An Aefi Is**: An AEFI is any untoward medical occurrence which follows immunization and which does not necessarily have a causal relationship with the usage of the vaccine. The adverse event may be any unfavourable or unintended sign, abnormal laboratory finding, symptom or disease.

CLASSIFICATION (WHO / MoHFW OPERATIONAL CATEGORIES)
| Type | Meaning | Examples |
|------|---------|----------|
| Vaccine product-related | Caused by one or more inherent properties of the vaccine | Anaphylaxis to a vaccine component; VAPP after OPV |
| Vaccine quality defect-related | Caused by a quality defect including the device | Contamination leading to toxic shock after reconstituted measles vaccine |
| Immunization error-related (programme error) | Inappropriate handling, prescribing, or administration | Wrong diluent; non-sterile syringe; reconstituted vaccine kept beyond permitted time; freeze-sensitive vaccine frozen |
| Immunization anxiety-related | Anxiety about immunization | Vasovagal syncope in adolescents |
| Coincidental | Caused by something other than vaccine, error, or anxiety | Concurrent infection; temporal association without causal link |

SEVERITY AND REPORTING

- **Serious AEFI**: death, life-threatening illness, hospitalization or its prolongation, persistent disability, congenital anomaly, or a cluster of events.
- **Cluster Investigation**: Clusters (for example multiple deaths after the same session, vial, or site) are treated as public-health emergencies for the immunization programme until investigated.

AS DISTRICT IMMUNIZATION OFFICER: FOUR SUSPECTED DEATHS WITHIN 24 HOURS OF MEASLES VACCINATION IN A REMOTE VILLAGE

1. Immediate actions
- **Notify The State**: Notify the State AEFI committee / SEPIO and district administration per cascade; do not wait for laboratory proof.
- **Suspend Use Of**: Suspend use of the implicated vaccine lot, vial, and session supplies; quarantine remaining vials, diluents, and syringes with batch numbers.
- **Secure Coldchain Logs**: Secure cold-chain logs, session microplan, tally sheets, reconstitution times, and the list of all children vaccinated in that session and nearby sessions using the same lot.
- **Arrange Clinical Verification**: Arrange clinical verification of deaths (verbal autopsy and medical records) while the AEFI pathway proceeds.

2. Field investigation team
- **Dio With District**: DIO with District AEFI committee members, a paediatrician or physician, cold-chain officer, ANM/ASHA of the village, and laboratory focal point; local administration support for community confidence.

3. Epidemiological investigation
- **Line list**: name, age, sex, time of vaccination, injection site, vaccine name/batch/expiry, diluent batch, time of reconstitution, onset of symptoms, clinical course, place of death.
- **Attack Rates Among**: Attack rates among vaccinated versus unvaccinated children; clustering by vial, vaccinator, site, or time of day.
- **Assess programme errors**: unsterile injections, wrong diluent, delayed use of reconstituted measles vaccine, toxic-shock pattern (cluster within hours with fever, vomiting, shock).

4. Laboratory and product investigation
- **Send Remaining Vaccine**: Send remaining vaccine and diluent for quality testing through the designated pathway; blood culture or autopsy samples when feasible and appropriate.
- **Evaluate For Sepsis**: Evaluate for sepsis or toxic shock when an error-related cluster is suspected.

5. Causality assessment
- **Use The National**: Use the national AEFI causality algorithm aligned with WHO: eligibility → checklist → algorithm → classification (consistent causal association to immunization / indeterminate / coincidental / unclassifiable).
- **Separate Preliminary Communication**: Separate preliminary communication from final classification.

6. Response and communication
- **Transparent Risk Communication**: Transparent risk communication with village leaders; continue unaffected routine immunization after risk assessment: avoid prolonged programme paralysis without cause.
- **Correct Errors Training**: Correct errors (training, supervision, open-vial policy, AD syringes, reconstitution rules); replace defective stock.
- **Support Families Document**: Support families; document for state and national AEFI databases.

7. Prevention of recurrence
- **Supportive Supervision Of**: Supportive supervision of session sites; monitor reconstitution clocks; never use non-vaccine diluents; discard reconstituted measles vaccine after 4 hours.

> **EXAM TIP:** AEFI definition → table of five causal types → DIO timed plan (notify → quarantine stock → line list → error vs coincidental → causality → communication). For measles-vaccine death clusters, explicitly discuss programme error, wrong diluent, and toxic shock.

[SN]Why live vaccines are more potent immunizing agents than killed vaccines[/SN]

WHY LIVE VACCINES ARE OFTEN MORE POTENT THAN KILLED VACCINES

DEFINITION CONTEXT

- **Therapeutic and Prophylactic Intervention**: Live attenuated vaccines contain organisms that replicate in the host in a controlled way; killed (inactivated) vaccines contain organisms or antigens that do not replicate.

REASONS FOR GREATER IMMUNOGENICITY OF MANY LIVE VACCINES

1. Replication amplifies antigen: a small administered dose yields ongoing antigen production, closer to natural infection.
2. Broader immune response: strong cellular (T-cell) and humoral immunity; killed vaccines are often mainly antibody-focused unless adjuvants or conjugates optimise the response.
3. Local mucosal immunity: oral or nasal live vaccines (for example OPV, LAIV) induce IgA at the portal of entry; most killed injectables do not.
4. Longer duration of protection after fewer doses for some antigens (context-specific).
5. Intracellular antigen processing pathways closer to natural infection.
6. Herd effects for some live vaccines: secondary spread of OPV historically boosted community immunity (with VAPP/VDPV trade-offs).

LIMITATIONS: WHY KILLED VACCINES REMAIN ESSENTIAL

- **Live Vaccines Are**: Live vaccines are contraindicated in severe immunodeficiency and often avoided in pregnancy; they are cold-chain sensitive; rare reversion can occur (VAPP/VDPV).
- **Killed Vaccines Ipv**: Killed vaccines (IPV, inactivated Hep A, modern rabies CCEEVs) offer safety in immunocompromised hosts without reversion risk.
- **Modern Schedules Often**: Modern schedules often combine both (for example bOPV + IPV) to gain intestinal plus humoral protection.

INDIA / PROGRAMME HOOK

- **Uip Uses Both**: UIP uses both live antigens (BCG, OPV, measles-containing vaccines, oral rotavirus, JE SA-14-14-2 in endemic districts) and inactivated, toxoid, or subunit antigens (IPV, pentavalent components, Hep B, PCV). Choice is risk–benefit, not potency alone.

> **EXAM TIP:** Define live vs killed → five to six potency mechanisms → three limitations → one India example pairing OPV with IPV. Do not claim live vaccines are always better.

[SN]Diseases for which toxoids are used for immunization[/SN]

DISEASES FOR WHICH TOXOIDS ARE USED

- **Biological Mechanism**: Toxoids are inactivated bacterial exotoxins that retain immunogenicity and induce protective antitoxin.
- **UIP Toxoid Formulations**: Classic examples in UIP-related practice: **diphtheria toxoid** and **tetanus toxoid** (as DPT/pentavalent, DT, Td/dT, TT-containing vaccines in pregnancy and boosters).
- **Toxoids Do Not**: Toxoids do not prevent colonization as reliably as some live vaccines prevent infection; they prevent toxin-mediated disease when circulating antitoxin is adequate.
- **Immunological Contrast**: Toxoid-preventable infections require neutralizing antitoxin antibodies against exotoxins, contrasting with whole-cell or acellular bacterial vaccines (pertussis) and replicating live viral vaccines (measles) that elicit multifaceted cellular and mucosal immune responses.

> **EXAM TIP:** Definition of toxoid → diphtheria + tetanus → schedule examples (primary series and boosters) → contrast with live vaccines in one line.

subsections.title: Respiratory Infections - Part B (Influenza, Acute Respiratory Infections, Pneumonia, Tuberculosis)
subsections.content:
INFLUENZA

OVERVIEW OF THE DISEASE

- **Disease Entity**: An acute respiratory tract infection caused by the influenza virus.
- **Clinical Features**: Characterized by a sudden onset of chills, malaise, fever, muscular pains, and cough.
- **Epidemiological Burden**: Occurs in all countries and affects millions of people every year. Causes 3-5 million cases of severe illness and about 290,000 to 650,000 deaths globally per year.
- **Viral Classification**: 3 types of influenza viruses: A, B, and C.
- **Epidemic Patterns**: Epidemics are caused by influenza A and B strains. Pandemics are caused by influenza A strains.
- **Viral Classification**: At present, 3 types of influenza viruses are circulating: A(H1N1), A(H3N2), and B viruses.
- **Epidemic Patterns**: Influenza A predominates in most countries, accounting for 59% of all influenza viruses detected.

AGENT FACTORS

- **Agent**: Influenza virus, family Orthomyxoviridae.
- **4 viral subtypes**: Type A, Type B, Type C, and Type D (antigenically distinct, no cross-immunity).
- **Influenza A Has**: Influenza A has 2 distinct surface antigens: Haemagglutinin (H) and Neuraminidase (N).
- **Antigenic Structure**: The H antigen initiates infection; the N antigen is responsible for the release of the virus from the infected cell.
- **Antigenic Structure**: There are 18 H subtypes and 11 N subtypes, but humans are mainly infected with H1, H2, or H3 and N1 or N2.
- **Antigenic Shift**: Sudden complete or major change in the virus resulting from genetic recombination. Causes major epidemics or pandemics. Occurred in 1918 (Spanish), 1957 (Asian), 1968 (Hong Kong).
- **Antigenic Drift**: Gradual change over a period of time due to point mutation. Causes minor epidemics.

HOST AND ENVIRONMENTAL FACTORS

- **Reservoir of infection**: Animals and birds (e.g., Swine, domestic poultry, wild birds, horses, dogs, cats).
- **Source of infection**: A case or subclinical case.
- **Period of infectivity**: 1 to 2 days before and 1 to 2 days after the onset of symptoms.
- **Age**: Affects all ages. Highest mortality in old people over 65 years of age and children under 18 months.
- **Immunity**: Antibodies appear 7 days after an attack and reach maximum in 2 weeks. After 1-2 months, drops to pre-infection level. Immunity is subtype-specific.
- **Environmental factors**: Epidemics usually occur in winter months in the Northern Hemisphere and winter or rainy season in the Southern Hemisphere. Overcrowding enhances transmission.

MODE OF TRANSMISSION AND INCUBATION

- **Mode of transmission**: Droplet infection or droplet nuclei created by sneezing, coughing, or talking.
- **Portal of entry**: Respiratory tract.
- **Incubation period**: 1 to 4 days (Notes mention 72 hours specifically).

CLINICAL FEATURES AND COMPLICATIONS

- **Fever Lasts 15**: Fever (lasts 1-5 days, averaging 3 days in adults), chills, aches, coughing, and generalized weakness.
- **Complications**: Acute sinusitis, otitis media, purulent bronchitis, and pneumonia (most dreaded).
- **Reye syndrome**: Fatty liver with encephalopathy. Rare but severe complication of influenza A and B in children (2-16 years), associated with aspirin use. Mortality rate 10-40%.

LABORATORY DIAGNOSIS

- **Laboratory Diagnosis**: Virus isolation from nasopharyngeal secretions.
- **Serology**: ELISA.

PREVENTION AND CONTROL

- **Preventive Measure**: Good ventilation of public buildings.
- **Preventive Measure**: Avoidance of crowded places during epidemics.
- **Encouraging Sufferers To**: Encouraging sufferers to cover their faces with a handkerchief when coughing and sneezing and to stay home.
- **Hygienic Practices During**: Hygienic practices during handling of poultry products.

INFLUENZA VACCINES

- **Vaccination Protocol**: Vaccines currently in use include egg-based, cell-cultured, and recombinant technologies.
- **1 Killed **: 1. Killed / Inactivated Vaccines (IIVs): Trivalent or Quadrivalent. Given via subcutaneous or intramuscular route as a single dose. Dose: 0.5 ml for adults and children over 3 years; 0.25 ml for children from 6 months to 36 months. Immunity lasts for 6-12 months (50-60% effective).
- **2 Live Attenuated**: 2. Live Attenuated Vaccines (LAIV): Trivalent. Single dose via intranasal spray. Given to individuals between 2 years and 49 years.
- **Highdose Iiv Hdiiv**: High-dose IIV (HD-IIV) and adjuvanted IIV (aIIV) are designed for persons aged 65 years and older.
- **Contraindications to inactivated vaccines**: Severe allergy to chicken eggs, history of anaphylactic reactions, history of Guillain-Barre syndrome within 6 weeks of previous vaccine, children less than 6 months of age.

ANTIVIRAL DRUGS (CHEMOPROPHYLAXIS & TREATMENT)

- **Oseltamivir**: 75 mg per day for prophylaxis; 75 mg twice daily for 5 days for therapy.
- **Zanamivir**: By inhaler (10 mg: two 5 mg inhalations) twice daily for therapy and once daily for prophylaxis.
- **Dosing Schedule For**: Dosing schedule for children is based on body weight (e.g., <15 kg: 30 mg twice a day for 5 days; 15-23 kg: 45 mg; 24-40 kg: 60 mg; >40 kg: 75 mg).

AVIAN INFLUENZA (BIRD FLU)

- **Primarily Affects Birds**: Primarily affects birds. Vast majority do not infect humans.
- **H5N1 Is A**: H5N1 is a strain with pandemic potential, since it might ultimately adapt into a strain that is contagious among humans.

PANDEMIC INFLUENZA A (H1N1) 2009 (SWINE FLU)

- **H1N1 Pandemic Epidemiology**: Emerged in March 2009. New nomenclature in 2011: influenza A(H1N1) pdm09.
- **Incubation period**: 1-4 days, could range up to 7 days.
- **Clinical Features Are**: Clinical Features are divided into:
- **1. Uncomplicated influenza**: Fever, cough, sore throat, rhinorrhoea, muscle pain, malaise, diarrhoea, vomiting.
- **2 Complicated Or**: 2. Complicated or severe influenza: Shortness of breath, dyspnoea, tachypnea, hypoxia, pneumonia, CNS involvement (encephalopathy, encephalitis), severe dehydration, renal failure, septic shock. Exacerbation of underlying chronic diseases (asthma, COPD, diabetes).
- **3 Signs **: 3. Signs & symptoms suggesting progressive disease: Cardiopulmonary insufficiency (turning blue, bloody sputum, low BP), CNS complications (altered mental status, unconsciousness, convulsions, paralysis), severe dehydration (decreased urinary output, dizziness, lethargy).
- **Lab diagnosis**: RT-PCR, nasopharyngeal samples, throat swab. Rapid influenza diagnostic tests (point-of-care).
- **Prevention  Control**: Prevention & Control: Hand hygiene, cover mouth and nose with tissue, ill persons should wear a face mask. Isolation of patients for 7 days after onset of illness or 24 hours after the resolution of fever & respiratory symptoms.
- **Pandemic Influenza A**: Pandemic Influenza A (H1N1) 2009 Vaccine:
- **Inactivated vaccine**: Monovalent vaccine containing antigen A/California/7/2009 (H1N1). Single dose, Intramuscular. Effective 14 days after vaccination.
- **Live attenuated vaccine**: Nasal spray.
- **Treatment**: Symptomatic care, antiviral drugs, oxygen therapy, fluid replacement, supportive care.
- **Antiviral Treatment**: Oseltamivir (Oral, 75 mg twice daily for 5 days), Zanamivir (Indicated for adults & children >5 years; 2 Inhalations / 2 x 5 mg twice daily for 5 days).

ACUTE RESPIRATORY INFECTIONS (ARI)

OVERVIEW OF THE DISEASE

- **Pathological Scope**: Cause inflammation of the respiratory tract anywhere from nose to alveoli, with a wide range of symptom combinations.
- **Clinical Features Include**: Clinical features include running nose, cough, sore throat, difficult breathing, ear problem, and fever.
- **Upper Respiratory Tract**: Upper respiratory tract infection (AURI): Common cold, pharyngitis, and otitis media.
- **Lower Respiratory Tract**: Lower respiratory tract infection (ALRI): Epiglottitis, laryngitis, laryngotracheitis, bronchitis, bronchiolitis, and pneumonia.

PROBLEM STATEMENT

- **Morbidity and Mortality**: About 90% of ARI deaths are due to pneumonia.
- **Morbidity and Mortality**: Pneumonia killed an estimated 0.80 million children in 2018 (>80% of deaths in children <2 years).
- **Incidence in developed countries**: 20-30%.
- **Responsible For 17**: Responsible for 17% of under-five deaths worldwide; 18% of all under-5 deaths in India.
- **India incidence**: 59 cases per lakh. In 2022, India reported 1,93,92,926 ARI cases (5,132 deaths) and 4,25,555 pneumonia cases (2,692 deaths).
- **Up To 13**: Up to 13% of inpatient deaths in pediatric wards are due to ARI.

EPIDEMIOLOGICAL DETERMINANTS

- **Agent factors**: 
- **Bacteria**: Klebsiella pneumoniae, Legionella pneumophila, Streptococcus pneumoniae (causes 78% of lobar pneumonia cases), Staphylococcus aureus, Haemophilus influenzae type b (2nd most common cause), Group B streptococcus.
- **Virus**: Influenza A, B, C; Parainfluenza 1, 2, 3; Respiratory syncytial virus (most common viral cause); Adenoviruses, Rhinoviruses, Coronaviruses.
- **Other agents**: Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Chlamydia type B, Coxiella burnetii. Pneumocystis jirovecii is the most common cause in HIV-infected infants.
- **Host factors**: Highest incidence in young children (developing countries) and the elderly (developed countries). Adult women experience more illness than men. Under 3 years of age, boys are affected more often and more severely.
- **Environmental factors**: Overcrowding, poor nutrition, low birth weight, maternal cigarette smoking, low socio-economic status, indoor smoke pollution.
- **Mode of transmission**: Air-borne route (inhalation of droplets) and direct person-to-person contact.

CLINICAL ASSESSMENT (IMCI GUIDELINES)

- **Clinical Examination**: Physical Examination (Look and Listen):
- **Fast breathing cut-offs**: 
- **Child Less Than**: Child less than 2 months: 60 breaths/min or more.
- **2 to 12 months**: 50 breaths/min or more.
- **12 Months To**: 12 months to 5 years: 40 breaths/min or more.
- **Chest indrawing**: Lower chest wall goes in when the child breathes IN.
- **Stridor**: Harsh noise when breathing IN (narrowing of larynx, trachea, epiglottis).
- **Wheeze**: Soft whistling sound on breathing OUT (narrowing of air passage in lungs).
- **Check For Severe**: Check for severe malnutrition, abnormally sleepy child, fever/low body temp, and cyanosis.

MANAGEMENT GUIDELINES (2 MONTHS TO 5 YEARS)

- **1. No Pneumonia (Cough and Cold)**: Signs: No chest indrawing, no fast breathing. Treatment: Advise mother to give home care, treat fever, treat wheezing if present.
- **2. Pneumonia**: Signs: Fast breathing and/or chest indrawing. Treatment: Advise home care, oral amoxicillin, treat fever, treat wheezing. Reassess after 2 days (Worse: refer urgently to hospital; Same: change antibiotics; Improving: finish 5 days of antibiotics).
- **3. Severe Pneumonia / Very Severe Disease**: Signs: Any general danger sign (not able to drink, persistent vomiting, convulsions, lethargic/unconscious, stridor in calm child, severe malnutrition). Treatment: Refer urgently to hospital, give first dose of injectable antibiotic, supportive therapy.

MANAGEMENT GUIDELINES (UNDER 2 MONTHS)

- **1. No Pneumonia**: Signs: No chest indrawing, no fast breathing. Treatment: Home care, keep young infant warm, frequent breastfeeding.
- **2 Severe **: 2. Severe / Very Severe Pneumonia: Signs: Chest indrawing, fast breathing, stopped feeding, convulsions, abnormally sleepy, stridor, wheezing. Treatment: Refer urgently to hospital, give first dose of an antibiotic.

TREATMENT REGIMENS (ANTIBIOTICS)

- **Pneumonia Cotrimoxazole Daily**: Pneumonia (Cotrimoxazole Daily Dose Schedule):
- **Sulphamethoxazole 100Mg **: Sulphamethoxazole (100mg) & Trimethoprim (20mg).
- ** 2 Months**: < 2 months: 1 tablet twice a day.
- **2-12 months**: 2 tablets twice a day.
- **1-5 years**: 3 tablets twice a day.
- **Pneumonia Amoxicillin Dispersible**: Pneumonia (Amoxicillin Dispersible Tablets - 250 mg):
- **2 Months To**: 2 months to <12 months (4-<10 kg): 1 tab twice a day x 5 days.
- **12 Months To**: 12 months to <3 years (10-<14 kg): 2 tabs twice a day x 5 days.
- **3 Years To**: 3 years to 5 years (14-19 kg): 3 tabs twice a day x 5 days.
- **Severe Pneumonia 2**: Severe Pneumonia (2 months - 5 years):
- **First 48 hours**: Benzyl penicillin (50,000 IU/kg/dose, 6 hourly, I/M) OR Ampicillin (50mg/kg/dose, 6 hourly, I/M) OR Chloramphenicol (25mg/kg/dose, 6 hourly, I/M).
- **If Condition Improves**: If condition improves (next 3 days): Procaine penicillin (50,000 IU/kg, once, I/M) OR Ampicillin (oral) OR Chloramphenicol (oral).
- **If No Improvement**: If no improvement (next 48 hours): Change antibiotic. (Ampicillin -> Chloramphenicol I/M. Chloramphenicol -> Cloxacillin + Gentamycin).
- **Severe Pneumonia **: Severe Pneumonia (< 2 months):
- **Benzyl Penicillin 50000**: Benzyl penicillin (50,000 IU/kg/dose, 12 hourly if <7 days or 6 hourly if 7 days-2 months, I/M) OR Ampicillin.
- **And Gentamycin 25Mgkgdose**: AND Gentamycin (2.5mg/kg/dose, 12 hourly if <7 days or 6 hourly if 7 days-2 months, I/M).
- **Chloramphenicol Is Not**: Chloramphenicol is NOT recommended as first line in young infants.

PREVENTION & CONTROL

- **Prevention and Control Strategy**: Improving living conditions, better nutrition, reduction in indoor smoke pollution, better MCH care.
- **Immunization**: 
- **Measles Vaccine**: Measles vaccine.
- **HIB vaccine**: Given in combination with Hep B & DPT & polio. 0.5 ml, I/M, at 6, 10 & 14 weeks. Not generally offered >24 months.
- **Pneumococcal pneumonia vaccine**: 
- **PPV23**: Polysaccharide non-conjugate vaccine. Routinely advised for everyone >65 years in USA. 0.5 ml, I/M, deltoid muscle, single dose.
- **PCV (Conjugate vaccine)**: PCV10 & PCV13. 3 doses at 6, 10 & 14 weeks.

[LAQ]Integrated Global Action Plan for Pneumonia and Diarrhoea (GAPPD)[/LAQ]

[SN]Treatment of pneumonia in under-five children[/SN]

INTEGRATED GLOBAL ACTION PLAN FOR PNEUMONIA & DIARRHOEA (GAPPD)

- **Brings Together Critical**: Brings together critical services & interventions to create healthy environments, promote protective practices, and ensure access to treatment.
- **Specific goals for 2025**: Reduce pneumonia mortality in children <5 years to <3 per 1000 live births; 90% full-dose coverage of relevant vaccines; 90% access to appropriate pneumonia management.

[SN]CBNAAT and Truenat in tuberculosis[/SN]

[SN]Rapid Molecular Diagnostic Testing in Tuberculosis (CBNAAT, Truenat)[/SN]

[LAQ]National Strategic Plan for TB Elimination / NTEP[/LAQ]

[SN]Strategies for TB elimination[/SN]

[SN]Nikshay Poshan Yojana[/SN]

[SN]Revised National Tuberculosis Control Programme (RNTCP) - now NTEP[/SN]

[SN]Tuberculosis drug resistance[/SN]

[SN]Treatment of MDR-TB and XDR-TB[/SN]

[SN]Challenges in Tuberculosis (TB) Control Programmes[/SN]

[SN]Sub-national TB free certification[/SN]

TUBERCULOSIS

OVERVIEW OF THE DISEASE

- **A Specific Infectious**: A specific infectious disease caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
- **Primarily Affects Lungs**: Primarily affects lungs (pulmonary tuberculosis) but can affect intestine, meninges, bones and joints, lymph glands, skin, and other tissues (extrapulmonary).
- **Affects Animals Like**: Affects animals like cattle (bovine tuberculosis), which can be communicated to man.

PROBLEM STATEMENT

- **Epidemiological Burden**: India is the highest TB burden country in the world (accounts for 26% of global incident cases in 2023).
- **Global Tb Incidence**: Global TB incidence in 2023: 10.8 million people.
- **Global Tb Deaths**: Global TB deaths in 2023: 1.25 million.
- **India Incidence Rate**: India Incidence rate of all forms of TB: 199 per lakh population.
- **India Prevalence Rate**: India Prevalence rate of all forms of TB: 195 per lakh (Notes) / 315 per lakh (Textbook 2023 estimate).

EPIDEMIOLOGICAL INDICES

- **1. Incidence**: Number of new and recurrent (relapse) episodes of TB occurring in a given year.
- **2. Prevalence**: Number of TB cases (all forms) at a given point in time.
- **3. Mortality from TB**: Number of deaths caused by TB in HIV-negative people.
- **4. Case fatality rate**: Risk of death from TB among people with active TB disease.
- **5. Case notification rate**: New and recurrent episodes notified to WHO per 100,000 population.
- **6. Case detection rate**: Number of notifications divided by estimated incidence.
- **7 Prevalence Of**: 7. Prevalence of drug-resistant cases: Patient excreting tubercle bacilli resistant to anti-TB drugs.

AGENT FACTORS

- **Agent**: M. tuberculosis. Human and bovine strains. Facultative intracellular parasite.
- **Atypical mycobacteria (4 groups)**: Photochromogens (M. kansasii), Scotochromogens (M. scrofulaceum), Non-photochromogens (M. intracellulare), Rapid growers (M. fortuitum).
- **Source of infection**: Human source (case whose sputum is positive). Bovine source (infected milk).
- **Communicability**: Patients are infective as long as they remain untreated. Effective anti-microbial treatment reduces infectivity by 90% within 48 hours.

HOST FACTORS

- **Age**: Affects all ages. In India, sharp rise in 15-24 years age group.
- **Sex**: More prevalent in males.
- **Nutrition**: Malnutrition heavily predisposes to TB.
- **Immunity**: No inherited immunity. Acquired via natural infection or BCG vaccine.

ENVIRONMENTAL FACTORS

- **Poor Housing Overcrowding**: Poor housing, overcrowding, undernutrition, smoking, alcohol abuse, indoor air pollution, diabetes.

MODE OF TRANSMISSION & INCUBATION

- **Mode of transmission**: Droplet infection and droplet nuclei generated by sputum-positive patients.
- **Incubation period**: 3 to 6 weeks from receipt of infection to positive tuberculin test. Disease development may take months or years.

LABORATORY DIAGNOSIS

- **1. Sputum Smear Microscopy**: Method of choice. 2 samples (Day 1 on the spot, Day 2 early morning sample). Zeihl-Neelsen (ZN) acid-fast stain or Diode-based fluorescent microscopy (LED FM).
- **2. Sputum Culture**: Solid medium (Lowenstein-Jensen). Liquid media (Middlebrook 7H9 broth, BACTEC MGIT 960 automated system, BacT Alert).
- **3 Rapid Molecular**: 3. Rapid Molecular Diagnostic Tests (NAAT):
- **Cbnaat Cartridge Based**: CBNAAT (Cartridge Based Nucleic Acid Amplification Test / GeneXpert MTB/RIF).
- **Truenat**: Truenat.
- **Line Probe Assay (LPA)**: FL LPA for RIF & INH resistance, SL LPA for fluoroquinolone & injectable resistance.
- **4. Insta test TB**: MycoDot (Dot-blot), Detect-TB (ELISA).
- **Diagnostic Modality**: 5. Tuberculin Skin Test (Mantoux Test): 1 TU of PPD-RT 23 with Tween 80 injected intradermally. Read at 48-96 hours. >10 mm induration is positive; <6 mm is negative; 6-9 mm is doubtful.
- **6 Tb Interferon**: 6. TB Interferon Gamma Release Assays (IGRAs): QuantiFERON TB Gold, T-SPOT. Blood tests measuring immune response.

TREATMENT: ANTI-TUBERCULOSIS DRUGS

- **First-line drugs**: 
- **Bactericidal**: Rifampicin (RMP/R), Isoniazid (INH/H), Streptomycin (S), Pyrazinamide (Z).
- **Bacteriostatic**: Ethambutol (E).
- **Second-line drugs**: 
- **Fluoroquinolones Levofloxacin Lfx**: Fluoroquinolones (Levofloxacin Lfx, Moxifloxacin Mfx).
- **Ethionamide Eto Protionamide**: Ethionamide (Eto), Protionamide (Pto).
- **Injectables**: Capreomycin, Kanamycin, Amikacin.
- **Cycloserine Cs Thioacetazone**: Cycloserine (Cs), Thioacetazone, Macrolides, PAS.
- **Newer drugs**: Bedaquiline (Bdq), Delamanid (Dlm), Linezolid (Lzd), Clofazimine (Cfz).

CHEMOTHERAPY PHASES (DOTS)

- **1. Intensive Phase (IP)**: 1-3 months. Health worker watches as patient swallows drugs. Rapidly kills bacilli.
- **2. Continuation Phase (CP)**: 6-9 months. Patient issued medicine in multiblister combipacks. Aimed at sterilizing dormant bacilli.

TREATMENT CATEGORIES & REGIMENS (HISTORICAL RNTCP INTERMITTENT DOTS: SUPERSEDED)

- **These Thriceweekly Category**: These thrice-weekly Category I/II boxes are **historical RNTCP intermittent regimens** and are no longer the current NTEP standard of care.
- **Category I Red**: Category I (Red Box, historical): New cases. Regimen: 2(HRZE)3 + 4(HR)3.
- **Category Ii Blue**: Category II (Blue Box, historical): Previously treated (relapse, failure, default). Regimen: 2(HRZES)3 + 1(HRZE)3 + 5(HRE)3.
- **Current practice**: daily fixed-dose combinations with universal drug-susceptibility testing / NAAT-first pathways (see NTEP revised daily regimen below).

NTEP REVISED DAILY DOSE REGIMEN (CURRENT)

- **All Patients Treated**: All patients treated with daily fixed-dose combinations (FDCs) based on weight bands.
- **New Cases**: IP - 2 HRZE; CP - 4 HRE.
- **Previously Treated Cases**: Treated exactly as new cases under recent guidelines unless drug resistance is detected.

DRUG-RESISTANT TB (DEFINITIONS: WHO 2021)

- **Mono-resistance**: Resistant to one first-line anti-TB drug only.
- **Poly-drug resistance**: Resistant to more than one first-line drug, other than both isoniazid and rifampicin.
- **Multidrug-resistant (MDR-TB)**: Resistant to at least isoniazid (H) and rifampicin (R).
- **Rifampicin-resistant (RR-TB)**: Resistant to rifampicin, with or without other resistance (managed on the MDR pathway).
- **Pre-XDR-TB**: MDR/RR-TB with additional resistance to any fluoroquinolone.
- **Extensively drug-resistant (XDR-TB)**: MDR/RR-TB with resistance to any fluoroquinolone AND at least one additional Group A drug (bedaquiline and/or linezolid). Group A also ranks the fluoroquinolones levofloxacin/moxifloxacin among the most potent second-line medicines.
- **Historical note**: Before 2021, XDR required resistance to a fluoroquinolone plus a second-line injectable (amikacin, kanamycin, or capreomycin). Injectables are no longer part of the XDR definition.

DRUG-RESISTANT TB TREATMENT REGIMENS

- **MDR-TB Regimen**: 1. Shorter Oral Bedaquiline-containing MDR/RR-TB regimen: 9-11 months.
- **IP (4-6 months)**: Bdq (6 months), Lfx, Cfz, Z, E, H(high dose), Eto.
- **CP (5 months)**: Lfx, Cfz, Z, E.
- **MDR-TB Regimen**: 2. Longer Oral M/XDR-TB regimen: 18-20 months.
- **Lfx Bdq 6M**: Lfx, Bdq (6m or longer), Lzd, Cfz, Cs.
- **3 Bpalm Regimen**: 3. BPaLM Regimen (New 6-month regimen): Bedaquiline, Pretomanid, Linezolid, Moxifloxacin. For MDR/RR-TB.
- **4 H Monopoly**: 4. H mono/poly DR-TB regimen: 6-9 months of Lfx, R, E, Z.

BCG VACCINATION

- **BCG Vaccination Profile**: Bacillus Calmette-Guerin. Live attenuated vaccine (Danish 1331 strain used in India).
- **Produced At Bcg**: Produced at BCG Laboratory at Guindy, Chennai.
- **Types**: Liquid (fresh) and Freeze-dried (stable for 1 year if kept below 10 C and away from sunlight).
- **Diluent**: Normal saline. Must be used within 3-4 hours after reconstitution.
- **Age**: At birth or at 6 weeks.
- **Dose**: <4 weeks = 0.05 ml; >4 weeks = 0.1 ml.
- **Route**: Intradermal using Tuberculin (Omega microstat) syringe. Site: Left deltoid muscle.
- **Phenomenon after vaccination**: 2-3 weeks (papule) -> 5 weeks (shallow ulcer) -> 6-12 weeks (heals with a permanent 4-8 mm scar).
- **Complications**: Severe ulceration, lymphadenitis, osteomyelitis, disseminated BCG infection.
- **Protective value**: Duration is 15-20 years. 80% effective in some trials, but highly effective in preventing severe childhood TB (meningitis, miliary).
- **Contraindications**: Infective dermatosis, immunodeficiency (HIV, leukemia, malignancy), immunosuppressive treatment, pregnancy.

[SN]Child without BCG scar: management preference[/SN]

BCG SCAR ABSENT: WHAT TO PREFER

- **BCG Scar Interpretation**: A visible BCG scar is a useful but imperfect marker of prior vaccination; absence of scar does not always mean the child never received BCG, and presence does not guarantee lifelong protection against all forms of TB.
- **For A Healthy**: For a healthy child presenting without a BCG scar and without documented vaccination: **give BCG** as per national schedule practice for unvaccinated eligible children (after excluding contraindications such as symptomatic immunodeficiency).
- **Do Not Use**: Do not use scar absence alone as proof of failed immunity requiring repeated BCG if vaccination is documented and the child is well; programme policy prioritises vaccinating the truly unvaccinated.
- **Bcg Is Most**: BCG is most valued for protection against severe childhood forms (miliary TB, TB meningitis), not as a perfect adult pulmonary-TB vaccine.
- **Record Vaccination In**: Record vaccination in the card; counsel caregivers on expected local reaction and when to return.

> **EXAM TIP:** One line on scar as imperfect marker → prefer vaccinate if undocumented/unvaccinated and eligible → contraindications → purpose of BCG (severe childhood TB).

CHEMOPROPHYLAXIS (TB PREVENTIVE TREATMENT - TPT)

- **TB Preventive Treatment**: Recommended for PLHIV, household contacts <5 years, and other clinical risk groups.
- **Regimens**: 
- **6H**: Isoniazid daily for 6 months (or 1 year for PLHIV in notes).
- **3HP**: Isoniazid + Rifapentine weekly for 3 months.

TB AND COMORBIDITIES

- **HIV**: Co-infected patients must receive CPT (Cotrimoxazole) and ART. Rifampicin interacts with ART, requiring careful management.
- **Diabetes**: Bidirectional relationship. Worsens TB outcomes.
- **Pregnancy**: First-line drugs are safe. Streptomycin is contraindicated (ototoxic to fetus).

GLOBAL TB STRATEGIES

- **DOTS Strategy (1994)**: 5 components (Government commitment, case detection via microscopy, standard short-course chemo, drug supply, monitoring).
- **Stop TB Strategy (2006)**: Expanded DOTS, addressed TB/HIV and MDR-TB.
- **End TB Strategy (2015-2035)**: 
- **Vision**: World free of TB (0 deaths, 0 disease).
- **Indicators  Targets**: Indicators & Targets (2020 / 2025 / 2030 / 2035):
- **Reduction in TB deaths**: 35% / 75% / 90% / 95%.
- **Reduction In Tb**: Reduction in TB incidence rate: 20% / 50% / 80% / 90%.
- **Tbaffected Families Facing**: TB-affected families facing catastrophic costs: 0% at all milestones.
- **Pillars**: 1. Integrated patient-centered care and prevention; 2. Bold policies and supportive systems; 3. Intensified research and innovation.
- **Global Plan 90-90-90 targets**: Reach at least 90% of all people with TB, Reach at least 90% of key populations, Achieve at least 90% treatment success.

[LAQ]Nutritional support scheme for patients with tuberculosis under NTEP[/LAQ]

NIKSHAY POSHAN YOJANA (NUTRITIONAL SUPPORT UNDER NTEP)

DEFINITION AND RATIONALE

- **Undernutrition Is Both**: Undernutrition is both a risk factor for progression from TB infection to disease and a predictor of poor treatment outcomes. Ni-kshay Poshan Yojana (NPY) is the NTEP direct benefit transfer (DBT) scheme providing financial support for nutrition to notified TB patients for the duration of treatment.

KEY FEATURES

1. Eligibility: Notified persons with TB on treatment under NTEP (as per programme notification rules).
2. Benefit: Monthly nutritional support transferred via DBT through Ni-kshay to the patient (or linked) bank account.
3. Amount (current national framing): **₹1,000 per month** for the duration of treatment (enhanced from the earlier ₹500 per month).
4. Timing: Linked to notification and continuation of treatment in Ni-kshay; follow-up rules as per operational guidance.
5. Complementary support: Ni-kshay Mitra and community support may add food baskets; Energy Dense Nutritional Supplementation (EDNS) for underweight patients has been introduced as an additional layer in recent national enhancements for eligible patients early in treatment.
6. Purpose: Improve adherence and outcomes; reduce catastrophic costs related to food insecurity during TB care.

OPERATIONAL CHALLENGES

- **Bankaccount Seeding And**: Bank-account seeding and DBT delays; awareness gaps; incomplete notification of private-sector patients until entered in Ni-kshay.

> **EXAM TIP:** TB-nutrition cycle → who is eligible → ₹1000/month DBT for treatment duration → complementary supports → three operational challenges.

[LAQ]National Strategic Plan for Tuberculosis Elimination[/LAQ]

[LAQ]Newer changes in management of TB under NTEP and problems in case management[/LAQ]

NATIONAL STRATEGIC PLAN / NTEP PROGRAMMATIC ARCHITECTURE

INTRODUCTION

- **Indias National Tb**: India’s National TB Elimination Programme (NTEP), formerly RNTCP, aligns with the WHO End TB Strategy and national commitment to accelerate decline in TB incidence, mortality, and catastrophic costs.

STRATEGIC PILLARS

1. Detect: early diagnosis with molecular NAAT (CBNAAT/Truenat), universal DST, active case finding in key populations, private-sector notification via Ni-kshay.
2. Treat: daily FDC regimens; DR-TB regimens including shorter oral regimens and BPaLM where eligible; adherence support.
3. Prevent: TB preventive treatment (TPT) for eligible contacts and PLHIV; airborne infection control; BCG for severe childhood forms.
4. Build: health-system strengthening, community engagement, Ni-kshay digital backbone, nutrition (NPY), research.

NEWER CHANGES IN CASE MANAGEMENT (HIGH-YIELD)

- **NTEP Case Management Advance**: Daily fixed-dose combinations; previously treated patients managed on daily regimens with DST rather than historical intermittent Category II as the default.
- **Naatfirst Diagnostic Algorithms**: NAAT-first diagnostic algorithms; universal DST for rifampicin resistance.
- **Alloral Drtb Regimens**: All-oral DR-TB regimens; introduction of bedaquiline-containing shorter and longer regimens and BPaLM where criteria met.
- **Tpt Expansion Tbhiv**: TPT expansion; TB-HIV and TB-diabetes bidirectional screening; Ni-kshay digital notification and DBT (NPY).

PROBLEMS IN CASE MANAGEMENT

- **Programmatic Challenge**: Delayed diagnosis and incomplete private-sector notification.
- **Programmatic Challenge**: Adherence challenges, stigma, and loss to follow-up.
- **Drugresistant Tb Capacity**: Drug-resistant TB capacity and adverse-drug-reaction management.
- **Undernutrition And Comorbidities**: Undernutrition and comorbidities (HIV, diabetes, tobacco, alcohol).
- **Dbt And Socialsupport**: DBT and social-support operational gaps.

SUB-NATIONAL TB-FREE CERTIFICATION

- **A National Verification**: A national verification process under NTEP recognizing states/districts that achieve predefined milestones toward TB-free status based on surveillance quality, burden trends, and programme performance.
- **Process**: claim by state → desk review → field verification by independent teams.
- **Recognizes Progress Continued**: Recognizes progress; continued surveillance is required to sustain gains.

CHALLENGES IN TB CONTROL PROGRAMMES (SUMMARY)

- **Incomplete Case Detection**: Incomplete case detection; DR-TB; TB-HIV and TB-diabetes; undernutrition; stigma; private-sector engagement; migrant populations; funding and human-resource gaps at the last mile.

> **EXAM TIP:** End TB vision → NTEP rename → Detect, Treat, Prevent, Build with India tools (Ni-kshay, NAAT, NPY) → newer regimen/DST changes → problems list. One table beats long prose.

[LAQ]Application of epidemiological principles in the Universal Immunization Programme[/LAQ]

[SN]Write briefly about vaccine logistics[/SN]

[LAQ]Plan for quality management and continuous quality improvement for the National Immunization Programme[/LAQ]

APPLICATION OF EPIDEMIOLOGICAL PRINCIPLES IN UIP

INTRODUCTION

- **The Universal Immunization**: The Universal Immunization Programme (UIP) delivers free vaccines against selected vaccine-preventable diseases through routine immunization and campaigns. Epidemiological principles guide antigen choice, target ages, coverage measurement, and outbreak control.

FRAMEWORK (PRINCIPLE → UIP APPLICATION)

| Epidemiological principle | Application in UIP |
|---------------------------|-------------------|
| Disease burden and priority | Antigens chosen for high under-5 mortality and morbidity |
| Host susceptibility by age | Age-specific schedule from birth through boosters |
| Herd immunity threshold | High two-dose measles-containing vaccine coverage to interrupt transmission |
| Cold chain and potency | Forward and reverse cold chain; open-vial policy for eligible vaccines |
| Surveillance | VPD, AFP (polio), measles-rubella laboratory-supported surveillance, AEFI |
| Outbreak investigation | Case definitions, laboratory confirmation, campaign immunization, RI gap analysis |
| Equity and risk groups | Left-out and drop-out children, urban poor, migrants; intensification drives |
| Evaluation | Full immunization coverage, dropout rates, session monitoring, coverage surveys |

VACCINE LOGISTICS (SHORT NOTE POINTS)

1. Forecasting and indent based on beneficiary load and wastage factors.
2. Storage at appropriate temperatures (ILR, deep freezer, cold boxes, vaccine carriers) with continuous temperature monitoring.
3. Freeze-sensitive versus heat-sensitive vaccines handled with correct conditioning of ice packs.
4. Open Vial Policy for eligible multidose vials; discard rules for reconstituted vaccines (for example measles within 4 hours).
5. Stock rotation (EEFO/FEFO), batch tracking, and prevention of stock-outs and overstocking.
6. Session-level logistics: AD syringes, diluents matched to vaccine, hub-cutters, waste disposal.
7. Reverse cold chain for samples when required (for example AFP stool specimens).

QUALITY MANAGEMENT AND CONTINUOUS QUALITY IMPROVEMENT (IMMUNIZATION)

1. Standards: national immunization schedule, session operational guidelines, cold-chain SOPs, AEFI SOPs.
2. Structure: cold-chain officers, AEFI committees, supportive supervision checklists.
3. Process measures: session held as planned, due-list use, safe injection, VVM status, temperature logs.
4. Outcome measures: coverage, dropout, VPD incidence, serious AEFI rates, timeliness of reporting.
5. PDCA cycle: plan microplans → do sessions → check coverage/AEFI/supervision data → act with training and corrective action.
6. Community accountability: headcount validation, urban strategy, missed-child tracking.

> **EXAM TIP:** Intro UIP → principle table with India examples → logistics 6 bullets → QI as structure-process-outcome + PDCA. Draw the childhood schedule only if time allows.

subsections.title: Intestinal Infections - Part A (Poliomyelitis, Viral Hepatitis A, B, C, D, E)
subsections.content:
POLIOMYELITIS

OVERVIEW OF THE DISEASE

- **Pathological Definition**: An acute viral infection caused by an RNA virus.
- **Pathological Definition**: Primarily an infection of the human alimentary tract, but the virus may infect the central nervous system in a very small percentage (about 1%) of cases, resulting in varying degrees of flaccid paralysis and possibly death.

PROBLEM STATEMENT

- **Eradication Status**: India was certified as polio-free on 27th March 2014.
- **Eradication Status**: Polio remains endemic in Afghanistan and Pakistan. (Nigeria was previously endemic but no longer sustains WPV1).
- **Eradication Status**: Wild Poliovirus (WPV) type 2 has not been detected since 1999 and was declared eradicated in September 2015.
- **Wpv Type 3**: WPV type 3 has not been detected since November 2012 and is declared eradicated.
- **Wpv Type 1**: WPV type 1 is the only wild poliovirus likely remaining in circulation.

AGENT FACTORS

- **Agent**: Poliovirus (RNA virus). Has 3 serotypes: 1, 2, and 3. Most outbreaks of paralytic polio are due to type-1 virus.
- **Resistance**: Survives for long periods in the external environment. In cold environments, it can live in water for 4 months and in faeces for 6 months. Rapidly inactivated by pasteurization and chemicals.
- **Reservoir of infection**: Man is the only known reservoir. Most infections are subclinical (1000 subclinical cases for every clinical case in children, 75 in adults). No chronic carriers.
- **Infective material**: Faeces and oropharyngeal secretions of an infected person.
- **Period of communicability**: 10 days before and 10 days after the onset of symptoms. Virus is excreted in the faeces for 2 to 3 weeks (sometimes up to 3 to 4 months), but is most infectious 7 to 10 days before and after onset.

HOST FACTORS

- **Age**: Affects all ages, but in India, it is essentially a disease of infancy and childhood. Between 6 months and 3 years is the most vulnerable age.
- **Sex**: Males are more affected. Sex ratio of 3 males to 1 female.
- **Immunity**: Maternal antibodies protect during the first 6 months. One attack confers solid, type-specific immunity.
- **Risk factors (provocative factors)**: Intramuscular injections, tonsillectomy undertaken especially during an epidemic, administration of alum-containing DPT, and fatigue can precipitate an attack of paralytic polio.

ENVIRONMENTAL FACTORS

- **Rainy season**: More likely to occur during the rainy season (June to September in India).
- **Overcrowding And Poor**: Overcrowding and poor sanitation provide opportunities for exposure.

MODE OF TRANSMISSION

- **Faecal-oral route**: Main route in developing countries (via contaminated water, food, flies, fingers).
- **Droplet infection**: May occur in the acute phase of the disease when the virus is in the throat.

INCUBATION PERIOD

- **7 To 14**: 7 to 14 days (range 3 to 35 days). Notes highlight 14 days.

CLINICAL SPECTRUM

- **1. Inapparent (Subclinical) infection**: 91-96% of infections. No presenting symptoms.
- **2. Abortive polio or Minor illness**: 4-8% of infections. Mild or self-limiting illness (viraemia) causing fever, malaise, sore throat. Patient recovers quickly.
- **3. Non-paralytic polio**: About 1% of infections. Features stiffness and pain in the neck and back (aseptic meningitis).
- **4. Paralytic polio**: Occurs in less than 1% of infections. Virus invades CNS. Asymmetrical flaccid paralysis. Deep tendon reflexes (DTRs) diminished. No sensory loss.
- **Tripod sign**: Child sits by supporting hands at the back and partially flexing the hips and knees.
- **Cause of death**: Respiratory insufficiency.

PREVENTION AND CONTROL

- **Vaccine Formulations**: 1. Inactivated (Salk) Polio Vaccine (IPV):
- **Immunological Mechanism**: Killed vaccine containing all 3 types (formulated to 40 D-antigen units of type 1, 8 of type 2, 32 of type 3).
- **Induces Circulating Humoral**: Induces circulating (humoral) antibodies but no local intestinal immunity.
- **Prevents Paralysis But**: Prevents paralysis but does not prevent reinfection of the gut by wild viruses.
- **Dose**: 0.5 ml Intramuscular (IM) in the anterolateral thigh, or as a fractional dose.
- **Fractional Dose Of**: Fractional dose of IPV (fIPV): 0.1 ml given intradermally (ID) at 6th and 14th weeks provides higher seroconversion rates than a single full dose of IPV given IM at 14 weeks.
- **Vaccine Formulations**: 2. Oral (Sabin) Polio Vaccine (OPV):
- **Immunological Mechanism**: Live attenuated virus. Given orally (2 drops).
- **Induces Both Humoral**: Induces both humoral and intestinal (local) immunity.
- **Excreted Virus Infects**: Excreted virus infects others, immunizing them (herd immunity).
- **Contains 1060 Ccid50**: Contains 10^6.0 CCID50 of type 1 and 10^5.8 CCID50 of type 3 (in bOPV).
- **Highly Effective In**: Highly effective in controlling epidemics.
- **Contraindications**: Immunocompromised individuals, leukemia, malignancy. Diarrhoea is not a contraindication, but an extra dose should be given later.
- **Vaccine Associated Paralytic**: Vaccine Associated Paralytic Poliomyelitis (VAPP): Rare adverse event. Frequently associated with Sabin 3 (60% of cases), followed by Sabin 2 and Sabin 1.
- **Vaccine Derived Poliovirus (VDPV)**: Mutated vaccine strains. Divided into cVDPVs (circulating), iVDPVs (immunodeficiency-associated), and aVDPVs (ambiguous).

POLIO ERADICATION AND ENDGAME STRATEGIC PLAN (2013-2018)

- **Objectives**: 1. Virus detection and interruption; 2. Routine Immunization (RI) strengthening and OPV withdrawal; 3. Containment and certification; 4. Legacy planning.
- **The Switch**: From trivalent OPV (tOPV) to bivalent OPV (bOPV) globally in April 2016.
- **Reason for Switch**: WPV type 2 has been eradicated since 1999. The risk of VAPP and cVDPV to the type 2 component of OPV outweighs its benefits.
- **IPV Introduction**: At least 1 dose of IPV introduced before the switch to maintain immunity against type 2 poliovirus.

PULSE POLIO IMMUNIZATION (PPI)

- **Pulse Polio Strategy**: Simultaneous, mass administration of OPV on a single day to all children 0-5 years of age.
- **First Round Was**: First round was held on 9th December 1995 and 20th January 1996 (initially targeted under 3 years, later WHO recommended under 5 years).
- **Conducted As 2**: Conducted as 2 rounds 6 weeks apart during the low transmission season of polio (November to February).
- **Doses During Ppi**: Doses during PPI are extra doses supplementing, and not replacing, routine immunization services.

ACUTE FLACCID PARALYSIS (AFP) SURVEILLANCE

- **AFP Surveillance Standards**: Finding and reporting children with AFP under 15 years of age.
- **Conducted Through Surveillance**: Conducted through Surveillance Medical Officers (SMOs) stationed at state headquarters.
- **Requires Transporting 2**: Requires transporting 2 stool samples collected 24-48 hours apart, within 14 days of paralysis onset.
- **Stool Specimens Are**: Stool specimens are shipped in a cold box (4-8 C) via reverse cold chain and must reach the lab within 72 hours.
- **Isolating And Mapping**: Isolating and mapping the virus by a WHO accredited laboratory.
- **Surveillance Indicator**: At least 2 cases of non-polio AFP per 100,000 population aged <15 years must be detected annually.

FACTORS THAT CONTRIBUTED TO POLIO ERADICATION IN INDIA

1. High-quality AFP surveillance with stool collection targets and WHO-accredited laboratories.
2. Pulse Polio / supplementary immunization activities with booths plus house-to-house “sweep” strategies.
3. Transition strategies: tOPV to bOPV switch (2016) with IPV introduction to maintain type-2 immunity.
4. Focus on high-risk areas, migrants, and underserved pockets with microplanning.
5. Political commitment, social mobilization (influencers, religious leaders), and partnership (NPSP/WHO, UNICEF, rotary-style partners).
6. Cold-chain and vaccinator workforce capacity; independent monitoring of coverage quality.
7. Last wild poliovirus case timing and subsequent certification (India polio-free 27 March 2014) sustained by continued vigilance against importations and cVDPV risk.

> **EXAM TIP:** Clinical spectrum → OPV vs IPV table → Endgame objectives + switch reason → AFP indicators → India success factors list.

VIRAL HEPATITIS

HEPATITIS A

OVERVIEW OF THE DISEASE

- **Formerly Known As**: Formerly known as infectious hepatitis or epidemic jaundice.
- **Caused By Hepatitis**: Caused by Hepatitis A virus (HAV).
- **Endemic In Most**: Endemic in most developing countries.

EPIDEMIOLOGICAL DETERMINANTS

- **Agent**: HAV, an RNA virus of the Picornaviridae family (genus Hepatovirus; formerly classified as Enterovirus type 72).
- **Reservoir of infection**: Human cases. No chronic carrier state.
- **Infective material**: Man's faeces.
- **Period of infectivity**: 2 weeks before to 1 week after onset of jaundice.
- **Virus excretion**: Excreted in faeces for about 2 weeks before jaundice and up to 2 weeks thereafter.
- **Host factors**: Children. The ratio of anicteric to icteric cases is 1:3 in adults, and up to 12:1 in children. One attack confers lifelong immunity.
- **Environmental factors**: Heavy rainfall, poor sanitation, overcrowding.
- **Mode of transmission**: Faecal-oral route is the major route (contaminated water, food). Parenteral and sexual routes are rare.
- **Incubation period**: 10 to 50 days (usually 14-28 days; Notes state 28 days).

CLINICAL SPECTRUM

- **Nausea Vomiting Anorexia**: Nausea, vomiting, anorexia, mild fever, followed by jaundice.

PREVENTION AND CONTROL

- **Control of reservoir**: Disinfection of faeces & fomites using sodium hypochlorite (0.5%).
- **Control of transmission**: Personal & community hygiene (hand washing), sanitary disposal of excreta, purification of water.
- **Vaccines**: 
- **Formaldehyde Inactivated Vaccine**: Formaldehyde inactivated vaccine (>12 months of age, 2 doses with 6-12 months interval, I/M in deltoid).
- **Immunological Mechanism**: Live attenuated vaccine (single dose, subcutaneous).

HEPATITIS B

OVERVIEW OF THE DISEASE

- **Formerly Known As**: Formerly known as Serum Hepatitis.
- **Accounts For 45**: Accounts for 45% of Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) and 30% of cirrhosis of liver.
- **Hepatitis B Prevalence**: Hepatitis B prevalence is highest in sub-Saharan Africa & East Asia.

EPIDEMIOLOGICAL DETERMINANTS

- **Agent**: Hepatitis B virus (HBV), a double-shelled DNA virus (Hepadnavirus family), originally known as the "Dane particle" (42-nm).
- **Antigens**: Surface antigen (HBsAg / Australia antigen), Core antigen (HBcAg), e antigen (HBeAg).
- **Reservoir of infection**: Man is the only reservoir. Carrier state is defined as the presence of HBsAg for more than 6 months.
- **Infective material**: Contaminated blood, body secretions (saliva, vaginal secretions, semen of infected persons).
- **Period of communicability**: Present in blood during the incubation period (month before jaundice).
- **Resistance**: Survives for at least 7 days on environmental surfaces. Destroyed by sodium hypochlorite or autoclaving.
- **Host Factors Age**: Host factors (Age & Chronicity): Chronic Hep B develops in 90% of perinatal infections, 30% in children <6 years, and 5% in >6 years (adults).
- **High-risk groups**: Surgeons, recipients of blood transfusion / organ transplants, laboratory personnel, homosexuals, prostitutes, percutaneous drug abusers, infants of HBV carrier mothers.
- **Mode of transmission**: 
- **Parenteral Route Bloodborne**: Parenteral route (Blood-borne infection).
- **Perinatal transmission (vertical)**: Leak of maternal blood into baby's circulation.
- **Sexual Transmission**: Sexual transmission.
- **Other routes**: Horizontal transmission (child to child through physical contact with skin cuts/grazes).
- **Incubation period**: 30 to 180 days (average 75 days).

CLINICAL PICTURE

- **Insidious Onset Can**: Insidious onset. Can lead to progressive liver fibrosis, cirrhosis, and markedly increased risk of hepatocellular carcinoma.
- **Diagnosis**: HBsAg is the primary marker. IgM anti-HBc confirms acute infection.

PREVENTION AND CONTROL

- **1. Hepatitis B Vaccine**: 
- **Recombinant Hep B**: Recombinant Hep B vaccine has replaced the plasma-derived vaccine. Active substance is HBsAg.
- **Available As Monovalent**: Available as monovalent or fixed combination (Pentavalent vaccine: DPT, Hep B & Hib).
- **Dose**: 0.5 ml, I/M.
- **Site**: Anterolateral aspect of mid-thigh.
- **Schedule**: Birth dose within 24 hours. Subsequent doses at 6, 10, and 14 weeks are administered as part of the Pentavalent vaccine.
- **2 Hepatitis B**: 2. Hepatitis B Immunoglobulin (HBIG):
- **Used For Those**: Used for those acutely exposed to HBsAg positive blood (surgeons, lab workers, newborn infants of carrier mothers, sexual contacts).
- **Given As Soon**: Given as soon as possible (ideally within 6 hours, preferably not later than 48 hours).
- **Dose**: 0.05 ml/kg body weight. 2 doses 30 days apart.

TREATMENT

- **Tenofovir Tdf Or**: Tenofovir (TDF) or Entecavir (ETV).

HEPATITIS C

OVERVIEW OF THE DISEASE

- **Agent**: Hepatitis C virus (HCV), a RNA virus of the Flavivirus family.
- **Major Cause Of**: Major cause of post-transfusion hepatitis.
- **High rate of chronicity**: 55-85% of persons will develop chronic HCV infection. Risk of cirrhosis is 15-30% within 20 years.

TRANSMISSION AND INCUBATION

- **Transmission**: Exposure to infectious blood (blood transfusions, contaminated syringes, injecting drug use). Sexual and perinatal transmission are less common.
- **Incubation period**: 2 weeks to 6 months (avg 40-120 days).

DIAGNOSIS AND TREATMENT

- **Diagnosis**: Anti-HCV antibody testing, followed by HCV RNA (viral load) testing for confirmation.
- **Treatment**: Direct Antiviral Agents (DAAs) such as Sofosbuvir/velpatasvir, Glecaprevir/pibrentasvir, Sofosbuvir/daclatasvir. Highly effective (cure rate high), short duration (8-24 weeks).
- **Prevention**: Blood safety, safe injections, harm reduction for IDUs. No vaccine is currently available.

HEPATITIS D

OVERVIEW OF THE DISEASE

- **Agent**: Hepatitis D virus (HDV), a defective RNA virus that requires HBV for its replication.
- **Transmission**: Co-infection or super-infection with HBV. Transmitted percutaneously or sexually.
- **Clinical**: Causes a more severe disease than HBV monoinfection. High prevalence in Mediterranean, Middle East, Pakistan.
- **Prevention**: Vaccination against HBV prevents HDV co-infection.

HEPATITIS E

OVERVIEW OF THE DISEASE

- **Agent**: Hepatitis E virus (HEV), an RNA virus (Calicivirus/Hepevirus).
- **Hepatitis E Epidemiology**: Enterically transmitted non-A, non-B hepatitis. Essentially a water-borne disease causing large epidemics in Asia and Africa.

TRANSMISSION AND INCUBATION

- **Transmission**: Faecal-oral route (contaminated drinking water). Food-borne and vertical transmission also possible.
- **Incubation period**: 2 to 9 weeks (average 40 days).

CLINICAL PICTURE

- **Usually Mild And**: Usually mild and self-limiting in young adults.
- **Can Result In**: Can result in fulminant hepatitis (acute liver failure) and death, particularly during pregnancy. Pregnant women are at greater risk of obstetrical complications and mortality.
- **Prevention**: Provision of safe drinking water and proper disposal of sanitary waste. No vaccine available globally (one registered only in China).

[LAQ]Investigation and control of a jaundice outbreak under a PHC[/LAQ]

JAUNDICE OUTBREAK: INVESTIGATION AND CONTROL (HAV/HEV CONTEXT)

1. Confirm and define: rising cases of acute jaundice; case definition (acute onset jaundice ± fever, dark urine, anorexia); line list age, sex, village, water source, date of onset.
2. Descriptive epi: epidemic curve, spot map, attack rates by water source and age.
3. Hypothesis: common-source water contamination (HAV/HEV) versus food-borne point source; rule out leptospirosis/malaria/drug injury as needed clinically.
4. Environmental: inspect drinking-water sources, pipelines, wells; free residual chlorine; sanitary survey of sewage cross-connection.
5. Laboratory: sample cases for IgM anti-HAV/HEV as available; water testing.
6. Control: ensure chlorinated safe water; boil-water advisory if needed; sanitary disposal of excreta; food hygiene; isolation of cases’ faeces disinfection practices; health education on handwashing.
7. No mass immunoglobulin as routine for large community outbreaks in most PHC settings; focus on water and sanitation. Hospitalize fulminant cases (especially pregnant women with suspected HEV).
8. Surveillance: continue active case search for two incubation periods after the last case linked to the source.

> **EXAM TIP:** Case definition → line list + curve + map → water hypothesis → chlorine/sanitation control → special warning for HEV in pregnancy.
