subsections.title: Intestinal Infections - Part B (Acute Diarrhoeal Diseases, Cholera, Typhoid Fever, Food Poisoning, Amoebiasis, Helminthiasis)
subsections.content:
ACUTE DIARRHOEAL DISEASES

OVERVIEW OF THE DISEASE

- **Clinical Definition**: Diarrhoea is defined as the passage of loose, liquid or watery stools, more than 3 times a day.
- **Clinical Definition**: The recent change in consistency and character of stools is more important than the number of stools.
- **Syndromic Classification**: Diarrhoeal diseases should be considered as a group of diseases in which the predominant symptom is diarrhoea.

CLINICAL TYPES OF DIARRHOEAL DISEASE

- **1. Acute watery diarrhoea**: Lasts several hours to days. Main danger is dehydration, weight loss also occurs if feeding is not continued. Pathogens: V. cholerae, E. coli, and Rotavirus.
- **2. Acute bloody diarrhoea**: Also called Dysentery. Main dangers are damage to the intestinal mucosa, sepsis, malnutrition, and dehydration. Pathogen: Shigella.
- **3. Persistent diarrhoea**: Lasts 14 days or longer. Main dangers are malnutrition, non-intestinal infections, and dehydration. Persons with other illnesses such as AIDS are more likely to develop persistent diarrhoea.
- **4. Diarrhoea with severe malnutrition**: Marasmus and kwashiorkor. Main dangers are severe systemic infection, dehydration, heart failure, and vitamin/mineral deficiency.

PROBLEM STATEMENT

- **Disease Burden**: Accounts for 9% (India 8%) of all under-5 deaths, mostly in children less than 2 years of age.

EPIDEMIOLOGICAL DETERMINANTS

AGENT FACTORS

- **1. Viruses**: 
- **Rotavirus**: Leading cause of severe, dehydrating diarrhoea in children under 5 years globally. Peaks during the winter season. Shed in very high concentration (>10^12 particles / gram).
- **Other viruses**: Astroviruses, Adenoviruses, Calciviruses, Coronaviruses, Norwalk group viruses, Enteroviruses, Cytomegalovirus.
- **2. Bacteria**: 
- **Enterotoxigenic Escherichia coli (ETEC)**: Important cause of acute watery diarrhoea in adults and children. Most common cause of traveler's diarrhoea. 2 toxins: heat labile (LT) and heat stable (ST).
- **Shigella**: Accounts for a high percentage of mortality due to diarrhoeal disease. Major cause of diarrhoea in India.
- **Campylobacter jejuni**: Commonest cause of enteritis.
- **Vibrio cholerae 01**: In cholera endemic areas, it accounts for 5-10% of all acute diarrhoeas yearly.
- **Salmonella**: Causes inflammation of bowel epithelium.
- **Other bacteria**: V. parahaemolyticus, Bacillus cereus, Staphylococcus aureus, Clostridium perfringens, Clostridium difficile, Enteroinvasive E. coli, Aeromonas, Yersinia enterocolitica, Chlamydia, Neisseria gonorrhoeae.
- **3. Others (Parasites)**: 
- **Cryptosporidium**: Coccidian parasite causing diarrhoea in infants, immunodeficient patients (e.g., AIDS), and domestic animals.
- **Giardia intestinalis**: Epithelial surface is smothered with them.
- **Entamoeba Histolytica Trichuriasis**: Entamoeba histolytica, Trichuriasis, Intestinal worms, Cyclospora.

BESIDES ABOVE CAUSES

- **1. Malnutrition**: May lead to kwashiorkor, sprue, coeliac disease, and pellagra which are all associated with diarrhoea.
- **2 Inborn Error**: 2. Inborn error of metabolism: Such as congenital enzyme deficiencies may lead to diarrhoea in the newborn.
- **3. AIDS**: Persistent diarrhoea is one of the main clinical signs.

RESERVOIR OF INFECTION

- **Man**: E. coli, Shigella, V. cholerae, G. lamblia, and E. histolytica.
- **Animal**: C. jejuni and Salmonella.

HOST FACTORS

- **Host Susceptibility**: Highest incidence in 6-11 months when weaning occurs.
- **Host Susceptibility**: Due to declining levels of maternal antibodies.
- **Contaminated Foods And**: Contaminated foods and direct contact with infections as infants start to crawl.
- **Due To Incorrect**: Due to incorrect feeding practices.

ENVIRONMENTAL FACTORS

- **Bacterial diarrhoea**: Occurs more frequently during the warm and rainy season.
- **Viral diarrhoea**: Peaks during the winter season.

MODE OF TRANSMISSION

- **Faecaloral Route Is**: Faecal-oral route is the primary mode of transmission.
- **Waterborne**: Water-borne.
- **Foodborne**: Food-borne.

DIARRHOEAL DISEASE CONTROL PROGRAMME IN INDIA

- **1978**: Started with objectives of reducing mortality due to diarrhoeal diseases.
- **1985-86**: Inception of National Oral Rehydration Therapy programme.
- **1992-93**: Became a part of the CSSM (Child Survival and Safe Motherhood) programme.
- **At present**: Part of NRHM (National Rural Health Mission).

SHORT TERM PROGRAMME (APPROPRIATE CLINICAL MANAGEMENT)

- **Clinical Management Component**: 1. Oral Rehydration Therapy (ORT)
- **Clinical Management Component**: 2. Intravenous rehydration
- **3 Maintenance Therapy**: 3. Maintenance therapy
- **4 Appropriate Feeding**: 4. Appropriate feeding
- **5 Chemotherapy**: 5. Chemotherapy
- **6 Zinc Supplementation**: 6. Zinc supplementation

LONG TERM PROGRAMME

- **Long-Term Preventive Component**: 1. Better MCH care practices: Maternal nutrition and Child nutrition.
- **2. Preventing strategies**: Sanitation, Health education, Immunization, Fly control.
- **3 Control And**: 3. Control and preventing diarrhoeal epidemics.
- **4 Integrated Global**: 4. Integrated global action plan for the prevention and control of pneumonia and diarrhoea (GAPPD).

APPROPRIATE CLINICAL MANAGEMENT DETAILS

ORAL REHYDRATION THERAPY (ORT)

- **Composition Of Reduced**: Composition of reduced osmolarity ORS in grams/litre:
- **Sodium chloride**: 2.6
- **Glucose, anhydrous**: 13.5
- **Potassium chloride**: 1.5
- **Trisodium citrate, dihydrate**: 2.9
- **Total weight**: 20.5
- **Composition Of Reduced**: Composition of reduced osmolarity ORS in mmol/litre:
- **Sodium**: 75
- **Chloride**: 65
- **Glucose, anhydrous**: 75
- **Potassium**: 20
- **Citrate**: 10
- **Total osmolarity**: 245 mmol/L

RULES FOR ORS DOSAGE

- **Children under 2 years**: 50-100ml after each loose stool.
- **2-10 years**: 100-200ml after each loose stool.
- **Older children and adults**: Give as much fluid as they want.
- **ORS Administration Guidance**: If the child vomits, wait for 10 minutes then try again slowly (a spoonful every 2 to 3 minutes).
- **Breastfeeding Should Be**: Breastfeeding should be continued during treatment with ORS.
- **Contents Of The**: Contents of the packet are to be dissolved in 1 litre of drinking water and should be used within 24 hours.
- **If Ors Is**: If ORS is not available: 1 teaspoon table salt and 6 teaspoons of sugar dissolved in 1 litre of drinking water is used until ORS is available.

INTRAVENOUS REHYDRATION

- **Intravenous Fluid Protocol**: Ringer lactate solution (RL) / Hartmann's solution is the best commercially available solution.
- **Diarrhoea treatment solution (DTS)**: 1 litre water, sodium chloride 4g, sodium acetate 6.5g, potassium chloride 1g, and glucose 10g.
- **If Nothing Is**: If nothing is available, normal saline can be given.
- **Dose for Infants**: 30ml/kg in 1 hour, then 70ml/kg in 5 hours.
- **Dose for Older Patients**: 30ml/kg in 30 min, then 70ml/kg in 2.5 hours.
- **Rehydration Must Continue**: Rehydration must continue until all signs of dehydration have disappeared.

MAINTENANCE THERAPY

- **Mild diarrhoea**: Not more than 1 stool every 2 hours or less than 5ml stool/kg/hr. Give 100ml of oral fluid / kg body weight / day until diarrhoea stops.
- **Severe diarrhoea**: More than 1 stool every 2 hours or more than 5ml stool/kg/hr. Give 15ml of oral fluid / kg body weight / hour.

APPROPRIATE FEEDING

- **During Episodes Of**: During episodes of diarrhoea, normal food intake should be promoted as soon as the child is able to eat.
- **Newborn Infants With**: Newborn infants with diarrhoea who show little or no signs of dehydration can be treated by breastfeeding alone.
- **Moderate Or Severe**: Moderate or severe dehydration receives oral rehydration solution.

CHEMOTHERAPY

- **Diarrhoea Due To**: Diarrhoea due to V. Cholerae: Doxycycline, tetracycline, TMP-SMX, and erythromycin.
- **Diarrhoea due to Shigella**: Ciprofloxacin.

[SN]Role of zinc in diarrhoeal disease management[/SN]

ZINC SUPPLEMENTATION

- **Zinc Protocol**: Adjunct to ORS in under-five diarrhoeal disease management (not a substitute for rehydration).
- **Reduces The Episodes**: Reduces the episode's duration and severity.
- **Lowers The Incidence**: Lowers the incidence of diarrhoea in the following 2 to 3 months.
- **Infants under 6 months**: 10 mg per day for 14 days.
- **Children Older Than**: Children older than 6 months: 20 mg per day for 14 days.
- **India programme hook**: zinc with ORS is a core short-term diarrhoeal disease control intervention under child health / IMNCI-linked practice.

> **EXAM TIP:** ORS first → zinc dose by age × 14 days → benefits (duration, severity, next 2 to 3 months) → not a substitute for rehydration.

LONG TERM PROGRAMME DETAILS

- **Better MCH care practices**: Improving prenatal nutrition will reduce LBW. Improving postnatal nutrition will improve quality of breast milk. Promotion of breastfeeding (limit commercial formulas). Appropriate weaning practices (not earlier than 6 months). Supplementary feeding (improve nutritional status aged 6-59 months). Vitamin A supplementation (reduces duration, severity, and complications).
- **Preventing strategies**: Sanitation (improve water supply, excreta disposal, food hygiene). Health education (breastfeeding, weaning, clean drinking water, proper excreta disposal).
- **Immunization**: 
- **Measles vaccine**: Can prevent up to 25% of diarrhoeal deaths in under-5 children.
- **Rotavirus vaccine**: Live oral vaccines used in UIP/national schedules as per state introduction: classic products taught: Rotarix (monovalent human, oral, 2-dose series in early infancy) and RotaTeq (pentavalent bovine-human reassortant, oral, 3-dose series). First dose is given early in infancy with upper age limits for the first and last doses as per national schedule to minimise intussusception risk window concerns.
- **Rotavirus Immunization Is**: Rotavirus immunization is a major long-term diarrhoea prevention strategy alongside measles vaccine, breastfeeding, WASH, and vitamin A programmes.

- **Fly control**: Flies breeding in association with faeces should be controlled.
- **Control And Preventing**: Control and preventing diarrhoeal epidemics: Requires strengthening of epidemiological surveillance systems.
- **Integrated Global Action**: Integrated global action plan for the prevention and control of pneumonia and diarrhoea (GAPPD): Brings together critical services and interventions to create healthy environments, promotes protective practices, and ensures access to proven preventive and treatment measures.

CHOLERA

OVERVIEW OF THE DISEASE

- **An Acute Diarrhoeal**: An acute diarrhoeal disease caused by V. Cholerae O1 (Classical or El Tor) and O139.
- **Characterized By Sudden**: Characterized by sudden onset of profuse, effortless, watery diarrhoea followed by vomiting, rapid dehydration, muscular cramps, and suppression of urine.

PROBLEM STATEMENT

- **Vibrio Cholerae Epidemiology**: El Tor biotype of V. Cholerae O1 has rapidly replaced the classical biotype in all parts of the country.
- **Most Of The**: Most of the El Tor biotype isolated today belongs to the serotype Ogawa.
- **During 2014 969**: During 2014, 969 cholera cases were reported in India with 4 deaths.
- **Majority Of Cases**: Majority of cases were reported from Maharashtra (253) followed by West Bengal (173).

EPIDEMIOLOGICAL DETERMINANTS

AGENT FACTORS

- **Agent**: V. Cholerae O group 1 or V. Cholerae O1 & O139 (epidemic strain). Non-O group 1V / O139 Cholerae (non-epidemic strain) includes Vibrio parahaemolyticus.
- **O Group 1**: O group 1 has 2 biotypes: Classical and El Tor.
- **Classical And El**: Classical and El Tor vibrios are further divided into 3 serological types: Inaba, Ogawa, and Hikojima.
- **Toxin production**: Vibrios multiply in the lumen of the small intestine and produce enterotoxins which produce diarrhoea through its effect on the adenylate cyclase-cyclic AMP system of mucosal cells of the small intestine.
- **Reservoir of infection**: Human (Cases and Carriers).
- **Infective material**: Stools and vomit of cases and carriers.

CARRIERS IN CHOLERA

- **1. Incubatory carriers**: 1 to 5 days.
- **2. Convalescent carriers**: 2 to 3 weeks (Notes mention 21 days).
- **3. Healthy carriers**: 10 days.
- **4. Chronic carriers**: 10 years. Affects the gall bladder.

HOST FACTORS

- **Age**: All ages and both sexes.
- **Population mobility**: Pilgrimages and fairs.
- **Economic status**: Low socio-economic status.

ENVIRONMENTAL FACTORS

- **Poor Environmental Sanitation**: Poor environmental sanitation.
- **Environmental Factors**: Contaminated water and food.
- **Low Standards Of**: Low standards of personal hygiene.

MODE OF TRANSMISSION

- **Faecally Contaminated Water**: Faecally contaminated water.
- **Contaminated Food**: Contaminated food.
- **Direct Contact With**: Direct contact with excreta and vomit of patients, and contaminated linen and fomites.

INCUBATION PERIOD

- **1 To 5**: 1 to 5 days (Notes mention 2 days specifically).

CLINICAL FEATURES

- **1. Stage of evacuation**: Profuse, painless, watery diarrhoea followed by vomiting. Up to 40 stools in a day.
- **2. Stage of collapse**: Sunken eyes, hollow cheeks, absent pulse, unrecordable blood pressure, loss of skin elasticity, and decreased urine output.
- **3. Stage of recovery**: Clinical improvement, blood pressure and temperature returns to normal, and urine output is reestablished.

DIAGNOSIS

- **Collection**: Venkatraman-Ramakrishnan (VR) medium or alkaline peptone water.
- **Transportation**: Cary-Blair Medium.
- **Direct examination**: Dark field illumination showing shooting stars in a dark sky.
- **Culture**: Bile Salt Agar medium.
- **Characterization**: Scintillating type of movement in hanging drop preparations.

PREVENTION AND CONTROL

- **1. Rehydration therapy**: ORS and I/V rehydration.
- **2. Sanitation measures**: Provision of piped water supplies, drinking water containing free residual chlorine, provision of sanitary latrines, sale of food under hygienic conditions, proper disinfection with cresol or bleaching powder.
- **3. Chemoprophylaxis**: Tetracycline for 3 days, twice daily, 500mg.
- **4. Vaccination**: 
- **Dukoral**: Monovalent, Oral, 2 doses given 7 days apart. For adults and children >2 years, 1 booster dose after 2 years.
- **Sanchol**: Bivalent, Oral, 2 doses given 14 days apart. For individuals > 1 year.
- **5. Health education**: Effectiveness of ORT, food hygiene practices, proper hand washing practices after defecation and before eating.

DIARRHOEAL DISEASE CONTROL PROGRAMME

- **Objective Is To**: Objective is to prevent diarrhoea-associated deaths in children due to dehydration.
- **Health Education Highlighting**: Health education highlighting the rational management of diarrhoea in children.
- **Ors Is Promoted**: ORS is promoted as the first line of treatment.

TYPHOID FEVER

OVERVIEW OF THE DISEASE

- **Systemic Infection Mainly**: Systemic infection mainly caused by S. typhi, found only in man.
- **Characterized By Continuous**: Characterized by continuous fever, bradycardia with involvement of lymphoid tissues.
- **The Term Enteric**: The term enteric fever includes both typhoid and paratyphoid fevers.

PROBLEM STATEMENT

- **Endemic In India**: Endemic in India.
- **Maximum Cases Were**: Maximum cases were reported from Bihar followed by UP.

EPIDEMIOLOGICAL DETERMINANTS

AGENT FACTORS

- **Agent**: S. typhi. Contains 3 antigens: O, H, and Vi.
- **Reservoir of infection**: Man (Cases and Carriers).
- **Carriers**: Convalescent carriers (6 to 8 weeks), Chronic carriers (> 1 year). Faecal carriers are more frequent than urinary carriers. "Typhoid Mary" is a famous example.
- **Source of infection**: Faeces and urine of cases and carriers.

HOST FACTORS

- **Age**: 5 to 19 years.
- **Sex**: Males (cases), Females (carriers).

ENVIRONMENTAL FACTORS

- **Rainy Season Julyseptember**: Rainy season (July-September coincides with the peak incidence).

INCUBATION PERIOD

- **10 To 14**: 10 to 14 days.

MODES OF TRANSMISSION

- **Faecaloral Route**: Faecal-oral route.
- **Urineoral Routes**: Urine-oral routes.

CLINICAL FEATURES

- **Enteric Fever Clinical Features**: Malaise, headache, cough, and sore throat.
- **Enteric Fever Clinical Features**: Abdominal pain and constipation.
- **Fever Ascends In**: Fever ascends in a step-ladder fashion.
- **Pea Soup Diarrhoea**: Pea soup diarrhoea.
- **Rash**: Rose spots.

COMPLICATIONS

- **Intestinal Hemorrhage**: Intestinal hemorrhage.
- **Intestinal Perforation**: Intestinal perforation.

DIAGNOSIS

- **Typhoid Diagnostic Assay**: Blood culture (mainstay of diagnosis).
- **Typhoid Diagnostic Assay**: Widal test.
- **Typhoid Diagnostic Assay**: IDL Tubex test.
- **Typhoid Diagnostic Assay**: Typhidot test (detects specific IgM and IgG antibodies).

PREVENTION AND CONTROL

- **1. Control of reservoir**: 
- **Cases**: Fluoroquinolones. Disinfection of stool and urine with 5% cresol and soiled clothes/linen with chlorine.
- **Carriers**: Amoxicillin with probenecid for 6 weeks. Cholecystectomy is the most successful approach for carriers.
- **2. Control of sanitation**: 
- **Purification Of Drinking**: Purification of drinking water supplies and improvement of basic sanitation.
- **3. Immunization**: 
- **Vi Polysaccharide Vaccine**: Ty2 S. typhi strain. S/C or I/M route. For > 2 years of age, 1 dose. Protection starts after 7 days of injection. Revaccination every 3 years.
- **Ty 21 A Vaccine**: Live attenuated Ty2 S. typhi strain. Orally (enteric coated capsules). For > 5 years of age, 3 doses on 1st, 3rd, and 5th day. Immunity is achieved in 7 days after the last dose. Revaccination every 3 years in endemic areas and every year for individuals travelling to endemic areas from non-endemic areas.

FOOD POISONING

OVERVIEW OF THE DISEASE

- **An Acute Gastroenteritis**: An acute gastroenteritis caused by ingestion of food or drink contaminated with either living bacteria or their toxins or inorganic chemical substances.
- **Characterized by**: History of ingestion of common food, attack of many persons at the same time, and similarity of signs and symptoms in the majority of cases.

TYPES OF FOOD POISONING

- **1. Non-bacterial**: Caused by chemicals like arsenic, mercury, cadmium, etc. Also caused by sea food, fertilizers, pesticides, etc.
- **2. Bacterial**: Foods contaminated with bacteria or their toxins.
- **Salmonella food poisoning**: Agents are S. typhimurium, S. enteritidis. Source: farm animals, poultry, contaminated meat. Incubation period: 12-24 hours.
- **Staphylococcal food poisoning**: Agents are enterotoxins of Staphylococcus aureus. Source: milk or milk products from cows suffering from mastitis, or from human food handlers. Incubation period: 1-6 hours (short because of preformed toxin).
- **Botulism**: Agent is the exotoxin of Clostridium botulinum. Source: canned food or pickled foods. Incubation period: 12-36 hours.
- **C. perfringens food poisoning**: Agent is Clostridium perfringens (welchii). Source: food consumed after 24 hours of preparation (meat dishes, poultry). Incubation period: 6-24 hours.
- **B. cereus food poisoning**: Agent is Bacillus cereus. Source: dried and processed food (e.g., fried rice). Incubation period: Emetic form (1-6 hours), Diarrheal form (12-24 hours).

INVESTIGATION OF FOOD POISONING

- **Outbreak Investigation Step**: 1. Secure a complete list of people involved.
- **Outbreak Investigation Step**: 2. Laboratory investigations.
- **3 Animal Experiments**: 3. Animal experiments.
- **4 Blood For**: 4. Blood for antibodies.
- **5 Environmental Study**: 5. Environmental study.
- **6 Data Analysis**: 6. Data analysis.

PREVENTION AND CONTROL

- **1. Food sanitation**: Meat inspection, personal hygiene, food handlers, food handling techniques, sanitary improvements, health education.
- **2. Refrigeration**: Below 4 deg. C (40 deg. F).

AMOEBIASIS

OVERVIEW OF THE DISEASE

- **The Condition Of**: The condition of harbouring the protozoan parasite Entamoeba histolytica with or without clinical manifestations.
- **A Common Infection**: A common infection of the human gastrointestinal tract. Worldwide distribution, major health problem in developing countries.

EPIDEMIOLOGICAL DETERMINANTS

- **Agent**: E. histolytica (exists in vegetative trophozoite and cystic forms).
- **Reservoir of Infection**: Man is the only reservoir (cases and carriers).
- **Infective material**: Faeces containing the cysts of E. histolytica.
- **Period of communicability**: As long as cysts are excreted (may be several years).
- **Host factors**: Affects all ages, no sex or racial difference. Often a household infection.
- **Environmental factors**: Closely related to poor sanitation and low socio-economic status. Use of nightsoil for agriculture favours spread.
- **Mode of transmission**: Faecal-oral route (contaminated water or food), sexual transmission (oral-rectal contact), and vectors (flies, cockroaches, rodents).
- **Incubation period**: About 2 to 4 weeks or longer.

CLINICAL FEATURES

- **Intestinal Amoebiasis Mild**: Intestinal amoebiasis (mild abdominal discomfort, diarrhoea to acute fulminating dysentery).
- **Extraintestinal Amoebiasis Involvement**: Extraintestinal amoebiasis (involvement of liver leading to liver abscess, lungs, brain, spleen, skin).

PREVENTION AND CONTROL

- **Primary prevention**: Sanitation (safe disposal of human excreta, hand washing), Water supply (protection, filtration, boiling), Food hygiene.
- **Secondary prevention**: Early diagnosis (demonstration of trophozoites/cysts in stool) and treatment (Metronidazole, Tinidazole for symptomatic cases; Diiodohyroxyquin or Diloxanide furoate for asymptomatic carriers).

SOIL-TRANSMITTED HELMINTHIASIS

OVERVIEW OF THE DISEASE

- **Includes Intestinal Roundworms**: Includes intestinal roundworms (Ascariasis), hookworms (Necator americanus, Ancylostoma duodenale), and whipworm (Trichuris trichiura).
- **Widely Distributed In**: Widely distributed in tropical and subtropical areas.

ASCARIASIS

- **Agent**: Ascaris lumbricoides (adult worm lives in small intestine).
- **Reservoir**: Man is the only reservoir.
- **Transmission**: Faecal-oral (ingestion of embryonated eggs via contaminated soil, vegetables, water).
- **Host factors**: Highest incidence in children aged 3-8 years.
- **Incubation period**: About 2 months for the life cycle to complete.

HOOKWORM INFECTION

- **Agent**: Ancylostoma duodenale and Necator americanus.
- **Reservoir**: Man.
- **Transmission**: Larvae penetrate the skin (usually walking barefoot on contaminated soil). Direct transmission can occur via oral route for A. duodenale.
- **Incubation period (prepatent period)**: 7 weeks for N. americanus, unpredictable for A. duodenale (up to 9 months).
- **Clinical**: Chronic blood loss leading to iron-deficiency anaemia, hypoalbuminaemia.
- **Chandler's Index**: Average number of hookworm eggs per gram of faeces in the population sampled; used to assess community hookworm load for epidemiological study (epidemiological stratification: light infection <200 EPG, moderate/transitional 200 to 250 EPG, heavy infection >250 EPG).

PREVENTION AND CONTROL

- **Primary prevention**: Sanitary disposal of human excreta, safe drinking water, food hygiene, health education, wearing protective footwear.
- **Secondary prevention**: Deworming with Albendazole (400 mg) or Mebendazole (100 mg twice daily for 3 days). Levamisole and Pyrantel are also used.

[SN]Role of deworming for school-going children[/SN]

DEWORMING FOR SCHOOL-GOING CHILDREN

- **National Deworming Protocol**: Soil-transmitted helminths (Ascaris, hookworm, Trichuris) impair nutrition, growth, and school performance; periodic deworming is a public-health intervention where prevalence justifies it.
- **Drugs**: Albendazole 400 mg single dose (or mebendazole regimens) as per national school deworming guidance; supervised administration on designated days (for example National Deworming Day platforms).
- **Benefits**: Reduces worm burden and related anaemia risk; complements WASH, footwear, and sanitation for durable control.
- **Target**: School-age and preschool children as per programme eligibility; coordination with education department for coverage.
- **Not a standalone solution**: sanitation and hygiene determine reinfection rates.
- **Safety**: Generally well tolerated; standard exclusions (for example first-trimester pregnancy for some anthelmintics in adult programmes) follow programme SOPs when co-administered populations differ.

> **EXAM TIP:** Name STH agents → albendazole single dose → school platform → link WASH → “deworming treats burden; sanitation prevents reinfection.”

subsections.content:
DENGUE SYNDROME

OVERVIEW OF THE DISEASE

- **Viral Characteristics**: Dengue viruses are arboviruses capable of infecting humans and causing disease.
- **Viral Characteristics**: Infections may be asymptomatic or may lead to classical dengue fever (DF), dengue haemorrhagic fever (DHF) without shock, or dengue haemorrhagic fever with shock (Dengue Shock Syndrome - DSS).
- **Epidemiological Transmission**: It is a self-limiting disease. Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus are the main vectors.
- **Epidemiological Transmission**: At present, DENV-1 and DENV-2 serotypes are widespread in India.

EPIDEMIOLOGICAL DETERMINANTS

AGENT FACTORS

- **Agent**: Dengue virus (genus Flavivirus) is an RNA virus.
- **4 virus serotypes exist**: DENV-1, DENV-2, DENV-3, and DENV-4.
- **Immune Response and ADE**: Infection with any one serotype confers lifelong immunity to that virus serotype only. They elicit cross-protection for only a few months against other types.
- **Immune Response and ADE**: Secondary infection with dengue serotype 2 or multiple infections with different serotypes lead to severe form (DHF/DSS).
- **Immune Response and ADE**: The first infection probably sensitizes the patient, while the second infection with a different serotype appears to produce immunological catastrophy (Antibody-dependent enhancement).
- **Vector**: Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus carry high vectorial competency.
- **Vector Biology**: Aedes aegypti is highly domesticated, strongly anthropophilic, and a nervous feeder (bites more than one host to complete one blood meal). It is a discordant species (needs more than one feed for gonotropic cycle completion). This results in multiple cases and clustering of dengue cases in cities.
- **Vector Biology**: Aedes albopictus partly invades peripheral areas, is an aggressive feeder, and is a concordant species (completes blood meal in one go on one person).

TRANSMISSION OF DISEASE

- **Vector Biology**: The Aedes mosquito becomes infective by feeding on a patient from the day before onset to the 5th day (viraemia stage) of illness.
- **Extrinsic incubation period**: 8 to 10 days. Once infective, the mosquito remains so for life.
- **Vector Biology**: Transovarian transmission of dengue virus occurs when the virus enters fully developed eggs at the time of oviposition.

ENVIRONMENTAL FACTORS

- **Being A Domestic**: Being a domestic breeder, it breeds in the containers in and around the houses (e.g., roof tops, stored water).
- **It Is An**: It is an endophagic and endophilic vector.
- **With A 2**: With a 2 C increase in temperature, the extrinsic incubation period is shortened.

INCUBATION PERIOD

- **3 To 10**: 3 to 10 days (commonly 5-6 days).

CLINICAL MANIFESTATIONS

1. UNDIFFERENTIATED FEVER

- **Infants Children And**: Infants, children, and adults infected for the first time may develop a simple fever indistinguishable from other viral infections.
- **Maculopapular Rashes May**: Maculopapular rashes may accompany the fever or appear during defervescence.

2. CLASSICAL DENGUE FEVER (DF)

- **Dengue Fever Manifestations**: Sudden onset with chills and high fever, intense headache, muscle and joint pain.
- **Within 24 Hours**: Within 24 hours, retroorbital pain (on eye movements) & photophobia develops.
- **Extreme Weakness Anorexia**: Extreme weakness, anorexia, constipation, altered taste, colicky pain, dragging pain in inguinal region.
- **Biphasic Fever Curve**: Biphasic fever curve (remission of a few hours to 2 days).
- **Skin Eruptions Maculopapular**: Skin eruptions (maculopapular rash) appear in 80% of cases during remission or second febrile phase (lasts 1-2 days), followed by desquamation.

3. DENGUE HAEMORRHAGIC FEVER (DHF)

- **A Severe Form**: A severe form characterized by plasma leakage and abnormal haemostasis.
- **Divided into three phases**: 
- **1. Febrile phase**: Lasts 2-7 days. Sudden high fever, facial flushing, headache, vomiting. Positive tourniquet test or petechiae, ecchymoses, purpura. Bleeding from mucosa, GI tract, injection sites. Mild hepatomegaly.
- **2. Critical phase**: Occurs around defervescence (days 3-7). Progressive leukopenia followed by rapid decrease in platelet count (<100,000 cells/cu.mm). Plasma leakage leads to haemoconcentration (Haematocrit rises >= 20%), pleural effusion, ascites, hypoproteinaemia.
- **3. Recovery phase**: 24-48 hours after critical phase. Gradual reabsorption of extravascular fluid. Rash of "isles of white in the sea of red". Haematocrit stabilizes. White blood cell count rises first, followed by platelet recovery.

4. DENGUE SHOCK SYNDROME (DSS)

- **Criteria For Dhf**: Criteria for DHF plus signs of shock: Tachycardia, cool extremities, delayed capillary refill, weak pulse, lethargy or restlessness.
- **Pulse Pressure **: Pulse pressure <= 20 mm Hg.
- **Systolic Pressure **: Systolic pressure < 80 mm Hg for < 5 years, or < 90 mm Hg for older children and adults.

LABORATORY DIAGNOSIS

- **Virus isolation**: From blood during the first 5 days (viraemic stage).
- **RT-PCR**: Detects viral RNA.
- **NS1 Antigen Test**: Highly conserved glycoprotein, abundant in serum during early stages. Simple test, high sensitivity, enables early detection.
- **MAC-ELISA (IgM-Capture ELISA)**: Detects IgM antibodies by day 5 of illness. Wanes off by 60 days (up to 90 days).
- **IgG ELISA**: Used for past infections. 4-fold rise in paired sera confirms infection.

GRADING OF SEVERITY AND MANAGEMENT

- **Mild Dengue (Group A)**: Managed on OPD basis. Patients can tolerate adequate oral fluids, pass urine every 6 hours, no warning signs. Treatment: ORS, paracetamol (avoid aspirin/NSAIDs), tepid sponging.
- **Moderate Dengue (Group B)**: Observation/in-hospital management. Dengue with warning signs (persistent vomiting, abdominal pain, lethargy, mucosal bleeding, liver >2cm, rising Hct with falling platelets) or co-morbidities (pregnancy, infancy, old age, diabetes). Treatment: IV fluid (0.9% NS or Ringer Lactate) if oral not tolerated.
- **Severe Dengue (Group C)**: Emergency treatment. Severe plasma leakage leading to shock (DSS), severe bleeding, or severe organ impairment (hepatic damage, cardiomyopathy, encephalitis). Treatment: Isotonic crystalloid solutions (10-20 ml/kg/hr over 1 hour), Colloids (Dextran 40) if massive leakage, Blood transfusion (10 ml/kg whole blood or 5 ml/kg packed RBC) if suspected severe overt bleed.

PREVENTION AND CONTROL

- **Mosquito control**: Anti-adult and anti-larval measures, source reduction (elimination of breeding places), covering stored water, weekly dry day.
- **Personal prophylaxis**: Bed nets, full sleeves, mosquito repellents.
- **Dengue Vaccines**: 
- **CYD-TDV (Dengvaxia, Sanofi)**: Tetravalent live-attenuated recombinant vaccine. 3 doses at 0, 6, and 12 months. Indicated for ages 9-45 years living in endemic areas. Safe ONLY in persons who have had a prior dengue virus infection (seropositive). Increases risk of severe dengue in seronegative individuals.
- **TAK-003 (Qdenga, Takeda)**: Tetravalent live-attenuated vaccine.

[LAQ]National Framework for Malaria Elimination Programme (2016-2030)[/LAQ]

[LAQ]Assessment of burden of malaria in a community and NVBDCP strategies[/LAQ]

[SN]Host factors in malaria[/SN]

[SN]Factors responsible for resurgence of malaria[/SN]

MALARIA

OVERVIEW OF THE DISEASE

- **Malaria Epidemiology**: A protozoal disease caused by Plasmodium parasites and transmitted by the bite of certain species of infected female Anopheline mosquitoes.
- **Global burden**: 249 million cases in 2022. Mostly in sub-Saharan Africa.
- **In India**: The majority of malaria cases and deaths are reported from high-burden states including Odisha, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, Madhya Pradesh, and the North Eastern states.
- **Substantial progress in India**: 80.53% reduction in morbidity and 78.38% reduction in mortality between 2015 and 2023. API was 0.16 per 1000 population in 2023.

MAJOR EPIDEMIOLOGICAL TYPES OF MALARIA IN INDIA

- **1. Tribal malaria**: Accounts for ~50% of P. falciparum cases.
- **2. Rural malaria**: Irrigated areas of arid and semiarid plains. An. culicifacies is the main vector. P. vivax predominant during lean periods, P. falciparum during periodic exacerbations.
- **3. Urban malaria**: An. stephensi is the vector. Influenced by poor sanitary conditions, unplanned settlements, overhead tanks, fountains.
- **4 Malaria In**: 4. Malaria in project areas: Tropical aggregation of labourers brings different strains of parasites. Ecological disturbance creates prolific vector breeding.
- **5. Border malaria**: High transmission belts along international/state borders.
- **6. Forest malaria**: An. dirus vector. Deforested areas harbour efficient vectors that bite humans and return to the forest, avoiding indoor residual sprays.
- **7. Floods and malaria**: Initial flush out of breeding, followed by pools of water creating mosquitogenic conditions. Lag time of 6-8 weeks.

DEFINITIONS

- **Malaria control**: Reducing disease burden to a level at which it is no longer a public health problem.
- **Malaria elimination**: Interruption of local mosquito-borne transmission (reduction to zero incidence in a defined area).
- **Certification of elimination**: Granted by WHO after proven interruption of local transmission for at least 3 consecutive years.
- **Malaria eradication**: Permanent reduction to zero worldwide incidence. Intervention measures no longer needed.

EPIDEMIOLOGICAL DETERMINANTS

AGENT FACTORS

- **Agent**: Four species of Plasmodium infect humans: P. vivax, P. falciparum, P. malariae, and P. ovale.
- **Parasite Biology**: In India, ~50% cases are P. falciparum, 4-8% mixed, and the rest P. vivax. P. malariae is <1% (Tumkur and Hassan districts in Karnataka). P. ovale is very rare (mostly tropical Africa).
- **Reservoir of infection**: Human reservoir (cases and carriers). A person must harbour both sexes of the gametocyte in the blood. Gametocytes must be mature and present in sufficient density (at least 12 per cu.mm).
- **Period of communicability**: As long as mature, viable gametocytes exist in circulating blood. In vivax, they appear in 4-5 days; in falciparum, 10-12 days after asexual parasites.
- **Relapses**: P. vivax and P. ovale can relapse >3 years after the first attack due to original sporozoite-induced liver schizonts (hypnozoites) lying dormant. P. falciparum and P. malariae do not have a true relapse (no latent liver phase); recrudescences are due to chronic blood infection.

HOST FACTORS

- **Age**: Affects all ages. Newborns have considerable resistance to P. falciparum due to high foetal haemoglobin.
- **Sex**: Males mostly exposed due to outdoor habits.
- **Race/Genetic**: Sickle cell trait (AS) causes milder illness with falciparum. "Duffy negative" RBCs are resistant to P. vivax.
- **Pregnancy**: Increases risk. Primigravid women are at greatest risk. May cause intrauterine death, premature labour, abortion.
- **Human Habits**: Sleeping outdoors, nomadism.
- **Immunity**: Acquired only after repeated exposure over years. Wanes when people migrate out of endemic regions.

ENVIRONMENTAL FACTORS

- **Season**: July to November (peak in India).
- **Temperature**: Optimum for parasite development in vector is 20 to 30 C. Below 16 C, development ceases. Above 30 C is lethal.
- **Humidity**: Relative humidity of 60% is necessary for mosquitoes to live their normal span. High humidity = more active, voracious feeding.
- **Rainfall**: Creates breeding opportunities.
- **Altitude**: Anophelines are not found above 2000-2500 metres.
- **Man-made malaria**: Burrow pits, garden pools, irrigation channels, dams, bridges.

VECTORS OF MALARIA (IN INDIA)

- **6 primary vectors**: An. culicifacies (rural/peri-urban), An. stephensi (urban/industrial), An. fluviatilis (hilly/forest fringes), An. minimus (foothills of NE states), An. dirus (forest vector in NE), An. epiroticus (Andaman & Nicobar Islands).
- **Life Span Of**: Life span of vector must be at least 10-12 days for parasite to complete sporogony and vector to become infective.

MODE OF TRANSMISSION

- **Vector transmission**: Bite of infected female anopheline mosquito.
- **Direct transmission**: Blood transfusion, hypodermic intramuscular/intravenous injections (drug addicts), transplacental (congenital).

INCUBATION PERIOD

- **P. falciparum**: 12 days (range 9-14)
- **P. vivax**: 14 days (range 8-17)
- **P. ovale**: 17 days (range 16-18)
- **P. malariae**: 28 days (range 18-40)

LIFE CYCLE

- **Malaria Life Cycle**: Asexual cycle (Schizogony in Human):
- **1. Hepatic phase**: Sporozoites enter liver cells. P. vivax and P. ovale have dormant forms (hypnozoites). P. falciparum bursts almost simultaneously (no exo-erythrocytic phase).
- **2. Erythrocytic phase**: Merozoites infect RBCs. Pass through trophozoite and schizont stages. Cycle is 48 hrs for Pf, Pv, Po; and 72 hrs for Pm.
- **3. Gametogeny**: Some forms become male/female gametocytes (infective to mosquito).
- **Malaria Life Cycle**: Sexual cycle (Sporogony in Mosquito):
- **Gametocytes Ingested **: Gametocytes ingested -> Exflagellation -> Microgametes fertilize macrogamete -> Zygote -> Ookinete -> Oocyst -> Sporozoites migrate to salivary glands.

CLINICAL FEATURES

- **Primary Fever Corresponds**: Primary fever corresponds to the release of merozoites into the blood.
- **1. Cold stage (15-60 mins)**: Lassitude, headache, nausea, chilly sensation, rigors. Temp rises to 39-41 C. Pulse rapid.
- **2. Hot stage (2-6 hours)**: Patient feels burning hot, casts off clothes. Skin hot and dry. Intense headache.
- **3. Sweating stage (2-4 hours)**: Fever comes down with profuse sweating. Temp drops to normal, skin cool/moist.
- **Complications (P. falciparum)**: Cerebral malaria, acute renal failure, liver damage, blackwater fever, dehydration, collapse.

LABORATORY DIAGNOSIS

- **1. Microscopy**: Thick smear (sensitive, 20x more rapidly detects parasites) and Thin smear (for species identification).
- **2 Rapid Diagnostic**: 2. Rapid Diagnostic Test (RDT): Dipstick format detecting circulating parasite antigens.
- **3. Serology**: Fluorescent antibody test.

MEASUREMENT OF MALARIA (PARAMETERS)

- **Annual Parasite Incidence (API)**: =(Confirmed cases during one year / Population under surveillance) x 1000.
- **Annual Blood Examination Rate (ABER)**: =(Number of slides examined / Population) x 100.
- **Annual Falciparum Incidence**: Annual Falciparum Incidence (AFI).
- **Slide Positivity Rate (SPR)**: =Percentage of slides positive for any malarial parasite.
- **Slide Falciparum Rate (SFR)**: =Percentage of slides positive for P. falciparum.

VECTOR INDICES

- **1. Human Blood Index**: Proportion of freshly-fed female mosquitoes containing human blood.
- **2. Sporozoite Rate**: Percentage of female anophelines with sporozoites in salivary glands.
- **3. Mosquito Density**: Number of mosquitoes per man-hour-catch.
- **4. Man-Biting Rate**: Average incidence of bites per day per person.
- **5. Inoculation Rate**: Man-biting rate multiplied by the infective sporozoite rate.

TREATMENT OF UNCOMPLICATED MALARIA

- **P. vivax**: 
- **Chloroquine (CQ)**: 25 mg/kg body weight divided over 3 days (10mg/kg day 1; 10mg/kg day 2; 5mg/kg day 3).
- **Primaquine (PQ)**: 0.25 mg/kg daily for 14 days (to prevent relapse/hypnozoites). Contraindicated in G6PD deficiency, infants, and pregnant women.
- **P. falciparum**: 
- **Artemisinin Based Combination**: Artemisinin Based Combination Therapy (ACT).
- **North-Eastern States**: Artemether (20mg) + Lumefantrine (120mg) for 3 days + Primaquine single dose (0.75 mg/kg) on day 2.
- **Other States**: Artesunate (4mg/kg) for 3 days + Sulfadoxine-Pyrimethamine (25mg/1.25mg/kg) on day 1 + Primaquine single dose (0.75 mg/kg) on day 2.
- **P Ovale And**: P. ovale and P. malariae: Treated same as P. vivax and P. falciparum respectively.
- **Mixed Infections Pv**: Mixed Infections (Pv + Pf): Full course of ACT + Primaquine 0.25 mg/kg/day for 14 days.
- **Pregnancy**: 
- **1st Trimester**: Quinine salt 10 mg/kg 3 times daily for 7 days (ACT is contraindicated).
- **2nd and 3rd Trimester**: Area-specific ACT.
- **Primaquine Is Contraindicated**: Primaquine is contraindicated in all trimesters.

TREATMENT OF SEVERE MALARIA

- **Severe Malaria Protocol**: Emergency management.
- **Severe Malaria Protocol**: Initial parenteral treatment for at least 48 hours with:
- **Quinine 20 Mgkg**: Quinine (20 mg/kg loading, 10 mg/kg maintenance)
- **Or Artesunate 24**: OR Artesunate (2.4 mg/kg IV/IM at 0, 12, 24 hrs, then daily)
- **Or Artemether 32**: OR Artemether (3.2 mg/kg IM then 1.6 mg/kg daily)
- **Or Arteether 150**: OR Arteether (150 mg daily IM for 3 days, adults only).
- **Followed By Full**: Followed by full oral course of area-specific ACT + PQ (for Pf) OR Quinine + Doxycycline/Clindamycin.
- **Corticosteroids Iv Mannitol**: Corticosteroids, IV mannitol, heparin are contraindicated.

CHEMOPROPHYLAXIS

- **Recommended For Travellers**: Recommended for travellers to endemic areas, soldiers, police, labour forces.
- **Shortterm 6 Weeks**: Short-term (<6 weeks): Doxycycline (started day before arrival) or Mefloquine (started 2-3 weeks before departure).
- **Prophylactic Drugs Taken**: Prophylactic drugs taken continuously and for 4 weeks after leaving the risk area.

VECTOR CONTROL STRATEGIES

- **Anti-adult measures**: Indoor Residual Spraying (IRS) using DDT, malathion. Space application (fog/mist), bed nets.
- **Anti-larval measures**: Oiling, Paris green, Temephos (chemical); Source reduction (drainage, filling); Integrated control.

MALARIA VACCINES

- **RTS,S/AS01 and R21/Matrix-M**: Pre-erythrocytic vaccines. Prevent P. falciparum infection in children.
- **Does Not Interrupt**: Does not interrupt transmission. No cross-protection for other species.
- **Schedule**: 4 doses (at 5-17 months age, 3 doses at 1-month intervals, 4th dose 18 months later).

[LAQ]Epidemiology, prevention and control of lymphatic filariasis in India[/LAQ]

[LAQ]Strategies to eliminate lymphatic filariasis from India with SWOT[/LAQ]

[SN]Strategies for elimination of lymphatic filariasis[/SN]

FACTORS RESPONSIBLE FOR RESURGENCE / PERSISTENCE OF MALARIA

- **Malaria Resurgence Determinants**: Incomplete surveillance and low ABER leading to undetected transmission.
- **Malaria Resurgence Determinants**: Drug resistance (historical CQ resistance in Pf) and incomplete radical cure for P. vivax hypnozoites.
- **Insecticide Resistance And**: Insecticide resistance and outdoor/early biting reducing IRS/LLIN impact.
- **Population Movement Project**: Population movement, project labour aggregation, and urban An. stephensi breeding in tanks/construction sites.
- **Ecological change**: irrigation, deforestation, flood aftermath breeding.
- **Programme Fatigue As**: Programme fatigue as cases fall (paradox of elimination) and stock-outs of diagnostics/drugs.

[LAQ]How will you assess malaria burden and current elimination strategies under NVBDCP[/LAQ]

ASSESSING MALARIA BURDEN IN A COMMUNITY

1. Review API, ABER, SPR, SFR, deaths, species mix, seasonality, and age pattern.
2. Judge surveillance quality: inadequate ABER underestimates burden.
3. Active case detection in high-risk pockets; fever surveys; RDT/microscopy camps.
4. Entomology: vector species, density, resting and biting behaviour, insecticide resistance.
5. Risk mapping: breeding sites, migration, forest fringe, project areas.
6. System check: ACT/RDT stocks, treatment compliance, private-sector leakage.

NATIONAL FRAMEWORK FOR MALARIA ELIMINATION (2016-2030) PROGRAMMATIC ARCHITECTURE

- **Definitions**: control vs elimination (zero indigenous cases in a defined area) vs eradication (global permanent zero). WHO certification requires evidence of interrupted local transmission for at least three consecutive years with capable surveillance.
- **Stratify Units By**: Stratify units by transmission intensity (API-based categories) with tailored packages: intensified control → elimination → prevention of re-establishment.
- **Strategies**: early diagnosis and complete treatment; integrated vector management; surveillance as intervention with case-based foci investigation; quality-assured labs; IEC/BCC; special strategies for tribal, forest, urban, border, and project malaria.
- **Tools**: area-specific ACT for Pf; primaquine radical cure for Pv where policy allows; IRS/LLIN/larviciding/source reduction as indicated.

> **EXAM TIP:** Write formulas for API and ABER → burden assessment steps → elimination definitions → stratified strategies → short SWOT if asked.

LYMPHATIC FILARIASIS

OVERVIEW OF THE DISEASE

- **Caused by nematode worms**: Wuchereria bancrofti (90% of cases globally), Brugia malayi, and Brugia timori.
- **Transmitted By The**: Transmitted by the bites of infective mosquitoes.
- **Chronic Manifestations Include**: Chronic manifestations include lymphangitis, lymphadenitis, elephantiasis of genitals, legs and arms, and hydrocele.

PROBLEM STATEMENT

- **More Than 657**: More than 657 million people live in at-risk areas. 120 million infected. 15 million with lymphoedema, 25 million men with scrotal hydrocele.
- **India**: Heavy endemic areas in UP, Bihar, Jharkhand, AP, Odisha, TN, Kerala, Gujarat.

EPIDEMIOLOGICAL DETERMINANTS

AGENT FACTORS

- **Agent**: W. bancrofti, B. malayi, B. timori.
- **Microfilariae (Mf) periodicity**: Nocturnal periodicity in India (appear in large numbers at night, 10 PM to 2 AM). Biological adaptation to the vector's biting habits.
- **Life span**: Adult worms live for up to 15 years. Mf live for up to a year or more.

HOST FACTORS

- **Host Factor**: Man is the definitive host.
- **Age**: Infection rates rise up to 20-30 years, then level off. Disease usually appears over 10 years of age.
- **Sex**: Mf rate higher in men.
- **Social factors**: Urbanization, industrialization, migration, poor sanitation.

ENVIRONMENTAL FACTORS

- **Climate**: Max prevalence of Culex quinquefasciatus at 22 to 38 C and 70% humidity.
- **Bad Drainage Polluted**: Bad drainage, polluted water, cesspools, open ditches favour breeding.

VECTORS

- **Mosquito Is The**: Mosquito is the intermediate host.
- **Bancroftian filariasis**: Culex quinquefasciatus (C. fatigans).
- **Brugian filariasis**: Mansonia annulifers and Mansonia uniformis.

MODE OF TRANSMISSION

- **Bite Of Infected**: Bite of infected vector mosquito. Parasite is deposited near the puncture site and penetrates the skin to reach the lymphatic system.

INCUBATION PERIOD

- **Pre-patent period**: Time from inoculation to first appearance of detectable Mf.
- **Clinical incubation period**: Time from invasion to clinical manifestations (8 to 16 months, or longer).

CLINICAL MANIFESTATIONS

- **1. Lymphatic Filariasis**: 
- **I Asymptomatic Amicrofilaraemia**: (i) Asymptomatic amicrofilaraemia.
- **(ii) Asymptomatic microfilaraemia**: Mf in blood, no symptoms. Important source of infection.
- **(iii) Acute manifestations**: Filarial fever, lymphangitis, lymphadenitis, lymphoedema, epididymo-orchitis.
- **(iv) Chronic obstructive lesions**: 10-15 years from onset. Fibrosis and obstruction. Hydrocele, elephantiasis (legs, scrotum, arms, penis, vulva, breasts), chyluria.
- **2 Occult **: 2. Occult / Cryptic Filariasis:
- **Classical Manifestations Absent**: Classical manifestations absent, Mf not found in blood.
- **Result Of Hypersensitivity**: Result of hypersensitivity reaction to filarial antigens.
- **Example**: Tropical pulmonary eosinophilia.

FILARIA SURVEY

- **1. Mass Blood Survey**: Thick film (20 cu.mm blood) collected by deep finger prick between 8:30 PM and 12 midnight.
- **2 Membrane Filter**: 2. Membrane filter concentration (MFC) method: For detecting low-density microfilaraemia. Venepuncture required.
- **3. DEC Provocation test**: 100 mg of Diethylcarbamazine (DEC) given orally. Mf peak in the blood within 15 mins. Blood examined after 1 hour in daytime.
- **4. Clinical survey**: For manifestations.
- **5 Entomological Survey**: 5. Entomological survey.

PARAMETERS ASSESSED

- **Microfilaria rate**: % showing Mf in peripheral blood.
- **Filarial endemicity rate**: % showing Mf or disease manifestation.
- **Microfilarial density**: Number of Mf per unit volume.
- **Average Infestation Rate**: Average infestation rate.

PREVENTION AND CONTROL

1. CHEMOTHERAPY

- **Diethylcarbamazine (DEC)**: Safe and effective. Kills Mf, uncertain effect on adults.
- **Dose for W. bancrofti**: 6 mg/kg daily for 12 days (72 mg/kg total).
- **Dose for B. malayi**: 3 to 6 mg/kg daily, up to total 36-72 mg/kg.
- **Mass Therapy **: Mass therapy / Selective treatment.
- **DEC-medicated salt**: 1-4 g of DEC per kg of common salt for 6 to 9 months.
- **Ivermectin**: 150-200 mcg/kg body weight single dose. Macrolide antibiotic.
- **Albendazole**: 400 mg single dose for adults and children >2 years.
- **Global Strategy (MDA)**: Annual mass drug administration of a 2-drug regimen (Ivermectin or DEC + Albendazole) for 4-6 years.

2. VECTOR CONTROL

- **Anti-larval measures**: 
- **Chemical**: Mosquito larvicidal oil (MLO), Pyrethrum-based emulsifiable larvicide (Pyrosene oil-E), Temephos, Fenthion.
- **Removal Of Pistia**: Removal of Pistia plant (for Mansonia mosquitoes).
- **Minor environmental measures**: filling ditches, drainage.
- **Anti-adult measures**: Pyrethrum space spray.
- **Personal prophylaxis**: Mosquito nets.

STRATEGIES TO ELIMINATE LYMPHATIC FILARIASIS (INDIA) WITH SWOT

PILLARS

1. Mass Drug Administration (MDA): annual supervised co-administration to the eligible endemic population for enough years to clear the microfilaria reservoir. Classic regimen DEC + albendazole; where policy adopts IDA (ivermectin + DEC + albendazole) in eligible settings, higher microfilaricidal impact is expected.
2. Morbidity Management and Disability Prevention (MMDP): hydrocele surgery access; lymphoedema hygiene, elevation, and exercises; home-based care training.
3. Vector control: anti-larval measures against Culex in polluted water; environmental sanitation; personal protection.
4. Surveillance: microfilaria surveys; transmission assessment surveys (TAS) after MDA criteria are met; investigation of persistent hotspots.
5. IEC and social mobilization: improve supervised swallowing and coverage.

SWOT

- **Strengths**: National elimination programme under NVBDCP; free MDA drugs; PHC/ASHA platform; historical endemicity mapping.
- **Weaknesses**: Incomplete MDA coverage/compliance; urban logistics; migrants; variable MMDP quality; night blood-survey operational difficulty.
- **Opportunities**: IDA where approved; integration with other NTD campaigns; digital microplanning; sanitation reducing Culex breeding.
- **Threats**: Programme fatigue; stopping MDA too early; drug hesitancy; urbanization creating new breeding sites.

STRENGTHENING

- **Premda House Listing**: Pre-MDA house listing and observed swallowing; independent coverage surveys; MMDP registers; larval control with municipal engineering; post-MDA surveillance before stopping MDA.

> **EXAM TIP:** Agent-vector-nocturnal periodicity → five pillars → SWOT table → four Comprehensive elimination demands integrated vector control, morbidity management and disability prevention (MMDP), and entomological surveillance alongside mass drug administration.

ZIKA VIRUS DISEASE

OVERVIEW OF THE DISEASE

- **Mosquitoborne Flavivirus Identified**: Mosquito-borne flavivirus identified in Uganda (1947).
- **Outbreaks In Yap**: Outbreaks in Yap Island (2007) and Brazil (2015).
- **Associated With Guillainbarre**: Associated with Guillain-Barre Syndrome and Microcephaly in newborns.

EPIDEMIOLOGICAL DETERMINANTS

- **Agent**: Zika virus (Flavivirus).
- **Vector**: Aedes mosquitoes (mainly Aedes aegypti).
- **Mode of transmission**: Bite of infected mosquito, sexual contact, transfusion of blood, and mother-to-child (transplacental or during birth).

INCUBATION PERIOD

- **A Few Days**: A few days (usually 2 to 14 days).

CLINICAL PICTURE

- **Zika Clinical Features**: Often asymptomatic (3 out of 4 cases).
- **Zika Clinical Features**: Mild symptoms similar to dengue: Fever, skin rashes, conjunctivitis, muscle and joint pain, malaise, headache. Lasts 2-7 days.
- **Severe Formshospitalization Are**: Severe forms/hospitalization are uncommon, fatalities are rare.
- **Major complications**: Microcephaly (congenital) and Guillain-Barre syndrome.

DIAGNOSIS

- **Dengue Diagnostic Test**: RT-PCR (Polymerase Chain Reaction) and virus isolation from blood samples.
- **Serology Is Not**: Serology is not recommended due to cross-reactivity.

PREVENTION AND TREATMENT

- **No Specific Treatment**: No specific treatment; symptomatic care (rest, fluids, paracetamol).
- **No Vaccine Currently**: No vaccine currently available.
- **Prevention Relies On**: Prevention relies on vector control (source reduction of Aedes breeding sites) and reducing mosquito-human contact.

ZOONOSES

DEFINITIONS AND CLASSIFICATION

- **Epidemiological Classification**: Zoonoses are defined as diseases and infections which are naturally transmitted between vertebrate animals and man.
- **Epidemiological Classification**: Classified in terms of their reservoir hosts, whether these are man or lower vertebrate animals:
- **Anthropo-zoo-nosis**: Infections transmitted from lower vertebrate to man (e.g., Rabies).
- **Zoo-anthropo-nosis**: Infections transmitted from man to lower vertebrate.
- **Amphi-xe-nosis**: Infection that may be transmitted in both directions.
- **Epidemiological Classification**: Classification based upon the type of life cycle of the infecting organism:
- **Direct-zoonosis**: Transmitted from an infected vertebrate host to a susceptible vertebrate host by direct contact, by contact with a fomite, or by a mechanical vector. The agent undergoes no propagative and developmental changes during transmission. Examples: Rabies, trichinosis, brucellosis.
- **Cyclo-zoonosis**: Requires more than one vertebrate host, but no invertebrate host, in order to complete the developmental cycle of the agent. Examples: Taeniasis, echinococcosis.
- **Meta-zoonosis**: Transmitted biologically by invertebrate vectors. In the invertebrate, the agent multiplies or develops, and there is always an extrinsic incubation period before transmission to another vertebrate host is possible. Examples: Arbovirus infection, plague, schistosomiasis.
- **Sapro-zoonosis**: Have both a vertebrate host and a non-animal developmental site or reservoir (food, soil, plants). Examples: various forms of larva migrans, mycoses.

[LAQ]Epidemiology, management and control of rabies in India[/LAQ]

[LAQ]Management of dog bite as well as rabies in man[/LAQ]

RABIES

OVERVIEW OF THE DISEASE

- **Disease Definition**: Also known as Hydrophobia.
- **Disease Definition**: An acute, highly fatal viral disease of the central nervous system.
- **Disease Definition**: Caused by Lyssavirus type 1.
- **Disease Definition**: Transmitted to man usually by bites or licks of rabid animals.
- **Disease Definition**: Always fatal.

PROBLEM STATEMENT

- **Rabies Burden**: Rabies is an enzootic and epizootic disease of worldwide importance.
- **Water Appears To**: Water appears to be the most effective natural barrier to rabies.
- **Australia Ireland New**: Australia, Ireland, New Zealand, Japan, Taiwan, etc., are free of the disease.
- **In India Lakshadweep**: In India, Lakshadweep and Andaman & Nicobar islands are free of the disease.
- **Although A Number**: Although a number of carnivorous and bat species serve as natural reservoirs, rabid dogs are the source of 99% of human infection.
- **India Reports 20000**: India reports 20,000 deaths annually.

AGENT FACTORS

- **Agent**: Lyssavirus type 1. A bullet-shaped neurotropic RNA containing virus belonging to the family Rhabdoviridae.
- **Serotypes 2 3**: Serotypes 2, 3, and 4 are rabies-related but antigenically distinct viruses.
- **Contains Two Distinct**: Contains two distinct major antigens: a glycoprotein (G protein) from the virus membrane (induces virus-neutralizing antibodies) and an internal nucleoprotein antigen.
- **Street virus**: Virus recovered from naturally occurring cases of rabies. Incubation period is long and variable (20-60 days in dogs).
- **Fixed virus**: Serial brain-to-brain passage of the street virus in rabbits modifies the virus such that its incubation period is progressively reduced until it becomes constant between 4-6 days. It does not form Negri bodies. Used in the preparation of antirabies vaccine.
- **Source of infection**: Saliva of rabid animals. Present in the saliva for 3-4 days (occasionally 5-6 days) before the onset of clinical symptoms and during the course of illness till death.

HOST FACTORS

- **Age/Sex**: Highest incidence in age group 1-24 years. Males are more frequently affected.
- **Rabies In Man**: Rabies in man is a dead-end infection.
- **Veterinarians Dog Handlers**: Veterinarians, dog handlers, and laboratory staff are at special risk of rabies.

MODES OF TRANSMISSION

- **Transmission Mode**: Deep bite or scratch by an infected animal.
- **Transmission Mode**: Saliva comes into direct contact with human mucosa or fresh skin wounds.
- **Humantohuman Transmission By**: Human-to-human transmission by bite is theoretically possible but never confirmed.
- **Rarely Contracted By**: Rarely contracted by inhalation of virus-containing aerosol or via transplantation of an infected organ.

INCUBATION PERIOD

- **Incubation Period**: Highly variable. Commonly 1-3 months following exposure, but may vary from 7 days to many years.
- **Depends On The**: Depends on the site of the bite, severity of the bite, number of wounds, amount of virus injected, species of the biting animal, clothing, and treatment undertaken.
- **Incubation Period Tends**: Incubation period tends to be shorter in severe exposures and bites on face, head, neck, and upper extremities.

PATHOGENESIS

- **Neuro-Pathogenesis**: Virus replicates in muscle or connective tissue cells at or near the site of introduction before it attaches to nerve endings and enters peripheral nerves.
- **Spreads Centripetally Via**: Spreads centripetally via the peripheral nerves towards the CNS.
- **Following Infection Of**: Following infection of the CNS, the virus spreads centrifugally in peripheral nerves to many tissues, including skeletal and myocardial muscle, adrenal glands, and skin.
- **Salivary Gland Invasion**: Salivary gland invasion is crucial for transmission to another animal or human.

CLINICAL PICTURE (RABIES IN MAN)

- **Prodromal symptoms**: Headache, malaise, sore throat, and slight fever lasting for 3-4 days.
- **80 Of Patients**: 80% of patients complain of pain or tingling at the site of the bite.
- **Aerophobia (fear of air)**: Fanning a current of air across the face causes violent spasms of the pharyngeal and neck muscles.
- **Spasms Of The**: Spasms of the muscles of deglutition on the mere sight or sound of water (Hydrophobia - fear of water) is pathognomonic of rabies.
- **Mental Changes Include**: Mental changes include fear of death, anger, irritability, and depression.
- **Duration Of Illness**: Duration of illness is 2 to 3 days, may be prolonged to 5-6 days. Patient dies abruptly during a convulsion or passes into paralysis and coma.

DIAGNOSIS

- **Clinical Diagnosis Based**: Clinical diagnosis based on history of bite and characteristic signs.
- **Confirmed Early In**: Confirmed early in illness by antigen detection using immunofluorescence of skin biopsy, and by virus isolation from saliva.
- **Neutralizing Antibodies Are**: Neutralizing antibodies are not usually detectable in serum or CSF before the eighth day.

TREATMENT

- **No Specific Treatment**: No specific treatment. Case management is supportive.
- **Isolate Patient In**: Isolate patient in a quiet room, protected from bright light, noise, or cold draughts.
- **Relieve Anxiety And**: Relieve anxiety and pain (Morphia 30-45 mg).
- **Muscle Relaxants Hydration**: Muscle relaxants, hydration, diuresis, and respiratory/cardiac support.

PREVENTION: POST-EXPOSURE PROPHYLAXIS (PEP)

- **Local treatment of wound**: 
- **Cleansing**: Immediate flushing and washing the wound(s), scratches, and adjoining areas with plenty of soap and water under a running tap for at least 15 minutes.
- **Chemical treatment**: Inactivate residual virus with virucidal agents - alcohol (400-700 ml/litre), tincture, or 0.01% aqueous iodine or povidone iodine.
- **Suturing**: Bite wounds should not be immediately sutured. If necessary, done 24-48 hours later, applying minimum stitches, under the cover of rabies immunoglobulin locally.
- **Antibiotics And Antitetanus**: Antibiotics and anti-tetanus measures when indicated.

CATEGORIES OF CONTACT AND PEP MEASURES

- **Category I**: Touching or feeding animals, licks on intact skin.
- **Measures**: None.
- **Category II**: Nibbling of uncovered skin, minor scratches or abrasions without bleeding.
- **Measures**: Immediate vaccination and local treatment of the wound.
- **Category III**: Single or multiple transdermal bites or scratches, licks on broken skin; contamination of mucous membrane with saliva; contacts with bats.
- **Measures**: Immediate vaccination and administration of rabies immunoglobulin; local treatment of the wound.

IMMUNIZATION (VACCINES)

- **Vaccine Administration**: Cell-culture and embryonated egg-based vaccines (CCEEVs) such as human diploid cells, Vero cells, chick embryo cells.
- **Must Comply With**: Must comply with WHO recommended potency of >= 2.5 IU per single IM dose (0.5 ml or 1.0 ml).
- **Intramuscular administration**: 
- **Essen regimen**: 5-dose regimen on days 0, 3, 7, 14, and 28 into deltoid (or thigh in children <2 years).
- **Zareb regimen**: 4-dose abbreviated multisite regimen (2-1-1). 2 doses on day 0 (one in each deltoid), 1 dose on day 7, 1 dose on day 21.
- **Intradermal administration**: 
- **2-site intradermal regimen**: 0.1 ml at 2 sites (deltoid or thigh) on days 0, 3, 7, and 28. (2+2+2+0+2 schedule).
- **Rabies Immunoglobulin (RIG)**: 
- **Administered Only Once**: Administered only once, preferably at or as soon as possible after initiation of PEP (not beyond the 7th day of vaccine).
- **Human rabies immunoglobulin (HRIG)**: 20 IU/kg body weight.
- **Equine rabies immunoglobulin (ERIG)**: 40 IU/kg body weight.
- **Administered Into Or**: Administered into or around the wound site. Remaining volume injected IM at a distant site.
- **Pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP)**: For high-risk groups. IM or ID doses on days 0, 7, and 21 or 28.
- **Previously vaccinated individuals**: 1 dose IM or ID on days 0 and 3. RIG is not indicated.

RABIES HUMAN MONOCLONAL ANTIBODY (RmAb)
- **Monoclonal Antibody Profile**: Laboratory-produced antibodies against rabies virus glycoprotein used for passive immunization in RIG-indicated exposures (typically Category III) where approved products are available.
- **Given Once Infiltrated**: Given once, infiltrated into and around the wound as anatomically feasible; any remaining volume intramuscularly distant from the vaccine site: same principles as RIG.
- **Always Combined With**: Always combined with thorough wound washing and a full vaccine course (IM or ID).
- **Advantages versus equine RIG**: more standardized manufacturing and lower risk of hypersensitivity than heterologous serum (product-specific).
- **Does Not Replace**: Does not replace vaccine; not indicated when only booster vaccine is required in previously adequately vaccinated persons.
- **Biological Dosing Specifications**: Human Rabies Immunoglobulin (HRIG) at 20 IU/kg body weight, Equine Rabies Immunoglobulin (ERIG) at 40 IU/kg body weight, or rabies human monoclonal antibodies (RmAb) at 3.33 IU/kg.

> **EXAM TIP:** Category III algorithm: wash 15 minutes → RIG/RmAb into wound → vaccine schedule. Table HRIG vs ERIG vs mAb.

POST-EXPOSURE PROPHYLAXIS IN PREVIOUSLY VACCINATED INDIVIDUALS

- **Re-Exposure Management**: If a person has completed a full pre- or post-exposure vaccine course previously and presents with a new exposure: give vaccine boosters on days **0 and 3** (IM or ID as per schedule used); **RIG/RmAb is not indicated**.
- **Documented Neutralizing Antibody**: Documented neutralizing antibody titre >0.5 IU/ml indicates adequate prior immunization; after a new Category II/III exposure the standard response remains vaccine boosters on days 0 and 3 without RIG/RmAb, plus thorough wound care.
- **Local Wound Care**: Local wound care remains mandatory even if prior vaccination is complete.

> **EXAM TIP:** New exposure + prior full course → wash → vaccine 0 and 3 → no RIG. Category I needs wound care only / no vaccine.

RABIES IN DOGS

- **Incubation period**: Ranges from 3-8 weeks (may be 10 days to a year).
- **Clinical Picture Manifests**: Clinical picture manifests in two forms:
- **Furious rabies (mad-dog syndrome)**: Change in behaviour, bites without provocation, runs amuck, hoarse voice, excessive salivation and foaming at the mouth, leads to paralytic stage and death.
- **Dumb rabies**: Excitative stage is lacking. Predominantly paralytic. Dog withdraws and dies in about 3 days.
- **Laboratory Diagnosis**: 
- **Fluorescent Antibody Test (FRA)**: Highly reliable, best single test for rapid diagnosis.
- **Microscopic examination**: Negri bodies identified in 75-90% of rabid dogs.
- **Mouse inoculation test**: 10% emulsion of brain tissue injected intracerebrally into 4 mice. Mice die in 6-8 days.
- **Corneal test**: Rabies virus antigen detected in live animals via corneal impressions.
- **Control of urban rabies**: 
- **Prophylactic vaccination**: Mass immunization covering 80-90% of dog population. Primary immunization at 3-4 months, boosters regularly.
- **Bpl Inactivated Nervous**: BPL inactivated nervous tissue vaccine (20% suspension of sheep brain). Dose 5 ml for dogs, 3 ml for cats.
- **Modified Live Virus**: Modified live virus vaccine (33% chick embryo). Dose 3 ml single injection.
- **Elimination Of Stray**: Elimination of stray dogs.

YELLOW FEVER

OVERVIEW OF THE DISEASE

- **A Zoonotic Disease**: A zoonotic disease caused by an arbovirus.
- **Affects Principally Monkeys**: Affects principally monkeys and other vertebrates in tropical America and Africa. Transmitted to man by culicine mosquitoes.
- **Shares Clinical Features**: Shares clinical features with other viral haemorrhagic fevers (dengue, Lassa fever) but characterized by more severe hepatic and renal involvement.

PROBLEM STATEMENT

- **47 Countries In**: 47 countries in Africa and Latin America are at risk.
- **Disease Has Never**: Disease has never been reported in India, but India is a "receptive" area because the conditions required for transmission (Aedes aegypti, susceptible monkeys) are present.

EPIDEMIOLOGICAL DETERMINANTS

- **Agent**: Flavivirus fibricus (Group B arbovirus / togavirus family). Shares group-specific antigens with West Nile, dengue. Virus is pantropic. In chick embryo cultures, it loses pathogenic properties but retains antigenicity.
- **Reservoir of infection**: Forest areas (monkeys and forest mosquitoes). Urban areas (man and Aedes aegypti).
- **Period of communicability**: Blood of patients is infective during the first 3 to 4 days of illness. Mosquitoes become infective after an extrinsic incubation period of 8 to 12 days and remain infective for life. Transovarian transmission occurs in mosquitoes.
- **Host factors**: All ages and sexes. Wood cutters and hunters at risk. One attack gives lifelong immunity. Infants of immune mothers have antibodies up to 6 months.
- **Environmental factors**: Temperature of 24 deg C or over and relative humidity >60% required for virus multiplication in mosquitoes. Urbanization leads to extension.

MODES OF TRANSMISSION

- **Sylvatic (jungle) yellow fever**: Monkeys -> wild mosquitoes -> man (mainly young men logging in forests).
- **Intermediate yellow fever**: Semi-domestic mosquitoes infect both monkeys and humans. Small-scale epidemics in Africa.
- **Urban yellow fever**: Infected people introduce virus into densely populated areas with Aedes mosquitoes -> man to man transmission.

INCUBATION PERIOD

- **3 To 6**: 3 to 6 days.

CLINICAL FEATURES & TREATMENT

- **Severe Cases Develop**: Severe cases develop jaundice with haemorrhagic manifestations (black vomit, epistaxis, melena), albuminuria, anuria, shock, coma.
- **Death Occurs Between**: Death occurs between the 5th and 10th day. CFR may reach 80% in severe cases.
- **No Specific Treatment**: No specific treatment. Supportive care for dehydration and fever.

PREVENTION AND CONTROL

- **1. Vaccination**: 17D vaccine (live attenuated, grown in chick embryo, freeze-dried).
- **Stored Between 5**: Stored between +5 and -30 deg C, preferably below zero.
- **Reconstituted With Cold**: Reconstituted with cold physiological saline. Discarded if not used within half an hour.
- **Dose**: 0.5 ml subcutaneously.
- **Immunity Appears On**: Immunity appears on 7th day and lasts for life.
- **Contraindications**: Children under 9 months (or 6 months during epidemic), pregnant women (unless outbreak risk is high), severe egg allergy, immunodeficiency/HIV.
- **2. Vector Control**: Anti-adult and anti-larval measures. Aedes aegypti index should not be more than 1% in towns and seaports in endemic areas.
- **3. International Measures (India)**: 
- **All Travellers Exposed**: All travellers exposed to risk must possess a valid international certificate of vaccination.
- **If No Certificate**: If no certificate, traveller is placed in quarantine in a mosquito-proof ward for 6 days.
- **Validity Of The**: Validity of the international certificate begins 10 days after vaccination and is **valid for the life of the person vaccinated** (IHR amendment). Older practice of 10-year validity is historical only.
- **Aircraftships Aerosol Sprayed**: Aircraft/ships aerosol sprayed on arrival. Airports kept free from breeding within 400 metres.
