JAPANESE ENCEPHALITIS (JE)

OVERVIEW OF THE DISEASE

- **A Mosquitoborne Encephalitis**: A mosquito-borne encephalitis caused by a Group B arbovirus (Flavivirus).
- **Zoonotic Disease Infecting**: Zoonotic disease infecting mainly animals and incidentally man.
- **Leading Cause Of**: Leading cause of viral encephalitis in Asia.

PROBLEM STATEMENT

- **Endemic In 21**: Endemic in 21 states of India. Assam, Bihar, UP, Karnataka, West Bengal, and Tamil Nadu report outbreaks every year (contributing ~55% of cases and deaths).

EPIDEMIOLOGICAL DETERMINANTS

- **Agent**: Group B arbovirus (Flavivirus).
- **Transmission cycle**: 
- **Pig  Mosquito**: Pig -> Mosquito -> Pig
- **Ardeid Bird **: Ardeid bird -> Mosquito -> Ardeid bird
- **Man Is An**: Man is an incidental "dead-end" host.
- **Animal hosts**: Pigs are the major vertebrate hosts and "amplifiers" of the virus. Cattle and buffaloes act as "mosquito attractants". Birds (pond herons, cattle egrets) are involved in the natural history.
- **Mosquito Vectors**: Culicine mosquitoes, notably Culex tritaeniorhynchus, C. vishnui, and C. gelidus. Breed in irrigated rice fields, shallow ditches. Zoophilic. Extrinsic incubation is 9-12 days.

INCUBATION PERIOD

- **5 To 15**: 5 to 15 days in man.

CLINICAL FEATURES

- **JE Clinical Course**: Ratio of overt disease to inapparent infection is about 1:250.
- **JE Clinical Course**: 1. Prodromal stage (1-6 days): Fever, headache, GI disturbances, lethargy.
- **2. Acute encephalitic stage**: High fever (38-40.7 C), nuchal rigidity, focal CNS signs, convulsions, speech difficulty, ocular palsies, hemiplegia, altered sensorium -> coma.
- **3 Late Stage**: 3. Late stage & sequelae: Temperature normalizes. Residual neurological deficits common. CFR varies between 20-40%.

DIAGNOSIS

- **Igmcapture Elisa Detecting**: IgM-capture ELISA detecting specific IgM in CSF or blood within 7 days of onset.

PREVENTION AND CONTROL

- **1. Vaccination**: 
- **Mouse Brainderived Nakayama**: Mouse brain-derived (Nakayama or Beijing strain, inactivated).
- **Cell Culturederived Inactivated**: Cell culture-derived inactivated (Beijing P-3 strain).
- **Cell Culturederived Live**: Cell culture-derived live attenuated (SA-14-14-2 strain). Integral part of Universal Immunization Programme in 83 endemic districts in India. Single dose + booster at 1 year interval.
- **2. Vector control**: Fogging with malathion or fenitrothion (ULV) within 2-3 km radius of infected villages. Use of mosquito nets.

OUTBREAK DEFINITION, JE WARNING SIGNS, AND RAPID RESPONSE TEAM

WORKING EPIDEMIOLOGICAL DEFINITION OF AN OUTBREAK

- **An Outbreak Is**: An outbreak is the occurrence of cases of a disease in a community or region clearly in excess of normal expectancy, or the appearance of a significant number of cases of an unusual disease. Even a single case of certain diseases (for example polio, yellow fever) may trigger outbreak response depending on context.

POINTERS / WARNING SIGNS OF IMPENDING JE ACTIVITY

- **Outbreak Warning Sign**: Seasonal rise in Acute Encephalitis Syndrome (AES) cases in known endemic blocks during transmission season.
- **Clustering Of Aesje**: Clustering of AES/JE in villages near rice fields with vector abundance (Culex tritaeniorhynchus complex).
- **Pig Amplification Settings**: Pig amplification settings and bird reservoir ecology with recent climatic favourability (rainfall, temperature).
- **Fall In Routine**: Fall in routine JE vaccine coverage in endemic districts; delayed case reporting from peripheral facilities.
- **Entomological alerts**: increased vector density; detection of virus in vectors where surveillance exists.

RAPID RESPONSE TEAM (COMPOSITION AND FUNCTIONS)

- **Typical composition**: epidemiologist/public-health officer, clinician (physician/paediatrician), entomologist, laboratory focal point, and local health administrator; veterinary input when zoonotic interface is relevant.
- **Functions**: verify diagnosis and case definitions; line listing and descriptive epidemiology; guide specimen collection (IgM in CSF/serum); vector control (fogging/ULV in defined radius); strengthen case management and referral; immunization response in eligible cohorts; risk communication; daily reporting to district/state.

AES PREVENTION AND MANAGEMENT (LINKED TO JE)

- **Prevention**: JE vaccination in endemic districts under UIP; vector control; personal protection; pigsty management away from dwellings where feasible.
- **Management of AES**: airway, anti-oedema measures as indicated, control of seizures and fever, fluid/electrolyte care, treat hypoglycaemia; specific etiology work-up (JE IgM); rehabilitation for sequelae.

> **EXAM TIP:** Outbreak definition → JE eco-epidemiology (pig-mosquito-man dead-end) → warning signs list → RRT composition + functions → vaccine + vector control.

RICKETTSIAL ZOONOSES

OVERVIEW OF THE DISEASE

- **Rickettsial Diseases Are**: Rickettsial diseases are caused by rickettsial organisms and transmitted to man by arthropod vectors (Q fever excepted).

CLASSIFICATION

- **Typhus group**: 
- **Epidemic typhus (louse-borne)**: R. prowazekii. Vector: Louse. Reservoir: Humans.
- **Murine typhus (endemic/flea-borne)**: R. typhi. Vector: Flea. Reservoir: Rodents.
- **Scrub typhus**: Orientia tsutsugamushi. Vector: Mite. Reservoir: Rodents.
- **Spotted fever group**: 
- **Rocky Mountain spotted fever**: R. rickettsii. Vector: Tick. Reservoir: Rodents, dogs.
- **Fievre Boutonneuse Indian**: Fievre boutonneuse, Indian tick typhus: R. conorii. Vector: Tick. Reservoir: Rodents, dogs.
- **Siberian tick typhus**: R. sibirica. Vector: Tick. Reservoir: Rodents.
- **Transitional group**: 
- **Rickettsial pox**: R. akari. Vector: Mite. Reservoir: Mice.
- **Queensland tick typhus**: R. australis. Vector: Tick. Reservoir: Rodents, marsupials.
- **Q fever**: 
- **Coxiella burnetii. Vector**: Airborne fomites/tick. Reservoir: Sheep, cattle, goats.

AGENT FACTORS

- **Rickettsiae Are Small**: Rickettsiae are small, obligate intracellular bacteria. Pleomorphic (short rods/cocci). Stain blue with Giemsa.
- **Grow Readily In**: Grow readily in the yolk sac of the embryonated egg.

CLINICAL FEATURES & DIAGNOSIS

- **Characterized By Fever**: Characterized by fever, headache, malaise, prostration, skin rash, and enlargement of spleen and liver.
- **Diagnosis**: Isolation, IFA test, complement fixation, Weil Felix reaction, ELISA.
- **Treatment**: Tetracycline is the drug of choice.

SCRUB TYPHUS

- **Agent**: Orientia tsutsugamushi.
- **Reservoir**: Trombiculid mite (transovarial transmission). Larva (chigger) feeds on vertebrate hosts.
- **Transmission**: Bite of infected larval mites.
- **Incubation period**: 10 to 12 days (range 6-21 days).
- **Clinical**: Acute onset chills, fever, headache. Macular rash on 5th day. Punched-out ulcer covered with a blackened scab (eschar) at mite bite site. Weil Felix reaction is strongly positive with Proteus strain OXK.
- **Control**: Tetracycline. Clearing vegetation, lindane/chlordane to ground. Mite repellents (benzyl benzoate, DEET).

MURINE TYPHUS (ENDEMIC TYPHUS)

- **Agent**: Rickettsia typhi (R. mooseri).
- **Reservoir**: Rats (R. rattus, R. norvegicus).
- **Transmission**: Spread from rat to rat by rat flea (X. cheopis). Transmitted to man by inoculation of infected faeces into skin or inhalation of dried faeces.
- **Incubation period**: 1 to 2 weeks (commonly 12 days).
- **Clinical**: Resembles louse-borne typhus but milder. Weil Felix reaction with Proteus OX-19 becomes positive in 2nd week.
- **Control**: Tetracycline. Rat flea control (residual insecticides like BHC, malathion).

INDIAN TICK TYPHUS

- **Agent**: Rickettsia conorii.
- **Reservoir**: Tick (Ixodidae family). Transovarial and trans-stadial passage.
- **Transmission**: Bite of an infected tick or contamination of skin with crushed tissues/faeces.
- **Incubation period**: 3 to 7 days.
- **Clinical**: Lesion or eschar at bite site. Maculopapular rash on 3rd day, appearing first on extremities (ankles, wrists) and moving centripetally.
- **Control**: Broad-spectrum antibiotics. Daily inspection of body for ticks, disinfection of dogs.

[SN]Coxiella burnetii[/SN]

Q FEVER

- **Agent**: Coxiella burnetii.
- **Reservoir**: Cattle, sheep, goats, ticks.
- **Transmission**: Inhalation of infected dust from contaminated soil/urine/faeces, aerosols during parturition, or ingestion of infected milk. No arthropod vector required for man.
- **Incubation period**: 2 to 3 weeks.
- **Clinical**: Acute fever, chills, headache. No rash or local lesion. Clinical picture is atypical pneumonia or hepatitis.
- **Control**: Doxycycline. Pasteurization or boiling of milk.

subsections.title: Surface Infections - Part A (Tetanus, Leprosy)
subsections.content:
TETANUS

OVERVIEW OF THE DISEASE

- **Disease Definition**: An acute disease induced by the exotoxin of Clostridium tetani.
- **Disease Definition**: Clinically characterized by muscular rigidity which persists throughout illness, punctuated by painful paroxysmal spasms of the voluntary muscles.
- **Disease Definition**: Specially affects the masseters (trismus or "lock-jaw"), facial muscles (risus sardonicus), muscles of the back and neck (opisthotonos), and those of the lower limbs and abdomen.
- **Tetanus Burden**: Mortality tends to be very high, varying from 40 to 80 per cent.

PROBLEM STATEMENT

- **Tetanus Burden**: Comparatively rare in developed countries but a major problem in developing countries.
- **Tetanus Burden**: Neonatal tetanus (NT) is a killer disease, second only to measles among the nine target diseases of the EPI.
- **Tetanus Burden**: Without high quality treatment, the case-fatality rate of NT can be as high as 80-90%.
- **Tetanus Burden**: Maternal and neonatal tetanus (MNT) is easily preventable by maternal immunization with tetanus toxoid containing vaccines (TTCV) and aseptic obstetric and postnatal umbilical cord care practices.
- **MNTE Elimination Status**: WHO defined elimination of NT as <1 case per 1000 live births in every district.
- **MNTE Elimination Status**: India was officially certified as achieving maternal and neonatal tetanus elimination (MNTE) in May 2015.
- **MNTE Elimination Status**: Success in India was aided by the National Rural Health Mission (NRHM) and the Janani Shishu Suraksha Karyakram (JSY) conditional cash transfer scheme to encourage institutional deliveries.

EPIDEMIOLOGICAL DETERMINANTS

AGENT FACTORS

- **Agent**: C. tetani. It is a gram-positive, anaerobic, spore-bearing organism.
- **Organism Characteristics**: The spores are terminal and give the organism a "drum-stick" appearance.
- **Resistance**: Spores are highly resistant to boiling, phenol, cresol, and autoclaving for 15 minutes at 120 C. They are best destroyed by steam under pressure at 120 C for 20 minutes or by gamma irradiation.
- **Reservoir of infection**: The natural habitat is soil and dust. Bacilli are found in the intestine of herbivorous animals (cattle, horses, goats, sheep) and excreted in their faeces. Spores survive for years in nature.
- **Exotoxin**: Tetanus bacilli produce a soluble exotoxin called tetanospasmin.
- **Toxicity**: It has astounding lethal toxicity, exceeded only by botulinum toxin. The lethal dose for a 70 kg man is about 0.1 mg.
- **Mechanism of action**: The toxin acts on 4 areas of the nervous system:
- **1 Motor End**: 1. Motor end plates in the skeletal system.
- **2 Spinal Cord**: 2. Spinal cord.
- **3 Brain**: 3. Brain.
- **4 Sympathetic Nervous**: 4. Sympathetic nervous system.
- **Its Principal Action**: Its principal action is to block the inhibition of spinal reflexes.
- **Period of communicability**: None. It is not transmitted from person to person.

HOST FACTORS

- **Age**: Commonly 5 to 40 years, which predisposes to all kinds of trauma. Tetanus in the newborn is "neonatal tetanus" (NT).
- **Nt Occurs When**: NT occurs when the umbilical cord is cut with unclean instruments or the stump is dressed with ashes, soil, or cowdung.
- **Sex**: Males have a higher incidence due to exposure, but females are exposed to the risk of "puerperal tetanus" during delivery or abortion.
- **Occupation**: Agricultural workers are at special risk due to contact with soil.
- **Rural-urban differences**: Incidence is much lower in urban than in rural areas.
- **Immunity**: No age is immune unless protected by previous immunization. Herd immunity does not protect the individual. The disease does not stimulate protective immunity because the lethal dose of the toxin is too small to be immunogenic. Patients who recover must be actively immunized.

ENVIRONMENTAL FACTORS

- **Tetanus Is A**: Tetanus is a positive environmental hazard. Depends on man's physical and ecological surroundings (soil, agriculture, animal husbandry) and unhygienic customs.

MODE OF TRANSMISSION

- **Infection Is Acquired**: Infection is acquired by contamination of wounds with tetanus spores.
- **Injuries include**: trivial pin prick, skin abrasion, puncture wounds, burns, human/animal bites, unsterile surgery, intra-uterine death, bowel surgery, dental extractions, injections, unsterile division of umbilical cord, compound fractures, otitis media, chronic skin ulcers, eye infections, and gangrenous limbs.

INCUBATION PERIOD

- **Usually 6 To**: Usually 6 to 10 days.
- **May Be As**: May be as short as one day or as long as several months.
- **Long Incubation Is**: Long incubation is explained by spores lying dormant in the wounds. Incubation is also prolonged by prophylaxis.

TYPES OF TETANUS

- **1. Traumatic**: Major and important cause. May result from trivial/unnoticed wounds.
- **2. Puerperal**: Follows abortion more frequently than normal labour. Post-abortal uterus is a favourable site.
- **3. Otogenic**: Ear may be a rare portal of entry (foreign bodies like infected pencils/matches). Occurs in children and adults.
- **4. Idiopathic**: No definite history of injury. Believed to be from microscopic trauma or absorption of toxin from the intestinal tract or inhaled spores.
- **5. Tetanus Neonatorum**: Infection of the umbilical stump after birth. First symptom seen around the 7th day. Known as "8th day disease" in Punjab.

PREVENTION AND CONTROL

1. ACTIVE IMMUNIZATION

- **Immunization Guidance**: Best prevented by active immunization with tetanus toxoid (stimulates antitoxin production).
- **Aim Is A**: Aim is a protective level of antitoxin (approximately 0.01 IU/ml serum) throughout life.
- **Combined Vaccines**: DPT, Pentavalent (DPT, Hep B, Hib), DT, dT (adult type).
- **Monovalent Vaccines**: Plain or fluid (formal) toxoid, and Tetanus vaccine adsorbed (PTAP, APT).
- **Schedule for Infants**: 3 doses of Pentavalent/DPT at 6, 10, 14 weeks. Boosters at 16-24 months, 5-6 years, and a TT/dT booster at 10 years and 16 years.

2. PASSIVE IMMUNIZATION

- **Human Tetanus Hyperimmunoglobulin (TIG)**: Best prophylactic. Dose for all ages is 250 IU. Gives passive protection up to 30 days. No serum sickness.
- **Antitetanus Serum Ats**: Anti-Tetanus Serum (ATS) - Equine: Used if TIG is unavailable. Standard dose is 1500 IU, injected subcutaneously after sensitivity testing. Protection lasts about 7-10 days. High risk of anaphylaxis and serum sickness.

3. ACTIVE AND PASSIVE IMMUNIZATION (SIMULTANEOUS)

- **Patient Is Given**: Patient is given 1500 IU of ATS or 250 IU of TIG in one arm, and 0.5 ml of adsorbed tetanus toxoid into the other arm or gluteal region.
- **Followed 6 Weeks**: Followed 6 weeks later by another 0.5 ml of toxoid, and a third dose one year later.

4. ANTIBIOTICS

- **Intramuscular Injection Of**: Intramuscular injection of 1.2 mega units of long-acting benzathine penicillin to kill vegetative forms.
- **Penicillin Has No**: Penicillin has no effect on tetanus spores.
- **If allergic to penicillin**: Erythromycin estolate 500 mg 6-hourly by mouth for 7 days.

PREVENTION OF NEONATAL TETANUS

- **1. Clean delivery practices**: The "Five Cleans" (Clean hands, clean delivery surface, clean blade for cutting cord, clean tie for the cord, and no application on the cord stump).
- **2. Maternal Immunization**: Two doses of tetanus toxoid to unimmunized pregnant women. First as early as possible, second at least a month later and at least 3 weeks before delivery. Previously immunized women require only one booster dose.

PREVENTION OF TETANUS AFTER INJURY

- **Wound Care**: All wounds must be thoroughly cleaned soon after injury (surgical toilet) to remove foreign bodies, soil, and necrotic tissue to abolish anaerobic conditions.
- **Categorization of Immunity**: 
- **Category A**: Has had a complete course of toxoid or a booster dose within the past 5 years.
- **Category B**: Has had a complete course of toxoid or a booster dose more than 5 years ago and less than 10 years ago.
- **Category C**: Has had a complete course of toxoid or a booster dose more than 10 years ago.
- **Category D**: Has not had a complete course of toxoid or immunity status is unknown.
- **Treatment Based On**: Treatment based on wound type:
- **Wounds Less Than**: Wounds less than 6 hours old, clean, non-penetrating, and with negligible tissue damage:
- **Category A**: Nothing more required.
- **Category B**: Toxoid 1 dose.
- **Category C**: Toxoid 1 dose.
- **Category D**: Toxoid complete course.
- **Other wounds**: 
- **Category A**: Nothing more required.
- **Category B**: Toxoid 1 dose.
- **Category C**: Toxoid 1 dose + Human Tet. Ig.
- **Category D**: Toxoid complete course + Human Tet. Ig.

[SN]SPARSH Leprosy Awareness Campaign[/SN]

[SN]Leprosy vaccine[/SN]

LEPROSY (HANSEN'S DISEASE)

OVERVIEW OF THE DISEASE

- **A Chronic Infectious**: A chronic infectious disease caused by Mycobacterium leprae.
- **Affects Mainly The**: Affects mainly the peripheral nerves, but also affects the skin, muscles, eyes, bones, testes, and internal organs.
- **Spectrum Ranges From**: Spectrum ranges from two polar forms: Lepromatous leprosy (LL) and Tuberculoid leprosy (TT), with borderline and indeterminate forms in between depending on host immune response.

CARDINAL FEATURES

- **Disease Definition**: Clinically characterized by one or more of the following:
- **Cardinal Sign of Leprosy**: 1. Hypopigmented or reddish skin patch(es) with definite loss of sensation (earliest sensation lost is usually light touch).
- **Cardinal Sign of Leprosy**: 2. Thickened peripheral nerves with loss of sensation and weakness/paralysis of corresponding muscles.
- **3 Presence Of**: 3. Presence of acid-fast bacilli (M. leprae) in the skin or nasal smears.
- **Advanced signs**: Nodules/lumps (face and ears), plantar ulcers, loss of fingers/toes, nasal depression, foot-drop, claw toes, facies leonina, madarosis (loss of eyebrows/eyelashes), gynaecomastia, and perforated palate.

PROBLEM STATEMENT

- **Leprosy Elimination Status**: India achieved the goal of leprosy elimination (<1 case per 10,000 population) at the national level in December 2005.
- **Global burden**: Dropped from 5.2 million cases in 1985 to 165,459 cases at the end of 2020.
- **In 2022 174087**: In 2022, 174,087 new cases were detected globally. SEAR accounted for 71.4% of the global burden (India, Brazil, and Indonesia contributed 78.1% of global new cases).
- **Multibacillary Cases Account**: Multibacillary cases account for ~68.9% of new cases.
- **Female cases**: 38.9%. Children <15 years: 5.1%.

EPIDEMIOLOGICAL DETERMINANTS

AGENT FACTORS

- **Agent**: M. leprae. Acid-fast, occurs both intracellularly and extracellularly in clumps or bundles called "globi".
- **Affinity For Schwann**: Affinity for Schwann cells and cells of the reticulo-endothelial system.
- **Generation Time Is**: Generation time is very long: 12-14 days for one bacterium to divide into two.
- **Mycobacterium Leprae Biology**: Cannot be grown in artificial media. Replicates in the 9-banded armadillo and nude mouse foot-pads.
- **Phenolic Glycolipid Pgl**: Phenolic glycolipid (PGL) is a highly specific M. leprae antigen.
- **Source of infection**: Multibacillary cases (lepromatous and borderline lepromatous). The current view is that all patients with "active leprosy" must be considered infectious.
- **Portal of exit**: The nose is a major portal of exit. Lepromatous cases harbour millions of bacilli in their nasal mucosa, discharged when sneezing or blowing the nose. Can also exit through ulcerated/broken skin.
- **Infectivity**: Highly infectious but of low pathogenicity. An infectious patient can be rendered non-infectious by treatment with dapsone for 90 days or rifampicin for 3 weeks (or local rifampicin drops/spray in 8 days).
- **Attack rates**: Among household contacts of lepromatous cases, 4.4% to 12% are expected to show signs within 5 years.

HOST FACTORS

- **Age**: Peaks between 20 and 30 years of age.
- **Sex**: Incidence and prevalence are higher in males. More marked among adults and lepromatous cases.
- **Migration**: Movement from rural to urban areas makes it an urban problem too.
- **Immunity**: Cell-mediated immunity (CMI) is responsible for resistance.
- **In Lepromatous Leprosy**: In lepromatous leprosy, there is a complete breakdown of CMI (Lepromin test is negative).
- **Anergy In Lepromatous**: Anergy in lepromatous leprosy is due to suppression of T cell production of interleukin-2 (IL-2).
- **Strong Cmi Restricts**: Strong CMI restricts disease to Pure Neural or Paucibacillary (PB) types.
- **Deficient Cmi Leads**: Deficient CMI leads to uncontrolled spread and Multibacillary (MB) type.
- **Genetic factors**: HLA-linked genes influence the immune response.

ENVIRONMENTAL FACTORS

- **Humidity Favours Survival**: Humidity favours survival of M. leprae. Viable in dried nasal secretions for at least 9 days, and in moist soil at room temperature for 46 days.
- **Overcrowding And Lack**: Overcrowding and lack of ventilation.

MODE OF TRANSMISSION

- **Droplet infection**: Aerosols containing M. leprae from the respiratory tract (nasal discharges).
- **Contact transmission**: Close, direct person-to-person contact, or indirect contact (soil, fomites, contaminated linen).
- **Other routes**: Insect vectors or tattooing needles cannot be completely ruled out.

INCUBATION PERIOD

- **Long Incubation Period**: Long incubation period. Average is 3 to 5 years, but can take up to 20 years. Often referred to as the "latent period".

PATHOGENESIS

- **Bacilli Enter The**: Bacilli enter the body (usually respiratory tract) -> migrate to neural tissue -> enter Schwann cells (prefer cooler places like cutaneous nerves & peripheral nerve trunks of limbs and face).
- **M Leprae Multiplies**: M. leprae multiplies slowly. Escapes to skin causing lesions.
- **Outcome Is Dictated**: Outcome is dictated by the patient's CMI.

CLASSIFICATION OF LEPROSY

1. INDIAN VS MADRID CLASSIFICATION

- **Indian**: Indeterminate type, Tuberculoid type, Borderline type, Lepromatous type, Pure neuritic type (no skin lesions).
- **Madrid**: Indeterminate, Tuberculoid (flat/raised), Borderline, Lepromatous.

2. RIDLEY-JOPLING CLASSIFICATION

- **Based On An**: Based on an immuno-histological scale: Tuberculoid (TT), Borderline tuberculoid (BT), Mid-borderline (BB), Borderline lepromatous (BL), Lepromatous (LL).

3. CLINICAL CLASSIFICATION FOR CONTROL PROGRAMMES (WHO)

- **Paucibacillary (PB) leprosy**: 1 to 5 skin lesions, and/or only one nerve involvement. Skin smear negative at all sites.
- **Multibacillary (MB) leprosy**: 6 and above skin lesions, and/or more than one nerve involvement. Skin smear positive at any site.

DIAGNOSTIC PROCEDURES

- **Clinical diagnosis**: Based on the 3 cardinal signs (Hypopigmented patch with sensory loss, thickened nerves, AFB positive smear).
- **Sensation testing**: Use a light ballpoint pen to test for touch sensation on the skin patch. Do not use a pin or cotton wool.
- **Nerve examination**: Palpate for thickening, tenderness. Assess motor/sensory function. Commonly affected nerves: Ulnar, Median, Radial, Facial, Posterior tibial, Lateral popliteal (common peroneal).
- **Bacteriological examination**: 
- **Slit And Scrape**: Slit and scrape method (Skin smears): Taken from active lesions and ear lobes.
- **Bacterial Index (BI)**: Measures density of living and dead bacilli on Ridley's logarithmic scale (0 to 6+ based on 100 oil-immersion fields). BI = 1+ means 1-10 bacilli in 100 fields; 6+ means >1000 bacilli per field.
- **Morphological Index (MI)**: Percentage of solid-staining (viable) bacilli among 200 pink-stained bacilli. Indicates drug response and resistance.
- **Solidfragmentedgranular Sfg Percentage**: Solid-fragmented-granular (SFG) percentage.
- **Foot-pad culture in mice**: Highly sensitive. Used for detecting drug resistance and evaluating drug potency.
- **Histamine test**: Detects early peripheral nerve damage (loss of flare response due to nerve destruction).
- **Immunological tests**: 
- **Lepromin test**: Injects 0.1 ml lepromin intradermally.
- **Early (Fernandez) reaction**: 48 hours. Indicates cell-mediated immunity to soluble antigens.
- **Late (Mitsuda) reaction**: 21 days. Nodule >5mm indicates CMI to bacillary component.
- **Used For Prognosis**: Used for prognosis and classification (positive in TT, negative in LL), NOT for diagnosis.
- **Fluorescent Leprosy Antibody**: Fluorescent Leprosy Antibody Absorption Test (FLA-ABS).
- **Monoclonal Antibodies And**: Monoclonal antibodies and ELISA (based on PGL antigen).

TREATMENT: MULTIDRUG THERAPY (MDT)

- **Rifampicin (RMP)**: Highly bactericidal. 600 mg monthly. Side effects: red urine, hepatotoxic, shock.
- **Dapsone (DDS)**: Bacteriostatic. 1-2 mg/kg/day. Side effects: haemolytic anaemia, methaemoglobinaemia, DDS syndrome (fever, rash, hepatitis).
- **Clofazimine (CLF)**: Anti-leprosy and anti-inflammatory. Weak bactericidal. Side effects: darkish red coloration of skin and body fluids, severe GI symptoms. (Ethionamide/Protionamide used if unacceptable).

MDT REGIMENS (REVISED WHO)

- **MDT Regimen Schedule**: Adult Multibacillary (MB) Leprosy (12 months within 18 months):
- **Rifampicin**: 600 mg once a month, supervised.
- **Dapsone**: 100 mg daily, self-administered.
- **Clofazimine**: 300 mg once a month supervised, and 50 mg daily self-administered.
- **MDT Regimen Schedule**: Adult Paucibacillary (PB) Leprosy (6 months within 9 months):
- **Rifampicin**: 600 mg once a month, supervised.
- **Dapsone**: 100 mg daily, self-administered.
- **Children 1014 Years**: Children 10-14 years MB Leprosy:
- **Rifampicin**: 450 mg/month supervised.
- **Dapsone**: 50 mg/day self.
- **Clofazimine**: 150 mg/month supervised + 50 mg every other day self.
- **Children 1014 Years**: Children 10-14 years PB Leprosy:
- **Rifampicin**: 450 mg/month supervised.
- **Dapsone**: 50 mg/day self.

TREATMENT DEFINITIONS

- **Defaulter**: Has not collected treatment for 12 consecutive months.
- **Relapse**: Appearance of new signs/symptoms after successfully completing an adequate course of MDT.

LEPRA REACTIONS

- **Immunologically Mediated Episodes**: Immunologically mediated episodes of acute/subacute inflammation. If untreated, leads to permanent deformities.
- **Type 1 (Reversal Reaction)**: 
- **Delayed Hypersensitivity**: Delayed hypersensitivity.
- **Occurs In Borderline**: Occurs in borderline cases (BT, BB, BL) due to shift in CMI.
- **Existing Lesions Become**: Existing lesions become reddish, swollen, warm, painful, tender. Nerves enlarged and painful (neuritis).
- **Treatment**: Prednisolone (corticosteroids).
- **Lepra Reaction Category**: Type 2 (Erythema Nodosum Leprosum - ENL):
- **Antigenantibody Arthustype Reaction**: Antigen-antibody (Arthus-type) reaction.
- **Occurs In Mb**: Occurs in MB cases only (BL and LL).
- **Red Painful Tender**: Red, painful, tender subcutaneous nodules appearing in crops. Evanescent (subside in a few days).
- **Systemic symptoms**: Fever, joint pain, iridocyclitis, orchitis, proteinuria, lymphadenitis.
- **Treatment**: Clofazimine (less potent but effective), analgesics, Prednisolone (for severe cases).

DISABILITY IN LEPROSY

- **Primary**: Direct result of nerve damage (loss of sensation, paralysis, dryness).
- **Secondary**: Result of neglected primary disability (ulcers, contractures).
- **Disability Grading (WHO)**: 
- **Hands and Feet**: 
- **Grade 0**: Sensation present, muscle power normal.
- **Grade 1**: Sensation absent, muscle power normal.
- **Grade 2**: Sensation absent, muscle power weak/paralyzed. Visible deformity (ulcer, contracture, claw hand, foot drop).
- **Eyes**: 
- **Grade 0**: Vision normal, no lid gap.
- **Grade 1**: N/A for eyes in this scale structure, or grouped with 0.
- **Grade 2**: Cannot count fingers at 6 metres (vision loss), gap present (lagophthalmos), red eye, corneal ulcer/opacity.

PREVENTION AND CONTROL STRATEGIES

- **Case finding**: Contact survey, Group surveys (school children, slums), Mass surveys (in hyperendemic areas, >1/1000 prevalence).
- **Chemoprophylaxis**: Single Dose Rifampicin (SDR) given as Post-Exposure Prophylaxis (PEP) to contacts.
- **Immunoprophylaxis**: BCG vaccine provides protective efficacy ranging from 28% to 60%.
- **Rehabilitation**: Physical and mental restoration to normal activity. Prevention of dehabilitation.
- **Global Leprosy Strategy**: Global Leprosy Strategy 2021-2030 ("Towards Zero Leprosy"):
- **Targets for 2030**: 120 countries with zero new autochthonous cases; 70% reduction in annual new cases; 90% reduction in rate per million of new cases with Grade-2 disability.
- **Key Indicators**: Annual New Case Detection Rate (ANCDR), Treatment Completion Rate (TCR >90%), Prevalence Rate (PR <1 per 10,000), Proportion of Grade II disabilities among new cases (<2%).

SPARSH LEPROSY AWARENESS CAMPAIGN

- **SPARSH Campaign Landmark**: SPARSH is a national IEC/BCC campaign under the leprosy programme to reduce stigma, promote early voluntary reporting of skin patches and nerve symptoms, and support discrimination-free services.
- **Emphasises That Leprosy**: Emphasises that leprosy is curable with free multidrug therapy (MDT).
- **SPARSH Campaign Landmark**: Encourages self-reporting and awareness of contact examination.
- **Addresses Stigma In**: Addresses stigma in school, workplace, and family settings.
- **Aligns With Goals**: Aligns with goals of zero discrimination and reduction of Grade-2 disability through earlier detection.
- **Uses Mass Media**: Uses mass media, local campaigns, and health-worker outreach (ASHA/ANM).
- **Complements Active Case**: Complements active case finding and single-dose rifampicin post-exposure prophylaxis (SDR-PEP) for contacts where implemented.

LEPROSY VACCINATION AND IMMUNOPROPHYLAXIS

- **Leprosy Immunoprophylaxis**: No universally deployed leprosy-specific vaccine equivalent to UIP antigens; **BCG** provides partial protection (efficacy varies widely across trials) and represents the principal operational immunoprophylactic agent evaluated in endemic settings.
- **Candidate vaccines**: Formulations such as Mycobacterium indicus pranii (MIP, formerly Mw) remain under operational research evaluation as adjunct immunotherapeutic or immunoprophylactic agents; they are not scheduled as routine UIP antigens.
- **Chemoprophylaxis With Singledose**: Chemoprophylaxis with single-dose rifampicin for contacts is the major current prevention adjunct alongside early MDT of cases.

PREVENTION OF DISABILITY AMONG PEOPLE AFFECTED BY LEPROSY

1. Early detection and complete MDT to halt nerve damage progression.
2. Prompt recognition and treatment of Type 1 and Type 2 reactions and neuritis (steroids as indicated).
3. Protective footwear, eye care (lagophthalmos), and self-care for anaesthetic hands/feet.
4. Prevention of secondary disabilities: ulcer care, physiotherapy, reconstructive surgery where needed.
5. Rehabilitation and anti-stigma measures (SPARSH, community inclusion).
6. WHO disability grading (0 to 2 for hands/feet/eyes) for monitoring Grade-2 disability among new cases.

> **EXAM TIP:** Cardinal signs → PB/MB → MDT table → reactions → disability grades 0 to 2 → prevention of disability list → SPARSH one-liners.

subsections.title: Surface Infections - Part B (STDs, HIV/AIDS) & 5.6 Emerging/Re-emerging Infections & 5.7 Hospital Acquired Infections

SEXUALLY TRANSMITTED DISEASES (STDS)

OVERVIEW OF THE DISEASE
- **A group:** A group of communicable diseases that are transmitted predominantly by sexual contact.
- **Caused by:** Caused by a wide range of bacterial, viral, protozoal, and fungal agents, as well as ectoparasites.
- **Have undergone:** Have undergone a dramatic transformation; the change in name from venereal diseases (VD) to sexually transmitted diseases (STD) indicates this transformation.
- **The list:** The list of pathogens has expanded from the 5 "classical" venereal diseases (syphilis, gonorrhoea, chancroid, lymphogranuloma venereum, and donovanosis) to include more than 20 agents.
- **Attention is:** Attention is now given to clinical syndromes associated with STDs (second generation STDs).

PROBLEM STATEMENT
- **Stds have:** STDs have a profound impact on sexual and reproductive health worldwide and rank among the top 5 disease categories for which adults seek health care.
- **More than:** More than 1 million STIs are acquired every day in the age group 15-49 years worldwide, majority of which are asymptomatic.
- **Each year, there are an estimated 374 million new infections with 1 of 4 STIs. During 2022:** chlamydia (129 million), gonorrhoea (82 million), syphilis (8 million), and trichomoniasis (156 million).
- **More than:** More than 500 million people are living with genital HSV (herpes) infections.
- **More than:** More than 300 million women have an HPV (Human Papilloma Virus) infection.
- **An estimated:** An estimated 254 million people are living with chronic hepatitis B globally.
- **Consequences:** STIs like herpes and syphilis can increase the risk of HIV acquisition three-fold or more. Mother-to-child transmission can result in stillbirth, neonatal death, low-birth-weight, prematurity, sepsis, pneumonia, neonatal conjunctivitis, and congenital deformities. HPV infection causes about 528,000 cases of cervical cancer and 311,000 cervical cancer deaths each year. STIs such as gonorrhoea and Chlamydia are major causes of pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) and infertility in women.
- **In India:** STDs are becoming a major public health problem. During 2022, about 38,587 cases of syphilis (14,747 males, 23,840 females) and 49 deaths were reported. Gonorrhoea is notoriously lacking in reporting but widely prevalent (30,250 cases reported, 9,989 males and 20,261 females, 10 deaths). 
- **Chancroid is:** Chancroid is fairly widely prevalent in India.
- **Lymphogranuloma venereum:** Lymphogranuloma venereum (LGV) is more prevalent in the southern states (Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh, Maharashtra, Karnataka) than in northern states.
- **Donovanosis (granuloma:** Donovanosis (granuloma inguinale) is endemic in Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh, Orissa, Karnataka, and Maharashtra, with greater prevalence along coastal areas.

EPIDEMIOLOGICAL DETERMINANTS

AGENT FACTORS
- **Bacterial agents:** Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Chlamydia trachomatis, Treponema pallidum, Haemophilus ducreyi, Mycoplasma hominis, Ureaplasma urealyticum, Calymmatobacterium granulomatis, Shigella spp., Campylobacter spp., Group B streptococcus, Bacterial vaginosis-associated organisms.
- **Viral agents:** Human (alpha) herpesvirus 1 or 2 (herpes simplex virus), Human (beta) herpesvirus 5 (cytomegalovirus), Hepatitis virus B, Human papilloma viruses, Molluscum contagiosum virus, Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV).
- **Protozoal agents:** Entamoeba histolytica, Giardia lamblia, Trichomonas vaginalis.
- **Fungal agents:** Candida albicans.
- **Ectoparasites:** Phthirus pubis (Pediculosis), Sarcoptes scabiei.

HOST FACTORS
- **Age:** Highest rates of incidence are observed in 20-24 year-olds, followed by 25-29 and 15-19 years age groups. 
- **Sex:** Overall morbidity rate is higher for men than for women, but morbidity caused by infection is generally much more severe in women (e.g., PID).
- **Marital status:** Frequency of STD infection is higher among single, divorced, and separated persons than among married couples.
- **Socio-economic status:** Individuals from the lowest socio-economic groups have the highest morbidity rate.

DEMOGRAPHIC FACTORS
- **Population explosion:** Population explosion, marked increase in the number of young people, and rural-to-urban migration.

SOCIAL AND BEHAVIOURAL FACTORS
- **Prostitution:** A major factor. The professional prostitute has largely been replaced by the "good-time girl" in developed countries. The male component (prostituant) is equally important.
- **Broken homes:** Promiscuous women are usually drawn from homes broken either due to death of one/both parents or separation.
- **Sexual disharmony:** Married people with strained relations, divorced, and separated persons.
- **Easy money:** Fostered by lack of female employment.
- **Emotional immaturity:** Often stressed as a social factor.
- **Urbanization and industrialization:** Long working hours, isolation from family, and mobility foster casual sexual relationships.
- **Social disruption:** Caused by disasters, wars, and civil unrest.
- **International travel:** Import/export of infection (e.g., resistant N. gonorrhoeae and HIV).
- **Changing behavioural patterns:** Values traditionally set on chastity are in conflict with ideas of independence and freedom from supervision.
- **Social stigma:** Accounts for non-detection, not disclosing contacts, dropping out of treatment, and going to quacks.
- **Alcoholism:** Indirect effect, may encourage prostitution or boost alcohol sales.

CLINICAL SPECTRUM
- **Gonococcal infection:** Inflammation of the genital tract involving the urethra in men and women, cervix and rectum in women, and rectum in men who have sex with men. Other sites: throat (pharyngitis) and eyes. Complications: PID, ectopic pregnancy, infertility, chronic pelvic pain, epididymitis, infant eye infection (blindness). Antibiotics: Ciprofloxacin, ceftriaxone, cefixime, spectinomycin.
- **Syphilis:** Ulceration of the uro-genital tract, mouth, or rectum. Later stages range from skin eruptions to cardiovascular and nervous system complications. Important cause of stillbirth. Antibiotics: Penicillin, doxycycline, erythromycin.
- **Chlamydial infection:** High percentage of women and men are asymptomatic. Complications similar to gonococcal infection. Antibiotics: Doxycycline, azithromycin, erythromycin, tetracycline, ofloxacin.
- **Trichomoniasis:** Vaginitis and vaginal discharge. Treatment: Metronidazole or tinidazole.
- **Chancroid:** Small papule develops at inoculation site (2-3 days), erodes into a deep, extremely painful ulcer. Painful swelling of inguinal lymph nodes (bubo). Antibiotics: Ciprofloxacin, erythromycin, ceftriaxone, azithromycin.
- **Lymphogranuloma venereum (LGV):** Swelling of lymph nodes in the groin. Small, painless ulcer (3-30 days) that may pass unrecognized. Extensive lymphatic damage causes elephantiasis of genitalia. Antibiotics: Doxycycline, erythromycin, tetracycline.
- **Donovanosis:** Granuloma inguinale. Small papule (3-40 days incubation) ruptures to form a granulomatous lesion that is characteristically pain-free and bleeds readily. Antibiotics: Azithromycin, doxycycline, erythromycin, tetracycline, TMP-SMX.
- **Genital herpes:** HSV-2. Papular lesions progressing to multiple blisters and ulcers. Lifelong infection with recurrences. Antivirals: Acyclovir, valacyclovir, famciclovir.
- **Human papilloma virus:** Ano-genital warts (soft flesh-coloured cauliflowers to flat warts). Cause of cervical cancer. Routine Papanicolaou staining recommended.

[SN]Syndromic approach to management of Sexually Transmitted Infections (STI)[/SN]

[SN]Advantages and disadvantages of syndromic approach in management of sexually transmitted diseases[/SN]

SYNDROMIC MANAGEMENT OF STDS
- **A scientifically:** A scientifically derived approach using flowcharts based on signs and symptoms, without waiting for lab tests.
- **Urethral discharge in males (Gonorrhoea + Chlamydia):** 
- **Tab cefixime:** Tab Cefixime 400 mg orally, single dose PLUS Tab Azithromycin 1 gram orally, single dose.
  - **If discharge persists after 7 days:** Tab Secnidazole 2 gm orally, single dose (to treat T. vaginalis).
- **Treat all:** Treat all recent partners. Advise sexual abstinence, provide condoms.
  - **Pregnant partner:** Cefixime 400 mg or Ceftriaxone 125 mg IM PLUS Erythromycin 500 mg QID for 7 days (or Amoxicillin 500 mg TDS for 7 days). Quinolones and doxycycline are contraindicated.
- **Vaginal discharge (Vaginitis:** T. vaginalis, Candida, Bacterial vaginosis / Cervicitis: N. gonorrhoeae, C. trachomatis):
  - **Vaginitis (Trichomonas - greenish frothy, Candida - curdy white, BV - adherent):** Tab Secnidazole 2 gm single dose OR Tinidazole 500 mg twice daily for 5 days PLUS Fluconazole 150 mg single dose OR local Clotrimazole 500 mg vaginal pessaries once.
  - **Cervicitis (Cervical erosion/ulcer):** Tab Cefixime 400 mg single dose PLUS Azithromycin 1 gram single dose.
  - **Pregnant women:** 1st trimester - Clotrimazole vaginal pessary only (Oral Fluconazole contraindicated). 2nd/3rd trimester - Oral Metronidazole/Secnidazole can be given.
- **Lower abdominal pain in females (PID:** N. gonorrhoeae, C. trachomatis, Anaerobes):
- **Tab cefixime:** Tab Cefixime 400 mg twice daily for 7 days PLUS Tab Metronidazole 400 mg twice daily for 14 days PLUS Doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 14 days.
  - **Pregnant women:** Refer to district hospital for hospitalization and parenteral regimen. Doxycycline is contraindicated.
- **Genital ulcers (Syphilis, Chancroid, Granuloma inguinale, LGV, Herpes):**
  - **Treat for syphilis and chancroid:** Inj Benzathine penicillin 2.4 million IU IM after test dose PLUS Azithromycin 1g orally single dose OR Ciprofloxacin 500 mg twice a day for 3 days.
  - **If vesicles present:** Treat for herpes with Tab Acyclovir 400 mg orally, 3 times a day for 7 days.
  - **Pregnant women:** Benzathine penicillin. If allergic to penicillin, treat with Erythromycin 500 mg QID for 15 days. Quinolones and doxycycline are contraindicated.
- **Scrotal swelling (Gonococcal and chlamydial):**
- **Tab cefixime:** Tab Cefixime 400 mg twice daily for 7 days PLUS Cap Doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 14 days. Supportive therapy (bed rest, scrotal elevation, analgesics).
- **Inguinal bubo (LGV and Chancroid):**
- **Cap doxycycline:** Cap Doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 21 days PLUS Tab Azithromycin 1 gram single dose (or Ciprofloxacin 500 mg BID for 3 days). A bubo should never be incised and drained; aspirate if fluctuant.
  - **Pregnant women:** Erythromycin base 500 mg 4 times daily for 21 days.


ADVANTAGES AND DISADVANTAGES OF THE SYNDROMIC APPROACH
Advantages:
- **Enables treatment:** Enables treatment at first visit without waiting for laboratory results ;  critical at primary care.
- **High sensitivity:** High sensitivity for public-health purposes when flowcharts are followed; reduces loss to follow-up.
- **Feasible where:** Feasible where laboratory capacity is limited; standardises care by less specialised staff.
- **Allows simultaneous:** Allows simultaneous treatment of co-pathogens (for example gonorrhoea + chlamydia in urethral discharge).
- **Facilitates partner:** Facilitates partner management and condom counselling in the same encounter.

Disadvantages:
- **Over-treatment possible:** Over-treatment possible (unnecessary antibiotics) with antimicrobial resistance risk.
- **Lower specificity:** Lower specificity than laboratory-confirmed diagnosis for some syndromes.
- **Genital ulcer:** Genital ulcer algorithms may miss or over-treat mixed aetiologies; herpes needs clinical recognition of vesicles.
- **Vaginal discharge:** Vaginal discharge flowchart has limited ability to distinguish cervicitis from vaginitis without speculum/risk assessment skill.
- **Still requires:** Still requires training, drugs in stock, and referral pathways for treatment failure and upper-tract disease.

> **EXAM TIP:** Define syndromic management → list major syndromes with first-line drugs → advantages vs disadvantages table → partner treatment + condoms.

CONTROL OF STDS
- **1. Initial planning:** Problem definition, establishing priorities, setting objectives, considering strategies.
- **2. Intervention strategies:**
  - **Case detection:** Screening (high priority for pregnant women, blood donors, sex workers), Contact tracing, Cluster testing (testing people in the same socio-sexual environment).
  - **Case holding and treatment:** Ensure complete and adequate treatment.
  - **Epidemiological treatment:** Administration of full therapeutic dose to persons recently exposed to STD while awaiting lab results.
  - **Personal prophylaxis:** Mechanical barriers (condoms, diaphragms), Vaccines (Hep B).
  - **Health education:** Help individuals alter their behaviour.
- **3. Support components:**
  - **STD clinics:** Consultation, investigation, treatment, contact tracing.
- **Laboratory services.:** Laboratory services.
  - **Primary health care:** Inclusion of PHC workers in the STD "health team".
  - **Information system:** Clinical notification, lab notification, sentinel/adhoc surveillance.
  - **Legislation:** To encourage early treatment and control commercial exploitation (e.g., The Immoral Traffic Prevention Act, 1986).
  - **Social welfare measures:** Rehabilitation of prostitutes, marriage counseling, prohibiting sexually stimulating literature.
- **4. Monitoring and evaluation:** Determine appropriateness and effectiveness of strategies.

[LAQ]Epidemiology, prevention and control of HIV/AIDS[/LAQ]

[LAQ]Epidemiological trends of HIV/AIDS in India[/LAQ]

[SN]National AIDS Control Programme (NACP)[/SN]

[SN]Voluntary Counselling and Testing Centre (VCTC) / Integrated Counselling and Testing Centre (ICTC)[/SN]

[SN]Sentinel surveillance of HIV/AIDS in India[/SN]

[SN]Highly Active Antiretroviral Therapy (HAART)[/SN]

[LAQ]Role of primary health centre in National AIDS Control Programme as per IPHS[/LAQ]

[LAQ]Surveillance for HIV/AIDS ;  strengths and weaknesses[/LAQ]

ACQUIRED IMMUNO DEFICIENCY SYNDROME (AIDS)

OVERVIEW OF THE DISEASE
- **Sometimes called:** Sometimes called "slim disease" in Africa.
- **Caused by:** Caused by the human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), a retrovirus.
- **Breaks down:** Breaks down the body's immune system, leaving the victim vulnerable to life-threatening opportunistic infections, neurological disorders, and unusual malignancies.
- **Aids refers:** AIDS refers only to the last stage of the HIV infection.

PROBLEM STATEMENT
- **Worldwide:** 39.9 million people living with HIV in 2023. 1.3 million new infections (reduced by 60% since 1995 peak). 630,000 AIDS-related deaths (reduced by 69% since 2004 peak).
- **Median hiv:** Median HIV prevalence among adults (15-49) is 0.8% globally.
- **Globally, 44%:** Globally, 44% of new infections are among women and girls.
- **Key populations are highly affected:** MSM (7.7x higher risk), sex workers (3x), injecting drug users (5x), transgender people (9.2x), prisoners (1.3x).
- **India:** Estimated adult HIV prevalence is about **0.20%** (India HIV Estimates 2023 family). Male and female prevalence are of similar order (approximately 0.22% male and 0.19% female in commonly cited disaggregation).
- **Number of PLHIV in India:** 25.44 lakh (2.54 million).
- **New HIV infections in India:** 68,450 in 2023. AIDS-related deaths: 35,870 in 2023.
- **Final Mother-to-Child Transmission (MTCT) rate:** 11.75%.
- **Epidemic in:** Epidemic in India is concentrated. High prevalence states include Mizoram, Nagaland, and Southern states.
- **India high-risk groups HIV prevalence:** IDU (9.9%), Transgender (8.8%), MSM (4.3%), Truckers (2.5%), FSW (2.2%), Migrants (0.99%), ANC attendees (0.29%).

EPIDEMIOLOGICAL DETERMINANTS

AGENT FACTORS
- **Agent:** First called lymphadenopathy associated virus (LAV). Two types: HIV-1 and HIV-2. HIV-1 is the most common.
- **Targets t4:** Targets T4 helper lymphocytes. Virus mutates rapidly.
- **Readily inactivated by heat, ether, acetone, 20% ethanol, and beta-propiolactone (1:**400 dilution). Relatively resistant to ionizing radiation and UV light.
- **Reservoir of infection:** Cases and carriers. Lifelong infection.
- **Source of infection:** Greatest concentration in blood, semen, and CSF. Lower concentrations in tears, saliva, breast milk, urine, cervical and vaginal secretions.

HOST FACTORS
- **Age:** Most cases in sexually active persons aged 20-49 years.
- **Sex:** High proportion of homosexual/bisexual men globally, but heterosexual transmission dominates in developing regions.
- **High-risk groups:** Male homosexuals/bisexuals, intravenous drug abusers, transfusion recipients, haemophiliacs, clients of STDs.

MODE OF TRANSMISSION (INDIA)
- **Heterosexual:** 88.2%
- **Parent to child (vertical):** 5%
- **Injectable drug users:** 1.7%
- **Homosexual:** 1.5%
- **Blood and blood products:** 1%
- **(not transmitted:** (Not transmitted by mosquitoes, casual contact, sharing food/water).

INCUBATION PERIOD
- **From a:** From a few months to 10 years or more from infection to development of AIDS.

CLINICAL MANIFESTATIONS
- **1. Initial infection:** 70% experience mild illness (fever, sore throat, rash). Window period: 2 to 12 weeks before antibodies are produced. Highly infectious but tests negative on standard antibody tests.
- **2. Asymptomatic carrier state:** Antibodies present but no overt signs of disease (except persistent generalized lymphadenopathy).
- **3. AIDS-related complex (ARC):** Illness without opportunistic infections. Unexplained diarrhoea lasting >1 month, loss of >10% body weight, generalized lymphadenopathy/enlarged spleen, decreased T-helper lymphocytes.
- **4. AIDS:** End stage. Appearance of opportunistic infections and cancers.

RELATIONSHIP OF CD4 COUNT TO OPPORTUNISTIC INFECTIONS
- **Normal CD4 count:** 500-1200 cells/mm3.
- **CD4 count 200-500:** Tuberculosis, Herpes simplex/zoster, Vaginal candidiasis, Hairy leukoplakia, Kaposi's sarcoma.
- **CD4 count 50-200:** Pneumocystis pneumonia, Toxoplasmosis, Cryptococcosis, Coccidioidomycosis, Cryptosporidiosis.
- **CD4 count Upto 50:** Histoplasmosis, CMV retinitis, CNS lymphoma.

WHO CLINICAL STAGING OF HIV DISEASE
- **Stage 1:** Asymptomatic, Persistent generalized lymphadenopathy.
- **Stage 2:** Moderate unexplained weight loss (<10%), recurrent respiratory tract infections, herpes zoster, angular cheilitis, recurrent oral ulcerations, papular pruritic eruptions, seborrhoeic dermatitis, fungal nail infection.
- **Stage 3:** Unexplained severe weight loss (>10%), unexplained chronic diarrhoea (>1 month), unexplained persistent fever (>1 month), unexplained anaemia (<8 g/dl)/neutropenia/thrombocytopenia, persistent oral candidiasis, oral hairy leukoplakia, pulmonary tuberculosis, severe bacterial infections.
- **Stage 4:** HIV wasting syndrome, Pneumocystis pneumonia, recurrent severe bacterial pneumonia, chronic herpes simplex, oesophageal candidiasis, extrapulmonary tuberculosis, Kaposi sarcoma, CMV disease (retinitis), CNS toxoplasmosis, HIV encephalopathy, disseminated mycosis.

CLINICAL DIAGNOSIS (SURVEILLANCE CASE DEFINITION)
- **Major signs:** Weight loss >10% body weight, chronic diarrhoea for >1 month, prolonged fever for >1 month.
- **Minor signs:** Cough for >1 month, generalized pruritic dermatitis, oropharyngeal candidiasis, history of herpes zoster, progressive/disseminated herpes, generalized lymphadenopathy.
- **Person has:** Person has AIDS if at least 2 major signs and 1 minor sign are present, in the absence of other known causes of immunosuppression (or presence of Kaposi sarcoma / cryptococcal meningitis alone is sufficient).

LABORATORY DIAGNOSIS
- **Screening tests:** ELISA (sensitivity test), Rapid diagnostic tests (point-of-care).
- **Confirmatory tests:** Western Blot (detects specific antibodies to viral core p24 and envelope gp41).
- **Other markers:** Absolute CD4 lymphocyte count, CD4 lymphocyte percentage, HIV viral load tests, p24 antigen, beta-2 microglobulin.

PREVENTION
- **Education:** Avoiding indiscriminate sex, not sharing razors/toothbrushes, avoiding pregnancy if infected, mass media campaigns.
- **Combination HIV prevention:** 
- **Biomedical/behavioral/structural interventions.:** Biomedical/behavioral/structural interventions.
- **Arv drugs:** ARV drugs for pre-exposure (PrEP) and post-exposure (PEP).
- **Condoms.:** Condoms.
- **Needle and:** Needle and syringe programmes.
- **Opioid substitution:** Opioid substitution therapy (methadone/buprenorphine).
- **Voluntary medical:** Voluntary medical male circumcision (VMMC) - reduces risk by approx 60%.
- **Prevention of blood-borne transmission:** Screening blood for HIV 1 & 2, strict sterilization practices.

TREATMENT (ANTIRETROVIRAL THERAPY - ART)
- **Art consists:** ART consists of combining at least three ARV drugs from different classes.
- **NRTIs:** Abacavir, Didanosine, Emtricitabine, Lamivudine (3TC), Stavudine, Zidovudine (AZT).
- **NtRTIs:** Tenofovir (TDF).
- **NNRTIs:** Efavirenz, Etravirine, Nevirapine.
- **Protease Inhibitors (PIs):** Atazanavir/r, Darunavir/r, Indinavir/r, Lopinavir/r.
- **Integrase Inhibitors (INSTIs):** Raltegravir, Dolutegravir (DTG).
- **Fusion Inhibitors:** Enfuvirtide.
- **NACO Guidelines (Treat All):** ART should be initiated in all adults living with HIV regardless of WHO clinical stage or CD4 count. Priority for stage 3 or 4 and CD4 <350.
- **First-line regimen (Adults >10 yrs, >30kg):** Tenofovir (300 mg) + Lamivudine (300 mg) + Dolutegravir (50 mg) [TLD regimen] as fixed-dose combination (FDC) once daily.
- **Paediatric regimens:** Abacavir + Lamivudine + Lopinavir/ritonavir (if <6 yrs and <20kg) or Dolutegravir (if >6 yrs and 20-30kg).

POST-EXPOSURE PROPHYLAXIS (PEP)
- **Initiated as:** Initiated as soon as possible (preferably within hours) for occupational exposure.
- **Adults & adolescents:** TDF + 3TC (or FTC) + third drug (like Dolutegravir or Raltegravir) for 28 days.
- **<10 years:** AZT + 3TC + third drug.

CO-TRIMOXAZOLE PROPHYLAXIS
- **Fixed dose:** Fixed dose combination (Sulphamethoxazole + Trimethoprim).
- **Recommended for:** Recommended for persons with WHO stage 3 or 4 and/or CD4 count <350 to prevent bacterial, fungal, and protozoan infections.

GLOBAL HEALTH SECTOR STRATEGY ON HIV (95-95-95 TARGETS)
- **UNAIDS Fast-Track / cascade targets for HIV:** **95%** of people living with HIV know their status; **95%** of those diagnosed receive sustained antiretroviral therapy; **95%** of those on treatment achieve viral suppression.
- **These are:** These are HIV programme targets (not the TB 90-90-90 case-finding framing).


NATIONAL AIDS CONTROL PROGRAMME (NACP)

DEFINITION AND EVOLUTION
- **Nacp is:** NACP is India’s national programme (NACO/SACS) for prevention, testing, treatment, and care of HIV/AIDS. Phases expanded from awareness and blood safety to combination prevention, Test and Treat, and elimination of vertical transmission goals.

KEY COMPONENTS
1. Targeted interventions for key populations (FSW, MSM, IDU/PWID, transgender persons, migrants, truckers).
2. ICTC and facility-based / community testing with linkage to care.
3. Prevention of parent-to-child transmission (PPTCT / EMTCT pathway).
4. ART centres and link ART; Treat All with optimized regimens (for example TLD first-line for eligible adults).
5. STI synergies, condom programming, needle-syringe programmes and opioid substitution for PWID.
6. Blood safety and standard precautions.
7. Strategic information: HSS, programme monitoring, PLHIV estimates.

ICTC / VCTC
- **VCTC (older term):** voluntary counselling and testing with informed consent, confidentiality, and pre-/post-test counselling.
- **ICTC:** integrated counselling and testing centres within health facilities ;  HIV testing services with counselling, linkage to ART/PPTCT, and often syphilis testing when co-located.
- **Functions:** risk assessment, consent, testing per national algorithm, disclosure support, partner services, condom promotion, referral.

SENTINEL SURVEILLANCE (HSS) OF HIV IN INDIA
- **Periodic surveys:** Periodic surveys at selected sentinel sites among defined groups (for example ANC attendees as a general-population proxy trend; high-risk groups at TI sites) to track prevalence trends over rounds.
- **Strengths:** standardized methodology across rounds; useful for trends and targeting; relatively feasible at scale.
- **Weaknesses:** clinic-based sampling bias; limited representativeness if sites are fixed; key populations are hard to sample representatively; not a substitute for case-based reporting and size estimates; ANC prevalence is only a proxy for population prevalence.
- **Classic MCQ teaching:** pregnant women included; high-risk groups monitored; general population is not the direct sampling frame of HSS high-risk rounds; periodicity is by surveillance rounds (not “yearly checkup of the general population”).

ROLE OF THE PRIMARY HEALTH CENTRE IN NACP (IPHS-ALIGNED)
1. IEC on safer sex, stigma reduction, and condom availability.
2. Offer of HIV testing as per guidelines and linkage to ICTC/ART.
3. ANC HIV testing and PPTCT linkage; safe delivery referral.
4. Syndromic STI management and condom promotion.
5. Community support for PLHIV (adherence, TB screening, cotrimoxazole where indicated).
6. Universal precautions, safe injections, biomedical waste, and staff awareness of PEP.
7. Recording, reporting, and coordination with ASHA and TI NGOs.

> **EXAM TIP:** Burden (0.20% adult prevalence, concentrated epidemic) → transmission modes India → NACP pillars → ICTC functions → HSS strengths/weaknesses table → PHC bullet list.


HUMAN PAPILLOMA VIRUS (HPV) VACCINES

DEFINITION AND RATIONALE
- **Persistent infection:** Persistent infection with high-risk HPV types (notably 16 and 18) causes most cervical cancers and a share of other anogenital and oropharyngeal cancers. [SN]Human Papilloma Virus Vaccines[/SN]

HPV vaccines are prophylactic subunit vaccines based on L1 virus-like particles (VLPs).

HIGH-YIELD POINTS
1. Types: bivalent (16/18), quadrivalent (6/11/16/18 ;  also protects against genital warts), nonavalent (adds further oncogenic types).
2. Target: primarily adolescents before sexual debut as per national operational age bands; catch-up cohorts may be included in campaigns.
3. Schedule: multi-dose intramuscular schedules (two-dose for younger adolescents meeting interval rules, or three-dose historically); follow the current national immunization/operational schedule for public-programme dosing.
4. High efficacy against vaccine-type persistent infection and precancerous lesions in HPV-naïve persons.
5. Not therapeutic ;  does not clear established infection; cervical screening remains essential.
6. Favourable safety profile; AEFI surveillance applies as for other vaccines.
7. India public-health angle: cervical cancer control pairs vaccination with screen-and-treat strategies under NCD/cervical cancer efforts.
8. Counselling: vaccination does not replace safer sex measures or later screening.

> **EXAM TIP:** HPV16/18 → cervical cancer → vaccine types table → prophylactic not therapeutic → screening still needed.


[SN]Endemic Treponematosis[/SN]

ENDEMIC TREPONEMATOSES (SHORT NOTE)
- **Non-venereal treponemal diseases of childhood in endemic foci:** yaws (*T. pallidum* subsp. *pertenue*), bejel/endemic syphilis, and pinta (*T. carateum*).
- **Transmission:** direct skin contact (not primarily sexual), favoured by overcrowding and poor hygiene.
- **Clinical:** early skin lesions; late destructive lesions of skin, bone, or cartilage depending on the disease.
- **Control:** mass or targeted treatment with benzathine penicillin (or azithromycin in yaws eradication strategies where used), active case finding, and improvement of hygiene.
- **Differ from:** Differ from venereal syphilis by epidemiology (childhood, non-sexual) though serology is treponemal-cross reactive.

> **EXAM TIP:** Name three endemic treponematoses → non-venereal childhood transmission → penicillin/azithromycin control → contrast with venereal syphilis.

[SN]Emerging zoonotic diseases[/SN]

[SN]Role of non-health sectors in the pandemic[/SN]

[LAQ]Lessons from COVID-19 for control of emerging infectious disease[/LAQ]

EMERGING AND RE-EMERGING INFECTIONS

OVERVIEW AND FACTORS RESPONSIBLE
- **Emerging diseases:** Infectious diseases whose incidence in humans has increased during the last 2 decades or threaten to increase in the near future (e.g., SARS, COVID-19, Nipah, Ebola).
- **Re-emerging diseases:** Diseases previously easily controlled but now developing antimicrobial resistance or appearing in epidemic form (e.g., MDR-TB, malaria, dengue, diphtheria in Russia).
- **Factors responsible:** Unplanned urbanization, overcrowding, poor sanitation, inadequate public health structure, increased exposure to disease vectors/reservoirs, microbial genetic mutation, antimicrobial resistance, international travel.


ROLE OF NON-HEALTH SECTORS IN A PANDEMIC
1. Home/home affairs and police: movement restrictions, public-order support for health measures without excessive coercion framing in exams ;  coordination role.
2. Local government and urban development: quarantine facilities, sanitation, burial/cremation logistics, migrant support.
3. Education: school closure/reopening protocols, mid-day meal adaptations, risk communication to families.
4. Transport and civil aviation: screening, travel advisories, evacuation logistics.
5. Industry/labour and finance: livelihood support, workplace SOPs, supply of essentials and oxygen/industry conversion.
6. Information/broadcasting and technology: rumour management, telemedicine platforms, digital vaccination certificates.
7. Animal husbandry/environment (for zoonoses): interface surveillance, market regulation, One Health coordination.
- **Exam line:** pandemics are whole-of-government and whole-of-society responses; health sector leads clinical and epi core but cannot succeed alone.

LESSONS FROM COVID-19 (PUBLIC HEALTH)
- **Early detection:** Early detection and genomic surveillance of variants; scalable testing algorithms.
- **Risk-based non-pharmaceutical:** Risk-based non-pharmaceutical interventions with attention to equity and livelihoods.
- **Oxygen, icu:** Oxygen, ICU, and supply-chain surge capacity as core preparedness ;  not optional.
- **Vaccination platforms:** Vaccination platforms at unprecedented scale; AEFI and cold-chain lessons transferable to UIP surge.
- **Infodemic management:** Infodemic management and community trust as determinants of compliance.
- **One health:** One Health and border health strengthening for the next zoonotic spillover.
- **Data systems:** Data systems (line lists, bed trackers) need interoperability before the crisis.

> **EXAM TIP:** Agent → transmission → severity strata → NPIs merits/demerits → vaccine strategy → five system lessons. For non-health sectors use a numbered multi-sector list.

EBOLA VIRUS DISEASE
- **Appeared for:** Appeared for the first time in Zaire & Sudan in 1976.
- **Family:** Filoviridae.
- **5 species:** Zaire ebolavirus, Reston ebolavirus, Sudan ebolavirus, Tai ebolavirus, Bundibugyo ebolavirus.
- **Incubation period:** 2 to 21 days.
- **Transmission:** Direct contact with blood, organs, body secretions of infected animals (chimpanzees, gorillas, fruit bats) or infected symptomatic persons/contaminated needles.
- **Clinical features:** Sudden onset of fever, intense weakness, muscle pain, headache, sore throat, vomiting, diarrhoea, rash, impaired kidney & liver function, internal and external bleeding.
- **CFR:** Up to 70%.
- **Treatment:** Supportive care is the mainstay. Specific therapeutics and vaccines (for example rVSV-ZEBOV for Zaire ebolavirus in outbreak response settings) have been developed since the major West African epidemic; availability depends on outbreak context and stockpiles.

HANTA PULMONARY SYNDROME
- **First recognized:** First recognized in 1993.
- **Carried by:** Carried by rodents, particularly deer mice.
- **Characterized by:** Characterized by respiratory failure and hemorrhagic fever with renal involvement. CFR >50%.

CORONAVIRUS DISEASE 2019 (COVID-19)
- **Agent:** SARS-CoV-2 (betacoronavirus, single-stranded RNA virus with a crown-like appearance under electron microscope). Identified in Wuhan, China in Dec 2019. Declared pandemic by WHO in Mar 2020.
- **Variants of concern:** Omicron (B.1.1.529), BA.1, BA.2, BA.3, BA.4, BA.5. Spreads more easily and quickly.
- **Transmission:** Direct/indirect contact with mucosal membranes, respiratory droplets, aerosols (airborne), and fomites.
- **Incubation period:** 2-14 days.
- **Clinical features:** 
  - **Common:** Fever, cough, fatigue, shortness of breath, loss of smell/taste, body aches.
  - **Progressive disease signs:** Oxygen impairment (hypoxia, cyanosis), CNS complications (altered mental status), severe dehydration.
  - **Complications:** ARDS, sepsis, septic shock, acute kidney injury, multi-organ dysfunction, acute pulmonary embolism.
- **Diagnosis:** RT-PCR is the gold standard. 
  - **CT (Cycle Threshold) score:** Number of cycles taken to detect viral load. Lower CT score = higher viral load and higher transmissibility. Range <25 = high viral load; 25-35 = moderate; >35 = negative or very low.
  - **Rapid Antigen Test (RDT):** High specificity, less sensitive.
- **Clinical Management:**
  - **Mild Disease:** SpO2 >94%. Home isolation. Hydration, antipyretics. Do NOT use Lopinavir-ritonavir, Hydroxychloroquine, Ivermectin, Molnupiravir, Favipiravir, Azithromycin, Doxycycline.
  - **Moderate Disease:** SpO2 90-93%, Respiratory rate >=24/min. Admit to ward. Oxygen support, awake proning. Anti-inflammatory: Dexamethasone 6mg/day or Methylprednisolone. Prophylactic anticoagulation (Enoxaparin). Remdesivir (within 10 days of onset for high-risk progression).
  - **Severe Disease:** SpO2 <90%, Respiratory rate >30/min. Admit to HDU/ICU. Respiratory support (NIV, HFNC, Intubation). Dexamethasone, Anticoagulation. Consider Tocilizumab if rapidly progressing and CRP/IL-6 is raised.
- **Post-COVID conditions:** Fatigue, brain fog, chest pain, palpitations, joint pain lasting weeks/months after initial infection.

BLACK FUNGUS INFECTION (MUCORMYCOSIS)
- **A rare:** A rare fungal infection caused by mucormycetes.
- **Risk factors:** Uncontrolled pre-existing diabetes, rampant overuse of steroids in COVID-19 management, prolonged ICU stay, broad-spectrum antibiotics.
- **Signs & Symptoms:** Facial pain, pain over sinuses, decreased sensation over half face, blackish discoloration of skin over nasolabial groove, nasal crusting, periorbital swelling, loosening of teeth.
- **Diagnosis:** KOH staining and microscopy, histopathology, CT scan of paranasal sinuses/lungs.
- **Treatment:** Liposomal Amphotericin B (initial dose 5 mg/kg body weight, up to 10 mg/kg if CNS involvement). Step down to oral Posaconazole or Isavuconazole. Surgery required to remove dead/infected tissues.

HOSPITAL ACQUIRED INFECTIONS (NOSOCOMIAL INFECTIONS)

OVERVIEW AND DEFINITION
- **Infections acquired:** Infections acquired during hospital care which were not present or incubating at admission.
- **Infections occurring:** Infections occurring more than 48 hours after admission are usually considered nosocomial.

SITES OF MOST COMMON NOSOCOMIAL INFECTIONS
- **1. urinary:** 1. Urinary tract (most common, often associated with catheterization)
- **2. lower:** 2. Lower respiratory tract (ventilator-associated pneumonia)
- **3. surgical:** 3. Surgical sites
- **4. skin:** 4. Skin & soft tissue
- **5. bacteraemia/septicaemia:** 5. Bacteraemia/Septicaemia (central line associated)
- **6. ent:** 6. ENT / Eye

EPIDEMIOLOGICAL DETERMINANTS
- **Sources:**
- **Patients (suffering:** Patients (suffering from infectious disease, e.g., B. coli).
- **Staff (doctors:** Staff (doctors, nurses, ward boys - S. aureus, Streptococcus, Salmonella).
- **Environment (hospital:** Environment (hospital dust, linen, bed clothes, basins, door handles, air).
- **Routes of spread:**
- **Direct contact:** Direct contact (hands of nurse or doctor to patient).
- **Droplet infection:** Droplet infection (coughing or sneezing).
- **Airborne (hospital:** Airborne (hospital dust).
- **Fomites.:** Fomites.
- **Various hospital:** Various hospital procedures (catheterization, intravenous procedures, infected cat gut, dressings).
- **Recipients:** Severely ill patients, those on corticosteroid therapy, immunocompromised, those in intensive care units, urological/geriatric wards, and special baby care units.

PREVENTIVE MEASURES
- **Isolation:** Of infectious patients.
- **Hospital staff:** Those suffering from skin diseases or sore throats should be kept away from patient care.
- **Hand washing:** Must be thorough. "Clean Care is Safer Care" guidelines. Most important step.
- **Dust control:** Wet dusting & vacuum cleaning.
- **Disinfection:** Patient's urine, faeces, sputum must be properly disinfected.
- **Control of droplet infection:** Face masks, proper bed spacing, preventing overcrowding, adequate ventilation.
- **Nursing techniques:** Barrier nursing & task nursing.
- **Precautions for clothing:** Gown (washable), Gloves (inexpensive plastic), Mask (cloth or paper).
- **For all patients (Standard Precautions):**
- **Use no-touch:** Use no-touch technique.
- **Wear gloves:** Wear gloves when in contact with blood, body fluids, mucous membranes, & contaminated items.
- **All sharps:** All sharps should be handled with extreme care.
- **Ensure patient:** Ensure patient care equipment & linen are either discarded, disinfected, or sterilized.
- **Ensure appropriate:** Ensure appropriate waste handling.

SPECIFIC PREVENTION
- **Urinary tract infections:** Aseptic catheter technique at insertion, limit duration, closed system.
- **Surgical site infections:** Local skin preparation of patients, clean operating environment, limiting preoperative hospital stay, optimal antibiotic prophylaxis.
- **Pneumonia:** Influenza vaccination for staff, aseptic intubation/suctioning, elevate head of bed.
- **Vascular device infections:** Local skin preparation, aseptic technique at insertion, limitation of dressing changes.

subsections.title: Chikungunya, Kala-azar, and Chandipura Virus Disease
subsections.content:
OVERVIEW OF THE SECTION
This section addresses three vector-borne infections of profound public health significance in India: Chikungunya, Visceral Leishmaniasis (Kala-azar), and Chandipura Virus Disease. While differing in their biological taxonomy, transmission vectors, and clinical presentations, all three diseases require coordinated surveillance, vector control, and clinical case management under the aegis of the National Center for Vector Borne Diseases Control (NCVBDC) and the National Centre for Disease Control (NCDC).

DEFINITIONS

- **Chikungunya**: An acute arboviral exanthematous disease caused by the Chikungunya virus (genus *Alphavirus*, family Togaviridae), transmitted by *Aedes* mosquitoes, classically presenting with sudden high fever and severe, often debilitating polyarthralgia.
- **Visceral Leishmaniasis (Kala-azar)**: A chronic, systemic protozoan infection caused by *Leishmania donovani*, transmitted by the phlebotomine sandfly *Phlebotomus argentipes*, characterized by irregular fever, hepatosplenomegaly, pancytopenia, progressive cachexia, and hyperpigmentation of the skin.
- **Chandipura Virus Disease**: A fulminant neurotropic viral infection caused by Chandipura vesiculovirus (family Rhabdoviridae), transmitted by phlebotomine sandflies, predominantly manifesting as rapid-onset Acute Encephalitis Syndrome (AES) with high mortality in young children.

[SN]Chikungunya[/SN]

CHIKUNGUNYA

- **Aetiological Agent**: Chikungunya virus (CHIKV), an enveloped single-stranded positive-sense RNA virus belonging to the genus *Alphavirus*, family Togaviridae.
- **Vectors**: Transmitted principally by *Aedes aegypti* (urban domestic vector) and *Aedes albopictus* (rural/peri-urban vector possessing the A226V envelope glycoprotein mutation that enhances viral dissemination). Both mosquitoes exhibit daytime biting habits with bimodal activity peaks at dawn and dusk.
- **Incubation Period**: Typically 3 to 7 days, with an operational range of 2 to 12 days.
- **Clinical Presentation**: Sudden onset of high fever, chills, cephalalgia, photophobia, and severe, symmetrical, crippling polyarthralgia predominantly involving peripheral small joints (wrists, ankles, interphalangeal joints). A maculopapular exanthem appears on the trunk and extremities within 3 to 5 days.
- **Chronic Morbidity**: Acute mortality is minimal (<0.1%), but persistent, disabling arthralgia, tenosynovitis, and joint stiffness endure for months or years in 30% to 50% of affected individuals, causing marked functional impairment.
- **Laboratory Confirmation**: Reverse Transcription-Polymerase Chain Reaction (RT-PCR) and viral isolation from serum during the initial viraemic window (days 1 to 5); IgM Enzyme-Linked Immunosorbent Assay (ELISA) demonstrates diagnostic seroconversion after day 5, persisting for up to 3 months.
- **Clinical Management**: Supportive and symptomatic care; paracetamol is the analgesic and antipyretic agent of choice. Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) must only be initiated after laboratory exclusion of dengue syndrome; aspirin is strictly contraindicated due to bleeding risk. No licensed human vaccine exists under the Universal Immunization Programme (UIP).
- **Integrated Vector Management**: Source reduction targeting peridomestic water collections, chemical larviciding with temephos (1 ppm), application of biological agents (*Gambusia affinis*, *Bacillus thuringiensis israelensis*), pyrethrum space spraying during epidemic clusters, and personal barrier protection.

CLINICAL DIFFERENTIATION: CHIKUNGUNYA VERSUS DENGUE SYNDROME

| Clinical / Epidemiological Feature | Chikungunya | Dengue Syndrome |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Aetiological Taxonomy** | *Alphavirus* (Family Togaviridae) | *Flavivirus* (Family Flaviviridae, Serotypes 1-4) |
| **Transmission Vector** | *Aedes aegypti*, *Aedes albopictus* | *Aedes aegypti*, *Aedes albopictus* |
| **Joint Involvement** | Severe, symmetrical, crippling polyarthralgia; common swelling and chronic arthropathy | Generalized myalgia, "breakbone" arthralgia; swelling and chronic arthropathy are rare |
| **Onset of Exanthem** | Early (days 1 to 4), maculopapular, centrifugal distribution | Late (days 4 to 7), maculopapular or scarlatiniform, convalescent islands of normal skin |
| **Plasma Leakage / Shock** | Extremely rare; no capillary leakage syndrome | Characteristic of severe dengue (DHF/DSS); pleural effusion, ascites, haemoconcentration |
| **Haemorrhagic Manifestations** | Mild, infrequent | Common in severe disease (petechiae, mucosal bleed, gastrointestinal haemorrhage) |
| **Thrombocytopenia** | Mild or absent | Marked and progressive (often <100,000/cu.mm in DHF) |
| **Long-Term Sequelae** | Prolonged, disabling arthralgia persisting for months to years | Asthenia and depression; prolonged arthritis absent |

> **EXAM TIP:** When differentiating Chikungunya from Dengue, emphasize that Chikungunya causes pronounced, debilitating, symmetric peripheral polyarthralgia with frequent chronic joint sequelae, whereas Dengue is distinguished by severe thrombocytopenia, plasma leakage, and potential progression to hypovolaemic shock. Always rule out Dengue before administering NSAIDs, and note that aspirin is strictly contraindicated.

[SN]Kala-azar[/SN]

[LAQ]Epidemiology, prevention and control of kala-azar in India[/LAQ]

KALA-AZAR (VISCERAL LEISHMANIASIS)

- **Causative Pathogen**: *Leishmania donovani*, an intracellular dimorphic protozoan parasite surviving as an aflagellated amastigote (Leishman-Donovan [LD] body) within host mononuclear phagocytes and as a flagellated promastigote in the sandfly vector.
- **Transmission Vector**: *Phlebotomus argentipes* (female sandfly); breeds in damp, organic-rich soil, cattle sheds, and earthen wall cracks; weak hopper flight (<400 metres), biting actively from dusk to dawn.
- **Reservoir and Transmission Dynamics**: Strictly anthroponotic in the Indian subcontinent (*Homo sapiens* is the sole established mammalian reservoir). Patients with Post-Kala-azar Dermal Leishmaniasis (PKDL) serve as persistent inter-epidemic transmission reservoirs.
- **Endemic Geography**: Historically confined to the alluvial plains of the Ganges and Brahmaputra basins: Bihar, Jharkhand, West Bengal, and eastern Uttar Pradesh.
- **Clinical Presentation**: Insidious or abrupt onset of persistent, irregular fever exhibiting a classic double daily spike; progressive, massive, non-tender splenomegaly; soft hepatomegaly; profound emaciation; and characteristic slate-grey hyperpigmentation of facial and extremity skin ("black sickness").
- **Haematological Triad**: Advanced disease manifests with severe pancytopenia (normocytic normochromic anaemia, marked leukopenia with absolute neutropenia, and thrombocytopenia) resulting from splenic sequestration and bone marrow infiltration.
- **Post-Kala-azar Dermal Leishmaniasis (PKDL)**: A non-ulcerative dermatosis arising in 5% to 10% of visceral leishmaniasis patients, typically months to years post-treatment; presents as macular hypopigmented patches, erythematous plaques, or nodular infiltrates laden with amastigotes, requiring targeted chemotherapy to eliminate the community reservoir.
- **Laboratory Diagnosis**:
  - **Immunochromatographic Screening**: Recombinant K39 (rK39) antigen dipstick test (sensitivity >98%, specificity >90% in active cases).
  - **Parasitological Demonstration**: Identification of amastigotes (LD bodies) on Giemsa-stained smears of splenic aspirate (diagnostic gold standard, sensitivity >95%) or bone marrow aspirate (sensitivity 70% to 85%).
  - **Molecular Assays**: Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR) and direct agglutination tests in specialized surveillance settings.
- **Therapeutic Regimens under NCVBDC Guidelines**:
  - **Preferred First-Line Therapy**: Single-dose intravenous infusion of Liposomal Amphotericin B (AmBisome) at 10 mg/kg body weight (achieving cure rates >95% under direct medical supervision).
  - **Alternative Regimens**: Oral Miltefosine (for 28 consecutive days) or combination therapy (Liposomal Amphotericin B plus Miltefosine or Paromomycin) for patients contraindicated for single-dose amphotericin.
  - **Treatment of PKDL**: Oral Miltefosine for 12 weeks or multiple courses of Liposomal Amphotericin B as prescribed by national programme protocols.
- **National Kala-azar Elimination Target and Strategy**:
  - **Elimination Benchmark**: Sustained reduction of annual Kala-azar incidence to less than 1 case per 10,000 population at the block (sub-district) administrative level.
  - **Core Operational Pillars**:
    1. **Early Case Detection and Complete Treatment**: Point-of-care rK39 rapid testing at Primary Health Centres and sub-centres, coupled with single-day liposomal amphotericin B therapy.
    2. **Integrated Vector Management**: Two annual rounds of Indoor Residual Spraying (IRS) using synthetic pyrethroids (alpha-cypermethrin 5% WP or deltamethrin) applied to mud walls of homes and cattle sheds up to 6 feet, supplemented by Long-Lasting Insecticidal Nets (LLINs).
