    3. **Active Surveillance and PKDL Search**: Coordinated bi-annual active search fortnights led by Accredited Social Health Activists (ASHAs) with performance-based cash incentives for case tracking.
    4. **Inter-sectoral Environmental Modification**: Upgradation of kachha mud dwellings to pucca brick houses under government housing schemes to permanently eliminate sandfly breeding crevices.

> **EXAM TIP:** In long-answer questions on Kala-azar elimination, clearly outline the epidemiological triad (Leishmania donovani - Phlebotomus argentipes - human reservoir), cite the block-level elimination benchmark (<1 case per 10,000 population), detail single-dose Liposomal Amphotericin B (10 mg/kg), and emphasize that identifying and treating PKDL cases is mandatory to prevent resurgence in post-elimination phases.

[SN]Chandipura virus disease[/SN]

CHANDIPURA VIRUS DISEASE

- **Aetiological Classification**: Chandipura virus (CHPV), an enveloped, bullet-shaped, negative-sense single-stranded RNA virus belonging to the genus *Vesiculovirus*, family Rhabdoviridae; first isolated in 1965 in Chandipura, Maharashtra.
- **Transmission Vectors**: Phlebotomine sandflies, particularly *Phlebotomus papatasi* and *Phlebotomus argentipes*, with suspected secondary involvement of *Sergentomyia* species; transovarial and trans-stadial transmission mechanisms allow viral persistence across seasons.
- **Susceptible Demographics**: High predilection for pediatric populations under 15 years of age, with maximum morbidity and mortality concentrated among rural and tribal children aged 9 months to 8 years.
- **Clinical Presentation**: Fulminant onset of Acute Encephalitis Syndrome (AES); characterized by sudden high-grade fever, recurrent vomiting, diarrhea, followed within 24 to 48 hours by altered sensorium, generalized convulsions, focal neurological deficits, decerebrate posturing, and rapid coma.
- **Case Fatality Rate**: Extremely severe disease course yielding a Case Fatality Rate (CFR) of 50% to 75% in recognized outbreak clusters, secondary to acute cerebral oedema, brainstem dysfunction, and shock.
- **Outbreak Epidemiology**: Documented outbreaks in central and western India (Andhra Pradesh, Maharashtra, Gujarat); in 2024, significant pediatric AES clusters in Gujarat and neighbouring districts were systematically investigated by the National Centre for Disease Control (NCDC) and confirmed as Chandipura encephalitis outbreaks.
- **Diagnostic Methods**: Real-time Reverse Transcription-Polymerase Chain Reaction (rRT-PCR) for viral RNA detection in blood or cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) collected during the early viraemic phase (first 1 to 4 days); IgM capture ELISA performed by reference laboratories such as the ICMR-National Institute of Virology (NIV), Pune.
- **Case Management and Public Health Response**: No specific antiviral drug or licensed human vaccine is available; therapeutic intervention relies upon intensive neuro-pediatric supportive care (control of cerebral oedema with hypertonic saline or mannitol, airway maintenance, seizure control with anticonvulsants, and fluid-electrolyte resuscitation); public health control centers on emergency indoor residual dusting with malathion/synthetic pyrethroids targeting sandfly harbourages, immediate notification of pediatric AES clusters, and community awareness regarding insect bite prevention.

> **EXAM TIP:** Frame Chandipura as an acute neurotropic rhabdovirus responsible for fulminant pediatric Acute Encephalitis Syndrome with catastrophic case fatality (50-75%). Structure answers around: 1) sandfly transmission, 2) rapid neurological deterioration within 24-48 hours, 3) early real-time RT-PCR diagnosis, 4) aggressive pediatric neuro-intensive supportive care, and 5) sandfly vector control.

INDIAN PROGRAMMATIC CONTEXT

- **NCVBDC and NCDC Integration**: All three conditions are coordinated under national vector-borne disease and outbreak control mechanisms. Visceral Leishmaniasis represents a targeted national elimination programme with defined block-level indicators, while Chikungunya and Chandipura virus diseases require vigilant entomological surveillance, AES laboratory networks, and rapid outbreak response protocols.

[REF]Reference: National Center for Vector Borne Diseases Control (NCVBDC) Guidelines on Kala-azar and Chikungunya; National Centre for Disease Control (NCDC) Investigational Protocols for Chandipura AES Outbreaks (2024); Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine.[/REF]

subsections.title: Plague, Leptospirosis, Kyasanur Forest Disease, and Nipah
subsections.content:
OVERVIEW OF THE SECTION
This section addresses four focal, high-fatality zoonotic infections of profound epidemiological importance: Plague, Leptospirosis, Kyasanur Forest Disease (KFD), and Nipah Virus Disease. These conditions exemplify the dynamic interface between wildlife reservoirs, arthropod vectors, domestic animals, and human populations under the One Health framework. Each disease requires rigorous surveillance, rapid diagnostic confirmation, and decisive containment protocols to prevent catastrophic outbreak amplification.

DEFINITIONS

- **Plague**: An acute, severe zoonotic bacterial disease caused by *Yersinia pestis*, maintained predominantly in rodent reservoirs and transmitted by fleas, presenting clinically in bubonic, pneumonic, or septicaemic forms.
- **Leptospirosis**: A worldwide spirochaetal zoonosis caused by pathogenic *Leptospira interrogans*, transmitted to humans through mucosal or cutaneous contact with water, moist soil, or mud contaminated with the urine of carrier animal hosts.
- **Kyasanur Forest Disease**: A tick-borne viral haemorrhagic and encephalitic disease caused by Kyasanur Forest disease virus (family Flaviviridae), geographically restricted to the Western Ghats biome, maintained in an enzootic cycle involving forest monkeys, small mammals, and *Haemaphysalis* ticks.
- **Nipah Virus Disease**: A high-consequence emerging zoonotic viral infection caused by Nipah henipavirus (family Paramyxoviridae), naturally harboured by *Pteropus* fruit bats, presenting as severe Acute Encephalitis Syndrome (AES) and respiratory distress, with marked potential for nosocomial transmission.

[SN]Plague[/SN]

PLAGUE

- **Aetiological Pathogen**: *Yersinia pestis*, a Gram-negative, facultative anaerobic, non-motile coccobacillus demonstrating characteristic bipolar "safety-pin" staining with Giemsa or Wayson stain.
- **Vector Biology and Flea Indices**: Transmitted primarily by the rodent flea *Xenopsylla cheopis* (oriental rat flea) and *Xenopsylla astia*. Bacterial coagulase produces proventricular blockage in the flea, prompting voracious feeding and regurgitation of infectious bacilli into the vertebrate host.
  - **General Flea Index**: Average number of fleas of all species found per rodent examined.
  - **Specific Cheopis Index**: Average number of *X. cheopis* fleas per rodent examined; a Cheopis Index exceeding 1.0 represents the critical epidemiological threshold indicating an explosive outbreak risk of human plague.
- **Natural Reservoirs and Epizootic Dynamics**: Enzootic maintenance occurs in wild forest rodents (*Tatera indica*, *Bandicota bengalensis*) in sylvatic foci. Transmission spillovers to domestic commensal rodents (*Rattus rattus*, *Rattus norvegicus*) precipitate urban epizootics. An abrupt epizootic "rat-fall" (sudden mortality among domestic rodents) heralds impending human bubonic infection as starving fleas abandon dead hosts.
- **Clinical Manifestations**:
  - **Bubonic Plague**: Represents 80% to 90% of clinical presentations; characterized by sudden fever, chills, profound prostration, and exquisitely painful, inflammatory regional lymphadenopathy ("buboes"), most commonly involving femoral, inguinal, and axillary nodes. Not directly contagious between humans.
  - **Pneumonic Plague**: Highly lethal, rapidly progressive form acquired either via aerosol inhalation from an infected human/animal (primary pneumonic plague) or via haematogenous dissemination from a bubo (secondary pneumonic plague). Characterized by severe cough, chest pain, hemoptysis, tachypnoea, and rapid respiratory failure; spreads directly person-to-person via infectious droplets.
  - **Septicaemic Plague**: Rapid bacteriological dissemination causing disseminated intravascular coagulation, purpuric lesions, acral gangrene ("black death"), and refractory endotoxic shock.
- **Indian Foci and Outbreak History**: Endemic sylvatic foci persist across the Deccan plateau (tri-junction of Maharashtra, Karnataka, and Andhra Pradesh) and northern sub-Himalayan belts. The 1994 Surat pneumonic outbreak and Beed bubonic cluster demonstrated the rapid resurgence potential of plague in post-monsoon urban settings.
- **Surveillance and Outbreak Containment**:
  - **Sequenced Vector and Rodent Control**: Vector flea control (insecticidal dusting with 5% malathion or synthetic pyrethroids applied to rodent burrows and wall crevices) MUST strictly precede rodent extermination; eradicating rats first forces hungry, infected fleas onto human populations.
  - **Antimicrobial Therapy**: Streptomycin (30 mg/kg/day IM in divided doses for 10 days) or Gentamicin serves as the first-line therapeutic regimen; oral Doxycycline or Ciprofloxacin provides effective secondary treatment.
  - **Strict Respiratory Isolation**: Mandatory droplet isolation of all pneumonic plague patients for at least 48 hours following initiation of effective bactericidal chemotherapy.
  - **Contact Chemoprophylaxis**: Oral Doxycycline (100 mg twice daily for 7 days) administered to close household and healthcare contacts of pneumonic cases.

CLINICAL AND EPIDEMIOLOGICAL DIFFERENTIATION: BUBONIC VERSUS PNEUMONIC PLAGUE

| Feature | Bubonic Plague | Pneumonic Plague |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Primary Route of Infection** | Bite of infected rodent flea (*Xenopsylla cheopis*) | Inhalation of infectious respiratory droplets or secondary haematogenous seeding |
| **Incubation Period** | 2 to 6 days | 1 to 3 days (exceptionally fulminant) |
| **Predominant Clinical Sign** | Exquisitely tender, swollen lymph nodes (buboes) | Productive cough, hemoptysis, tachypnoea, respiratory failure |
| **Person-to-Person Transmission** | Absent; requires flea vector | Highly contagious via droplet nuclei; initiates explosive epidemics |
| **Untreated Mortality** | 50% to 60% | Approaching 100% within 24 to 48 hours |
| **Public Health Precaution** | Standard precautions plus flea dusting | Strict respiratory/droplet isolation plus mandatory contact chemoprophylaxis |

> **EXAM TIP:** In questions on plague epidemiology, highlight the sequential rule of pest management: always apply insecticidal flea dusting before implementing rodent eradication to prevent hungry fleas from attacking humans. Cite the Cheopis Index threshold (>1.0), explain the droplet transmission hazard of pneumonic plague, and detail doxycycline chemoprophylaxis for contacts.

[SN]Leptospirosis[/SN]

LEPTOSPIROSIS

- **Causative Microorganism**: Pathogenic spirochaetes of the species *Leptospira interrogans* (encompassing over 250 antigenically distinct serovars classified into 25 serogroups, including *icterohaemorrhagiae*, *autumnalis*, *australis*, and *canicola*).
- **Reservoirs and Transmission Ecology**: Chronically harboured within the renal proximal tubules of rodents, cattle, pigs, and dogs without producing systemic disease; viable spirochaetes are shed continuously in animal urine into environmental soil and water. Humans acquire infection through percutaneous entry via abraded skin or exposed mucous membranes (conjunctiva, oral mucosa) contacting water, mud, or slush contaminated with animal urine during agricultural labor (paddy, sugarcane) or monsoon urban inundations.
- **Clinical Spectra**: Biphasic illness:
  - **Anicteric Leptospirosis (85% to 90%)**: Abrupt onset of high fever, rigors, intense headache, pathognomonic severe calf muscle tenderness, and prominent bilateral conjunctival suffusion without purulent discharge. Frequently self-limiting or rapidly aborting with early antimicrobial therapy.
  - **Icteric Leptospirosis / Weil's Disease (5% to 10%)**: Severe multi-organ crisis marked by the classic clinical triad of profound jaundice (hepatic necrosis), acute oliguric or non-oliguric renal failure (interstitial nephritis), and extensive haemorrhagic diathesis (pulmonary haemorrhage, hemoptysis, gastrointestinal bleeding).
- **Laboratory Confirmation**:
  - **Microscopic Agglutination Test (MAT)**: Gold-standard serological assay; demonstration of a fourfold or greater increase in agglutination titre between acute and convalescent sera, or a single diagnostic titre >=1:400 in endemic areas.
  - **Enzyme-Linked Immunosorbent Assay (ELISA)**: Rapid detection of Leptospira-specific IgM antibodies, widely utilized for peripheral hospital screening from the fifth day of clinical symptoms.
  - **Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR)**: Sensitive detection of leptospiral DNA in blood or CSF during the initial leptospiraemic window (first 4 to 7 days).
- **Therapeutic Protocols**:
  - **Severe Leptospirosis**: Intravenous Benzylpenicillin (1.5 million units IV every 6 hours for 7 days) or IV Ceftriaxone (1 g once daily); antimicrobial therapy must be initiated immediately on clinical suspicion without delaying for MAT confirmation.
  - **Mild Leptospirosis**: Oral Doxycycline (100 mg twice daily for 7 days) or oral Azithromycin (500 mg once daily for 5 days).
- **Prevention and Prophylaxis**:
  - **Targeted Chemoprophylaxis**: Oral Doxycycline (200 mg once weekly) administered to disaster rescue workers, sanitation staff, and agricultural laborers during flood crises as mandated by national outbreak guidelines.
  - **Occupational Hygiene**: Wearing waterproof gumboots and gloves, drainage of stagnant agricultural collections, and rigorous rodent control around residential zones.

CLINICAL FEATURES: ANICTERIC LEPTOSPIROSIS VERSUS WEIL'S DISEASE

| Clinical Parameter | Anicteric Leptospirosis | Icteric Leptospirosis (Weil's Disease) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Proportion of Cases** | 85% to 90% of clinical presentations | 5% to 10% of clinical presentations |
| **Clinical Triad** | Absent; fever, headache, calf myalgia | Classical triad: deep jaundice, renal failure, haemorrhage |
| **Renal Involvement** | Transient, mild proteinuria | Acute tubular and interstitial nephritis, oliguria, uremia |
| **Haemorrhagic Diathesis** | Rare, mild epistaxis or petechiae | Severe; pulmonary alveolar haemorrhage, hemoptysis, purpura |
| **Case Fatality Rate** | Low (<1%) | High (10% to 40%), highest with pulmonary haemorrhage |
| **Therapeutic Approach** | Oral doxycycline or azithromycin | Urgent hospitalization, IV penicillin/ceftriaxone, hemodialysis |

> **EXAM TIP:** Detail the clinical triad of Weil's disease: deep jaundice, acute renal impairment, and haemorrhagic manifestations (particularly pulmonary haemorrhage). Emphasize that severe calf tenderness and non-purulent conjunctival suffusion provide crucial early diagnostic clues, and highlight oral doxycycline (200 mg once weekly) for post-exposure prophylaxis during floods.

[SN]Kyasanur Forest Disease[/SN]

KYASANUR FOREST DISEASE (KFD / MONKEY FEVER)

- **Aetiological Classification**: Kyasanur Forest disease virus (KFDV), an enveloped, positive-sense single-stranded RNA virus belonging to the tick-borne encephalitis antigenic complex, family Flaviviridae.
- **Vector Transmission Dynamics**: Transmitted by hard ticks of the genus *Haemaphysalis*, predominantly *Haemaphysalis spinigera*. The nymphal developmental stage serves as the principal vector for human infection, exhibiting maximum questing and biting activity during dry post-monsoon months (November to May).
- **Host Ecology and Sentinel Monkeys**: Forest monkeys, particularly the black-faced langur (*Semnopithecus entellus*) and bonnet macaque (*Macaca radiata*), are exquisitely susceptible amplifying hosts. Epizootic monkey deaths ("monkey falls") function as crucial natural sentinels alerting surveillance units to active viral circulation within forest tracts. Enzootic maintenance involves forest rodents, shrews, and ground-feeding birds.
- **Endemic Geography**: Geographically confined to the Western Ghats ecosystem; originally isolated in Shimoga district (Karnataka) in 1957, with documented contiguous expansion into adjoining districts of Karnataka (Chikmagalur, Uttara Kannada, Dakshina Kannada, Udupi), Kerala (Wayanad), Tamil Nadu (Nilgiris), Goa, and Maharashtra.
- **Clinical Course**: Characteristically biphasic disease evolution:
  - **Initial Viraemic Phase**: Sudden onset of high fever, frontal cephalalgia, severe myalgia, prostration, vomiting, diarrhea, conjunctival suffusion, and haemorrhagic manifestations (epistaxis, gingival oozing, gastrointestinal bleeding).
  - **Secondary Convalescent / Neurological Phase**: In 15% to 20% of patients, following a transient afebrile lull of 1 to 2 weeks, a secondary phase ensues, marked by recrudescent fever, severe tremors, mental confusion, neck stiffness, and meningoencephalitis. Case fatality ranges from 3% to 5%.
- **Diagnostic Confirmation**: Real-time RT-PCR for viral RNA detection in blood during the first 8 days of viraemia; IgM and IgG ELISA processed in reference virology centres (e.g., ICMR-NIV Pune).
- **Prevention and Control Strategies**:
  - **KFD Vaccination**: Formalin-inactivated, tissue-culture derived KFD vaccine administered in endemic taluks; primary immunization comprises two doses given 1 month apart to residents and forest laborers aged 7 to 65 years, followed by a booster dose at 6 to 9 months and annual booster doses.
  - **Personal Barrier Protection**: Topical application of repellents (DEET or DMP oil) to exposed skin before forest entry; wearing tick-protective clothing; avoidance of handling dead monkey carcasses; prompt reporting of monkey mortality to the district surveillance unit.

> **EXAM TIP:** In questions on Kyasanur Forest Disease, describe the tick-monkey-human cycle, identify Haemaphysalis spinigera nymphs as the primary vector, explain "monkey falls" as an epizootic sentinel warning, detail the biphasic clinical course (haemorrhagic followed by encephalitic), and cite the formalin-inactivated KFD vaccine schedule.

[SN]Nipah virus disease[/SN]

[LAQ]Nipah virus: reservoir, outbreaks, and control[/LAQ]

NIPAH VIRUS DISEASE

- **Pathogen Biology**: Nipah virus (NiV), an enveloped, negative-sense single-stranded RNA virus belonging to the genus *Henipavirus*, family Paramyxoviridae; classified globally as a high-consequence Biosafety Level 4 (BSL-4) priority pathogen.
- **Natural Wildlife Reservoir**: Frugivorous megabats of the genus *Pteropus* (fruit bats or flying foxes, predominantly *Pteropus medius* / *Pteropus giganteus* in India). The virus persists subclinically in bat colonies and is shed intermittently in urine, saliva, and birth fluids.
- **Transmission Pathways**:
  - **Bat-to-Human Spillover**: Consumption of fresh, unpasteurized date palm sap (toddy/tari) contaminated with bat excretions, or ingestion of fruits contaminated with bat saliva or urine.
  - **Intermediate Host Transmission**: Direct contact with infected intermediate amplifying domestic hosts (notably pigs in the index 1998 Malaysian epidemic).
  - **Human-to-Human Nosocomial Transmission**: Direct contact with respiratory droplets, tracheal secretions, urine, or bodily fluids of acutely ill patients; nosocomial clustering among healthcare personnel, hospital attendants, and family caregivers represents a catastrophic amplification hazard.
- **Indian Outbreak Chronology**:
  - **Siliguri, West Bengal (2001)**: 66 cases with a Case Fatality Rate of 74%, characterized by pronounced nosocomial transmission in clinical hospital settings.
  - **Nadia, West Bengal (2007)**: 30 cases with 100% case fatality.
  - **Kerala Outbreaks (2018, 2019, 2021, 2023, 2024)**: Recurrent localized outbreaks in Kozhikode and Malappuram districts, originating from index bat spillover events with subsequent household and hospital secondary transmission; overall CFR of 70% to 90%.
- **Clinical Presentation**: Incubation period averages 4 to 14 days (extreme ranges up to 45 days recorded). Presents initially as an acute febrile syndrome with severe headache, vomiting, myalgia, progressing rapidly to Acute Encephalitis Syndrome (drowsiness, myoclonus, cerebellar ataxia, brainstem dysfunction, and coma within 24 to 48 hours). Over 50% of patients exhibit acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) or atypical pneumonia.
- **Diagnostic Confirmation**: Real-time RT-PCR and viral RNA detection from throat swabs, CSF, and urine samples processed under strict BSL-4 biocontainment at ICMR-NIV, Pune; serological confirmation via IgM capture ELISA.
- **Therapeutic and Supportive Care**: No approved specific antiviral chemotherapy or licensed human vaccine; intensive supportive neuro-intensive care, mechanical ventilation for ARDS, and hemodynamic support; investigational therapeutics include intravenous remdesivir and human monoclonal antibody m102.4 under compassionate-use emergency protocols.
- **Infection Prevention and Public Health Containment**:
  - **Hospital Infection Control**: Immediate isolation of suspected cases in negative-pressure isolation wards; mandatory deployment of Level-3 Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) including N95/FFP3 respirators, double gloves, eye protection, and impervious gowns; strict barrier nursing.
  - **Contact Tracing and Quarantine**: Systematic identification, risk stratification (high-risk vs low-risk), and mandatory 21-day quarantine of all primary and secondary contacts with daily symptom monitoring.
  - **Community Prevention**: Banning consumption of raw, uncovered date palm sap; installation of protective bamboo skirts over sap-collection pots; thorough washing and peeling of fruits; avoidance of fallen, damaged fruits; safe, dignified protocolized burial or cremation of deceased victims without ritual touching.
  - **One Health Integration**: Collaborative surveillance linking public health authorities, veterinary departments, wildlife biologists, and forest rangers to monitor bat roosting sites and animal-human interfaces.

> **EXAM TIP:** In long-answer questions on Nipah virus, frame the response around the One Health paradigm. Highlight Pteropus fruit bats as the reservoir, ingestion of contaminated date palm sap as the spillover mechanism, and nosocomial transmission as the primary amplification danger. Emphasize strict BSL-4 infection control, mandatory 21-day contact quarantine, and compassionate use of monoclonal antibody m102.4.

INDIAN PROGRAMMATIC CONTEXT

- **Zoonoses Surveillance Architecture**: Under the Integrated Disease Surveillance Programme (IDSP) and the National One Health Mission, focal zoonoses require immediate electronic reporting. Plague and KFD surveillance operate through specialized field research units, Leptospirosis control is coordinated under the National Programme for Prevention and Control of Leptospirosis (NPCL), and Nipah containment utilizes rapid multidisciplinary outbreak response teams.

[REF]Reference: National Centre for Disease Control (NCDC) Guidelines on Plague, Leptospirosis, and KFD; State Protocol for Nipah Virus Disease Containment (Government of Kerala); Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine.[/REF]

subsections.title: Trachoma, Yaws, Scabies, and Pediculosis
subsections.content:
OVERVIEW OF THE SECTION
This section addresses communicable surface and ectoparasitic diseases of significant public health importance: Trachoma, Yaws, Scabies, and Pediculosis. These conditions reflect environmental hygiene, socioeconomic status, water accessibility, and community overcrowding. They encompass historical public health triumphs, such as the national elimination of active trachoma and yaws, alongside recurrent dermatological infestations managed at community, school, and primary healthcare levels.

DEFINITIONS

- **Trachoma**: A chronic, contagious keratoconjunctivitis caused by *Chlamydia trachomatis* (serovars A, B, Ba, C), characterized by progressive conjunctival follicular hypertrophy, papillary hyperplasia, and conjunctival scarring leading to trichiasis, corneal opacity, and irreversible blindness.
- **Yaws**: A chronic, non-venereal endemic treponematosis caused by *Treponema pallidum* subspecies *pertenue*, transmitted primarily among children in humid tropical biomes by direct skin contact, producing lesions of skin, cartilage, and bone.
- **Scabies**: A highly contagious, intensely pruritic ectoparasitic dermatosis caused by the microscopic itch mite *Sarcoptes scabiei* var. *hominis*, transmitted via direct, prolonged skin-to-skin contact.
- **Pediculosis**: Cutaneous and hair infestation caused by blood-sucking human lice: *Pediculus humanus capitis* (head louse), *Pediculus humanus corporis* (body louse), or *Pthirus pubis* (pubic louse).

[SN]Trachoma[/SN]

TRACHOMA

- **Aetiological Pathogen**: *Chlamydia trachomatis*, an obligate intracellular bacterium; serovars A, B, Ba, and C are responsible for endemic blinding trachoma.
- **Transmission Mechanisms**: Direct transmission via personal contact with ocular and nasal discharges of infected individuals (especially children under 9 years), indirect transmission via contaminated fomites (towels, clothing, bedclothes), and mechanical vector transmission by eye-seeking synanthropic flies (*Musca sorbens*).
- **Environmental and Social Determinants**: Inadequate domestic water supply, poor personal hygiene (unwashed faces in children), overcrowded domestic quarters, inadequate sanitation (open defecation promoting fly breeding), and arid, dusty rural climates.
- **WHO Simplified Grading System (FISTO)**:
  - **TF (Trachomatous inflammation - Follicular)**: Presence of five or more follicles of at least 0.5 mm diameter in the upper tarsal conjunctiva (indicates active infection).
  - **TI (Trachomatous inflammation - Intense)**: Pronounced inflammatory thickening of the tarsal conjunctiva obscuring more than half of the normal deep tarsal vessels.
  - **TS (Trachomatous Scarring)**: Presence of easily visible fibrous scarring bands in the tarsal conjunctiva.
  - **TT (Trachomatous Trichiasis)**: At least one eyelash rubbing against the eyeball, or evidence of recent epilation of in-turned eyelashes.
  - **CO (Corneal Opacity)**: Easily visible corneal opacity overlying at least part of the pupil margin, producing visual impairment.
- **WHO SAFE Strategy**: Comprehensive multi-sectoral intervention framework:
  - **S - Surgery**: Corrective bilamellar tarsal rotation surgery for individuals presenting with trichiasis (TT) to prevent corneal trauma and blindness.
  - **A - Antibiotics**: Mass drug administration (MDA) of single-dose oral Azithromycin (20 mg/kg, up to maximum 1 g) or topical 1% tetracycline eye ointment (twice daily for 6 weeks) in communities where TF prevalence in children aged 1 to 9 years equals or exceeds 5%.
  - **F - Facial Cleanliness**: Community and school-based hygiene education promoting frequent face washing in young children to eliminate ocular-nasal secretions that attract *Musca sorbens* flies.
  - **E - Environmental Improvement**: Expanding community access to potable water, constructing household sanitary latrines to suppress fly populations, and improving waste disposal.
- **India's Elimination Milestone**: Under the National Programme for Control of Blindness and Visual Impairment (NPCBVI), India systematically implemented the SAFE strategy and nationwide surveillance surveys; in 2024, the World Health Organization officially validated India as having eliminated trachoma as a public health problem (TF prevalence sustained <5% across all children aged 1 to 9 years nationwide).

WHO SIMPLIFIED TRACHOMA GRADING CLASSIFICATION (FISTO FRAMEWORK)

| Grade | Clinical Feature | Diagnostic Significance |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **TF** | Trachomatous inflammation - Follicular (>=5 follicles of >=0.5 mm on upper tarsal conjunctiva) | Primary indicator of active community transmission; guides antibiotic MDA |
| **TI** | Trachomatous inflammation - Intense (inflammatory thickening obscuring >50% of deep vessels) | Indicates severe active infection carrying high risk of cicatricial progression |
| **TS** | Trachomatous Scarring (visible fibrous cicatricial bands in tarsal conjunctiva) | Indicates past cumulative infection and architectural remodelling |
| **TT** | Trachomatous Trichiasis (at least one eyelash in contact with globe or recent epilation) | Critical surgical indication; prevents impending mechanical corneal scarring |
| **CO** | Corneal Opacity (visible opacity over pupil margin) | End-stage cicatricial complication causing permanent visual loss |

> **EXAM TIP:** Detail the WHO SAFE strategy (Surgery, Antibiotics, Facial cleanliness, Environmental improvement) and the FISTO grading system. Highlight the public health elimination benchmark: TF prevalence <5% in children aged 1 to 9 years, and note that WHO officially validated India's elimination of blinding trachoma as a public health problem in 2024.

[SN]Yaws[/SN]

YAWS (ENDEMIC TREPONEMATOSIS)

- **Aetiological Classification**: *Treponema pallidum* subspecies *pertenue*, a slender, spiral-shaped spirochaete morphologically and serologically indistinguishable from the venereal syphilis agent *Treponema pallidum* subsp. *pallidum*.
- **Epidemiological Features**: Transmitted non-venereally through direct skin-to-skin contact, gaining entry through minor abrasions or cuts. Primarily afflicts rural, socioeconomically disadvantaged children under 15 years residing in warm, humid, tropical forest communities with scarce water and inadequate clothing.
- **Clinical Evolution and Staging**:
  - **Primary Stage (Early Yaws)**: Solitary, painless, pruritic, raspberry-like papilloma ("mother yaw") developing at the inoculation site after an incubation period of 2 to 4 weeks; ulcerates, forms an amber crust, and heals with an atrophic scar.
  - **Secondary Stage (Early Yaws)**: Disseminated generalized papillomas, condylomatous eruptions in skin folds, painful palmar and plantar hyperkeratotic fissures ("crab yaws" producing a characteristic crab-like gait), and painful periostitis/dactylitis in long bones.
  - **Latent Stage**: Quiescent, asymptomatic phase with positive treponemal serology.
  - **Tertiary Stage (Late Yaws)**: Destructive, non-infectious gummatous necrosis developing in roughly 10% of untreated individuals years later; causes severe osteoperiostitis, bowed anterior deformities of the tibia ("sabre tibia"), destructive ulceration of the palate and nasal septum ("gangosa" / rhinopharyngitis mutilans), and paranasal exostoses ("goundou"). Yaws does not cause cardiovascular or central nervous system lesions.
- **Laboratory Diagnosis**: Rapid treponemal (TPHA, TPPA) and non-treponemal (VDRL, RPR) serology; Dual Path Platform (DPP) rapid point-of-care syphilis/yaws test; multiplex real-time PCR for definitive differentiation from other treponematoses.
- **WHO Morges Eradication Strategy**: Community mass treatment using a single oral dose of Azithromycin (30 mg/kg, maximum 2 g); intramuscular Benzathine Penicillin G serves as an effective alternative.
- **India's Historic Eradication Milestone**: India launched the National Yaws Eradication Programme (N-YEP) in 1996-1997 in hyper-endemic tribal districts of Odisha, Andhra Pradesh, and Madhya Pradesh; achieving zero transmission in 2003, India was formally certified free of yaws by WHO in 2016. Sustained rumour surveillance, cash incentives for case reporting, and school screening continue in formerly endemic pockets.

COMPARATIVE DIFFERENTIATION: YAWS VERSUS VENEREAL SYPHILIS

| Feature | Yaws | Venereal Syphilis |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Causative Organism** | *Treponema pallidum* subsp. *pertenue* | *Treponema pallidum* subsp. *pallidum* |
| **Transmission Route** | Non-venereal; direct skin contact via abrasions | Sexual intercourse, vertical/transplacental, blood |
| **Predominant Age Group** | Children under 15 years in rural/tribal foci | Sexually active adolescents and adults |
| **Primary Lesion** | Extragenital papilloma / ulcer ("mother yaw") | Genital painless indurated ulcer (hard chancre) |
| **Late Complications** | Sabre tibia, gangosa, goundou | Tabes dorsalis, general paresis, aortic aneurysm |
| **Neurological / Cardiac** | Never occurs | Classical tertiary syphilis features |
| **Congenital Transmission** | Never occurs | Congenital syphilis (Hutchinson triad, snuffles) |
| **Treatment of Choice** | Single-dose oral azithromycin (30 mg/kg) | Intramuscular benzathine penicillin G |

> **EXAM TIP:** Differentiate Yaws from Venereal Syphilis: Yaws is caused by Treponema pallidum subspecies pertenue, transmitted non-venereally by skin contact during childhood, produces skin and bone destruction (mother yaw, crab yaws, gangosa, sabre tibia), but never produces neurosyphilis, cardiovascular lesions, or congenital transmission. Note India's WHO certification as yaws-free in 2016.

[SN]Scabies[/SN]

SCABIES

- **Aetiological Organism**: *Sarcoptes scabiei* var. *hominis*, a microscopic, obligate human itch mite. The fertilized adult female mite burrows into the stratum corneum of the epidermis, depositing 2 to 3 eggs daily over a lifespan of 4 to 6 weeks.
- **Transmission Dynamics**: Acquired predominantly via direct, prolonged skin-to-skin contact (typically requiring at least 15 to 20 minutes of physical intimacy or contact). Indirect transmission via contaminated clothing, bedclothes, or towels is uncommon in classical scabies due to low mite burden, but common in crusted scabies.
- **Predisposing Settings**: Severe overcrowding, institutional living (prisons, boarding schools, orphanages, residential care facilities, refugee camps), poverty, and substandard personal hygiene.
- **Pathognomonic Clinical Features**:
  - **Intense Nocturnal Pruritus**: Exacerbated at night due to host warmth and hypersensitivity reaction to mite proteins, faeces (scybala), and ova.
  - **Characteristic Burrows**: Slender, raised, greyish-white or serpiginous lines (1 to 10 mm in length) terminating in a tiny pinpoint papulovesicle harboring the female mite.
  - **Classical Anatomical Distribution**: Interdigital web spaces of fingers, anterior flexor creases of wrists, extensor aspects of elbows, anterior axillary folds, periumbilical skin, waistline, buttocks, genitalia (penis and scrotum in males), and areolae in females. The head and neck are classically spared in adults, but may be involved in infants and the elderly.
- **Crusted (Norwegian) Scabies**: Highly contagious, virulent form occurring in immunocompromised individuals (HIV/AIDS, haematological malignancy, organ transplant recipients, leprosy) and debilitated elderly patients; characterized by thick, hyperkeratotic, psoriasiform crusting over large body surfaces, harboring millions of live mites with minimal or absent itching due to defective cell-mediated immunity.
- **Therapeutic Protocol**:
  - **Topical Permethrin 5% Dermal Cream**: Therapeutic drug of choice; applied meticulously from the chin/neck downwards over the entire body surface (including scalp, face, and ears in infants), left on for 8 to 14 hours, and thoroughly washed off. A repeat application 7 days later is mandatory to eradicate newly hatched nymphs.
  - **Oral Ivermectin**: 200 micrograms/kg body weight administered as a single dose, repeated after 14 days; indicated for institutional outbreaks, crusted scabies, and refractory cases.
  - **Simultaneous Household Contact Treatment**: All household members and close physical contacts must be treated simultaneously, regardless of whether cutaneous symptoms are present.
  - **Fomite Decontamination**: Laundering of bedding, linen, and clothing in hot water (>=50 degrees C) or sealing in plastic bags for at least 72 hours (as mites die within 48 to 72 hours off the human host).

CLINICAL DIFFERENTIATION: CLASSICAL SCABIES VERSUS CRUSTED (NORWEGIAN) SCABIES

| Feature | Classical Scabies | Crusted (Norwegian) Scabies |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Mite Burden** | Typically 10 to 15 live female mites per host | Millions of live mites across crusted scales |
| **Pruritus** | Severe, intractable, nocturnal hypersensitivity itch | Minimal or absent due to deficient cell-mediated immunity |
| **Skin Lesions** | Discrete burrows, papulovesicles, excoriations | Extensive, thick, psoriasiform hyperkeratotic crusts |
| **Infectivity** | Requires prolonged, direct skin-to-skin contact | Highly contagious; spreads rapidly via bedding, dust, clothes |
| **Host Immune Status** | Immunocompetent individuals | Immunocompromised (HIV, transplant, steroids, leprosy) |
| **Management** | Topical 5% permethrin cream (single application + 7-day repeat) | Combined oral ivermectin + repeated topical permethrin + keratolytic agents |

> **EXAM TIP:** In scabies management, stress the three golden rules: 1) apply topical permethrin 5% from neck to toes (including head in infants) and repeat at 7 days, 2) treat all household members simultaneously whether symptomatic or not, and 3) hot-wash or seal all clothing and bedding for 72 hours. Contrast classic scabies (10-15 mites, intense nocturnal itch) with crusted scabies (millions of mites, minimal itch, immunocompromised host).

[SN]Pediculosis[/SN]

PEDICULOSIS

- **Aetiological Taxonomy**: Blood-sucking ectoparasitic lice specific to humans:
  - **Pediculus humanus capitis (Head Louse)**: Infests scalp hair, cementing oval white egg cases ("nits") firmly to the base of hair shafts; spread via direct head-to-head contact or shared combs, caps, and bedding, predominantly among primary school children.
  - **Pediculus humanus corporis (Body Louse)**: Resides and lays eggs in the seams and folds of inner clothing rather than on the skin, migrating to skin only to feed; highly associated with extreme poverty, homelessness, lack of laundry facilities, and refugee camps.
  - **Pthirus pubis (Pubic / Crab Louse)**: Infests coarse pubic and perianal hair (occasionally eyelashes and axillary hair); transmitted almost exclusively via sexual contact or close physical cohabitation.
- **Vector Potential of Body Lice**: Crucial public health vector transmitting three major historical epidemic infections:
  - **Epidemic Typhus**: Caused by *Rickettsia prowazekii*; transmitted through contamination of bite wounds with infectious louse faeces scratched into skin.
  - **Trench Fever**: Caused by *Bartonella quintana*; transmitted via louse faeces.
  - **Louse-Borne Relapsing Fever**: Caused by *Borrelia recurrentis*; transmitted when infected lice are crushed onto abraded skin.
- **Therapeutic and Control Measures**:
  - **Head Lice Control**: Topical Permethrin 1% lotion or 5% cream applied to dry hair and scalp, rinsed after 10 minutes, and repeated after 7 to 9 days to destroy emerging nymphs; mechanical wet-combing with a fine-toothed nit comb.
  - **Body Lice Control**: Thorough laundering of clothing and bed linen in hot water (>60 degrees C) or dry cleaning, accompanied by hot ironing of inner clothing seams; insecticidal dusting (1% permethrin powder) in refugee or disaster camp settings.
  - **Pubic Lice Control**: Permethrin 1% lotion applied to pubic and adjacent hairy regions, washed off after 10 minutes; simultaneous screening and treatment of sexual partners.

COMPARATIVE PROFILE OF HUMAN LICE INFESTATIONS

| Feature | Head Louse (*P. humanus capitis*) | Body Louse (*P. humanus corporis*) | Pubic Louse (*Pthirus pubis*) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Habitat** | Scalp hair, especially occipital and retroauricular | Seams and folds of inner clothing | Coarse pubic hair, perianal, axillary, lashes |
| **Primary Transmission** | Head-to-head contact, shared combs/hats | Shared clothing, unwashed bedding, overcrowding | Sexual intercourse, close bodily cohabitation |
| **Vector of Disease** | No known disease transmission | Epidemic typhus, relapsing fever, trench fever | No known disease transmission |
| **Primary Control Focus** | Topical pediculicide and fine-toothed combing | Clothing laundering (>60°C), ironing seams | Topical pediculicide, treat sexual partners |

> **EXAM TIP:** Remember that among human lice, only the body louse (Pediculus humanus corporis) acts as a vector for systemic human infections: Epidemic Typhus (Rickettsia prowazekii), Trench Fever (Bartonella quintana), and Relapsing Fever (Borrelia recurrentis). Body louse control is achieved through clothing hygiene and laundering (>60°C) rather than topical body application.

INDIAN PROGRAMMATIC CONTEXT

- **Integration with National Health Programmes**: Surface infections intersect multiple national public health initiatives. Trachoma elimination is maintained under the National Programme for Control of Blindness and Visual Impairment (NPCBVI), post-eradication surveillance for Yaws is sustained under the National Center for Vector Borne Diseases Control (NCVBDC), and Scabies and Pediculosis are managed through School Health and Wellness Programmes under Ayushman Bharat.

[REF]Reference: World Health Organization (WHO) SAFE Strategy Guidelines for Trachoma; National Yaws Eradication Programme (N-YEP) Verification Dossier; Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine.[/REF]

title: Non Communicable Diseases
description: Epidemiology and prevention of major non-communicable diseases in India, in textbook order: cardiovascular diseases, cancers, diabetes and obesity, blindness, accidents, then the expanded NP-NCD 2023-2030 package.

subsections.title: Coronary Heart Disease, Hypertension, Stroke, and Rheumatic Heart Disease
subsections.content:
OVERVIEW OF THE CHAPTER
The global and Indian health landscapes have undergone a profound epidemiological transition, shifting disease burden from acute infectious pestilence to chronic degenerative non-communicable diseases (NCDs). In India, this transition is marked by an Epidemiological Transition Ratio falling well below one, with NCDs inflicting disproportionate premature mortality and morbidity during peak productive years (ages 35 to 64).

South Asian populations exhibit a distinctive vascular and metabolic phenotype marked by accelerated atherogenesis, premature coronary artery disease, central adiposity, atherogenic dyslipidaemia, and insulin resistance. Arising from a complex web of causation driven by tobacco, unhealthy diets, physical inactivity, and environmental stressors, these permanent conditions resist curative approaches. Public health strategy therefore mandates population-wide primordial and primary prevention, risk-factor modification, and integrated primary healthcare screening.

DEFINITIONS
- **Non-Communicable Diseases (NCDs)**: Impairment of bodily structure and/or function that necessitates a modification of the patient's normal life, and has persisted over an extended period of time. Caused by non-reversible pathological alterations.
- **Epidemiological Transition Ratio (ETR)**: The ratio of Disability-Adjusted Life Years (DALYs) from Communicable, Maternal, Neonatal, and Nutritional Diseases (CMNNDs) to DALYs from NCDs and injuries. A ratio less than 1.0 indicates a higher burden of NCDs and injuries.
- **Coronary Heart Disease (CHD)**: Impairment of heart function due to inadequate blood flow to the heart compared to its needs, caused by obstructive changes in the coronary circulation.
- **Hypertension (HTN)**: A chronic condition of persistently elevated systemic arterial blood pressure, distributed continuously across populations, and representing a major modifiable risk factor for cardiovascular death and disability.
- **Stroke (Cerebrovascular Accident, CVA)**: Rapidly developed clinical signs of focal or global disturbance of cerebral function lasting more than 24 hours or leading to death, with no apparent cause other than that of vascular origin.
- **Rheumatic Heart Disease (RHD)**: Chronic valvular heart disease that follows Acute Rheumatic Fever (ARF), itself a non-suppurative delayed autoimmune sequela of pharyngitis caused by Group A Streptococcus (GAS), specifically Streptococcus pyogenes.

CORONARY HEART DISEASE (CHD)
- **Clinical Manifestations**: Angina pectoris, myocardial infarction (MI), congestive cardiac failure, cardiac dysrhythmias, and sudden cardiac death (cessation of circulation within 24 hours of acute symptom onset).
- **Indian Epidemiological Context**: Coronary heart disease presents approximately a decade earlier in South Asians than in Western cohorts, with peak onset classically occurring in the fifth and sixth decades. Males demonstrate higher incidence in classic registry series. Underlying hypertension, diabetes mellitus, central adiposity, and heavy tobacco consumption account for the majority of the population attributable risk.
- **Epidemiological Measurement of Burden**: Quantified using Proportional Mortality Rates, incidence rates, age-specific mortality rates, prevalence, and Case Fatality Rate (CFR).
- **Non-Modifiable Risk Factors**: Advanced age, male sex, positive family history, genetic polymorphisms, Type A behavioural patterns (excessive competitive drive, time urgency, and hostility), and South Asian ethnicity.
- **Modifiable Behavioural and Biological Risk Factors**:
  - **Tobacco Consumption**: Major driver of premature vascular mortality. Carbon monoxide promotes endothelial injury and atherogenesis; nicotine stimulates adrenergic overdrive, elevating heart rate, systemic blood pressure, and myocardial oxygen consumption. Risk demonstrates a linear dose-response relationship with daily cigarette consumption and exhibits progressive decline following sustained cessation.
  - **Elevated Blood Pressure**: Systemic arterial hypertension accelerates endothelial shear stress and atheroma formation; systolic blood pressure serves as the strongest continuous predictor of vascular risk.
  - **Dysglycaemia and Diabetes Mellitus**: Induces accelerated microvascular and macrovascular pathology through advanced glycation end-products and endothelial dysfunction.
  - **Adiposity and Physical Inactivity**: Elevated Body Mass Index (BMI), abdominal (visceral) adiposity, and sedentary lifestyle promote insulin resistance and chronic systemic inflammation.
  - **Atherogenic Dyslipidaemia**: Serum total cholesterol levels exceeding 200 mg/dL represent elevated risk. Low-Density Lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol is the primary atherogenic lipoprotein. Very-Low-Density Lipoprotein (VLDL) correlates with accelerated atherosclerosis and peripheral vascular disease. High-Density Lipoprotein (HDL) acts as a protective anti-atherogenic marker through reverse cholesterol transport.
  - **Dietary and Psychosocial Factors**: Excessive dietary sodium, trans-fatty acids, refined sugars, hazardous alcohol intake, emotional distress, and socio-economic deprivation.
- **Cardiovascular Prevention and Management**:
  - **Medical and Interventional Revascularization**: Guideline-directed pharmacotherapy (including beta-blockers, antiplatelet agents, and statins) alongside Coronary Artery Bypass Grafting (CABG) or Percutaneous Transluminal Coronary Angioplasty (PTCA) based on clinical stratification.
  - **Prudent Cardioprotective Diet**: Limiting total dietary fat to under 20% to 30% of daily energy intake, restricting saturated fats to under 7%, minimizing dietary cholesterol, maintaining sodium chloride intake below 5 g/day, eliminating trans-fats, and increasing complex carbohydrates, pulses, and dietary fibre.
  - **Lifestyle Modification**: Regular moderate aerobic exercise, structured weight control, smoking cessation, and stress reduction.
- **New York Heart Association (NYHA) Functional Classification**: Class I (no limitation of physical activity), Class II (slight limitation; comfortable at rest), Class III (marked limitation; comfortable only at rest), and Class IV (inability to carry out any physical activity without discomfort; symptoms present at rest).
- **Landmark Community Intervention Trials**:
  - **North Karelia Project (Finland)**: Pioneer comprehensive community-based intervention demonstrating dramatic reductions in cardiovascular mortality through dietary modification, smoking reduction, and hypertension control.
  - **Stanford Three-Community Study (USA)**: Evaluated mass-media public health education combined with intensive individual counselling in reducing cardiovascular risk factor profiles.
  - **Oslo Diet and Antismoking Trial (Norway)**: Randomized controlled trial confirming that dietary fat reduction and smoking cessation significantly reduce serum lipids and coronary incidence.
  - **Multiple Risk Factor Intervention Trial (MRFIT, USA)**: Large-scale trial assessing simultaneous intervention on smoking, hypercholesterolaemia, and hypertension in high-risk men.
  - **Multinational Monitoring of Trends and Determinants in Cardiovascular Disease (MONICA Project)**: Landmark World Health Organization (WHO) international collaborative study validating whether temporal changes in cardiovascular mortality reflect changes in known risk factor levels and healthcare delivery.

HYPERTENSION (HTN)

[SN]Hypertension: definition and measurement[/SN]

[LAQ]Natural history of hypertension[/LAQ]

- **Global and National Burden**: Major modifiable contributor to global Disability-Adjusted Life Years (DALYs) and cardiovascular mortality. Approximately 90% of cases are essential (primary) hypertension, with the remaining 10% secondary to renovascular, endocrine (e.g., Cushing syndrome, phaeochromocytoma), gestational, or pharmacological causes (including Oral Contraceptive Pills, OCPs).
- **Clinical Definition**: Under Indian Standard Treatment Guidelines (STG) and national program criteria, hypertension is defined as persistent elevation of blood pressure with systolic blood pressure (SBP) ≥140 mmHg and/or diastolic blood pressure (DBP) ≥90 mmHg, confirmed across multiple standardized readings. Blood pressure is a continuous variable without a true biological cut-off; cardiovascular risk rises progressively across all adult ranges.
- **Blood Pressure Classification (Standard Treatment Guidelines)**:
  - **Optimal Blood Pressure**: SBP <120 mmHg and DBP <80 mmHg.
  - **Normal Blood Pressure**: SBP 120 to 129 mmHg and/or DBP 80 to 84 mmHg.
  - **High-Normal Blood Pressure**: SBP 130 to 139 mmHg and/or DBP 85 to 89 mmHg.
  - **Grade 1 Hypertension (Mild)**: SBP 140 to 159 mmHg and/or DBP 90 to 99 mmHg.
  - **Grade 2 Hypertension (Moderate)**: SBP 160 to 179 mmHg and/or DBP 100 to 109 mmHg.
  - **Grade 3 Hypertension (Severe)**: SBP ≥180 mmHg and/or DBP ≥110 mmHg.
  - **Isolated Systolic Hypertension**: SBP ≥140 mmHg with DBP <90 mmHg.
- **Standardized Measurement Protocol**: Use of validated digital or aneroid sphygmomanometers; appropriate cuff bladder dimensions covering 80% of arm circumference; patient seated quietly for at least 5 minutes with back and supported arm at heart level, feet uncrossed on the floor; avoidance of caffeine or smoking for 30 minutes prior; taking multiple readings and recording the average. Opportunistic screening is mandated for all adults aged 30 years and above at primary healthcare contacts under the National Programme for Prevention and Control of Non-Communicable Diseases (NP-NCD).
- **Rule of Halves (Iceberg Phenomenon)**: Epidemiological principle describing community hypertension distribution: approximately one-half of hypertensive individuals remain undiagnosed; of those diagnosed, approximately one-half receive pharmacotherapy; and of those treated, only one-half achieve optimal blood pressure control.
- **Etiological Determinants**: Age-related vascular stiffening, genetic predisposition, South Asian ethnicity, excess sodium intake (>5 g/day), high dietary saturated fats, low dietary potassium, physical inactivity, abdominal obesity, hazardous alcohol intake, chronic psychological stress, and exposure to vasoconstrictive drugs.
- **Natural History and Target-Organ Damage**: Left untreated, chronic systemic hypertension accelerates systemic arteriolosclerosis and atheroma progression, culminating in end-organ damage: cerebrovascular disease (ischaemic and haemorrhagic stroke), coronary artery disease, left ventricular hypertrophy and heart failure, chronic kidney disease (nephrosclerosis), hypertensive retinopathy, and peripheral vascular disease. Blood pressure tracking from childhood into adulthood underscores the importance of primordial interventions.
- **Comprehensive Prevention Strategies**:
  - **Population-Wide (Mass) Strategy**: Aims to shift the entire community blood pressure distribution curve downward through primordial and primary measures, including population salt reduction, reduction of trans-fats, promotion of physical activity, and tobacco control.
  - **High-Risk (Targeted) Strategy**: Identifies individuals with established hypertension or high cardiovascular risk scores through opportunistic and community screening, followed by lifestyle intervention and guideline-directed antihypertensive pharmacotherapy.

[SN]DASH diet[/SN]

DASH DIET (Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension)
- **Dietary Architecture**: Evidence-based cardioprotective nutritional pattern rich in vegetables, fruits, and low-fat dairy products, while substantially reducing saturated and total fats. Emphasizes micronutrients that foster vasodilation, including potassium, calcium, magnesium, and dietary fibre.
- **Promoted Components**: Fresh leafy green vegetables, whole fruits, whole grains, pulses, low-fat dairy items, poultry, fish, and unsalted nuts and seeds in controlled quantities.
- **Restricted Components**: Dietary sodium chloride, red and processed meats, sugar-sweetened beverages, commercial sweets, and saturated fats.
- **Clinical Efficacy**: Randomized controlled trials demonstrate significant reductions in systolic and diastolic blood pressure, an effect potentiated when combined with sodium restriction, regular aerobic exercise, and weight optimization.
- **Indian Context Adaptations**: Promoting higher daily intake of seasonal green vegetables and lentils; substituting unrefined whole grains for polished rice; restricting high-sodium accompaniments (pickles, papads, commercial chutneys); and minimizing deep-fried snacks prepared in hydrogenated vegetable oils.

STROKE (CEREBROVASCULAR ACCIDENT)
- **Clinical Definition**: Rapidly developed clinical signs of focal or global disturbance of cerebral function lasting more than 24 hours or leading to death, with no apparent cause other than vascular origin. Transient Ischaemic Attack (TIA) is defined as a brief episode of neurological dysfunction caused by focal brain ischaemia without acute infarction, clinically resolving within 24 hours and functioning as an ominous herald of impending major stroke.
- **Pathological Classification**:
  - **Ischaemic Stroke (approximately 80% to 85% of cases)**: Encompasses large-artery cerebral thrombosis, cardioembolic stroke (frequently associated with atrial fibrillation, valvular disease, or mural thrombi), and small-vessel lacunar infarction.
  - **Haemorrhagic Stroke (approximately 15% to 20% of cases)**: Encompasses primary intracerebral haemorrhage (most often secondary to chronic uncontrolled hypertension) and subarachnoid haemorrhage (frequently resulting from ruptured saccular aneurysms or Arteriovenous Malformations, AVM).
- **Epidemiological Risk Factors**: Advanced age, male sex, prior TIA or stroke, systemic arterial hypertension (the single strongest modifiable determinant for both ischaemic and haemorrhagic varieties), cardiac disorders (atrial fibrillation, valvular defects), diabetes mellitus, cigarette smoking, dyslipidaemia, central obesity, and use of oral contraceptive pills in high-risk women.
- **Indian Epidemiological Context**: Stroke among young adults (under 45 years) accounts for a notably higher proportion of cases (15% to 30%) in India compared to Western populations, linked to premature atherosclerosis, rheumatic heart disease embolism, metabolic syndrome, and hypercoagulable states.
- **Levels of Prevention and Management**:
  - **Primary Prevention**: Population-wide blood pressure control, smoking cessation, salt reduction, management of diabetes, anticoagulation in non-valvular atrial fibrillation, and promotion of physical activity.
  - **Secondary Prevention**: Rapid acute clinical recognition using pre-hospital assessment tools (e.g., Face Arm Speech Time, FAST protocol); emergency non-contrast cranial Computed Tomography (CT) or Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI); intravenous thrombolysis within the therapeutic window (under 4.5 hours from symptom onset) or mechanical thrombectomy for eligible ischaemic cases; neurosurgical and blood pressure stabilization in haemorrhagic events.
  - **Tertiary Prevention**: Multidisciplinary neuro-rehabilitation, encompassing physical therapy, speech and language therapy, occupational retraining, and long-term secondary chemoprophylaxis (antiplatelets or anticoagulants, statins, and antihypertensives).

RHEUMATIC HEART DISEASE (RHD)
- **Natural History and Pathogenesis**: Acute Rheumatic Fever (ARF) represents a non-suppurative delayed autoimmune sequela occurring 2 to 3 weeks after pharyngeal infection by Group A Streptococcus (GAS), specifically Streptococcus pyogenes. It is not an active communicable disease itself, but an autoimmune complication of an antecedent respiratory infection. Approximately 1% to 3% of untreated streptococcal pharyngitis episodes culminate in ARF; recurrent bouts of ARF trigger progressive immune-mediated fibrovascular damage to cardiac valves, culminating in permanent Rheumatic Heart Disease (RHD).
- **Epidemiological Triad**:
  - **Agent Factors**: Group A β-haemolytic Streptococcus; rheumatogenicity is linked to specific cell-wall M protein serotypes (notably M types 1, 3, 5, 6, 14, 18, 19, and 24) characterized by molecular mimicry with human cardiac myosin.
  - **Host Factors**: Children aged 5 to 15 years; equal sex incidence for acute attacks (though chronic mitral stenosis predominates in adult females); genetic susceptibility involving specific Human Leukocyte Antigen (HLA) class II alleles (such as HLA-DR4, HLA-DR7).
  - **Environmental Factors**: Overcrowded living quarters, poor housing, low socio-economic status, inadequate access to primary healthcare, and seasonal variations corresponding to streptococcal respiratory epidemics.
- **Indian Epidemiological Context**: Rheumatic heart disease remains a notable cause of cardiovascular morbidity and mortality in developing settings. In India, juvenile mitral stenosis (rapidly progressive mitral valve stenosis developing in children and adolescents under 20 years of age) is uniquely prevalent due to repeated, untreated streptococcal throat infections and exuberant host immune response.
- **Clinical Features**: Migratory polyarthritis affecting large joints (knees, ankles, wrists, elbows); carditis involving endocardium, myocardium, and pericardium (pancarditis, presenting as new pathological murmurs, cardiomegaly, pericardial friction rub, or heart failure); Sydenham chorea; subcutaneous nodules over bony prominences; and erythema marginatum (serpiginous evanescent non-pruritic erythematous rash with central clearing).
- **Diagnostic Framework (Revised Jones Criteria)**: Requires documented evidence of preceding GAS pharyngeal infection (elevated or rising Antistreptolysin O, ASO titre, anti-DNase B, positive throat swab culture, or rapid antigen detection test) plus either two major manifestations, or one major and two minor manifestations.
  - **Major Manifestations**: Carditis (clinical or subclinical on echocardiography); arthritis (polyarthritis in low-risk settings; monoarthritis, polyarthritis, or polyarthralgia in moderate-to-high-risk populations); chorea; erythema marginatum; and subcutaneous nodules.
  - **Minor Manifestations**: Arthralgia (if arthritis is not counted as a major criterion); fever (≥38.5°C in low-risk, ≥38.0°C in moderate-to-high-risk); elevated inflammatory markers (Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate, ESR ≥60 mm/hour or C-Reactive Protein, CRP ≥3.0 mg/dL in low-risk; ESR ≥30 mm/hour or CRP ≥3.0 mg/dL in moderate-to-high-risk); and prolonged PR interval on Electrocardiogram (ECG) after adjusting for age (unless carditis is counted as a major criterion).
- **Levels of Prevention**:
  - **Primary Prevention**: Prompt and adequate antimicrobial treatment of GAS pharyngitis before the development of rheumatic fever. Drug of choice: single intramuscular injection of Benzathine Benzylpenicillin (1.2 million units for individuals weighing ≥27 kg; 600,000 units for children weighing <27 kg), or oral Penicillin V for a full 10-day course. For penicillin-allergic patients: oral erythromycin, azithromycin, or first-generation cephalosporins.
  - **Secondary Prophylaxis**: Continuous administration of an effective antimicrobial agent to prevent recurrent GAS colonization and recurrent ARF attacks. Drug of choice: intramuscular Benzathine Benzylpenicillin administered every 3 to 4 weeks (1.2 million units for ≥27 kg; 600,000 units for <27 kg).
  - **Duration of Secondary Prophylaxis**:
    - **Rheumatic Fever Without Carditis**: Minimum 5 years from last attack or until 21 years of age, whichever is longer.
    - **Rheumatic Fever With Carditis Without Valvular Defect**: Minimum 10 years from last attack or until 21 years of age, whichever is longer.
    - **Rheumatic Heart Disease With Residual Valvular Defect**: Minimum 10 years from last attack or until 40 years of age (sometimes lifelong in high-risk occupational environments), whichever is longer.
  - **Jai Vigyan Mission (ICMR)**: Initiated in 2000 by the Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR) as a national mission-mode project for community- and school-based screening, registry maintenance, penicillin chemoprophylaxis adherence, and public awareness.

> **EXAM TIP:** In written answers for Rheumatic Heart Disease, differentiate clearly between primary prevention (eradicating GAS pharyngitis with a single dose of intramuscular benzathine penicillin) and secondary prophylaxis (regular penicillin injections every 3 to 4 weeks to prevent recurrent attacks). Always state the three duration tiers of secondary prophylaxis based on valvular involvement.

KEY POINTS
- **Epidemiological Transition Ratio**: Falls below 1.0 as non-communicable diseases and injuries outpace communicable, maternal, neonatal, and nutritional disorders.
- **Case Fatality Rate**: Quantifies the acute killing power and clinical severity among diagnosed cases of a disease.
- **Tobacco Exposure Intensity**: Filter cigarettes do not confer cardiovascular protection; coronary risk correlates directly with cumulative exposure duration and daily volume.
- **Rule of Halves in Hypertension**: Reflects substantial community attrition across the detection, treatment, and clinical control cascade.
- **Predominant Stroke Mechanism**: Cerebral ischaemia and arterial thrombosis account for the overwhelming majority of stroke presentations.
- **Juvenile Mitral Stenosis**: Distinctive South Asian presentation characterized by rapid valvular cicatrization within 5 to 10 years of initial acute rheumatic fever attacks.

FORMULAS AND CALCULATIONS
Mortality metrics:
- **Proportional Mortality Rate (PMR)**: (deaths from a specific cause / total deaths from all causes) × 100
- **Case Fatality Rate (CFR)**: (deaths from a specific disease / total diagnosed cases of that disease) × 100
- **Epidemiological Transition Ratio (ETR)**: Total DALYs from CMNNDs / Total DALYs from NCDs and Injuries

[REF]Reference: Standard Community Medicine NCD chapter (cardiovascular cluster); World Health Organization Stroke Diagnostic Criteria; Revised Jones Criteria (AHA 2015 update); Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (MoHFW) Standard Treatment Guidelines and NP-NCD 2023-2030 Guidelines; ICMR Jai Vigyan Mission on RF/RHD.[/REF]

subsections.title: Cancers: Epidemiology, Downstaging, and Cervical Cancer Elimination
subsections.content:
OVERVIEW OF THE CHAPTER
Malignant neoplasms represent a diverse collective of non-communicable disorders marked by autonomous cellular proliferation, local tissue invasion, and distant metastatic dissemination. In India, cancers represent a leading cause of premature adult mortality. Cancer epidemiology elucidates behavioural, environmental, and oncogenic infectious determinants to deploy primordial safeguards, while implementing secondary strategies, notably clinical downstaging and organized screening, to interrupt carcinogenesis at early, curable stages.

DEFINITIONS
- **Cancer (Malignant Neoplasm)**: A heterogeneous group of diseases characterized by uncontrolled cellular proliferation, loss of contact inhibition, local infiltration into adjacent tissue architectures, and systemic dissemination via haematogenous or lymphatic metastasis.
- **Carcinoma**: Malignant epithelial neoplasm arising from ectodermal or endodermal tissue layers (e.g., squamous cell carcinoma, adenocarcinoma).
- **Sarcoma**: Malignant mesenchymal neoplasm arising from connective tissues, including bone, cartilage, striated or smooth muscle, and fat.
- **Downstaging of Cancer**: A public health strategy utilizing health education, clinical suspicion, and basic physical examination to detect cancer at an earlier, localized clinical stage in populations lacking access to high-resource organized screening programs.
- **Cervical Cancer Elimination Threshold**: The World Health Organization (WHO) benchmark defining elimination as a public health problem when sustained national incidence reaches 4 or fewer cases per 100,000 women-years.

CANCERS

[LAQ]Epidemiology of cancers and levels of prevention[/LAQ]

[SN]Strategies to reduce burden of cancers[/SN]

- **Epidemiological Classification**: Malignant neoplasms are classified by histogenesis into carcinomas (epithelial origin), sarcomas (mesenchymal connective tissue origin), lymphomas and leukaemias (haematopoietic and lymphoid lineages), and neuroectodermal tumours.
- **Global and National Disease Burden**: Cancers constitute the second leading non-communicable cause of death globally. In India, tobacco-related malignancies (oral cavity, lung, oesophagus, and hypopharynx) dominate among males, whereas breast, cervix uteri, and ovarian carcinomas account for the major burden among females. Exact site-specific rankings reflect National Cancer Registry Programme (NCRP) data from the Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR).
- **Major Etiological Determinants and Risk Factors**:
  - **Tobacco and Areca Nut**: Principal preventable cause of malignant transformation. Smoked tobacco (cigarettes, bidis, hookahs) drives carcinomas of the lung, larynx, and oesophagus; smokeless tobacco (khaini, gutkha, zarda) and betel quid with areca nut drive oral and pharyngeal malignancies through direct chemical carcinogens including tobacco-specific nitrosamines (TSNAs).
  - **Alcohol Abuse**: Synergistic co-carcinogen with tobacco, precipitating upper aerodigestive tract, hepatic, and colorectal carcinomas.
  - **Dietary and Metabolic Risk Factors**: Diets high in processed meats, aflatoxins (hepatocellular carcinoma), and low in dietary fibre and fresh vegetables; obesity and physical inactivity (endometrial, postmenopausal breast, and colorectal cancers).
  - **Oncogenic Biological Agents**: Human Papillomavirus (HPV types 16, 18, 31, 33, 45) in cervical, anogenital, and oropharyngeal cancers; Hepatitis B Virus (HBV) and Hepatitis C Virus (HCV) in hepatocellular carcinoma; Helicobacter pylori in gastric adenocarcinoma and MALT lymphoma; Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV) in nasopharyngeal carcinoma and Burkitt lymphoma; and Schistosoma haematobium in squamous cell carcinoma of the bladder.
  - **Occupational and Environmental Carcinogens**: Asbestos (malignant pleural mesothelioma and lung cancer), aromatic amines such as 2-naphthylamine (bladder carcinoma), benzene (acute myeloid leukaemia), arsenic, and ionizing/ultraviolet radiation (melanoma, non-melanoma skin cancers).
  - **Genetic and Familial Susceptibility**: Inherited cancer syndromes such as BRCA1 and BRCA2 mutations in breast and ovarian cancers, and familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP) in colorectal malignancies.
- **Seven Warning Signs of Cancer (American Cancer Society)**:
  - **Change in Bowel or Bladder Habits**: Persistent alteration in colorectal motility or urinary frequency indicative of colorectal or urological malignancy.
  - **A Sore That Does Not Heal**: Chronic non-healing mucosal or cutaneous ulceration persisting beyond two to three weeks.
  - **Unusual Bleeding or Discharge**: Spontaneous postmenopausal, intermenstrual, haemoptysis, haematuria, or rectal bleeding.
  - **Thickening or Lump in Breast or Elsewhere**: Painless, firm, discrete mass in mammary gland, soft tissue, or lymph nodes.
  - **Indigestion or Difficulty in Swallowing**: Progressive dysphagia or persistent dyspepsia suggestive of oesophageal or gastric neoplasia.
  - **Obvious Change in Wart or Mole**: Alteration in color, diameter, shape, symmetry, or elevation.
  - **Nagging Cough or Hoarseness**: Unresolved cough or dysphonia persisting beyond two weeks in smokers.
- **Mnemonic Formulation**: **CAUTION**
  - **C**: Change in bowel or bladder habits
  - **A**: A sore that does not heal
  - **U**: Unusual bleeding or discharge
  - **T**: Thickening or lump in breast or elsewhere
  - **I**: Indigestion or difficulty in swallowing
  - **O**: Obvious change in a wart or mole
  - **N**: Nagging cough or persistent hoarseness
- **Comprehensive Levels of Prevention**:
  - **Primordial Prevention**: Macro-level national policies curbing environmental carcinogens, strict taxation and advertising bans on tobacco products, and public food environment regulation.
  - **Primary Prevention**: Tobacco cessation campaigns; alcohol restriction; universal immunization with Hepatitis B vaccine (National Immunization Schedule) and HPV vaccine; occupational hygiene; elimination of asbestos; and treatment of precancerous conditions.
  - **Secondary Prevention**: Population screening and early clinical detection, including Visual Inspection with Acetic Acid (VIA) or Visual Inspection with Lugol's Iodine (VILI) and HPV DNA screening for cervical cancer; clinical breast examination (CBE) and mammography; oral visual examination (OVE) for tobacco users; and faecal occult blood testing or colonoscopy for colorectal neoplasms.
  - **Tertiary Prevention**: Multimodality oncological treatment (surgery, radiotherapy, systemic chemotherapy, immunotherapy), symptom palliation, psychological support, and structured pain relief following the WHO Pain Ladder.
- **Statutory Framework for Tobacco Control**: The Cigarettes and Other Tobacco Products (Prohibition of Advertisement and Regulation of Trade and Commerce, Production, Supply and Distribution) Act (COTPA), 2003:
  - **Public Smoking Ban (Section 4)**: Prohibition of smoking in all public spaces and healthcare/educational premises.
  - **Advertising Prohibition (Section 5)**: Prohibition of direct and indirect commercial advertising, promotion, and brand sponsorship.
  - **Minor Protection (Section 6)**: Prohibition of tobacco sale to individuals under 18 years of age and within a 100-yard radius of educational institutions.
  - **Packaging Mandates (Section 7)**: Mandatory conspicuous pictorial health warnings covering specified packaging surface areas alongside toxic emission disclosures.

[SN]Downstaging of cancers[/SN]

DOWNSTAGING OF CANCERS
- **Conceptual Definition**: A population-level secondary prevention strategy focused on early clinical diagnosis, where community awareness, primary healthcare worker training, and prompt diagnostic referral shift the distribution of clinical stages at presentation from advanced, untreatable stages (Stage III and IV) to early, treatable stages (Stage I and II).
- **Epidemiological Rationale**: Cancer prognosis, disease-free survival, and treatment costs correlate inversely with clinical stage at presentation. In resource-constrained settings where mass screening is logistically infeasible, downstaging represents a cost-effective operational bridge.
- **Operational Components**:
  - **Community Sensitization**: Educating populations on early warning symptoms (CAUTION signs) to reduce patient delay.
  - **Primary Health Worker Empowerment**: Equipping Accredited Social Health Activists (ASHAs), Auxiliary Nurse Midwives (ANMs), and Community Health Officers (CHOs) at Ayushman Arogya Mandirs to conduct basic physical examinations (oral cavity inspection, clinical breast examination).
  - **Health Systems Strengthening**: Streamlining fast-track referral pathways to eliminate provider and diagnostic delay.
  - **Standardized Treatment Protocols**: Providing prompt oncological care and tracking stage distribution trends at district and tertiary cancer centres.
- **Operational Contrast With Screening**: Screening identifies unrecognized, asymptomatic disease in apparently healthy individuals through standardized tests, whereas downstaging aims at earlier clinical identification of symptomatic patients presenting with early warning signs. Both approaches are harmonized under the NP-NCD service package.

[SN]Cervical cancer elimination strategies[/SN]

CERVICAL CANCER ELIMINATION STRATEGIES
- **Global Elimination Benchmark**: The World Health Organization (WHO) Global Strategy aims to achieve an incidence threshold of 4 or fewer cases per 100,000 women-years across all countries.
- **WHO 90-70-90 Targets for 2030**:
  - **Primary Prevention (90%)**: 90% of girls fully vaccinated with the Human Papillomavirus (HPV) vaccine by 15 years of age.
  - **Secondary Prevention (70%)**: 70% of women screened with a high-performance test (such as HPV DNA testing) by 35 years of age, and again by 45 years of age.
  - **Tertiary Prevention and Management (90%)**: 90% of women identified with cervical disease treated (90% of precancerous lesions managed; 90% of invasive cervical cancers treated).
- **Operational Screening Modalities**:
  - **HPV DNA Molecular Testing**: Gold-standard high-performance test with high negative predictive value, enabling longer screening intervals (every 5 to 10 years).
  - **Visual Inspection with Acetic Acid (VIA)**: Application of 3% to 5% dilute acetic acid to the cervix; opaque white aceto-white lesions near the squamocolumnar junction indicate precancerous dysplasia. Feasible in low-resource settings allowing a single-visit screen-and-treat approach (thermal ablation or cryotherapy).
  - **Visual Inspection with Lugol's Iodine (VILI)**: Application of Lugol's iodine; non-staining mustard-yellow areas represent glycogen-depleted precancerous tissue.
  - **Cervical Cytology (Papanicolaou Pap Smear)**: Conventional or liquid-based cytology detecting dysplastic cellular morphology.
- **Implementation in Indian Public Health**: Delivery of HPV immunization through national platforms; opportunistic screening of women aged 30 to 65 years at Ayushman Arogya Mandir and Primary Health Centre (PHC) facilities under NP-NCD; and linkage of screen-positive individuals to District Hospitals and Medical Colleges for colposcopy, biopsy, and treatment.

[SN]Oral leukoplakia: approach to risk-factor study[/SN]

ORAL LEUKOPLAKIA: EPIDEMIOLOGICAL INVESTIGATION PROTOCOL
- **Investigation Objective**: To evaluate the epidemiological association and calculate the strength of association (Odds Ratio) between putative risk factors (tobacco, areca nut, alcohol) and oral leukoplakia in a designated population.
- **Optimal Methodological Design**: Unmatched or matched case-control study design, representing the most logistically efficient, rapid, and cost-effective approach for investigating risk factors of relatively uncommon premalignant conditions.
- **Case Definition and Selection**: Individuals clinically diagnosed with oral leukoplakia (defined by the WHO as a white plaque or patch of questionable risk having excluded other known diseases or disorders that carry no increased risk for cancer), confirmed by histopathological biopsy showing hyperkeratosis or dysplasia.
- **Control Selection**: Age- and sex-matched individuals selected from the same catchment community or hospital outpatient clinic without evidence of oral mucosal lesions.
- **Exposure Measurement**: Standardized interviewer-administered questionnaire capturing duration, frequency, type of tobacco (bidis, cigarettes, khaini, gutkha, paan with tobacco), areca nut consumption, alcohol use, oral hygiene practices, and nutritional history.
- **Statistical Analysis**: Calculation of Odds Ratios (OR) with 95% Confidence Intervals (CI); stratified Mantel-Haenszel analysis or multivariable logistic regression modeling to adjust for confounding variables and assess synergistic interactions (e.g., tobacco plus alcohol); evaluation of dose-response relationships.
- **Ethical Safeguards**: Institutional Ethics Committee clearance; informed voluntary written consent; and provision of structured tobacco and areca nut cessation counselling and referral for all participants.

> **EXAM TIP:** In questions detailing cancer prevention, structure answers systematically according to the four levels: Primordial (tobacco taxation/COTPA), Primary (HPV/HBV vaccination, lifestyle), Secondary (Downstaging, VIA/Pap/HPV screening), and Tertiary (Palliative care, WHO pain ladder). Examiners award high marks for citing the specific WHO 90-70-90 targets for cervical cancer elimination.

KEY POINTS
- **Leading Malignancy Profiles**: Tobacco-related oral and lung cancers predominate among Indian men; breast and cervical carcinomas dominate among Indian women.
- **Downstaging Versus Screening**: Downstaging focuses on earlier clinical detection of symptomatic cases, whereas screening tests asymptomatic populations.
- **Triple Elimination Targets**: The WHO 2030 targets mandate 90% HPV immunization, 70% high-performance screening, and 90% treatment of precancer and invasive cancer.
- **Statutory Enforcement**: COTPA 2003 forms the cornerstone of Indian legislative tobacco control across public spaces, advertising, and packaging.

[REF]Reference: WHO cervical cancer elimination 90-70-90; COTPA 2003; NP-NCD cancer screening pathways; National Cancer Registry Programme (ICMR-NCRP).[/REF]

subsections.title: Diabetes Mellitus, Obesity, Physical Activity, and WHO STEPS
subsections.content:
OVERVIEW OF THE CHAPTER
Diabetes mellitus and obesity constitute twin metabolic epidemics accelerating cardiovascular risk and microvascular end-organ damage across populations. Driven by nutritional transitions and sedentary behaviours, their surging prevalence in developing countries imposes heavy disease burdens. Managing this crisis requires standardized risk-factor surveillance, grounded in the World Health Organization (WHO) STEPwise approach, combined with primary healthcare screening, lifestyle intervention, and integrated community prevention frameworks.

DEFINITIONS
- **Diabetes Mellitus (DM)**: A heterogeneous group of metabolic disorders characterized by persistent chronic hyperglycaemia resulting from defects in insulin secretion, insulin action, or both, leading to disturbances in carbohydrate, lipid, and protein metabolism.
