- **Obesity**: A state of abnormal or excessive accumulation of adipose tissue in the body resulting from an imbalance between energy intake and energy expenditure, which impairs physical health and elevates morbidity and mortality.
- **Impaired Fasting Glucose (IFG)**: An intermediate metabolic state defined by fasting plasma glucose levels between 100 mg/dL and 125 mg/dL (5.6 to 6.9 mmol/L).
- **Impaired Glucose Tolerance (IGT)**: An intermediate metabolic state characterized by a two-hour post-load plasma glucose between 140 mg/dL and 199 mg/dL (7.8 to 11.0 mmol/L) following a 75 g oral glucose tolerance test.
- **Metabolic Syndrome**: A constellation of interconnected physiological, biochemical, and metabolic risk factors, including abdominal adiposity, insulin resistance, atherogenic dyslipidaemia, and elevated systemic arterial blood pressure.

DIABETES MELLITUS (DM)
- **Global and National Epidemiology**: Characterized as a global pandemic; India carries one of the largest national caseloads worldwide. Marked by accelerated onset at younger adult ages and lower body mass thresholds compared to Western populations. World Diabetes Day is observed annually on 14 November.
- **Etiological Classification**:
  - **Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus**: Results from autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta cells, causing absolute insulin deficiency; typically manifests during childhood or adolescence; associated with Human Leukocyte Antigen (HLA) class II genotypes (specifically HLA-DR3 and HLA-DR4).
  - **Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus**: Accounts for over 90% of global diabetes cases; characterized by peripheral insulin resistance accompanied by progressive relative secretory defect of beta cells; strongly linked to genetic susceptibility, central adiposity, physical inactivity, and unhealthy diet.
  - **Gestational Diabetes Mellitus (GDM)**: Hyperglycaemia with onset or first recognition during pregnancy; elevates maternal-fetal perinatal risks and conveys high lifetime risk of future Type 2 diabetes.
  - **Other Specific Types**: Genetic defects of beta-cell function (Maturity-Onset Diabetes of the Young, MODY), genetic defects in insulin action, exocrine pancreatic diseases (chronic pancreatitis, fibrocalculous pancreatic diabetes), endocrinopathies (Cushing syndrome, acromegaly), and drug-induced forms (corticosteroids, thiazides).
- **Etiological Determinants and Pathogenesis**: Genetic predisposition; environmental triggers; viral agents (implicated in Type 1 pathogenesis, including Coxsackie B4, mumps, and congenital rubella); chemical toxins; nutritional transition towards ultra-processed foods; and sedentary behaviour.
- **World Health Organization Diagnostic Criteria**:
  - **Fasting Plasma Glucose (FPG)**: ≥126 mg/dL (7.0 mmol/L) after an overnight fast of at least 8 hours.
  - **Two-Hour Post-Load Plasma Glucose**: ≥200 mg/dL (11.1 mmol/L) during a standard 75 g Oral Glucose Tolerance Test (OGTT).
  - **Random Plasma Glucose**: ≥200 mg/dL (11.1 mmol/L) in the presence of classic diabetic symptoms (polyuria, polydipsia, polyphagia, unexplained weight loss).
  - **Glycated Haemoglobin (HbA1c)**: ≥6.5% (48 mmol/mol) measured using a standardized National Glycohemoglobin Standardization Program (NGSP) certified assay.
- **Screening Methodologies**: High-risk targeted screening is prioritized, evaluating individuals with age ≥30 years, central adiposity, positive family history, hypertension, prior GDM, or polycystic ovary syndrome. Glucosuria (urine glucose) is insensitive for early or mild disease due to the renal threshold for glucose (approximately 180 mg/dL).
- **Levels of Prevention**:
  - **Primordial Prevention**: Societal policies promoting whole foods, physical activity spaces, and taxation on sugar-sweetened beverages.
  - **Primary Prevention**: Lifestyle modification (5% to 7% sustained weight reduction, moderate physical activity of 150 minutes/week, reduction of saturated fat, and tobacco cessation); pharmacotherapy (metformin in high-risk prediabetes).
  - **Secondary Prevention**: Opportunistic screening under the National Programme for Prevention and Control of Non-Communicable Diseases (NP-NCD); tight glycaemic control; blood pressure control (<130/80 mmHg); lipid-lowering therapy with statins; regular screening for microvascular complications.
  - **Tertiary Prevention**: Management of established complications: diabetic retinopathy (laser photocoagulation), diabetic nephropathy (ACE inhibitors/ARBs, dialysis), diabetic neuropathy and diabetic foot care (ulcer prevention, offloading, amputation prevention).

[SN]Diabetic care indicators in the community[/SN]

PROCESS AND OUTCOME INDICATORS FOR DIABETIC CARE
- **Purpose and Programmatic Role**: Systematically assess the operational quality, coverage, and clinical effectiveness of community- and facility-based diabetes care under public health programs.
- **Process Indicators (Health Systems and Delivery)**:
  - **Screening Coverage**: Proportion of eligible adult population (aged 30 years and above) screened for elevated blood glucose in the catchment community per year.
  - **Registration and Follow-up Rate**: Proportion of newly diagnosed diabetic individuals registered in NCD clinics who attend regular monthly or quarterly follow-up visits.
  - **Blood Pressure Assessment Rate**: Proportion of registered diabetic patients with documented blood pressure measurement at each clinical visit.
  - **Comprehensive Complication Screening**: Proportion of diabetic patients undergoing annual visual acuity/fundus examination, monofilament foot assessment, and urinary microalbuminuria/serum creatinine testing.
  - **Therapeutic Adherence and Supply**: Proportion of clinical encounters where essential anti-diabetic pharmacotherapy is fully dispensed without stock-outs.
- **Outcome Indicators (Clinical and Epidemiological Impact)**:
  - **Glycaemic Control Rate**: Proportion of registered diabetic patients achieving target glycaemic control (HbA1c <7.0% or fasting plasma glucose <130 mg/dL).
  - **Blood Pressure Control in Diabetics**: Proportion of diabetic patients with coexisting hypertension achieving target blood pressure (<130/80 mmHg).
  - **Acute Metabolic Complication Incidence**: Hospitalization rates for severe hypoglycaemia, Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA), or Hyperosmolar Hyperglycaemic State (HHS).
  - **End-Stage Organ Damage Incidence**: Incidence of lower-extremity non-traumatic amputations, new-onset end-stage renal disease (ESRD) requiring dialysis, and vision-threatening diabetic retinopathy.

OBESITY

[LAQ]Community assessment of obesity[/LAQ]

[SN]Anthropometric indices of obesity[/SN]

- **Overview and Phenotypes**: Abnormal expansion of adipose tissue mass. Android (central, abdominal, visceral) obesity represents a far more powerful driver of atherogenesis, dyslipidaemia, and type 2 diabetes than gynoid (peripheral, gluteofemoral) adiposity.
- **Anthropometric Indices and Diagnostic Cut-Offs**:
  - **Body Mass Index (BMI, Quetelet Index)**: Calculated as weight in kilograms divided by height in metres squared (kg/m²).
    - **WHO International Classification**: Underweight: <18.5; Normal weight: 18.5 to 24.9; Overweight (Pre-obese): 25.0 to 29.9; Class I Obesity: 30.0 to 34.9; Class II Obesity: 35.0 to 39.9; Class III Obesity (Severe/Morbid): ≥40.0.
    - **WHO Asian / Indian Revised Criteria**: Underweight: <18.5; Normal weight: 18.5 to 22.9; Overweight (At risk): 23.0 to 24.9; Obese: ≥25.0.
  - **Waist Circumference (WC)**: Direct surrogate of visceral adipose tissue volume. International cut-offs: >102 cm in men and >88 cm in women. South Asian action thresholds: ≥90 cm in men and ≥80 cm in women indicate central obesity.
  - **Waist-to-Hip Ratio (WHR)**: Ratio of waist circumference to maximum hip circumference. Central obesity cut-offs: >0.90 in men and >0.85 in women.
  - **Waist-to-Height Ratio (WHtR)**: Simple population metric; values ≥0.5 indicate elevated cardiometabolic risk across all sexes and ethnic groups.
  - **Broca Index**: Quick estimate of ideal body weight: Ideal Weight (kg) = Height (cm) − 100.
  - **Lorentz Formula**: Sex-adjusted modification of Broca index: Ideal Weight (kg) = Height (cm) − 100 − [(Height (cm) − 150) / 4 (men) or 2 (women)].
  - **Corpulence Index**: Calculated as Actual Body Weight / Desirable Body Weight; values exceeding 1.20 indicate obesity.
  - **Ponderal Index**: Calculated as Height (cm) / cube root of Weight (kg).
  - **Skinfold Thickness**: Caliper measurement of subcutaneous adipose folds (triceps, biceps, subscapular, suprailiac); triceps skinfold thickness exceeding 20 mm in males or 30 mm in females indicates excessive adiposity.
- **Community Assessment Protocol for Obesity**:
  - **Step 1: Objectives and Operational Criteria**: Formulating clear epidemiological objectives and designating explicit anthropometric diagnostic cut-offs (incorporating revised Asian BMI and waist circumference standards).
  - **Step 2: Study Design and Sampling Frame**: Selecting a cross-sectional population survey utilizing multistage probability cluster sampling representative of urban and rural strata.
  - **Step 3: Sample Size Calculation**: Estimating sample size based on anticipated obesity prevalence, desired precision, design effect, and non-response allowance.
  - **Step 4: Standardized Equipment and Field Training**: Calibrating electronic scales to the nearest 0.1 kg, stadiometers to the nearest 0.1 cm, and non-stretchable tension-controlled measuring tapes; conducting inter- and intra-observer reliability calibration.
  - **Step 5: Anthropometric Data Collection**: Measuring body weight, stature, waist circumference, and hip circumference following standardized WHO protocols.
  - **Step 6: Statistical Analysis and Stratification**: Calculating prevalence rates of overweight, obesity, and central adiposity, stratified by age, sex, socio-economic status, and rural-urban domicile.
  - **Step 7: Ethical Referral and Community Feedback**: Obtaining institutional ethics clearance, delivering individual dietary feedback, and referring high-risk individuals to primary health centres under NP-NCD.

COUCH POTATO SYNDROME

[SN]Couch potato syndrome[/SN]

- **Conceptual Definition**: A sociological and public health term denoting a chronic sedentary lifestyle characterized by prolonged bouts of sitting or reclining, high consumption of screen entertainment, and negligible expenditure of physical energy, typically accompanied by passive overconsumption of hyper-palatable, energy-dense foods.
- **Pathophysiological Consequences**: Suppressed lipoprotein lipase activity in skeletal muscle, diminished insulin-mediated glucose uptake, accelerated atherogenesis, and elevated risk of metabolic syndrome, type 2 diabetes, and premature cardiovascular death.
- **Public Health Countermeasures**: Active transport infrastructure, workplace sit-stand workstations, school movement breaks, enforcement of screen-time guidelines in children, and integration of physical activity counselling into primary care contacts.

[SN]WHO physical activity recommendations[/SN]

PHYSICAL ACTIVITY GUIDELINES (WHO 2020)
- **Adults Aged 18 to 64 Years**: Should perform at least 150 to 300 minutes of moderate-intensity aerobic physical activity, or at least 75 to 150 minutes of vigorous-intensity aerobic physical activity per week, or an equivalent combination. Additionally, muscle-strengthening activities involving all major muscle groups should be conducted on 2 or more days per week.
- **Children and Adolescents Aged 5 to 17 Years**: Should engage in an average of at least 60 minutes per day of moderate-to-vigorous intensity, mostly aerobic, physical activity throughout the week, incorporating vigorous-intensity and bone-strengthening activities on at least 3 days per week.
- **Sedentary Behaviour Guidance**: Limit total daily sedentary time; replace prolonged seated intervals with physical activity of any intensity (including light intensity); disrupt prolonged sitting every 30 to 60 minutes.
- **National Initiatives in India**: Integration of lifestyle counselling into NP-NCD, physical literacy in school curricula, and national physical fitness campaigns (Fit India Movement).

[SN]NCD risk factor survey (WHO STEPS)[/SN]

WHO STEPwise APPROACH TO NCD RISK FACTOR SURVEILLANCE (STEPS)
- **Core Purpose**: A standardized, sequential surveillance framework developed by the World Health Organization to gather representative, high-quality, and longitudinal non-communicable disease risk-factor data across populations and over time.
- **Hierarchical Surveillance Architecture**:
  - **STEP 1 (Behavioural Assessment)**: Administering a standardized questionnaire to collect socio-demographic details, tobacco consumption patterns, harmful alcohol use, nutritional practices (fruit, vegetable, and salt intake), physical activity levels, and personal/family history of raised blood pressure or diabetes.
  - **STEP 2 (Physical Measurements)**: Obtaining standardized physical measurements, including systolic and diastolic blood pressure, height, body weight, and waist circumference (with optional hip circumference).
  - **STEP 3 (Biochemical Assessment)**: Collecting biological specimens to measure fasting blood glucose, total cholesterol, HDL cholesterol, and triglycerides, with expanded modules assessing 24-hour urinary sodium and creatinine excretion.
- **Module Composition**: Each step incorporates core items (mandatory for basic cross-national comparability), expanded items (detailed epidemiological insights), and optional items (context-specific inquiries).
- **Public Health Applications**: Establishing national baseline prevalence; evaluating the effectiveness of public health interventions and policies; forecasting future chronic disease burdens; and monitoring progress toward national and global NCD monitoring frameworks.

> **EXAM TIP:** When writing community assessment of obesity, distinguish clearly between the WHO international BMI criteria and the revised Asian-specific criteria (overweight ≥23 kg/m², obesity ≥25 kg/m²). Do not confuse the viral associations of Type 1 diabetes (Coxsackie B, mumps) with the streptococcal origin of acute rheumatic fever.

FORMULAS AND CALCULATIONS
Obesity indicators:
- **Body Mass Index (BMI)**: Weight (kg) / Height² (m²)
- **Ponderal Index**: Height (cm) / cube root of Weight (kg)
- **Broca Index**: Height (cm) − 100
- **Lorentz Formula**: Height (cm) − 100 − [(Height (cm) − 150) / 4 (men) or 2 (women)]
- **Corpulence Index**: Actual Weight / Desirable Weight

KEY POINTS
- **Metabolic Amplification**: Obesity and physical inactivity significantly multiply the relative risk of developing Type 2 diabetes.
- **Tripartite Surveillance Architecture**: WHO STEPS systematically builds from behavioural questionnaires (Step 1) to physical anthropometry (Step 2) to biochemical laboratory assays (Step 3).
- **Asian Cut-Off Specificity**: South Asian populations experience substantial metabolic dysregulation at lower BMI (≥23 kg/m²) and waist circumference (≥90 cm in men, ≥80 cm in women) than Western populations.

[REF]Reference: WHO diagnostic bands for diabetes; WHO 2020 Guidelines on Physical Activity and Sedentary Behaviour; WHO STEPwise approach to NCD risk factor surveillance; NP-NCD diabetes and obesity pathways.[/REF]

subsections.title: Blindness, Deafness, Disability Rights, and Pesticide Genetic Effects
subsections.content:
OVERVIEW OF THE CHAPTER
Sensory impairments and chronic physical disabilities impose profound personal suffering, social exclusion, and socioeconomic dependency upon populations. Within community medicine, the public health burden of visual loss and hearing impairment is largely preventable or surgically remediable through primary healthcare screening, timely nutritional prophylaxis, modern surgical techniques, and early rehabilitation under statutory human rights protections.

DEFINITIONS
- **Blindness (WHO and NPCBVI Standard)**: Visual acuity of less than 3/60 (Snellen) or inability to count fingers at a distance of 3 metres in the better eye with the best possible optical correction.
- **Low Vision (Visual Impairment)**: Visual acuity of less than 6/18 down to 3/60 in the better eye with the best possible optical correction.
- **Social Blindness**: Visual acuity of less than 6/60 in the better eye, rendering an individual unable to perform occupations requiring normal vision.
- **Deafness and Hearing Impairment**: Complete or partial loss of the ability to hear sound in one or both ears; disabling hearing impairment in adults is defined by hearing loss exceeding 35 decibels (dB) in the better-hearing ear.
- **Disability**: Any restriction or lack of ability (resulting from an impairment) to perform an activity in the manner or within the range considered normal for a human being.

BLINDNESS AND VISUAL IMPAIRMENT
- **Epidemiological Definition and Cut-Offs**: The World Health Organization (WHO) and the National Programme for Control of Blindness and Visual Impairment (NPCBVI) define blindness as presenting visual acuity <3/60 in the better eye with best refractive correction.
- **WHO Visual Impairment Categories**:
  - **Category 0 (Mild or No Impairment)**: Visual acuity 6/18 or better.
  - **Category 1 (Moderate Impairment)**: Visual acuity <6/18 to 6/60.
  - **Category 2 (Severe Impairment)**: Visual acuity <6/60 to 3/60.
  - **Category 3 (Blindness)**: Visual acuity <3/60 to 1/60 (finger counting at 1 metre).
  - **Category 4 (Blindness)**: Visual acuity <1/60 to perception of light.
  - **Category 5 (Blindness)**: No perception of light.
- **Major Etiological Determinants**: Cataract constitutes the leading cause of blindness globally and in India (accounting for approximately 50% to 62% of national blindness). Other major causes include uncorrected refractive errors, glaucoma, diabetic retinopathy, corneal opacities (including trachoma, nutritional xerophthalmia, and trauma), and childhood blindness.
- **Preventive Tiers and Community Interventions**:
  - **Primary Level**: Prophylaxis against nutritional xerophthalmia with vitamin A supplementation (National Vitamin A Prophylaxis Programme); trachoma hygiene and face washing; measles immunization; eye protection in industry and agriculture; rubella immunization to avert congenital cataracts.
  - **Secondary Level**: Early diagnosis and high-volume, high-quality cataract surgery (manual small-incision cataract surgery, SICS, or phacoemulsification with intraocular lens, IOL implantation); school eye screening for early correction of refractive errors; screening for diabetic retinopathy and glaucoma.
  - **Tertiary Level**: Corneal grafting and eye banking networks; visual rehabilitation, orientation, and mobility training; low-vision aid distribution.
- **Vision 2020: The Right to Sight**: A global collaborative initiative launched by WHO and the International Agency for the Prevention of Blindness (IAPB) to eliminate avoidable blindness by the year 2020. Globally, it targeted five conditions: cataract, refractive errors, trachoma, onchocerciasis, and childhood blindness. In the Indian epidemiological context, priority was expanded to seven conditions: cataract, refractive errors, childhood blindness, corneal blindness, glaucoma, diabetic retinopathy, and low vision.
- **National Programme for Control of Blindness and Visual Impairment (NPCBVI)**: Launched in 1976 as a 100% centrally sponsored scheme. Focuses on decentralization via District Health Societies, establishment of dedicated vision centres at Primary Health Centres (PHCs), upgrading Regional Institutes of Ophthalmology (RIOs), free IOL surgeries, school eye screening programs, and voluntary eye donation networks, with the national goal of reducing blindness prevalence to 0.3%.

DEAFNESS AND HEARING IMPAIRMENT

[LAQ]Prevention and control of deafness and hearing impairment[/LAQ]

- **Public Health Significance**: Pervasive sensory disorder impairing cognitive speech development in young children, educational attainment, occupational productivity, and social interaction in adults.
- **Comprehensive Levels of Prevention**:
  - **Primary Prevention**: Immunization against rubella, measles, mumps, and meningitis; clean and safe obstetric care preventing birth asphyxia and neonatal hyperbilirubinaemia; strict avoidance and rational administration of ototoxic pharmacotherapy (aminoglycosides, loop diuretics, cisplatin); occupational noise control (engineering safeguards, acoustic insulation, hearing protection devices in work environments exceeding 85 dB); public awareness against inserting unhygienic objects into the auditory canal.
  - **Secondary Prevention**: Universal newborn hearing screening utilizing Automated Auditory Brainstem Response (AABR) or Otoacoustic Emissions (OAE); preschool and school hearing screening; prompt medical management of acute otitis media and surgical clearance of chronic suppurative otitis media (CSOM); cerumen impaction removal.
  - **Tertiary Prevention**: Provision of subsidized, tailored hearing aids; cochlear implantation for profound sensorineural hearing loss in early childhood; auditory-verbal therapy; sign language instruction; and vocational rehabilitation.
- **National Programme for Prevention and Control of Deafness (NPPCD)**: Implemented under the National Health Mission (NHM) to prevent avoidable hearing loss, provide early detection and medical/surgical rehabilitation of ear ailments, upgrade district hospital ENT capacity, and train primary healthcare personnel.

DISABILITY RIGHTS AND GOVERNMENT PROVISIONS

[SN]Disability rights and government provisions[/SN]

- **Public Health Paradigm**: Disability represents a complex biosocial phenomenon demanding an evolution from paternalistic medical charity to a human-rights-based empowerment model. Public health mandates primary prevention of disabling diseases, timely therapeutic mitigation, barrier-free healthcare environments, and full socio-economic inclusion.
- **Statutory Framework (RPwD Act, 2016)**: The Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016, enacted to fulfill commitments under the United Nations Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (UNCRPD):
  - **Expansion of Categories**: Broadened recognized disability categories from 7 (under the 1995 Act) to 21 distinct conditions, including acid attack victims, Parkinson disease, multiple sclerosis, intellectual disabilities, autism spectrum disorder, and chronic neurological conditions.
  - **Non-Discrimination and Employment Quotas**: Mandating reasonable accommodation, non-discrimination in employment, and 4% reservation in government establishments for benchmark disabilities (≥40% certified impairment).
  - **Educational Entitlements**: Guaranteed free education for children with benchmark disabilities between 6 and 18 years of age in neighborhood or special schools.
  - **Statutory Penalties**: Legal liabilities and penalties for offenses and atrocities committed against persons with disabilities.
- **Health System Responsibilities**: Ensuring barrier-free architectural accessibility in all public hospitals; providing subsidized assistive technologies; instituting early intervention centres; and maintaining dignity, privacy, and informed consent in clinical management.
- **Community Medicine Integration**: Preventing major disabling conditions (stroke hemiplegia, diabetic peripheral neuropathy and amputation, traumatic brain injury from road crashes) through NP-NCD and trauma care, while orchestrating community-based rehabilitation (CBR).

PESTICIDES AND GENETIC EFFECTS

[SN]Pesticides and genetic effects[/SN]

- **Toxicological Spectrum and Exposure Pathways**: Agricultural pesticides (organophosphates, organochlorines, carbamates, synthetic pyrethroids) enter human systems via inhalation, dermal absorption, and ingestion of contaminated food and groundwater. Chronic occupational and bystander exposures are linked to endocrine disruption, reproductive toxicity, neurodegenerative disorders, and potential genotoxicity.
- **Genotoxic and Mutagenic Mechanisms**: Certain pesticide compounds generate reactive oxygen species (ROS), causing oxidative stress, DNA single- and double-strand breaks, sister chromatid exchanges, and chromosomal aberrations in exposed human lymphocytes.
- **Hierarchy of Occupational and Environmental Controls**:
  - **Elimination and Substitution**: Phasing out and banning highly hazardous pesticides (Class Ia and Ib under WHO classification); substituting safer chemical agents; and adopting Integrated Pest Management (IPM) to minimize chemical reliance.
  - **Engineering and Administrative Safeguards**: Implementing closed mixing systems; adhering to prescribed pre-harvest waiting periods; enforcing proper storage and disposal of empty pesticide containers.
  - **Personal Protection**: Mandating the continuous use of specialized Personal Protective Equipment (PPE), including non-permeable gloves, aprons, eye protection, and respirators during application.
  - **Medical Surveillance and Health Education**: Conducting periodic biomonitoring (such as blood cholinesterase activity for organophosphates) among agricultural workers, establishing poison control centres, and training peripheral healthcare workers in toxidrome identification and antidotal therapy (atropine, pralidoxime).

> **EXAM TIP:** For questions on Vision 2020, examiners evaluate whether you can contrast the five global target diseases (cataract, refractive errors, trachoma, onchocerciasis, childhood blindness) with India's expanded seven-disease priority list (which adds diabetic retinopathy, glaucoma, and corneal blindness). In disability rights, remember that the RPwD Act 2016 expanded protected categories from 7 to 21.

KEY POINTS
- **Primary Cause of Blindness**: Cataract remains the foremost cause of avoidable visual impairment both globally and within India.
- **Vision 2020 Expansion**: India expanded the global five-condition mandate to seven priority conditions reflecting regional epidemiological burdens.
- **Legislative Empowerment**: The RPwD Act 2016 establishes 21 recognized disability conditions and guarantees non-discrimination, education, and employment quotas.

[REF]Reference: WHO/NPCBVI blindness definition; NPPCD; Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016; National Programme for Control of Blindness and Visual Impairment (NPCBVI).[/REF]

subsections.title: Accidents, Injuries, Haddon Matrix, and Snakebite Envenoming
subsections.content:
OVERVIEW OF THE CHAPTER
Accidents and acute physical trauma represent major, preventable causes of premature mortality and long-term disability worldwide. Modern epidemiology approaches injuries not as random misfortune, but as predictable events resulting from interactions between human hosts, environmental hazards, and technological vectors. Applying systematic epidemiological models, particularly the Haddon matrix, enables multifaceted interventions across pre-event, event, and post-event phases, complemented by structured burn management and national envenomation control strategies.

DEFINITIONS
- **Accident**: An unexpected, unplanned, and unintended event that occurs suddenly and results in recognizable physical harm, bodily injury, death, or property damage.
- **Injury**: Physical damage to the human body resulting from acute exposure to energy (mechanical, thermal, electrical, chemical, or radiant) in amounts exceeding physiological tolerance, or from the acute deprivation of vital environmental elements (such as oxygen in drowning).
- **Accidentology**: The scientific study of accidents, examining their epidemiology, distribution, etiological determinants, behavioral dynamics, and evidence-based preventive countermeasures.
- **Haddon Matrix**: An analytical public health framework conceptualizing injury causation and prevention across a 3-by-3 grid intersecting the epidemiological triad (Host, Vector/Agent, Physical and Socioeconomic Environment) with the three temporal phases of an event (Pre-event, Event, Post-event).
- **Snakebite Envenoming**: A life-threatening, neglected tropical disease and acute medical emergency resulting from the injection of venomous toxins following the bite of a venomous snake.

ACCIDENTS AND INJURIES

[SN]Road traffic accidents and accidentology[/SN]

- **Accidentology and Preventability**: In contemporary public health, accidents are recognized as preventable events with distinct epidemiological patterns, risk factors, and causal pathways.
- **Road Traffic Accident (RTA) Fatality Definition**: Standard international epidemiological convention defines a road traffic death as any fatality occurring within 30 days of the vehicular crash as a direct consequence of the collision.
- **Classification of Unintentional and Intentional Injuries**:
  - **Unintentional Injuries**: Road traffic crashes, accidental falls, burns and scalds, drowning, accidental poisonings, and occupational injuries.
  - **Intentional Injuries**: Interpersonal violence, self-harm and suicide, and collective/war violence.
- **Etiological Determinants of Road Traffic Crashes**:
  - **Human (Host) Factors**: Young age, male sex, excessive speed, driving under the influence of alcohol or psychotropic substances, driver fatigue, mobile device distraction, failure to use safety restraints (helmets, seatbelts, child car seats), and aggressive driving behaviour.
  - **Vehicular (Vector) Factors**: Inadequate brake maintenance, worn tyres, absent anti-lock braking systems (ABS), lack of airbags, structural instability, overloaded commercial vehicles, and defective lighting systems.
  - **Environmental Factors**: Defective highway engineering, poorly demarcated pedestrian crossings, absent street lighting, potholed surfaces, lack of physical lane segregation between high-speed vehicles and vulnerable road users (pedestrians, cyclists, two-wheelers), adverse weather conditions, and lax traffic enforcement.
- **Comprehensive Prevention and the Haddon Matrix**:
  - **Pre-Event Phase**: Measures preventing the crash from occurring: speed calming, drink-driving checkpoints, road signage, public education, vehicle roadworthiness certifications, and graduated licensing.
  - **Event Phase**: Measures minimizing injury severity during crash impact: mandatory crash helmets conforming to safety standards, three-point seatbelts, automotive crumple zones, side-impact airbags, and energy-absorbing roadside crash barriers.
  - **Post-Event Phase**: Measures mitigating trauma consequences after impact: bystander first aid, prompt emergency medical response (108 ambulance systems), Golden Hour trauma care at designated trauma centres, surgical stabilization, and long-term neuro-orthopaedic rehabilitation.
- **Emergency Burn Management Protocol**:
  - **Scene Safety and Extinguishment**: Extinguish active flames by having the victim stop, drop, and roll or smothering flames with heavy woollen blankets; disconnect electrical sources; remove smouldering garments and constricting jewelry immediately.
  - **Thermal Neutralization**: Irrigate burned surfaces with clean, cool running water (15°C to 20°C) for 10 to 20 minutes to halt thermal penetration. Avoid applying ice, ice water, or freezing compresses which induce vasoconstriction and worsen tissue ischemia.
  - **Harmful Practices to Avoid**: Never apply unproven topical agents, toothpaste, cooking oils, cow dung, or raw turmeric; never puncture or aspirate intact blisters; avoid prolonged cold immersion which precipitates hypothermia in extensive burns.
  - **Wound Protection and Transport**: Cover cleansed burn wounds with clean, dry, sterile non-adherent dressings or clean linen, initiate early oral or intravenous fluid resuscitation following Parkland formulas for extensive burns, and transfer rapidly to a specialized burns unit.
- **Snakebite First Aid and Clinical Protocol**:
  - **Pre-Hospital First Aid Guidelines**: Reassure the patient (the majority of bites are by non-venomous species or represent dry bites without venom transfer); keep the victim calm and warm; immobilize the bitten limb using a broad splint and crepe bandage as for a bone fracture, maintaining the limb below heart level; remove rings and tight items before edema develops; ensure immediate, calm transport to a health facility stocking Anti-Snake Venom (ASV).
  - **Harmful Traditional Practices to Avoid**: Do not apply arterial tourniquets or tight bands (causes tissue necrosis, ischaemia, and massive venom release upon loosening); do not cut, incise, or suction the bite site; do not apply electrical shocks, herbal powders, or ice packs; do not administer unverified indigenous medications.
  - **Definitive In-Hospital Pharmacotherapy**: Administration of polyvalent Anti-Snake Venom (effective in India against the Big Four venomous species: Russell's viper, Spectacled cobra, Common krait, and Saw-scaled viper) upon development of systemic neurotoxic, haemotoxic, or severe local signs, managed alongside supportive airway and renal care.

[SN]National Action Plan for Snakebite Envenoming[/SN]

NATIONAL ACTION PLAN FOR PREVENTION AND CONTROL OF SNAKEBITE ENVENOMING (NAP-SE)
- **Programmatic Genesis**: Launched in 2024 by the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (MoHFW) to provide a strategic, multisectoral roadmap to curb snakebite mortality across India.
- **Strategic Targets**: Reduce snakebite-related deaths and morbidities by 50% by the year 2030, in full alignment with the World Health Organization (WHO) Global Snakebite Roadmap.
- **Core Strategic Pillars**:
  - **Human Health and Treatment Capabilities**: Strengthening primary and secondary public healthcare facilities (Ayushman Arogya Mandir, PHCs, CHCs, District Hospitals) by ensuring continuous supply of quality polyvalent Anti-Snake Venom (ASV), essential resuscitation equipment, and round-the-clock trained medical officers.
  - **Community Education and Early First Aid**: Conducting mass awareness campaigns educating agricultural workers and rural communities on protective footwear, torch usage at night, mosquito nets, and the lifesaving first-aid protocols.
  - **Disease Surveillance and Mandatory Notification**: Establishing snakebite envenoming as an officially notifiable condition across implementing States and Union Territories on the Integrated Health Information Platform (IHIP).
  - **One Health and Cross-Sectoral Convergence**: Collaborating actively with the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change, Department of Agriculture, and local Panchayati Raj institutions for ecological habitat management and farmer training.

> **EXAM TIP:** In written answers on injury prevention, construct the 3x3 Haddon Matrix table explicitly crossing Pre-event, Event, and Post-event phases with Host, Agent/Vehicle, and Environmental factors. For snakebite management, highlight the 'Big Four' venomous snakes in India (Cobra, Krait, Russell's viper, Saw-scaled viper) and contrast correct immobilization with dangerous traditional practices (no tourniquets, no incisions).

KEY POINTS
- **Structural Framework**: The Haddon Matrix remains the global paradigm for deconstructing and preventing physical trauma.
- **Thirty-Day Fatality Standard**: International convention classifies road traffic deaths as fatalities occurring within 30 days of the event.
- **National Envenomation Target**: NAP-SE (2024) commits to halving Indian snakebite mortality by 2030 through ASV availability, community training, and One Health convergence.

[REF]Reference: Haddon matrix teaching; MoHFW National Action Plan for Snakebite Envenoming (NAP-SE) 2024; WHO Global Snakebite Roadmap.[/REF]

subsections.title: COPD, Fatty Liver Disease, and NP-NCD 2023-2030
subsections.content:
OVERVIEW OF THE CHAPTER
The programmatic control of non-communicable diseases in India has strategically evolved beyond the original quaternary cluster of cardiovascular diseases, diabetes, cancer, and stroke. Under the updated National Programme for Prevention and Control of Non-Communicable Diseases (NP-NCD 2023 to 2030), the national policy architecture incorporates chronic respiratory illnesses, metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease, chronic kidney disease, and decentralized emergency networks for acute myocardial infarction.

DEFINITIONS
- **Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD)**: A common, preventable, and treatable chronic lung disease characterized by persistent respiratory symptoms and progressive airflow limitation resulting from airway and/or alveolar abnormalities, predominantly triggered by significant exposure to noxious particles or gases (Global Initiative for Chronic Obstructive Lung Disease, GOLD).
- **Non-Alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease (NAFLD)**: An umbrella clinicopathological condition defined by excessive hepatic fat accumulation (steatosis exceeding 5% of hepatocytes) in the absence of significant alcohol consumption or other secondary causes of hepatic lipid accrual, as designated in Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (MoHFW) operational guidelines.
- **Metabolic Dysfunction-Associated Steatotic Liver Disease (MASLD)**: The 2023 multi-society international consensus designation replacing NAFLD, defining hepatic steatosis in the presence of at least one of five cardiometabolic risk factors (overweight/obesity, impaired glucose tolerance/type 2 diabetes, hypertension, hypertriglyceridaemia, or low HDL cholesterol).
- **MetALD**: A distinct clinical category within the steatotic liver disease spectrum describing individuals with MASLD who additionally consume moderate quantities of alcohol (140 to 350 g/week for females, 210 to 420 g/week for males).
- **ST-Elevation Myocardial Infarction (STEMI)**: An acute cardiovascular emergency characterized by transmural myocardial ischemia resulting from abrupt occlusive thrombosis of an epicardial coronary artery, manifested on Electrocardiogram (ECG) by persistent ST-segment elevation.

[SN]COPD and asthma under NP-NCD[/SN]

COPD AND ASTHMA UNDER NP-NCD
- **Epidemiological Drivers in India**: Inhalation of tobacco smoke (active and passive smoking), household air pollution from the combustion of solid biomass fuels (wood, dung, crop residues) in poorly ventilated rural kitchens, ambient outdoor particulate pollution (PM2.5 and PM10), and occupational exposures to mineral dusts, chemical vapours, and noxious gases.
- **Programmatic Integration Under NP-NCD (2023 to 2030)**: Chronic respiratory diseases, specifically COPD and bronchial asthma, have been formally integrated into NP-NCD, broadening health system capacity beyond cardiovascular and metabolic targets.
- **Screening and Diagnostic Pathways**: While population-based community screening at Ayushman Arogya Mandir remains dedicated to adults aged 30 years and above for hypertension, diabetes, and oral, breast, and cervical cancers, COPD and asthma are systematically screened among symptomatic Outpatient Department (OPD) attendees at Primary Health Centres (PHCs) and Community Health Centres (CHCs).
- **Primary and Secondary Care Interventions**: Delivering brief opportunistic tobacco cessation interventions; counselling rural households on cleaner cooking fuels and kitchen ventilation; administering annual influenza and pneumococcal immunizations for vulnerable cohorts; training healthcare providers and patients on proper metered-dose inhaler (MDI) technique; and establishing spirometry testing networks at Sub-District Hospital (SDH) and District Hospital (DH) levels.
- **Environmental Policy Linkages**: Intersectoral convergence with the National Programme on Climate Change and Human Health (NPCCHH), the National Clean Air Programme (NCAP), and the Pradhan Mantri Ujjwala Yojana (PMUY) to lower ambient and household biomass exposures.

[SN]NAFLD, MASLD, and MetALD[/SN]

[LAQ]Fatty liver disease: terminology and NP-NCD integration[/LAQ]

FATTY LIVER DISEASE
- **Terminology and International Consensus Evolution**: In 2023, global hepatology and metabolic consensus panels adopted Metabolic Dysfunction-Associated Steatotic Liver Disease (MASLD) to replace the non-stigmatizing and physiologically affirmative nomenclature of Non-Alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease (NAFLD). The classification establishes MetALD to categorize individuals possessing metabolic risk factors who also consume moderate quantities of alcohol.
- **Indian National Policy Nomenclature**: The Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (MoHFW) maintains the operational title Non-Alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease (NAFLD) within national programme architecture, issuing the updated Operational Guidelines for NAFLD under NP-NCD (Version 2.0, 2024). In academic and clinical settings, both operational designations (NAFLD in programme delivery; MASLD in clinical taxonomy) are referenced.
- **Metabolic Interrelationships**: Deeply intertwined with central adiposity, insulin resistance, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and atherogenic dyslipidaemia, acting as both an end-organ manifestation of the metabolic syndrome and an independent amplifier of cardiovascular risk.
- **Public Health Interventions**: Because pharmacotherapy cannot fully reverse advanced hepatic fibrosis, core public health levers emphasize primordial and primary lifestyle modification: sustained 7% to 10% weight loss, adherence to cardioprotective dietary patterns (restricting refined carbohydrates and fructose, eliminating ultra-processed foods), regular moderate aerobic physical activity, strict glycemic control, and reduction or complete cessation of alcohol intake.
- **Operational Delivery in Public Facilities**: Institutionalized within NP-NCD Medical Officer modules, incorporating opportunistic screening and metabolic evaluation among overweight and diabetic patients attending CHC and District Hospital NCD clinics.

[LAQ]NPCDCS / NP-NCD: goals, objectives and strategies[/LAQ]

[SN]NPCDCS and NP-NCD[/SN]

NATIONAL PROGRAMME FOR PREVENTION AND CONTROL OF NON-COMMUNICABLE DISEASES (NP-NCD)
- **Programmatic Identity and Evolution**: Launched in 2010 under the National Health Mission (NHM) as the National Programme for Prevention and Control of Cancer, Diabetes, Cardiovascular Diseases and Stroke (NPCDCS). In 2023, the Union Ministry of Health and Family Welfare expanded and renamed the scheme as the National Programme for Prevention and Control of Non-Communicable Diseases (NP-NCD) to incorporate an expanded spectrum of chronic diseases.
- **Overarching Goal**: To prevent and control common non-communicable diseases through multi-sectoral coordination; reduce premature mortality, morbidity, and preventable disability; and establish an integrated continuum of comprehensive care from village health sub-centres to tertiary teaching hospitals.
- **Key Programmatic Objectives**:
  - **Health Promotion and Behavioural Change**: Promoting population-wide lifestyle modifications targeting four major behavioural risk factors (tobacco consumption, alcohol abuse, unhealthy diet, and physical inactivity).
  - **Screening and Early Detection**: Conducting opportunistic and population-based screening for hypertension, diabetes, and common oral, breast, and cervical cancers among adults aged 30 years and above.
  - **Tiered Clinical Care Networks**: Providing accessible diagnosis, treatment, continuous follow-up, and timely referrals through institutionalized NCD clinics across primary, secondary, and tertiary health facilities.
  - **Health System Capacity Building**: Upgrading physical infrastructure, human resources, essential diagnostic equipment, and uninterrupted supplies of anti-hypertensive and anti-diabetic medications.
  - **Programmatic Convergence**: Integrating with complementary health initiatives, including the National Tobacco Control Programme (NTCP), National Programme for Health Care of the Elderly (NPHCE), and National Oral Health Programme (NOHP).
  - **Digital Surveillance and Monitoring**: Implementing longitudinal electronic patient tracking and screening records through the National NCD Portal linked to individual Ayushman Bharat Health Account (ABHA) IDs.
- **Level-Wise Service Delivery Framework**:
  - **Community and Ayushman Arogya Mandir (Sub-Health Centre level)**: Enumeration of all individuals aged 30 years and above using the Community-Based Assessment Checklist (CBAC); opportunistic screening for hypertension, diabetes, and oral cancer by ASHAs and ANMs; clinical breast and visual acetic acid cervical exams by trained Community Health Officers (CHOs); and community lifestyle counselling.
  - **Primary Health Centre (PHC / UPHC)**: Confirmation of screening results, initiation of first-line pharmacotherapy as per Standard Treatment Guidelines (STGs), dispensing monthly drug refills, and monitoring treatment adherence.
  - **Community Health Centre (CHC / Sub-District Hospital)**: Specialized First Referral Unit establishing dedicated Day Care NCD Clinics; diagnostic ultrasonography, electrocardiography, and laboratory panels; management of complications; and referral coordination.
  - **District Hospital (DH)**: Comprehensive district NCD clinics, intensive coronary care units (ICCU), stroke care units, haemodialysis units under the Pradhan Mantri National Dialysis Programme (PMNDP), daycare chemotherapy, and palliative care units.
  - **Tertiary Level (Medical Colleges and State Cancer Institutes)**: Advanced super-specialty interventions, complex revascularization, radiation oncology, tertiary rehabilitation, and professional medical education.

[LAQ]NP-NCD 2023-2030: expanded conditions and STEMI levels[/LAQ]

NP-NCD 2023 TO 2030 (EXPANDED OPERATIONAL FRAMEWORK)
- **Policy Horizon and Scope**: The MoHFW Operational Guidelines 2023 to 2030 delineate an expanded programmatic ambit addressing the epidemiological burden of non-communicable conditions across India.
- **Expanded Clinical Portfolio**: Phased integration of chronic respiratory diseases (COPD and asthma), Non-Alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease (NAFLD), Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD) with institutional dialysis linkages, dedicated Acute Stroke care pathways, and decentralized ST-Elevation Myocardial Infarction (STEMI) management networks.
- **Technological and Service Innovations**: Transition to digitized longitudinal care records via the National NCD Portal; integration with Ayushman Bharat Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana (AB-PMJAY) for secondary and tertiary financial protection; and strengthening of decentralized drug dispensing at Ayushman Arogya Mandirs.

STEMI FACILITY LEVELS UNDER NP-NCD
- **Level 1 Facilities (Spoke Facilities without On-Site Thrombolysis)**: Primary health centres or rural outposts staffed by Medical Officers without ECG or thrombolytic capabilities. Responsibilities: immediate recognition of acute ischaemic chest pain, administration of emergency oral loading doses of antiplatelets (aspirin and clopidogrel) and high-intensity statin according to national protocol, and immediate tele-consultation and expedited ambulance dispatch to a Level 2 or Level 3 centre.
- **Level 2 Facilities (Spoke Facilities with Thrombolytic Capabilities)**: Community Health Centres or Sub-District Hospitals staffed by Medical Officers with 12-lead ECG and thrombolytic infrastructure. Responsibilities: rapid acquisition and tele-interpretation of 12-lead ECG within 10 minutes of arrival; prompt intravenous thrombolysis (tenecteplase, reteplase, or streptokinase) for eligible STEMI patients presenting within the therapeutic window (ideal door-to-needle time <30 minutes); and immediate post-thrombolysis transfer to a Level 3 facility for rescue or routine invasive coronarography (pharmacoinvasive strategy).
- **Level 3 Facilities (Hub Facilities with Primary PCI Capabilities)**: District Hospitals, Medical Colleges, or tertiary cardiac institutes equipped with dedicated Cardiac Catheterization Laboratories (Cath Labs). Responsibilities: 24/7 Primary Percutaneous Coronary Intervention (PCI) with an ideal door-to-balloon time of <90 minutes, critical cardiac intensive care, and advanced haemodynamic monitoring.

INDIAN CONTEXT:
- **Governance and Implementation**: NP-NCD is financed through the National Health Mission (NHM) as a centrally sponsored partnership between the Union Government and States/UTs. State and District NCD Cells drive administrative execution.
- **Decentralized Service Delivery**: The operationalization of Ayushman Arogya Mandirs (formerly Sub-Health Centres and Primary Health Centres transformed into Health and Wellness Centres) ensures universal population-based screening and medication continuity at the grassroots level.
- **Programmatic Milestones**: National targets align with the WHO Global NCD Action Plan, pursuing a 25% relative reduction in premature mortality from cardiovascular diseases, cancer, diabetes, and chronic respiratory diseases by 2025/2030.

> **EXAM TIP:** In questions on NP-NCD, highlight the 2023 rebranding from NPCDCS to NP-NCD and detail the expanded condition package (COPD, NAFLD, CKD, and STEMI network levels). Always tabulate the STEMI Level 1, Level 2, and Level 3 spoke-hub model with door-to-needle (<30 minutes) and door-to-balloon (<90 minutes) time standards.

KEY POINTS
- **Rebranding and Horizon**: Renamed in 2023 from NPCDCS to NP-NCD, governed by Operational Guidelines covering 2023 to 2030.
- **Broadened Scope**: Encompasses chronic respiratory diseases, metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease, chronic kidney disease, and acute STEMI networks.
- **Tiered STEMI Architecture**: Organizes emergency coronary care into Level 1 (loading dose/transfer), Level 2 (door-to-needle thrombolysis <30 min), and Level 3 (PCI hub door-to-balloon <90 min).
- **Population Screening Focus**: Maintains universal screening of adults aged 30 and above for hypertension, diabetes, and oral, breast, and cervical malignancies via the Community-Based Assessment Checklist (CBAC).

[REF]Reference: MoHFW NP-NCD Operational Guidelines 2023-2030; MoHFW Operational Guidelines for NAFLD Version 2.0 (2024); GOLD COPD definition; National Health Mission (NHM).[/REF]

subsections.title: Understanding the Administrative Hierarchy
subsections.content:
OVERVIEW: HEALTH PROGRAMMES IN INDIA

National health programmes represent deliberate, state-directed public health interventions designed to curb major disease burdens, stabilize population growth, and build resilient health infrastructure across India. Since Independence, India's public health trajectory has evolved from vertical, disease-specific campaigns (eradicating smallpox, eliminating guinea worm, and banishing wild poliovirus) to horizontal health systems strengthening.

The launch of the National Rural Health Mission in 2005 and its consolidation into the National Health Mission bridged the historic rural-urban divide, deploying over one million Accredited Social Health Activists (ASHAs) as the community vanguard. Modern Indian public health advances this paradigm through Ayushman Bharat, uniting comprehensive primary care at Ayushman Arogya Mandirs with financial risk protection under PM-JAY. Alongside targeted missions for tuberculosis elimination, vector-borne disease control, and non-communicable diseases, these flagship initiatives operationalize universal health coverage, transforming healthcare from fragmented curative encounters into a lifelong continuum of preventive, promotive, and curative care.

ADMINISTRATIVE ARCHITECTURE OF HEALTH IN INDIA

The delivery of public health in India operates through a structured administrative and financial continuum. Public health interventions follow a cascading framework from national constitutional vision to grassroots community delivery.

THE ROLE OF A UNION MINISTRY

A central Ministry functions as the overarching policymaking and administrative authority. Rather than operating under a single mandate, a Ministry formulates multiple distinct national policies addressing specific sectors within its jurisdiction. Each policy establishes strategic directions that subsequently operationalise into missions, programmes, and schemes.

For example, the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (MoHFW) manages several distinct national policies simultaneously:
- **National Health Policy (NHP 2017):** Outlines universal health coverage goals, preventive and promotive frameworks, and public health expenditure targets.
- **National Population Policy (NPP 2000):** Addresses reproductive health needs, maternal-child survival, and voluntary fertility regulation toward population stabilization.
- **National Blood Policy (2002):** Governs voluntary blood donation systems, transfusion safety standards, testing protocols, and fractional blood component availability.

Similarly, the Ministry of Women and Child Development (MWCD) directs complementary sectoral policies:
- **National Nutrition Policy (1993):** Directs intersectoral action to combat undernutrition, micronutrient deficiencies, and maternal-child dietary deficits.
- **National Policy for Children (2013):** Supersedes the 1974 policy, safeguarding fundamental child rights to survival, health, nutrition, education, and protection.
- **National Early Childhood Care and Education Policy (ECCE 2013):** Promotes holistic development and foundational learning during early critical developmental windows.

THE FOUR TIERS EXPLAINED

Following the enactment of a policy by a Ministry, the implementation architecture operationalises across four functional tiers:

1. **Policy (The Vision):**
  - **Strategic direction:** Defines broad national priorities, ethical frameworks, and demographic targets for successive decades.
  - **Macro framework:** Policies establish long-term governance principles rather than day-to-day administrative instructions.

2. **Mission (The Execution Vehicle):**
  - **Time-bound delivery:** Represents a heavily funded, structured strategic vehicle (such as the National Health Mission or Ayushman Bharat) designed to achieve the targets set by national policy.
  - **Integrated funding:** Pools financial resources, establishes flexible funding mechanisms, and bridges horizontal inter-departmental divides across central and state tiers.

3. **Programme (The Technical Strategy):**
  - **Operational design:** Implements specific condition-focused or disease-targeted public health interventions.
  - **Clinical protocols:** Formulates standard technical guidelines, treatment regimens, diagnostic criteria, and disease surveillance metrics.

4. **Scheme or Initiative (The Targeted Tool):**
  - **Demand-side levers:** Deploys specific financial, operational, or logistics mechanisms to overcome social and financial barriers to healthcare access.
  - **Direct entitlements:** Delivers conditional cash transfers, free diagnostics, subsidized pharmaceuticals, or designated community-level mobilisations.

HIERARCHY EXAMPLES ACROSS SECTORS

1. **Healthcare Sector (MoHFW):**
  - **Policy:** National Health Policy (NHP 2017)
  - **Mission:** National Health Mission (NHM) and Ayushman Bharat
  - **Programme:** Reproductive, Maternal, Newborn, Child, Adolescent Health and Nutrition (RMNCAH+N)
  - **Scheme:** Janani Suraksha Yojana (JSY), Janani Shishu Suraksha Karyakram (JSSK), Rashtriya Bal Swasthya Karyakram (RBSK), Rashtriya Kishor Swasthya Karyakram (RKSK), Navjat Shishu Suraksha Karyakram (NSSK), Samagra Shishu Bal Swasthya Karyakram (SSBSK), and Weekly Iron and Folic Acid Supplementation Programme (WIFS).

2. **Education Sector (Ministry of Education):**
  - **Policy:** National Education Policy (NEP 2020)
  - **Mission:** National Mission on Foundational Literacy and Numeracy (NIPUN Bharat)
  - **Programme:** Samagra Shiksha
  - **Scheme:** Pradhan Mantri Poshan Shakti Nirman (PM POSHAN, formerly Mid-Day Meal Scheme) and Padhe Bharat Badhe Bharat.

3. **Nutrition and Child Development Sector (MWCD):**
  - **Policy:** National Nutrition Policy and National ECCE Policy
  - **Mission:** POSHAN Abhiyaan (National Nutrition Mission)
  - **Programme:** Saksham Anganwadi and POSHAN 2.0
  - **Scheme:** Anganwadi Services Scheme and Scheme for Adolescent Girls (SAG).

CROSS-SECTORAL SOCIAL DETERMINANTS OF HEALTH

Effective public health outcomes depend upon intersectoral action managed by partner central ministries:

- **Ministry of Rural Development:**
  - **Poverty alleviation:** Deendayal Antyodaya Yojana - National Rural Livelihoods Mission (DAY-NRLM) mobilises rural women into self-help groups, directly enhancing household nutritional security and health-seeking behaviour.

- **Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs (MoHUA):**
  - **Urban living environments:** Pradhan Mantri Awas Yojana - Urban (PMAY-U) and Swachh Bharat Mission - Urban (SBM-U) improve structural housing, environmental sanitation, and vector-breeding containment in urban slums.

- **Ministry of Jal Shakti:**
  - **Safe drinking water:** Jal Jeevan Mission (JJM) provides Functional Household Tap Connections (FHTC) providing 55 litres per capita per day (lpcd) of potable water, interrupting the transmission of water-borne diarrhoeal illnesses.

- **Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment (MoSJE):**
  - **Social protection:** Implements targeted de-addiction initiatives (Nasha Mukt Bharat Abhiyaan) and rehabilitation schemes for marginalised and vulnerable communities.

> **EXAM TIP:** For questions on health planning and programme organization: draw the 4-tier hierarchy (Policy → Mission → Programme → Scheme) with vertical examples (NHP 2017 → NHM → RMNCAH+N → JSY/JSSK). Differentiate between strategic vision (Policy) and targeted delivery tools (Schemes).

[REF]Reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine (28th Edition), Chapter on Health Programmes in India; Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (MoHFW), Government of India Guidelines.[/REF]

subsections.title: National Health Mission (NHM)
subsections.content:
NATIONAL HEALTH MISSION (NHM)
Nodal Ministry: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (MoHFW)

CURRENT INDIA FIGURES (AGAINST NHM TARGETS)

National Health Mission (NHM) targets remain the programme goals. Latest official achievement:

| Indicator | NHM target | Latest official | Year | Source |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Infant mortality rate | 25 per 1,000 live births | 24 | 2024 | SRS 2024, RGI |
| Maternal mortality ratio | 100 per 100,000 live births (NHM); SDG 3.1 is below 70 | 87 | 2022-24 | SRS Special Bulletin on Maternal Mortality 2022-24, RGI |
| Total fertility rate | 2.1 | 2.0 (NFHS); 1.9 (SRS) | 2023-24 / 2023 | NFHS-6, 2023-24, IIPS/MoHFW; SRS Statistical Report 2023, RGI |

[SN]National Health Mission (NHM)[/SN]

[LAQ]National Health Mission: components, strategies and targets[/LAQ]

INTRODUCTION AND KEY MILESTONES

The National Health Mission (NHM) was launched in 2013 by integrating the National Rural Health Mission (NRHM, 2005) and the National Urban Health Mission (NUHM, 2013), along with flexible support for many national disease-control and RMNCAH activities. NHM remains the core umbrella for strengthening public health systems at primary and secondary levels through state and district health societies.

NHM aims to increase access to the decentralized health system by establishing new infrastructure in deficient areas and upgrading the infrastructure in existing institutions.

COMPONENTS UNDER NHM (2013)

- **National Rural:** Health Mission (launched in 2005)
- **National Urban:** Health Mission (launched in 2013)
- **Communicable Disease:** programmes
- **Non-communicable Disease:** programmes
- **Administrative components:** Programmatic priority area.
- **RMNCAH+N (Reproductive,:** Maternal, Neonatal, Child, Adolescent Health + Nutrition)
*(Note: Detailed initiatives under RMNCAH+N, including maternal and child health schemes, are covered in a dedicated section.)*

TARGETS AND GOALS OF NHM

- **Reduce Maternal:** Mortality Ratio (MMR) to < 1 / 1000 live births (or 100 / 100,000 live births).
- **Reduce Infant:** Mortality Rate (IMR) to 25 / 1000 live births. Latest official IMR is 24 (SRS 2024, RGI), so the numerical NHM IMR target has been reached at national level; state gaps remain.
- **Reduce Total:** Fertility Rate (TFR) to 2.1.
- **Maternal anaemia reduction:** Prevent and reduce anaemia prevalence in women (15–49 years).
- **Morbidity and mortality containment:** Prevent and lower mortality and morbidity from communicable, non-communicable, and emerging diseases.
- **Catastrophic expenditure reduction:** Lower out-of-pocket spending on total healthcare.
- **Tuberculosis reduction targets:** Lower annual incidence and mortality from TB by 50%.
- **Leprosy elimination targets:** Lower prevalence of leprosy to <1 case per 10,000 population and Grade 2 disability incidence to zero across all districts.
- **Malaria incidence targets:** Lower Annual Parasite Incidence (API) to <1 per 1,000 population.
- **Lymphatic filariasis targets:** Lower microfilaria prevalence in all endemic districts to <1 percent.
- **Eliminate Kala-azar:** by 2010 (Original historical target; India officially achieved elimination at the block level in 2023).

NATIONAL URBAN HEALTH MISSION (NUHM)
Nodal Ministry: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (MoHFW)

NUHM seeks to improve the health status of the urban population, particularly slum dwellers and other vulnerable sections (homeless, rag pickers, street children, rickshaw pullers, brick / lime kiln workers, sex workers, and migrants) by facilitating their access to quality health care. It focuses on sanitation, clean drinking water, vector control, and strengthening of public health capacity.

Urban Health Care Services and Infrastructure:
- **Mahila Arogya Samiti (MAS):** Covers 50-100 households (250-500 beneficiaries). NUHM provides an annual untied grant of Rs. 5000 to MAS every year.
- **ASHA / Link Worker (LW):** Covers 1000-2500 population. Ensures participation by creation of MAS and Rogi Kalyan Samitis (RKS).
- **ANM:** Covers 10,000 population.
- **Urban Primary Health Centre (U-PHC):** Covers 50,000 population. Located within or near slums. Functional from 12 pm to 8 pm. No IPD services. Services include OPD, Lab, Drugs, RCH services, and Counseling for diseases.
- **Urban Community Health Centre (U-CHC):** Serves as a satellite hospital for 4-5 U-PHCs. Covers 2,50,000 population (5,00,000 and 100 bedded in metro cities). Has 30-50 beds with IPD services. Services include medical care, minor surgery, and institutional delivery.

Services rendered by ASHA in NUHM:
- **Health promotion role:** Functions as a promoter of good health practices and health-seeking behaviour.
- **Facilitate awareness:** on RCH services.
- **Facilitate access:** to health-related services at AWC / PHC.
- **Accompany pregnant:** woman and children requiring treatment.
- **Community action:** for prevention of diseases.
- **Community mobilization:** Facilitates formation and promotion of Mahila Arogya Samitis (MAS).
- **Maintain records:** about births and deaths, immunization, and ANC services.

Indicators in NUHM:
- **Community process:** Number of MAS formed, Number of ASHA trained.
- **Health system:** Number of ANM recruited, Number of U-PHCs and U-CHCs made operational, Number of RKS created.
- **RCH services:** ANCs registered in 1st trimester, TT 2nd dose coverage in pregnant women, Number of children fully immunized.
- **Communicable diseases:** Number of malaria cases detected, Number of TB cases identified.
- **Non-communicable diseases:** Number of diabetes, cancer, and hypertension cases screened.

Targets of NUHM:
- **40 percent:** reduction in Under-5 Mortality Rate (U5MR).
- **50 percent:** reduction in MMR.
- **100 percent:** ANC coverage.
- **100 percent:** institutional delivery.
- **Total fertility rate:** TFR target of 2.1 (achieved nationally at replacement level).

NATIONAL RURAL HEALTH MISSION (NRHM)
Nodal Ministry: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (MoHFW)

[SN]ASHA Worker[/SN]

The aim of NRHM is to provide accessible, affordable, accountable, effective, and reliable primary health care, and bridge the gap in rural health care by creating a cadre of Accredited Social Health Activists (ASHA). It brings the Indian system of medicine (AYUSH) to the mainstream of health care.

Plan of Action and Infrastructure Pyramid:
1. Creation of ASHA: Must be a female resident of the village, preferably married/widow/divorced, aged 25-45 years, with communication skills and leadership qualities. General norm is one ASHA per 1000 population (relaxed to one per habitation in tribal, hilly, and desert areas).
2. Village Level (1000 Population): ASHA, Anganwadi Worker (AWW), Village Health Sanitation and Nutrition Committee (VHSNC). Focus on Village Health and Nutrition Days (VHND), drug kits, and referral chains.
3. Gram Panchayat / Sub Health Centre Level (5-6 villages): Strengthening of SCs with additional ANM. Skill up-gradation of educated RMPs. Staffing of 2 ANMs and 1 male MPW. Services include telephone links, MCH/Immunization days, drugs, and MCH clinics.
4. Cluster of GPs / PHC Level (30-40 villages): Strengthening of PHCs with a Medical Officer in charge and an AYUSH practitioner. Staffing includes 3 Staff Nurses and 1 LHV for 4-5 SCs. Services include ambulance/hired vehicle, fixed day MCH/Immunization clinics, mobile app-based clinical workflow for CHOs, emergencies handled by nurses 24x7, round the clock services, drugs, and TB/Malaria tests.
5. Block Level Hospital (100,000 population / 100 villages): Strengthening of CHCs with posting of anesthetist and promotion of RKS for hospital management. Services include ambulance, telephone, obstetric/surgical medical emergencies 24x7, and round the clock services.
6. District Level: All vertical health and family welfare programmes merged into a common District Health Mission. Provision of Mobile Medical Unit (MMU) for improved outreach services.

Major Initiatives under NRHM:
- **Frontline deployment:** Selection and deployment of Accredited Social Health Activists (ASHAs).
- **Rogi Kalyan Samiti (RKS):** Patient welfare committee / hospital management society. Members act as trustees to manage the affairs of the hospital and upkeep of facilities.
- **Untied grants to the sub-centres:** SCs are better equipped with blood pressure measuring equipments, haemoglobin (Hb) measuring equipment, stethoscope, and weighing machine.
- **Village Health:** Sanitation and Nutrition Committee (VHSNC): Important tool for community empowerment and participation at the grass-root level.
- **National Mobile Medical Units (NMMUs):** Repositioned with universal colour and design.
- **National Ambulance Services:** Free ambulance services for patient transport (e.g., Dial 108 and 102).
- **Web enabled:** Mother and Child Tracking System (MCTS): Name-based tracking of pregnant women, infants, and children up to the age of three years to ensure delivery of services like ANC, PNC, and immunization.

[SN]Kayakalp scheme[/SN]

KAYAKALP SCHEME
Nodal Ministry: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (MoHFW)

Definition
Kayakalp is a MoHFW/NHM initiative to promote cleanliness, hygiene, and infection control in public health facilities and to recognise and reward well-performing facilities.

Background and purpose
- **Institutional objective:** Launched to enhance public facility cleanliness, hygiene standards, and healthcare-associated infection prevention.
- **Complements National:** Quality Assurance Standards (NQAS) and other quality frameworks (e.g. LaQshya for labour rooms).

Key focus areas
1. Hospital/facility upkeep: wards, OPDs, toilets, water, waste zones.
2. Sanitation and hygiene: cleaning schedules, materials, monitoring.
3. Waste management: segregation, Bio-Medical Waste Rules compliance, sharps.
4. Infection control: hand hygiene, PPE, asepsis, sterilisation practices as applicable.
5. Support services: laundry, kitchen, water quality, drainage.
6. Hygiene promotion: IEC for patients/attendants and staff behaviour.
7. Assessment and awards: external assessment against a checklist; awards at facility levels (PHC/CHC/DH/medical college categories as per scheme cycles).

Link to other initiatives
- **Works alongside:** NQAS certification and health-sector cleanliness drives.
- **Clean, infection-safe:** facilities support RMNCAH outcomes, surgical safety, and community trust in public care.

> **EXAM TIP:** Define Kayakalp → list 6–7 thematic domains of the checklist → mention award/assessment cycle → link to NQAS/infection control → one line on why cleanliness is a public-health intervention.

[SN]Health Management Information System (HMIS) in India[/SN]

[LAQ]Health Management Information System (HMIS) in India: district improvement[/LAQ]

HMIS IN INDIA

Definition
HMIS is a routine system for collecting, processing, analysing, and using health service data for planning, monitoring, and management decisions at facility, block, district, state, and national levels.

Features and flow
1. Facility registers and monthly reports → block/district consolidation → state/national portals.
2. Indicators across RMNCAH, disease control, facility services, human resources, and stocks (as configured).
3. Complements disease-specific systems (Nikshay, IHIP/IDSP, U-WIN, and others); interoperability is the modern agenda.

Uses
- **Gap analysis,:** target setting, supervisory focus, resource allocation, and programme review meetings.

Problems
- **Over-reporting or:** under-reporting; delayed data; multiple parallel formats; weak analysis skills; data not used for local action (“reporting for upward consumption only”).

District-level improvements
1. Limit parallel registers; promote single-source entry and interoperability.
2. Monthly data quality audits (completeness, consistency, outliers).
3. Train MO/BPM/data managers to convert indicators into action plans.
4. Display dashboards in review meetings; close the loop with supervisory visits.
5. Integrate private-sector reporting for notifiable conditions where mandated.
6. Feedback to ANM/CHO on data they generate: ownership improves quality.

> **EXAM TIP:** Definition → data cycle → uses → 4 weaknesses → 6 district fixes → mention coexistence with IHIP/Nikshay/U-WIN.

[SN]Coordination between functioning of ASHA, Anganwadi Worker (AWW), and Auxiliary Nurse Midwife (ANM) for better output[/SN]

ASHA–AWW–ANM COORDINATION (THE COMMUNITY TRIAD)

Definition
Effective primary care outreach in India depends on coordinated roles of ASHA (community mobiliser under health), AWW (ICDS nutrition/ECD worker under WCD), and ANM (multipurpose peripheral health functionary at sub-centre level).

Role clarity
- **ASHA:** mobilisation, home visits, escort, incentive-linked tasks (ANC mobilisation, SSBSK home visits, treatment support, disease notification support).
- **AWW:** supplementary nutrition, growth monitoring, preschool, counselling; hosts many community contact days.
- **ANM:** clinical outreach, routine immunisation, antenatal procedures, records and due-lists.

Coordination platforms
1. Village Health Sanitation and Nutrition Day (VHSND/VHND): common service day.
2. Shared due-lists for pregnant women and children.
3. Joint home visits for drop-outs, SAM, and high-risk pregnancies.
4. Referral feedback loops to PHC/CHO-led Ayushman Arogya Mandir.
5. Local committees (VHSNC) for accountability.

Why coordination improves output
- **Reduces missed:** ANC/RI/nutrition contacts; unifies messaging; improves follow-up after discharge (SSBSK continuum).

> **EXAM TIP:** Draw the triad table → VHND as the hinge → 5 joint activities → one line that incentives alone fail without role clarity and shared microplans.

> **EXAM TIP:** For NHM: NRHM+NUHM → ASHA/VHSNC/RKS/untied funds → key targets (MMR/IMR/TFR) → flexible financing via health societies. For ASHA SN: selection norms → roles → incentives → community triad with AWW/ANM.

[REF]Reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine (28th Edition), National Health Mission; Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (MoHFW), Government of India Operational Guidelines.[/REF]

subsections.title: RMNCAH+N (Reproductive, Maternal, Newborn, Child, Adolescent Health and Nutrition)
subsections.content:
RMNCAH+N STRATEGY
Nodal Ministry: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (MoHFW)

CURRENT INDIA FIGURES (MATERNAL AND CHILD HEALTH)

NFHS-6 India fact sheets (May 2026) do not publish infant, neonatal, or under-five mortality. Use SRS for those rates.

| Indicator | Latest | Year | Source | Previous |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Maternal mortality ratio | 87 per 100,000 live births | 2022-24 | SRS Special Bulletin on Maternal Mortality 2022-24, RGI | 88 (SRS 2021-23); 93 (SRS 2019-21); 97 (SRS 2018-20) |
| Infant mortality rate | 24 per 1,000 live births (rural 28 / urban 18 in 2023) | 2024 | SRS 2024, RGI | 25 (SRS Bulletin 2023, RGI); 32 (SRS 2020) |
| Neonatal mortality rate | 18 per 1,000 live births | 2024 | SRS 2024, RGI | SRS 2020 teaching tables ~20 |
| Under-five mortality rate | 28 per 1,000 live births | 2024 | SRS 2024, RGI | 29 (SRS 2023) |
| Institutional births | 90.6% | 2023-24 | NFHS-6, 2023-24, IIPS/MoHFW | 88.6% (NFHS-5, 2019-21, IIPS/MoHFW) |
| ANC in first trimester | 76.2% | 2023-24 | NFHS-6, 2023-24, IIPS/MoHFW | 70.0% (NFHS-5, 2019-21, IIPS/MoHFW) |
| At least 4 ANC visits | 65.2% | 2023-24 | NFHS-6, 2023-24, IIPS/MoHFW | 58.5% (NFHS-5, 2019-21, IIPS/MoHFW) |
| IFA for 180 days or more | 37.8% | 2023-24 | NFHS-6, 2023-24, IIPS/MoHFW | 26.0% (NFHS-5, 2019-21, IIPS/MoHFW) |
| Caesarean section | 27.2% | 2023-24 | NFHS-6, 2023-24, IIPS/MoHFW | 21.5% (NFHS-5, 2019-21, IIPS/MoHFW) |
| Exclusive breastfeeding (under 6 months) | 55.8% | 2023-24 | NFHS-6, 2023-24, IIPS/MoHFW | 63.7% (NFHS-5, 2019-21, IIPS/MoHFW). Coverage fell |
| Breastfed within 1 hour of birth | 50.1% | 2023-24 | NFHS-6, 2023-24, IIPS/MoHFW | 41.8% (NFHS-5, 2019-21, IIPS/MoHFW) |
| Fully vaccinated (12-23 months, fact-sheet definition) | 82.6% | 2023-24 | NFHS-6, 2023-24, IIPS/MoHFW | PIB also quotes 87.1% from vaccination-card information |

[LAQ]Evolution of RCH and operational components of RMNCH+A[/LAQ]

INTRODUCTION TO RMNCAH+N STRATEGY
Nodal Ministry: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (MoHFW)

Launched by the Government of India in 2013, the RMNCH+A strategy evolved to link maternal and child health to reproductive health, family planning, adolescent health, HIV, gender, and preconception care. It has now evolved into the RMNCAH+N framework, explicitly integrating Nutrition.

Key Interventions across the RMNCAH+N Framework:
1. Reproductive Health: Spacing methods (PPIUCD), Interval IUCD, Home Delivery of Contraceptives (HDC) and Ensuring Birth Spacing (ESB), Pregnancy test kits (PTK - "Nischay Kits"), and Sterilization services.
2. Maternal Health: Mother and Child Tracking System (MCTS), identification of high-risk pregnancies, highly trained HR, review of maternal and infant deaths, identifying low institutional delivery areas, and incentivizing ANMs for domiciliary care.
3. Newborn Health: Exclusive breastfeeding, Samagra Shishu Bal Swasthya Karyakram (SSBSK: HBNC+HBYC continuum) through ASHA/AAA, Essential Newborn Care, Special Newborn Care Units (SNCUs), and use of Gentamycin by ANMs.
4. Child Health: Focus on nutrition, diarrhea management, pneumonia management, full immunization coverage, and Rashtriya Bal Swasthya Karyakram (RBSK).
5. Adolescent Health: Addressing teenage pregnancy, Peer educators, strengthening ARSH clinics, Iron Plus Initiative, and promoting Menstrual Hygiene.
6. Nutrition (Cross-cutting): Anemia Mukt Bharat Abhiyaan, Poshan Abhiyaan, Integrated Child Development Services (ICDS), and PM Poshan Scheme.

 MATERNAL HEALTH INITIATIVES 

CHILD SURVIVAL AND SAFE MOTHERHOOD PROGRAMME (CSSM)
Nodal Ministry: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (MoHFW)
- **Launch year:** 1992 under the Eighth Five Year Plan.
- **Focus:** Antenatal services, safe delivery, and child survival interventions.
- **Evolved into:** the Reproductive and Child Health (RCH) Phase I & II programmes, which introduced essential obstetric care, 24-hour delivery services, safe abortion, and the Vandemataram scheme.

[SN]Janani Suraksha Yojana[/SN]

[LAQ]Critical review of Janani Suraksha Yojana (JSY)[/LAQ]

JANANI SURAKSHA YOJANA (JSY)
Nodal Ministry: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (MoHFW)
- **Programme inception:** Launched in 2005 under NRHM, modifying the National Maternity Benefit Scheme (NMBS).
- **Goal:** Reduce maternal and infant mortality by promoting institutional deliveries.
- **Obstetric complication subsidy:** Subsidizes the cost of Caesarean delivery and management of obstetric complications up to Rs. 1,500.
- **All BPL:** women who deliver at home are entitled to Rs. 500 per delivery irrespective of age and parity.
- **Cash Assistance:** Structure for Institutional Delivery (In Rupees):
  1. Rural Area:
     - **Low Performing States (LPS) (Rural):** Mother's package Rs. 1400, ASHA's package Rs. 600. Total = Rs. 2000.
     - **High Performing States (HPS) (Rural):** Mother's package Rs. 700, ASHA's package Rs. 600. Total = Rs. 1300.
  2. Urban Area:
     - **Low Performing States (LPS) (Urban):** Mother's package Rs. 1000, ASHA's package Rs. 400. Total = Rs. 1400.
     - **High Performing States (HPS) (Urban):** Mother's package Rs. 600, ASHA's package Rs. 400. Total = Rs. 1000.
- **Eligibility:** In LPS, given to all women delivering in government health centres. In HPS, given to BPL and SC/ST women delivering in government centres.

CRITICAL APPRAISAL OF JSY

What worked
1. Rapid rise in institutional deliveries in many low-performing states via demand-side cash incentive.
2. Clear LPS/HPS differential packages and ASHA linkage improved outreach.
3. Synergy later with JSSK (cost barrier reduction) and quality initiatives (LaQshya, SUMAN).

Problems in implementation
1. Focus on place of delivery sometimes outpaced readiness for quality EmOC, blood storage, and referral.
2. Overcrowding of facilities; variable respectful maternity care.
3. Documentation/payment delays; exclusion errors and leakage risks if verification is weak.
4. Home-delivery incentives and LPS vs HPS eligibility nuances create confusion if not counselled well.
5. Continuum of care (ANC quality, PNC, newborn care) may be neglected if only delivery cash is emphasised.
6. Transport and complications management still fail in hard-to-reach geographies without functional referral.

Recommendations
1. Tie incentives to quality metrics (NQAS/LaQshya) and complication readiness, not headcount alone.
2. Strengthen FRUs, blood storage, and 102/108 linkages before pushing footfall.
3. Real-time DBT tracking, grievance redressal (e.g. 104/SUMAN pathways), and social audits.
4. Integrate JSY messaging with PMSMA high-risk identification and SSBSK (home-based) follow-up.
5. Support ASHA with timely payment and skill reinforcement for birth preparedness.

> **EXAM TIP:** Half page scheme facts (definition, LPS/HPS table) → half page achievements vs problems vs recommendations → end with JSY+JSSK+quality trilogy.

JANANI SHISHU SURAKSHA KARYAKRAM (JSSK)
Nodal Ministry: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (MoHFW)
- **Launch year:** Launched in June 2011 to eliminate out-of-pocket expenses for pregnant women and sick neonates.
- **Beneficiaries:** Pregnant females up to 42 days post-delivery, and sick infants.
- **Goal:** Reduce maternal mortality and out-of-pocket expenditure.
