- **Assured Services:** Cashless delivery (vaginal and C-section), free drugs and diagnostics, free diet (3 days for normal delivery, 7 days for C-section), free blood, and free transport (home to facility, inter-facility referral, and drop back home after 48 hours of stay).

LAQSHYA: LABOR ROOM QUALITY IMPROVEMENT GUIDELINES
Nodal Ministry: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (MoHFW)
- **Goal:** To reduce maternal mortality.
- **Eligible facilities:** Medical college hospitals, District Hospitals (DHs), Sub-District Hospitals (SDHs), and high-load Community Health Centres (CHCs); Sub-Centres and primary health centres are excluded from LaQshya certification.
- **Quality Improvement:** is assessed through NQAS (National Quality Assurance Standards). Every facility achieving a 70 percent score on NQAS will be certified.
- **Badges:** Platinum (>90%), Gold (>80%), and Silver (>70%).
- **Financial incentives:** Facility-level cash rewards for NQAS-certified facilities achieving ≥80% client satisfaction (≥70% for OT/ICU).
  - **Medical College Hospitals:** Rs. 6 lakhs.
  - **District Hospitals:** Rs. 3 lakhs.
  - **FRUs:** Rs. 2 lakhs.

PRADHAN MANTRI MATRU VANDANA YOJANA (PMMVY)
Nodal Ministry: Ministry of Women and Child Development (MWCD)
- **Nodal governance:** Administered under the Ministry of Women and Child Development (MWCD), representing a non-MoHFW cross-sectoral entitlement.
- **Goal:** Reduce maternal mortality and provide partial wage compensation.
- **Incentive:** Cash assistance given to pregnant females > 19 years of age, ONLY for the first live birth.
- **Cash incentive:** is given up to Rs. 5000 in two installments:
  - **1st installment (Rs. 3000):** On registration at a health facility and receiving at least one ANC within 6 months.
  - **2nd installment (Rs. 2000):** After birth registration and the child receives BCG, OPV, and Pentavalent vaccines.
- **Special Provision:** In case the second birth is a girl child, an incentive of Rs. 6000 will be given as a single installment.

PRADHAN MANTRI SURAKSHIT MATRITVA ABHIYAN (PMSMA)
Nodal Ministry: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (MoHFW)
- **Goal:** Reduce maternal mortality and identify high-risk pregnancies.
- **Fixed-day service delivery:** Dedicated antenatal check-ups provided on the 9th of every month by medical officers and obstetricians.
- **Color-coded Cards:** 
  - **Red Card:** High risk.
  - **Green Card:** No risk.
  - **Blue Card:** PIH (Pregnancy Induced Hypertension).
  - **Yellow Card:** Any other comorbidities.

DAKSHATA
- **An initiative:** to train health workers in intrapartum and immediate postpartum care.

[SN]SUMAN[/SN]

SURAKSHIT MATRITVA AASHWASAN (SUMAN) SCHEME
Nodal Ministry: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (MoHFW)
- **Launch year:** Launched in October 2019 to provide guaranteed, zero-cost dignified maternal-child healthcare.
- **Goal:** Zero preventable maternal and newborn deaths.
- **Beneficiaries:** Pregnant women during the antenatal period, during delivery, women up to 6 months post-delivery, and children up to 1 year.
- **Provides 18:** assured services.
- **Service Guarantee Charter:** Dignified, respectful quality care; denial of services is not tolerated; ensures a positive birth experience; grievance redressal mechanism (Toll-free 104).

[SN]SUMAN Roadmap 2030[/SN]

[LAQ]SUMAN Roadmap 2030: strategy, targets and interventions[/LAQ]

SUMAN ROADMAP 2030

DEFINITION AND LAUNCH
- **SUMAN Roadmap:** 2030 is a comprehensive, evidence-driven strategic framework of the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (MoHFW) to strengthen maternal and newborn healthcare and accelerate progress towards the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) by 2030.
- **Launched on:** 29 June 2026 by the Union Health Minister at the 16th Conference of the Central Council of Health and Family Welfare (CCHFW).
- **Lead division:** Spearheaded by the Maternal Health Division under the RMNCAH+N operational framework.
- **Combines national:** priorities with local realities, with extra focus on high-burden geographies where maternal and newborn mortality remains a challenge.

RELATION TO THE 2019 SUMAN CHARTER
- **SUMAN (2019):** remains the service-guarantee charter: assured, dignified, respectful, free care with zero tolerance for denial of services.
- **The 2030:** Roadmap is the operational matrix built on that charter: life-cycle interventions, high-risk pregnancy tracking, high-focus district action, community accountability, and digital monitoring to reach SDG maternal and newborn targets.

GOALS AND TARGETS
- **Maternal Mortality Ratio (MMR):** below 70 per 100,000 live births by 2030 (SDG 3.1).
- **Further lowering:** of Neonatal Mortality Rate (NMR) and Infant Mortality Rate (IMR).
- **Universal saturation:** of quality maternal and newborn health services in all States and Union Territories.
- **Zero preventable:** maternal and newborn deaths.

LIFE-CYCLE AND HIGH-RISK FRAMEWORK
- **Life-cycle continuum:** pre-pregnancy, pregnancy, childbirth, and the postnatal period, with convergence to child health, adolescent health, family planning, and nutrition.
- **High-risk pregnancies:** are identified, tracked, and managed through four stages:
  1. Antenatal care
  2. Third-trimester care
  3. Intrapartum care
  4. Postnatal period
- **Also addresses:** transport, tribal and hard-to-reach access, quality emergency obstetric care, SUMAN Panchayats, and climate-related risks to mothers and newborns.

**Mnemonic:** ATIP
- **A:** Antenatal care
- **T:** Third-trimester care
- **I:** Intrapartum care
- **P:** Postnatal period

HIGH-FOCUS GEOGRAPHY
- **Time-bound, focused:** interventions in 130 districts across 13 high-focus States: Assam, Bihar, Chhattisgarh, Haryana, Jharkhand, Karnataka, Madhya Pradesh, Odisha, Punjab, Rajasthan, Uttar Pradesh, Uttarakhand, and West Bengal.
- **Remaining States and Union Territories:** sustain gains and achieve universal coverage of quality maternal and newborn services.

KEY INTERVENTIONS

High-focus States (additional package)
- **SUMAN Package for Pregnant Women:** early registration, complete antenatal care, quality clinical assessment, and adequate post-partum institutional stay.
- **Bi-weekly home:** visits by Accredited Social Health Activists (ASHAs) in the eighth and ninth months: danger-sign detection, nutrition counselling, birth preparedness, and institutional delivery.
- **Financial support:** for designated caregivers in the critical postnatal period.
- **Special incentives:** for referral transport during obstetric emergencies.
- **Hard-to-reach infrastructure:** Establishment of Birth Waiting Homes and Mobile Medical Units in difficult and tribal terrains.

All States and Union Territories
- **Pre-pregnancy care:** folic acid supplementation for women planning pregnancy.
- **Nutrition interventions:** for maternal anaemia and undernutrition.
- **High-risk pregnancy tracking:** Systematic identification, line-listing, and specialist referral of high-risk pregnancies.
- **Strengthen Maternal:** Death Surveillance and Response (MDSR) and Maternal Near Miss (MNM) reviews.
- **Wider use:** of Non-Pneumatic Anti-Shock Garments (NASG) for obstetric haemorrhage.
- **Caesarean audit:** Clinical audit and rationalization of Caesarean section rates against Robson ten-group classification criteria.
- **Climate-responsive planning:** for pregnant women and newborns.
- **Continuum linkage:** Full integration with SSBSK for post-discharge home visitation and infant tracking.

COMMUNITY AND ACCOUNTABILITY
- **SUMAN Panchayats:** (Jan Bhagidari / community partnership): community ownership aimed at zero maternal deaths, zero infant deaths, universal antenatal care, institutional deliveries, full immunisation, and local accountability.
- **Mothers' Picnic:** community engagement to promote positive newborn-care practices.

DIGITAL AND QUALITY ENABLERS
- **JANANI (Journey:** of Antenatal, Natal and Neonatal Integrated Care) Portal: digital monitoring and reporting across the continuum.
- **Centralised SUMAN:** Call Centre for grievance redressal.
- **Apex clinical hubs:** Upgradation of medical colleges as Centres of Excellence (CoE) for maternal and newborn healthcare.
- **Stronger referral:** linkages across facilities.
- **Artificial intelligence:** (AI)-enabled labour rooms.

> **EXAM TIP:** Open with 2019 SUMAN charter versus 2030 Roadmap → targets (MMR below 70) → ATIP four-stage high-risk tracking → 130 districts in 13 high-focus States → high-focus package versus all-State package → close with SUMAN Panchayat, JANANI Portal, and SSBSK linkage. Do not recycle the 2019 18-service list as if it were the 2030 document.

MAA (MOTHERS ABSOLUTE AFFECTION) PROGRAMME
Nodal Ministry: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (MoHFW)
- **Promotes breastfeeding:** Encourages exclusive breastfeeding for 6 months and continuation till 2 years.
- **Human Milk Banks:** Functions include lactation counseling, stimulation and expression support (electric pumps), collection, storage, processing, and dispensing of donor human milk.
- **Hierarchy:** CLMC (Comprehensive Lactation Management Centres in Med Colleges/District hospitals with NICU), LMC (Lactation Management Centres in district/sub-district hospitals with functional SNCU), and LSU (Lactation Supporting Units at all delivery points).

ORGANIZATION OF MATERNAL AND CHILD HEALTHCARE
- **3 Delay Model:** 
  1. Phase I (Decision to seek care): Influenced by socioeconomic/cultural factors.
  2. Phase II (Identifying and reaching medical facility): Influenced by accessibility.
  3. Phase III (Receipt of adequate and appropriate treatment): Influenced by quality of care.

- **Levels of MCH Care:** 
  1. Level 1 (Sub-centre & non-24x7 PHC): Normal vaginal delivery, newborn care, refer high-risk babies. 2-6 beds. < 10 deliveries/month. Staff: ANM, MO.
  2. Level 2 (24x7 PHC, CHC): Vaginal delivery, C-section, basic emergency obstetric care. 10-30 beds. 10-20 deliveries/month. Staff: 1-3 MOs, LHV.
  3. Level 3 (FRU-CHC, District Hospital, Med College): Comprehensive emergency obstetric care. >30 beds. > 20 deliveries/month. Staff: 6 specialties, neonatologist.

- **First Referral Units (FRU):** 
  - **3 Critical Determinants:** Blood storage facility, C-section facility, Newborn care.
  - **Criteria:** 20-30 beds, functional labor room and OT, 24 hr water/electricity, ambulance.
  - **Types:** Non-FRU-CHC (30 beds), FRU-CHC (30-50 beds), FRU-UCHC (Metro 100 beds, Non-metro 50 beds).

 NEWBORN AND CHILD HEALTH INITIATIVES 

NAVJAT SHISHU SURAKSHA KARYAKRAM (NSSK)
Nodal Ministry: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (MoHFW)
- **Provides 2:** days training to healthcare workers / medical officers on basic newborn care and resuscitation services.

RASHTRIYA BAL SWASTHYA KARYAKRAM (RBSK 2.0)
Nodal Ministry: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (MoHFW)
- **Launched 2013:** under NHM; Operational Guidelines updated as RBSK 2.0 (2026), Child Health Division, MoHFW.
- **Aim:** Continuum of early identification → screening → referral → free treatment → follow-up for children and adolescents 0-18 years (curative + preventive + promotive; participatory engagement of child and family).
- **Target age:** Birth to 18 years: universal coverage across facility, Anganwadi and school platforms.
- **Delivery platforms & screening frequency:** 
  - **Birth–6 weeks:** Facility newborn screening at public delivery points (MO / SN / ANM); ASHA via SSBSK (home-based newborn care arm) for home births.
  - **6 weeks to 6 years:** Anganwadi Centres: Mobile Health Team (MHT) screening ≥ twice a year.
  - **6-18 years:** Government and government-aided schools: MHT screening ≥ once every academic year (block = planning hub).
- **Comprehensive 4Ds screening:** Systematic screening across ~38 health conditions categorized under Defects at birth, Diseases, Deficiencies, and Developmental delays.
  1. Defects at birth: Neural tube defects, Down syndrome, Cleft lip and/or palate, Talipes (club foot), Developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH), Congenital cataract, Congenital deafness, Congenital heart diseases, Retinopathy of prematurity, CAKUT (new emphasis under 2.0).
  2. Deficiencies: Anaemia (especially severe), Vitamin A deficiency (Bitot's spot), Vitamin D deficiency (rickets), Severe Acute Malnutrition (SAM), Goitre.
  3. Diseases of childhood (incl. NCDs): Skin conditions, Otitis media (ASOM/CSOM), Rheumatic heart disease, Reactive airway disease, Dental caries, Convulsive disorders, Tuberculosis, Leprosy; expanded NCD screening: Diabetes mellitus (T1 & T2), Hypertension, Kidney disorders (e.g. nephrotic syndrome / glomerulonephritis).
  4. Developmental delays including disabilities: Vision impairment, Hearing impairment, Neuro-motor impairment, Motor / Cognitive / Language delay, Behavioural concerns (anxiety, ADHD, sleep), Neurodevelopmental (ASD, SLD), Global developmental delay (GDD).
  - **Optional / special:** Congenital hypothyroidism (optional); adolescent-specific health concerns; red-flag referral to facility.
  - **Target screening exclusions:** Congenital glaucoma is excluded from the standard 4Ds newborn screening panel (which specifically screens for congenital cataract and congenital deafness).
- **Mobile Health:** Team (core 4; composition flexible under RBSK 2.0): 2 Medical Officers (MBBS / BDS / AYUSH) + 1 ANM / MPW / Staff Nurse / B.Sc Nursing + 1 Pharmacist (or Lab Technician / Ophthalmic Assistant). Support cadres (CHO, School Health & Wellness Ambassadors, peer educators, RKSK / mental health counsellors, interns) reinforce: they do not replace: core MHT.
- **District Early Intervention Centre (DEIC):** District multidisciplinary hub for diagnosis confirmation, early intervention therapies, high-risk follow-up (preterm, LBW, SNCU graduates, birth defects) and tertiary linkage; all DEIC services free of cost for 0-18 years.
- **Care pathway:** Screen (MHT / facility / ASHA) → Identify 4Ds + NCDs → Refer (3-part referral card) → DEIC confirm + therapy → Tertiary hub-and-spoke if needed → MHT / digital loop closure (minimise loss to follow-up).
- **Digital framework (2.0):** Longitudinal Health Report Card via integrated modules: CNS (Comprehensive Newborn Screening), MHT module, DEIC module; interoperability with JANANI / RCH, UDISE+, U-WIN, Poshan Tracker, ABDM (ABHA / BAL ABHA).
- **Financial protection (2.0):** PMJAY-aligned secondary/tertiary packages plus RBSK / State / CSR mix; cochlear implant eligibility expanded to 0-6 years (was 0-2 years under earlier RBSK).
- **Convergence:** MoHFW (NHM, RKSK, AMB, NP-NCD, SSBSK (HBNC+HBYC), eSanjeevani, Tele-MANAS, PMJAY) + MoWCD (AWC, Poshan Tracker) + MoE (schools, UDISE+, SHWAs) + disability rehabilitation linkages.

[SN]Samagra Shishu Bal Swasthya Karyakram (SSBSK)[/SN]

[LAQ]SSBSK: continuum, visit schedule and risk stratification[/LAQ]

SAMAGRA SHISHU BAL SWASTHYA KARYAKRAM (SSBSK)
Nodal Ministry: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (MoHFW)
- **Unified, family-centric:** programme (Operational Guidelines 2026, MoHFW) integrating HBNC (2011/2014) and HBYC (2018) into one continuum of home-based care from birth to 36 months, with risk-stratified follow-up and stronger CPHC linkages through Ayushman Arogya Mandirs (AAM).
- **Tagline:** pehle teen saal, sampoorna dekhbhal (first three years, complete care).
- **Delivery model:** AAA team (ASHA-AWW-ANM) with CHO (rural) or MO (urban) for joint visits; digitally enabled via Shaishav App interoperable with JANANI, U-WIN, RBSK 2.0, POSHAN Tracker, MPCDSR.

Why unify (high yield)
- **First ~3:** years are critical for brain development; care does not stop at 15 months (old HBYC end).
- **Preterm/LBW/SNCU graduates:** remain vulnerable beyond the neonatal period.
- **Post-neonatal bridge:** Closes the historic service vacuum between Day 42 (conclusion of classic HBNC) and 3 months of age.
- **Aligns with INAP "Care Beyond Survival":** Survive, Thrive, Transform.

What changed vs separate HBNC/HBYC
- **Duration:** single continuum birth-36 months (was HBNC 0-42 days; HBYC 3-15 months).
- **Risk focus:** full risk stratification with entry/exit criteria (not limited high-risk only).
- **Maternal mental health:** PHQ-2/CBAC screen then counsel then Tele-MANAS or AAM (CHO/MO).
- **Digital:** Shaishav App for risk flag, visit scheduling, danger-sign prompts (paper-heavy reporting reduced).
- **Team:** AAA + CHO/MO joint care, not ASHA+ANM alone.
- **Programme consolidation:** The Home Based Newborn Care (HBNC) and Home Based Young Child Care (HBYC) visitation schedules are unified under the SSBSK continuum.

HOME VISIT SCHEDULE: NEWBORN (0-42 DAYS)
Healthy newborn
- **Institutional delivery:** 4 visits - Day 3, 7, 14, 42.
- **Home delivery:** 5 visits - Day 1, 3, 7, 14, 42.
- **Focus:** exclusive breastfeeding, warmth, danger signs, immunization linkage, maternal PNC, ECD (talk/touch/play).

At-risk newborn: 9 visits
- **Days 1,:** 3, 5, 7, 10, 14, 21, 28, 42.
- **Joint visits Day 3 and Day 7:** rural ASHA+ANM+CHO; urban ASHA+ANM+MO.
- **Mandatory facility:** follow-up for at-risk within 8 days of discharge.
- **All SNCU graduates:** facility reviews at 8 days, 1 month, 3 months, 6 months, 12 months.

At-risk newborn criteria
1. LBW (<2500 g) or preterm (<37 weeks).
2. Feeding failure (breastfeeding not initiated or unable to breastfeed).
3. SNCU/NBSU/MNCU/NICU graduate (hospitalised/discharged).
4. Life-threatening or feeding-impairing congenital anomaly.
5. Low weight-for-age trajectory: not regained birth weight by Day 14, or no weight gain on 2 consecutive visits after Day 14.

YOUNG CHILD CONTACTS (6 WEEKS TO 36 MONTHS)
- **Bridge the old HBNC-HBYC gap:** VHSND/UIP contacts at 1.5 months and 2.5 months (screen danger signs, weigh and plot, reinforce EBF, ECD and safety counselling).
- **ASHA home:** visits for ALL young children - 8 visits: 3, 6, 9, 12, 18, 24, 30, 36 months.
- **Joint visits:** at Month 3 and Month 6 for at-risk children (same AAA+CHO/MO pattern).
- **Well-Baby Sessions:** on every VHSND/UHND continue till 3 years as extra contacts beyond home visits.

At-risk young child (6 weeks to 36 months): entry
- **Moderately underweight (yellow):** WFA -2 to -3 SD or WFL/H -2 to -3 SD.
- **Severely underweight (red):** WFA < -3 SD or WFL/H < -3 SD.
- **Nutritional rehabilitation follow-up:** Post-NRC discharge follow-up care.
- **Developmental delay:** (MCP card red flags / milestones).
- **Recurrent illness:** (>=2 episodes in 1 year needing hospital/doctor).
- **Partial/incomplete age-appropriate:** immunization.

Exit from at-risk (all must be met)
- **Low-risk criteria:** Weight-for-age within green growth chart zone, age-appropriate developmental milestones, and age-appropriate routine vaccination.
- **Re-entry allowed:** anytime till 36 months if criteria reappear. Continuous reassessment is mandatory.

CRITICAL DISTINCTION: AT-RISK vs DANGER SIGNS
- **At-risk:** closer observation, intensified home visits, joint visits, growth monitoring, line-list/digital flag, referral only when indicated.
- **Danger signs:** pre-referral stabilization, urgent referral, inform ANM/CHO, arrange transport (JSSK), keep warm, prevent hypoglycaemia. Any child (healthy or at-risk) can develop danger signs.

CORE CARE PACKAGE (HOME)
- **Home-based KMC:** for LBW/small/SNCU-NBSU-MNCU graduates: skin-to-skin >=8 hours/day when possible; EBF 10-12 times/day; EBM by katori-paladai (no bottle).
- **Nutrition:** EBF 6 months; complementary feeding after 6 months with continued BF; growth monitoring and plot on MCP card every visit.
- **ECD (5 domains):** good health, adequate nutrition, responsive caregiving, security and safety, early learning.
- **Maternal PNC:** and mental health embedded in every scheduled visit.

> **EXAM TIP:** Open with definition (HBNC+HBYC to birth-36 mo continuum). Table healthy vs at-risk visit days. State at-risk is not the same as danger signs. End with AAA+CHO joint visits, VHSND bridge at 1.5/2.5 mo, and Well-Baby Session till 3 years.


FACILITY BASED NEWBORN CARE
1. MCH Level I (PHC, Sub-centre): Newborn Care Corner (NBCC) in the labour room. Care of normal newborn, BF support, prompt referral.
2. MCH Level II (CHC, First referral unit): Newborn Stabilization Unit (NBSU). Advanced resuscitation, phototherapy, newborn sepsis management, stabilization and referral of very low birth weight (1800-2500 gms).
3. MCH Level III (District Hospital): Special Newborn Care Unit (SNCU) away from labour room. 24x7 neonatologist/pediatrician, management of LBW < 1.8 kg, follow-up of discharged babies.

NUTRITIONAL REHABILITATION CENTRES (NRCs)
- **Facility-based units:** providing medical and nutritional care to Severe Acute Malnutrition (SAM) children under 5 years of age with medical complications.

IMNCI: INTEGRATED MANAGEMENT OF NEONATAL & CHILDHOOD ILLNESSES
Nodal Ministry: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (MoHFW)
- **Target:** 0-5 years old infants.
- **Illnesses included:** Acute respiratory infections (Pneumonia), Diarrhoea, Measles, Malaria, Malnutrition, Otitis media.
- **Colour Coded Management:** 
  - **Green:** Home management.
  - **Yellow:** OPD & medical treatment.
  - **Pink:** Referral to CHC/Hospital.

INDIAN NEWBORN ACTION PLAN (INAP)
Nodal Ministry: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (MoHFW)
- **Aim:** Achieve single-digit stillbirth rate & neonatal mortality rate (< 10 / 1000 live births) by 2030.
- **Epidemiological milestone:** India has achieved a single-digit national stillbirth rate ahead of the 2030 target.
- **6 Pillars of Care:** Pre-conception & antenatal, Care during labour & childbirth, Immediate newborn care, Care of healthy newborn, Care of small & sick newborn, Care beyond survival.

 ADOLESCENT HEALTH INITIATIVES 

RASHTRIYA KISHOR SWASTHYA KARYAKRAM (RKSK)
Nodal Ministry: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (MoHFW)
- **Targets:** Girls and boys, married/unmarried, poor/affluent, school/out of school.
- **Objectives:** Improve nutrition, enable sexual and reproductive health, enhance mental health, prevent injuries and violence, prevent substance misuse, and address NCDs.
- **7C Strategy:** Coverage, Content, Communities, Clinics, Counselling, Communication, Convergence.

ADOLESCENT FRIENDLY HEALTH CLINICS (AFHC) / ARSH
- **Objectives:** 
  - **Weekly Iron:** Folic Acid Supplementation (WIFS): 60mg elemental iron & 500 mcg Folic acid weekly.
  - **Promote menstrual hygiene:** Access to good quality sanitary pads.
  - **Decrease RTI:** / STI.

MENSTRUAL HYGIENE SCHEME (MHS)
Nodal Ministry: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (MoHFW)
- **Aim:** Promote menstrual hygiene among adolescent girls (10-19 years) in rural areas.
- **FREEDAYS:** Sanitary packs provided to adolescent girls in rural areas at a subsidized rate of Rs. 6 for a pack of 6 sanitary pads.
- **ASHA workers:** receive an incentive of Rs. 1 per pack sold, plus a free pack of napkins every month for personal use.

KISHORI SHAKTI YOJANA (KSY)
Nodal Ministry: Ministry of Women and Child Development (MWCD)
- **ICDS adolescent platform:** Nutrition and life-skills initiative for adolescent girls delivered via Anganwadi platforms.
- **Multi-sectoral oversight:** Administered by the Ministry of Women and Child Development in convergence with POSHAN Abhiyaan.

[SN]Intensified National iron plus initiative (I-NIPI)[/SN]

INTENSIFIED NATIONAL IRON PLUS INITIATIVE (I-NIPI) / ANAEMIA MUKT BHARAT
Nodal Ministry: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (MoHFW)

Definition
I-NIPI is the intensified national strategy (repositioned under Anaemia Mukt Bharat) to reduce anaemia across life-cycle groups through prophylactic IFA, deworming, behavioural change, testing and treatment, and intersectoral convergence.

Why it matters
- **Anaemia contributes:** to maternal morbidity, low birth weight, child development deficits, and reduced work capacity.
- **Strategic priority:** Functions as a cross-cutting priority across RMNCAH+N and POSHAN Abhiyaan frameworks.

Core intervention packages
1. Prophylactic IFA supplementation by age and physiological group (children; adolescents via WIFS; women of reproductive age; pregnant and lactating women: as per national schedules).
2. Deworming in target age groups (linked to National Deworming Day where applicable).
3. Behaviour change: dietary diversity, delayed cord clamping messaging, compliance support.
4. Testing and treatment of anaemic cases using point-of-care screening where available and facility confirmation/treatment.
5. Mandatory IFA provision at programme contact points (pregnancy contacts, school/AWC platforms).
6. Convergence with RKSK, PMSMA, SUMAN service contacts, ICDS/POSHAN platforms, and schools.

Indian context:
- **Implementation platform:** Delivered through NHM/RMNCAH+N contacts (ASHA/ANM), schools (WIFS), and Anganwadi platforms; links to POSHAN Abhiyaan outcomes.

> **EXAM TIP:** Define I-NIPI/AMB → life-cycle groups → IFA + deworming + diet + test-treat → convergence with WIFS/PMSMA/POSHAN → close with “anaemia control is multi-platform, not a single pill programme”.

[SN]Poshan Abhiyaan[/SN]

[LAQ]Nutritional strategies under POSHAN Abhiyaan and integration with health programmes[/LAQ]

POSHAN ABHIYAAN (NATIONAL NUTRITION MISSION)
Nodal Ministry: Ministry of Women and Child Development (MWCD)

Definition
POSHAN Abhiyaan is India’s flagship nutrition mission to improve nutritional outcomes of children, adolescents, pregnant women and lactating mothers through a convergent, technology-supported, Jan Andolan approach.

Objectives (scaffold)
- **Improve nutritional:** outcomes for children under 6 years, adolescent girls, pregnant women and lactating mothers.
- **Strengthen service:** delivery quality and coverage under the ICDS/Anganwadi ecosystem.
- **Drive behaviour:** change on diet diversity, hygiene, breastfeeding, and complementary feeding.

Strategic pillars
1. Convergence: Health (NHM/RMNCAH+N), WCD (ICDS/Anganwadi), drinking water and sanitation, Education, PRI.
2. ICT-enabled real-time monitoring: growth monitoring and service tracking tools for frontline workers.
3. Capacity building: Incremental Learning Approach for workers.
4. Jan Andolan: community mobilisation, POSHAN Maah/Pakhwada.
5. Service package quality: supplementary nutrition, IYCF counselling, anaemia interventions, SAM referral pathways.

Integration with health programmes
- **ANC/PMSMA/SUMAN:** maternal nutrition, IFA, weight gain, counselling.
- **SSBSK:** breastfeeding, complementary feeding, illness care, ECD.
- **RBSK 2.0/NRC:** 4Ds (incl. SAM) with DEIC/NRC linkage; facility rehabilitation.
- **UIP sessions:** contact point for growth/IYCF messages.
- **Anaemia Mukt Bharat / I-NIPI:** IFA, deworming, diet.
- **Swachh Bharat / Jal Jeevan:** WASH: diarrhoea-nutrition cycle.

Conclusion
POSHAN Abhiyaan converts nutrition from a narrow food-supplementation idea into a multi-sector outcome mission; health systems supply the clinical and community contact density.

> **EXAM TIP:** Definition → objectives → 5 pillars → integration list with RMNCAH schemes → Jan Andolan → short conclusion on convergence.

> **EXAM TIP:** For RMNCH+A LAQ: evolution CSSM→RCH→RMNCH+A/RMNCAH+N → continuum table (R/M/N/C/A + Nutrition) → flagship schemes (JSY/JSSK/SUMAN/RBSK/RKSK) → challenges and strategies. For SUMAN SN: zero preventable deaths → beneficiaries → service guarantee/grievance → link JSSK + LaQshya.

[REF]Reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine (28th Edition), RMNCAH+N; MoHFW Operational Guidelines for Maternal, Newborn, Child, and Adolescent Health.[/REF]

subsections.title: National Vector Borne Disease Control Programme (NVBDCP)
subsections.content:
[LAQ]National Vector Borne Disease Control Programme: strategies and vector management[/LAQ]

INTRODUCTION
Nodal Ministry: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (MoHFW)

The National Vector Borne Disease Control Programme (NVBDCP) is implemented in the States and Union Territories for the prevention and control of vector-borne diseases. The Directorate of NVBDCP is the nodal agency for planning, policy-making, technical guidance, monitoring, and evaluation under the overall umbrella of the National Health Mission (NHM).

The programme covers the following six vector-borne diseases:
1. Malaria (Anopheles mosquito)
2. Filariasis (Culex mosquito)
3. Kala-azar (Sand flies - Visceral leishmaniasis)
4. Japanese Encephalitis (Culex mosquito)
5. Dengue (Aedes mosquito)
6. Chikungunya (Aedes mosquito)

STRATEGIES AND INTERVENTIONS

The three-pronged strategy for the prevention and control of vector-borne diseases is as follows:
1. Disease Management
- **Early case:** detection and complete treatment (Most important).
- **Referral strengthening:** Upgrade of first referral units and district hospitals for severe vector-borne disease management.
- **Epidemic preparedness:** and rapid response.
2. Integrated Vector Management (IVM)
- **Anti-larval measures:** (Chemical, biological, and environmental methods).
- **Anti-adult measures:** (Indoor Residual Sprays - IRS, Space sprays, Genetic control).
- **Personal protection:** (Nets, Repellents, Screening).
- **Legislative measures:** (Civil laws).
3. Supportive Interventions
- **Behaviour Change:** Communication (BCC) focusing on health education.
- **Public-private partnership:** Collaborative engagement with private health providers.
- **Inter-sectoral convergence:** Coordinated multi-departmental vector abatement.
- **Capacity building:** and operational research.

INTEGRATED VECTOR CONTROL APPROACH

1. Anti-Larval Measures (Preferred in Urban Areas, specifically >50,000 population & Slide Positivity Rate ≥ 5%)
- **Environmental Control:** Yields permanent results focusing on source reduction (levelling ground, filling drains/ditches, intermittent irrigation, altering salinity).
- **Chemical Control:** Spraying larvicides like Paris green, Temephos (Abate - 200L/hectare), Fenthion, and Chlorpyrifos.
- **Biological Control:** Larvivorous fish (Gambusia affine and Lebistes reticulates/Barbados Millions), Toxorhynchites splendens (predator mosquito for Aedes), and Antilarval bacilli (Bacillus thuringiensis). Used in burrow pits, sewage oxidation ponds, and cisterns.

2. Anti-Adult Measures (Preferred in Rural Areas)
- **Space Spray (Fogging):** Malathion / Pyrethroids.
- **Indoor Residual Spray (IRS):** DDT 50% WP, Malathion 25% WP, Pyrethroids (Deltamethrin, Cyfluthrin).
- **IRS Rules:** based on API (Annual Parasite Incidence):
  - **Areas with API > 2:** IRS at regular intervals (6 weeks) using DDT/Malathion/Pyrethroids.
  - **Areas with API < 2:** Focal space spray with Malathion/DDT whenever a case of P. falciparum is reported.
- **Insecticide Application:** DDT (2 rounds of 1 gm/m² in transmission season; if refractory, shift to Malathion), Malathion (3 rounds of 2 gm/m²), Synthetic pyrethroids (2 rounds of 0.25 gm/m² conducted at 6-week intervals).

3. Personal Protection and Programme Targeting (do not conflate)
- **Programme stratification:** high API / high-burden areas prioritise LLIN coverage, IRS as per insecticide susceptibility, and intensified surveillance; lower-burden areas emphasise surveillance, early diagnosis and complete treatment, and focal outbreak response.
- **Personal protection:** insecticide-treated nets / LLINs, protective clothing, repellents, and screening reduce man-vector contact wherever Anopheles transmission risk exists. API categories guide public-programme resource allocation; they do not mean individuals in low-API settings need no net.
- **LLINs:** long-lasting insecticide-treated nets (programme shelf-life commonly cited around 3 years of useful life under field conditions).
- **Common repellents:** DEET, lemon grass oil, soybean oil, neem oil, chrysanthemum oil.

MALARIA CONTROL AND ELIMINATION

KEY MILESTONES
- **1953:** Launching of National Malaria Control Programme (NMCP).
- **1958:** NMCP changed to National Malaria Eradication Programme (NMEP).
- **1971:** Urban Malaria Scheme launched (Focus on anti-larval measures).
- **1977:** Modified Plan of Operations implemented (Stratified by API < 2 and API > 2).
- **1997:** World Bank assisted Enhanced Malaria Control Project (EMCP) launched (Tribal areas with API > 2 for last 3 years).
- **1998:** Roll Back Malaria (received WHO funding, focused on insecticides and bed nets).
- **2003-04:** Renamed to National Vector Borne Disease Control Programme (NVBDCP).
- **2005:** Introduction of Rapid Diagnostic Tests (RDT).
- **2016:** National Framework for Malaria Elimination in India 2016-2030 launched.

NATIONAL FRAMEWORK FOR MALARIA ELIMINATION IN INDIA (2016-2030)
- **Goals:** Eliminate malaria (0 indigenous cases) throughout the entire country by 2030, with an interim target of zero indigenous cases by 2027, and maintain malaria-free status.
- **Global Targets:** Reduction in malaria incidence by 90% and reduction in malaria-related deaths by 90%.
- **Programme Phasing and Category Status:** 
  - **Category 0:** Prevention of re-establishment phase (Zero indigenous cases).
  - **Category 1:** Elimination phase (API < 1 case/1000 population at risk).
  - **Category 2:** Pre-elimination phase (API < 1 but some districts API 1/1000 or more).
  - **Category 3:** Intensified control phase (API > 1 case/ 1000 population at risk).

SURVEILLANCE AND CASE DETECTION
- **Active Case Detection:** Done by Male Multipurpose Workers via fortnightly door-to-door fever surveillance and blood smear collection.
- **Passive Case Detection:** Malaria clinics setup under Urban Malaria Scheme; fever treatment depots in villages.
- **Link Worker Scheme:** One link worker for every 2000 population in high P. falciparum areas to collect smears and provide presumptive treatment.
- **Diagnosis:** 
  - **Peripheral Blood Smear:** Thick smear (sensitivity for detecting parasite), Thin smear (specificity for identifying species). Stains used: JSB (Jaswant Rai Bhattacharya) and Giemsa.
  - **Rapid Diagnostic Test (Dipstick):** Rapid detection of P. falciparum (3-5 minutes) based on Histidine-rich protein II Ag detection.
  - **Optimal Test:** Detects both Pf and Pv, based on Parasite Lactate Dehydrogenase (PLDH) antigen. More superior and quicker than dipstick if parasite load is 60-100/microliter.

[SN]Treatment of different types of Malaria according to NVBDCP[/SN]

MALARIA TREATMENT PROTOCOLS (NATIONAL GUIDELINES)

1. Uncomplicated Malaria
- **P. Vivax or P. Ovale:** Chloroquine (DOC: 25mg/kg total dose over 3 days) + Primaquine (0.25mg/kg for 14 days to prevent relapse).
- **P. Falciparum or P. Malariae:** 
  - **Other States (uncomplicated P. falciparum):** ACT-SP [Artesunate (3 days) + Sulphadoxine/Pyrimethamine (Day 1)] + Primaquine (0.75 mg/kg single dose on Day 2 for gametocytocidal action).
  - **Northeastern States:** ACT-AL [Artemether + Lumefantrine] + Primaquine (Day 2).
- **Mixed Infection:** ACT-AL or ACT-SP for 3 days + Primaquine for 14 days.

2. Pregnancy Guidelines
- **Pregnancy with Vivax:** Chloroquine (DOC).
- **Pregnancy with Falciparum:** 
  - **1st Trimester:** Oral Quinine Salts.
  - **2nd/3rd Trimester:** ACT-AL or ACT-SP.
- **Note:** Primaquine is strictly contraindicated in Pregnancy, Infants, and G6PD deficiency.

3. ACT Blister Packs (Age-Based Color Coding)
- **0-1 years:** Pink
- **1-4 years:** Yellow
- **5-8 years:** Green
- **9-14 years:** Red
- **15 & above:** White

4. Severe Malaria Management
- **Diagnosis:** Acute malaria with >5% parasitaemia and/or organ dysfunction (ARDS, circulatory collapse, DIC, severe anemia, hypoglycaemia).
- **Drug of Choice:** Artesunate 2.4 mg/kg body weight IV or IM given on admission (time=0), then at 12 hrs and 24 hrs, then once a day. (Used for adults and children).
- **Alternatives:** Quinine (20 mg salt/kg IV infusion) or Artemether (3.2 mg/kg IM on admission).

5. Chemoprophylaxis
- **Short Term (< 6 weeks):** Doxycycline 100mg daily. Start 1-2 days before travel, continue 4 weeks post-travel.
- **Long Term (> 6 weeks):** Mefloquine 250mg weekly. Start 2-3 weeks before travel, continue 4 weeks post-travel.

FILARIASIS, KALA-AZAR, AND OTHER DISEASES
*(Note: Maintained from the existing programme data)*

Filariasis:
- **Elimination Criteria:** Filaria carriers < 1 percent and children born free from circulating antigenaemia.
- **Mass Drug Administration (MDA):** Recently utilizes Ivermectin + DEC + Albendazole (IDA) for >= 5 years (except pregnant women and children < 2 years).

[LAQ]National Vector Borne Disease Control Programme with reference to Kala-azar[/LAQ]

KALA-AZAR (VISCERAL LEISHMANIASIS) UNDER NVBDCP

Definition
Kala-azar (visceral leishmaniasis) is a protozoal disease caused by Leishmania donovani, transmitted by the bite of infected female sandflies (Phlebotomus argentipes in India), characterised by prolonged fever, weight loss, hepatosplenomegaly, and anaemia.

Public health importance
- **Geographical distribution:** Historically concentrated in endemic foci across Bihar, Jharkhand, West Bengal, and eastern Uttar Pradesh.
- **Poverty, mud:** housing, cattle sheds, and peri-domestic sandfly resting favour transmission.
- **Goal:** elimination as a public health problem , defined as incidence below 1 case per 10,000 population at block/sub-district level, sustained. India reached this incidence threshold at block level nationwide around end-2023; sustained surveillance remains essential.

NVBDCP strategies specific to kala-azar
1. Early case detection: Active case search, camp approaches, and ASHA incentives for suspect referral and treatment-support tasks.
2. Rapid diagnosis: rK39 rapid diagnostic test in programme settings; confirmatory pathways as per national guidelines.
3. Complete treatment: Liposomal amphotericin B (single-dose regimen used in the programme algorithm at 10 mg/kg IV) or alternatives such as miltefosine as per protocol and contraindications.
4. Vector control: Indoor residual spray focused on sandfly resting sites, alongside environmental sanitation around dwellings.
5. Surveillance of post-kala-azar dermal leishmaniasis (PKDL) as a potential reservoir.
6. IEC/BCC and intersectoral action (housing, poverty programmes).
7. Cross-border and inter-state coordination in the endemic belt.

Incentives (programme teaching points)
- **Active case:** search / treatment-support incentives to ASHA and patient support as notified under the programme (commonly taught figures include incentive to ASHA for case detection/support and support to the patient completing treatment).

Challenges
- **Residual transmission:** pockets; PKDL detection; IRS coverage and acceptance; private-sector under-notification; migration; sustaining gains after the threshold is achieved.

Conclusion
Kala-azar control is elimination-oriented NVBDCP work: diagnose early, treat fully, suppress sandfly contact, and sustain surveillance after incidence falls below the elimination threshold.

Japanese Encephalitis & Dengue:
- **JE:** IRS is not effective (outdoor resters). Malathion outdoor fogging is used. Vaccination for 1-15 years.
- **Dengue:** Diagnosis via IgM capture ELISA (after 5th day) and NS1 kits (from 1st day). Vector management focuses on Aedes control.

[LAQ]Environmental determinants of vector-borne diseases and NVBDCP strategies[/LAQ]

ENV DETERMINANTS OF VECTOR-BORNE DISEASES (LAQ FRAME)

Environmental determinants (with examples)
1. Water management: Irrigation, water storage, and blocked drains (Anopheles, Aedes, Culex breeding).
2. Housing and sanitation: Mud plaster cracks (sandfly resting) and improper solid waste disposal (Aedes breeding containers).
3. Climate and seasonality: Temperature, humidity, and rainfall shaping vector longevity and seasonal transmission peaks.
4. Land use and urbanisation: Peri-urban expansion, construction sites, and scrap tyre dumps (Aedes breeding).
5. Animal husbandry and agriculture: Cattle sheds adjacent to dwellings (sandfly proliferation) and waterlogged paddy fields (Culex and Anopheles breeding).
6. Human behaviour and mobility: Outdoor sleeping habits, migration into endemic pockets, and intermittent household water storage practices.

How NVBDCP addresses them
- **Integrated vector management:** source reduction, larviciding, biological control, IRS/space spray as indicated, personal protection (LLINs), and legislative measures.
- **Disease management:** early case detection and complete treatment, epidemic preparedness, rapid response.
- **Supportive interventions:** BCC, intersectoral convergence (municipalities, water/sanitation, agriculture), capacity building.

> **EXAM TIP:** Open with env-determinant list × disease examples → three-pronged NVBDCP strategy table → one disease deep-dive (malaria or kala-azar) → improvements (One Health, urban Aedes, climate early warning).

> **EXAM TIP:** Malaria treatment SN: species × regimen table (Pv CQ+PQ; Pf ACT-SP vs NE ACT-AL; pregnancy rules; severe artesunate) → always state primaquine contraindications. Kala-azar LAQ: agent-vector-host → elimination definition → diagnosis/treatment/vector control → PKDL → sustainability.

[REF]Reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine (28th Edition), National Vector Borne Disease Control Programme; Directorate of NVBDCP / NCVBDC Guidelines, MoHFW.[/REF]

subsections.title: National Leprosy Eradication Programme (NLEP)
subsections.content:
[LAQ]National Leprosy Eradication Programme (NLEP)[/LAQ]

INTRODUCTION AND EPIDEMIOLOGY
Nodal Ministry: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (MoHFW)

Leprosy (Hansen's Disease) is a chronic infectious disease caused by Mycobacterium leprae affecting the peripheral nerves. It is the oldest disease known to mankind and is often referred to as a "social disease." The youngest case of leprosy reported in India was a 2.5-month-old baby.

Epidemiological Determinants:
- **Agent Factors:** Mycobacterium leprae (acid-fast bacilli). High infectivity (affects 4-12 percent of household contacts within 5 years), but low pathogenicity (more subclinical cases, following the iceberg phenomenon). Persists in soil for 1-2 months. Source of infection is humans only. Affects the reticuloendothelial system and Schwann cells.
- **Host Factors:** Males > Females. Peak age: 20-40 years.
- **Environmental Factors:** Lower socioeconomic status, overcrowding, poverty, and winters.
- **Mode of Transmission:** Droplet infection, contact transmission (direct skin-to-skin or indirect via soil/fomites), breast milk from lepromatous mothers, transplacental, insect vectors, and tattooing needles.

Why Leprosy is NOT Amenable to Complete Eradication:
- **Prolonged incubation period:** Extended latency of 5–7 years complicates prompt transmission interruption.
- **Disputed modes:** of transmission.
- **Subclinical reservoir:** Extensive subclinical infections (iceberg phenomenon) undetectable by standard field screening.
- **Complicated spectrum:** of disease manifestations.
- **Cell-mediated immune anergy:** Profound antigen-specific cell-mediated immune failure in lepromatous patients.
- **Bacterial resistance:** and persistence in the human body.
- **Vaccine deficit:** Absence of a dedicated, universally protective preventive vaccine (Mycobacterium indicus pranii under clinical evaluation).
- **Social stigma:** Entrenched cultural stigma and prejudice causing voluntary disease concealment.

KEY MILESTONES
- **1955:** National Leprosy Control Programme (NLCP) launched focusing on monotherapy.
- **1982:** Introduction of Multi Drug Therapy (MDT).
- **1983:** Upgraded and renamed as National Leprosy Eradication Programme (NLEP).
- **2005:** Case load came down to less than 1 per 10,000 population at the national level, achieving the goal of leprosy elimination.

GOALS AND OBJECTIVES
- **Elimination Criteria:** Prevalence rate < 1 case / 10,000 population at the sub-national and district level.
- **Annual New Case Detection Rate (ANCDR):** < 10 cases / lakh population.
- **Grade II Disability:** Reduce Grade II disability percentage to < 1 percent among new cases at the National level, and < 1 case / million population.
- **Zero disabilities:** among new child cases.
- **Zero stigma:** and discrimination against persons affected by leprosy.

LEVELS OF PREVENTION & STRATEGIES

1. PRIMARY PREVENTION
- **Health Education:** Spread awareness through the SPARSH initiative using mascots like Sapna (a cured village school girl) and Meena (concept adopted from UNICEF child rights).
- **Prophylaxis (Post-Exposure:** Prophylaxis - PEP): Single dose Rifampicin is given to close contacts.
  - **Indications:** All household contacts > 2 years. Social contacts (close contact > 20 hours in the last 3 weeks). Neighbourhood contacts within a 75-100 metre radius or 3 houses on either side.
  - **Contraindications:** Children < 2 years old and pregnant women.
  - **PEP Dosage (Single dose Rifampicin):** 
    - **≥ 15 years:** 600mg
    - **10-14 years:** 450mg
    - **Children 6-9 years (weight ≥ 20kg):** 300mg
    - **Children < 20 kg:** 10-15mg/kg

2. SECONDARY PREVENTION (EARLY DIAGNOSIS AND TREATMENT)
- **Early Diagnosis Initiatives:** 
  - **ASBULS (ASHA-Based:** Surveillance of Leprosy Suspects): Door-to-door surveillance. ASHA gets an incentive of Rs. 250 for detecting a case without disability, and Rs. 200 for detecting a case with disability.
  - **Active leprosy:** case detection campaigns (14 days) in high endemic zones, and focused campaigns in low endemic zones.
- **Clinical Diagnosis:** 
  - **Skin Lesion:** Hypopigmented or hyperpigmented patches with sensory loss (Anaesthetic patch). Hypoanaesthetic patch is the most specific type.
  - **Nerve Involvement:** Thickening and enlargement of peripheral nerves + loss of sensation ± weakness of muscle supplied. Most common nerve involved: Ulnar nerve. (Sensory deficit usually precedes motor deficit).
- **Laboratory Diagnosis:** (Skin Slit Smear Examination):
  - **Bacteriological Index:** (BI) calculation indicates disease prognosis.
  - **BI =:** Total score in all smears / No. of smears.
  - **Scoring:** 0 (0 bacilli in 100 fields), 1+ (1-10 bacilli in 100 fields), 2+ (1-10 bacilli in 10 fields), up to 6+ (>1000 bacilli in each field).
  - **BI <:** 2 -> Paucibacillary (PB); BI ≥ 2 -> Multibacillary (MB).

CLASSIFICATION IN LEPROSY
- **Based on:** Clinical Grounds (NLEP standard for treatment):
  - **Paucibacillary (PB):** 1-5 skin lesions, NO nerve involved, negative skin smear at all sites.
  - **Multibacillary (MB):** > 5 skin lesions, ≥ 1 nerve involved, positive skin smear at any site.
- **Other Classifications (Prognostic use only):** Ridley-Jopling (TT, BT, BB, BL, LL), Indian Classification (Indeterminate, Tuberculoid, Borderline, Lepromatous, Pure Neuritic), Madrid Classification.

TREATMENT (NLEP REGIMEN)
- **Blister Packs:** Color-coded as Pink for adults and Brown for children. Contains a supervised monthly dose and a daily dose.
- **Standard MDT:** 
  - **Adults (>14 years):** Rifampicin 600 mg once a month (supervised); Clofazimine 300 mg once a month (supervised) + 50 mg daily; Dapsone 100 mg daily.
  - **Children (10-14 years):** Rifampicin 450 mg once a month (supervised); Clofazimine 150 mg once a month (supervised) + 50 mg alternate days; Dapsone 50 mg daily.
  - **Children (<10 years / <40 kg):** Requires single formulation medications (Rifampicin 10 mg/kg monthly, Clofazimine 100 mg monthly + 50 mg twice weekly, Dapsone 2 mg/kg daily).
- **Recent Update (Effective April 1, 2025):** India transitioned to a uniform 3-drug regimen (Rifampicin, Dapsone, and Clofazimine) for both Paucibacillary (PB) and Multibacillary (MB) cases. The duration remains 6 months for PB and 12 months for MB.
- **Defaulter:** A patient on MDT who has not collected treatment for 12 consecutive months.
- **Relapse:** A patient whose therapy was terminated successfully but subsequently develops new signs and symptoms.

FOLLOW-UP AND DRUG-RESISTANT LEPROSY
- **Follow-up post-treatment:** Patients released from treatment are followed up for at least 5 years. ASHA workers receive Rs. 400 for PB and Rs. 600 for MB completion.
- **Drug-Resistant Leprosy:** 24 months treatment duration. Uses Ofloxacin, Minocycline, and Clofazimine (with Clarithromycin added for Rifampicin+Ofloxacin resistance).

3. TERTIARY PREVENTION (DPMR)
- **Disability Prevention:** and Medical Rehabilitation (DPMR) includes disability limitation, free reconstructive surgeries, crutches, and free microcellular (MCR) footwear.
- **Reconstructive surgery (RCS) incentives:** Rs. 12,000 as a welfare allowance to the patient (raised from Rs. 8,000), and Rs. 5,000 to the government institution/PMR center.
- **3 Tier System for DPMR:** Primary (PHC/CHC), Secondary (District Hospital/Nucleus), Tertiary (JALMA, PMR institutes).

INDICATORS AND MONITORING
- **NIKUSHTH:** Real-time leprosy monitoring software across India.
- **Primary / Core Indicator:** Annual New Case Detection Rate (ANCDR). Target < 10 cases/lakh population. Most important epidemiological indicator.
- **Operational / Health Awareness Indicator:** Grade 2 disability rate (target < 1% among new cases, current 1.31 per million population in 2024-25).
- **Long-Term Impact Indicator:** Prevalence rate.

IMMUNITY TESTING: LEPROMIN TEST
- **Immunological assessment:** Lepromin test measures host cell-mediated immune competence, serving prognostic and classification purposes rather than diagnosis.
- **0.1 ml:** Lepromin (Dharmendra or Mitsuda antigen) injected intradermally on the forearm.
- **Early Reaction (Fernandez reaction):** Read at 48 hours. Redness > 10 mm indicates +ve. Indicates prior exposure/hypersensitivity (Corresponds to Mantoux reaction).
- **Late Reaction (Mitsuda reaction):** Read at 21 days. Nodule > 5 mm diameter is +ve. Indicates active cell-mediated immunity.
- **Note:** The Lepromin test is negative in lepromatous cases and in most infants < 6 months, but BCG vaccination can convert a lepromin test result from negative to positive.

URBAN LEPROSY CONTROL AND NGOS
- **Urban leprosy assistance:** Dedicated technical and financial assistance provided to municipal corporations and townships with population >1 lakh.
- **612 self-settled:** colonies house around 50,000 leprosy-affected persons.
- **NGOs (e.g.,:** Leprosy Mission, Lepra India) are involved in DPMR, IEC, and SET (Survey Education and Treatment) schemes, with 54 NGOs receiving grant-in-aid.

NATIONAL STRATEGIC PLAN AND ROADMAP FOR LEPROSY (2023-2027)
- **Pillar 1:** Strengthen leadership, commitment, and partnerships.
- **Pillar 2:** Accelerate Case Detection.
- **Pillar 3:** Provide Quality Services.
- **Pillar 4:** Prevention of Disease, Disabilities, Stigma, and Discrimination (including PEP).
- **Pillar 5:** Develop Digital Surveillance Systems (Nikusth 2.0).

> **EXAM TIP:** For NLEP LAQ: Define elimination (<1 case/10,000) vs eradication → obstacles to eradication → WHO classification (PB vs MB) → MDT blister packs and drug regimens (Rifampicin, Dapsone, Clofazimine) → DPMR (RCS, MCR footwear) → National Strategic Plan 2023–2027 (Nikusth 2.0, SDR-PEP, zero child disability).

[REF]Reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine (28th Edition), National Leprosy Eradication Programme; Central Leprosy Division, MoHFW Guidelines.[/REF]

subsections.title: National Tuberculosis Elimination Programme (NTEP)
subsections.content:
[LAQ]National Tuberculosis Elimination Programme (NTEP)[/LAQ]

INTRODUCTION AND HISTORY
Nodal Ministry: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (MoHFW)

The National Tuberculosis Programme (NTP) has been in operation since 1962. Due to low treatment success rates, it was revitalized as the Revised National Tuberculosis Control Programme (RNTCP) in 1997, adopting the Directly Observed Treatment Short-course (DOTS) strategy. In 2020, the programme was officially renamed the National Tuberculosis Elimination Programme (NTEP) to align with the goal of ending TB.

GOALS AND OBJECTIVES

- **National Strategic Plan (2017-2025):** Vision of 0 death, 0 disease, and 0 poverty.
- **Primary Goal:** End TB by 2025.
- **Mortality reduction:** 90 percent reduction.
- **Incidence reduction:** 80 percent reduction.
- **0 percent:** of patients having catastrophic expenditure due to TB.

STRATEGIES AND INTERVENTIONS (DTPB)

- **Detect:** Find all TB cases with an emphasis on reaching every TB patient in the private sector.
- **Treat:** Initiate and sustain all patients on appropriate anti-TB treatment wherever they seek care, with high-quality anti-TB drugs.
- **Prevent:** Prevent the emergence of TB in susceptible populations and stop catastrophic expenditure.
- **Build:** Build and strengthen supportive systems including enabling policies, empowered institutions, and human resources.

HIGH RISK GROUPS AND CASE DETECTION

1. High Risk Groups:
- **Comorbidities:** Diabetes, COVID-19, PLHIV, Organ transplant recipients, Dialysis patients, Malignancies, and those on immunosuppressants.
- **Social / Occupational:** Prisoners, Migrant populations, Shelter/Old age homes, and Occupational exposure like Silicosis (sandstone, glass, pottery, mines, coal industries).
- **Geographical:** Urban slums, Tribal areas.

2. Types of Case Detection:
- **Active Case Finding:** Screening for TB in the community among high-risk groups (urban slums, prisoners, tribal areas).
- **Intensified Case Finding:** Screening people attending clinics with comorbidities like diabetes, PLHIV, COVID, and malignancy.
- **Passive Case Finding:** TB clinic reporting.

DIAGNOSTICS AND LABORATORY NETWORK

Definitions:
- **Presumptive TB Case (formerly TB suspect):** Any person with cough ≥ 2 weeks duration; fever/night sweats/weight loss ≥ 2 weeks; contacts of a smear-positive TB patient having cough of any duration; suspected extra-pulmonary TB; or an HIV positive patient having a cough of any duration.
- **Sputum Positive TB:** Bacteriologically confirmed case.
- **Sputum Negative TB:** Clinically confirmed case.

Diagnostic Modalities & Algorithm:
- **Universal Drug Susceptibility Testing (DST):** CBNAAT is done at baseline for any TB suspect to rule out rifampicin resistance.
- **Pediatric & Extra-Pulmonary TB:** Investigation of Choice (IOC) is CBNAAT. For pediatric cases, Chest X-ray + CBNAAT + Tuberculin test is used.
- **Algorithm:** Upfront NAAT (CBNAAT/Truenat) is the primary diagnostic test for all presumptive TB cases to detect MTB and Rifampicin resistance simultaneously.
  - **If MTB:** is detected, assess Rifampicin resistance via CBNAAT.
  - **Rifampicin Sensitive:** -> Start Drug Sensitive TB regime & first-line LPA (Line Probe Assay).
  - **Rifampicin Resistance:** -> Refer for resistant TB management -> 1st line LPA, 2nd line LPA, and Liquid Culture.

CLASSIFICATION OF DRUG RESISTANT TB (DRTB)

- **Mono-Resistant (MR):** Resistant to any 1 TB drug other than rifampicin.
- **H-Mono Resistant:** Resistant to isoniazid (most common).
- **Rifampicin Resistant (RR):** Resistant to rifampicin only.
- **Multi Drug Resistant (MDR):** Resistant to both rifampicin and isoniazid.
- **Poly-Drug Resistant (PDR):** Drug resistance to any drugs but NOT rifampicin and isoniazid.
- **Pre-extensively drug-resistant (pre-XDR-TB):** MDR/RR-TB with additional resistance to any fluoroquinolone (WHO 2021).
- **Extensively drug-resistant (XDR-TB):** MDR/RR-TB with resistance to any fluoroquinolone and to at least one Group A drug (bedaquiline and/or linezolid) (WHO 2021).
- **Presumptive MDR:** Non/poor response to 1st line therapy, treatment after loss to follow up, recurrent TB, or contact history of MDR-TB/PLHIV/TB death in household.

TREATMENT REGIMENS

1. Drug Sensitive TB (Weight Band Categories for FDCs):
- **Intensive Phase (IP):** 2 months of HRZE.
- **Continuation Phase (CP):** 4 months of HRE.
- **Adult Weight Bands (Kg) / Number of FDCs:** 25-34 (2 tabs), 35-49 (3 tabs), 50-64 (4 tabs), 65-75 (5 tabs), >75 (6 tabs). Individualise if higher bands are not tolerated.
- **Pediatric Weight:** Bands (Kg) / Number of Dispersible FDCs: 4-7 (1 tab), 8-11 (2 tabs), 12-15 (3 tabs), 16-24 (4 tabs), 25-29 (3+1A tabs), 30-39 (2+2A tabs).

2. Drug Resistant TB:
- **BPaLM Regimen (6 months):** Adopted by MoHFW in 2024 for RR/MDR/Pre-XDR. Includes Bedaquiline, Pretomanid, Linezolid, and Moxifloxacin. (Pretomanid is C/I in pregnant/lactating women and hypothyroidism; Linezolid causes anemia/neuropathy; Bedaquiline causes cardiac conduction disorders).
- **Older Regimens:** 9-11 months of CHOBZEE or 18-20 months of BC2L2 for XDR.
- **H-Mono/Poly Drug DXTB:** 6 months of Pyrazinamide, Ethambutol, Rifampicin, Levofloxacin (6 ZERO IP) & No CP.

3. Treatment in Pregnancy:
- **Drug-sensitive TB:** standard first-line daily FDC regimen (HRZE → HRE) is used; streptomycin is avoided.
- **Pyridoxine supplementation:** is important with isoniazid.
- **Drug-resistant TB:** managed under PMDT with regimen individualisation (certain newer agents carry pregnancy-specific cautions; for example, pretomanid is contraindicated during pregnancy).
- **Pregnancy continuation:** Medical termination of pregnancy is never routinely indicated solely due to maternal tuberculosis diagnosis.

4. Prophylaxis & Evaluation:
- **Contacts of Resistant TB:** Rifampicin resistant + FQ sensitive -> Levofloxacin (6 months). Isoniazid resistant + Rifampicin sensitive -> Rifampicin (4 months).
- **Pyridoxine Supplementation:** Added for patients on ATT (Children 10 mg/day, Adults 25 mg/day, PLHIV 50 mg/day).
- **Treatment Evaluation:** CBC, UPT, Urea/Creatinine (Ethambutol/Rifampicin nephrotoxic), LFT (Pyrazinamide/Isoniazid hepatotoxic), TSH (Pretomanid/Ethionamide cause hypothyroidism), ECG (Bedaquiline/Delamanid).

TB-HIV COINFECTION

- **Start ATT:** first, then 2 weeks later start ART to prevent immune reconstitution syndrome.
- **Prophylaxis of TB in PLHIV:** Evaluated via CBNAAT. If TB negative, TB preventive therapy given to those > 13 years old -> Isoniazid + Rifapentine.

INCENTIVES AND IT SYSTEMS

- **Nikshay Poshan Yojana:** Nutritional incentive of Rs. 1000/month given to all notified TB patients.
- **Informant Incentive:** Any individual who helps identify a case of TB in the community is given Rs. 500.
- **Private Practitioners:** Rs. 500 on notifying a case, and Rs. 500 on treatment completion. Failure to notify is a punishable offence with imprisonment for a term which may extend from six months to two years, or fine, or both.
- **IT Systems:** NIKSHAY (web portal for notification/surveillance).
- **Compliance Tech:** DOTS 99 (toll-free number inside the tablet strip) and MERM Box (Medicine Event Reminder Monitor - digital pillbox for MDR-TB capturing data on pillbox opening).

NEW INITIATIVES AND PARTNERSHIPS

- **TB Mukt Bharat Abhiyan & Nikshay Mitra:** Any individual, NGO, or corporate can adopt a TB patient for a minimum of 6 months to a maximum of 3 years to provide nutritional, additional diagnostic, and vocational support.
- **SAKSHAM PRAVAAH:** National trainers provide training to frontline workers on soft skills and psychosocial aspects.
- **NISHTHA:** Aims at providing quality care for control of TB by strengthening primary healthcare.
- **PROJECT ECHO:** Extension for community healthcare outcomes to provide treatment/diagnostics at the periphery.
- **JEET (Joint:** Effort for Elimination of Tuberculosis): Increasing notification rates by private practitioners.
- **National TB SAMPARK Helpline:** 1800-11-6666.
- **TB CHAMP:** Trial to see the use of levofloxacin in children for multidrug-resistant preventive therapy.

INFECTION CONTROL
- **Isolation:** Patient on TB treatment should be isolated for 3 weeks (Within 48hrs bacterial load reduces by 50-90%; 2 weeks 95%; 3 weeks 99%).
- **BMW Handling:** Sputum disposed in 5% cresol or 5% phenol after 12 hours into hospital effluent system, or collected in handkerchief and burned. Autoclave slides at 121°C for 15 mins.

> **EXAM TIP:** Open NTEP with history NTP→RNTCP→NTEP → NSP goals → Detect-Treat-Prevent-Build → diagnostics (upfront NAAT) → DS vs DR regimens with correct weight bands and WHO DR definitions → Nikshay/Nikshay Poshan → close with End TB framing.

[REF]Reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine (28th Edition), National Tuberculosis Elimination Programme; Central TB Division, MoHFW Guidelines.[/REF]

subsections.title: National AIDS Control Programme (NACP)
subsections.content:
[LAQ]National AIDS Control Programme (NACP Phase V)[/LAQ]

INTRODUCTION AND HISTORY
Nodal Ministry: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (MoHFW)

The National AIDS Control Organization (NACO) was set up in 1992 under the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, headquartered in New Delhi. The first case of HIV/AIDS in India was detected in 1986 in Chennai, Tamil Nadu.

The primary aim of the National AIDS Control Programme (NACP) is to prevent further transmission of HIV, decrease morbidity and mortality, and minimize socio-economic impact. NACP merged with the National Health Mission in 2021.

NACP PHASE-V (2021-2026) GOALS & STRATEGY

- **Reduce Annual:** New HIV Infections by 80 percent by 2025-26 from the 2010 baseline.
- **Reduce AIDS-related:** mortality by 80 percent by 2025-26 from the 2010 baseline.
- **Eliminate vertical:** transmission of HIV and Syphilis.
- **Promote Universal:** Access to Quality STI/RTI services.
- **Eliminate HIV/AIDS-related:** stigma and discrimination.
- **Broad Strategy:** PTT (Prevent, Test, Treat) for HIV & AIDS.

GLOBAL AIDS STRATEGY (2021-2026)

- **Eliminate AIDS:** by 2030.
- **95-95-95 Targets:** 
  - **95 percent:** of PLHIV should know their status.
  - **95 percent:** on treatment.
  - **95 percent:** undergo adequate viral suppression.
  - **95 percent:** at risk of HIV use combination treatment.
  - **95 percent:** of women have access to sexual and reproductive health.
  - **95 percent:** coverage of services for eliminating vertical transmission.

HIV SERO SURVEILLANCE

The purpose of Sentinel Surveillance is to detect missing cases and track the bridge population.
1. High Risk Groups (Sentinel Size - 250): Commercial sex workers (CSW), Men having sex with men (MSM), Injectable drug abusers (IDU), Transgenders (TGs).
2. Bridge Population (Sentinel Size - 250): Single male migrants (SMM), Truck drivers, Clients of CSW.
3. General Population (Sentinel Size - 400): Antenatal women are used as proxy indicators to assess HIV prevalence among the general population (Currently 0.22).

- **Antenatal Clinic Surveillance Framework:** Sample size 400, Duration 3 months, Frequency Biennial (once in 2 years), Consecutive sampling. Pregnant women aged 15-49 years attending ANC clinic for the first time in the current round of surveillance. Linked-anonymous testing using venous blood sample via 2-step testing.
- **Important Note:** STD clinics and TB clinics are NOT included in sentinel surveillance.
- **Active Surveillance:** Going house to house collecting info. Passive Surveillance: Hospital reporting of diseases.

DIAGNOSIS AND SCREENING OF HIV

- **Screening test for HIV:** ELISA.
- **Confirmatory Test:** Western Blot.
- **p24 Antigen Detection Test:** Done in the window period.
- **Confirmatory test for adults:** qPCR done by nucleic acid amplification test.
- **Gold standard for diagnosis in children:** HIV DNA RTPCR.
- **Best Test:** Viral load estimation (to assess response to treatment and effect of ART therapy).
- **Reliable Test:** CD4 count (to assess response to treatment and progression of disease).
- **Screening Method:** By triple testing (ERS battery: ELISA, RAPID, Spot test). ELISA (highly sensitive) > triple testing.

TESTING STRATEGIES AND SCENARIOS

- **Opt-In Testing:** Testing is offered and the patient is required to actively give permission before it can occur.
- **Opt-Out Testing:** Performing an HIV test after notifying the patient; assent is assumed unless the patient actively declines. (Recommended by WHO and CDC).
- **Probable HIV Scenarios:** 
  - **Blood Donation (1/3 tests positive):** Unlinked anonymous testing. Discard blood.
  - **Symptomatic Person (2/3 tests positive):** Counselling and refer for confirmation.
  - **Asymptomatic Person:** e.g., ANC checkup (3/3 tests positive): Opt-Out Testing.
- **Strategy Settings:** 
  - **Mandatory ->:** Blood donation.
  - **Unlinked anonymous testing:** Used strictly for epidemiological research and sentinel surveillance without individual notification.
  - **Voluntary confidential testing:** Standard diagnostic protocol with informed pre- and post-test counselling.

TREATMENT (UNDER NACP)

Treat All Strategy (WHO): Any HIV-positive individual is started on ART irrespective of CD4 count.

1. Regimens Preferred:
- **Adults and adolescents (1st line regimen):** TLD[Tenofovir (300mg) + Lamivudine (300mg) + Dolutegravir (50mg)].
  *TLD is C/I in Children <10 years, Weight <30kg, or known case of renal/hepatic dysfunction.*
- **Children (1st line regimen):** ZLD/ALD[Zidovudine/Abacavir + Lamivudine + Dolutegravir].
- **Neonate:** Zidovudine + Lamivudine + Raltegravir.

PREVENTION OF PARENT TO CHILD TRANSMISSION (PPTCT)

For HIV-positive pregnant women, the TLD regimen is given irrespective of gestational age.
Management of the newborn born to an HIV-positive mother:
- **Early Infant Diagnosis:** Done at 6 weeks via HIV DNA RTPCR. If positive, start ART. If negative, 6 months follow up for 2 years -> Confirm HIV status at 18 months.
- **Low Risk Infant (Mother on ART > 4 weeks):** Syrup Nevirapine 10 mg OD x 6 weeks irrespective of feeding type. (If mother is already taking nevirapine, Syrup Zidovudine is given for 6 weeks).
- **High Risk:** Infant (Mother NOT on ART, or < 4 weeks, or high viral load > 1000 RNA copies/ml after 32 weeks): Syrup Nevirapine & Syrup Zidovudine. If on exclusive replacement feeds -> given for 6 weeks. If on exclusive breast feeds -> given for 12 weeks.

BREAST FEEDING PROTOCOL
- **Breast feeding:** is NOT contraindicated for an HIV-positive woman.
- **Do not:** switch between types of milk. Avoid abrupt stopping of breast milk.
- **If the baby is HIV positive:** Exclusive breastfeeding for 6 months and continue till 2 years.
- **If the baby is HIV negative:** Exclusive breastfeeding for 6 months and continue till 1 year.

PROPHYLAXIS

1. Post Exposure Prophylaxis (PEP): For accidental needle prick injury.
- **Drug of choice:** Tenofovir + Lamivudine + Dolutegravir (Single FDC tablet taken preferably at night).
- **Should be:** taken within 72 hours (Best if started within 2 hours).
- **Regimen duration:** Post-exposure prophylaxis must be continued uninterrupted for 28 days.

2. Prophylaxis for TB in PLHIV:
- **Most common:** Opportunistic Infection among PLHIV in India is TB.
- **Bidirectional screening:** is done (PLHIV tested for TB by CBNAAT, and TB patients tested for HIV).
- **If TB Negative:** TB preventive therapy is given (For PLHIV ≥13 years: Isoniazid + Rifapentine daily for 28 days (1HP) or weekly for 3 months (3HP)). Pyridoxine given along with Isoniazid.
- **For HIV-TB Coinfection:** Start ATT first, then 2 weeks later start ART to prevent Immune Reconstitution Syndrome.

3. Cotrimoxazole Preventive Therapy:
- **Opportunistic infection prophylaxis:** Cotrimoxazole preventive therapy (CPT) to protect against Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PCP) and toxoplasmosis.
- **Start:** CD4 < 350 cells/mm³.
- **Stop:** CD4 > 350 on two occasions six months apart + ascending trend + no WHO stage 3/4.
- **DOC:** Cotrimoxazole (Trimethoprim 160mg + Sulfamethoxazole 800mg double-strength tablet).

ORGANIZATIONAL SET-UP & INITIATIVES

- **ICTC centres:** Integrated counselling and testing centres.
  - **Stand-alone ICTC:** Special labs in cities/high-burden areas.
  - **Facility-integrated ICTC:** Designated areas in labs, most common, cost-effective.
  - **Mobile ICTC:** For low-burden areas, village/communities.
- **Sampoorna Suraksha Strategy:** Integrated response reaching out to diverse populations (low-risk and high-risk) where every person is safe from HIV/AIDS and treated with ART.
- **ALL IN Initiative:** Global initiative to end adolescent AIDS. Focuses on adolescents as leaders of social change, improving data, and placing adolescent HIV on political agendas.

> **EXAM TIP:** For NACP questions: Structure by Phase V (2021–2026) targets (80% reduction in new infections and deaths, eliminate vertical transmission) → 95-95-95 Fast-Track targets → Targeted Interventions (TI for FSW, MSM, IDU) → Testing strategy (ICTC, 3-test algorithm) → ART regimens (TLD: Tenofovir + Lamivudine + Dolutegravir) → PPTCT protocol.

[REF]Reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine (28th Edition), National AIDS Control Programme; NACO National Operational Guidelines, MoHFW.[/REF]

subsections.title: National Programme for Control of Blindness and Visual Impairment (NPCB&VI)
subsections.content:
[SN]National Programme for Control of blindness[/SN]

INTRODUCTION AND HISTORY
Nodal Ministry: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (MoHFW)

The National Programme for Control of Blindness was launched in the year 1976 as a 100 per cent centrally sponsored programme (now 60:40 in all states and 90:10 in North-Eastern States). It incorporates the earlier National Trachoma Control Programme which was started in the year 1963. The programme was launched with the goal to reduce the prevalence of blindness from 1.4 per cent (1974) to 0.3 per cent.

GOALS AND OBJECTIVES

- **To reduce:** the prevalence of blindness to 0.3 per cent. (Recently, the goal is set to reduce the prevalence to 0.25 per cent. As per the 2015-19 survey, the prevalence of blindness was 0.36 per cent).
- **To continue:** signature activities i.e., performance of cataract operations, school eye screening and distribution of free spectacles, and collection of donated eyes for keratoplasty.
- **Curable blindness identification:** Early detection and comprehensive treatment of preventable visual loss across primary, secondary, and tertiary levels.
- **Universal eye care delivery:** Comprehensive diagnostic and therapeutic ophthalmic services with focus on surgical quality.
- **Apex institute upgrading:** Enhancing Regional Institutes of Ophthalmology (RIOs) into sub-specialty centres of excellence.
- **To enhance:** community awareness on eye care and lay stress on preventive measures.
- **Ophthalmic research expansion:** Promoting operational and epidemiological research on blindness prevention and health services.
- **To secure:** participation of voluntary organizations and private practitioners in delivering eye care.

STRATEGIES AND INTERVENTIONS

- **Free cataract:** surgery through health care delivery system as well as by NGO and private practitioner.
- **Active screening:** of population above 50 years of age.
- **Paediatric vision screening:** School-based visual acuity assessment to detect and correct amblyopia and refractive errors.
- **Outreach to underserved areas:** Expanding eye care coverage to remote geographies via public-private partnerships.
- **Information Education:** Communication (IEC) activities for creating awareness on eye care and promotion of preventive eye care.
- **District hospital:** strengthened by upgrading manpower like ophthalmologists and paramedical ophthalmic assistants (PMOA) on contractual basis.
- **Establishing vision:** centers in all PHCs with a PMOA.
- **Multipurpose District:** Mobile Ophthalmic Units: At present, there are 80 central mobile units attached to medical colleges and 341 district mobile units to provide eye care in mobile eye camps, particularly in rural areas.
- **Mobile and tele-ophthalmology:** Deploying mobile surgical vans and tele-ophthalmology networks to extend service reach.
- **Clearing cataract:** backlog in a campaign mode to take care of pending cases, especially following the Covid-19 pandemic. District Collectors lead the campaign in their respective districts.
- **Cataract surgery:** packages are included in AB-PMJAY (transitioning to auto-adjudication) and State Insurance Schemes.
- **Involving voluntary:** organizations such as Lions International, Rotary International, and NGOs to organize eye camps in remote rural and urban areas.

ORGANIZATIONAL STRUCTURE AND ADMINISTRATION

- **Central Level:** Ophthalmology Section, Directorate General of Health Services, Ministry of Health & FW, New Delhi (National Institute of Ophthalmology AIIMS Delhi).
- **State Level:** State Ophthalmic Cell, Directorate of Health Services. (Merged with State Health Society under NRHM).
- **District Level:** District Blindness Control Society. (Merged with District Health Societies).
- **Tertiary Level:** Medical Colleges, Regional Institutes of Ophthalmology, and Centres of Excellence in Eye Care.
- **Secondary Level:** District Hospital and NGO Eye Hospital.
- **Primary Level:** Sub-district level hospitals / CHCs, Mobile Ophthalmic Units, Upgraded PHCs, Ophthalmic Assistants, Link Workers / Panchayats.

CARE DELIVERY LEVELS

1. Primary eye care services
- **Preventive and promotive eye care services:** Under comprehensive primary health care, Health and Wellness Centres (HWC) are providing preventive and promotive eye care services.
- **IEC activities:** for promotion and preventive eye care and eye donation.

2. Secondary eye care services
- **Cataract surgeries:** Reduction in the backlog of cataract by performing cataract surgeries in Governmental/Non-Governmental Eye Hospitals and private practitioners. Facilities for intra-ocular lens implantation have been expanded to the taluka level.
- **Refractive error screening:** Screening school children for visual deficits and distributing free spectacles to needy students.
- **Management of visual impairment:** The programme is now geared to take care of all categories of visual impairment including low vision cases. Focus is on treatment and management of diabetic retinopathy, vitreo-retinal diseases, glaucoma, corneal blindness, childhood blindness, retinopathy of prematurity (ROP), and age-related macular degeneration (AMD).
- **Eye banking services:** Strengthening of eye banking services and collection of donated eyes.

3. Tertiary eye care services
- **Apex facility strengthening:** Grant-in-aid support to upgrade Regional Institutes of Ophthalmology (RIOs) and medical colleges.
- **Superspeciality eye:** care services.
- **Personnel skill up-gradation:** Continuous professional training for ophthalmic surgeons, nurses, and technicians.

4. Infrastructure development and capacity building
- **Apex facility strengthening:** Grant-in-aid support to upgrade Regional Institutes of Ophthalmology (RIOs) and medical colleges.
- **Surgical capacity building:** Structured training for ophthalmologists and Ophthalmic Assistants in high-volume cataract surgery.

SCHOOL EYE SCREENING PROGRAMME

- **Paediatric refractive burden:** Approximately 6% to 7% of children aged 10–14 years suffer from uncorrected visual impairment.
- **School vision screening:** Schoolteachers trained to administer preliminary visual acuity screening using Snellen charts.
- **Suspected children:** are seen by ophthalmic assistants.
- **Corrective spectacles:** are prescribed or given free of cost for persons below the poverty line (BPL).

COLLECTION AND UTILIZATION OF DONATED EYES

- **Hospital retrieval programme:** Motivation of relatives of terminally ill patients with grave disease, or accident victims, to donate eyes.
- **Eye donation fortnight:** Organized from 25th August to 8th September every year to promote eye donation.
- **During 2022-23,:** approximately 62,370 corneas were collected nationally.
- **Gujarat, Tamil:** Nadu, Maharashtra, and Andhra Pradesh are leading states in this activity.

EXTERNALLY AIDED PROJECTS

- **World Bank:** assisted cataract blindness control project.
- **Danish assistance:** to NPCB.
- **WHO assistance for prevention of blindness:** Includes intra-country fellowships in corneal transplantation, vitreo-retinal surgery, lasers in ophthalmology, and paediatric ophthalmology; pilot survey on childhood blindness in Delhi.

VISION 2020: THE RIGHT TO SIGHT

- **Global mandate:** Collaborative WHO and IAPB global initiative launched to eliminate avoidable blindness by 2020.
- **Objective:** To eliminate avoidable causes of blindness by the year 2020.
- **Main features:** 
  - **Target blinding conditions:** Cataract, childhood blindness (xerophthalmia), refractive errors, trachoma, and low vision.
  - **Human resource:** development as well as infrastructure and technology development at various levels of the health system.
- **Proposed 4 tier system structure:** 
  1. Centers of excellence (Tertiary): Focus on Research (20 Centres).
  2. Training centers (Tertiary): Focus on Retinal surgery, Corneal transplantation, Glaucoma surgery (200 Centres).
  3. Service centers (Secondary): Focus on Cataract surgery (2,000 Centres).
  4. Vision centers (Primary): Focus on Refraction and Prescription of glasses (20,000 Centres).

> **EXAM TIP:** Launch year + goal prevalence → cataract/school screening/eye bank → Vision 2020 disease list → primary to tertiary structure.

[REF]Reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine (28th Edition), National Programme for Control of Blindness; NPCB&VI Guidelines, MoHFW.[/REF]

subsections.title: National Iodine Deficiency Disorders Control Programme (NIDDCP)
subsections.content:
[SN]National Iodine Deficiency Disorders Control Programme (NIDDCP)[/SN]

INTRODUCTION AND HISTORY
Nodal Ministry: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (MoHFW)

India commenced a Goitre Control Programme in 1962, which was initially based on the provision of iodized salt to endemic regions. At the end of three decades, the prevalence of the disease still remained high.

As a result, a major national programme, renamed as the "National Iodine Deficiency Disorders (IDD) Control Programme", was initiated. The new approach shifted the focus from area-specific use to nation-wide promotion of iodized salt.

It was decided as a national policy to fortify all edible salt in a phased manner by 1992, which coincided with the beginning of the 8th Five Year Plan (and supported by policies initiated since the 3rd Five Year Plan).

GOALS AND OBJECTIVES

- **To assess:** the magnitude of Iodine Deficiency Disorders (IDD) through surveys in districts.
- **Salt iodization:** Phased substitution of common edible salt with potassium iodate-fortified salt.
- **Periodic impact surveys:** Epidemiological resurveys every 5 years to measure IDD prevalence and salt iodization impact.
- **Laboratory monitoring:** of iodized salt and urinary iodine excretion.
- **Health education:** and publicity.

COMPONENTS AND STRATEGIES

The essential components of the national IDD programme are:
- **Universal iodized salt:** Mandatory household consumption of iodized salt.
- **Laboratory surveillance:** Quality control of salt iodine levels at production and retail, alongside urinary iodine monitoring.
- **Manpower training:** Capacity building for laboratory technicians and district health staff.
- **Mass communication:** Public education and awareness on iodized salt consumption.

CURRENT STATUS AND ACHIEVEMENTS

- **Notification banning:** the sale of non-iodized salt for human consumption in the entire country has been issued under the "Food Safety and Standards Act 2006 and Regulations 2011".
- **For effective:** implementation of the National Iodine Deficiency Disorders Control Programme, 35 States/UTs have established Iodine Deficiency Disorders Control Cells in their State Health Directorate.
