- **Consequent upon:** the liberalization of iodized salt production, the Salt Commissioner has issued licenses to 824 salt manufacturers, out of which 777 units have commenced production.
- **These manufacturing:** units have an annual production capacity of 222 lakh metric tonnes of iodized salt.
- **Nation-wide universal:** salt iodisation (USI) is the central strategy, with laboratory monitoring of salt iodine and urinary iodine excretion.

HIGH-YIELD PROGRAMME POINTS (SN DEPTH)

- **Universal salt iodisation (USI):** all edible salt iodised in a phased national policy approach.
- **Monitoring indicators commonly examined:** iodine content of salt at production and consumer levels; median urinary iodine excretion; goitre prevalence in school-age children on resurvey cycles.
- **District-level resurveys:** Scheduled epidemiological surveys every 5 years to track total goitre rate and programme progress.
- **Ban on:** sale of non-iodised salt for human consumption under food safety regulations supports USI.
- **Health education:** and laboratory monitoring cells in states are essential operational components.

> **EXAM TIP:** History goitre programme → rename to NIDDCP/USI → salt iodine monitoring + UIE → resurvey cycle → food safety ban line.

[REF]Reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine (28th Edition), National Iodine Deficiency Disorders Control Programme; Nutrition Division, MoHFW.[/REF]

subsections.title: Universal Immunization Programme (UIP)
subsections.content:
INTRODUCTION AND HISTORY
Nodal Ministry: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (MoHFW)

The Expanded Programme on Immunization (EPI) was launched by the WHO in 1974 globally and introduced in India in 1978. The primary objective was to reduce mortality and morbidity from vaccine-preventable diseases of childhood. Achieving self-sufficiency in vaccine production became an objective under India's Universal Immunization Programme (UIP), which evolved from EPI in 1985.

In 1985, the programme was renamed as the Universal Immunization Programme (UIP) in India. The aim was to achieve 100 percent coverage of pregnant women with 2 doses of tetanus toxoid (or a booster dose) and at least 85 percent coverage of infants with 3 doses each of DPT and OPV, one dose of BCG, and one dose of measles vaccine by 1990.

UIP targets 12 vaccine-preventable diseases: Diphtheria, Pertussis, Tetanus, Polio, Measles, Rubella, severe form of Childhood Tuberculosis, Hepatitis B, and Meningitis & Pneumonia caused by Haemophilus Influenzae type B, Japanese Encephalitis, Pneumococcal Pneumonia, and Rotavirus diarrhea.

PULSE POLIO IMMUNIZATION PROGRAMME
Nodal Ministry: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (MoHFW)

The Pulse Polio Immunization Programme was launched in the country in the year 1995. 

KEY MILESTONES AND TARGETS
- **1st round:** Conducted over 2 immunization days 6 weeks apart on 9th December 1995 and 20th January 1996, targeting children aged less than 3 years.
- **Pulse Polio:** Immunization Programme target age: Initially targeted children under 3 years of age. Later on, as per WHO guidelines, it was expanded to children under 5 years of age.
- **Pulse:** Refers to the sudden simultaneous mass administration of OPV on a single day to all children 0-5 years of age, regardless of their previous immunization status.
- **PPI rounds:** occur in 2 rounds about 4 to 6 weeks apart during the low transmission season of polio, i.e., between November to February.

STEPS TAKEN TO MAINTAIN POLIO FREE STATUS
- **All states:** and UTs to develop Rapid Response Teams (RRT) and Emergency Preparedness and Response Plans (EPRP).
- **In UP:** and Bihar, every newborn is vaccinated and tracked for 8 subsequent rounds.
- **Apart from:** vaccinating at fixed booths and through house-to-house visits, vaccination is also done at railway stations, bus stops, and religious congregations.
- **Special booths:** are established in areas bordering neighboring countries like Wagah border, Attari station, and Munabo train station.
- **High level:** of vigilance is maintained through surveillance across the country for Vaccine-Derived Poliovirus (VDPV).
- **Multi-pronged strategy:** implemented to ensure sanitation, hygiene, and clean drinking water in 107 high-risk blocks.
- **Social mobilizing:** activities are conducted by involving local influencers, community, and religious leaders.
- **Emergency stock:** of OPV is maintained to respond to Wild Poliovirus (WPV) and circulating Vaccine-Derived Poliovirus (cVDPV).

POLIO ENDGAME STRATEGIC PLAN
- **Inactivated Poliovirus:** Vaccine (IPV) introduced into the national immunization programme from November 2015, initially in 6 states and expanded nationwide by April 2016.
- **Trivalent OPV:** (tOPV) switched to Bivalent OPV (bOPV) from April 2016 (The Big Switch).

MISSION INDRADHANUSH
Nodal Ministry: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (MoHFW)

Mission Indradhanush was launched by the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare in December 2014.

GOALS AND STRATEGY
- **Indradhanush depicts:** 7 colours of the rainbow for prevention against 7 vaccine-preventable diseases.
- **Diseases included:** Diphtheria, Whooping cough, Tetanus, Polio, Tubercular meningitis, Measles, and Hepatitis B. It also includes Japanese Encephalitis (JE) and Haemophilus influenzae type B in selected districts.
- **Pregnant women:** are also immunized against tetanus.
- **Objective:** To fully immunize children who are either unvaccinated or partially vaccinated and those who have not been covered during routine vaccination sessions.

PHASES OF MISSION INDRADHANUSH
- **1st Phase:** 
  - **1st round:** started from 7th April 2015.
  - **Covered 201:** high-focus districts.
  - **Carried out:** for more than a week.
  - **Successive phases:** Three monthly follow-up phases conducted on the 7th of May, June, and July 2015.
- **2nd Phase:** 
  - **Started from:** 7th October 2015.
  - **Covered 352:** districts.
  - **Phase duration:** Four intensified monthly rounds covering persistently low-coverage districts.
  - **Covering all:** eligible children and pregnant women.

[SN]Intensified Mission Indradhanush[/SN]

INTENSIFIED MISSION INDRADHANUSH (IMI)
Nodal Ministry: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (MoHFW)

Definition
IMI is an intensified, drive-mode strategy under UIP to vaccinate left-out and dropped-out children and pregnant women who missed routine immunisation, using headcount, session planning, and intersectoral mobilisation beyond fixed RI days.

Relation to Mission Indradhanush
- **Mission Indradhanush (from 2014):** phased drives to raise full immunisation coverage.
- **IMI:** intensified approach with sharper focus on low-coverage pockets, urban slums, remote/tribal areas, migrants, and stronger monitoring.

High-yield points
1. Target: unvaccinated/partially vaccinated children and due pregnant women.
2. Strategy: identify missed beneficiaries → special sessions → track completion of due antigens.
3. Microplanning: high-risk areas, brick kilns, nomadic groups, urban poor.
4. Convergence: Health + WCD (AWW) + local bodies + influencers for mobilisation.
5. Monitoring: readiness assessment, session monitoring, coverage feedback.
6. Digital support: progressive use of platforms such as U-WIN for registration and due-listing in recent rounds.
7. IMI 5.0 (2023): conducted across districts with inclusion of children up to 5 years (earlier focus often up to 2 years), with special attention to measles-rubella dose catch-up alongside other UIP antigens.

Indian context:
- **Equity bridge:** Intensified Mission Indradhanush (IMI) bridges routine immunisation gaps across underserved geographies; complete immunisation prevents vaccine-preventable disease (VPD) outbreaks and accelerates national measles-rubella elimination targets.

> **EXAM TIP:** Define MI vs IMI → targets → microplanning/high-risk areas → strategy bullets → one line on IMI 5.0 age expansion and MR focus.

[SN]Electronic Vaccine Intelligence Network (eVIN)[/SN]

ELECTRONIC VACCINE INTELLIGENCE NETWORK (eVIN)

Definition
eVIN is a technology system under the Universal Immunization Programme that digitises vaccine stocks and cold-chain temperature logistics to reduce stock-outs, overstocking, and wastage.

What it does
1. Near real-time visibility of vaccine stock at stores and cold-chain points.
2. Continuous temperature monitoring of cold-chain equipment with alerts for excursions.
3. Improves indenting, distribution, and redistribution of vaccines.
4. Strengthens accountability of cold-chain handlers and programme managers.
5. Supports coverage improvement indirectly by ensuring the right vaccine is available at the right session site.
6. Generates dashboards for state/district review (stock sufficiency, wastage patterns, equipment downtime).

Components (answer scaffold)
- **People:** trained cold-chain handlers / vaccine store keepers.
- **Process:** stock transactions recorded digitally; SOPs for temperature breach.
- **Technology:** application + temperature loggers + central dashboards.
- **Network:** from national/state stores down to last cold-chain points linked to sessions.

Indian context:
- **Supply chain modernisation:** Deployed across all states and districts under Universal Immunization Programme (UIP) and NHM support to eliminate vaccine stock-outs and cold-chain temperature breaches; functions symbiotically with U-WIN (which digitises individual beneficiary records and session due-lists).

> **EXAM TIP:** One-line definition → stock + temperature pillars → 5 operational benefits → contrast eVIN (logistics) vs U-WIN (beneficiary tracking) if asked digital immunisation tools.

MEASLES-RUBELLA (MR) CAMPAIGN
Nodal Ministry: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (MoHFW)

The Government of India expanded the measles vaccine across the country in 1985 under the UIP. In 2010, a second dose of measles was introduced at 16-24 months of age, which led to a significant reduction in the disease burden. In 2017, the Measles-Rubella (MR) Vaccine was introduced through a phased campaign.

GOAL
- **Disease elimination targets:** Elimination of measles and control of rubella and Congenital Rubella Syndrome (CRS).
- **Population immunity goal:** Achieving and maintaining ≥95% population immunity through two routine vaccine doses.

PHASING AND TARGETS
- **Targets over:** 400 million children in 36 states and UTs in a span of two years. Included under the National Health Mission (NHM).
- **1st Phase:** February 2017 in 5 states (Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Goa, Lakshadweep, and Puducherry).
- **Next Round:** August 2017 in 8 states/UTs (Andhra Pradesh, Chandigarh, Dadra & Nagar Haveli, Daman & Diu, Himachal Pradesh, Kerala, Telangana, and Uttarakhand).

STRATEGY FOR MR CAMPAIGNS
- **MR vaccine:** introduced through a campaign in a phased manner across the country without sub-phasing within the states.
- **Target group:** All children in the target age group are vaccinated irrespective of previous immunization status or history of measles/rubella disease.
- **MR vaccination:** is given at fixed and outreach session sites (schools, CHC/PHC/AWC, community halls, village headmen houses, or private doctor clinics).
- **Mobile teams:** are deployed to cover high-risk areas and populations during the campaign.
- **MR Vaccine:** Introduced into the routine program by replacing the two doses of measles vaccine currently administered. The first dose is given between 9 and 12 months of age, and the second dose is given at 16-24 months of age.

COMMUNICATION OBJECTIVES AND STRATEGY
- **Positive positioning:** of the MR campaign among stakeholders, communities, and media.
- **Facilitate community:** acceptance of MR vaccination through social mobilization interventions.
- **Build an:** enabling environment through positive media reporting.
- **Crisis communication:** Proactive media engagement and community counter-messaging to address vaccine hesitancy and rumours.
- **Components of communication strategy:** Pre-campaign building of an enabling environment, social media monitoring and reporting, AEFI crisis communication, advocacy with stakeholders and medical practitioners, social mobilization to create demand, and maximizing reach through mass media and IEC materials.
- **Steps for community mobilization:** Training of frontline workers (ANM, AWW, ASHA, and community volunteers), name-based enlisting of educational institutions and beneficiaries by ASHA and AWW, preparation of due lists, and making plans to mobilize schools and communities.
- **IEC Activities:** Auto miking (loudspeakers), posters, banners, hoardings, leaflets to parents and community leaders, and organizing rallies at the community level.

ROLES AND RESPONSIBILITIES
- **State Level:** High-level political commitment, use of social media, printing and distribution of IEC materials, media sensitization, AEFI crisis communication, and campaign monitoring.
- **District Level:** CMO has overall accountability and District Immunization Officer (DIO) is the programme officer. Responsible for ensuring intersectoral coordination, monitoring implementation, and reviewing planned activities daily.
- **Block Level:** BMO has overall accountability. Responsible for building a team, supervising activities, preparing plans for sub-centres, IPC training of ANM, ASHA, and AWW, meeting local leaders, and ensuring IEC materials are displayed.
- **Village Level:** 
  - **ANM:** Visit all schools for seeking support, organize MR vaccination session sites with the help of ASHA and AWW.
  - **ASHA / AWW:** Identify children and pregnant women in their area who are not immunized, mobilize the community and beneficiaries to the session site, and conduct IPC with families of the target age groups.

MR VACCINE CHARACTERISTICS
- **Live attenuated:** vaccine.
- **Contains Measles:** vaccine (Edmonston strain) and Rubella vaccine (RA 27/3 strain).
- **For certain:** vaccines in the UIP, such as Measles and Rubella, vaccination results in high (> 95 percent) seroconversion rates, and protection is generally assumed to be lifelong.
- **Before reconstitution,:** it is stable when stored between 2 to 8 degrees Celsius.
- **Very sensitive:** to sunlight, hence it comes in colored glass vials.
- **Open vial:** policy is NOT applicable to reconstituted MR vaccine.
- **Must be:** used within 4 hours after reconstitution. At the session site, the reconstituted vaccine should be kept inside the well of the icepack.
- **Induces both:** humoral and cellular immune responses.

DOSAGE AND ADMINISTRATION
- **Formulation and reconstitution:** Supplied as a freeze-dried pellet reconstituted exclusively with manufacturer-supplied diluent.
- **MR Vaccine Dose:** 0.5 ml.
- **Administered subcutaneously:** in the right upper arm.
- **Other live:** and inactivated bacterial and viral vaccines can be administered simultaneously on the same day along with MR vaccine, at different sites.

ADVERSE REACTIONS AND CONTRAINDICATIONS
- **Adverse reactions:** Slight pain and tenderness at the site of injection, mild fever, febrile seizures, transient rash, thrombocytopenic purpura, arthralgia/joint pain, and anaphylaxis (very rare).
- **Contraindications:** 
  - **High fever:** (> 102 degrees F / 38-39 degrees C).
  - **Serious systemic illness:** Acute moderate-to-severe illness warranting clinical recovery before vaccination.
  - **Pregnancy precautions:** Live attenuated vaccines contraindicated during pregnancy.
  - **Anaphylactic contraindication:** Documented history of severe anaphylaxis to neomycin, gelatin, or prior vaccine dose.
  - **Severely immune-compromised:** individuals.
  - **Individuals receiving:** immunosuppressive therapeutic radiation.
  - **Vaccination should:** be delayed for 3 to 11 months after the administration of blood or blood products.
  - **Following MR:** vaccination, the administration of blood products should be avoided for 2 weeks.

LESSONS LEARNT AND RECOMMENDATIONS FROM CATCH-UP CAMPAIGNS
- **Geographical campaign phasing:** Campaign rollout prioritises state-wide contiguous coverage to avoid cross-border transmission.
- **Interdepartmental coordination:** between Health, Education, and Women and Child Development (WCD) is crucial.
- **Stakeholder mobilization:** Structured sensitization of professional bodies (IAP, IMA), religious leaders, and education departments.
- **Social mobilization:** through IPC, developing special strategies for high-risk areas.
- **Focus on:** injection safety, AEFI surveillance, cold chain management, safe injection practices, and waste management.
- **AEFI preparedness:** Pre-positioning of standard AEFI emergency kits (including Adrenaline 1:1000) at every vaccination post.
- **Establishing an:** alternate pool of vaccinators identified from medical colleges, nursing colleges, and pharmacy colleges trained in advance.
- **Ensure quality:** monitoring and supervision by identifying supportive supervisors and independent external monitors at all levels.

[REF]Reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine (28th Edition), Immunization Programmes in India; UIP Operational Guidelines, MoHFW.[/REF]

subsections.title: National Programme for Prevention & Control of Non-Communicable Diseases (NP-NCD)
subsections.content:
[LAQ]National Programme for Prevention and Control of Non-Communicable Diseases (NP-NCD)[/LAQ]

INTRODUCTION AND BACKGROUND
Nodal Ministry: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (MoHFW)

India is experiencing a rapid health transition with a rising burden of chronic non-communicable diseases (NCDs). Originally integrated in 2010 as the National Programme for Prevention and Control of Cancer, Diabetes, Cardiovascular Diseases and Stroke (NPCDCS), the Government of India officially renamed it in May 2023 to the National Programme for Prevention & Control of Non-Communicable Diseases (NP-NCD).

This renaming reflects its broadened scope, which now officially subsumes conditions like Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD), Non-Alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease (NAFLD), Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD), Non-ST elevation MI, and Rheumatic Heart Disease (RHD). The programme has also integrated AYUSH systems.

- **Logo Tagline:** "Health in your own hands"
- **Level of Prevention:** The best level of prevention to control NCDs is Primordial Prevention. However, most national health programs, including NP-NCD, primarily operate at the Secondary level of prevention (early diagnosis and treatment).

WHO GLOBAL ACTION PLAN FOR CONTROL OF NCDS (Extended to 2030)

The WHO Global Action Plan includes 9 voluntary global NCD targets to be achieved by 2025:
1. 25% reduction in premature mortality from NCDs.
2. 10% reduction in the harmful use of alcohol.
3. 10% reduction in physical inactivity.
4. 30% reduction in salt/sodium intake.
5. 30% reduction in tobacco use.
6. 25% reduction in raised blood pressure.
7. 0% increase in diabetes and obesity.
8. 50% coverage of drug therapy and counselling.
9. 80% coverage of essential NCD medicines and technologies.

WHO STEPS APPROACH FOR NCD SURVEILLANCE

The STEPS approach is a standardized method for collecting and analyzing data on NCD risk factors, based on household surveys:
- **STEP 1 (Questionnaire):** Information based on sociodemographic profile, risk behaviours (lifestyle, psychological behaviour), and medical treatment.
- **STEP 2 (Physical Measurements):** Anthropometry (Height, Weight, BMI, Waist circumference) & Blood Pressure.
- **STEP 3 (Biochemical Measurements):** Lab investigations (e.g., Blood glucose level, lipid profile).

GOALS AND OBJECTIVES OF NP-NCD

- **Lifestyle modification:** Primary prevention through community health promotion, physical activity, and dietary interventions.
- **Provide early:** diagnosis and management of common NCDs.
- **Build capacity:** at various levels of health care for prevention, diagnosis, and treatment of common NCDs.
- **Train human:** resources within the public health setup to cope with the increasing burden of NCDs.
- **Palliative and rehabilitation capacity:** Building intermediate and home-based palliative care services across district health networks.

ADMINISTRATIVE SET-UP AND COMPONENTS

The programme functions through a cascading administrative structure:
- **Tertiary Level:** State NCD Cell & Cancer Care facilities in Medical Colleges/Regional Cancer Centres (RCC).
- **District Level:** District NCD Cell & NCD Clinics at District Hospitals (Cardiac Care Units, Cancer Care facilities).
- **CHC Level:** Block CHC managed by Rogi Kalyan Samiti. Provides early diagnosis, management, and laboratory referral.
- **Sub-Centre Level:** Managed with the Village Health Committee. Focuses on health promotions and opportunistic screening.

A. DIABETES, CARDIOVASCULAR DISEASE AND STROKE (DCS) COMPONENT

1. Activities at Sub-Centre
- **Health promotion:** for behaviour and lifestyle change through organizing camps, interpersonal communications, posters, etc.
- **Opportunistic screening:** of the population > 30 years of age using BP measurement and blood glucose by strip method.
- **Suspected cases:** are referred to CHCs.
- **Diagnostic consumables:** Point-of-care provision of blood glucometers, diagnostic strips, and auto-disabled lancets at HWCs.
- **Regular home:** visits by ANM/Male Health Workers to elderly and bedridden persons.

2. Activities at Community Health Centre (CHC)
- **CHC NCD clinic:** Specialized weekly and daily non-communicable disease outpatient services at Community Health Centres.
- **Diagnostic profiling:** Essential biochemical investigations (fasting blood glucose, lipid profile, serum creatinine) and ECG.
- **Clinical case management:** Standardised treatment, protocol-based medicine refills, and stabilization of cardiovascular and diabetic complications.
- **Complicated cases:** referred to the district hospital.

3. Activities at District Hospital
- **District hospital NCD clinic:** Comprehensive NCD outpatient clinic and Day Care Chemotherapy Centre.
- **Population-based screening:** of persons > 30 years to identify individuals at high-risk of diabetes, hypertension, and common cancers.
- **Tertiary follow-up:** Comprehensive diagnostic staging, specialized therapy, and annual multi-organ complication screening.
- **Home-based palliative:** care for chronic, debilitating, and progressive patients.

URBAN HEALTH CHECK-UP SCHEME & REFERRAL GUIDELINES

- **Urban Health Check-up Scheme:** Screens the urban slum population (> 30 years and pregnant females) for diabetes and high blood pressure, creating a database for prevalence in slums.
- **Referral Guidelines:** Individuals with a systolic BP > 140 mm of Hg and diastolic BP > 90 mm of Hg, or random blood sugar >= 140 mg/dl, are referred to a medical officer.
- **Once diagnosed,:** the patient receives at least a month's supply of drugs (up to 3 months via ASHA/ANM) through the CHO-led clinical workflow at Ayushman Arogya Mandirs.

B. CANCER COMPONENT UNDER NP-NCD

Cancer Objectives:
1. Primary prevention: Health education.
2. Secondary prevention: Early diagnosis and screening (cervix, mouth, breast, and tobacco-related cancers).
3. Tertiary prevention: Palliative care and strengthening of existing institutions.

Cancer Schemes and Services:
- **Regional Cancer Centre Scheme:** Acts as referral centres for complicated cases at the tertiary level.
- **Oncology Wing Development Department:** Fills geographic gaps with central assistance for equipment (e.g., cobalt units).
- **Decentralized NGO Scheme:** Financial assistance for health education and early detection.
- **Treatment provided:** Surgery, Chemotherapy (drugs for 100 patients at district hospitals), and Home-based palliative care.

TOBACCO CONTROL LEGISLATION AND MPOWER MEASURES

National Tobacco Control Programme (NTCP) components and the COTPA 2003 Act enforce the prohibition of smoking in public, ban sales to minors (<18, with proposed amendments to raise to <21), and mandate pictorial warnings.

To strengthen tobacco control, WHO's MPOWER measures are heavily utilized:
- **M:** Monitor tobacco use and prevention policies.
- **P:** Protect people from tobacco smoke.
- **O:** Offer help to quit tobacco use (Tobacco cessation facilities).
- **W:** Warn about the dangers of tobacco.
- **E:** Enforce bans on tobacco advertising, promotion, and sponsorship.
- **R:** Raise taxes on tobacco.

NEW INITIATIVES AND INTEGRATIONS

1. Bidirectional Screening for TB and Diabetes: A joint collaborative activity where TB patients are screened for Diabetes, and diabetic patients are screened for TB. 
  - **ASHA workers:** fill out the Community-Based Assessment Checklist (CBAC) form for this screening and receive an incentive of Rs. 10 per form.
2. Intervention for prevention and control of Rheumatic Heart Disease (RHD) and Rheumatic Fever under the platform of NP-NCD and RBSK.
3. Integration of AYUSH with NP-NCD.
4. Population-based screening of women and men aged 30 years and above is now integrated into Comprehensive Primary Health Care under Ayushman Bharat at Health and Wellness Centres (Ayushman Arogya Mandirs).

> **EXAM TIP:** For NP-NCD answers: Trace evolution from NPCDCS to NP-NCD (May 2023 expansion to CKD, COPD, NAFLD) → 3-tier delivery structure (Sub-centre/HWC, CHC NCD clinic, District Hospital NCD clinic/CCU) → Population-Based Screening (PBS for ≥30 years using CBAC form) → 5 common conditions (Hypertension, Diabetes, Oral, Breast, Cervical cancer) → WHO 25×25 targets and MPOWER.

[REF]Reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine (28th Edition), NP-NCD; Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS), MoHFW Operational Guidelines.[/REF]

subsections.title: National Mental Health Programme (NMHP)
subsections.content:
[LAQ]National Mental Health Programme (NMHP)[/LAQ]

INTRODUCTION AND HISTORY
Nodal Ministry: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (MoHFW)

The National Mental Health Programme (NMHP) was launched in 1982 with a view to ensure the availability of mental health care services for all, especially the community at risk and underprivileged sections of the population.

The programme covers 767 districts and has expanded its reach across the country to encourage the application of mental health knowledge in general healthcare and social development.

AIMS AND OBJECTIVES

Aims:
1. Prevention and treatment of mental and neurological disorders and their associated disabilities.
2. Improve quality of life of the population.
3. Application of mental health technology to improve general health services.

Objectives:
1. To ensure availability and accessibility of minimum mental health care for all in the foreseeable future, particularly to the most vulnerable and underprivileged sections of the population.
2. To encourage application of mental health knowledge in general health care and in social development.
3. To promote community participation in mental health services development, and to stimulate efforts towards self-help in the community.

STRATEGIES

The programme strategies are:
1. Integration of mental health with primary health care through the NMHP.
2. Provision of tertiary care institutions for treatment of mental disorders.
3. Eradicating stigmatization of mentally ill patients and protecting their rights through regulatory institutions like the Central Mental Health Authority and State Mental Health Authority.

DISTRICT MENTAL HEALTH PROGRAMME

Components:
1. Training of all workers in the mental health team at the identified nodal institute in the state.
2. Public education in mental health to increase awareness and to reduce stigma.
3. For early detection and treatment, OPD and indoor services are provided.
4. Providing valuable data and experience at the level of community to the state and centre for future planning and improvement in service and research.

Activities:
The District Mental Health Programme has incorporated promotive and preventive activities for positive mental health which includes:
1. School mental health activities:
  - **Life skills:** education in schools.
  - **Counselling services:** Psychosocial support and clinical mental health counselling.
2. College counseling services:
  - **Provided through:** trained teachers and counselors.
3. Workplace stress management:
  - **Covers formal:** and informal sectors, including farmers, women, etc.
4. Suicide prevention services:
  - **Counseling centre:** at the district level.
  - **Sensitization workshops:** and IEC.
  - **Tele-counselling helplines:** 24×7 distress and crisis intervention hotlines.

THRUST AREAS

1. District mental health programme in an enlarged and more effective form covering the entire country.
2. Streamlining and modernization of mental hospitals in order to modify their present custodial role.
3. Upgrading departments of psychiatry in medical colleges and enhancing the psychiatric content of the medical curriculum at the undergraduate as well as postgraduate level.
4. Strengthening the central and state mental health authorities with a permanent secretariat. Appointment of medical officers at state headquarters in order to make the monitoring role more effective.
5. Research and training in the field of community mental health, substance abuse, and child adolescent psychiatric clinics.


[SN]Tele-MANAS[/SN]

[LAQ]National Tele Mental Health Programme (Tele-MANAS)[/LAQ]

TELE-MANAS (NATIONAL TELE MENTAL HEALTH PROGRAMME)
DEFINITION
Tele Mental Health Assistance and Networking Across States (Tele-MANAS) is the National Tele Mental Health Programme (NTMHP). It is the digital arm of the District Mental Health Programme (DMHP). It was launched on 10 October 2022 (World Mental Health Day) to provide 24×7 tele-mental health counselling.

HIGH-YIELD POINTS
- **Toll-free number:** 14416 (a second access number 1-800-891-4416 is also used in programme material).
- **Nodal technical centre:** National Institute of Mental Health and Neuro Sciences (NIMHANS), Bengaluru.
- **As on:** 03 March 2026 (Press Information Bureau): 36 States and Union Territories have set up 53 Tele-MANAS Cells; services in 20 languages as opted by States; more than 34.34 lakh calls handled since inception.
- **Tele-MANAS Mobile:** Application launched on 10 October 2024. By December 2025 it included English, Hindi, and ten additional regional languages (Assamese, Bengali, Gujarati, Kannada, Malayalam, Marathi, Tamil, Telugu, Odia, Punjabi), with a screen-free path for visually challenged users via the helpline.
- **Dedicated Tele-MANAS:** cell at Armed Forces Medical College (AFMC), Pune, for serving personnel and dependents.
- **Two-tier idea for answers:** trained counsellor on first contact; specialist/psychiatrist on escalation; in-person referral to DMHP, medical officers, or mental health professionals.
- **Mental health:** services are also in the Comprehensive Primary Health Care package at Ayushman Arogya Mandirs.

> **EXAM TIP:** Tele-MANAS: Launch 10 Oct 2022 → 24×7 toll-free helpline 14416 → NIMHANS nodal technical apex → 2-tier service delivery (counsellor triage → psychiatrist escalation) → multimodal access via mobile app and regional languages → integration with DMHP and Ayushman Arogya Mandirs.


THE MENTAL HEALTHCARE ACT, 2017

The United Nations convention on the rights of persons with disabilities was ratified by the Government of India, thus making it obligatory to align the policies and laws of the country with the convention.

Key provisions and milestones:
- **The Mental:** Healthcare Bill, 2013 was introduced in Parliament and subsequently enacted as The Mental Healthcare Act, 2017, in order to protect, promote and fulfill the rights of persons with mental illness during the delivery of healthcare in institutions and in the community.
- **It ensures:** healthcare, treatment, and rehabilitation of persons with mental illness is provided in the least restrictive environment possible.
- **Statutory regulatory framework:** Regulates public and private mental healthcare delivery within a rights-based framework, ensuring equity, least restrictive care environments, and patient autonomy.
- **Suicide has:** been decriminalized under the Act.
- **The Mental:** Healthcare Act, 2017 received the assent of the President of India on 07.04.2017.

[REF]Reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine (28th Edition), National Mental Health Programme; Mental Healthcare Act, 2017; Tele-MANAS Guidelines, NIMHANS/MoHFW.[/REF]

subsections.title: Integrated Disease Surveillance Programme (IDSP)
subsections.content:
[LAQ]Integrated Disease Surveillance Programme (IDSP)[/LAQ]

INTRODUCTION AND HISTORY
Nodal Ministry: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (MoHFW)

The Integrated Disease Surveillance Project (IDSP) is a decentralized state-based surveillance system in the country. It was launched in November 2004 as a 5-year project up to March 2010. The project was restructured and extended up to March 2012, and continues as the Integrated Disease Surveillance Programme under the National Health Mission (NHM) for all states, with its digital platform now evolved into the Integrated Health Information Platform (IHIP) 2.0 to enhance integrated surveillance and preparedness against zoonotic disease threats.

GOALS AND OBJECTIVES

- **Early warning and response:** Designed to capture early epidemic signals to trigger rapid containment responses across rural and urban jurisdictions.
- **To provide:** essential data to monitor the progress of ongoing disease control programmes and help allocate health resources more efficiently.
- **The important:** information in disease surveillance involves identifying who gets the disease, how many get the disease, where they get the disease, why they get the disease, and what needs to be done as a public health response.

ORGANIZATIONAL STRUCTURE AND ADMINISTRATION

- **Central Surveillance Unit (CSU):** Established and integrated in the National Centre for Disease Control (NCDC), Delhi.
- **State Surveillance Unit (SSU):** Established at all State / UT headquarters.
- **District Surveillance Unit (DSU):** Established at all districts in the country.
- **An IT:** network connecting 776 sites in states / district headquarters and premier institutes has been established with the help of the National Information Centre (NIC) and ISRO (Indian Space Research Organization) for data entry, training, video conferencing, and outbreak discussions.

TYPES OF INTEGRATIONS IN IDSP

Different types of integration are proposed and implemented in the project:
1. Health and non-health sectors (Developing effective partnership).
2. Non-communicable and communicable diseases surveillance.
3. Private sector and NGOs.
4. Academic institutions and medical colleges (Bringing them into the primary public health activity of disease surveillance).
5. Sharing of surveillance information of disease control programmes.

COMPONENTS OF SURVEILLANCE

The prerequisite of effective surveillance is the use of standard case definitions, ensuring regularity of reports, and action on reports. The components are:
1. Collection of data
2. Compilation of data
3. Analysis and interpretation of data
4. Follow up action
5. Feedback

CLASSIFICATION OF SURVEILLANCE

Weekly disease surveillance data on epidemic-prone diseases are collected on 'S' (syndromic), 'P' (probable/presumptive), and 'L' (laboratory) formats. 

[SN]Integrated Health Information Platform (IHIP)[/SN]

Districts report this data primarily through the Integrated Health Information Platform (IHIP) portal. IHIP represents a major upgrade from the older IDSP reporting structure, enabling real-time, case-based, geo-tagged reporting rather than relying solely on weekly aggregate syndromic data.

1. Syndromic diagnosis: Diagnosis is made on the basis of the clinical pattern by paramedical personnel and members of the community (e.g., Sub-centre health worker / ANM).
2. Presumptive (Probable) diagnosis: Diagnosis made on typical history and clinical examination by a Medical Officer (e.g., PHC / CHC MO).
3. Confirmed diagnosis: Clinical diagnosis confirmed by a medical officer and positive laboratory identification.

SYNDROMES LISTED UNDER SURVEILLANCE

The paramedical health staff undertake disease surveillance based on broad categories of presentation. These syndromes are intended to pick up all priority diseases listed under regular surveillance.
- **Fever:** 
  - **Less than:** 7 days duration without any localizing signs (Malaria, Typhoid, JE, Dengue, Measles).
  - **With rash:** (Measles, Dengue).
  - **With altered:** sensorium or convulsions (JE, Meningitis).
  - **Bleeding from:** skin or mucus membrane (Dengue, Haemorrhagic fevers).
  - **More than:** 7 days with or without localizing signs (Typhoid, Malaria).
- **Cough:** More than 3 weeks duration (Tuberculosis).
- **Acute flaccid paralysis:** Polio.
- **Diarrhoea:** Cholera, Acute diarrhoeal disease.
- **Jaundice:** Hepatitis, Leptospirosis, Dengue, Malaria, Yellow fever.
- **Unusual events:** causing death or hospitalization: Anthrax, Plague, Emerging epidemics.

CONDITIONS UNDER SURVEILLANCE

1. Regular Surveillance:
  - **Vector borne diseases:** Malaria.
  - **Water borne diseases:** Acute diarrhoeal disease (Cholera), Typhoid.
  - **Respiratory diseases:** Tuberculosis.
  - **Vaccine preventable diseases:** Measles.
  - **Diseases under eradication:** Polio.
  - **Other conditions:** Road traffic accidents (Link-up with police computers).
  - **International commitments:** Plague.
  - **Unusual clinical syndromes:** Meningoencephalitis / Respiratory distress, Haemorrhagic fevers, other undiagnosed conditions.
2. Sentinel Surveillance:
  - **Sexually transmitted diseases / blood borne:** HIV / HBV / HCV.
  - **Other conditions:** Water quality monitoring, Outdoor air quality (Large urban centres).
3. Regular periodic surveys:
  - **NCD risk factors:** Anthropometry, Physical activity, Blood pressure, Tobacco, Nutrition, etc.
4. Additional state priorities:
  - **Each state:** may identify up to five additional conditions for surveillance.

OUTBREAK AND RAPID RESPONSE

In epidemiology, an outbreak is a sudden increase in the occurrence of a disease in a particular time and place. Whenever there is a rising trend of illness, it is investigated by the Rapid Response Team (RRT) to diagnose and control the outbreak. It is a multi-specialty team typically comprising an epidemiologist, a microbiologist, a medical officer, laboratory technicians, data managers, and other specialists, including veterinary officers for zoonotic diseases, as per requirement, aligned with the One Health approach for zoonoses.

Warning signs of an impending outbreak:
- **Spatiotemporal clustering:** Unusual spatial or temporal grouping of disease cases or unexplained deaths.
- **Unusual increase:** in the number of cases or deaths.
- **Even a:** single case of measles, AFP, cholera, plague, dengue, or JE.
- **Acute febrile:** illness of unknown aetiology.
- **Epidemiologically linked cases:** Occurrence of two or more linked cases of acute meningoencephalitis or severe hemorrhagic illness.
- **Unusual isolate:** Detection of rare, drug-resistant, or unexpected pathogens.
- **Demographic shift in morbidity:** Significant deviation in age distribution of affected individuals compared to baseline surveillance data.
- **Sudden increase:** or high vector density.
- **Disaster surveillance:** Epidemic surveillance following floods, cyclones, or earthquakes.

Trigger events for investigation:
- **Acute watery stools:** A single case of severe dehydration or death in a patient > 5 years of age with diarrhoea, OR more than 10 houses having at least one case of loose stools irrespective of age, per village or urban ward.
- **Fever < 7 days duration:** (Syndromic surveillance category, further classified as 'Only Fever', 'With Rash', 'With Altered Sensorium / Convulsions', or 'With Bleeding').
  - **Only fever:** 5 cases in 1000 population.
  - **With rash (Measles / Dengue):** 2 similar cases in a village (1000 population).
  - **Altered consciousness:** 2 cases of fever with altered consciousness in the village / 1000 population.
  - **Fever with bleeding:** 2 cases of fever with bleeding in a village / 1000 population.
  - **Fever with convulsions:** 2 cases of fever with convulsions in a village / 1000 population.
- **Fever more than 7 days:** More than 2 cases in a village / 1000 population.
- **Jaundice:** More than 2 cases in a village / 1000 population.
- **Unusual event:** More than 2 deaths or hospitalizations.

REPORTING UNITS IN IDSP

1. Public Health Sector:
  - **Rural:** CHCs, District hospitals.
  - **Urban:** Urban hospitals, ESI / Railway / Medical college hospitals.
2. Private Health Sector:
  - **Rural:** Sentinel private practitioners and Sentinel hospitals.
  - **Urban:** Sentinel private nursing homes, Sentinel hospitals, Medical colleges, Private and NGO laboratories.

> **EXAM TIP:** Define IDSP → CSU/SSU/DSU → S/P/L forms → syndromes and triggers → RRT → IHIP as real-time case-based geo-tagged upgrade from weekly aggregate reporting.

[REF]Reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine (28th Edition), Integrated Disease Surveillance Programme; NCDC / MoHFW Operational Guidelines.[/REF]

subsections.title: Ayushman Bharat Programme (AB-PMJAY & Health and Wellness Centres)
subsections.content:
[LAQ]Ayushman Bharat: AB-PMJAY and Health and Wellness Centres[/LAQ]

INTRODUCTION AND HISTORY
Nodal Ministry: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (MoHFW)

In February 2018, the Government of India announced two major initiatives in the health sector under the Ayushman Bharat Programme. The aim is to cover preventive and health promotive interventions at the primary, secondary, and tertiary care systems. 

Ayushman Bharat is a National Health Protection Scheme which will cover over 10 crore poor and vulnerable families (approximately 50 crore beneficiaries), providing coverage up to 5 lakh rupees per family per year for secondary and tertiary care hospitalization. It subsumes the on-going centrally sponsored schemes like the Rashtriya Swasthya Bima Yojana (RSBY) and the Senior Citizen Health Insurance Scheme (SCHIS).

GOALS AND OBJECTIVES (2018-2022)

- **Focus on:** the wellness of poor families.
- **Providing medical:** benefits to poor families.
- **Establishing Health:** and Wellness Centers at a nearer distance, so that patients will not have to travel a long distance.
- **Financial risk protection:** Drastic reduction of catastrophic out-of-pocket health expenditure (OOPE) for hospitalization.

COMPONENTS OF AYUSHMAN BHARAT

The programme consists of two main pillars:
1. Ayushman Arogya Mandir (AAM) (Previously known as Health and Wellness Centre).
2. Ayushman Bharat - Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana (AB-PMJAY).

AYUSHMAN AROGYA MANDIR (HEALTH AND WELLNESS CENTRES)
Nodal Ministry: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (MoHFW)

The National Health Policy 2017 envisioned Health and Wellness Centres as the foundation of India's health system. 

Key features and achievements:
- **Infrastructure scale:** Over 1.84 lakh Ayushman Arogya Mandirs operationalized nationwide to deliver Comprehensive Primary Health Care.
- **The first:** Health and Wellness Centre was inaugurated on 14th April 2018 in Bijapur district of Chhattisgarh.
- **Operational progress:** Nationwide operationalization of 172,148 centres as of March 2024, delivering promotive and curative services.
- **The centres:** provide comprehensive health care, including maternal and child health services, communicable diseases services, and services related to Non-Communicable Diseases (NCDs) such as hypertension, diabetes, and 3 common cancers of the oral cavity, breast, and cervix.
- **Incremental addition:** of primary healthcare services for mental health, ENT, ophthalmology, oral health, geriatric and palliative health care, and trauma care.
- **Wellness activities:** like Yoga, cyclathons, marathons, EAT RIGHT, SAFE, cessation of tobacco and drugs, meditation, laughter clubs, and open gyms are promoted. An annual health calendar guides planned activities.
- **The centres:** also provide free essential drugs and diagnostic services.

Primary Healthcare Team at Sub Health Centre level AAM:
- **Primary care team lead:** Headed by a Community Health Officer (B.Sc. Nursing / BAMS with Certificate in Community Health) utilizing digital decision-support apps.
- **Other members:** of the team include multi-purpose workers (Male and Female) and Accredited Social Health Activists (ASHAs).
- **Standardized competency training:** Formal six-month bridge training conducted in collaboration with IGNOU and state health institutions.

Expanded service packages planned to be provided at functional AAMs:
1. Care in pregnancy and child birth.
2. Neonatal and infant health care services.
3. Childhood and adolescent health care services.
4. Family planning, contraceptive services, and other reproductive health care services.
5. Management of communicable diseases: National Health programmes.
6. General out-patient care for acute simple illnesses and minor ailments.
7. Screening, prevention, control, and management of non-communicable diseases and chronic communicable diseases like tuberculosis and leprosy.
8. Basic oral health care.
9. Screening and basic management of mental health ailments.
10. Care for common ophthalmic and ENT problems.
11. Elderly and palliative health care services.
12. Emergency medical services including burns and trauma.

[SN]The Ayushman Bharat Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana (PMJAY)[/SN]

PRADHAN MANTRI JAN AROGYA YOJANA (AB-PMJAY)
Nodal Ministry: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (MoHFW)
Implementing agency: National Health Authority (NHA), an attached office of MoHFW

AB-PMJAY provides health coverage up to Rs. 5.00 lakh per family per year to poor and vulnerable families identified on the basis of Socio Economic Caste Census (SECC) data.

Salient Features:
- **Benefit cover:** of Rs. 5 lakh per family per year.
- **Entire family:** covered with no limit on family size, age, or number of members.
- **All pre-existing:** illnesses are covered from day one.
- **Fully portable:** across the country.
- **Covers poor,:** deprived rural families and identified occupational urban workers.
- **Beneficiaries covered:** under the scheme are allowed to take cashless benefits from any public or private empanelled hospitals across the country.
- **Flexible financial flow:** Direct electronic fund disbursement via dedicated Escrow accounts to ensure timely claim settlements.
- **IT platform:** is made operational which entails a paperless, cashless transaction.

Expansion to Senior Citizens (September 2024): All senior citizens aged 70 and above are eligible for health coverage of up to ₹5 lakh per family per year under AB PM-JAY, irrespective of income.
- **The Union:** Cabinet approved a major expansion of AB-PMJAY on September 11, 2024, to cover all senior citizens aged 70 and above, regardless of their socio-economic status or income.
- **Benefits around:** 4.5 crore families, including 6 crore senior citizens.
- **New distinct card:** Eligible senior citizens aged 70 and above receive a new, distinct card under the AB PM-JAY scheme.
- **Top-up coverage:** Senior citizens within families already covered by AB PM-JAY receive an additional top-up cover of up to Rs 5 lakh per year, exclusively for family members aged 70 and above.
- **Family coverage:** Senior citizens who are not part of an existing AB PM-JAY family receive a cover of up to Rs 5 lakh per year on a family basis.
- **Choice of schemes:** Senior citizens already benefiting from CGHS, ECHS, or CAPF have the option to either continue with their current scheme or opt for AB PM-JAY.
- **Eligibility with private insurance:** Senior citizens aged 70 years and above, even if covered by private health insurance policies or the Employees' State Insurance (ESI) scheme, are also eligible for benefits under Ayushman Bharat PM-JAY, as approved in September 2024.

TARGET BENEFICIARIES

Target Group for Rural (based on SECC deprivation criteria): Households with only one room with kucha walls and kucha roof (D1); households with no adult member aged 16-59 years (D2); female-headed households with no adult male member aged 16-59 years (D3); households with a disabled member and no able-bodied adult member (D4); SC/ST households (D5); and landless households deriving a major part of their income from manual casual labour (D7).
- **D1:** Only one room with kachha walls and kachha roof.
- **D2:** No adult member between age 16 to 59.
- **D3:** Female headed households with no adult male member between age 16 to 59.
- **D4:** Disabled member and no able-bodied adult member.
- **D5:** SC/ST households.
- **D7:** Landless households deriving major part of their income from manual casual labour.
- **Automatically included:** Households without shelter, Destitute/living on alms, Manual scavenger families, Primitive tribal groups, Legally released bonded labour.

Target Group for Urban (based on occupational categories):
- **Rag picker:** / Beggar.
- **Domestic worker:** / Street vendor.
- **Construction worker:** / Plumber / Labour.
- **Sweeper /:** Sanitation worker.
- **Transport worker:** / Driver / Conductor / Helper.
- **Cart puller:** / Rickshaw puller / Coolie.
- **Shop worker:** / Peon / Waiter.
- **Electrician /:** Mechanic / Washer-man (dhobi) / Gardener (Mali) / Tailor / Welder / Security guard.

IMPLEMENTATION STRATEGY

- **National level:** An Ayushman Bharat National Health Protection Mission Agency (AB-NHPMA) has been established.
- **State level:** State Health Agency (SHA) implements the scheme.
- **Funding:** The expenditure incurred in premium payments is shared between Central and State Governments in a specified ratio.
- **Modes of Implementation:** States/UTs can decide to implement the scheme through an insurance company, directly through a Trust/Society, or use an integrated model.
  - **Insurance Mode:** States/UTs select an Insurance Company.
  - **Trust / Assurance Mode:** Implemented through Society/Trust of State Health Department, utilizing AI-driven Auto-Adjudication for claims under the Strategy for AI in Healthcare in India (SAHI) framework.
  - **Mixed Model:** Combination of Insurance and Assurance.

MAJOR IMPACT

- **Financial risk protection:** Drastic reduction of catastrophic out-of-pocket health expenditure (OOPE) for hospitalization.
- **Increased benefit:** cover to nearly 40 percent of the population.
- **Covering almost:** all secondary and many tertiary hospitalizations.
- **Universal family entitlement:** Annual floater hospitalization cover of Rs. 5 lakh per family with zero restrictions on family size, age, or gender.
- **Increased access:** to quality health and medication.
- **Unmet needs:** of the population which remained hidden due to lack of financial resources are catered to.
- **Timely treatments,:** improvements in health outcomes, patient satisfaction, improvement in productivity and efficiency, and job creation thus leading to improvement in quality of life.

PREVENTING MONETARY IRREGULARITY UNDER AB-PM-JAY
1. Robust beneficiary identification (authorised databases) and authentication at admission.
2. Hospital empanelment criteria, de-empanelment for fraud, and package master with defined rates.
3. Pre-auth and claims adjudication (including automated/AI-assisted checks where implemented).
4. Medical audit, trigger-based review of high-value/high-frequency procedures, and anti-fraud cells at State Health Agency.
5. IT trail: Paperless claims reduce informal cash points, backed by whistle-blower and grievance channels.
6. Portability with transaction visibility across states reduces duplicate claims when systems interoperate.

CRITICAL APPRAISAL: AYUSHMAN AROGYA MANDIR (HWC) vs IPHS
- **Purpose:** AAM expands comprehensive primary care close to community (wellness + continuum); IPHS prescribes minimum standards for infrastructure, HR, services, and quality by facility type.
- **Strength of AAM:** population coverage, CHO-led team, NCD screening, free drugs/diagnostics push.
- **Strength of IPHS:** benchmarking and quality floor for SC/PHC/CHC/DH.
- **Tension:** rapid AAM scale may outrun HR skills, diagnostics uptime, and referral maturity if inputs lag; IPHS norms remain unmet if rebranding outpaces investment.
- **Way forward:** use IPHS as the quality/HR/infrastructure checklist while AAM expands the service package and wellness activities; fund gaps inside the AAM network.

ADVANTAGES AND LIMITATIONS OF AB-PM-JAY (OOPE LENS)
Advantages
- **Large reduction:** potential in catastrophic hospital expenditure for covered secondary/tertiary care.
- **Cashless, portable:** cover up to ₹5 lakh per family per year with no family-size cap; pre-existing conditions covered from day one.
- **Universal senior citizen coverage:** Universal Rs. 5 lakh top-up cover for all senior citizens aged 70 and above, regardless of household income (Cabinet approval, September 2024).
Limitations
- **Outpatient care:** and many non-hospital costs still drive OOPE if primary care is weak.
- **Empanelment quality:** variation; package rates and fraud control require constant vigilance.
- **Awareness, card:** generation, and denial/grievance handling determine real access.
- **Supply-side readiness:** (beds, specialists) in underserved areas can limit utilisation of the entitlement.

[LAQ]Components of Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission[/LAQ]

[SN]National Digital Health Mission[/SN]

AYUSHMAN BHARAT DIGITAL MISSION (ABDM) / NATIONAL DIGITAL HEALTH MISSION
Nodal Ministry: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (MoHFW)
Implementing agency: National Health Authority (NHA), an attached office of MoHFW

Definition
ABDM (earlier popularised as National Digital Health Mission) builds a national digital health ecosystem so that health records, facility/professional registries, and service transactions can interoperate with consent, improving continuity of care and programme efficiency.

Core building blocks
1. Ayushman Bharat Health Account (ABHA / Health ID): Unique identifier for individuals to link longitudinal health records with informed consent.
2. Healthcare Professionals Registry (HPR): Verified digital registry of medical doctors, nurses, and allied healthcare professionals.
3. Health Facility Registry (HFR): Comprehensive verified repository of public and private health facilities across modern and traditional medicine systems.
4. Unified Health Interface (UHI): Open network protocols enabling seamless digital discovery, teleconsultations, and booking across diverse digital health applications.
5. Personal Health Records (PHR) / longitudinal electronic health record exchange: Citizen-centric, consent-based digital health data exchange across healthcare providers.
6. Supporting architecture: Privacy and security by design, robust grievance redressal mechanisms, and seamless technical integration with existing health IT platforms.

Expected public health benefits
- **Lifelong care continuum:** Seamless digital linkage connecting primary preventative care with tertiary specialized treatment.
- **Reduced duplication:** of tests; better referral feedback.
- **Stronger fraud:** analytics for insurance/assurance schemes when linked appropriately.
- **Population health:** insights from aggregated, anonymised data for planning.

Cautions (balanced exam line)
- **Digital divide,:** consent literacy, cybersecurity, and private-sector onboarding determine real-world equity gains.

> **EXAM TIP:** One-line definition → ABHA/HPR/HFR/UHI/PHR list → benefits → privacy/equity caution → link to PM-JAY claims and CPHC continuity.

> **EXAM TIP:** Eligibility table (rural deprivation criteria + urban occupations + 70+ expansion) → ₹5 lakh features → fraud-control bullets → AAM vs IPHS mini-comparison → OOPE reduction conclusion with advantages/limitations.

[REF]Reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine (28th Edition), Ayushman Bharat; National Health Authority (NHA) & MoHFW Operational Guidelines.[/REF]

subsections.title: National Tobacco Control Programme (NTCP)
subsections.content:
[SN]National Tobacco Control Programme (NTCP)[/SN]

INTRODUCTION AND HISTORY
Nodal Ministry: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (MoHFW)

In order to facilitate the implementation of the Tobacco Control Laws, to bring about greater awareness about the harmful effects of tobacco, and to fulfill the obligations under the WHO-Framework convention on tobacco control, the Government of India launched a new National Tobacco Control Programme in the 11th Five Year Plan.

KEY MILESTONES
- **2007-08:** Pilot phase was launched in 16 districts covering 9 states.
- **The programme:** has since expanded and now covers around 612 districts in all 36 States/Union Territories across the country.

CIGARETTE AND OTHER TOBACCO PRODUCTS ACT (COTPA) 2003

A comprehensive tobacco control legislation titled "The Cigarettes and other Tobacco Products (Prohibition of Advertisement and Regulation of Trade and Commerce, Production, Supply and Distribution) Act, 2003" was assented to on 18th May 2003 and notified in the Gazette of India on 25th Feb 2004.

The important provisions of the Act are:
- **Public smoking prohibition:** Section 4 bans smoking in all defined public places and workplaces.
- **Advertisement ban:** Section 5 strictly prohibits direct and indirect commercial advertising, sponsorship, and brand promotion of tobacco products.
- **Underage sales prohibition:** Section 6(a) bans tobacco sales to or by individuals under 18 years of age.
- **Educational campus protection:** Section 6(b) prohibits sale of tobacco products within a radius of 100 yards from any educational institution.
- **Mandatory depiction:** of statutory warnings (including pictorial warnings) on tobacco packs.
- **Mandatory depiction:** of tar and nicotine contents along with maximum permissible limits on tobacco packs.

KEY RULES AND REGULATIONS

- **The rules:** related to the prohibition of smoking in public places came into force from 2nd October 2008. As per rules, it is mandatory to display smoke-free signages at all public places.
- **Graphic health warnings:** Section 7 mandates display of pictorial and text health warnings covering specified surface areas of all tobacco packaging.
- **On account:** of sustained efforts on the part of the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, all States/UTs issued orders for the implementation of the Food Safety Regulations banning the manufacture, sale, and storage of gutka and pan masala containing tobacco or nicotine by the year 2014-15.
- **Several States/UTs:** have banned all forms of smokeless tobacco products such as chewing tobacco, zarda, khaini, and other flavoured and processed tobacco irrespective of name and form.
- **On 24th:** September 2015, the Government of India notified that the rules on "tobacco pack pictorial warnings" would come into effect from 1st April 2016. These rules mandate the display of pictorial health warnings on 85 per cent of the principle display area of the tobacco product pack on both sides (60 per cent of the picture and 25 per cent of the text).

PROGRAMME COMPONENTS AND STRATEGIES

The main components of the programme are:
1. Public awareness and mass media campaigns for awareness building and for behavioural change.
2. Establishment of tobacco product testing laboratories, to build regulatory capacity, as required under COTPA 2003.
3. Mainstreaming the programme components as a part of the health delivery mechanism under the National Health Mission (NHM) framework.
4. Mainstream research and training on alternate crops and livelihood, with other nodal ministries.
5. Monitoring and evaluation, including surveillance, e.g., adult tobacco surveys.
6. Dedicated tobacco control cells at National, State, and District levels for effective implementation and monitoring of anti-tobacco initiatives.
7. Training of health and social workers, NGOs, school teachers, etc.
8. School programme.
9. Provision of tobacco cessation facilities.

> **EXAM TIP:** For NTCP questions: Outline COTPA 2003 key sections (Sec 4 smoking ban in public places, Sec 5 advertising ban, Sec 6 sales to minors / near schools, Sec 7 pictorial warnings) → 3-tier organizational structure (NTCC, STCC, DTCC) → Tobacco Cessation Centres (TCC) and Quitline (1800-11-2356) → MPOWER strategy alignment.

[REF]Reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine (28th Edition), National Tobacco Control Programme; COTPA 2003; MoHFW Operational Guidelines.[/REF]

subsections.title: National Programme for Healthcare of the Elderly (NPHCE)
subsections.content:
[SN]National Programme for Health Care of the Elderly (NPHCE)[/SN]

INTRODUCTION AND HISTORY
Nodal Ministry: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (MoHFW)

The Government of India launched the National Programme for Health Care of the Elderly (NPHCE) to address health-related problems of elderly people. The programme initially identified districts in 21 states during the 11th Five Year Plan period to implement its strategies and interventions.

AIMS AND OBJECTIVES

- **To provide:** separate, specialized, and comprehensive healthcare to senior citizens at various levels of the state healthcare delivery system, including outreach services.
- **To ensure:** preventive and promotive care, and management of illness.
- **To focus:** on health manpower development for geriatric services.
- **To provide:** medical rehabilitation and therapeutic intervention.
- **To carry:** out Information, Education, and Communication (IEC) activities.

PROGRAMME INFRASTRUCTURE AND HEALTHCARE LEVELS

The details of the geriatric setup and activities undertaken at various healthcare levels are as follows:

1. National Centres of Ageing (NCA)
- **2 National:** Centres of Ageing are being established at AIIMS, New Delhi and Madras Medical College, Chennai.
- **Core functions:** include training of health professionals, research activity, and healthcare delivery in the field of geriatrics.

2. Regional Geriatric Centres
- **8 regional:** geriatric centres have been developed as referral units in different regions of the country.
- **Tertiary phased expansion:** Planned expansion across additional medical colleges to establish dedicated Regional Geriatric Centres (RGCs).

3. Department of Geriatric at 20 Super Specialized Institutions
- **Geriatric Departments:** are being developed at 8 identified medical institutions located in various regions of the country, with a 30-bedded in-patient facility.
- **Apart from:** providing referral treatment, research, and manpower development, these institutions are involved in developing and updating training materials for various levels of health functionaries, and developing IEC material and guidelines.
- **Funds have:** been provided for manpower, equipment, medicines (consumables & drugs), construction of buildings, and training.

4. Geriatric Unit at District Hospitals
- **The programme:** was approved for implementation in 2017-2018 in 520 districts, covering 35 states.
- **Provision exists:** for establishing 10-bedded geriatric wards and dedicated OPD services exclusively for geriatric patients.
- **Financial and infrastructure support:** Central grant-in-aid allocated for specialized geriatric ward infrastructure, consumables, and human resource contracting.

5. Rehabilitation Units at Community Health Centres (CHCs)
- **In identified:** districts, there is a provision for dedicated health clinics for elderly persons twice a week.
- **A rehabilitation:** unit is being set up at all the CHCs falling under identified districts.
- **A dedicated:** rehabilitation worker is supposed to provide physiotherapy to needy elderly persons.

6. Activity at Primary Health Centres (PHCs)
- **Weekly geriatric:** clinics are arranged at the identified PHCs by a trained Medical Officer.
- **For diseases:** needing further investigation and treatment, persons are referred to the first referral unit (CHC or District Hospital) as per need.
- **A one-time:** grant is given to PHCs for the procurement of equipment.

7. Activity at Sub-Centre Level
- **The ANMs:** and Male Health Workers posted in sub-centres make domiciliary visits to elderly persons in their jurisdiction.
- **They arrange:** suitable calipers and supportive devices from the PHC and provide them to elderly disabled persons to make them ambulatory.
- **Sub-centre rehabilitation support:** Domiciliary visits by frontline workers providing basic mobility aids and primary ailment management.

RECENT UPDATES

- **The tertiary:** component of the programme has been renamed as Rashtriya Varishth Jan Swasthya Yojana (RVJSY).

> **EXAM TIP:** Pyramid from sub-centre domiciliary care → PHC clinic → CHC rehab → DH geriatric unit → regional/national centres; mention RVJSY tertiary rename if asked recent updates.

[REF]Reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine (28th Edition), National Programme for Health Care of the Elderly; MoHFW Guidelines.[/REF]

subsections.title: National Programme for Prevention and Management of Trauma and Burn Injuries (NPPMTBI)
subsections.content:
[SN]Trauma Care and Burn Management Programme[/SN]

INTRODUCTION
Nodal Ministry: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (MoHFW)

The National Programme for Prevention and Management of Trauma and Burn Injuries (NPPMTBI) addresses two major causes of mortality, morbidity, and disability in India: road traffic crashes and burn injuries. The programme operates through two distinct components.

A. TRAUMA CARE COMPONENT

BACKGROUND AND MILESTONES
- **Road traffic:** crashes are one of the major causes of disability, morbidity, and mortality. As per the Road Accident Report for 2019, a total of 4,49,002 accidents took place in the country leading to 1,51,113 deaths and 4,51,361 injuries.
- **9th and 10th Five Year Plans:** The programme for trauma care started as a "Pilot Project for Strengthening Emergency Facilities along the Highways".
- **11th Five Year Plan:** The programme was approved as "Assistance for Capacity Building for Developing Trauma Care Facilities in Government Hospitals on National Highways" for developing a network of trauma care facilities (TCFs) along the Golden Quadrilateral highway corridor as well as North-South & East-West Corridors. 116 TCFs were identified and funded under the Programme during the 11th FYP with 100 percent central assistance.
- **12th Five Year Plan:** The scheme was further extended as "Capacity Building for Developing Trauma Care Facilities in Govt. Hospitals on National Highways" wherein 80 Hospitals/Medical Colleges were approved for financial assistance.

OBJECTIVES
- **To establish:** a network of Trauma Care Facilities on National/State Highways in order to reduce the incidence of preventable deaths and disabilities due to road traffic accidents by observing the golden hour principle.
- **To develop:** Surveillance, Trauma Registry, and Capacity Building Centre for collection, compilation, analysis, and dissemination of information for policy formulation and preventive interventions.
- **To improve:** the awareness about trauma care among the general masses and vulnerable groups by developing and disseminating IEC material.

B. BURN INJURIES COMPONENT

BACKGROUND AND EPIDEMIOLOGY
- **India has:** one of the largest burdens of burns with an estimated 7,000,000 burn injuries per year, an estimated 1.4 lakh deaths, and 2.4 lakh disabilities.
- **Burn injuries:** are the second largest group of injuries after road accidents. This translates to a mortality rate of over 8.3 / 100,000 population, and a loss of 5 million disability-adjusted life years (DALYs).
- **This high:** incidence has been attributed to illiteracy, poverty, and low safety consciousness in the population.
- **The epidemiology:** of mortality after burns is unique in India; most burn injuries are in young adults and deaths are more common in women than men, contrasting trends observed in other low-and middle-income countries.

MILESTONES AND OBJECTIVES
- **2010:** A pilot programme on burn care was initiated by the Ministry of Health & Family Welfare in the name of "Pilot Programme for Prevention of Burn Injuries" (PPPBI).
- **It was:** initially implemented in 3 Medical Colleges and six District Hospitals.
- **The goal:** of PPPBI was to ensure the prevention of burn injuries, provide timely and adequate treatment in case of burn injuries to reduce mortality, complications, and ensuing disabilities, to provide effective rehabilitative interventions if disability has set in, and to establish a central burn registry.
- **12th Five Year Plan:** The pilot project continued as a full-fledged programme for the tertiary care level.
- **Financial assistance:** towards the District Hospital component was undertaken under the National Health Mission (NHM). The scheme is being extended since then.

> **EXAM TIP:** For NPPMTBI: Golden Hour concept (first 60 minutes) → 4-tier trauma network along National/State Highways (Levels I–IV with defined beds, CT/OT readiness, and triage) → Burn care units (skin banking, acute fluid resuscitation Parkland formula, rehabilitation) → National Injury and Burn Registries.

[REF]Reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine (28th Edition), NPPMTBI; Trauma & Burn Care Guidelines, Directorate General of Health Services, MoHFW.[/REF]

subsections.title: National Water Supply and Sanitation Programme & Swachh Bharat Mission
subsections.content:
[SN]Swachh Bharat Mission (Gramin and Urban)[/SN]

INTRODUCTION AND HISTORY
Historical nodal ministry: Ministry of Health; current rural water and sanitation rest with the Ministry of Jal Shakti

The National Water Supply and Sanitation Programme was initiated in 1954 with the objective of providing safe water supply and adequate drainage facilities for the entire urban and rural population of the country.

In 1972, a supplement to the national water supply and sanitation programme known as the Accelerated Rural Water Supply Programme was started. During the Fifth Five Year Plan, rural water supply was included in the Minimum Needs Programme of the State Plans. The Central Government supported the efforts of the States in identifying problem villages.

ACCELERATED RURAL WATER SUPPLY PROGRAMME (ARWSP)
Historical nodal ministry: Department of Drinking Water Supply (later Department of Drinking Water and Sanitation, Ministry of Jal Shakti)

A "problem village" was defined as one where no source of safe water is available within a distance of 1.6 km, or where water is available at a depth of more than 15 metres, or where the water source has excess salinity, iron, fluorides and other toxic elements, or where water is exposed to the risk of cholera.

The stipulated norm of water supply under earlier programs was 40 litres per capita per day (lpcd), and at least one hand pump/spot-source for every 250 persons. The National Drinking Water Mission, launched in 1986, was subsequently renamed as the Rajiv Gandhi National Drinking Water Mission in 1991. The current norm under the Jal Jeevan Mission is 55 lpcd.

In 1999-2000, the Sector Reform Project was started to involve the community in planning, implementation and management of drinking water schemes, which was in 2002 scaled up as the Swajaldhara Programme.

SWAJALDHARA AND BHARAT NIRMAN

Swajaldhara was launched on 25th December 2002 as a community-led participatory programme aiming at providing safe drinking water in rural areas with full community ownership. It had two components:
- **Swajaldhara I (First Dhara):** For a gram panchayat or a group of panchayats at the block/tahsil level.
- **Swajaldhara II (Second Dhara):** With the district as the project area.

The programme was revised from 1st April 2009 and named as the National Rural Drinking Water Programme (NRDWP).

Bharat Nirman was launched in 2005 to build rural infrastructure. Phase-I was implemented from 2005-06 to 2008-09, and Phase-II from 2009-10 to 2011-12. Priority was given to cover water quality problems and habitations affected by arsenic, fluoride, iron, salinity, and nitrate.

During the 12th Five Year Plan (2012-2017), service levels for rural water supply were enhanced from the norm of 40 lpcd to 55 lpcd for designing systems, with a target of at least 50 per cent of the rural population having access to water within their household premises or within 100 metres radius, and at least 30 per cent having individual household connections (up from 13 per cent). Currently, the Jal Jeevan Mission (launched in 2019) aims to provide functional household tap connections with 55 lpcd to every rural household by 2024.

THE NAL JAL YOJANA (JAL JEEVAN MISSION)
Nodal Ministry: Department of Drinking Water and Sanitation, Ministry of Jal Shakti

The Jal Jeevan Mission (JJM) is a programme that aims to provide every rural household with access to safe and reliable tap water, initially by 2024, and subsequently extended till 2028.

Goal of Jal Jeevan Mission: To provide every rural household with a Functional Household Tap Connection (FHTC) that delivers at least 55 liters of tap water per person per day, meeting prescribed quality standards, with an extended target of December 2028.

RURAL SANITATION PROGRAMME AND NIRMAL BHARAT ABHIYAN

In 2012, a paradigm shift was made in the Total Sanitation Campaign by launching the Nirmal Bharat Abhiyan (NBA) in the 12th Five Year Plan. 

- **Objective:** To achieve sustainable behavioural change with the provision of sanitary facilities in entire communities in a phased manner, adopting a saturation mode with "Nirmal Grams" as outcomes.

SWACHH BHARAT MISSION (SBM)
Nodal ministries: SBM-Gramin under Ministry of Jal Shakti; SBM-Urban under Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs (MoHUA)

Swachh Bharat Abhiyan or Swachh Bharat Mission is a national campaign by the Government of India to clean streets, roads, and infrastructure of the country. It was officially launched by the Prime Minister of India on 2nd October 2014 at Rajghat, New Delhi.

- **Aim:** To eradicate open defecation by year 2019 by constructing over 100 million toilets in rural India.
- **Sub-missions:** Swachh Bharat Mission Gramin and Swachh Bharat Mission Urban.

SWACHH BHARAT MISSION GRAMIN (SBM-G)
Nodal Ministry: Department of Drinking Water and Sanitation, Ministry of Jal Shakti

- **Objectives:** Bring about an improvement in the general quality of life in rural areas, accelerate sanitation coverage to achieve the vision of Swachh Bharat by 2nd October 2019, motivate communities and Panchayati Raj Institutions, encourage cost-effective technologies, and develop community-managed sanitation systems focusing on solid and liquid waste management.
- **Components:** Start-up activities, IEC and capacity building, construction of household toilets, and construction of community sanitary complexes.
- **School Sanitation:** Construction of toilets in government schools and anganwadi centres (focusing on separate toilets for girls and boys) implemented by the Ministry of Education and Ministry of Women and Child Development.
- **Incentives:** Provided for the construction of household toilets for Below Poverty Line (BPL) households, and restricted Above Poverty Line (APL) households including SCs/STs, small and marginal farmers, landless labourers, physically handicapped, and women-headed families.

SWACHH BHARAT MISSION URBAN (SBM-U)
Nodal Ministry: Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs (MoHUA)

Implemented by the Ministry of Urban Development. 

- **Objectives:** Elimination of open defecation, eradication of manual scavenging, modern and scientific municipal solid waste management, effecting behavioural change, generating awareness, capacity augmentation for Urban Local Bodies (ULBs), and creating an enabling environment for private sector participation in Capital Expenditure (Capex) and Operation and Maintenance (Opex).
- **Mission Components:** Household toilets (including conversion of insanitary latrines into pour-flush latrines), Community toilets, Public toilets, Solid waste management, IEC and public awareness, and Capacity building and administrative office expenses.
- **Public vs. Community Toilets:** 
  - **Public Toilets:** are for the floating population/general public in places such as markets, train stations, and tourist places.
  - **Community Toilets:** are shared facilities provided for a group of residents or an entire settlement, used primarily by low-income/informal settlements or slums where household space constraints exist.
- **Special Focus Groups:** Manual scavengers adequately rehabilitated; informal waste management workers (rag pickers) integrated into formal systems; temporary accommodation provided with toilets for migrants and homeless; mandatory temporary toilets at construction sites; priority accorded to vulnerable sections (pensioners, girl children, pregnant and lactating mothers).
- **Target Group for Household Toilets:** 80 per cent of urban households engaging in open defecation, all households with insanitary latrines, and all households with single-pit latrines. The remaining 20 per cent practicing open defecation are targeted by community toilets due to space constraints.

CLEAN TOILETS CAMPAIGN 2024

- **Sanitation transformation:** A decade of Swachh Bharat Mission has positioned universal sanitation and safe waste containment at the forefront of rural development.
- **Public toilet hygiene:** Targeted campaign to enforce continuous maintenance, hygiene audits, and water availability in public and community toilets.
- **Achievements:** Over 800 Toilet Blocks retrofitted/upgraded and 400+ new toilet blocks constructed. Over 10,000+ toilets nominated adhering to FACES (Functional, Accessible, Clean, Eco-friendly, Safe) parameters. 1,500+ women-led SHGs completed basic maintenance.
- **Clean Toilets Campaign:** A 5-week 'Clean Toilets Campaign' was conducted from 19th November (World Toilet Day 2024) to 25th December (Good Governance Day 2024) to transform all 70,000+ Community and Public Toilets across the country in terms of cleaning and maintenance.

SOLID WASTE MANAGEMENT COMPONENT

Municipal Solid Waste Management (MSWM) refers to a systematic process that comprises waste segregation and storage at source, primary collection, secondary storage, transportation, secondary segregation, resource recovery, processing, treatment, and final disposal of solid waste.

> **EXAM TIP:** For sanitation questions: Evolution from CRSP/TSC/NBA to Swachh Bharat Mission (SBM 2014) → SBM-G vs SBM-U components → ODF criteria (zero open defecation + safe containment) → ODF+ (toilet functionality + O&M) → ODF++ (faecal sludge and septage management) → link to Jal Jeevan Mission (JJM: 55 lpcd potable tap water by FHTC).

[REF]Reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine (28th Edition), Environmental Health; Ministry of Jal Shakti Guidelines for SBM-G and JJM.[/REF]

subsections.title: Polio Endgame Strategy & Surveillance Programme
subsections.content:
[SN]Polio Endgame Strategy and AFP Surveillance[/SN]

INTRODUCTION AND POLIO ENDGAME ERADICATION STRATEGY
Nodal Ministry: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (MoHFW)

The Polio Endgame Strategy (established for 2019-2023, and subsequently revised for 2022-2026) consists of a comprehensive set of actions representing a collective commitment to eradicate polio. It focuses heavily on eradication, integration, certification, and containment.

GOALS OF THE POLIO ENDGAME STRATEGY (2022-2026)

1. Goal One (Eradication):
