[SN]Maternal Mortality Ratio[/SN]

[LAQ]Maternal mortality: trends, determinants, and national response[/LAQ]

MATERNAL MORTALITY RATIO (MMR)

CURRENT INDIA FIGURES (MATERNAL AND CHILD HEALTH)

NFHS-6 India fact sheets (May 2026) do not publish infant, neonatal, or under-five mortality. Use SRS for those rates.

| Indicator | Latest | Year | Source | Previous |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Maternal mortality ratio | 87 per 100,000 live births | 2022-24 | SRS Special Bulletin on Maternal Mortality 2022-24, RGI | 88 (SRS 2021-23); 93 (SRS 2019-21); 97 (SRS 2018-20) |
| Infant mortality rate | 24 per 1,000 live births (rural 28 / urban 18 in 2023) | 2024 | SRS 2024, RGI | 25 (SRS Bulletin 2023, RGI); 32 (SRS 2020) |
| Neonatal mortality rate | 18 per 1,000 live births | 2024 | SRS 2024, RGI | SRS 2020 teaching tables ~20 |
| Under-five mortality rate | 28 per 1,000 live births | 2024 | SRS 2024, RGI | 29 (SRS 2023) |
| Institutional births | 90.6% | 2023-24 | NFHS-6, 2023-24, IIPS/MoHFW | 88.6% (NFHS-5, 2019-21, IIPS/MoHFW) |
| ANC in first trimester | 76.2% | 2023-24 | NFHS-6, 2023-24, IIPS/MoHFW | 70.0% (NFHS-5, 2019-21, IIPS/MoHFW) |
| At least 4 ANC visits | 65.2% | 2023-24 | NFHS-6, 2023-24, IIPS/MoHFW | 58.5% (NFHS-5, 2019-21, IIPS/MoHFW) |
| IFA for 180 days or more | 37.8% | 2023-24 | NFHS-6, 2023-24, IIPS/MoHFW | 26.0% (NFHS-5, 2019-21, IIPS/MoHFW) |
| Caesarean section | 27.2% | 2023-24 | NFHS-6, 2023-24, IIPS/MoHFW | 21.5% (NFHS-5, 2019-21, IIPS/MoHFW) |
| Exclusive breastfeeding (under 6 months) | 55.8% | 2023-24 | NFHS-6, 2023-24, IIPS/MoHFW | 63.7% (NFHS-5, 2019-21, IIPS/MoHFW). Coverage fell |
| Breastfed within 1 hour of birth | 50.1% | 2023-24 | NFHS-6, 2023-24, IIPS/MoHFW | 41.8% (NFHS-5, 2019-21, IIPS/MoHFW) |
| Fully vaccinated (12-23 months, fact-sheet definition) | 82.6% | 2023-24 | NFHS-6, 2023-24, IIPS/MoHFW | PIB also quotes 87.1% from vaccination-card information |

DEFINITIONS
- **Maternal death:** The death of a woman while pregnant or within 42 days (6 weeks) of termination of pregnancy, irrespective of the duration and anatomical site of the pregnancy, from any cause related to or aggravated by the pregnancy or its management, but not from accidental or incidental causes.
- **Late maternal death:** The death of a woman from direct or indirect obstetric causes occurring more than 42 days but less than one year after the termination of pregnancy.
- **Pregnancy-related death:** The death of a woman while pregnant or within 42 days of termination of pregnancy, irrespective of the cause of death (including accidental and incidental causes).

ICD CLASSIFICATION OF MATERNAL DEATHS
- **Direct obstetric deaths:** Deaths resulting from obstetric complications of the pregnant state (pregnancy, labour, and puerperium), interventions, omissions, incorrect medical treatment, or a chain of events resulting from any of the above (e.g., eclampsia, severe haemorrhage, sepsis, obstructed labour).
- **Indirect obstetric deaths:** Deaths resulting from previous existing disease, or disease that developed during pregnancy, which was not due to direct obstetric causes but was aggravated by the physiological changes of pregnancy (e.g., cardiac disease, viral hepatitis, severe anemia).

STATISTICAL MEASURES OF MATERNAL MORTALITY
- **Maternal Mortality Ratio (MMR):** Number of maternal deaths in a given period per 100,000 live births during the same period. Formula: (Number of maternal deaths / Total live births) x 100,000. It measures obstetric risk per pregnancy.
- **Maternal Mortality Rate (MMRt):** Number of maternal deaths in a given period per 100,000 women of reproductive age (15 to 49 years). Formula: (Number of maternal deaths / Total women aged 15-49 years) x 100,000. It reflects both the obstetric risk per birth and the population fertility rate.
- **Proportion of maternal deaths (PMD):** Number of maternal deaths expressed as a proportion of all deaths among women of reproductive age. Formula: (Number of maternal deaths / Total deaths among women aged 15-49 years) x 1,000.
- **Adult lifetime risk of maternal death:** The cumulative probability that a 15-year-old female will die from a maternal cause during her reproductive lifespan.

[SN]Approaches to measuring maternal mortality[/SN]

APPROACHES FOR MEASURING MATERNAL MORTALITY
- **Civil Registration and Vital Statistics (CRVS):** Routine continuous registration of all births and maternal deaths; standard method in developed settings, often limited by under-registration in developing countries.
- **Sample Registration System (SRS):** A dual-record system operating large representative sample units across Indian states, providing the authoritative national estimates of maternal mortality.
- **Sisterhood method:** A population survey technique interviewing a representative sample of adults regarding the survival of all their biological sisters through their childbearing years.
- **Reproductive Age Mortality Studies (RAMOS):** Comprehensive identification of all deaths among women of reproductive age in a defined population using multiple overlapping data sources (hospital records, burial grounds, police registers).
- **Verbal autopsy:** Structured questionnaire administered to family and community members regarding signs, symptoms, and circumstances preceding death where medical certification is unavailable.
- **RHIME protocol:** Representative, Resampled, Routine Household Interview of Mortality with Medical Evaluation, an enhanced verbal autopsy tool with physician review utilized in the Indian SRS framework.
- **Decennial national census:** Incorporating targeted questions on household pregnancy-related deaths within the preceding 12 months.

INCIDENCE AND EPIDEMIOLOGY OF MATERNAL MORTALITY
- **Global burden:** Global average is estimated at approximately 223 maternal deaths per 100,000 live births.
- **Indian national estimates:** The Maternal Mortality Ratio in India stands at 87 per 100,000 live births (SRS Special Bulletin on Maternal Mortality 2022-24, Office of the Registrar General of India).
- **Progressive decline:** India's MMR has fallen consistently from 97 (SRS 2018-20), 93 (SRS 2019-21), and 88 (SRS 2021-23) to 87 (SRS 2022-24).
- **Sustainable Development Goal (SDG 3.1):** Targets reducing the global maternal mortality ratio to less than 70 per 100,000 live births by 2030.
- **Inter-state disparities:** High-burden states in SRS 2022-24 include Uttar Pradesh (154), Madhya Pradesh (135), and Chhattisgarh (124). Low-burden states achieving the SDG target include Kerala (24), Tamil Nadu (25), and Maharashtra (37).

DETERMINANTS AND CAUSES OF MATERNAL MORTALITY IN INDIA

1. Medical Causes
- **Direct obstetric causes:** Postpartum haemorrhage (most common single cause), puerperal sepsis, hypertensive disorders of pregnancy (preeclampsia and eclampsia), obstructed labour, and unsafe abortion.
- **Indirect obstetric causes:** Severe nutritional anaemia, cardiovascular diseases, infectious hepatitis, and pulmonary tuberculosis.

2. Social and Demographic Determinants
- **Maternal age:** Childbirth under 18 years or over 35 years carries significantly elevated risk.
- **Parity:** Grand multiparity (fourth birth and above) increases risk of uterine atony, rupture, and haemorrhage.
- **Birth spacing:** Inter-pregnancy intervals less than 24 months deplete maternal nutrient stores.
- **Socioeconomic vulnerability:** Low maternal education, poverty, gender inequality, and lack of emergency obstetric transport.

TEMPORAL DISTRIBUTION OF MATERNAL DEATHS
- **Vulnerable window:** Maternal mortality peaks during the third trimester, labour, and the immediate puerperium.
- **Postpartum concentration:** Approximately 70 percent of maternal deaths occur during the postpartum period, with 45 percent concentrated within the first 24 hours of childbirth.
- **Global distribution:** Severe haemorrhage (25%), indirect causes (20%), puerperal infections (15%), unsafe abortion (13%), eclampsia (12%), and obstructed labour (8%).
- **Indian distribution:** Severe haemorrhage (38%), other conditions/indirect causes (34%), puerperal sepsis (16%), unsafe abortion (8%), and obstructed labour (5%). Postpartum haemorrhage and puerperal sepsis jointly account for over half of all maternal deaths.

PREVENTIVE MEASURES AND NATIONAL INITIATIVES
- **Antenatal care:** Early registration within 12 weeks and minimum four clinical checkups for risk stratification.
- **Prophylaxis:** Anemia Mukt Bharat IFA supplementation and Td immunization.
- **Institutional delivery promotion:** Financial incentives under Janani Suraksha Yojana (JSY) and zero out-of-pocket expenditure under Janani Shishu Suraksha Karyakram (JSSK).
- **Quality improvement: LaQshya:** Labour Room Quality Improvement Initiative to enhance clinical quality in labour rooms and maternity operating theatres.
- **Pradhan Mantri Surakshit Matritva Abhiyan (PMSMA):** Guarantees free, comprehensive antenatal checkups by specialists on the 9th of every month.
- **Dakshata initiative:** Competency-based clinical training of medical officers and staff nurses in intrapartum and immediate postpartum care.
- **Surakshit Matritva Aashwasan (SUMAN) Roadmap 2030:** A national policy framework aiming to lower India's MMR below 70 by 2030, establishing a four-stage tracking continuum for high-risk pregnancies across priority districts, reinforced by community SUMAN Panchayats ensuring a service-guarantee charter with zero denial of care.

> **EXAM TIP:** MMR exam structure: ICD definition (42 days, non-accidental) → MMR (live births) vs MMRt (women of reproductive age) vs Lifetime risk → Direct vs Indirect causes table → Three Delays model → National initiatives (JSY cash assistance, JSSK cashless entitlements, LaQshya certification, and SUMAN service guarantee). Always cite the specific SRS survey period when quoting vital rates.

[SN]Perinatal mortality[/SN]

PERINATAL MORTALITY RATE (PNMR)
- **Perinatal period definition:** Commences at 28 completed weeks of gestation (fetal weight approximately 1,000 g) and terminates at 7 completed days after birth (ICD criteria). The WHO international definition commences at 22 completed weeks of gestation (500 g fetal weight).
- **Viability criteria:** Fetal weight of at least 1,000 g; where birth weight is unknown, gestational age of at least 28 completed weeks, or crown-heel body length of at least 35 cm.
- **Perinatal mortality rate formulas:**
  - **Standard epidemiological formula:** (Late fetal deaths [stillbirths after 28 weeks] + early neonatal deaths [0-7 days]) / (Total live births in the same year) x 1,000.
  - **WHO preferred formula:** (Late fetal deaths + early neonatal deaths) / (Live births + late fetal deaths) x 1,000.
- **Clinical and public health significance:** Reflects the joint quality and efficacy of antenatal, intrapartum, and early neonatal care.
- **National child survival indicators:** National child survival indicators record a Neonatal Mortality Rate of 18 and an Infant Mortality Rate of 24 per 1,000 live births (SRS 2024, Office of the Registrar General of India). The older SRS 2020 perinatal teaching figure was 18 per 1,000 live births.

CAUSES OF PERINATAL MORTALITY
- **Antenatal determinants:** Maternal hypertensive disorders, gestational diabetes, severe maternal anaemia, maternal infections (syphilis, toxoplasmosis), and placental insufficiency.
- **Intrapartum determinants:** Birth trauma, intrapartum fetal hypoxia, obstructed labour, cord prolapse, and uterine rupture.
- **Postnatal determinants:** Prematurity, respiratory distress syndrome, severe congenital anomalies, and early neonatal sepsis.
- **Biological and social risk factors:** Low maternal socioeconomic status, maternal height below 140 cm, extreme reproductive age (<16 or >35 years), and lack of skilled attendance at delivery.

PREVENTION OF PERINATAL MORTALITY
- **Pre-conceptional and antenatal interventions:** Early risk screening, gestational weight monitoring, balanced nutrition, iron-folic acid prophylaxis, and Td vaccination.
- **Intrapartum management:** Delivery by Skilled Birth Attendants, partograph-based labour monitoring, and emergency obstetric care at First Referral Units (FRUs).
- **Early neonatal care:** Immediate resuscitation, thermal control, clean cord management, and prompt initiation of exclusive breastfeeding.

NEONATAL MORTALITY RATE (NMR)
- **NMR formula:** (Number of deaths of neonates under 28 days of age / Total live births in the same year) x 1,000.
- **Neonatal mortality (NM):** Deaths occurring within the first 28 completed days of life.
  - **Early neonatal mortality (ENM):** Deaths occurring within the first 7 completed days of life (0 to 6 days).
  - **Late neonatal mortality (LNM):** Deaths occurring from the 8th to 28th day of life.
- **Incidence in India:** Neonatal Mortality Rate stands at 18 per 1,000 live births (SRS 2024, RGI; compared to ~20 in SRS 2020). Early neonatal deaths account for approximately 75 percent of all neonatal deaths.
- **Global causes of neonatal mortality:** Preterm birth complications (35%), intrapartum complications / birth asphyxia (24%), neonatal sepsis (15%), and congenital anomalies (11%).
- **Causes in India:** Prematurity and low birth weight represent the primary cause of neonatal deaths. Early neonatal deaths are driven by prematurity, birth asphyxia, and congenital malformations; late neonatal deaths are predominantly caused by community-acquired infections (pneumonia, septicaemia, and diarrhoea).

NEONATAL SCREENING
- **Screening profile:** Routine neonatal screening programs evaluate newborns for treatable congenital and metabolic conditions:
  - **Congenital hypothyroidism:** Most frequently screened congenital endocrinopathy worldwide.
  - **Phenylketonuria (PKU):** Evaluated via newborn heel-prick dried blood spots using the Guthrie bacterial inhibition assay or tandem mass spectrometry.
  - **Hemoglobinopathies:** Screening for sickle cell disease and beta-thalassemia.
  - **Developmental dysplasia of the hip:** Clinical screening via Ortolani and Barlow maneuvers.
  - **Glucose-6-Phosphate Dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency:** Prevents severe neonatal hyperbilirubinemia and kernicterus.

NEONATAL TETANUS
- **Clinical nomenclature:** Historically referred to as "8th day disease" due to typical clinical onset during the second week of life.
- **Elimination milestone:** In August 2015, India achieved validation for the Elimination of Maternal and Neonatal Tetanus (defined as less than 1 case of neonatal tetanus per 1,000 live births in every district).
- **The Five Cleans:** Hygienic delivery practices essential for sustaining neonatal tetanus elimination:
  1. **Clean delivery surface:** Disinfected plastic sheet or sterile delivery surface.
  2. **Clean hands:** Thorough handwashing with soap and clean running water.
  3. **Clean cord cut:** Sterile, newly opened razor blade.
  4. **Clean cord tie:** Sterile, uncontaminated ligature thread.
  5. **Clean cord stump:** Leaving the stump dry with nothing applied.

POST NEONATAL MORTALITY RATE (PNMR)
- **PNMR formula:** (Number of deaths of infants between 28 days and 1 year of age / Total live births in the same year) x 1,000.
- **Mathematical relationship:** Calculated as Infant Mortality Rate minus Neonatal Mortality Rate (IMR - NMR). With an IMR of 24 and NMR of 18 (SRS 2024, RGI), the post-neonatal mortality rate in India is approximately 6 per 1,000 live births.
- **Primary etiologies:** Driven primarily by environmental, dietary, and infectious factors: acute respiratory infections (pneumonia), acute diarrhoeal diseases, and severe acute malnutrition.

[SN]Infant Mortality Rate[/SN]

INFANT MORTALITY RATE (IMR)
- **IMR formula:** (Number of deaths of infants under one year of age in a given year / Total live births in the same year) x 1,000.
- **Public health significance:**
  - **Community health barometer:** Widely regarded as the single most sensitive barometer of community health status, sanitation, and availability and accessibility of basic healthcare services.
  - **Socioeconomic indicator:** Universally acknowledged as the second most sensitive indicator of socioeconomic development (ranked second only to the Under-Five Mortality Rate).
- **Incidence in India:** Infant Mortality Rate is 24 per 1,000 live births (SRS 2024, RGI). According to the SRS Bulletin 2023, the national rate was 25 (rural: 28, urban: 18), showing significant progress from 32 in SRS 2020.
  - **High-burden states:** Madhya Pradesh, Uttar Pradesh, and Chhattisgarh record highest rates (~37 per 1,000).
  - **Low-burden states:** Kerala records the lowest rate (5 per 1,000 live births in SRS 2023).
- **Mortality timeline:** Approximately 68 percent of infant deaths occur within the first month of life (neonatal period), of which 75 percent occur in the first week. The highest risk of demise is concentrated in the first 24 to 48 hours of life. After the first month, mortality in India shows higher rates among female infants due to gender-based disparities in nutrition and healthcare access.
- **Primary causes in India:** Prematurity and low birth weight, acute respiratory infections (pneumonia), diarrhoeal illnesses, congenital malformations, and umbilical sepsis.

CRITERIA FOR AT-RISK INFANTS
- **Anthropometric criteria:** Birth weight below 2,500 g, failure to gain weight over three consecutive monthly evaluations, or weight falling below 70 percent of median reference standards.
- **Clinical vulnerability:** Presence of severe protein-energy malnutrition, persistent diarrhoea, or congenital malformations.
- **Familial and social criteria:** Birth order 5 or higher, twin or multiple births, artificial formula feeding, maternal deprivation, single-parent household, or working mother with poor substitute care.

FACTORS AFFECTING INFANT MORTALITY
- **Maternal biological age:** Highest IMR is documented in adolescent mothers under 19 years and older mothers over 35 years.
- **Maternal literacy:** Strong inverse correlation with infant mortality; higher maternal education enhances health literacy, timely immunization, and hygienic feeding.
- **Birth order:** Displays a U-shaped pattern: elevated in first-borns, lowest in second-borns, and progressively escalating from third-born infants onward.
- **Birth spacing:** Infant mortality is highest with inter-pregnancy intervals under 12 months, and lowest with intervals of 24 to 36 months.
- **Feeding practices:** Delayed initiation of breastfeeding, administration of prelacteal feeds, non-exclusive breastfeeding, and unhygienic bottle-feeding markedly elevate death risks.
- **Harmful traditional practices:** Discarding colostrum, delayed umbilical cord clamping, and application of cow dung or ash to the cord stump.

CHILD DEATH RATE (1 TO 4 YEAR MORTALITY RATE)
- **Mathematical formula:** (Number of deaths of children aged 1 to 4 completed years in a given year / Mid-year population of children aged 1 to 4 years) x 1,000.
- **Denominator specification:** Uses the mid-year population of the specific age cohort (1 to 4 years), not total live births.
- **Leading causes:** In developing nations, acute diarrhoeal diseases and lower respiratory infections predominate; in developed nations, accidental injuries represent the leading cause.
- **Age-specific risk:** Highest mortality within this cohort occurs during the second year of life (12 to 23 months) during the critical transition to solid family diets.
- **Socioeconomic indicator:** Reflects the environmental hygiene, community nutrition, and living standards of a country more specifically than the crude birth or death rates.

CHILD SURVIVAL RATE (CSR) / CHILD SURVIVAL INDEX
- **Calculation formula:** (1,000 - Under-Five Mortality Rate) / 10.
- **Interpretation:** Converts the Under-Five Mortality Rate into a percentage metric of child survival; in India, an Under-Five Mortality Rate of 28 corresponds to a Child Survival Rate of approximately 97.2.

UNDER-5 MORTALITY RATE (U5MR) / CHILD MORTALITY RATE (CMR)
- **Calculation formula:** (Number of deaths of children under five years of age in a given year / Total live births in the same year) x 1,000.
- **Indian national figures:** Under-Five Mortality Rate is 28 per 1,000 live births (SRS 2024, RGI; compared to 29 in SRS 2023 and 32 in SRS 2020).
- **Public health primacy:** Recognized as the single best overall indicator of socioeconomic development, environmental health, and national child wellbeing.
- **Neonatal share:** Neonatal conditions account for approximately 47 to 50 percent of all global and national under-five deaths.

[SN]Maternal death surveillance and response (MDSR)[/SN]

MATERNAL DEATH SURVEILLANCE AND RESPONSE (MDSR)

DEFINITION
Maternal Death Surveillance and Response (MDSR) is an active, continuous epidemiological cycle that identifies, notifies, and quantifies maternal deaths, investigates medical and social causes, and implements actionable clinical and health system interventions to eliminate preventable maternal mortality.

OBJECTIVES
- **Universal enumeration:** Identify and count every maternal death occurring within health facilities and communities.
- **Etiological investigation:** Elucidate the precise clinical causes, systemic lapses, and delay factors contributing to death.
- **Evidence-based response:** Formulate targeted, corrective health system actions at facility, district, and state levels.
- **Accountability tracking:** Monitor the sustained implementation and impact of recommendations.

THE MDSR CYCLE
1. **Identification and notification:** Immediate identification and notification of all deaths among women of reproductive age (15-49 years) to screen for pregnancy-related deaths.
2. **Investigation:** Comprehensive maternal death audit utilizing facility case records, physician reviews, and community verbal autopsies.
3. **Review and analysis:** Multidisciplinary review by facility and district Maternal Death Review Committees conducted in a confidential, no-blame environment.
4. **Actionable response:** Remedying identified bottlenecks (e.g., blood availability, emergency referral transport, clinical protocol adherence, emergency obstetric staffing).
5. **Surveillance reporting:** Aggregation of district findings into state and national registries for policy recalibration.

OPERATIONAL LEVELS
- **Community level:** Frontline notification of maternal deaths by ASHAs and ANMs within 24 to 48 hours, followed by structured verbal autopsy interviews with family members.
- **Facility level:** Internal audit of every institutional maternal death within 24 hours by hospital clinical committees; reviewing maternal near-miss cases to enhance clinical resilience.
- **District and state levels:** Monthly district review meetings chaired by the District Magistrate/Collector to review systemic delays and allocate emergency funds.

LINK TO QUALITY INITIATIVES
- **Complementary role:** Complements population-level MMR estimates by delivering real-time, actionable local epidemiological intelligence.
- **Quality linkages:** Drives infrastructure and operational readiness across LaQshya certified labour rooms, First Referral Units (FRUs), and dedicated blood storage centers.

> **EXAM TIP:** MDSR framework: Draw the 4-stage cycle (Identify → Review → Respond → Monitor). Highlight the non-punitive, no-blame culture. Differentiate MDSR (real-time local quality improvement) from MMR (sample-based population mortality metric). Link to the Three Delays model.

[SN]Child death review[/SN]

CHILD DEATH REVIEW (CDR)

DEFINITION
Child Death Review is a systematic public health process of notifying, investigating, and clinically reviewing deaths of children under five years of age to delineate preventable medical, nutritional, and socio-environmental factors and institute remedial actions.

OPERATIONAL PURPOSE
- **Institutional learning:** Transform every child death into an actionable learning opportunity for the health system and community.
- **Identification of systemic delays:** Pinpoint preventable delays in parental care-seeking, emergency transport, and clinical triage.
- **Local prioritization:** Optimize deployment of frontline interventions, including Oral Rehydration Therapy corners, Special Newborn Care Units, and facility IMNCI protocols.

STEPWISE CDR PROCESS
1. **Frontline notification:** Prompt notification of child deaths by ASHAs and ANMs at community level, and medical record personnel at facility level.
2. **Classification and line listing:** Categorization into neonatal versus post-neonatal deaths, and community versus facility deaths.
3. **Case investigation:** Conducting structured verbal autopsy interviews with caregivers and performing detailed facility case sheet reviews.
4. **District review:** Multidisciplinary case review at block and district levels to assign primary and secondary causes of death.
5. **Systemic response:** Implementing remedial actions, including retraining workers, augmenting vaccine cold chains, and providing feedback to frontline staff.

PROGRAMMATIC LINKAGES IN INDIA
- **Community child health:** Integrated with Home-Based Newborn Care (HBNC) and Home-Based Care for Young Child (HBYC) home visits.
- **Clinical child health:** Linked to the Integrated Management of Neonatal and Childhood Illness (IMNCI) guidelines and facility-based newborn units.

> **EXAM TIP:** CDR core structure: Definition → 5-step operational cascade (Notify, Classify, Investigate, Review, Respond) → Systemic delay examples (care-seeking delay, transport gap, clinical management lapse) → Programmatic integration with HBNC and IMNCI.

[SN]Action plan for single-digit stillbirth rate by 2030[/SN]

STILLBIRTH REDUCTION TOWARDS 2030

DEFINITION
A stillbirth is defined as the death of a fetus prior to complete expulsion or extraction from the mother, using standard statistical viability thresholds (fetal weight ≥1,000 g, gestational age ≥28 completed weeks, or body length ≥35 cm).

PUBLIC HEALTH IMPORTANCE
- **Shared etiology:** Stillbirths share common pathophysiological determinants with maternal mortality and early neonatal deaths, reflecting maternal hypertension, intrapartum asphyxia, obstructed labour, and infections.
- **Invisible burden:** Accurate enumeration and stillbirth audits are vital to unmasking hidden fetal mortality.

STRATEGIC ACTIONS FOR STILLBIRTH REDUCTION
1. **High-quality antenatal surveillance:** Early registration, screening for gestational hypertension, and maternal syphilis and HIV testing.
2. **Skilled birth attendance:** Continuous intrapartum fetal heart rate monitoring and partograph-assisted labour management.
3. **Emergency obstetric care:** 24x7 comprehensive emergency obstetric and caesarean capabilities at First Referral Units (FRUs).
4. **Fetal growth restriction monitoring:** Detection of fetal growth deceleration and appropriate timing of delivery.
5. **Infection screening and prophylaxis:** Universal screening and treatment for maternal syphilis and prevention of malaria.
6. **Stillbirth death audits:** Systematic maternal and perinatal death audits across all delivery points to identify intrapartum stillbirths.
7. **Community awareness:** Educating pregnant women regarding fetal movements (kick counts) and obstetric warning signs.

NATIONAL POLICY FRAMING
- **India Newborn Action Plan (INAP):** Aligned with the global Every Newborn Action Plan (ENAP), targeting the achievement of single-digit stillbirth rates (less than 10 per 1,000 total births) by 2030.

> **EXAM TIP:** Stillbirth reduction framework: Definition (≥28 weeks / ≥1000 g) → Antenatal vs Intrapartum determinants table → Strategic action points → India Newborn Action Plan (INAP) target of single-digit stillbirth rate (<10 per 1,000 births) by 2030.

SOLVED EXERCISES

[EX]102. Mid-year population 5,00,000. Live births 15,000, deaths 7,000, infant deaths 1,875. Calculate crude birth rate, crude death rate, and infant mortality rate.[/EX]
[ANS]
- **Crude Birth Rate (CBR):**
  CBR = (15,000 / 5,00,000) x 1,000 = **30 per 1,000 population**

- **Crude Death Rate (CDR):**
  CDR = (7,000 / 5,00,000) x 1,000 = **14 per 1,000 population**

- **Infant Mortality Rate (IMR):**
  IMR = (1,875 / 15,000) x 1,000 = **125 per 1,000 live births**
[/ANS]

[EX]103. Mid-year population 2,00,000. Live births 6,050, stillbirths 110, deaths in the first week 250, in the first month 480, in the first year 750. Calculate stillbirth, perinatal, neonatal, and infant mortality rates.[/EX]
[ANS]
- **Stillbirth Rate (SBR):**
  SBR = (110 / (6,050 + 110)) x 1,000 = **17.86 per 1,000 total births**

- **Neonatal Mortality Rate (NMR):**
  NMR = (480 / 6,050) x 1,000 = **79.34 per 1,000 live births**

- **Infant Mortality Rate (IMR):**
  IMR = (750 / 6,050) x 1,000 = **123.97 per 1,000 live births**

- **Perinatal Mortality Rate (Standard WHO formula):**
  PMR = ((110 + 250) / (6,050 + 110)) x 1,000 = **58.44 per 1,000 total births**
[/ANS]

subsections.title: Under-5 Clinic, Congenital Disorders, and Battered Baby Syndrome
subsections.content:
OVERVIEW OF THE CHAPTER

The delivery of comprehensive primary child healthcare requires integrated institutional mechanisms such as the Under-Five Clinic, combining curative therapy, nutritional surveillance, immunization, and parental education within a single operational setting. Concurrently, preventive pediatrics encompasses the early screening and prenatal diagnosis of congenital disorders, alongside vigilance for clinical and medico-legal emergencies of child abuse and Non-Accidental Injury (Battered Baby Syndrome).

[SN]Under-5 Clinic[/SN]

UNDER-5 CLINIC
- **Operational definition:** A specialized primary healthcare facility delivering an integrated package of preventive, promotive, curative, referral, and educational services to children under five years of age, predominantly staffed and managed by trained nursing personnel.
- **Core goal:** To provide comprehensive, continuous, low-cost community health care to young children within an accessible, child-friendly facility.
- **Essential activities:**
  - **Health surveillance:** Continuous health surveillance and developmental monitoring of all children from birth up to five years of age.
  - **Disease control:** Prevention and control of common childhood infections (measles, pertussis, tuberculosis, malaria, and gastroenteritis).
  - **Outpatient treatment:** Rapid, outpatient treatment of acute dehydration, lower respiratory infections, and dermatological conditions.

SYMBOLIC ARCHITECTURE: LOGO OF THE UNDER-5 CLINIC
- **Design layout:** Composed of one large outer enveloping triangle containing four smaller internal triangles.
- **Outer enveloping triangle:** Represents Health Education, indicating that educational and communication activities encompass, permeate, and sustain all other functional clinical components.
- **Four internal service triangles:**
  - **Apex triangle (top):** Care in Illness (curative services and diagnostic assessment).
  - **Left internal triangle:** Growth Monitoring (weight charting and nutritional tracking).
  - **Right internal triangle:** Preventive Care (immunization and nutritional prophylaxis).
  - **Central inverted triangle:** Family Planning (counselling and birth spacing services for parents).

FUNCTIONS OF THE UNDER-5 CLINIC

1. Care in Illness
- **Diagnostic services:** Basic laboratory investigations (hemoglobin, urine, stool examination, malaria smears) and clinical evaluation.
- **Therapeutic services:** Standardized protocol-based management of acute respiratory infections, acute diarrhoeal diseases with dehydration, skin infections, and protein-energy malnutrition.
- **Referral linkages:** Timely stabilization and referral of severely ill children to Community Health Centres or District Hospitals.

2. Growth Monitoring
- **Anthropometric surveillance:** Periodic recording of weight, recumbent length/height, and mid-upper arm circumference.
- **Weighing frequency schedule:**
  - **First year of life:** Monthly weight evaluation.
  - **Second and third years:** Weighing every 2 months.
  - **Fourth and fifth years:** Weighing every 3 months.
- **Growth charting:** Weight is plotted on sex-specific growth charts to identify early growth deceleration; developmental milestones are simultaneously evaluated.

3. Preventive Care
- **Universal immunization:** Delivery of all scheduled vaccines under the Universal Immunization Programme.
- **Nutritional supplementation:** High-dose Vitamin A prophylaxis, Iron and Folic Acid syrups, and biannual deworming.
- **Diarrhoeal prevention:** Promotion of hygienic feeding, safe water, and community distribution of Oral Rehydration Salts (ORS) and zinc.

4. Family Planning
- **Postpartum family welfare:** Integrated counselling on contraceptive choices, emphasizing lactational amenorrhoea, barrier methods, intrauterine devices (IUDs), and postpartum tubal ligation.

5. Health Education
- **Caregiver guidance:** Structured group and individual health education covering exclusive breastfeeding, timely complementary feeding, personal hygiene, and home management of fever and cough.

CONGENITAL DISORDERS AMONG NEWBORNS

DEFINITIONS AND EPIDEMIOLOGY
- **Clinical definition:** Structural, functional, or biochemical abnormalities determined before or during gestation and recognizable at birth or in early life.
- **Global incidence:** Affects approximately 30 per 1,000 live births; cardiovascular malformations and central nervous system defects represent the most prevalent forms.
- **Incidence in India:** Congenital anomalies account for approximately 2.5 percent of all live births.
- **Regional patterns in India:** Neural tube defects (anencephaly, spina bifida) predominate across Northern India, whereas musculoskeletal and cardiac malformations represent the most common anomalies across other regions.

CAUSES OF CONGENITAL DISORDERS
- **Genetic factors:**
  - **Chromosomal aneuploidies:** Down's syndrome (trisomy 21), Edwards syndrome (trisomy 18), Turner's syndrome (45,X), and Klinefelter's syndrome (47,XXY).
  - **Inborn errors of metabolism:** Phenylketonuria, galactosemia, and Tay-Sachs disease.
  - **Monogenic disorders:** Beta-thalassemia, sickle cell anemia, cystic fibrosis, and hemophilia.
- **Environmental teratogens:**
  - **Intrauterine infections (TORCH):** Toxoplasmosis, Rubella, Cytomegalovirus, and Herpes simplex virus.
  - **Teratogenic pharmaceuticals:** Thalidomide (phocomelia), anticonvulsants (phenytoin, sodium valproate), and excessive Vitamin A intake.
  - **Maternal metabolic illnesses:** Uncontrolled gestational diabetes mellitus (caudal regression syndrome, cardiac defects) and chronic hypertension.
  - **Physical and chemical exposures:** Ionizing radiation, organic solvents, maternal alcoholism, and maternal periconceptional folic acid deficiency.

RISK STRATIFICATION AND PRENATAL DIAGNOSTIC MODALITIES
- **Major maternal risk factors:** Advanced maternal age (>35 years, sharply elevating Down's syndrome risk to 1 in 67 at age 40) and parental consanguinity (elevating risks of autosomal recessive disorders).
- **Prenatal screening and diagnostic techniques:**
  - **Maternal serum alpha-fetoprotein (MSAFP):** Elevated levels indicate open neural tube defects (spina bifida, anencephaly); reduced levels suggest trisomy 21.
  - **High-resolution ultrasonography:** Fetal anomaly scan at 18 to 20 weeks detects major structural cardiovascular and neural malformations.
  - **Amniocentesis:** Performed after 15 completed weeks of gestation for fetal karyotyping and biochemical diagnostics.
  - **Chorionic villus sampling (CVS):** Performed between 10 and 12 weeks of gestation, providing rapid first-trimester chromosomal analysis.

[SN]Battered Baby Syndrome[/SN]

BATTERED BABY SYNDROME AND CHILD ABUSE

NOMENCLATURE AND DEFINITIONS
- **Clinical synonyms:** Known variously as Caffey Syndrome, Shaken Baby Syndrome, Infantile Whiplash Syndrome, or Non-Accidental Injury (NAI).
- **Clinical definition:** A clinical condition observed in young children, predominantly under 3 years of age, who have suffered non-accidental, intentional physical trauma inflicted by a parent, guardian, or caregiver.
- **World Health Organization definition of child abuse:** All forms of physical and emotional ill-treatment, sexual abuse, neglect, or negligent treatment resulting in actual or potential harm to the child's health, survival, development, or dignity in the context of a relationship of responsibility, trust, or power.

PATHOGNOMONIC CLINICAL FEATURES
- **Cranial trauma:** Head injury represents the primary cause of mortality; manifestation includes diastatic skull fractures with egg-shell calcification.
- **Intracranial injury:** Vigorous shaking results in subdural haematoma, retinal haemorrhages, and periorbital ecchymosis without overt external head impact.
- **Skeletal trauma:** Multiple fractures of differing radiological ages; pathognomonic posterior rib fractures showing callus formation with a "string of beads" appearance, and metaphyseal "bucket-handle" fractures of long bones.
- **Cutaneous injuries:** Multiple contusions, human bite marks, cigarette burns, and characteristic "sixpence bruises" (circular finger-tip contusions resulting from violent grasping).

CLASSIFICATION OF CHILD ABUSE
1. **Physical abuse:** Intentional infliction of physical bodily harm (hitting, shaking, burning, poisoning).
2. **Sexual abuse:** Exploitation or coercion of a child to participate in sexual activities.
3. **Emotional abuse:** Persistent psychological hostility, verbal degradation, terrorizing, or withholding affection.
4. **Child neglect:** Persistent failure to provide basic physiological necessities (nutrition, clothing, shelter, affection, supervision, and medical care).

PREVENTION STRATEGIES: THE WHO INSPIRE FRAMEWORK
The INSPIRE framework represents seven evidence-based public health strategies to end violence against children:
- **I:** Implementation and enforcement of protective child legislation.
- **N:** Norms and values change through community sensitization.
- **S:** Safe physical environments in schools and neighborhoods.
- **P:** Parent and caregiver support through positive parenting education.
- **I:** Income and economic strengthening for vulnerable households.
- **R:** Response and support services for victims of violence.
- **E:** Education and life skills training for children and adolescents.

> **EXAM TIP:** Under-5 clinic: Draw the emblem (Outer triangle = Health Education; 4 inner triangles = Care in illness [Apex], Growth monitoring [Left], Preventive care [Right], Family planning [Base]). Battered Baby Syndrome: Caffey syndrome triad (subdural haematoma, retinal haemorrhages, multiple skeletal fractures of varying ages + sixpence bruises). Classify abuse into 4 types → summarize the INSPIRE framework.

subsections.title: Behavioral Problems, Juvenile Delinquency, Child Rights, and APGAR Score
subsections.content:
OVERVIEW OF THE CHAPTER

Child health extends beyond somatic growth to encompass emotional equilibrium, cognitive maturation, and social adaptation. Behavioral maladjustments, juvenile delinquency, and vulnerability to neglect or exploitation represent complex biosocial problems requiring multi-disciplinary interventions, child guidance clinics, and robust legal protections. In perinatal care, prompt functional assessment via the APGAR scoring system guides immediate resuscitation, while epidemiological risk stratification optimizes resource allocation across maternal and child health services.

BEHAVIORAL PROBLEMS IN CHILDREN
- **Etiological determinants:** Behavioral maladjustments arise from a complex interplay of subnormal cognitive ability, unrecognized organic neurodevelopmental disorders, and environmental maladaptation within stressful family or school milieus.
- **Intervention principles:** Primary resolution requires improving living conditions, enhancing family emotional stability, and providing structured educational support.
- **Classification of behavioral disorders:**
  - **Antisocial disorders:** Truancy, lying, persistent stealing, destructiveness, and overt aggression towards peers or animals.
  - **Habit disorders:** Persistent thumb sucking, onychophagia (nail biting), enuresis (bed-wetting), encopresis, and compulsive masturbation.
  - **Personality disorders:** Intense jealousy, pathological temper tantrums, excessive shyness, specific phobias, generalised anxiety, and social withdrawal.
  - **Psychosomatic manifestations:** Psychogenic headaches, recurrent abdominal pain, functional tremors, conversion reactions, and psychogenic asthma.
  - **Educational difficulties:** School phobia, scholastic backwardness, and learning disabilities (dyslexia, dyscalculia).

[SN]Juvenile delinquency[/SN]

JUVENILE DELINQUENCY
- **Legal definitions:**
  - **Juvenile delinquent:** A child or adolescent who has engaged in acts violating criminal statutes or social codes.
  - **Juvenile age limit:** Under Indian statutory law, any person who has not completed 18 years of age.
  - **Statutory modification:** Under the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act 2015, juveniles aged 16 to 18 years accused of committing heinous offences (such as murder or rape) may be transferred for trial as adults following preliminary psychological and social assessment.
  - **Delinquency:** Significant deviation from normal youthful behavior, embracing incorrigibility, ungovernability, habitual desertion from home, and antisocial acts.
- **Epidemiological pattern:** Peak incidence occurs in adolescents aged 15 years and above; rates are approximately five times higher among boys than girls.

CAUSES OF JUVENILE DELINQUENCY
- **Biological and genetic factors:** Genetic vulnerabilities, intellectual disability, sensory and physical handicaps, neuroendocrine imbalances, and chromosomal variations (e.g., 47,XYY karyotype).
- **Familial and social environment:** Parental deprivation, broken homes (parental divorce, separation, desertion), domestic violence, child neglect, parental alcoholism, and overcrowded slum dwellings.
- **Societal and economic pressures:** Rapid uncontrolled urbanization, commercial exploitation of youth, peer gang pressures, substance abuse, and exposure to media violence.

PREVENTIVE MEASURES
- **Primary family-level prevention:** Pre-marital counselling, family life education, and parental guidance to foster positive parenting and emotional security.
- **School-based interventions:** Positive student-teacher relationships, active remedial teaching, and early identification of behavioral maladjustments.
- **Community social welfare:** Recreational playgrounds, community youth clubs, vocational training centres, and specialized child guidance clinics.

CHILD GUIDANCE CLINIC
- **Historical background:** Established first in Chicago in 1909 to manage juvenile delinquency through psychiatric and psycho-social methods.
- **Clinical scope:** Provides multidisciplinary diagnosis and therapy for children and adolescents experiencing emotional, behavioral, and educational maladjustments.
- **Core preventive objective:** Resolves early neurotic, behavioral, and conduct disorders in childhood to avert psychiatric illness and personality disorders in adult life.
- **Multidisciplinary clinical team:**
  - **Mental health professionals:** Child psychiatrist (team leader), clinical psychologist, educational psychologist, and psychiatric social workers.
  - **Medical and pediatric specialists:** Pediatrician, neurologist, and public health nurses.
  - **Rehabilitative therapists:** Speech language pathologist and occupational therapist.
- **Clinical therapeutic modalities:**
  - **Medical management:** Medical treatment of underlying organic disease and correction of sensory deficits.
  - **Psychotherapy:** Play therapy, behavioral modification, and cognitive psychotherapy to rebuild emotional security.
  - **Parental counselling:** Family therapy, parental guidance, and environmental restructuring to reform the domestic setting.

CHILDREN IN DIFFICULT CIRCUMSTANCES
- **Vulnerable childhood populations:**
  - **Homeless and abandoned children:** Pavement dwellers, displaced youth, and evicted children lacking shelter.
  - **Orphaned and destitute children:** Children deprived of parental care and family support.
  - **Migrant and refugee children:** Displaced street children, unregistered migrants, and unaccompanied minors.
  - **Exploited youth:** Children engaged in hazardous child labor, debt bondage, or commercial sexual exploitation.
  - **Incarcerated mothers' children:** Children residing in correctional facilities with incarcerated mothers.
  - **Children with chronic disabilities:** Children living with terminal illnesses, congenital anomalies, or severe physical and mental handicaps.
- **Protective statutory frameworks in India:**
  - **Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act 2015:** Primary legislative instrument guaranteeing care, protection, and rehabilitation for children in conflict with law and children in need of care and protection.
  - **Immoral Traffic (Prevention) Act 1956:** Prohibits trafficking of children and women for commercial sexual exploitation.
  - **Ujjawala Scheme:** Comprehensive centrally sponsored scheme for prevention of trafficking and for rescue, rehabilitation, and reintegration of commercial sexual exploitation victims.

RIGHTS OF WOMEN AND CHILDREN
- **Constitutional safeguards in India:**
  - **Article 21A:** Guarantees free and compulsory education for all children aged 6 to 14 years as a fundamental right.
  - **Article 24:** Prohibits employment of children under 14 years of age in hazardous occupations, factories, or mines.
  - **Article 39(e) & (f):** Directs state policy to prevent abuse of children and ensure children develop in a healthy manner with freedom and dignity.
  - **Article 45:** Mandates early childhood care and education for all children until they complete six years of age.
- **International child rights declarations:** Universal rights to identity, survival, development, protection, and participation under the United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child (UNCRC).

CHILD PLACEMENT AND REHABILITATION
- **Orphanages:** Institutional facilities caring for destitute and parentless children; group institutional care is generally recognized as inferior to family-based rearing.
- **Foster home placement:** Temporary or prolonged arrangement placing a child in the protective care of a licensed foster family when biological parents cannot provide care.
- **Legal adoption:** The permanent legal transfer of all parental rights and responsibilities from biological parents to adoptive parents, conferring full legal status upon the child.
- **Observation and remand homes:** Temporary custodial institutions where children in conflict with the law are accommodated during legal inquiries, receiving education, psychiatric evaluation, and vocational training.
- **Special homes and Borstal institutions:**
  - **Borstal schools:** Semi-custodial educational and reformatory institutions designed for youthful offenders aged 16 to 21 years who require discipline and vocational training.
  - **Rehabilitation focus:** Operates on principles of reformation, moral re-education, and industrial apprenticeship to reintegrate youth into society.
  - **Statutory governance:** Governed by state Borstal School Acts (e.g., Bombay Borstal Schools Act 1929), providing reformative detention from 3 to 5 years in lieu of imprisonment.

[SN]Risk approach in MCH[/SN]

RISK APPROACH IN MATERNAL AND CHILD HEALTH
- **Managerial concept:** An epidemiological and administrative managerial strategy that directs extra clinical attention and resources toward individuals identified as having high risk factors.
- **Core public health objective:** Ensures optimal allocation of limited health personnel, diagnostic facilities, and hospital beds, providing "something for all, but more for those in need".
- **Risk assessment parameters:**
  1. **Magnitude:** Prevalence and demographic extent of the specific risk condition in the community.
  2. **Treatability:** Responsiveness of the risk factor to cost-effective medical or public health interventions.
  3. **Cost-effectiveness:** Ratio of health gains and disability reduction relative to expenditure.
  4. **Community attitude:** Social acceptability, cultural values, and felt need of the population.

[SN]APGAR Score[/SN]

APGAR SCORE
- **Clinical definition:** A rapid, objective scoring system evaluated at 1 minute and 5 minutes after birth to assess the clinical status of the newborn and determine the immediate need for resuscitation.
- **Timing and clinical interpretation:**
  - **1-minute score:** Reflects the immediate physiological condition at birth and dictates the urgency of neonatal resuscitation.
  - **5-minute score:** Reflects the physiological response to resuscitative interventions and correlates with survival and neurological prognosis.
- **Stratification of total score:**
  - **7 to 10:** Normal physiological transition; infant in excellent condition requiring routine supportive care.
  - **4 to 6:** Moderately depressed infant; mandates immediate tactile stimulation, clearing airway, and positive pressure bag-and-mask ventilation.
  - **0 to 3:** Severely depressed infant; mandates emergency cardiopulmonary resuscitation, tracheal intubation, and medications.

PARAMETERS OF THE APGAR SCORE

| Parameter | Score 0 | Score 1 | Score 2 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **A** - Appearance (Skin colour) | Blue, pale all over | Pink body, cyanotic extremities (Acrocyanosis) | Completely pink body and extremities |
| **P** - Pulse (Heart rate) | Absent | Slow (<100 beats/min) | >100 beats/min |
| **G** - Grimace (Reflex irritability) | No response to suction | Grimace, faint facial response | Vigorous cry, cough, sneeze, pulls away |
| **A** - Activity (Muscle tone) | Completely limp, flaccid | Some flexion of extremities | Active motion, well-flexed extremities |
| **R** - Respiration (Respiratory effort) | Absent | Slow, irregular, hypopneic | Strong, vigorous lusty cry |

> **EXAM TIP:** APGAR scoring: Evaluated at 1 min (status at birth) and 5 min (response to resuscitation). The mnemonic APGAR corresponds to Appearance, Pulse, Grimace, Activity, Respiration. Scores: 0-3 (severe asphyxia), 4-6 (moderate depression), 7-10 (normal). Note: Acrocyanosis (pink trunk, blue hands/feet) scores 1 for Appearance, which is common in normal neonates. For Juvenile Delinquency: cite JJ Act 2015 (16-18 heinous offence adult trial), Chicago 1909 origin, and Borstal school reformatory purpose.

subsections.title: School Health Services
subsections.content:
OVERVIEW OF THE CHAPTER

School health services constitute a highly strategic and cost-effective investment in community health, capitalizing on the formative educational years to cultivate enduring health practices and detect latent childhood morbidities. The school provides a controlled micro-environment where preventive surveillance, nutritional supplementation, environmental hygiene, and early clinical referral converge. The schoolteacher acts as the critical frontline observer linking students, parents, and healthcare personnel.

[SN]School Health Services[/SN]

[LAQ]School health services: objectives, components, and school environment[/LAQ]

SCHOOL HEALTH SERVICES
- **Historical origin:** School health services were initiated in India in 1909 in Baroda city.
- **Systematic national expansion:** A systematic nationwide program was established in 1960 following national expert recommendations.
- **Primary frontline observer:** The school teacher serves as the most important functionary for observing day-to-day changes in child behavior and conducting morning inspections.
- **Scope of health focus:** Focuses on prevention and control of malnutrition, communicable infections, intestinal helminthiasis, skin infestations, sensory deficits (vision and hearing), and dental caries.

COMMON HEALTH PROBLEMS OF SCHOOL CHILDREN
1. **Dental conditions:** Dental caries and periodontal diseases (statistically the most prevalent health defect).
2. **Nutritional deficiencies:** Protein-energy malnutrition, iron deficiency anaemia, and iodine deficiency disorders (goitre).
3. **Infectious diseases and parasitic infestations:** Intestinal worm infestations, pediculosis, scabies, and impetigo.
4. **Sensory disorders:** Uncorrected refractive errors, trachoma, and chronic suppurative otitis media.
5. **Behavioral and emotional problems:** School phobia, scholastic backwardness, and adjustment problems.

OBJECTIVES OF SCHOOL HEALTH SERVICES
- **Promotion of positive health:** Fostering optimal physical, mental, and social potential in the child.
- **Disease prevention:** Protecting children against vaccine-preventable infections and environmental risks.
- **Early diagnosis and treatment:** Detecting physical, sensory, or mental defects early and establishing prompt treatment.
- **Health consciousness:** Inculcating positive health attitudes, personal hygiene, and lifelong health-promoting habits.
- **Provision of a healthful environment:** Ensuring an aesthetically pleasing, physically safe, and sanitary school micro-environment.

SCHOOL HEALTH EXAMINATION RECOMMENDATIONS

1. Renuka Ray School Health Committee (1961)
- **Policy foundation:** Laid the foundational policy framework for school health services in India.
- **Examination frequency:** Recommended a thorough medical examination of every child at the time of school entry, followed by re-examination every 4 years.

2. National Health Mission Guidelines
- **Screening frequency:** Recommends periodic comprehensive health screening of school children once every 6 months, executed via mobile health teams under the Rashtriya Bal Swasthya Karyakram (RBSK).

3. School Eye Screening Protocol
- **Target population:** Children enrolled in classes V to VIII (approximate age: 10 to 14 years).
- **Staffing ratio:** One trained schoolteacher designated to screen 150 students.
- **Referral threshold:** Visual acuity worse than 6/9 in either eye triggers prompt referral to the Primary Health Centre ophthalmic assistant for refraction.

COMPONENTS OF SCHOOL HEALTH SERVICES

1. Healthful School Environment
- **Location and acoustic zoning:** Centrally located with accessible approach roads, situated away from noisy thoroughfares, railway tracks, factories, cinemas, and markets; securely fenced.
- **Site acreage:** Minimum 5 acres for a primary school and 10 acres for a higher secondary school (providing adequate playing fields).
- **Structural construction:** Single-storied buildings are preferred for ease of evacuation and child safety.
- **Classroom specifications:** Maximum capacity of 40 students; minimum floor space allowance of 10 sq ft (~1 sq metre) per pupil.
- **Ergonomic seating:** Single desk-and-chair units recommended. "Minus-type" desks (where the vertical line from the front edge of the seat overlaps the edge of the desk) are recommended to maintain proper posture and prevent spinal deformities.
- **Ventilation and windows:** Combined door and window area must constitute at least 25 percent of the floor space, positioned on opposite walls to ensure cross-ventilation. High ventilators should comprise at least 2 percent of floor space.
- **Internal wall finish:** White-washed walls to maximize light diffusion.
- **Illumination:** Natural daylight illumination entering preferably from the student's left.
- **Potable water supply:** Adequate and continuous supply of safe, chlorinated drinking water.
- **Mid-day meal area:** Dedicated, hygienic dining room for storing and consuming meals.
- **Sanitary facilities:** Separate, private sanitary conveniences for boys and girls. Standards: 1 urinal per 60 students; 1 latrine per 100 students.

2. Health Appraisal
- **Periodic medical examinations:** Comprehensive physician-led examinations to detect refractive errors, cardiac murmurs, anaemia, and orthopedic defects.
- **Daily morning inspection:** Teacher-led rapid inspection checking cleanliness of skin, hair, nails, and teeth, and observing for early signs of contagious disease (rash, conjunctival erythema, coryza).

3. Nutritional Services
- **PM POSHAN (Mid-Day Meal Scheme):** Provides hot cooked meals fulfilling one-third of daily caloric requirements and half of daily protein requirements.
- **School nutrition gardens:** Establishment of vegetable and fruit gardens within school grounds to promote dietary diversification.

4. First Aid and Emergency Care
- **Teacher emergency readiness:** Structured training of teachers to administer immediate first aid for lacerations, fractures, epistaxis, seizures, and foreign body choking.

5. Dental Health Services
- **Preventive oral surveillance:** Annual dental screening to detect dental caries, plaque accumulation, and malocclusion, supplemented by oral hygiene instruction.

6. Eye Health Services
- **Sensory defect screening:** Systematic screening for refractive errors, color blindness, and trachoma.
- **Nutritional blindness prevention:** Identification of Bitot's spots and administration of prophylactic Vitamin A.

7. Personal Hygiene Instruction
- **Health education curriculum:** Cultivating daily personal habits including handwashing with soap before meals, oral hygiene, nail trimming, and environmental sanitation.

> **EXAM TIP:** School health services blueprint: Historical origin (Baroda 1909, Renuka Ray Committee 1961) → Common health defects (dental caries most prevalent) → Environmental norms table (classroom 10 sq ft/child, 40 pupils, minus-type desk, windows 25% floor space, 1 urinal/60, 1 latrine/100) → Core services (Health appraisal + Daily teacher inspection + PM POSHAN + Eye screening acuity cutoff <6/9).

subsections.title: Geriatrics and Health Care of the Elderly
subsections.content:
OVERVIEW OF THE CHAPTER

Demographic ageing represents an inevitable consequence of the epidemiological transition, driven by sustained declines in fertility and increasing life expectancy. In India, persons aged 60 years and above represent an expanding demographic segment characterized by chronic multi-morbidity, physical functional decline, and biosocial vulnerabilities. Preventive geriatrics addresses this expanding burden through health promotion, screening for the classical 'geriatric giants', and establishing continuum of care via the National Programme for Health Care of the Elderly (NPHCE).

DEFINITIONS
- **Gerontology:** The scientific multidisciplinary study of the biological, physical, sociological, and psychological processes associated with ageing.
- **Clinical Gerontology (Geriatrics):** The branch of clinical medicine concerned with the diagnosis, treatment, and preventive care of elderly individuals.
- **Social Gerontology:** The specialized subfield of gerontology addressing social structures, retirement, family relationships, community attitudes, and policies impacting older populations.
- **Experimental Gerontology:** Biological research investigating cellular senescence, biochemical changes, genetic regulation, and pathology of the ageing organism.
- **Geriatric Gynaecology:** Clinical subspecialty addressing postmenopausal gynaecological disorders in elderly women, including pelvic organ prolapse, atrophic vaginitis, and ovarian and endometrial malignancies.

DEMOGRAPHICS OF AGEING
- **Demographic definition in India:** Persons aged 60 completed years and above are classified as elderly.
- **Global demographic patterns:** Italy and Japan demonstrate the highest proportions of older persons globally.
- **Indian demographic transition:** Elderly individuals constitute approximately 8.6 to 10.1 percent of India's population; however, due to overall population size, India is home to over 140 million older citizens, presenting substantial chronic care requirements.

HEALTH PROBLEMS OF THE AGED

1. Physiological Consequences of Senescence
- **Sensory impairment:** Senile cataract (leading cause of visual impairment), open-angle glaucoma, presbyopia, and presbycusis (sensorineural deafness).
- **Musculoskeletal changes:** Generalized sarcopenia, progressive osteoporosis predisposing to fractures, and reduced joint flexibility.
- **Cardiovascular and respiratory changes:** Decreased vascular compliance, diminished cardiac reserve, and senile emphysema.
- **Failure of homeostatic reserves:** Blunted thermoregulation, diminished thirst reflex, and altered drug clearance.

2. Chronic Degenerative Pathologies
- **Cardiovascular diseases:** Systemic atherosclerosis, hypertension, ischemic heart disease, and heart failure.
- **Orthopedic trauma and osteoarticular disorders:** Osteoarthritis of weight-bearing joints, cervical and lumbar spondylosis, and fracture neck of femur following low-energy falls.
- **Metabolic and endocrine disorders:** Type 2 diabetes mellitus, metabolic syndrome, and thyroid dysfunction.
- **Chronic respiratory diseases:** Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and bronchial asthma.
- **Oncological conditions:** Benign prostatic hyperplasia, prostate carcinoma, colorectal malignancies, and breast carcinoma.

3. Psychosocial and Cognitive Disorders
- **Cognitive decline:** Age-associated memory impairment, vascular dementia, and Alzheimer's disease.
- **Affective disorders:** Late-life depression, anxiety, hypochondriasis, loneliness, and emotional despondency.
- **Social maladjustment:** Loss of spouse, bereavement, social isolation, loss of earning power, and vulnerability to elder abuse or neglect.

COMMON MORBIDITIES AND MORTALITY HIERARCHY
- **Frequency of common health complaints:** Visual impairment > Locomotive disorders > Neurological conditions > Cardiovascular disorders > Respiratory ailments.
- **Primary cause of disability:** Visual impairment (primarily unoperated senile cataract).
- **Primary cause of mortality:** Cardiovascular disorders represent the leading cause of death among persons aged 70 years and above.

LIFESTYLE INTERVENTIONS FOR HEALTHY AGEING
- **Dietary and nutritional modulation:** Reduction of saturated fats, free sugars, and refined salt; adequate intake of dietary fiber, micronutrients, calcium, and vitamin D.
- **Regular physical activity:** Moderate aerobic exercise, resistance training, and balance conditioning to prevent sarcopenia and preserve functional autonomy.
- **Body mass maintenance:** Prevention of obesity, reducing metabolic risk factors and joint strain.
- **Substance cessation:** Complete cessation of tobacco smoking and moderation of alcohol consumption.
- **Social connectedness:** Active community participation, intellectual pursuits, and intergenerational social networks to prevent psychological isolation.

SERVICES AND SOCIAL SECURITY FOR THE ELDERLY IN INDIA
- **National Policy on Older Persons (1999):** Provides a comprehensive national framework for financial security, healthcare, nutrition, shelter, and education for senior citizens.
- **National Council for Older Persons (NCOP):** Established to operationalize, coordinate, and review the National Policy.
- **National Social Assistance Programme (NSAP):** Central umbrella programme administering social pensions for destitute older citizens below the poverty line.
- **Indira Gandhi National Old Age Pension Scheme (IGNOAPS):** Component of NSAP for citizens below the poverty line aged 60 years and above. The Central Government provides ₹200 per month for individuals aged 60 to 79 years, and ₹500 per month for individuals aged 80 years and above, supplemented by variable state-specific top-up contributions.
- **Project OASIS (Old Age Social and Income Security):** National commission report outlining pension reforms and institutional savings mechanisms for unorganized-sector workers.
- **Voluntary sector initiatives (HelpAge India):** Premier non-governmental organization providing mobile medical units, cataract surgery, day-care centres, and community support programs.
- **Statutory and fiscal protections:** Concessions in railway and public transportation, dedicated counters in public hospitals, and enhanced income tax exemptions for senior and super-senior citizens.
- **Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act 2007:** Establishes a legal obligation for children and heirs to provide maintenance to elderly parents, supported by summary tribunals and criminal penalties for abandonment.

LEVELS OF PREVENTION IN GERIATRIC HEALTH

1. Primary Prevention
- **Habit modification:** Cessation of tobacco and alcohol consumption.
- **Physical conditioning:** Daily balance training, gait retraining, and physical therapy.
- **Environmental safety:** Modification of domestic hazards to prevent accidental falls.
- **Immunization in older adults:** Annual influenza vaccination, pneumococcal polysaccharide immunization, and decennial Td boosters.

2. Secondary Prevention (Early Screening)
- **Non-communicable disease screening:** Periodic blood pressure monitoring and fasting blood glucose evaluation.
- **Sensory defect screening:** Annual visual acuity testing and hearing assessments.
- **Cancer screening:** Mammography, cervical screening, fecal occult blood testing, and prostate examination.
- **Geriatric syndromes screening:** Comprehensive assessment for urinary incontinence, depressive symptoms, polypharmacy, and nutritional deficiency.

3. Tertiary Prevention (Disability Limitation and Rehabilitation)
- **Functional rehabilitation:** Occupational and physical therapy for stroke deficits, osteoarthritis, and fracture recovery.
- **Assistive mobility devices:** Provision of canes, walkers, wheelchairs, and hearing aids.
- **Caregiver support:** Respite care, caregiver counselling, and palliative care networks to maintain dignity.

[LAQ]National Programme for Health Care of the Elderly: challenges and district plan[/LAQ]

[SN]Geriatric policy in India[/SN]

[SN]Social welfare schemes for the elderly in India[/SN]

NATIONAL PROGRAMME FOR HEALTH CARE OF THE ELDERLY (NPHCE)

DEFINITION AND RATIONALE
The National Programme for Health Care of the Elderly (NPHCE) is an integrated national health initiative dedicated to providing accessible, comprehensive, and high-quality healthcare services to India's senior citizens (aged 60 years and above) across primary, secondary, and tertiary health tiers.

PROGRAMME SERVICE ARCHITECTURE
| Level of Care | Primary Facility | Dedicated Service Package |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Primary tier | Sub-centre / Ayushman Arogya Mandir & Primary Health Centre (PHC) | Domiciliary visits by frontline workers, screening for hypertension and diabetes, weekly geriatric clinics, and provision of assistive devices |
| Secondary tier | Community Health Centre (CHC) & District Hospital | Biweekly geriatric clinics, 10-bedded dedicated geriatric ward at District Hospital, specialized physiotherapy units, and diagnostic laboratories |
| Tertiary tier | Regional Geriatric Centres (RGCs) & National Centres of Ageing (NCAs) | Inpatient geriatric beds, post-graduate medical training (MD Geriatrics), advanced rehabilitative therapies, and clinical research |

CORE SERVICE COMPONENTS
- **Dedicated clinical facilities:** Earmarked outpatient queues, specialized weekly clinics, and dedicated inpatient beds.
- **Rehabilitative services:** Comprehensive physiotherapy and occupational therapy units.
- **Chronic disease management:** Assured supply of essential anti-hypertensive, anti-diabetic, and analgesics.
- **Workforce training:** Structured capacity building of medical officers, staff nurses, and community health workers in geriatric competencies.
- **Continuum of care:** Domiciliary health check-ups for bedridden elderly through ASHAs and ANMs.

THE "GERIATRIC GIANTS" (CLASSIC CLINICAL SYNDROMES)
1. **Immobility:** Severe restriction of movement resulting from stroke, osteoarthritis, or severe Parkinsonism.
2. **Instability:** Recurrent accidental falls resulting from loss of postural reflexes, visual deficits, or orthostatic hypotension.
3. **Incontinence:** Urinary and fecal incontinence leading to skin maceration, social withdrawal, and severe caregiver burden.
4. **Intellectual impairment:** Dementia and acute delirium resulting in progressive loss of personal autonomy.

SYSTEMIC CHALLENGES IN DISTRICT GERIATRIC HEALTHCARE DELIVERY
- **Specialized human resource shortages:** Acute scarcity of trained geriatricians, physiotherapists, and geriatric nurses.
- **Multi-morbidity and polypharmacy:** Concurrent chronic conditions leading to complex drug-drug interactions and adverse drug reactions.
- **Inadequate long-term care infrastructure:** Absence of institutional day-care centres, respite care facilities, and home-based palliative care.
- **Physical accessibility barriers:** Public healthcare buildings lacking ramps, elevators, grab-rails, and disabled-friendly toilets.
- **Economic distress:** High out-of-pocket expenditure for diagnostic tests, assistive hearing aids, and chronic medications.

SEVEN-POINT DISTRICT IMPLEMENTATION PLAN
1. **Situational demographic mapping:** Enumerate the elderly population (aged 60+), estimate multi-morbidity burden, and map primary and secondary health infrastructure.
2. **Dedicated clinical service delivery:** Operationalize weekly geriatric clinics and a 10-bedded geriatric ward with assigned physiotherapy sessions at the District Hospital.
3. **Community-based outreach:** Mobilize ASHAs and Multi-Purpose Workers for quarterly home-based assessments of bedridden and housebound elderly.
4. **Referral and counter-referral protocols:** Formalize transport pathways linking Primary Health Centres with the District Hospital and Regional Geriatric Centres.
5. **Programmatic convergence:** Integrate geriatric healthcare with IGNOAPS social pensions, National Blindness Control cataract surgeries, and Ayushman Arogya Mandir NCD packages.
6. **Infrastructure age-proofing:** Implement age-friendly retrofits including non-slip flooring, corridor handrails, ramps, and dedicated seating areas.
7. **Epidemiological surveillance:** Maintain a district geriatric registry to track outpatient footfall, cataract surgical volume, hypertension-diabetes control, and fall injuries.

[SN]Prevention of falls in elderly[/SN]

PREVENTION OF FALLS IN THE ELDERLY
- **Epidemiological importance:** Accidental falls represent the leading cause of accidental injury, fracture neck of femur, traumatic brain injury, chronic institutionalization, and loss of independence in older persons.
- **Intrinsic risk factors:** Age-related sarcopenia, gait ataxia, visual deterioration, orthostatic hypotension, vestibulocochlear impairment, cognitive deficits, and consumption of psychotropic or sedative medications.
- **Extrinsic environmental risk factors:** Inadequate illumination, slippery polished surfaces, loose floor rugs, lack of stair handrails, absence of bathroom grab-rails, and inappropriate footwear.
- **Three-tier prevention strategy:**
  - **Primary prevention:** Regular gait and balance retraining exercises (e.g., Tai Chi), domestic hazard modification, correction of visual refractive errors, and rationalization of sedative medications.
  - **Secondary prevention:** Routine annual screening for fall history in geriatric outpatient clinics, bone mineral density assessment, and pharmacotherapy for osteoporosis.
  - **Tertiary prevention:** Specialized post-fall orthopedic rehabilitation, gait re-education with mobility aids (walkers, canes), and home environmental adaptations to prevent recurrent trauma.

> **EXAM TIP:** Geriatric medicine blueprint: Definition (60+ years in India) → Health problems classification (senescence vs chronic disease vs psychosocial) → Geriatric Giants (Immobility, Instability, Incontinence, Intellectual impairment) → NPHCE multi-tier architecture (PHC, CHC, District Hospital 10-bed ward, Regional Geriatric Centre) → 7-point district plan. For short notes on falls: Intrinsic vs Extrinsic risk factors → Primary, Secondary, and Tertiary prevention.

subsections.title: National Programs and Schemes in Maternal and Child Health
subsections.content:
OVERVIEW OF THE CHAPTER

To combat high rates of preventable maternal, neonatal, and childhood mortality, the Government of India has established comprehensive vertical and integrated public health initiatives. Central national programs include the Integrated Child Development Services (ICDS), Integrated Management of Neonatal and Childhood Illness (IMNCI), Janani Suraksha Yojana (JSY), Janani Shishu Suraksha Karyakram (JSSK), Rashtriya Kishor Swasthya Karyakram (RKSK), and Rashtriya Bal Swasthya Karyakram (RBSK 2.0). These initiatives bridge facility-based clinical excellence with grassroots community participation.

INTEGRATED CHILD DEVELOPMENT SERVICES (ICDS) SCHEME
- **Nodal administrative agency:** Ministry of Women and Child Development (MWCD), Government of India.
- **Launch date and framework:** Launched on 2 October 1975; operates as a centrally sponsored flagship scheme.
- **Central operational locus:** The Anganwadi Centre (AWC) functions as the community hub for service delivery.
- **Primary frontline functionary:** The Anganwadi Worker (AWW), a resident honorary female voluntary worker, delivers frontline services.

ICDS PROJECT STRUCTURE
- **Administrative unit:** One Community Development Block constitutes one administrative ICDS project unit in rural areas.
- **Population coverage norms:**
  - **Rural / Urban projects:** Covers approximately 100,000 population.
  - **Tribal projects:** Covers approximately 35,000 population.

STAFFING HIERARCHY
- **Child Development Project Officer (CDPO):** Administrative head of one ICDS project block (1 CDPO per 100,000 population).
- **Supervisor (Mukhya Sevika):** Direct supervisor of Anganwadi Workers; 4 Supervisors per CDPO, each covering 25 Anganwadi centres (1 Supervisor per 25,000 population).
- **Anganwadi Worker (AWW):** Approximately 100 AWWs operate within a block project, each serving 800 to 1,000 population.

ANGANWADI CENTRE SPECIFICATIONS
- **Staffing norm:** One Anganwadi Worker and one Anganwadi Helper (Sahayika).
- **Population coverage standards:**
  - **Rural / Urban centre:** Covers 400 to 800 population.
  - **Tribal / Difficult terrain centre:** Covers 300 to 800 population.
  - **Mini-Anganwadi centre:** Covers 150 to 300 population.
  - **Anganwadi on demand:** Established for habitations with at least 40 children under six years lacking an Anganwadi centre.
- **Community platforms (Mahila Mandals):** Local women's collectives mobilized to support service delivery, maternal nutrition, and community ownership.

OBJECTIVES OF THE ICDS SCHEME
- **Nutritional and health advancement:** Improve the nutritional and health status of children aged 0 to 6 years.
- **Holistic child development:** Lay the foundation for proper psychological, physical, and cognitive development of the child.
- **Mortality and dropout reduction:** Reduce the incidence of child mortality, morbidity, malnutrition, and school dropout.
- **Inter-sectoral coordination:** Achieve effective coordination of policy and implementation among various departments to promote child development.
- **Maternal health enhancement:** Enhance maternal capability to care for the health and nutritional needs of the child through health education.

TARGET BENEFICIARIES
- **Young infants and toddlers:** Children under 3 years of age.
- **Pre-school children:** Children aged 3 to 6 years.
- **Adolescent girls:** Girls aged 10 to 19 years (special focus on out-of-school girls).
- **Reproductive-age women:** Women in the reproductive age group (15 to 49 years).
- **Expectant mothers:** Pregnant women throughout gestation.
- **Lactating mothers:** Nursing mothers for the first 6 months postpartum.

PACKAGE OF SIX SERVICES UNDER ICDS

1. Supplementary Nutrition
- **Annual feeding norm:** Supplementary nutrition is provided for at least 300 feeding days in a calendar year:
  - **Children (6 to 72 months):** 500 kcal of energy and 12 to 15 g of protein provided daily at the Anganwadi Centre (unit cost: ₹8.00).
  - **Severely malnourished children:** 800 kcal of energy and 20 to 25 g of protein provided daily as double rations (unit cost: ₹12.00).
  - **Pregnant and lactating mothers:** 600 kcal of energy and 18 to 20 g of protein provided daily as Take-Home Rations (THR; unit cost: ₹9.50).

2. Nutrition and Health Education (NHE)
- **Target audience and curriculum:** Delivered to women aged 15 to 49 years, particularly pregnant and nursing mothers, focusing on infant feeding, maternal diet, and hygiene.

3. Non-Formal Pre-School Education
- **Play-based early learning:** Provided to children aged 3 to 6 years at the Anganwadi Centre using indigenous, child-friendly play materials.

4. Universal Immunization
- **Universal vaccine delivery:** Frontline mobilization and coordination for child immunization and maternal Td vaccination, delivered jointly with ANMs.

5. Health Check-ups
- **Routine clinical surveillance:** Routine antenatal and postnatal care check-ups, monthly growth monitoring (weight-for-age plotting on MCP cards), and screening for childhood illnesses.

6. Referral Services
- **Secondary clinical referral:** Prompt referral of severely malnourished or critically ill children to Nutrition Rehabilitation Centres (NRCs), Community Health Centres, or District Hospitals.

SUBSIDIARY PROGRAMMES LINKED WITH ICDS
- **Kishori Shakti Yojana (KSY):** Empowering adolescent girls (11 to 18 years) through life skills, vocational training, and nutrition awareness.
- **Scheme for Adolescent Girls (SAG / SABLA):** Improving the nutrition and health status of out-of-school adolescent girls aged 11 to 14 years.
- **Pradhan Mantri Matru Vandana Yojana (PMMVY):** Direct conditional maternity benefit cash transfer of ₹5,000 in two installments to compensate for wage loss and promote institutional birth.
- **Poshan Abhiyaan (National Nutrition Mission):** Multi-ministerial convergence mission utilizing digital tracking (Poshan Tracker) to eliminate stunting, wasting, and anemia.

[SN]Integrated Management of Neonatal and Childhood Illness (IMNCI)[/SN]

[LAQ]IMNCI strategy and standard case management[/LAQ]

INTEGRATED MANAGEMENT OF NEONATAL AND CHILDHOOD ILLNESS (IMNCI)
- **Nodal ministry:** Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (MoHFW), Government of India.
- **Origin:** Indian adaptation of the WHO/UNICEF Integrated Management of Childhood Illness (IMCI) strategy.
- **Key adaptations in the Indian context:**
  - **Neonatal inclusion:** Inclusion of young neonates from birth through the first week of life (0 to 7 days).
  - **Sick young infant focus:** Special clinical emphasis on managing sick neonates and young infants (under 2 months of age).
  - **National protocol alignment:** Complete harmonization with national guidelines on malaria, anaemia, vitamin A prophylaxis, and the Universal Immunization Programme.
  - **Frontline workforce training:** Systematic skill-building across auxiliary nurse midwives, ASHAs, and Anganwadi workers.
- **Definition of young infant:** Under IMNCI, infants under 2 months of age are classified as Young Infants.
- **Three core strategic components:**
  1. **Clinical skills improvement:** Enhancing the diagnostic and case management competencies of healthcare staff.
  2. **Health systems strengthening:** Ensuring availability of essential pediatric medicines, vaccines, and referral mechanisms.
