Data thus collected are used in demography and public health practice. They may be qualitative (stillbirths, persons with peptic ulcer) or quantitative (birth weights, haemoglobin readings). Regular administrative machinery is necessary to record the events.

DATA AND VARIABLES

A variable is any character, characteristic, or quality that varies.

[SN]Qualitative and quantitative data[/SN]

[SN]Scales of measurement[/SN]

Classification based on nature of data

Do not treat qualitative as a synonym of discrete, or quantitative as a synonym of continuous. Those are two different splits.

1. Qualitative (categorical) data
- There is no notion of magnitude or size of the characteristic because it cannot be measured on a metric scale.
- Persons with the same attribute are counted to form groups: attacked, escaped, died, cured, vaccinated, male, treated, on placebo.
- Only the frequency varies, not a measured size of the attribute. Survival remains the same; the number of survivors varies.
- Results are expressed as a ratio, proportion, percentage, or rate.
- Methods commonly employed: standard error of proportion and chi-square tests.
- Examples: sex, ABO blood group, treated versus not treated.

2. Quantitative (numerical) data
- The characteristic has a magnitude. It is counted or measured.
- There are two things that can vary: the value of the characteristic and the frequency of persons with that value.
- Methods commonly employed: mean, standard deviation, standard error of mean, t and Z tests, correlation and regression.
- Examples: serum cholesterol, weight, mid-upper arm circumference (MUAC), blood pressure, number of children.

Classification of quantitative data by how values occur
- Discrete quantitative: only isolated countable values (no meaningful in-between). Examples: parity, number of children, number of deaths in a year, platelet count.
- Continuous quantitative: any value in a range is possible (limited only by the measuring instrument). Examples: height, body temperature, haemoglobin, MUAC.

A count such as "number of children" is quantitative and discrete. It is not qualitative merely because it is a whole number.

Classification based on number of values
- Dichotomous (binary) variable: only 2 possible values. Examples: Rh group (positive or negative), sex (male or female), diabetes (present or absent).
- Polytomous variable: more than 2 possible values. Examples: ABO blood group; Body Mass Index (BMI) groups (underweight, normal, overweight, obese); anaemia grades. Raw MUAC or raw BMI in centimetres or kg/m² are continuous measurements, not polytomous labels, until they are cut into classes.

Classification based on dependency in a study
- Independent variable: the factor that is changed or used to predict. Example: the liquid used to water plants; dose of a drug.
- Dependent variable: the change that happens due to the independent variable. Example: height of the plants; fall in blood pressure.
- Controlled variable: a factor held unchanged. Example: the type of plant used.

SCALES OF MEASUREMENT (I.R.O.N. SCALE)

A useful exam mnemonic: Interval, Ratio, Ordinal, Nominal.

Categorical scales (qualitative variables)

1. Nominal scale: based on names. No sequence or specific order.
   - Examples: Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) status (positive or negative), race, blood groups, types of hospitals, sex.
   - Appropriate average: mode. Appropriate test family: chi-square.

2. Ordinal scale: a sequence or specific order is present. Used for grading into categories.
   - Examples: severity of anaemia (mild, moderate, severe); hypertension grades; social class; Child-Pugh score categories A, B, C.
   - Likert scale: a bipolar ordinal scale used to quantify attitudes (strongly agree to strongly disagree), usually 3, 5, or 7 points.
   - Appropriate average: median (or mode). Tests: rank-based (Wilcoxon, Mann–Whitney, Kruskal–Wallis).

Dimensional (metric) scales (quantitative variables)

Mean and standard deviation can be worked out only on an interval or ratio scale.

1. Interval scale: equal intervals, but absolute zero is absent. There is no true starting point.
   - Example: temperature in Celsius or Fahrenheit. 20 °C is not "twice as hot" as 10 °C.
   - Appropriate average for symmetric data: mean.

2. Ratio scale: equal intervals and an absolute zero is present. There is a true starting point.
   - Examples: temperature in Kelvin, weight, height, age, MUAC, blood pressure, pulse rate.
   - Ratios are meaningful: 80 kg is twice 40 kg.

**Mnemonic:** IRON
- I: Interval (no true zero)
- R: Ratio (true zero)
- O: Ordinal (ordered categories)
- N: Nominal (named categories)

> **EXAM TIP:** Define the scale, give two examples, then state which average and which test family fit. Draw a 4-row table (scale | example | zero | average). Do not confuse ordinal grades with interval measurements.

KEY POINTS

- Biostatistics is statistics applied to biological and medical data (quantitative medicine).
- Health, medical, and vital statistics overlap; they are not exclusive labels.
- A parameter describes a population (Greek). A statistic describes a sample (Roman).
- Data come from experiments, surveys, and records.
- A datum is one fact. Statistics (plural) are many figures. Statistics (singular) is the science of those figures.
- Qualitative data are named categories. Quantitative data are numbers (discrete counts or continuous measurements).
- Nominal and ordinal are categorical. Interval and ratio are metric.
- Mean and SD belong to interval or ratio scales. Median belongs to ordinal or skewed metric data. Mode belongs to nominal data.

FORMULAS AND CALCULATIONS

Not the home of computational formulas. Remember only:
- Population mean μ versus sample mean x-bar
- Population SD σ versus sample SD s
- Complement of a proportion: q = 1 − p (or Q = 1 − P)

SOLVED EXERCISES

[EX]1. Discuss briefly the application and usefulness of methods in biostatistics in different disciplines of medicine, in a general way.[/EX]
[ANS]
**Definition.** Biostatistics is the application of statistical methods to data derived from biological sciences, especially medicine (quantitative medicine).

**Why it is useful.** Everything in medicine that is to be compared or judged (blood pressure, attack rate, drug effect) must be expressed in figures. Figures vary from person to person. Methods in biostatistics decide whether that variation is chance (biological) or due to a real factor.

**By discipline**
- **Anatomy and physiology:** define normality and its limits (pulse 72 per minute is a mean, not a single "normal" number); compare means of height or blood pressure between places or years; correlate height with weight.
- **Pharmacology:** decide whether a change after a drug is chance; compare two drugs or two doses; find relative potency of a new drug against a standard.
- **Clinical medicine:** compare cure, relief, or death rates in treated versus control groups; test association (smoking and cancer); decide which signs are characteristic of a syndrome.
- **Community medicine:** test sera and vaccines in the field; test a causative factor (iodized salt and goitre); evaluate a programme (pasteurization and typhoid morbidity; family planning and birth rate).

**As figures (vital and health statistics).** They tell leading causes of death and sickness, whether a disease is rising or falling, who is affected, the age-sex structure, and which programme should have priority. They are the eyes and ears of the health administrator.

**Close.** He who accepts statistics indiscriminately will be duped; he who distrusts them indiscriminately will remain ignorant. The student must both compute and interpret.
[/ANS]

[EX]2. Write short notes on: (iv) quantitative data; (v) qualitative data.[/EX]
[ANS]
**(v) Qualitative (categorical) data**
- No notion of metric magnitude; the attribute is named, not measured.
- Persons sharing an attribute form a class: attacked, died, vaccinated, blood group A.
- Only the frequency varies. Results are a ratio, proportion, percentage, or rate.
- Typical tools: standard error of proportion, chi-square test.
- Examples: sex, ABO group, treated versus not treated.

**(iv) Quantitative (numerical) data**
- The characteristic has magnitude. It is counted (discrete) or measured (continuous).
- Discrete examples: parity, number of children, number of attacks.
- Continuous examples: temperature, haemoglobin, birth weight, serum cholesterol.
- Typical tools: mean, standard deviation, standard error of the mean, t and Z tests, correlation.

**Contrast line.** Qualitative = named categories. Quantitative = numbers. Discrete versus continuous is a further split of quantitative data, not a synonym of qualitative versus quantitative.
[/ANS]

subsections.title: Presentation of Statistical Data
subsections.content:
OVERVIEW OF DATA PRESENTATION

Data collected and compiled from experimental work, records, and surveys must be accurate and complete. Sorting or classification of data into characteristic groups or classes is the first step before presentation. Presentation methods must be concise without losing details, arouse interest, be simple and meaningful, define the problem, and suggest solutions.

There are two main methods of presenting frequencies of a variable: tabulation and drawing (charts and diagrams).

[SN]Presentation of statistical data[/SN]

[LAQ]Tabulation and diagrams for qualitative and quantitative data[/LAQ]

TABULATION

Tables are devices for presenting data from a mass of statistical data.

Rules for a good table
- Number tables sequentially.
- Give each table a clear title (what, where, when).
- Headings of columns and rows must be extremely clear (height in cm, age in years).
- Present data according to size, chronologically, or alphabetically.
- Footnotes may explain excluded data or abbreviations.
- Units belong in the heading, not repeated in every cell.

Types of tabulation
- Simple tables: one characteristic, such as year of admission and number of postgraduate students.
- Frequency distribution table: data split into class intervals and frequencies.
  - Number of groups: ideally a maximum of about 20 and a minimum of 5 (ordinarily 6 to 16, depending on the detail needed).
  - Class intervals should be equal throughout the table.
  - State whether the interval is inclusive or exclusive (for example 60 to less than 61).
- Master table: one line per person; all subjective and objective information opposite identification data.

FREQUENCY, RELATIVE FREQUENCY, AND CUMULATIVE FREQUENCY

- Frequency (f): number of observations falling in a class.
- Relative frequency: f / n, often written as a percentage. Useful when two samples of different size are compared.
- Cumulative frequency: running total of frequencies from the lowest class upward (less-than type) or from the highest downward (more-than type). Needed to draw an ogive and to locate median, quartiles, and percentiles.

CHARTS AND DIAGRAMS FOR QUALITATIVE DATA

Bar chart / bar diagram
- Used to compare the magnitude of different frequencies in discrete or qualitative data.
- The most versatile of all statistical diagrams.
- Rectangular bars represent data. Bars may be vertical or horizontal.
- Bars are usually separated by spaces nearly equal to half the width of the bar.
- For visual comparison of magnitudes. Not used to show the relationship between two continuous variables (that is a scatter or a line of regression).
- Types:
  - Simple bar chart: one bar per category.
  - Multiple / compound bar chart: two or more bars grouped (males and females per year).
  - Component / proportional bar chart: each bar divided into parts; each part is a proportion. Write the percentage on top of the bar when asked.

Pie chart / sector diagram
- Discrete data of qualitative characters (blood groups, causes of mortality, types of leprosy).
- Frequencies shown in a circle. The angle of the sector is proportional to the frequency.
- Formula: angle (degrees) = (class frequency / total observations) × 360.
- Gives a comparative difference at a glance. Avoid when there are many tiny slices.

Pictogram / picture diagram
- Popular method to impress the frequency of events on the common person.
- Pictures or symbols represent counts (one human figure = 1,000 persons).

Statistical maps (spot map, shaded map, dot-density map)
- Geographical distribution of frequencies.
- Classic example: John Snow's cholera spot map.

CHARTS AND DIAGRAMS FOR QUANTITATIVE DATA

Histogram
- Used for continuous quantitative data.
- Pictorial diagram of a frequency distribution.
- Series of adjacent rectangles with **no spaces** between them.
- Class intervals on the horizontal axis (abscissa); frequencies on the vertical axis (ordinate).
- It is an **area** diagram: the area of each rectangle is proportional to the frequency. If class widths are unequal, height must be adjusted so that area still equals frequency.

Frequency polygon
- Area diagram of frequency distribution developed over a histogram.
- Join the midpoints of class intervals at the heights of the frequencies with straight lines.
- Close the polygon to the baseline at the midpoints of the empty classes on either side.

Frequency curve
- When the number of observations is very large and the group interval is reduced, the polygon loses its angulation and becomes a smooth frequency curve.

Line chart / line diagram
- A special frequency polygon drawn between a value (or frequency) and time.
- Shows the trend of an event over a period (rising, falling, or fluctuating).
- Best method to show the trend of incidence or a programme indicator with the passage of time.
- Does **not** replace a scatter diagram for the relationship between two measured variables.

Cumulative frequency diagram (ogive)
- Plot cumulative frequency against the upper (or lower) class boundary.
- The curve is always uprising for a less-than ogive.
- Helps in defining cut-off limits and locating percentiles, quartiles, and the median.
- The less-than ogive and the greater-than ogive intersect at the median.

Scatter diagram / dot diagram
- Relationship between two continuous variables.
- Vertical axis generally represents the dependent or outcome variable.
- A cluster around a straight line suggests a linear relationship. No cluster means no relationship.
- Indicates strong positive, weak positive, or negative correlation visually. It does not give the numerical coefficient r.

OTHER IMPORTANT PLOTS

Stem and leaf plot
- Frequency distribution in which stems are the tens place and leaves are the ones place. A stem of 1 and a leaf of 2 represents 12.

Tree diagram
- Possible outcomes of an event (used in probability and clinical decision paths).

Box and whisker plot (related to tiles)
- Tertile: 2 intercepts, 3 tiles.
- Quartile: 3 intercepts, 4 tiles. Represented by a box plot.
- The box contains the middle 50 percent of values (interquartile range). Each whisker covers 25 percent unless outliers are plotted separately.
- Components: minimum, lower quartile (Q1), median (Q2), upper quartile (Q3), maximum, interquartile range (IQR = Q3 − Q1).
- Pentile (4 intercepts), decile (9), centile / percentile (99 intercepts, 100 equal parts). Median is the 50th centile.
- Percentile location in an ordered series of n values: position of Px = (n + 1) × x / 100.

HOW TO CHOOSE A DIAGRAM

| Data / question | Diagram |
|---|---|
| Categories, counts | Simple or multiple bar |
| Parts of a whole (few classes) | Pie / sector, or component bar |
| Continuous frequency distribution | Histogram, then polygon or curve |
| Trend over years | Line diagram |
| Two measured variables | Scatter |
| Geography | Spot or shaded map |
| Lay audience | Pictogram |
| Median and spread, outliers | Box and whisker |

Bar versus histogram (classic viva)
- Bar: qualitative or discrete; gaps between bars; height = frequency.
- Histogram: continuous; no gaps; **area** = frequency.

Bar versus pie
- Both can show the same qualitative frequencies. A bar is better for comparing magnitudes. A pie is better for showing shares of a total. They serve a similar purpose only when the question is "parts of one whole."

> **EXAM TIP:** First say table, then diagram. Always match diagram to data type. Write the pie-angle formula if a sector diagram is asked. For histogram versus bar: continuous and no gaps versus categorical with gaps.

KEY POINTS

- Classify first, then tabulate, then draw.
- Equal class intervals; 6 to 16 groups is a practical range.
- Qualitative: bar, pie, pictogram, map.
- Quantitative: histogram, polygon, curve, line (time), ogive, scatter.
- Ogive locates median, quartiles, and percentiles.
- Histogram is an area diagram.

FORMULAS AND CALCULATIONS

- Pie angle (degrees) = (class frequency / n) × 360
- Relative frequency = f / n
- Cumulative frequency of class k = f1 + f2 + … + fk
- Position of percentile Px in ordered data = (n + 1) × x / 100

SOLVED EXERCISES

[EX]2. Write short notes on: (i) frequency distribution; (ii) relative frequency; (iii) cumulative frequency.[/EX]
[ANS]
**(i) Frequency distribution**
A table (or its graph) that shows how many observations fall in each class of a variable. After raw data are sorted, equal class intervals are chosen (commonly 6 to 16 groups) and tallies are converted to frequencies (f). It is the starting point for the mean of grouped data, the histogram, and the polygon.

**(ii) Relative frequency**
The class frequency divided by the total n, often as a percentage: (f / n) × 100. It lets two samples of different size be compared class by class.

**(iii) Cumulative frequency**
The running total of frequencies from the lowest class up (less-than type) or from the highest down (more-than type). Plotted against the class boundary it gives the ogive, from which median, quartiles, and any percentile are read.
[/ANS]

[EX]3. State which type of diagrams are used for presentation of: (i) quantitative data; (ii) qualitative data. Illustrate giving familiar examples.[/EX]
[ANS]
**(i) Quantitative (continuous) data**
Histogram (frequency of haemoglobin classes; no gaps). Frequency polygon or curve (same data, midpoints joined). Line diagram (year-wise incidence of measles). Ogive (cumulative heights of students). Scatter diagram (height versus weight). Box plot (quartiles of birth weight).

**(ii) Qualitative (discrete) data**
Simple or multiple bar (sex-wise admissions by year). Component or proportional bar (birth-order shares rural versus urban). Pie / sector diagram (types of leprosy among 240 patients). Pictogram (hospital beds). Spot or shaded map (cholera cases by street).

**Rule.** If you measured it on a scale, start with a histogram. If you counted a named category, start with a bar or a pie.
[/ANS]

[EX]4. The following data give creatinine (mg per 100 ml) in a 24-hour urine specimen for normal males. (i) Tabulate the data in appropriate class intervals using the tally-mark system. (ii) Present the data graphically as a histogram and a polygon.[/EX]
[ANS]
**Transcribed series (n = 84; range 1.08 to 2.34 mg/100 ml).** Convenient equal interval = 0.20 mg/100 ml, starting at 1.00.

**i. Frequency table**

| Class interval (mg/100 ml) | Tally idea | f |
|---|---|---|
| 1.00–1.19 | || | 2 |
| 1.20–1.39 | 13 marks | 13 |
| 1.40–1.59 | 32 marks | 32 |
| 1.60–1.79 | 21 marks | 21 |
| 1.80–1.99 | 12 marks | 12 |
| 2.00–2.19 | || | 2 |
| 2.20–2.39 | || | 2 |
| Total |  | 84 |

**ii. Graphs**
- Histogram: class intervals on X, frequency on Y, adjacent rectangles, **no gaps**. The 1.40–1.59 block is the tallest (modal class).
- Frequency polygon: plot the midpoint of each class at height f and join with straight lines. Close to the baseline at midpoints 0.90 and 2.50. The polygon peaks at midpoint 1.50.

**Comment.** The distribution is unimodal and slightly right-skewed (a thin tail toward 2.3).
[/ANS]

[EX]5. Illustrate the following sterilization data (Family Planning Programme, India, figures in thousands) by a bar chart. The book asks for a component bar and the percentage written on top of the bar.[/EX]
[ANS]
**How to draw**
- X-axis: years 1969–70 through 1981–82 (13 bars).
- Each year is one **component bar** of height = target (thousands).
- Shade the lower part = achieved; the remainder = shortfall (or draw achieved as the filled component).
- Write the given percent achieved on top of each bar (64.2, 51.2, 105.2, 54.8, 41.6, 67.7, 107.1, 192.2, 23.8, 37.4, 58.3, 70.9, 96.4).

**What the chart shows**
Achievement crossed the target in 1971–72, 1975–76, and especially 1976–77 (192.2 percent). It collapsed in 1977–78 (23.8 percent) and recovered slowly toward 1981–82 (96.4 percent). A component bar plus the printed percentage is the correct qualitative-time presentation; a line diagram of percent achieved is an acceptable extra for trend.
[/ANS]

[EX]6. Present the live-births by order of birth (India, rural and urban, 1972 and 1978) by a component or proportional bar chart.[/EX]
[ANS]
Draw **four proportional bars** of equal height 100 percent (rural 1972, rural 1978, urban 1972, urban 1978). Divide each bar into birth orders 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, and 6 or more using the printed percentages.

**Reading the figure**
- First-order shares rose (rural 19.85 to 23.45 percent; urban 21.60 to 25.65 percent).
- Sixth-or-more shares fell (rural 22.00 to 15.36 percent; urban 20.02 to 12.99 percent).
- Urban bars show a larger shift toward low order than rural bars.

This is the correct diagram: one whole (all live births) split into ordered qualitative parts, compared across place and year.
[/ANS]

[EX]7. Illustrate progress in medical termination of pregnancy in India by a line chart using the tabulated year-wise numbers.[/EX]
[ANS]
**Data (numbers of MTP).** 1972–73: 20,143; 1973–74: 41,212; 1974–75: 1,05,531; 1975–76: 2,14,205; 1976–77: 2,78,870; 1977–78: 2,47,049; 1978–79: 3,17,732; 1979–80: 3,60,832; 1980–81: 3,88,405; 1981–82: 4,26,451.

**Line chart.** Years on X, number of MTPs on Y. Plot each point and join. The line rises steeply from 1972–73 to 1976–77, dips in 1977–78, then climbs steadily to 1981–82.

**Conclusion.** A line diagram is the correct choice because the question is **trend over time**, not a frequency distribution (so not a histogram) and not parts of a whole (so not a pie).
[/ANS]

[EX]8. Prepare a linear diagram of serum oxytetracycline after intramuscular and intravenous injection and draw conclusions.[/EX]
[ANS]
Plot time (1, 2, 12, 18, 24 hours) on X and serum level (μg/ml) on Y. Two lines: intramuscular (0.2, 1.5, 0.9, 0.4, 0.1) and intravenous (5.91, 3.39, 0.493, 0.035, 0.0076).

**Conclusions**
- Intravenous injection gives a high peak at 1 hour (5.91) and then falls steeply; by 18–24 hours the level is almost nil.
- Intramuscular injection peaks later (2 hours, 1.5) at a much lower height but remains measurable longer than the intravenous tail.
- For a rapid high blood level, intravenous is superior. For a more sustained low level, intramuscular is superior. The linear (line) diagram is the right graph because both series are the same variable followed through time.
[/ANS]

[EX]9. Prepare a sector diagram for type of leprosy among 240 patients (tuberculoid 148, lepromatous 64, indeterminate 18, borderline 10).[/EX]
[ANS]
Angle = (frequency / 240) × 360.

| Type | n | Angle |
|---|---|---|
| Tuberculoid | 148 | 222.0° |
| Lepromatous | 64 | 96.0° |
| Indeterminate | 18 | 27.0° |
| Borderline | 10 | 15.0° |
| Total | 240 | 360° |

Draw a circle, mark the four sectors from a radius, and label each with type, number, and percent (61.7, 26.7, 7.5, 4.2 percent). Tuberculoid dominates the pie.
[/ANS]

[EX]10. State briefly, giving reasons, the diagrams you can draw for: (i) year-wise and sex-wise distribution of children less than 5 years per family in a large town; (ii) number of persons using different contraceptives (diaphragm, jelly, Nirodh, pills, Saheli, copper T) in the same town, as a proportional bar.[/EX]
[ANS]
**(i)** Qualitative (year) × qualitative (sex) counts: a **multiple (compound) bar diagram**, two bars (boys, girls) grouped under each year. A line diagram with two lines is acceptable if the emphasis is trend. Not a histogram (the count is not a continuous measurement). Not a single pie (two factors).

**(ii)** Several methods as parts of one total: **one proportional (component) bar** of height 100 percent, sliced by method; or a pie. The question itself asks for a proportional bar. A cluster of simple bars would compare magnitudes but would not show shares of the same whole as clearly.
[/ANS]

[EX]11. Comment: (i) Bar and pie diagrams serve the same purpose. (ii) Histogram and bar diagrams are not the same.[/EX]
[ANS]
**(i)** Partly true. Both display qualitative frequencies. A pie shows shares of one total; a bar compares magnitudes and can handle many categories, grouped years, or components. They are interchangeable only for a few parts of one whole. They are not the same tool for trends or for two-way classifications.

**(ii)** True. A bar has gaps and is for discrete or named classes; height = frequency. A histogram has **no gaps** and is for continuous data; **area** = frequency. Swapping them is a standard examination error.
[/ANS]

[EX]13. Stillbirth rates per 1,000 total births in 30 towns (1977): 27, 28, 40, 32, 30, 36, 25, 29, 30, 29, 26, 30, 20, 35, 32, 36, 37, 29, 29, 42, 32, 27, 35, 36, 29, 33, 27, 41, 49, 34. (i) Prepare a frequency table with classes 20–24, 25–29, …. (ii) Transform to a graph. Can the data be presented by line diagram, simple bar, or histogram?[/EX]
[ANS]
**i. Frequency table**

| Class | Tally | f |
|---|---|---|
| 20–24 | | | 1 |
| 25–29 | 12 marks | 12 |
| 30–34 | 8 marks | 8 |
| 35–39 | 5 marks | 5 |
| 40–44 | 3 marks | 3 |
| 45–49 | | | 1 |
| Total |  | 30 |

(Check: 1+12+8+5+3+1 = 30.)

**ii. Graph.** The proper graph is a **histogram** (continuous rate, equal intervals, no gaps), with a frequency polygon over the midpoints 22, 27, 32, 37, 42, 47.

**Which diagrams are allowed?**
- Histogram: yes (continuous grouped data).
- Simple bar: not preferred (would insert misleading gaps).
- Line diagram: no, because the X variable is a class of rates, not calendar time.
[/ANS]

[EX]26. (ii) Draw a histogram for the number of children born to 350 women (0: 171; 1: 82; 2: 50; 3: 25; 4: 13; 5: 7; 6: 2).[/EX]
[ANS]
Number of children is discrete but can be drawn as adjacent bars of width 1 (a histogram-like column chart with classes centred on 0, 1, 2, …). Height = number of women. The figure is sharply right-skewed: the 0-child column (171) dominates; the tail runs to 6 children (2 women). Label X as "number of children born" and Y as "number of women."
[/ANS]

subsections.title: Measures of Central Tendency and Measures of Dispersion
subsections.content:
OVERVIEW

After collection and presentation, quantitative data are summarized by answering three questions:
1. What is the average or central value?
2. How are the other values dispersed around this value?
3. What is the shape of the distribution: is it normal?

Normal is not the mean alone. It is the accepted range of variation on either side of the average. Normal blood pressure is not "the mean 120" but a range such as mean 120 ± 20, that is 100 to 140, with still some chance that higher or lower values are compatible with health.

[SN]Measures of central tendency[/SN]

[LAQ]Measures of central tendency and measures of dispersion[/LAQ]

MEASURES OF CENTRAL TENDENCY (AVERAGES)

An average is the one central value around which all other observations are dispersed. The **median** splits an ordered series so that half the observations lie above it and half below it. The mean does that only when the distribution is symmetric. An average helps:
- To see that most normal observations lie close to the centre, while a few too large or too small lie at the ends.
- To compare groups: mean incubation of cholera versus typhoid; mean daily attendance of two hospitals. After finding the difference, one reasons why.

There are three common measures of central position: mean, median, and mode.

MEAN (ARITHMETIC AVERAGE)

The sum of all observations divided by the number of observations. Denoted x-bar for a sample and μ for a population.

x-bar = ΣX / n

It uses every observation and is the average most used in further tests of significance. It is the measure most affected by extreme values.

Types of mean
- Arithmetic mean (AM): the ordinary average.
- Geometric mean (GM): useful for exponentially growing data and for data with extreme values (titres, some rates). GM = (X1 × X2 × … × Xn)^(1/n).
- Harmonic mean (HM): useful for rates and for data that are inverses (average speed). HM = n / Σ(1/Xi).

Ungrouped series
- Small numbers: add and divide by n.
- Large numbers: assume a working origin w (assumed mean). Let x = X − w. Then x-bar = w + (Σx / n).

Example (direct). Erythrocyte sedimentation rates of 7 subjects: 7, 5, 3, 4, 6, 4, 5.
ΣX = 34, n = 7, mean = 34 / 7 = 4.86.

Example (assumed mean). Incubation periods of 9 polio cases around w = 20: deviations sum to 0, so mean = 20 + 0 = 20 days.

Grouped series: weighted mean
When n is large, prepare a frequency table. The mean is a weighted mean (mean of means):

x-bar = Σ(f × Xg) / n

where Xg is the midpoint of the class and f is the class frequency. Do **not** average class means without weights.

Example. Average income of 10 lady doctors is Rs 40,000 and of 20 male doctors is Rs 60,000. The combined mean is not (40,000 + 60,000) / 2 = 50,000. It is (40,000 × 10 + 60,000 × 20) / 30 = 16,00,000 / 30 = Rs 53,333.

Working-unit shortcut for grouped data
1. Place 0 opposite a convenient central class (working origin w = that class midpoint).
2. Code other classes as −2, −1, 0, +1, +2, … in units of the class interval i.
3. Mean in working units = Σ(f x) / n.
4. Mean in real units: x-bar = w + [Σ(f x) / n] × i.

Never forget to multiply the coded mean by the class interval when i is not 1.

MEDIAN

The middle observation after the series is arranged in ascending or descending order.

- Odd n: the middle value. Serial number of the median = (n + 1) / 2.
- Even n: the mean of the two central values.

Median is preferred when one or more of the lowest or highest observations are wide apart (hospital stay, income, age at marriage in a skewed series). Mean of 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14, 32 is 12.3; median is 10. The value 32 distorts the mean.

Grouped series: locate the class that contains n/2, then interpolate:

Median = L + [(n/2 − cf) / f] × i

where L is the lower boundary of the median class, cf is the cumulative frequency before that class, f is the frequency of the median class, and i is the class width.

MODE

The most frequently occurring observation (the most fashionable value). Example: in tuberculin reactions 3, 5, 7, 7, 8, 8, 8, 10, 11, 12 the mode is 8 mm.

Mode is rarely used alone in medical statistics. A series may be bimodal (two peaks), which often means two dissimilar groups are mixed.

Empirical relation (moderately skewed unimodal data):

Mode ≈ 3 Median − 2 Mean

WHICH AVERAGE TO USE

| Scale / shape | Prefer |
|---|---|
| Nominal | Mode |
| Ordinal | Median |
| Metric, roughly symmetric | Mean (with SD) |
| Metric, skewed or open-ended | Median (with IQR) |
| Combining group averages | Weighted mean |

> **EXAM TIP:** Define average, then mean / median / mode with one worked mini-example each. Stress weighted mean for grouped data. Close with the scale table.

[SN]Measures of variability[/SN]

MEASURES OF DISPERSION (VARIABILITY)

An average without a measure of scatter is incomplete. Types of variability taught in medical statistics:
- Biological (normal) variability: pulse, blood pressure, height among healthy people.
- Real (pathological) variability: beyond biological limits, due to disease or an external factor.
- Experimental / observer / instrument variability: parallax, uncalibrated sphygmomanometer.
- Sampling variability: sample statistics differ from sample to sample (measured later as standard error).

1. RANGE
Highest minus lowest. Simple, but ignores all intermediate values and is unstable in small samples.

2. MEAN DEVIATION (AVERAGE DEVIATION)
Average of absolute deviations from the mean.

MD = Σ |X − mean| / n

3. VARIANCE
Mean of squared deviations.

Population: σ² = Σ(X − μ)² / N
Sample (unbiased): s² = Σ(X − x-bar)² / (n − 1)

The divisor n − 1 is Bessel's correction (degrees of freedom). Classic teaching sometimes uses n when n is large (greater than 30).

4. STANDARD DEVIATION (SD)
The root mean square deviation from the arithmetic mean. The principal measure of spread around the mean. Denoted σ (population) or s (sample).

s = √[ Σ(X − x-bar)² / (n − 1) ]

It uses every observation, unlike the range. It is the unit of distance on the baseline of the normal curve.

Assumed-mean computing formula (ungrouped):

s = √[ (Σx² − (Σx)² / n) / (n − 1) ]

where x = X − w.

Grouped:

s = i × √[ (Σf x² − (Σf x)² / n) / (n − 1) ]

5. COEFFICIENT OF VARIATION (CV)
Relative variation, so two series in different units or of different magnitude can be compared.

CV = (SD / mean) × 100 (percent)

Example. Systolic blood pressure: children mean 100, SD 8, CV = 8 percent. Adults mean 120, SD 12, CV = 10 percent. Adults are relatively more variable.

6. STANDARD ERROR (SE)
Not a measure of scatter **within** one sample. It measures how much a sample statistic (usually the mean) is expected to vary from sample to sample. Bridge to confidence intervals and tests.

SE of mean = SD / √n

SE of a proportion = √(pq / n)

Percentiles, quartiles, and the semi-interquartile range belong with location as well as spread. Q1, Q2 (median), Q3 divide the ordered series into four equal parts. Semi-interquartile range (SIQR) = (Q3 − Q1) / 2. IQR = Q3 − Q1 is less sensitive to extremes than the range.

> **EXAM TIP:** Define variability, then list range, MD, variance, SD, CV, and SE with one line each on **when** to use them. CV is the answer whenever units differ. SE is sampling variation, not biological spread.

KEY POINTS

- Mean uses all data and feeds significance tests. Median resists outliers. Mode is the commonest value.
- Grouped mean is always weighted. Multiply coded means by the class interval.
- SD is the working measure of dispersion. CV compares relative spread. SE judges the sample mean.
- Empirical: Mode ≈ 3 Median − 2 Mean.

FORMULAS AND CALCULATIONS

- x-bar = ΣX / n
- Grouped: x-bar = Σ f Xg / n = w + (Σ f x / n) × i
- Median (raw): middle of the ordered series
- Median (grouped): L + [(n/2 − cf) / f] × i
- Mode ≈ 3 Median − 2 Mean
- Range = Xmax − Xmin
- MD = Σ |X − mean| / n
- s² = Σ(X − x-bar)² / (n − 1)
- s = √s²
- CV = (s / x-bar) × 100
- SE(mean) = s / √n
- SIQR = (Q3 − Q1) / 2

SOLVED EXERCISES

[EX]12. Name and define the statistical measures of central tendency (centring constants) and of variability.[/EX]
[ANS]
**Central tendency (averages)**
- Mean: ΣX / n. Uses every value; distorted by extremes.
- Median: middle value of the ordered series. Robust to outliers.
- Mode: most frequent value. Little used alone in medical series.

**Variability (dispersion)**
- Range: highest − lowest.
- Mean deviation: mean of absolute deviations from the mean.
- Variance: mean of squared deviations.
- Standard deviation: square root of variance; the working measure of spread.
- Coefficient of variation: (SD / mean) × 100; compares series in different units.
- Standard error of the mean: SD / √n; sampling variation of the mean, not scatter inside one sample.
- Interquartile range / semi-interquartile range: based on Q3 − Q1; resistant to extremes.
[/ANS]

[EX]14. Calculate mean, median, and mode of the 30 stillbirth rates in Exercise 13.[/EX]
[ANS]
ΣX = 965, n = 30.
**Mean** = 965 / 30 = **32.17** per 1,000.

Ordered series: 20, 25, 26, 27, 27, 27, 28, 29, 29, 29, 29, 29, 30, 30, 30, 32, 32, 32, 33, 34, 35, 35, 36, 36, 36, 37, 40, 41, 42, 49.
**Median** (mean of 15th and 16th) = (30 + 32) / 2 = **31**.

**Mode** = **29** (occurs five times; the next values occur only three times).

(Matches the printed key: 32.167, 31, 29.)
[/ANS]

[EX]15. Determine the range, mean deviation, variance, standard deviation, and coefficient of variation of the data in Exercise 13.[/EX]
[ANS]
n = 30, mean = 32.167, Xmin = 20, Xmax = 49.

- **Range** = 49 − 20 = **29**
- **Mean deviation** = Σ|X − mean| / 30 = 136 / 30 = **4.53**
- **Sample variance** (divisor n − 1) = **34.70**
- **Sample SD** = √34.70 = **5.89**
- **CV** = (5.89 / 32.167) × 100 = **18.3 percent**

(Printed key: range 29, MD 4.5, Var 34.69, SD 5.89, CV 18.31 percent. The key uses n − 1 for variance.)
[/ANS]

[EX]16. (i) Sex ratio males:females = 1,000 : 933. Literacy 40 percent in males and 20 percent in females (1981). Calculate the general literacy rate. (ii) Birth rate 32 per 1,000 males and 28 per 1,000 females. Calculate the combined birth rate.[/EX]
[ANS]
These are **weighted means**. Take a notional 1,933 persons (1,000 males + 933 females).

**(i) General literacy rate**
Literates = 0.40 × 1,000 + 0.20 × 933 = 400 + 186.6 = 586.6
GLR = 586.6 / 1,933 × 100 = **30.35 percent**

**(ii) Combined birth rate**
Births per 1,933 people = 32 × 1 + 28 × 0.933 = 32 + 26.124 = 58.124
Combined rate = 58.124 / 1.933 = **30.07 per 1,000**

(Printed key: GLR 30.346; combined birth rate 30.06.)
[/ANS]

[EX]17. Calculate the mean number of living children per woman: x = 0,1,2,3,4,5 and f = 42, 49, 57, 40, 31, 22 (n = 241).[/EX]
[ANS]
The printed table omitted the zero class; the total n = 241 implies 42 women with no living child.

Σf x = 0×42 + 1×49 + 2×57 + 3×40 + 4×31 + 5×22 = 517
Mean = 517 / 241 = **2.145 children per woman**
[/ANS]

[EX]18. Calculate mean and standard deviation of protein content of local sorghum varieties: 9, 8, 8, 9, 8, 9, 10.[/EX]
[ANS]
n = 7, ΣX = 61, mean = **8.71**
Σ(X − mean)² = 3.429
Sample SD (n − 1) = √(3.429 / 6) = **0.76**

(Printed key: 8.71 and 0.760.)
[/ANS]

[EX]19. From the frequency table of Exercise 13, show that the mean from grouped data does not exactly agree with the mean from the raw 30 observations.[/EX]
[ANS]
Raw mean (Exercise 14) = 32.167.

Grouped mid-points 22, 27, 32, 37, 42, 47 with frequencies 1, 12, 8, 5, 3, 1:
Σf Xg = 22 + 324 + 256 + 185 + 126 + 47 = 960
Grouped mean = 960 / 30 = **32.00** (or 32.3 if an inclusive coding / different mid-point convention is used, as in the printed key).

**Reason.** Grouping replaces every value in a class by the mid-point. That approximation (and the assumption of even spread inside the class) shifts the mean slightly. Always state which mean you are quoting.
[/ANS]

[EX]20. Compare variability of systolic blood pressure: children 5–10 years, mean 100, SD 8; adults 30–40 years, mean 120, SD 12.[/EX]
[ANS]
Units are the same, but the means differ, so compare **coefficients of variation**.

- Children: CV = 8 / 100 × 100 = **8 percent**
- Adults: CV = 12 / 120 × 100 = **10 percent**

Adults are relatively more variable. Comparing the raw SDs (8 versus 12) alone would overstate the adult excess because the adult mean is higher.
[/ANS]

[EX]21. Define percentiles and discuss their applications. Compute Q1, Q2, Q3 and the semi-interquartile range for the height table (n = 200 students, classes 145.0–147.4 … 167.5–169.9 with frequencies 2, 4, 8, 18, 30, 40, 40, 28, 24, 6).[/EX]
[ANS]
**Definition.** Percentiles (centiles) are values that divide an ordered distribution into 100 equal parts. The 50th percentile is the median. Quartiles Q1, Q2, Q3 are the 25th, 50th, and 75th percentiles.

**Applications.** Locate a child on a growth chart; prepare a standard median weight card (ICDS-style grades as percent of the reference median); compare two samples (Harvard versus Indian ogives); find what percent of people exceed a given height.

**Computation (n = 200).** Cumulative frequencies: 2, 6, 14, 32, 62, 102, 142, 170, 194, 200.
Class width i = 2.5 cm.

- Q2 (100th value) lies in 157.5–159.9 (cf before = 62, f = 40):
  Q2 = 157.5 + [(100 − 62) / 40] × 2.5 = 157.5 + 2.375 = **159.88 cm**
- Q1 (50th value) lies in 155.0–157.4 (cf before = 32, f = 30):
  Q1 = 155.0 + [(50 − 32) / 30] × 2.5 = 155.0 + 1.50 = **156.50 cm**
- Q3 (150th value) lies in 160.0–162.4 (cf before = 102, f = 40):
  Q3 = 160.0 + [(150 − 102) / 40] × 2.5 = 160.0 + 3.00 = **163.00 cm** (printed key 163.2; a 0.2 cm shift appears if the class is treated as 160.0–162.5).
- SIQR = (Q3 − Q1) / 2 ≈ (163.2 − 156.5) / 2 = **3.35 cm**
[/ANS]

[EX]22. Write short notes on: (i) variability; (ii) biological variability; (iii) standard deviation; (iv) coefficient of variation.[/EX]
[ANS]
**(i) Variability:** scatter of observations around the centre. Types: biological, real (pathological), experimental (observer or instrument), and sampling.

**(ii) Biological variability:** the usual person-to-person spread in health (pulse 55–90, birth weight 1.8–4.5 kg). It defines the normal range as mean ± 2 SD, not a single number.

**(iii) Standard deviation:** root mean square deviation from the mean. Uses all observations. Unit of distance on the normal curve. Sample formula uses n − 1.

**(iv) Coefficient of variation:** (SD / mean) × 100. Dimensionless. The correct way to compare variability of systolic pressure in children versus adults, or of weight versus height.
[/ANS]

[EX]23. Serum cholesterol of 10 subjects: 240, 260, 290, 245, 255, 288, 272, 263, 277, 250. Calculate mean and SD with an assumed mean.[/EX]
[ANS]
Take w = 260. Deviations x = −20, 0, 30, −15, −5, 28, 12, 3, 17, −10.
Σx = 40, Σx² = 2,716, n = 10.
Mean = 260 + 40/10 = **264 mg/100 ml**
s = √[(2,716 − 40²/10) / 9] = √(2,556 / 9) = √284 = **16.85** (printed key 17.37 if divisor n is used: √271.6 = 16.48; the 17.37 figure matches √(Σ(X−264)² / 9) with arithmetic on the raw list = 17.37).

Using raw values: Σ(X − 264)² = 2,714, s = √(2714/9) = **17.37 mg/100 ml**.
[/ANS]

[EX]24. Mid-arm circumference (cm) of 25 boys aged 4 months: 14, 11, 11, 10, 12, 13, 10, 14, 11, 11, 10, 12, 12, 13, 13, 11, 14, 12, 12, 12, 13, 12, 12, 13, 12. Calculate mean, median, mode, and SD.[/EX]
[ANS]
n = 25, ΣX = 300, mean = **12.00 cm**
Ordered series: ten 12s sit in the middle, so **median = 12**. The value 12 occurs 9 times, more than any other, so **mode = 12**.
Σ(X − 12)² = 34, s = √(34/24) = **1.19 cm**

Mean = median = mode, so the sample is symmetric about 12 cm.
[/ANS]

[EX]25. Monthly operations in an oral surgery unit: 15, 18, 25, 40, 25, 18, 25, 21, 30, 33, 25. Find the range, mean, and SD.[/EX]
[ANS]
n = 11, min 15, max 40.
**Range** = 25
ΣX = 275, **mean** = 25
Σ(X − 25)² = 528, s = √(528/10) = **7.27**

(Printed key: range 25, mean 25, SD 7.266.)
[/ANS]

[EX]26. (i) Calculate the mean number of children born per woman from: 0 children, 171 women; 1, 82; 2, 50; 3, 25; 4, 13; 5, 7; 6, 2 (n = 350).[/EX]
[ANS]
Σf x = 0×171 + 82 + 100 + 75 + 52 + 35 + 12 = 356
Mean = 356 / 350 = **1.02 children per woman**
(Printed key 1.05; the difference is rounding or a slightly different zero-class count in the original table. With the frequencies as listed, 1.02 is exact.)
[/ANS]

[EX]27. Total serum proteins (g percent) of 31 subjects: 7.8, 7.2, 7.0, 6.8, 7.4, 7.2, 7.2, 7.4, 7.2, 6.6, 7.1, 7.3, 7.5, 7.4, 7.4, 7.2, 7.2, 6.6, 7.1, 7.3, 7.5, 7.4, 7.2, 7.2, 6.9, 5.8, 7.2, 7.3, 7.0, 7.3, 6.8. Determine range, mean, and SD.[/EX]
[ANS]
n = 31, min 5.8, max 7.8, **range = 2.0**
ΣX = 221.65, **mean = 7.15 g percent**
s ≈ **0.36 g percent** (printed key 0.359). The low value 5.8 is the only clear outlier; it widens the range more than the SD.
[/ANS]

[EX]28. Mean and coefficient of variation of weights (kg) of children 18–21 months: 8,5,10,10,9, 6,8,8,10,8, 6,8,10,10,7, 9,9,8,10,9, 10,5,9,8,9, 8,6,9,6,9.[/EX]
[ANS]
n = 30, ΣX = 247, mean = **8.23 kg**
Sample SD = **1.55 kg**
CV = 1.55 / 8.23 × 100 = **18.8 percent**

(Printed key: 8.23, 1.55, 18.83 percent.)
[/ANS]

subsections.title: Z-Score, Normal Distribution Curve, and Skewness
subsections.content:
OVERVIEW

Range, averages, and percentiles all describe a series, but they do not by themselves tell the **probability** that a new observation is usual. For that one needs the shape of the distribution around the mean, expressed in units of standard deviation (SD). The reference shape is the normal (Gaussian) distribution.

So much physiological variation exists that an isolated observation should not be labelled abnormal without referring it to mean and SD.

[SN]Normal distribution and normal curve[/SN]

[LAQ]Normal curve, standard normal deviate, and skewness[/LAQ]

NORMAL DISTRIBUTION (GAUSSIAN DISTRIBUTION)

When a large number of observations of a variable (height, blood pressure, pulse, birth weight) are taken at random and class intervals are kept small, it is seen that:
- Some observations lie above the mean and some below.
- Frequencies are greatest around the mean and decrease smoothly toward both extremes.
- Almost half the observations lie above and half below the mean, and the two sides are symmetrical.

A distribution of this shape is a normal or Gaussian distribution. It is a virtue of a large random sample.

Areas under a normal curve (memorize)

If the variable has mean μ and standard deviation σ:

| Interval | Area included | Outside |
|---|---|---|
| μ ± 1 σ | 68.27 percent (about two-thirds) | about 32 percent |
| μ ± 1.96 σ | 95 percent | 5 percent |
| μ ± 2 σ | 95.45 percent | 4.55 percent |
| μ ± 2.58 σ | 99 percent | 1 percent |
| μ ± 3 σ | 99.73 percent | 0.27 percent |

Thus six standard deviations (three on either side of the mean) cover almost the entire range. Values farther than 2 SD from the mean are uncommon (about 5 percent). Values farther than 3 SD are rare (about 0.3 percent) and may be unusual or pathological. "Normal" here means **usual**, not a clinical diagnosis.

Worked illustration. Heights of students, mean 160 cm, SD 5 cm.
- Mean ± 1 SD = 155 to 165 cm contains about 68 percent.
- Mean ± 2 SD = 150 to 170 cm contains about 95 percent.
- Mean ± 3 SD = 145 to 175 cm contains about 99.7 percent.
A height of 177 cm lies beyond mean + 3 SD; the chance that it belongs to this population is very small.

THE NORMAL CURVE

A histogram of a large normal sample with a small class interval becomes a smooth, symmetrical, bell-shaped (or "breast-shaped") curve.

Characteristics
1. Bell-shaped.
2. Bilaterally symmetrical.
3. Mean, median, and mode coincide at the centre.
4. The curve is asymptotic: the tails approach the baseline but never touch it.
5. Two points of inflection: the curve changes from convex to concave. A perpendicular from each inflection meets the baseline at a distance of **one SD** from the mean.
6. Total area under the curve = 1 (or 100 percent).

These properties belong to **every** normal curve of a variable X ~ N(μ, σ²). They do **not** mean that the mean is 0 and the SD is 1. That is true only after standardizing (see Z).

[SN]Z-score or standard normal deviate[/SN]

RELATIVE OR STANDARD NORMAL DEVIATE (Z)

Deviation from the mean, measured in units of SD, is the standard normal deviate Z.

Z = (X − μ) / σ

Z states how many SDs an observation is above or below the mean.
- Z = +1: X is one SD above the mean. About 84 percent of values lie below it; about 16 percent lie above it.
- Z = −1.5: only about 7 percent of values lie below X.
- Z = 0: X equals the mean.

The **standard normal** variable is Z ~ N(0, 1): mean 0, SD 1, variance 1. Areas for Z are read from the unit normal table (single tail).

Example 1. Mean birth weight 3.05 kg, SD 0.39 kg.
Normal limits at ±1.96 SD: 3.05 ± 1.96 × 0.39 = 2.29 to 3.81 kg.
- 4 kg is greater than 3.81, so it is unusual (outside 95 percent limits).
- 2.5 kg lies inside 2.29–3.81, so it is not labelled unusual on this rule.

Example 2. Menstrual cycle mean 28 days, SD 2 days.
Z for 30 days = (30 − 28) / 2 = +1. Table area beyond Z = 1 is 0.1587. About 16 percent of women have a cycle longer than 30 days.
Z for 22 days = (22 − 28) / 2 = −3. Area beyond is 0.0013 (0.13 percent).

Example 3. Pulse mean 72 / min, SD 3.5.
The central 50 percent of a normal curve lies between mean ± 0.6745 SD (often taught as 0.67 SD): 72 ± 2.3, that is about 69.7 to 74.3.

SKEWNESS (ASYMMETRY)

Not all biological series are symmetric. Duration of labour in a first child is typically skewed to the right (long right tail). Age at death is often bimodal (peaks in infancy and in old age), which suggests two dissimilar groups mixed in one population.

- No skew (symmetric): mean = median = mode.
- Positive (right) skew: long tail to the right. Mean is pulled toward the high values. Mean > median > mode.
- Negative (left) skew: long tail to the left. Mean < median < mode.

Pearson's measures
- First (mode) coefficient: (mean − mode) / SD
- Second (median) coefficient: 3 (mean − median) / SD

For skewed data, prefer the median and a non-parametric test rather than mean ± SD.

KURTOSIS

Kurtosis describes tailedness and peakedness relative to a normal curve.
- Mesokurtic: normal-like.
- Leptokurtic: heavier tails or sharper peak.
- Platykurtic: lighter tails or flatter peak.

Skewness is left-right asymmetry. Kurtosis is not skewness.

> **EXAM TIP:** Draw a labelled bell with 68 / 95 / 99.7. Write Z = (X − mean) / SD. State that mean 0 and SD 1 apply to the **standard** normal, not to every normal curve. Add one sentence on right versus left skew.

KEY POINTS

- Large random samples of many biological measurements follow a normal distribution.
- μ ± 1.96 σ covers 95 percent. μ ± 3 σ covers almost all.
- Z converts any normal X to the unit normal.
- Right skew: mean greater than median. Left skew: mean less than median.
- Bimodality suggests a mixed (heterogeneous) sample.

FORMULAS AND CALCULATIONS

- Z = (X − μ) / σ
- 95 percent usual limits ≈ μ ± 1.96 σ
- 99 percent usual limits ≈ μ ± 2.58 σ
- Pearson skewness (median form) = 3 (mean − median) / SD

SOLVED EXERCISES

[EX]29. Write short notes on: (i) normal distribution; (ii) normal curve.[/EX]
[ANS]
**(i) Normal distribution**
A large random sample of a continuous biological variable (height, pulse, birth weight), grouped in small class intervals, piles up around the mean and falls off symmetrically. About 68 percent of values lie within mean ± 1 SD, 95 percent within mean ± 1.96 SD, and 99.7 percent within mean ± 3 SD. Values beyond 2 SD are uncommon; beyond 3 SD are rare. This arithmetic description is the normal (Gaussian) distribution. It is the reference for Z, confidence limits, and many tests of significance.

**(ii) Normal curve**
The graph of that distribution is a smooth, bell-shaped, symmetrical curve. Mean, median, and mode coincide. Tails approach the baseline but never meet it. Points of inflection stand one SD from the mean on each side. Total area is 1. The **standard** normal curve is the special case with mean 0 and SD 1, obtained by Z = (X − μ) / σ. An ordinary height curve with mean 160 cm and SD 5 cm is still a normal curve; it is not "mean 0, SD 1" until it is standardized.

**Use.** The curve converts a raw measurement into a probability of being usual, which range and mean alone cannot do.
[/ANS]

subsections.title: Hypothesis Testing, P-Value, Errors, Power of a Test, and Confidence Intervals
subsections.content:
OVERVIEW

A sample mean or proportion is not the population value. Repeated samples from the same universe give slightly different statistics. That fluctuation is **sampling variation**. Tests of significance and confidence intervals exist to decide whether an observed difference is likely to be this chance variation, or is large enough to reject the idea of "no real difference."

[SN]Null hypothesis[/SN]

[SN]P-value[/SN]

[LAQ]Hypothesis testing, errors, power, and confidence intervals[/LAQ]

SAMPLING DISTRIBUTION AND STANDARD ERROR

The sampling distribution of the mean is the distribution of x-bar values obtained from many samples of size n drawn from the same population. If n is reasonably large, this sampling distribution is approximately normal even when the parent distribution is not perfectly normal (central limit idea as taught for large samples).

Standard error of the mean (SEM) measures the spread of sample means around the population mean:

SEM = SD / √n

It shrinks as n rises. It is **not** the same as SD (SD is spread of individual observations inside one sample).

Standard error of a proportion:

SE(p) = √(pq / n)

where p is the sample proportion and q = 1 − p (or 100 − p if p is a percent).

HYPOTHESIS TESTING

Hypothesis (H): an assumption about the status of a phenomenon.

Null hypothesis (H0)
The hypothesis of **no difference** (or no association) beyond chance. It is the working assumption the test tries to disprove.
- Research claim: the new treatment differs from (or is better than) the old.
- H0: there is no real difference between the two treatments; any observed difference is a chance finding.

Alternative hypothesis (H1 or Ha)
The hypothesis of a real difference. It may be two-sided (different in either direction) or one-sided when only one direction is scientifically plausible.

STEPS (exam scaffold)
1. State H0 and H1.
2. Choose the test and the significance level α (usually 0.05).
3. Compute the test statistic (Z, t, χ², F) and the p-value, or compare with a critical table value.
4. If p < α (or |statistic| exceeds the critical value), reject H0.
5. Interpret in words: statistically significant is not the same as clinically important, and is not causation.

P-VALUE

The p-value is the probability, **assuming H0 is true**, of obtaining a result as extreme as (or more extreme than) the one observed.

- p > 0.05: not significant at the 5 percent level. Do not reject H0.
- p < 0.05: significant at the 5 percent level. Reject H0.
- p = 0.01: a result this extreme would occur about 1 time in 100 if H0 were true.

Changing the confidence level changes the critical bar:
- Moving from a 95 percent to a 68 percent interval makes it easier to call a difference "significant."
- Moving from 95 percent to 99 percent makes it harder.

Never write "p proves the treatment works." Write "the difference is unlikely under H0 at the stated α."

STATISTICAL ERRORS

|  | H0 true in nature | H0 false in nature |
|---|---|---|
| Reject H0 | Type I error (α, false positive) | Correct (power) |
| Do not reject H0 | Correct | Type II error (β, false negative) |

Type I error (alpha error)
- H0 is true but is rejected.
- Mnemonic: NTR 1 (Null True, Rejected = Type I).
- Its maximum tolerated probability is the significance level α, usually 0.05.
- In medical studies a Type I error is often considered more serious than a Type II error (declaring a useless drug effective).
- Analogous to a false-positive error rate.

Type II error (beta error)
- H0 is false but is accepted (not rejected).
- Mnemonic: NFA 2 (Null False, Accepted = Type II).
- Analogous to a false-negative error.

There is no equation "1 = Alpha." The two identities to remember are:
- Probability of Type I error (when H0 is true) = α
- Power = 1 − β

POWER OF A TEST

Power is the probability of correctly rejecting a false null hypothesis. It is the ability of the test to detect a real difference.

Power = 1 − β

Power rises when:
- The true effect is larger.
- n is larger.
- The SD is smaller.
- α is larger (a more lenient bar; this increases Type I risk).

CONFIDENCE INTERVALS (CI)

A confidence interval is a range, calculated from the sample, that is likely to include the unknown population parameter at a stated confidence level (commonly 95 percent).

Large-sample CI for a mean:

CI = x-bar ± Z × SEM
SEM = SD / √n

| Confidence | Z (two-sided) | Everyday teaching |
|---|---|---|
| 68.27 percent | 1 | mean ± 1 SE |
| 95 percent | 1.96 | often taught as mean ± 2 SE |
| 99 percent | 2.58 | mean ± 2.58 SE |

Interpretation (classical)
If the study were repeated many times, about 95 percent of such intervals would contain the true population value. Do not say "there is a 95 percent probability that this particular interval contains the mean" in a frequentist exam answer; use the long-run wording.

Width of the CI shrinks when n rises or SD falls. A 95 percent CI for a difference that excludes 0 (or for a ratio that excludes 1) usually agrees with p < 0.05.

CI versus p
- p: evidence against H0.
- CI: range of plausible effect sizes; preferred for reporting magnitude.

Example structure
Mean body temperature 98.14 °F, SD 0.6, n = 25.
SEM = 0.6 / √25 = 0.12.
Approximate 95 percent limits: 98.14 ± 1.96 × 0.12 ≈ 97.90 to 98.38 °F.

LEVEL OF SIGNIFICANCE

The conventional 5 percent level (α = 0.05) means: we accept a 5 percent risk of rejecting a true H0. Other levels (1 percent, 0.1 percent) are used when a false positive would be especially costly.

> **EXAM TIP:** Define H0 as no difference. Then SEM formula, then p < 0.05 rule, then the 2 × 2 error table, then power = 1 − β, then CI = mean ± 1.96 SE. One line: SD is within-sample scatter; SE is from-sample-to-sample scatter.

KEY POINTS

- Sampling distribution of the mean has SE = SD / √n.
- H0 is the hypothesis of chance only.
- Type I = α = false positive. Type II = β = false negative. Power = 1 − β.
- 95 percent CI for a mean ≈ x-bar ± 1.96 SE.
- Statistical significance is not clinical importance.

FORMULAS AND CALCULATIONS

- SEM = SD / √n
- SE(p) = √(pq / n)
- Z (for a mean) = (x-bar − μ0) / SEM
- 95 percent CI (mean) = x-bar ± 1.96 × SEM
- 95 percent CI (proportion) = p ± 1.96 × SE(p)
- Power = 1 − β

SOLVED EXERCISES

[EX]30. Explain: (i) standard error of mean; (ii) confidence limits; (iii) null hypothesis; (iv) level of significance.[/EX]
[ANS]
**(i) Standard error of the mean.** SEM = SD / √n. It is the SD of the sampling distribution of the mean: how much x-bar is expected to bounce from sample to sample. It is not the SD of the raw observations.

**(ii) Confidence limits.** The two ends of a confidence interval. Large-sample 95 percent limits for a mean: x-bar ± 1.96 SEM (often taught as ± 2 SE). About 95 percent of such intervals from repeated samples would contain μ.

**(iii) Null hypothesis (H0).** The working assumption of no real difference (or no association) beyond chance. Tests try to reject it.

**(iv) Level of significance (α).** The pre-set risk of a Type I error, usually 0.05. If p < α, H0 is rejected.
[/ANS]

[EX]31. Calculate the standard error of the mean for the 30 stillbirth rates of Exercise 13.[/EX]
[ANS]
From Exercise 15, s = 5.89, n = 30.
SEM = 5.89 / √30 = 5.89 / 5.477 = **1.08** (printed key 1.1).

Interpretation: a sample mean of 32.2 from 30 towns would typically wander by about 1.1 stillbirths per 1,000 from the universe mean.
[/ANS]

[EX]32. A random sample of 900 children had mean fat-fold thickness at triceps 3.4 mm, SD 2.3 mm. Can it reasonably be regarded as a representative sample of a population whose mean thickness is 3.2 mm? Discuss estimation of a population mean from a sample.[/EX]
[ANS]
SEM = 2.3 / √900 = 2.3 / 30 = 0.0767
Z = (3.4 − 3.2) / 0.0767 = 2.61
|Z| = 2.61 > 1.96, p < 0.01.

**Conclusion.** The sample mean is significantly higher than 3.2 mm. It should **not** be regarded as a representative sample of that universe (printed key: No; Z = 2.61, p < 0.01).

**Estimation.** The sample mean estimates μ. A 95 percent CI is 3.4 ± 1.96 × 0.0767 = 3.25 to 3.55 mm, which excludes 3.2 and agrees with the test.
[/ANS]

[EX]33. Ten random weights (kg): 68, 63, 66, 69, 63, 67, 70, 70, 71, 71. Does this sample adequately represent a population of mean 66 kg?[/EX]
[ANS]
n = 10, ΣX = 678, mean = 67.8
s = 3.01 (sample)
SEM = 3.01 / √10 = 0.95
t = (67.8 − 66) / 0.95 = 1.89
df = 9; two-sided 5 percent critical t ≈ 2.262.
|t| = 1.89 < 2.262, p > 0.05.

**Yes.** 66 kg lies inside the sample's 95 percent interval (printed key: Yes; t = 1.89, SE = 0.95). The sample is compatible with a universe mean of 66 kg.
[/ANS]

[EX]34. Define standard error of the mean. Mean haemoglobin of the population is 14.3. Can a sample of 15 individuals with mean 13.5 and SD 1.5 come from that population?[/EX]
[ANS]
SEM = SD / √n, the sampling SD of the mean.

SEM = 1.5 / √15 = 0.387
t = (13.5 − 14.3) / 0.387 = −2.07
df = 14; 5 percent critical t ≈ 2.145.
|t| = 2.07 < 2.145, p > 0.05.

**Yes**, the sample can come from that population (printed key: Yes; t = 2.05, SE = 0.39, p > 0.05). The shortfall of 0.8 g/dL is still compatible with chance in a sample of 15.
[/ANS]

[EX]35. Universe mean attacks of common cold 4.5, SD 2.87. Sample of 20: 7,2,5,0,1, 5,5,6,7,6, 2,6,9,4,8, 8,6,7,9,3. (i) Mean, SD, and SE of the mean. (ii) Why SD and SE differ. (iii) 95 percent confidence limits of attacks in the universe; do all sample observations lie inside them?[/EX]
[ANS]
**(i)** n = 20, ΣX = 106, mean = **5.30**
s = **2.59**, SEM = 2.59 / √20 = **0.58**

**(ii)** SD is the scatter of the **20 individual counts** around 5.30. SE is the scatter expected of the **sample mean** if the study were repeated. SE is always smaller (SD / √n).

**(iii)** 95 percent CI for the universe mean: 5.30 ± 1.96 × 0.58 = **4.16 to 6.44** (printed key 4.08 and 6.52, using a slightly different s or t0.05,19 = 2.093: 5.30 ± 2.093 × 0.58 = 4.09 to 6.51).

Individual observations run from 0 to 9. They need **not** all lie inside the CI of the **mean**. The CI is for μ, not for every person. Several counts (0, 1, 8, 9) lie outside 4–6.5 and that is expected.
[/ANS]

subsections.title: Tests of Statistical Significance
subsections.content:
OVERVIEW OF STATISTICAL TESTS

Tests of statistical significance are mathematical devices used to obtain a p-value (or a test statistic to compare with a table) and to decide whether an observed difference or association is likely due to chance.

There are two families:
- Parametric tests: assume an approximate normal distribution (or a large n) and usually compare means on an interval or ratio scale.
- Non-parametric tests: fewer distributional assumptions; used for ranks, ordinal data, and categorical frequencies.

[SN]Test of significance[/SN]

[LAQ]Parametric and non-parametric tests[/LAQ]

[SN]t-test[/SN]

[SN]Chi-square test[/SN]

[LAQ]Analysis of Variance (ANOVA)[/LAQ]

WHICH TEST WHEN

| Question | Data | Typical test |
|---|---|---|
| One large sample mean versus a known μ | Quantitative, n large or σ known | Z test for a mean |
| One small sample mean versus a known μ | Quantitative, σ unknown | One-sample t |
| Two independent means | Quantitative, ~normal | Unpaired (Student) t; Z if both samples large |
| Two paired means (before/after, matched) | Quantitative | Paired t |
| Three or more independent means | Quantitative | One-way ANOVA (F), then post-hoc |
| One proportion versus a known P | Categorical | Z for a proportion |
| Two independent proportions | Categorical | SE(p1 − p2) / Z, or χ² |
| Association in a contingency table | Categorical | Chi-square (Fisher if cells tiny) |
| Two independent ordinal / skewed samples | Ranks | Mann–Whitney (Wilcoxon rank-sum) |
| Paired ordinal / skewed | Ranks | Wilcoxon signed-rank (or sign test) |
| Three or more independent ranks | Ranks | Kruskal–Wallis |

Z is a large-sample (or known-σ) form of a mean or proportion test. t is used when σ is estimated from a small or moderate sample. There is no magic wall at n = 30, but that figure is the conventional teaching cut for "large."

PARAMETRIC TESTS FOR MEANS

1. Standard error of the mean and Z
Z = (x-bar − μ0) / (s / √n)

Used when n is large. Compare |Z| with 1.96 (5 percent, two-sided) or 2.58 (1 percent).

2. Standard error of the difference between two means (large samples)

SE(x1 − x2) = √(s1²/n1 + s2²/n2)

Z = (x1 − x2) / SE(x1 − x2)

Example pattern. Boys n = 169, mean height 168 cm, SD 14. Girls n = 54, mean 153, SD 8.
SE = √(196/169 + 64/54) = √(1.160 + 1.185) ≈ 1.53
Z = 15 / 1.53 ≈ 9.8, p < 0.001. Height differs with sex.

3. Student's t-test (small samples, σ unknown)

t = (x-bar − μ0) / (s / √n)    with df = n − 1

Unpaired (independent) two-sample t, equal-variance form:

t = (x1 − x2) / [s_p × √(1/n1 + 1/n2)]

s_p² = [(n1 − 1)s1² + (n2 − 1)s2²] / (n1 + n2 − 2)

df = n1 + n2 − 2

Paired t (same subjects before and after, or matched pairs):

Work on the differences d.

t = d-bar / (s_d / √n)    df = n − 1

Use paired t when each subject is his or her own control (breathing capacity before and after tapping ascites; haemoglobin before and after vitamin B12). Use unpaired t when two separate groups are compared (normal versus malnourished chest circumference).

4. Analysis of variance (ANOVA, F test)
Compares means of **three or more** independent groups by splitting total variance into between-group and within-group parts.

F = MS_between / MS_within

H0: all group means are equal. A significant F says at least one mean differs; it does not say which pair. Then use a post-hoc test (Tukey or Bonferroni-adjusted comparisons).

Why not many t-tests? Each extra pairwise t inflates Type I error.

Assumptions: independent observations, approximate normality of residuals, similar variances. If badly violated, consider Kruskal–Wallis.

NON-PARAMETRIC AND CATEGORICAL TESTS

Selection map (nominal versus ordinal):

| Groups | Nominal / frequencies | Ordinal / ranks |
|---|---|---|
| 1 (paired 2×2) | McNemar | Wilcoxon signed-rank |
| 2 independent | Chi-square (or Fisher) | Mann–Whitney (Wilcoxon rank-sum) |
| 3 or more independent | Chi-square (r × c) | Kruskal–Wallis |

Other named tests
- Cronbach's alpha: internal consistency of a questionnaire.
- Kolmogorov–Smirnov: assess whether a sample matches a stated distribution (including normality).
- Dixon Q: a simple outlier screen.
- Log-rank / Cox: compare survival curves (Kaplan–Meier).
- Bland–Altman: agreement of a new measurement with a reference, not correlation.
- Fisher exact: 2×2 table with small expected counts.

CHI-SQUARE TEST

A test of significance for association (or for goodness of fit) with **qualitative** (categorical) data. It tells whether an association is present, not how strong it is (strength needs a coefficient such as Cramer's V, or an odds ratio).

χ² = Σ [(O − E)² / E]

Expected cell: E = (row total × column total) / grand total

Degrees of freedom for a contingency table: df = (r − 1)(c − 1). For 2×2, df = 1. Critical value at df = 1, p = 0.05 is **3.84**.

Yates' continuity correction (2×2, small n): subtract 0.5 from |O − E| before squaring. Use when any expected cell is small (classic teaching: less than 5). If expected counts are very small, prefer Fisher exact.

Goodness of fit: compare observed class frequencies with frequencies expected from a ratio (for example 1 : 8 : 16) or from an earlier study. df = k − 1 (minus extra estimated parameters if any).

Worked 2×2 (vaccines)
Vaccine A: attacked 22, not attacked 68, n = 90.
Vaccine B: attacked 14, not attacked 72, n = 86.
Totals: attacked 36, not attacked 140, N = 176.

H0: no difference in attack rates.

E(A, attacked) = 90 × 36 / 176 = 18.41
E(A, not) = 90 × 140 / 176 = 71.59
E(B, attacked) = 86 × 36 / 176 = 17.59
E(B, not) = 86 × 140 / 176 = 68.41

χ² = (22−18.41)²/18.41 + (68−71.59)²/71.59 + (14−17.59)²/17.59 + (72−68.41)²/68.41 ≈ 1.79

df = 1, 1.79 < 3.84. Do not reject H0. The data do not show that vaccine B is superior.

STANDARD ERROR OF A PROPORTION AND OF THE DIFFERENCE

SE(p) = √(pq / n)

95 percent limits for a single proportion: p ± 1.96 SE(p).

Example. 10 percent eosinophils in 200 white cells: p = 0.10, SE = √(0.10×0.90/200) = 0.0212.
95 percent limits: 0.10 ± 1.96×0.0212 = 0.058 to 0.142, that is 5.8 percent to 14.2 percent.

SE of the difference of two independent proportions:

SE(p1 − p2) = √[p1 q1 / n1 + p2 q2 / n2]

(Some texts use a pooled p under H0 of equal proportions.)

Z = (p1 − p2) / SE(p1 − p2)

The same 2×2 data can usually be tested by Z or by χ²; χ² with df = 1 equals Z².

SPECIAL NOTES

- Cronbach's alpha, Kolmogorov–Smirnov, Bland–Altman, and Cox models are one-line viva tools; they are not substitutes for t or χ² in ordinary theory answers.
- Always end a numerical answer with a **sentence**: "The difference is / is not statistically significant at the 5 percent level; H0 is rejected / not rejected."

**Mnemonic:** CQ, TQ
- C: Chi-square is for Qualitative data (proportions, categories).
- T: t-test is for Quantitative data (means).

> **EXAM TIP:** Draw the which-test table first. For a long answer on t: define, unpaired versus paired, formula, df, one medical example each. For χ²: formula, E, df, 3.84, Yates, one 2×2. Never list Kruskal–Wallis under nominal data.

KEY POINTS

- Z / t / ANOVA compare means. χ² compares frequencies.
- Paired t uses differences. Unpaired t uses two samples. ANOVA is for three or more means.
- Mann–Whitney and Kruskal–Wallis are rank analogues of unpaired t and ANOVA.
- χ² = Σ(O − E)² / E; 2×2 critical value 3.84 at 5 percent.
- SE(p1 − p2) tests two percentages.

FORMULAS AND CALCULATIONS

- Z = (x-bar − μ) / (s / √n)
- SE(x1 − x2) = √(s1²/n1 + s2²/n2)
- t_paired = d-bar / (s_d / √n)
- t_unpaired = (x1 − x2) / [s_p √(1/n1 + 1/n2)]
- F = MS_between / MS_within
- χ² = Σ(O − E)² / E
- E = (row total × column total) / N
- df = (r − 1)(c − 1)
- SE(p) = √(pq / n)
- SE(p1 − p2) = √(p1q1/n1 + p2q2/n2)

SOLVED EXERCISES

[EX]36. Determine if height differs with sex. Boys: n 169, mean 168 cm, SD 14. Girls: n 54, mean 153 cm, SD 8.[/EX]
[ANS]
H0: μB = μG.
SE = √(14²/169 + 8²/54) = √(1.160 + 1.185) = 1.53
Z = (168 − 153) / 1.53 = **9.8**, p < 0.001.
Reject H0. Mean height differs highly significantly with sex.
[/ANS]

[EX]37. Serum protein: males n 18, mean 7.21, SD 0.26; females n 7, mean 6.90, SD 1.28. Is the female mean lower?[/EX]
[ANS]
Pooled two-sample t (df = 18 + 7 − 2 = 23).
s_p² = [17 × 0.26² + 6 × 1.28²] / 23 = 0.477
s_p = 0.691
SE = 0.691 × √(1/18 + 1/7) = 0.308
t = (7.21 − 6.90) / 0.308 = **1.01** (or −1.01 if female minus male).
|t| = 1.01, p > 0.10.
The apparent female deficit is **not significant**. Do not conclude that serum protein is lower in females from these data.
[/ANS]

[EX]38. Mean difference in systolic pressure of 100 patients before and after treatment = 30 mmHg; SD of differences = 10. Was treatment effective?[/EX]
[ANS]
Paired design. SE(d) = 10 / √100 = 1
Z = 30 / 1 = **30**, p < 0.001.
Highly significant. The fall of 30 mmHg is not a chance finding; treatment was effective.
[/ANS]

[EX]39. Social class I: n 196, mean cholesterol 180, SD 42. Class V: n 144, mean 150, SD 48. Is the difference significant?[/EX]
[ANS]
SE = √(42²/196 + 48²/144) = √(9.00 + 16.00) = 5.00
Z = (180 − 150) / 5 = **6.0**, p < 0.001.
Yes. Class I has a significantly higher mean cholesterol than class V.
[/ANS]

[EX]42. Two infant groups at the 8th month: n 100, mean 6.9 kg, SD 1.10 versus n 169, mean 7.3 kg, SD 0.91. Are the means different?[/EX]
[ANS]
SE = √(1.10²/100 + 0.91²/169) = √(0.0121 + 0.00490) = 0.130
Z = (7.3 − 6.9) / 0.130 = **3.07**, p < 0.01.
Yes, mean weights differ significantly.
[/ANS]

[EX]43. Neonatal systolic pressure: normal n 54, mean 75, SD 6; asphyxia n 14, mean 69, SD 5. Is the difference significant?[/EX]
[ANS]
SE = √(36/54 + 25/14) = √(0.667 + 1.786) = 1.57
Z (or t) = (75 − 69) / 1.57 = **3.83**, p < 0.001.
Yes. Mean systolic pressure is significantly lower after neonatal asphyxia.
[/ANS]

[EX]44. Mean plasma K+ in 50 diseased men = 3.35 mEq/L, SD 0.50. Normal adult value 4.6. Do they have lower potassium?[/EX]
[ANS]
SEM = 0.50 / √50 = 0.0707
Z = (3.35 − 4.6) / 0.0707 = **−17.7**, p < 0.001.
Yes. The diseased men have significantly lower plasma potassium than the normal value.
[/ANS]

[EX]45. Define the t-test and give situations for unpaired and paired t.[/EX]
[ANS]
Student's t compares a sample mean (or a mean difference) with a hypothesized value when σ is unknown and n is small or moderate. t = (estimate − H0 value) / SE, with df = n − 1 (one sample or paired) or n1 + n2 − 2 (two samples).

**Unpaired (independent) t:** two separate groups (normal versus malnourished chest circumference; boys versus girls; drug versus control animals).

**Paired t:** two readings on the same (or matched) subjects (blood pressure before and after a drug; haemoglobin before and after vitamin B12; breathing capacity before and after relief of ascites). Analyse the differences.
[/ANS]

[EX]46. Chest circumference (cm) at 1 year. Normal: 42, 46, 50, 48, 50, 52, 41, 49, 51, 56. Malnourished: 38, 41, 36, 35, 30, 42, 31, 29, 31, 35. Test the difference.[/EX]
[ANS]
Normal mean 48.5, malnourished mean 34.8, difference 13.7.
Pooled SE = **2.03**, t = **6.73**, df = 18, p < 0.001.
Highly significant. Mean chest circumference is lower in the malnourished group.
[/ANS]

[EX]47. Uterine weights (mg) of 20 rats: 14, 18, 9, 18, 21, 22, 27, 26, 15, 19, 15, 19, 22, 21, 24, 30, 16, 20, 24, 32. Can the lot mean be 24 mg? t0.05,19 = 2.093.[/EX]
[ANS]
Mean = 20.6, s ≈ 5.59, SE = 1.25
t = (20.6 − 24) / 1.25 = **−2.72**
|t| = 2.72 > 2.093, p < 0.05.
**No.** The sample is not compatible with a universe mean of 24 mg.
[/ANS]

[EX]48. Maximum breathing capacity (L/min) in 7 patients with ascites, before versus after treatment. Could the change be attributed to treatment?[/EX]
[ANS]
Paired t on the seven differences. Printed result: **t = 4.18**, p < 0.01.
Yes. The rise in breathing capacity after reduction of ascites is significant and can be attributed to treatment.
[/ANS]

[EX]49. Cord clamping and blood volume as percent of body weight. Early (n 11): 13.8, 8.0, 8.4, 8.8, 9.6, 9.8, 8.2, 10.3, 8.5, 11.5, 8.2. Late (n 16): 10.4, 13.1, 11.4, 9.0, 11.9, 11.0, 16.2, 14.0, 8.2, 13.0, 8.8, 14.9, 12.2, 13.9, 13.4. Is there a relationship?[/EX]
[ANS]
Unpaired t. Printed result: **t = −3.06**, p < 0.01.
Yes. Late clamping is associated with a significantly higher blood volume (as percent of body weight) than early clamping.
[/ANS]

[EX]50. Additional hours of sleep on drugs A and B in 10 patients each. A: 0.7, 1.6, 0.2, 1.2, 0.1, 3.4, 3.7, 0.8, 0.0, 2.0. B: 1.9, 0.8, 1.1, 0.1, 0.1, 4.4, 5.5, 1.6, 4.6, 3.6. Compare.[/EX]
[ANS]
Unpaired t. SD of the difference scale 1.6, SE 0.50, **t = 1.99**, p > 0.05.
The extra sleep on B is **not** statistically significant at 5 percent. Do not declare B superior.
[/ANS]

[EX]51. Weight gain (g) on ration A versus B, 12 guinea-pigs each. A: 31,34,34,29,26,32,35,38,34,30,29,32. B: 26,24,28,29,30,29,32,26,35,29,32,28.[/EX]
[ANS]
**t = 2.34**, p < 0.05.
Significant. Mean gain is higher on ration A.
[/ANS]

[EX]52. Pigeon blood glucose after 55 °C for 1 hour versus control. Control: 200,186,176,184,170,172,170,163,176,173. Heat: 173,249,188,215,230,196,184,186,189,200.[/EX]
[ANS]
Unpaired t. **t = 2.95**, p < 0.01.
Significant. Blood glucose is higher in the heat-exposed group.
[/ANS]

[EX]53. Pigeon versus rabbit blood glucose (pigeons as in Q52 control list; rabbits: 145,125,100,112,127,139,151,140,159,132).[/EX]
[ANS]
**t = 6.72**, p < 0.001.
Significant. Pigeon glucose is higher than rabbit glucose (ether anaesthesia in rabbits is a caveat on interpretation, not on the arithmetic).
[/ANS]

[EX]54. Serum iron: 15 normal children, mean 148 μg percent, SD 44.03; 15 with infantile cirrhosis, mean 151, SD 49.04. Significant?[/EX]
[ANS]
**t = 0.17**, p > 0.10.
Not significant. The 3 μg percent difference is chance.
[/ANS]

[EX]55. Serum bilirubin: 15 normal, mean 1.05, SD 0.34; 15 cirrhosis, mean 4.99, SD 2.52. Significant?[/EX]
[ANS]
**t = 6.00**, p < 0.001.
Yes. Mean bilirubin is significantly higher in infantile cirrhosis.
[/ANS]

[EX]56. Maximum breathing capacity before versus after relief of ascites in 15 patients; calculated t = 1.82. Is the difference significant?[/EX]
[ANS]
df = 14, two-sided 5 percent critical t ≈ 2.145.
1.82 < 2.145, **p > 0.05**.
**No.** This t does not establish a significant change.
[/ANS]

[EX]57. Haemoglobin (g) in 6 patients before and after 3 months of vitamin B12: 12.2→13.0, 11.3→13.4, 14.7→16.0, 11.4→13.6, 11.5→14.0, 12.7→13.8. Real improvement?[/EX]
[ANS]
Paired t. **t = 5.93**, p < 0.01.
Yes. The rise in haemoglobin is highly significant.
[/ANS]

[EX]58. Explain null hypothesis and list tests that prove or disprove it. Then test a tranquillizer: anxiety scores before 22,18,17,19,22,12,14,11,19,7 and after 19,11,14,17,23,11,15,19,11,8.[/EX]
[ANS]
**H0** is the hypothesis of no real difference (or no association) beyond chance. Tests used to confront it: Z (large-sample means or proportions), unpaired and paired t, ANOVA (F), χ², Fisher exact, Mann–Whitney, Wilcoxon signed-rank, Kruskal–Wallis, log-rank.

**This trial.** Paired t on the 10 differences. **t = 0.90**, p > 0.05.
Not significant. These scores do not prove the tranquillizer effective.
[/ANS]

[EX]59. Systolic pressures of 6 hypertensives: 179,190,183,165,180,175; after one week of a drug: 175,180,187,150,170,180. Could the differences arise by chance?[/EX]
[ANS]
Paired t. **t = 1.5**, p > 0.10.
Yes, such differences could arise by chance. The fall is **not** significant.
[/ANS]

[EX]60. Serum digoxin (μg/ml) at 4 h versus 8 h in 9 men: (1.0,1.0), (1.3,1.3), (0.9,0.7), (1.0,1.0), (1.0,0.9), (0.9,0.8), (1.3,1.2), (1.1,1.0), (1.0,1.0). Significant?[/EX]
[ANS]
Paired t. **t = 3.0**, p < 0.05.
Yes. The fall from 4 hours to 8 hours is significant at the 5 percent level.
[/ANS]

[EX]61. Weight (kg) of 9 women before and after 3 months of an oral contraceptive: 48.0→49.2, 56.4→57.2, 52.0→56.0, 60.0→58.0, 54.0→56.0, 56.0→57.2, 48.0→47.2, 56.0→56.4, 52.0→52.8. Evidence of weight gain?[/EX]
[ANS]
Paired t. **t = 1.5**, p > 0.10.
No sufficient evidence of a real gain.
[/ANS]

[EX]62. Drug on group A (before/after, n 10) versus control group B (n 12). (i) Are A (before) and B from the same universe? (ii) Is the drug effective in A?[/EX]
[ANS]
**(i)** Unpaired t on A-before versus B: **t = 2.07**, p > 0.05. Compatible with one universe (borderline; do not reject H0 at 5 percent).
**(ii)** Paired t on A before versus after: **t = 5.58**, p < 0.001. The drug produces a highly significant fall in group A.
[/ANS]

[EX]63. Define standard error of a proportion. Eosinophils 10 percent in 200 white cells. What are the lowest and highest percentages expected on repeating the count?[/EX]
[ANS]
SE(p) = √(pq / n), the sampling SD of a sample proportion.

p = 0.10, n = 200, SE = √(0.09/200) = 0.0212
95 percent limits: 0.10 ± 1.96 × 0.0212 = **0.058 to 0.142**, that is **5.8 percent to 14.2 percent**.
[/ANS]

[EX]64. Oral contraceptive users n 40, hypertensive 8; other devices n 60, hypertensive 15. Same hypertension proportion?[/EX]
[ANS]
p1 = 8/40 = 0.20, p2 = 15/60 = 0.25
Z = 0.59, χ² (Yates) = 0.12, p > 0.10.
**Not significant.** Do not reject equal proportions.
[/ANS]

[EX]65. Untrained workers 36 injured of 120; trained 8 injured of 80. Justify the role of training.[/EX]
[ANS]
p1 = 0.30, p2 = 0.10, SE(p1−p2) = 0.059, **Z = 3.35**, p < 0.001.
Significant. Injury is lower among the trained; the data support a protective role of training.
[/ANS]

[EX]66. Define SE of the difference between two proportions. Caries in 234/1000 males and 266/1000 females. Significant?[/EX]
[ANS]
SE(p1−p2) = √(p1q1/n1 + p2q2/n2).

SE = 0.0194, Z = 1.65, χ² = 2.56, p > 0.05.
**Not significant.** The sex difference in caries may be chance.
[/ANS]

[EX]67. Protein-calorie malnutrition 15 percent of 400 children versus 5 percent of 300. Significant?[/EX]
[ANS]
SE = 0.023, Z = 4.23, χ² = 16.89, p < 0.001.
**Yes.** The two prevalence rates differ significantly.
[/ANS]

[EX]68. In 1,000 unprotected people, 8 percent died of smallpox. Of 250 then vaccinated, 12 died the next year. Justify the vaccinator's claim.[/EX]
[ANS]
First-year deaths among 1,000: 80. Next-year vaccinated 12/250 = 4.8 percent versus a naive 8 percent.
SE ≈ 0.020, Z = 2.15, but χ² = 2.55 (not < 0.05 on the χ² criterion in the key).
