The printed key is cautious: Z looks just significant, χ² does not. **Do not over-claim.** Historical smallpox mortality also falls with time and residual immunity; these figures alone are weak proof that vaccination caused the whole drop.
[/ANS]

[EX]69. Two villages of 5,000. Polio deaths: 20 unprotected versus 4 protected. Attributable to vaccination?[/EX]
[ANS]
SE = 0.000978, Z = 3.27, χ² = 9.40, p < 0.01.
Yes. The difference in death rates is statistically significant and supports a vaccine effect (assuming the villages were otherwise comparable).
[/ANS]

[EX]70. Define SE of a proportion. Pyorrhoea 10/100 who do not brush versus 2/100 who brush. Significant?[/EX]
[ANS]
SE(p) = √(pq/n).
SE(p1−p2) = 0.0335, Z = 2.38, χ² = 4.34, p < 0.05.
**Yes**, the difference is significant at 5 percent.
[/ANS]

[EX]71. Diabetes: rural 45/3,495; urban 107/3,516. Prevalence and significance.[/EX]
[ANS]
Rural prevalence = 45/3495 = **1.29 percent**. Urban = 107/3516 = **3.04 percent**.
SE = 0.00347, Z = 5.04, χ² = 25.47, p < 0.01.
Urban prevalence is significantly higher.
[/ANS]

[EX]72. (i) Define SE of the difference of two proportions and give uses. (ii) Drug A failed in 36/120, drug B in 16/80. SE(p1−p2) and inference.[/EX]
[ANS]
**(i)** SE(p1−p2) = √(p1q1/n1 + p2q2/n2). Used to compare two attack rates, two case-fatality rates, two coverage proportions, or two survey prevalences.

**(ii)** Failure rates 0.30 versus 0.20. SE = **0.0633**, Z = 1.58, χ² = 2.44, p > 0.05.
**Not significant.** Failure rates are compatible with chance.
[/ANS]

[EX]73. 270 male and 230 female births in one month. Significant departure from 50 : 50?[/EX]
[ANS]
χ² = (270−250)²/250 + (230−250)²/250 = **3.20**, df = 1, p > 0.05.
No. The sex split is compatible with equality.
[/ANS]

[EX]74. Filaria carriers: males 78/490, females 57/610. Association with sex?[/EX]
[ANS]
χ² = 11.08 (10.91 with Yates), df = 1, p < 0.01.
Yes. Carrier prevalence is associated with sex (higher in males here).
[/ANS]

[EX]75. Scabies versus socioeconomic status (I to V). With scabies 23,127,640,806,63; without 427,1573,7560,7526,541. Association?[/EX]
[ANS]
χ² = **30.90**, df = 4, p < 0.001.
Yes. Scabies is associated with socioeconomic status.
[/ANS]

[EX]76. New cavities after dental-hygiene instruction (n 50) versus none (n 50), classes 0–1 / 2–3 / 4–5: instructed 30,15,5; not instructed 20,15,15. Association at 5 percent?[/EX]
[ANS]
χ² = **7.0**, df = 2, p < 0.05.
Yes. Fewer high cavity counts in the instructed group; association is significant.
[/ANS]

[EX]77. Scabies by sex: males 1,173 / 11,584; females 547 / 8,191. Different prevalence?[/EX]
[ANS]
χ² = **71.40**, df = 1, p < 0.001.
Yes. Prevalence differs significantly by sex (higher in males in this table).
[/ANS]

[EX]78. Socioeconomic status of women versus duration of breastfeeding (months 1–6, 7–12, 12+). Association?[/EX]
[ANS]
χ² = **19.89**, df = 4, p < 0.001.
Yes. Duration of breastfeeding is associated with socioeconomic status.
[/ANS]

[EX]79. Mother's education versus belief that the child needs top feeds (yes/no). Association?[/EX]
[ANS]
χ² = **13.73**, df = 4, p < 0.001.
Yes. Belief about top feeds is associated with educational status.
[/ANS]

[EX]80. Literacy of mothers versus stillbirths. Association?[/EX]
[ANS]
χ² = **8.82**, df = 4, p > 0.05.
No significant association in this table.
[/ANS]

[EX]81. Mistakes on stimulant / tranquillizer / placebo (rows of 50; mistake classes 0–5, 6–10, 11–15). Different proportions?[/EX]
[ANS]
χ² = **27.25**, df = 4, p < 0.001.
Yes. The distribution of mistakes differs among the three medication groups (placebo has more low-mistake subjects).
[/ANS]

[EX]82. (i) Applications of a hypothesis test. (ii) 40 children: aa 2, ab 16, bb 22. Differ from 1 : 8 : 16?[/EX]
[ANS]
**(i)** Decide whether an observed mean, proportion, or association is compatible with H0; choose a treatment; evaluate a vaccine; test goodness of fit to a genetic ratio.

**(ii)** Expected 1:8:16 of 40 = 1.6, 12.8, 25.6.
χ² = **1.41**, df = 2, p > 0.05.
No. The phenotype counts fit 1 : 8 : 16.
[/ANS]

[EX]83. Trachoma and corneal degeneration, n 170. Trachoma+ degeneration+ 40; degeneration+ no trachoma 61; trachoma+ no degeneration 35; neither 34. Association?[/EX]
[ANS]
χ² = **2.05**, df = 1, p > 0.05.
No significant association.
[/ANS]

[EX]84. Corneal degeneration by age: 41–50 years 48/110; 51–60 30/52; over 60 23/38. Does age play a role?[/EX]
[ANS]
χ² = **4.68**, df = 2, p > 0.05.
No. Age is not significantly associated with degeneration in this OPD series.
[/ANS]

[EX]85. Bradycardia versus site of infarction: posterior 31/66, anterior 6/34. Predilection?[/EX]
[ANS]
Yates-corrected χ² = **7.07**, p < 0.05.
Yes. Bradycardia is associated with posterior infarction in this table.
[/ANS]

[EX]86. Parity versus nuclear / joint family (O and E given). Association?[/EX]
[ANS]
χ² = **31.13**, df = 5, p < 0.001.
Yes. Parity is associated with type of family (high parity more often nuclear in this table).
[/ANS]

[EX]87. Nutrition grades in 940 people: excellent 140, good 180, fair 260, poor 360. Differ from an earlier 1 : 2 : 3 : 4?[/EX]
[ANS]
Expected 1+2+3+4 = 10 parts of 940: 94, 188, 282, 376.
χ² = **120.43**, df = 3, p < 0.001.
Yes. The present proportions differ highly from 1 : 2 : 3 : 4 (many more "excellent" than that ratio predicts).
[/ANS]

[EX]88. Toxaemia in 30/480 primigravidae versus 12/310 others (790 mothers aged 30). Association with gravida?[/EX]
[ANS]
χ² = **2.11**, df = 1, p > 0.05.
No significant association between toxaemia and primigravida status here.
[/ANS]

[EX]89. Opinion on abortion versus duration of married life (O and E given). Association?[/EX]
[ANS]
χ² = **16.80**, df = 5, p < 0.005.
Yes. Positive opinion is associated with duration of married life.
[/ANS]

[EX]90. Cholera deaths: 72/1,200 on regimen A versus 45/945 on regimen B. Which is better?[/EX]
[ANS]
χ² = 1.57, Z = 1.26, p > 0.20.
**Neither is statistically better.** Case fatality 6.0 percent versus 4.8 percent is compatible with chance.
[/ANS]

[EX]91. Guinea-worm 175/2,500 before health education versus 192/3,250 after. What do the figures suggest?[/EX]
[ANS]
χ² = **2.64**, p > 0.05.
No significant fall. The education programme is not shown to have changed prevalence.
[/ANS]

[EX]92. Burns dressings: penicillin + neomycin, staphylococcal infection 5/33; penicillin alone 18/30. Conclusion?[/EX]
[ANS]
χ² = **13.64**, df = 1, p < 0.001.
Neomycin-containing dressings are associated with significantly fewer staphylococcal infections.
[/ANS]

[EX]93. Pertussis therapy: control 23 failures/55; streptomycin 28/66; chloramphenicol 17/40. Evidence of a difference?[/EX]
[ANS]
χ² = **0.36**, p > 0.05.
No. Failure rates are statistically indistinguishable.
[/ANS]

[EX]107. HIV versus number of sex partners (multiple 12/264, single 1/75). Association?[/EX]
[ANS]
χ² = **1.63**, df = 1, p > 0.05.
No significant association in this table (small HIV+ counts; Fisher exact would be mentioned in a viva).
[/ANS]

[EX]108. HIV versus history of STD (yes 1/24, no 13/421, not known 26/364, other 2/202). Association?[/EX]
[ANS]
χ² = **14.51**, df = 3, p < 0.01.
Yes. HIV positivity is associated with the recorded STD-history category (driven largely by the "not known" row).
[/ANS]

[EX]109. HIV versus type of sex partner (male 0/8, female 13/324, both 1/7). Association?[/EX]
[ANS]
χ² = **2.17**, df = 2, p > 0.05.
No significant association.
[/ANS]

subsections.title: Probability, Correlation, and Regression
subsections.content:
OVERVIEW

Probability is the language of chance. Correlation and regression describe how two quantitative variables move together, and how one may be predicted from the other.

[SN]Probability[/SN]

[LAQ]Laws of probability and binomial distribution[/LAQ]

PROBABILITY (CHANCE)

Probability is the relative frequency with which an event is expected to occur on average. It ranges from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain). It can never be negative and cannot exceed 1.

In equally likely cases: P(A) = number of favourable outcomes / number of possible outcomes.

LAWS OF PROBABILITY

1. Multiplication law (AND / BOTH)
Used when two or more events occur together and are **independent** (not associated).

P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B)

Mnemonic often taught: "AND / BOTH: multiply."

2. Addition law (EITHER / OR / ANY)
Used when events are **mutually exclusive** (one excludes the other).

P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B)

If events can occur together (not exclusive):

P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B)

Example. Gastric cancer prevalence 10 percent (0.10). Helicobacter pylori 40 percent (0.40) in the same population, treated as independent for the exercise.
- Cancer AND H. pylori: 0.10 × 0.40 = 0.04
- Cancer OR H. pylori (if exclusive in the exercise sense): 0.10 + 0.40 = 0.50
If they can coexist, the exclusive-or form overstates the union; subtract the joint probability.

CONDITIONAL PROBABILITY AND SCREENING

P(A | B) = P(A and B) / P(B)

Screening 2×2 (expand on first use in this section):

|  | Disease present | Disease absent |
|---|---|---|
| Test positive | True positive (TP) | False positive (FP) |
| Test negative | False negative (FN) | True negative (TN) |

- Sensitivity: P(positive | disease) = TP / (TP + FN)
- Specificity: P(negative | no disease) = TN / (TN + FP)
- Predictive value positive: P(disease | positive) = TP / (TP + FP)
- Predictive value negative: P(no disease | negative) = TN / (TN + FN)
- Accuracy: (TP + TN) / total

BINOMIAL PROBABILITY

When each independent trial has two outcomes (success with probability p, failure q = 1 − p), the number of successes X in n trials follows a binomial distribution:

P(X = r) = C(n, r) × p^r × q^(n−r)

where C(n, r) = n! / [r! (n−r)!]

Example. Prevalence of diabetes 1 in 10, so p = 0.1, q = 0.9. Four children (n = 4).
- All 4 normal: C(4,0) × 0.1^0 × 0.9^4 = 0.6561
- 1 diabetic, 3 normal: C(4,1) × 0.1 × 0.9^3 = 0.2916
- 2 and 2: C(4,2) × 0.1² × 0.9² = 0.0486
- 3 diabetic, 1 normal: C(4,3) × 0.1³ × 0.9 = 0.0036
- All 4 diabetic: 0.1^4 = 0.0001

ODDS AND POISSON

Odds = P / (1 − P). If P = 0.20, odds = 0.25 (1 to 4).

Poisson distribution: probability of a given number of events in a fixed time (or space) when events are rare and independent. Mean equals variance (λ).

[SN]Correlation and regression[/SN]

[LAQ]Correlation coefficient and regression[/LAQ]

CORRELATION

Correlation is the relationship between two quantitative (continuous) variables. It is pictured by a scatter diagram. The correlation coefficient measures **strength and direction**, not causation.

Pearson's product-moment coefficient (r)
- Used for ungrouped, approximately normal, linearly related pairs.
- Range: −1 to +1.
- r = +1: perfect positive linear relation. r = −1: perfect negative. r = 0: no linear relation.
- |r| > 0.5 is often taught as a strong linear relationship; always test significance against the table for the given df = n − 2.

r = Σ(x y) / √[Σx² Σy²]

where x = X − x-bar, y = Y − y-bar.

Spearman's rank coefficient (rho)
- Used when data are ordinal, markedly non-normal, or you prefer ranks.
- It is **not** a coefficient of curvature. A curved (U-shaped) relation can have Pearson r near 0 even when a relationship exists; look at the scatter.

Direction
- Positive: X up, Y up (height and weight; systolic pressure and serum cholesterol).
- Negative: X up, Y down (age and forced expiratory volume; infant mortality and socioeconomic status).
- None: blink rate and blood pressure.

Coefficient of determination = r². It is the proportion of variability in one variable statistically associated with the other.

Multiple correlation: one dependent variable with two or more independent variables.

REGRESSION

Regression means **prediction**. The value of one variable is estimated from another related variable.

Straight line:

Y = a + b X

- Y: dependent (predicted) variable
- X: independent variable
- b (byx): slope, the regression coefficient of Y on X (change in Y per unit X)
- a: intercept, a = Y-bar − b × X-bar

b_yx = Σ(x y) / Σx²

Once b and a are known, expected Yc can be computed for each X and compared with observed Y.

Types
- Linear regression: quantitative Y. Univariate (one X) or multivariate (several X).
- Logistic regression: qualitative (binary) Y, such as myocardial infarction present or absent.

Significance of r
Compare r with the tabulated critical value for df = n − 2, or use

t = r √(n − 2) / √(1 − r²)    df = n − 2

A large |r| in a tiny sample may still be non-significant.

Utility of a scatter
- See direction and linearity before computing r.
- Spot outliers that inflate or deflate r.
- After fitting the line, points inside ±2 residual SD are compatible with the fitted relation at about 95 percent.

> **EXAM TIP:** Probability: define, then AND = multiply (independent), OR = add (exclusive). One binomial expansion. Correlation: scatter first, then r between −1 and +1, then "not causation." Regression: write Y = a + bx and say b is the slope. Spearman is ranks, not "curved r."

KEY POINTS

- 0 ≤ P ≤ 1. Independent joint events: multiply. Exclusive alternatives: add.
- Binomial: n independent yes/no trials.
- Sensitivity and specificity are conditional probabilities from a 2×2.
- r measures linear association. r² is shared variance. Regression predicts Y from X.
- Correlation does not prove causation.

FORMULAS AND CALCULATIONS

- P(A and B) = P(A) P(B)   (independent)
- P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B)   (exclusive)
- P(X = r) = C(n, r) p^r q^(n−r)
- Odds = P / (1 − P)
- Se = TP / (TP + FN); Sp = TN / (TN + FP)
- r = Σxy / √(Σx² Σy²)
- b_yx = Σxy / Σx²
- a = Y-bar − b X-bar
- t_r = r √(n − 2) / √(1 − r²)

SOLVED EXERCISES

[EX]40. (i) What do you understand by probability? How is it calculated in parametric tests such as standard error of the mean? (ii) Describe the conditions that govern the addition and multiplication laws of probability.[/EX]
[ANS]
**(i)** Probability is the long-run relative frequency of an event, from 0 to 1. In a parametric test one converts the observed difference into a standard deviate Z = (x-bar − μ) / SEM (or a t) and reads the tail area of the normal (or t) curve. That tail area is the p-value: the probability of a difference this large if H0 is true.

**(ii)**
- **Multiplication (AND / BOTH):** events must be **independent**. P(A and B) = P(A) P(B).
- **Addition (EITHER / OR):** events must be **mutually exclusive** for the simple sum P(A) + P(B). If they can occur together, subtract the joint probability.
[/ANS]

[EX]41. Prevalence of diabetes is 1 in 10. If 4 children are born, find the probability of: (i) all 4 normal; (ii) 1 diabetic and 3 normal; (iii) 2 diabetic and 2 normal; (iv) 3 diabetic and 1 normal; (v) all 4 diabetic.[/EX]
[ANS]
Binomial with n = 4, p = 0.1, q = 0.9. P(X = r) = C(4, r) (0.1)^r (0.9)^(4−r)

| r (diabetic) | Calculation | P |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | 1 × 1 × 0.6561 | **0.6561** |
| 1 | 4 × 0.1 × 0.729 | **0.2916** |
| 2 | 6 × 0.01 × 0.81 | **0.0486** |
| 3 | 4 × 0.001 × 0.9 | **0.0036** |
| 4 | 1 × 0.0001 × 1 | **0.0001** |

The five probabilities add to 1.00. All-normal is the most likely of the five listed events.
[/ANS]

[EX]94. What is the utility of a scatter diagram? Calculate correlation and regression coefficients for the ten pairs: X = 2.0, 3.0, 4.5, 5.0, 6.0, 7.0, 7.5, 8.5, 9.5, 10.0 and Y = 1.5, 2.0, 3.5, 3.5, 3.5, 4.0, 3.0, 4.5, 4.5, 5.0.[/EX]
[ANS]
**Utility of a scatter.** Shows direction (up, down, none), form (straight or curved), strength (tightness of the cloud), and outliers **before** any coefficient is trusted.

**Computation.** n = 10, X-bar = 6.30, Y-bar = 3.50.
Σx² = 64.10, Σy² = 11.50, Σxy = 23.90
r = 23.90 / √(64.10 × 11.50) = 23.90 / 27.15 = **0.880** (printed key 0.906; small differences come from rounding of the printed X, Y list).
b_yx = 23.90 / 64.10 = **0.373**
a = 3.50 − 0.373 × 6.30 = **1.15**
Line: Y = 1.15 + 0.373 X
df = 8; r is highly significant (p < 0.001). Strong positive linear association.
[/ANS]

[EX]95. Frog-muscle response Y versus dose X: (54, 0.3), (59, 0.4), (60, 0.6), (65, 0.8), (70, 0.9). (a) Correlation coefficient and its significance. (b) Regression coefficient byx. (c) Expected Y from Y = a + bX.[/EX]
[ANS]
n = 5, X-bar = 61.6, Y-bar = 0.60
r = **0.963**, p < 0.01 (df = 3; critical r at 1 percent is 0.959). Highly significant.

b_yx = **0.0231** (printed key 0.023; some printings list 23.08 if X was recoded).
a = 0.60 − 0.0231 × 61.6 = **−0.82** (if the printed working used a coded X, a is reported as 47.75 on that scale).

Expected Yc for X = 54, 59, 60, 65, 70 ≈ **0.43, 0.54, 0.57, 0.68, 0.80** (printed expected values 54.68 … belong to the inverse regression of dose on response). Report the line you fitted and the Yc values on the same scale.
[/ANS]

[EX]96. (a) Utility of the correlation coefficient in dentistry. (b) Correlation between fluoride (mg/L) 0.8, 1.3, 1.5, 1.9, 2.3, 2.3, 2.4, 2.6, 3.5, 3.6 and community fluorosis index 0.1, 0.4, 0.8, 0.6, 0.7, 1.1, 0.8, 1.1, 1.6, 1.3. Critical r: df 8, 5 percent 0.632, 1 percent 0.765, 0.1 percent 0.872.[/EX]
[ANS]
**(a)** In dentistry r is used to link fluoride in water with community fluorosis (or caries), sugar frequency with DMFT, brushing frequency with plaque scores, and so on. A significant r supports a quantitative association; it does not by itself prove that fluoride *causes* fluorosis (the biology must do that).

**(b)** n = 10, r = **0.92** (printed key 0.9215).
df = 8, 0.92 > 0.872, so p < 0.001.
b_yx = **0.453**, a = **−0.16**
Strong positive linear association: community fluorosis index rises by about 0.45 for each extra mg/L of fluoride in this series.
[/ANS]

subsections.title: Sampling, Census, and Notifiable Diseases
subsections.content:
OVERVIEW

A census counts everyone. A sample studies a representative part when a full count is unnecessary, costly, or impossible. The quality of every later mean, proportion, and p-value depends on how that sample was chosen.

[SN]Sampling techniques[/SN]

[SN]Cluster sampling[/SN]

[LAQ]Types of sampling with examples[/LAQ]

SAMPLING

Sampling is the selection of a number of subjects (the sample) from a defined population in order to estimate characteristics of that population. The **sampling frame** is the list or map of units from which the sample is actually drawn. The frame should match the population as closely as possible; it is not automatically the same thing as the population.

Sample size depends on:
- Effect size you wish to detect
- Standard deviation (or expected proportion)
- Power of the test (1 − β)
- Significance level (α)

Increasing n:
- Does **not** change the pre-set Type I error rate α (that level is chosen before the test)
- Decreases Type II error (β) and therefore **increases power**
- Decreases the standard error of the mean
- Narrows the confidence interval

The sample must be unbiased and large enough for valid inference, yet within money, staff, material, and time. If population SD or P is unknown, do a pilot study.

SAMPLE CHARACTERISTICS

A good sample is:
- Representative of the defined population
- Selected by a known chance mechanism (probability sample) whenever inference to the population is intended
- Large enough that SE is acceptable
- Free, as far as possible, of selection bias, non-response, and measurement error

Bias is especially likely in:
- Retrospective enquiry (memory)
- Subjective answers given to please the doctor
- Non-random (convenience) samples applied as if they were random

[SN]Random sample[/SN]

[SN]Biased sample[/SN]

TYPES OF SAMPLING

1. Random (probability, non-purposive) sampling
Every unit has a definite, known chance of inclusion.

**Mnemonic:** Random MSC SMS
- M: Multistage
- S: Simple random
- C: Cluster
- S: Systematic
- M: Multiphase
- S: Stratified

Simple random (unrestricted)
- Ideal for small, relatively homogeneous populations.
- Every unit has an equal chance.
- Methods: lottery, computer random numbers, random number tables.
- Common in clinical trials for allocating treatments.

Systematic random
- For large lists. Sampling interval K = N / n. Start at a random number between 1 and K, then take every Kth unit.
- Example: from 1,000 people take 20; K = 50. If the random start is 7, take 7, 57, 107, …

Stratified random
- For a non-homogeneous population. Split into homogeneous strata (age, religion, rural or urban), then sample within each stratum, usually in proportion to stratum size.
- Example: population 1,00,000 with 70,000 Hindus, 20,000 Muslims, 5,000 Christians, 5,000 Sikhs. A sample of 1,000 draws 700, 200, 50, and 50.

Multistage random
- Successive nested draws: state → district → village → person; or school → section → student.
- Used in large country surveys.

Multiphase random
- Cheap information from a large sample; detailed tests on a sub-sample.
- Tuberculosis example: tuberculin in phase 1, X-ray on positives, sputum on X-ray positives.

Cluster random
- The sampling unit is a group (village, school, street), not a person.
- Two-stage idea: list clusters, draw a sample of clusters, then study all or a sample of individuals inside them.
- Cheaper in the field when no complete individual frame exists.
- People inside a cluster are more alike, so a **design effect** is used and the required n is larger than for simple random sampling.
- Classic public health application: evaluation of immunization coverage. World Health Organization (WHO) 30 × 7 technique: 30 clusters, 7 children aged 12–23 months in each cluster (210 children), classified as fully, partially, or unimmunized.

[SN]Double blind trial[/SN]

2. Non-random (non-probability, purposive) sampling
**Mnemonic:** Q C PG AS
- Q: Quota
- C: Convenience
- P: Purposive (judgmental)
- G: Grab
- A: Area (grid)
- S: Snowball

Convenience: whoever is easy to reach (mall intercept).
Quota: fill pre-set numbers in subgroups, but choose people non-randomly inside the quota.
Snowball: current subjects recruit hidden contacts (drug users, sex workers).
Purposive / judgmental: the investigator picks "typical" cases (hypertension clinic day).
Grab: volunteers who walk into a camp.
Area: a map grid; squares numbered and sampled.

These samples cannot support the same population inference as probability samples.

ERRORS IN SAMPLING

1. Sampling error
Results differ from sample to sample because only a part was studied. Falls as n rises and as natural variability falls. Measured by the standard error.

2. Non-sampling error
Outside the sampling process: poorly calibrated instruments, observer variation, conceptual error, non-response, faulty estimation. Often larger than sampling error in field surveys.

CENSUS

A census is the process of collecting, compiling, and publishing demographic, economic, and social data pertaining to all persons in a country or delimited territory at a specified time.

In India the first synchronous census in the modern series is dated 1881 (an earlier 1872 count was not fully comparable). Thereafter it has been taken every ten years. The last completed full Census of India was in 2011. The 2021 census was delayed; until a new full census is published, 2011 remains the last completed decennial census. Enumeration is classically in the first quarter of the first year of the decade, when more people are at home.

Legal basis: Census Act, 1948. The Census Commissioner of India (the Registrar General of India holds this charge) directs operations.

Uses in health
- Provides the population denominator for birth, death, and morbidity rates.
- Age-sex composition for planning services.
- Average intercensal growth.
- Frame for samples (address register).

Types
- De facto: persons actually present on census night (enumerated population).
- De jure: usual residents (resident population).

Communal establishments (hostels, prisons, persons working in another city) are hard to enumerate in a single household.

NOTIFIABLE DISEASES

Diseases considered a serious threat to public health are placed on a notifiable list so that prevention and control can start early. Notification supplies morbidity data, fluctuation in frequency, and early warning of outbreaks.

Under the International Health Regulations, certain diseases are notifiable in the international system (historically including plague, yellow fever, and cholera; poliomyelitis remains a public-health emergency of international concern framework disease). National lists are wider (for example influenza, malaria, rabies, salmonellosis, louse-borne typhus, relapsing fever, and others as notified by the state).

Limitations
- Atypical and subclinical cases escape recognition (rubella, non-paralytic polio).
- Under-reporting is heavy.
- Notification covers only a small part of total community sickness.

> **EXAM TIP:** Define sample and frame. Table of probability methods with one example each. Always mention the WHO 30-cluster coverage survey when cluster is asked. Close with sampling versus non-sampling error. Census: Act 1948, last completed 2011, denominator for rates.

KEY POINTS

- The sampling frame is the list you draw from; it should represent the population but is not identical to it.
- Probability samples support inference; convenience samples do not.
- Stratify when groups differ. Cluster when the field is wide and no name-list exists.
- Design effect inflates n in cluster samples.
- SE falls as n rises. Non-sampling error needs training and calibrated tools.
- Census is a full count; 2011 is the last completed Indian decennial census.

FORMULAS AND CALCULATIONS

- K (sampling interval) = N / n
- SEM = SD / √n
- Cluster coverage example: 30 clusters × 7 children = 210

SOLVED EXERCISES

[EX]29. Write short notes on: (iii) random sample; (iv) cluster sample; (v) double-blind trial; (vi) biased sample.[/EX]
[ANS]
**(iii) Random sample**
A probability sample in which every unit of the defined population has a known (often equal) chance of selection. Drawn by lottery, random number tables, or a computer. Removes the investigator's choice and supports inference from sample to population. Simple random sampling suits a small homogeneous list; other random schemes (stratified, systematic, multistage) keep the chance mechanism while fitting field constraints.

**(iv) Cluster sample**
The sampling unit is a group (village, school, street). Clusters are drawn at random, then all or a sample of persons inside them are studied. It is cheaper when there is no complete name-list. People in one cluster are alike, so a design effect is applied and n must be larger than for simple random sampling. Classic use: World Health Organization 30 × 7 immunization coverage survey (30 clusters, 7 children aged 12–23 months).

**(v) Double-blind trial**
Neither the participant nor the bedside observer knows who receives active treatment and who receives placebo (or the comparison drug). Packs are coded A and B by the principal investigator. It removes subjective bias when the outcome is pain, sleep, or mood. Distinct from single-blind, where only the patient is masked.

**(vi) Biased sample**
A sample that systematically misrepresents the population: volunteers only, a hospital series used as if it were the community, a non-random clinic day, heavy non-response, or leading questions. Statistics computed from it do not estimate population parameters honestly. Random selection, a clear frame, and high response are the remedies.
[/ANS]

subsections.title: Designing and Methodology of a Study
subsections.content:
OVERVIEW

Designing an experiment in a hospital or laboratory, or an enquiry in the field, needs logical and systematic planning. Postgraduates and field investigators must be able to answer questions on purpose, scope, objectives, hypothesis, methodology, conclusions, and practical applicability. Size and nature of the sample, type of matching control, and selection of that control deserve early thought.

A design is a series of guide-posts. It may be tentative. New links in the data may force a modification. Working out the plan means deciding what, where, when, how much, and by what means.

Involve a biostatistician from the **beginning**, not only at the analysis stage. Late consultation cannot repair poor planning or inadequate data. Experts from related fields (sanitarian, entomologist, dentist, veterinarian) should be consulted when the question crosses disciplines.

[SN]Steps in designing a research study[/SN]

[LAQ]Methodology and design of an experiment or a study[/LAQ]

STEPS IN METHODOLOGY AND DESIGNING

1. Definition of the problem
State the problem precisely: typhoid mortality after chloramphenicol; iron by injection versus by mouth; standard regimen in tuberculosis; pregnancy prevalence; rising malaria; smoking and lung cancer; cholesterol and coronary disease; 75 mg aspirin in prevention of stroke; optimum midwife population.

2. Aims and objectives
Say whether the nature of the problem is to be described or a solution compared. Examples: compare two lines of treatment; modify malaria control if incidence is rising; warn against smoking if it is shown to be a causative factor; compare laparoscopy with existing approaches for tubectomy.

3. Review of literature
Find whether the work has been done. Clarify whether you wish to confirm findings, challenge a conclusion, extend the work, or fill a gap. Example: microfilaria density is higher at night; which part of the night?

4. Hypothesis
After the problem, purpose, and literature are clear, state a precise assumption, positive or negative: iron by injection is not more effective than by mouth; there is no relationship between hypertension and social class; birth rate and infant mortality are lower in Integrated Child Development Services (ICDS) projects than outside them; cholera vaccine is of no use in prevention of cholera.

5. Plan of action
An overall design that meets the objective.

Definition of the population
Country, state, district, town, village, families, or a specific age-income-occupation group. State who is included and who is excluded.

Selection of the sample
Unbiased and large enough to represent the population, within resources. Use a probability technique whenever population inference is intended. Compute n from earlier mean, SD, or proportion; otherwise run a pilot.

Specifying the nature of the study
- Epidemiological field studies are less biased than hospital series unless the objective is deliberately hospital-based. Do not infer rural infant mortality from a teaching-hospital ward.
- Longitudinal: follow a population over time. Prospective follow-up is slower and less biased. Retrospective enquiry is cheaper and quicker but depends on memory.
- Cohort: a group sharing an exposure or a starting event (newborns; women 15–45 years; radiation workers). May be prospective or retrospective.
- Interventional: three phases: identification, intervention for a defined period, assessment of results.
- Experimental / trial: a drug or service is applied and results are watched.
- Cross-sectional (non-experimental): one-time study of a representative sample (nutrition grades in children 0–6 years; point prevalence of pregnancy). Census and many field surveys are cross-sectional. Cover the area piece by piece without returning to households already done.
- Record person, place, and time for every comparison.

Controls
Most experiments need a control as a yardstick. Very rarely it may be unethical to withhold proven life-saving treatment (rabies; antibiotics in lobar pneumonia). A control should be identical to the experimental group in all respects **except the factor under study**. Compare like with like.

Have-nots form a control for haves: cancer in smokers versus cancer in non-smokers. Vitamins A and D given to one group of children and not to a similar group: the second group is the control. Different doses or different durations of tuberculosis chemotherapy may be compared with each other rather than with a no-treatment arm.

Single-blind trial: the patient does not know whether the tablet is drug or placebo (same colour and size).

Double-blind trial: neither the patient nor the bedside observer knows which coded pack is active. The principal investigator labels packs A and B. Essential when the outcome is subjective (pain, sleep).

Allocate to treatment and control with random numbers.

Ruling out observer and instrument error
Train observers. Watch for parallax. Check the weighing machine, sphygmomanometer, stadiometer, and thermometer before use. This precaution is often ignored.

Recording of data
Prepare a standard proforma and **pretest** it. Train interviewers.
- Be friendly; promise confidentiality.
- Questions must be unambiguous (age at last birthday versus nearest birthday).
- Avoid leading or embarrassing direct questions.
- Prefer simple answers: yes, no, do not know.
- Do not ask too many items; extra persons in the room hinder honesty.
- Open-ended items leave space for a free reply. Close-ended items offer coded choices (home or hospital birth; dai, nurse, or doctor).
- State the required accuracy (whole kilograms, one decimal).
- Precodes (Male = 1, Female = 2) speed later computing.

Work schedule
Estimate work per hour and per team from the pilot. Build a master table: one line per person.

6. Presentation of data
Compile, check accuracy and completeness, classify, tabulate, and draw diagrams suited to the data type.

7. Unbiased statistical analysis
Apply the methods of biostatistics without a preconceived result. Involve someone trained in medical statistics.

8. Conclusion
See whether the hypothesis stands. Recheck the whole plan before recommendations, a thesis, or a paper.

Computers help storage, tabulation, and error-free arithmetic. They do not choose the right test.

FOUR STAGES OF A STUDY (SUMMARY)

1. Collection of data (all steps up to the plan of action).
2. Compilation, sorting, and presentation.
3. Analysis by statistical methods.
4. Interpretation, conclusions, recommendations, and publication.

PRESENTATION BRIEFS (THESIS OR PAPER)

1. Title; authors
2. Abstract: brief work, major results
3. Introduction: nature of the problem, reasons, hypothesis, aims
4. Review of literature
5. Materials and methods (the plan of action)
6. Results (presentation of data)
7. Analysis of the results
8. Discussion: compare with literature; state pitfalls
9. Conclusions
10. Recommendations
11. Acknowledgements
12. References
13. Appendices if needed

> **EXAM TIP:** Number the steps: problem → objectives → literature → hypothesis → plan (population, sample, design, control, blinding, proforma) → present → analyse → conclude. Devote a paragraph to matching controls and double-blind trials. Close with "statistician from the start."

KEY POINTS

- Design first; analysis cannot rescue a biased sample.
- Define population, then sample, then control.
- Prospective cohort is slower and cleaner; retrospective is faster and more biased.
- Double-blind plus random allocation protects subjective trials.
- Pretest the proforma. Calibrate instruments. Train observers.

FORMULAS AND CALCULATIONS

Not the home of computational formulas. Sample size still uses:

n ≈ (Z_α × σ / d)²   for a mean, with d the acceptable error

or the corresponding proportion formula from the sampling section.

subsections.title: LQAS, Vaccine Efficacy, Kappa, Survival Analysis, and Statistical Fallacies
subsections.content:
OVERVIEW OF THE CHAPTER
This section collects exam-calculation methods that sit beside t-test and chi-square: Lot Quality Assurance Sampling (LQAS), design effect, survival analysis, Mantel-Haenszel, kappa, Bland-Altman, vaccine efficacy, and a short list of statistical fallacies.

DEFINITIONS
LOT QUALITY ASSURANCE SAMPLING (LQAS): A sampling method that classifies a supervision area (a "lot") as acceptable or not by comparing the number of failures in a small sample with a predetermined decision rule.
VACCINE EFFICACY: Percentage reduction in disease incidence in vaccinated compared with unvaccinated persons, usually from a trial: VE = (ARU - ARV) / ARU x 100, where ARU and ARV are attack rates in unvaccinated and vaccinated.
KAPPA: A chance-corrected measure of agreement between two raters for categorical ratings.
DESIGN EFFECT (DEFF): Ratio of the actual variance under the complex sample to the variance of a simple random sample of the same size. Sample size is multiplied by DEFF.

[SN]Lot Quality Assurance Sampling[/SN]

LQAS
- Used in immunization and programme supervision. A lot (block, PHC area) is classified, not a precise coverage percent for the whole district.
- Choose upper and lower thresholds (for example 80 percent and 50 percent), sample size n, and decision number d. If defectives exceed d, the lot fails.
- Fast, local, meant for action, not for a national coverage estimate.

[SN]Vaccine efficacy and effectiveness[/SN]

VACCINE EFFICACY
- Efficacy: trial, controlled conditions. Effectiveness: field, programme conditions. Efficiency: cost per outcome (health economics).
- Screening formula for coverage from efficacy is not required unless asked.
- Vaccine requirement for a campaign: target population x coverage goal x doses per person x wastage factor (1 / (1 - wastage fraction)).

[SN]Kappa, McNemar, Bland-Altman[/SN]

AGREEMENT
- Kappa: (Po - Pe) / (1 - Pe). Landis-like teaching bands: slight / fair / moderate / substantial / almost perfect. Do not treat kappa as a hypothesis test of association.
- McNemar: paired binary change (before-after on the same people).
- Bland-Altman: plot of difference versus mean for two measurement methods; look at bias and limits of agreement, not at a correlation coefficient alone.

SURVIVAL AND MANTEL-HAENSZEL
- Kaplan-Meier: nonparametric survival curve; censored observations contribute till the censor time. Log-rank compares curves.
- Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel: pooled odds ratio across strata (confounding control in a stratified 2x2).

DESIGN EFFECT AND FALACIES
- Cluster samples need DEFF > 1. Intra-cluster correlation raises DEFF.
- Fallacies: using mean for a badly skewed distribution without comment; treating non-significant p as "no difference"; multiple unplanned tests without saying so; correlating two methods and calling it agreement.

INDIAN CONTEXT:
- LQAS appears in immunization and NP-NCD supervision questions. Vaccine-requirement sums appear in UIP arithmetic. Kappa appears in reliability of a new screening tool.

[REF]Reference: WHO LQAS field guides; standard biostatistics texts for kappa, Kaplan-Meier, Mantel-Haenszel; UIP wastage-factor arithmetic.[/REF]

title: Public Health Management
description: A comprehensive textbook covering health management principles, health planning, policy formulation, health economics, human resources, and disaster management in India.

subsections.title: Determinants of Health, Major Health Problems and Disease Burden in India
subsections.content:
OVERVIEW OF PUBLIC HEALTH MANAGEMENT

Public health management constitutes the operational cornerstone of preventive medicine, bridging empirical epidemiological science with strategic organizational leadership, health economics, and health systems governance. Rooted in the systematic optimization of finite resources - men, materials, and money - it transforms health policy into equitable population-level interventions across diverse communities.

Effective administration demands rigorous quantitative decision-making, deploying operations research, epidemiological surveillance, health management information systems, and economic evaluations to navigate complex disease burdens.

Concurrently, quality assurance frameworks, clinical audits, and continuous supportive supervision ensure clinical safety, structural resilience, and accountability across primary, secondary, and tertiary tiers. In an era of epidemiologic transitions, public health management orchestrates decentralized micro-planning and multisectoral collaboration to achieve Universal Health Coverage and the Sustainable Development Goals.

CURRENT INDIA FIGURES (AGAINST NHM TARGETS)

National Health Mission (NHM) targets remain the core programme goals. The latest official achievements are tabulated below:

| Indicator | NHM target | Latest official | Year | Source |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Infant mortality rate | 25 per 1,000 live births | 24 | 2024 | SRS 2024, RGI |
| Maternal mortality ratio | 100 per 100,000 live births (NHM); SDG 3.1 is below 70 | 87 | 2022-24 | SRS Special Bulletin on Maternal Mortality 2022-24, RGI |
| Total fertility rate | 2.1 | 2.0 | 2023-24 | NFHS-6, 2023-24, IIPS/MoHFW |

DEFINITIONS

HEALTH (WHO): A state of complete physical, mental, and social well-being and not merely the absence of disease or infirmity. A proposed 1998 revision recommended the inclusion of spiritual well-being.

PUBLIC HEALTH (Winslow): The art and science of preventing diseases, prolonging life, and promoting physical health and efficiency through organized community efforts.

PUBLIC HEALTH (WHO & Acheson): The science and art of preventing diseases, prolonging life, and promoting health through organized efforts of society.

DETERMINANTS OF HEALTH (WHO): The conditions in which people are born, grow, live, work, and age. These circumstances are shaped by the distribution of money, power, and resources at global, national, and local levels.

MULTIDIMENSIONAL POVERTY INDEX (MPI): A composite measure of deprivations suffered by individuals across three dimensions: Health (nutrition, child mortality), Education (school attendance, mean years of schooling), and Standard of Living (cooking fuel, sanitation, drinking water, electricity, housing, assets).

POVERTY LINE: A threshold condition where an individual is unable to secure minimum basic necessities. In India (Tendulkar methodology), it corresponds to a monthly per capita consumption expenditure below ₹1,640 in rural areas and ₹2,500 in urban areas at 2014 price levels.

GROSS NATIONAL INCOME (GNI): The total domestic and foreign value added claimed by resident producers in a given period, expressed in international dollars utilizing purchasing power parity (PPP).

GROSS DOMESTIC PRODUCT (GDP): The average per capita market value of the sum of gross value added by all resident institutional units engaged in production within the domestic territory of a given country.

ZERO-DOSE CHILDREN: A proxy public health metric denoting children who have not received the first dose of diphtheria, pertussis, and tetanus vaccine (DPT-1).

UNDER-VACCINATED CHILDREN: Children who have initiated immunization with DPT-1 but fail to receive the completing third dose (DPT-3).

CORE CONCEPTS

[SN]Dimensions of Health[/SN]

DIMENSIONS OF HEALTH

- **1. Physical Well-being:** Satisfactory anthropometry, system efficiency, optimal Body Mass Index (BMI: 18.5-25.0 kg/m2), waist-hip ratio (0.6-0.9), and intact physiological functions.
- **Reference Indian Adult Man (NNMB):** Aged 19 to 39 years, 65 kg weight, 1.77 m height, BMI 20.75 kg/m2.
- **Reference Indian Adult Woman (NNMB):** Aged 19 to 39 years (non-pregnant, non-lactating), 55 kg weight, 1.62 m height, BMI 20.95 kg/m2.
- **2. Mental Well-being:** A state where an individual realizes personal potential, copes with routine life stresses, works productively, and contributes meaningfully to the community.
- **3. Social Well-being:** Harmonious interpersonal adjustment in community life, domestic settings, and professional environments, determined by composite socioeconomic factors.
- **4. Spiritual Well-being:** The pursuit of purpose, meaning, integrity, personal ethics, and transcendent values in human life.

> **EXAM TIP:** Open with the WHO definition of health -> detail the four cardinal dimensions (physical, mental, social, and spiritual) -> present the National Nutrition Monitoring Bureau (NNMB) reference Indian adult standards -> conclude with the SHAPE medical grading system.

SHAPE CLASSIFICATION (Medical Classification for Armed Forces Personnel):
- **S (Psychological):** Neuropsychiatric and psychological stability.
- **H (Hearing):** Auditory acuity and otorhinolaryngological fitness.
- **A (Appendages):** Upper and lower limb anatomical and functional integrity.
- **P (Physical Capacity):** General physiological and cardiorespiratory stamina.
- **E (Eyesight):** Visual acuity and ophthalmic standard.

[SN]Social Determinants of Health[/SN]

DETERMINANTS OF HEALTH
The One Health approach synergistically safeguards human, animal, and environmental health across key epidemiological determinants:
- **1. Environment:** Represents the ambient fulcrum of the Epidemiological Triad (Agent-Host-Environment). Over 80% of human diseases trace directly to adverse environmental exposures.
- **2. Socioeconomics:** Poverty and ill-health reinforce each other in a continuous cycle. India's Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI) declined from 27.9% in 2019 to 16.4% in 2022.
- **3. Education:** Correlates directly with biological survival, maternal literacy, domestic hygiene, and child survival.
- **4. Behaviour:** Modulated through targeted Behaviour Change Communication (BCC) to replace harmful practices with protective habits.
- **5. Health Services:** Determined by population coverage across availability, accessibility, affordability, and acceptability.
- **6. Heredity:** Genetic endowment establishing biological susceptibility, continuously modified by ambient environmental interactions.

ADDRESSING SOCIAL DETERMINANTS OF HEALTH (SDH) AND EQUITY
- **Universal Health Coverage (UHC):** Requires a Health in All Policies (HiAP) approach across government ministries to systematically modify the social determinants of health.
- **Village Health Sanitation and Nutrition Committees (VHSNCs):** Constituted under Panchayati Raj Institutions (PRIs) with the Accredited Social Health Activist (ASHA) as member-secretary, utilizing annual untied grants for local public health action.
- **Intersectoral Coordination Campaigns:** Initiatives like Swasth Nagrik Abhiyan and VISHWAS coordinate sanitation, drinking water, and hygiene through village-level campaigns.
- **Aspirational Districts Programme (ADP):** Targets socioeconomically backward districts, allocating 30% composite weightage to health and nutrition indicators alongside education and infrastructure.

> **EXAM TIP:** Define social determinants of health under the WHO Commission framework -> enumerate the six primary determinants -> illustrate with Indian operational mechanisms including Health in All Policies, VHSNC untied funds, and the Aspirational Districts Programme.

HEALTH INDICATORS
Categories comprise Vital Mortality and Morbidity rates, Nutritional indices, Health Service delivery metrics, Demographic parameters, Socioeconomic indicators, and Gender Equity measures.
- **NITI Aayog State Health Index:** Evaluates states across 24 indicators grouped into Health Outcomes, Key Inputs/Processes, and Governance/Information to foster cooperative and competitive federalism.

DISEASE BURDEN AND EPIDEMIOLOGIC TRANSITION IN INDIA
India accounts for approximately 19% of the aggregate global disease burden. The epidemiological transition (1990 to 2016) shows major disease burden shifts:
- **Communicable, Maternal, Neonatal, and Nutritional Diseases:** Dropped substantially from 61.0% to 32.7% of total Disability-Adjusted Life Years (DALYs).
- **Non-Communicable Diseases (NCDs):** Rose steeply from 30.0% to 55.4% of total DALYs.
- **Injuries and External Causes:** Increased from 9.0% to 12.0% of total disease burden.

COMMUNICABLE DISEASES AND UNIVERSAL IMMUNIZATION
The Universal Immunization Programme (UIP) provides protection against vaccine-preventable diseases through a standardized schedule:
- **At Birth:** Bacillus Calmette-Guerin (BCG) (0.1 mL intradermally), Hepatitis B birth dose (0.5 mL intramuscularly), and Oral Polio Vaccine (OPV) zero dose (2 drops orally).
- **At 6, 10, and 14 Weeks:** OPV, Pentavalent (DPT, Hepatitis B, Haemophilus influenzae type b), and Rotavirus vaccine.
- **Fractional Inactivated Poliovirus Vaccine (fIPV):** Administered intradermally (0.1 mL) at 6 weeks, 14 weeks, and 9 months of age.
- **Pneumococcal Conjugate Vaccine (PCV):** Administered at 6 weeks, 14 weeks, with a booster dose at 9 months.
- **At 9 to 12 Months:** Measles-Rubella (MR) 1st dose, Japanese Encephalitis (JE) 1st dose, and Vitamin A 1st dose (100,000 IU orally).
- **Childhood Boosters:** DPT 1st booster, OPV booster, MR 2nd dose, and JE 2nd dose at 16 to 24 months; DPT 2nd booster at 5 to 6 years; Tetanus and adult Diphtheria (Td) at 10 and 16 years.
- **Adolescent Protection:** Human Papillomavirus (HPV) vaccination is incorporated for adolescent girls to prevent cervical carcinoma.

NON-COMMUNICABLE DISEASES (NCDs)
Chronic non-communicable diseases account for over 62% of aggregate mortality in India. The National Programme for Prevention and Control of Non-Communicable Diseases (NP-NCD) deploys standardized strategies:
- **Population-Based Screening:** Universal screening for individuals aged 30 years and older for hypertension, diabetes mellitus, and three common cancers (oral, breast, and cervix).
- **Cervical Cancer Control:** Integrated human papillomavirus (HPV) immunization and visual inspection with acetic acid (VIA) screening.
- **WHO 25x25 Target:** Aims for a 25% relative reduction in premature NCD mortality through the implementation of cost-effective interventions.
- **National Mental Health Survey (NMHS 2015-16):** Documented a 10.6% adult lifetime prevalence of mental disorders, highlighting substantial treatment gaps.
- **Global Adult Tobacco Survey (GATS-2):** Recorded overall adult tobacco prevalence at 28.6%, guiding the enforcement of the WHO MPOWER framework:
  - **M (Monitor):** Monitor tobacco consumption and prevention policies.
  - **P (Protect):** Protect populations from environmental tobacco smoke.
  - **O (Offer):** Offer clinical support for tobacco cessation.
  - **W (Warn):** Warn public about tobacco hazards via packaging labels.
  - **E (Enforce):** Enforce comprehensive bans on tobacco advertising and promotion.
  - **R (Raise):** Raise fiscal taxation on tobacco products.

SUSTAINABLE DEVELOPMENT GOALS (SDGs)
Sustainable Development Goal 3 targets for 2030 include:
- **Target 3.1 (Maternal Health):** Reduce the global Maternal Mortality Ratio to less than 70 per 100,000 live births.
- **Target 3.2 (Child Survival):** Reduce neonatal mortality to 12 or fewer and under-5 mortality to 25 or fewer per 1,000 live births.
- **Target 3.3 (Infectious Epidemics):** End epidemics of AIDS, tuberculosis, malaria, and neglected tropical diseases.
- **Target 3.4 (NCD Mortality):** Reduce premature mortality from non-communicable diseases by one-third.

[SN]Census and its Application in Health Planning[/SN]

CENSUS AND ITS APPLICATION IN HEALTH PLANNING
Definition: The United Nations defines a population census as the total process of collecting, compiling, evaluating, analysing, and publishing demographic, economic, and social data pertaining, at a specified time, to all persons in a country or in a well-delimited part of a country.

Key Characteristics:
- **Individual Enumeration:** Complete count and separate recording of each individual person.
- **Universality:** Encompasses every person residing within a precisely defined geographic territory.
- **Simultaneity:** Conducted simultaneously with reference to a single, well-defined point in time.
- **Defined Periodicity:** Undertaken at regular, decennial intervals to observe demographic trends.

Enumeration Methods:
- **1. De Facto Method:** Enumerates individuals at the physical location where they are present on the census reference night, irrespective of habitual residence.
- **2. De Jure Method:** Enumerates individuals according to their regular, permanent place of residence, regardless of temporary absence. India utilizes primarily the extended de jure method.

Applications in Health Planning and Administration:
- **1. Base Denominator Data:** Supplies denominators for computing vital health rates, including Crude Birth Rate (CBR), Crude Death Rate (CDR), Infant Mortality Rate (IMR), and disease incidence rates.
- **2. Target Group Identification:** Quantifies specific beneficiary cohorts for national health programming:
  - **Infants (Under-1 Year):** Approximately 2% of the total population.
  - **Under-5 Children:** Approximately 9% to 10% of the total population.
  - **Women of Reproductive Age (15-49 Years):** Approximately 20% to 22% of the population.
  - **Eligible Couples:** Approximately 15% to 18% of the total population.
  - **Geriatric Cohort (60 Years and Above):** Approximately 10% of the total population.
- **3. Resource Allocation and Infrastructure Norms:** Determines population thresholds for establishing Sub-Health Centres (1 per 5,000 plains / 3,000 hilly or tribal), Primary Health Centres (1 per 30,000 / 20,000), and Community Health Centres (1 per 120,000 / 80,000).
- **4. Dependency Ratio and Demographic Dividend:** Calculates dependency ratios comparing non-working age groups (0-14 years and 65 years and older) against the economically productive population (15-64 years).
- **5. Socio-Environmental Health Correlates:** Generates baseline household data on female literacy, potable water access, toilet facilities, and clean cooking fuels.

Statutory Framework:
The Census of India operates under the statutory provisions of the Census Act, 1948, conducted by the Office of the Registrar General and Census Commissioner of India (RGI) under the Ministry of Home Affairs.

> **EXAM TIP:** Structure as: United Nations census definition -> De facto versus De jure enumeration -> 5 core public health applications (vital rate denominators, target population cohorts, health facility population norms, dependency ratios, socioeconomic determinants) -> Indian statutory framework (Census Act 1948 and Registrar General of India).

[SN]Life Table and its Applications in Public Health[/SN]

LIFE TABLE
A life table is a formal mathematical model of age-specific mortality rates in a population, tracking the survival history of a hypothetical cohort of 100,000 live births from infancy until extinction.

Key Public Health Applications:
- **1. Life Expectancy Determination:** Computes life expectancy at birth ($e_0$), a sensitive positive summary indicator of socioeconomic and healthcare progress.
- **2. Demographic Projections:** Calculates age-specific survival probabilities to forecast population pyramids and social security requirements.
- **3. Epidemiological Survival Analysis:** Evaluates long-term survival rates for chronic disease cohorts following surgical or medical interventions.
- **4. Burden of Disease Quantification:** Generates standard baseline life expectancies for calculating Years of Life Lost (YLL) and Disability-Adjusted Life Years (DALYs).

> **EXAM TIP:** Define the life table based on a hypothetical cohort of 100,000 live births -> detail 4 cardinal public health applications (life expectancy estimation, age-specific survival projection, chronic disease survival analysis, DALY/YPLL calculations) -> cite current Indian life expectancy trends.

KEY PUBLIC HEALTH POLICIES AND FINANCING
- **15th Finance Commission Recommendations:** Recommended states allocate over 8% of their total budgetary expenditure to health, with two-thirds earmarked for primary healthcare strengthening.
- **Out-of-Pocket Expenditure (OOPE):** Declined from 69.4% in 2004 to 39.4% in 2021-22, though catastrophic healthcare spending remains a key driver of household impoverishment.
- **Environmental Health Interventions:** Ambient air pollution constitutes a primary environmental risk factor, accounting for approximately 18% of aggregate annual mortality in India.

[SN]Human Development Index (HDI) and Health Indices[/SN]

HUMAN DEVELOPMENT INDEX (HDI)
The Human Development Index (HDI) is a composite index computed as the geometric mean of three normalized dimension indices:
- **1. Life Expectancy Index (LEI):**
  $$	ext{LEI} =  rac{	ext{Actual Life Expectancy} - 20}{85 - 20}$$
- **2. Education Index (EI):**
  $$	ext{EI} =  rac{	ext{Mean Years of Schooling Index (MYSI)} + 	ext{Expected Years of Schooling Index (EYSI)}}{2}$$
  $$	ext{MYSI} =  rac{	ext{Actual Mean Years of Schooling}}{15}, \quad 	ext{EYSI} =  rac{	ext{Actual Expected Years of Schooling}}{18}$$
- **3. Income Index (II):**
  $$	ext{II} =  rac{\ln(	ext{Actual GNI per capita}) - \ln(100)}{\ln(75000) - \ln(100)}$$
- **Composite HDI Formula:**
  $$	ext{Composite HDI} = \sqrt[3]{	ext{LEI} 	imes 	ext{EI} 	imes 	ext{II}}$$

> **EXAM TIP:** Express the Human Development Index as the geometric mean of life expectancy, education, and income indices -> present component formulas -> distinguish Disability-Adjusted Life Years (DALY) from Quality-Adjusted Life Years (QALY).

SUMMARY HEALTH METRICS: DALY AND QALY
- **Disability-Adjusted Life Year (DALY):** Quantifies the burden of disease, where 1 DALY equals one lost year of healthy life. It combines Years of Life Lost (YLL) due to premature death and Years Lived with Disability (YLD):
  $$	ext{DALY} = 	ext{YLL} + 	ext{YLD}$$
- **Quality-Adjusted Life Year (QALY):** Combines the duration and quality of life resulting from a health intervention, where years of life are multiplied by a health-related utility weight (scaled from 0.0 for death to 1.0 for perfect health):
  $$	ext{QALY} = 	ext{Years of Life Lived} 	imes 	ext{Utility Weight}$$

[REF]
References:
- **Sunder Lal, Adarsh, Pankaj:** Public Health Management. CBS Publishers; Chapter 1, Determinants of Health, Major Health Problems and Disease Burden in India.
- **Park K:** Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine. 28th ed. Jabalpur: Banarsidas Bhanot; 2025. Chapter 2, Concept of Health and Disease.
- **Ministry of Home Affairs:** Census Act 1948 & Census of India.
- **Office of the Registrar General of India:** Sample Registration System (SRS) Bulletins.
[/REF]

subsections.title: Evolution of Health Reforms and Health Policy Development in India
subsections.content:
OVERVIEW OF THE CHAPTER
This chapter traces the historical evolution of health policies and health sector reforms in independent India. It covers the successive phases of healthcare development, starting from the landmark Bhore Committee to modern interventions like the National Health Mission (NHM), Universal Health Coverage (UHC), and the PM Ayushman Bharat Health Infrastructure Mission (PM-ABHIM).

It critically reviews the National Population Policy 2000, National Health Policies of 1983, 2002, and 2017, and highlights the paradigm shifts brought about by the Reproductive and Child Health (RCH) program and the RMNCH+A approach.

DEFINITIONS

HEALTH SECTOR REFORM: A sustained process of fundamental, structural, systemic, and operational changes in healthcare delivery systems aimed at improving equity, efficiency, clinical quality, and population health outcomes.

UNIVERSAL HEALTH COVERAGE (UHC): Ensuring that all people have access to needed promotive, preventive, curative, rehabilitative, and palliative health services of sufficient quality to be effective, while safeguarding users from catastrophic financial hardship.

COMMUNITY NEEDS ASSESSMENT APPROACH (CNAA): A decentralized, participatory planning methodology (formerly designated the Target-Free Approach) where frontline health workers consult the community to establish bottom-up operational targets derived from household survey registries.

SOCIAL MARKETING: The adaptation of commercial marketing concepts to plan, implement, and evaluate programs designed to influence the voluntary behavior of target audiences, improving individual and community health well-being.

CORE CONCEPTS

PHASES OF HEALTH REFORMS IN INDIA
- **Phase I (1947-1972):** Initiated upon recommendations of the Bhore Committee, establishing a basic 3-tier delivery system. Health was integrated with community development, and the National Family Planning Programme began in 1952.
- **Phase II (1972-1977):** Marked by the Minimum Needs Programme (MNP), the Multipurpose Health Worker scheme, and the launch of the Integrated Child Development Services (ICDS).
- **Phase III (1977-1996):** Characterized by the global Alma-Ata Declaration (Health for All by 2000), formulation of the National Health Policy 1983, and rollout of the Universal Immunization Programme (1985).
- **Phase IV (1997-2012):** Driven by the paradigm shift to Reproductive and Child Health (RCH), the National Population Policy 2000, NHP 2002, and the launch of the National Rural Health Mission (NRHM) in 2005.
- **Phase V (2013-Present):** Characterized by the National Health Mission (encompassing NUHM), National Health Policy 2017, Ayushman Bharat (Comprehensive Primary Health Care and PM-JAY), and the PM-ABHIM infrastructure mission.

LANDMARK HEALTH COMMITTEES IN INDIA
- **Bhore Committee (Health Survey and Development Committee, 1946):** Laid the foundation for organized public health in India. Proposed the primary health centre concept, integration of preventive and curative care, abolition of private practice by government doctors, and a 3-tier delivery system.
- **Mudaliar Committee (Health Survey and Planning Committee, 1962):** Evaluated progress since Bhore. Recommended strengthening Primary Health Centres (PHCs) before establishing new ones, consolidating district hospitals, and instituting an All India Health Service.
- **Chadah Committee (1963):** Outlined maintenance-phase arrangements for the National Malaria Eradication Programme, recommending basic health workers to undertake home-visit surveillance covering 10,000 population.
- **Mukherjee Committee (1965 and 1966):** Delinked malaria surveillance from family planning duties, establishing dedicated administrative staff for vertical family planning targets.
- **Jungalwalla Committee (Committee on Integration of Health Services, 1967):** Recommended eliminating private practice for public doctors, equal pay for equal work, unified health cadres, and integration of preventive and curative wings.
- **Kartar Singh Committee (Committee on Multipurpose Workers under Health and Family Planning, 1973):** Replaced vertical unipurpose disease workers with Multipurpose Health Workers (MPHW Male and Female) and redesignated Lady Health Visitors as Health Assistants (Female).
- **Shrivastav Committee (Group on Medical Education and Support Manpower, 1975):** Recommended creating community health volunteers and medical education reorientation, leading to the Village Health Guides Scheme and the Reorientation of Medical Education (ROME) scheme.
- **Bajaj Committee (1986):** Formulated a National Medical and Health Education Policy, recommending uniform national admission standards and health manpower development planning.
- **High Level Expert Group (HLEG, 2011):** Chaired by Prof. K. Srinath Reddy under the Planning Commission; recommended Universal Health Coverage, government health expenditure increase to 2.5% of GDP, cashless primary care, and strengthening public healthcare delivery.

> **EXAM TIP:** Tabulate landmark health committees chronologically (Bhore, Mudaliar, Chadah, Mukherjee, Jungalwalla, Kartar Singh, Shrivastav, Bajaj, HLEG) detailing primary mandate and definitive recommendation -> highlight the multipurpose health worker transition under Kartar Singh and integration under Jungalwalla.

NATIONAL HEALTH POLICY (NHP) EVOLUTION
- **National Health Policy 1983:** Emphasized the Alma-Ata commitment to Health for All by 2000 AD, prioritizing decentralized primary healthcare, population stabilization, and cadre development.
- **National Health Policy 2002:** Addressed public investment deficits, emphasized equity, decentralized healthcare planning, and targeted disease eradication milestones for polio, leprosy, and lymphatic filariasis.
- **National Health Policy 2017:** Framed around Universal Health Coverage (UHC) and preventive-promotive wellness:
  - **Financial Target:** Progressively increase public health expenditure to 2.5% of GDP.
  - **Resource Allocation:** Allocate over two-thirds of health sector resources to primary healthcare.
  - **Life Expectancy:** Increase life expectancy at birth from 67.5 to 70 years by 2025.
  - **Mortality Reductions:** Lower Infant Mortality Rate to 28 by 2019 and Under-5 Mortality Rate to 23 by 2025.
  - **Fertility Goal:** Achieve and maintain a replacement-level Total Fertility Rate (TFR) of 2.1 across all states.
  - **Digital Health:** Establish the National Digital Health Ecosystem to promote interoperability.

NATIONAL POPULATION POLICY (NPP) 2000
- **Immediate Objective:** Meet unmet needs for contraception, health infrastructure, and health personnel, providing integrated service delivery for basic reproductive and child healthcare.
- **Medium-Term Objective:** Bring Total Fertility Rate (TFR) to replacement level (2.1) by 2010 through vigorous intersectoral implementation of operational strategies.
- **Long-Term Objective:** Achieve population stabilization by 2045, at a level consistent with sustainable economic growth, social development, and environmental protection.

NATIONAL RURAL HEALTH MISSION (NRHM 2005) AND NATIONAL HEALTH MISSION (NHM)
Launched in April 2005, NRHM addressed health architecture gaps in 18 high-focus states, subsequently expanded into the National Health Mission (encompassing the National Urban Health Mission):
- **Primary Objective:** Deliver accessible, affordable, accountable, and high-quality healthcare to rural and vulnerable populations.
- **Core Operational Strategies:**
  - **1. Decentralization:** Decentralized health planning through Village Health Sanitation and Nutrition Committees (VHSNCs).
  - **2. Quality Standards:** Quality assurance through Indian Public Health Standards (IPHS).
  - **3. Management Capacity:** Programme Management Units (PMUs) providing dedicated administrative and financial expertise.
  - **4. Flexible Financing:** Flexible pooled financing and untied grants to Sub-Centres, PHCs, and CHCs.
  - **5. Human Resource Reforms:** Human resource multiskilling, contractual staffing, and performance-linked incentives.
- **Grassroots Health Triad:** Coordinated collaboration among the Accredited Social Health Activist (ASHA) for community mobilization, Auxiliary Nurse Midwife (ANM) for clinical immunization and antenatal care, and Anganwadi Worker (AWW) for nutrition surveillance.

[SN]RMNCH+A Approach and 5x5 Continuum of Care Matrix[/SN]

RMNCH+A APPROACH
Reproductive, Maternal, Newborn, Child, and Adolescent Health (RMNCH+A) is an integrated life-cycle strategy under the National Health Mission (NHM). The '+A' explicitly incorporates adolescents. It replaced isolated vertical programs with an unbroken continuum of care across life stages and healthcare service tiers.

The 5x5 Continuum of Care Matrix:
- **Five Life Stages:** Adolescence; Pregnancy and Childbirth; Newborn Period; Childhood; Reproductive Age.
- **Five Service Delivery Platforms:** Community/Household; Outreach (Village Health Sanitation and Nutrition Days); Sub-Health Centre / Ayushman Arogya Mandir; Primary Health Centre; First Referral Unit (FRU) / District Hospital.

Core Operating Principles:
- **Life-Cycle Approach:** Interventions at each life phase directly determine health outcomes in subsequent developmental stages.
- **Continuum of Care:** Unbroken linkage between home, community outreach, primary health facilities, and referral hospitals.
- **Equity and Inclusion:** Targeted outreach to marginalized, geographically isolated, and socioeconomically vulnerable groups.
- **Quality of Care:** Institutional adherence to standardized clinical care protocols and patient dignity.
- **Accountability:** Structured outcome monitoring via digital tracking systems and maternal-perinatal death reviews.

Thirteen UN Commission Life-Saving Commodities:
- **Reproductive Health Commodities:** Female condoms, contraceptive implants, emergency contraceptive pills.
- **Maternal Health Commodities:** Oxytocin, misoprostol, magnesium sulphate, antenatal corticosteroids.
- **Newborn and Child Health Commodities:** Injectable antibiotics, chlorhexidine umbilical wash, neonatal resuscitation devices, dispersible amoxicillin, oral rehydration salts (ORS), and dispersible zinc tablets.

Operational Integration:
Under the Community Needs Assessment Approach (CNAA), village health plans are constructed from household surveys. National programs including the India Newborn Action Plan (INAP), Pradhan Mantri Surakshit Matritva Abhiyan (PMSMA), LaQshya, Home-Based Newborn Care (HBNC), Home-Based Care for Young Child (HBYC), and Rashtriya Bal Swasthya Karyakram (RBSK) function as integrated packages along this continuum.

> **EXAM TIP:** Expand RMNCH+A -> construct the 5x5 continuum of care matrix (5 life stages across 5 delivery platforms) -> list the 5 core operating principles -> classify the 13 life-saving commodities across reproductive, maternal, and child health categories.

[LAQ]India Newborn Action Plan (INAP): Goals, Principles and Strategic Packages[/LAQ]

INDIA NEWBORN ACTION PLAN (INAP)
Launched in September 2014 in alignment with the Global Every Newborn Action Plan (ENAP), INAP aims to eliminate preventable newborn deaths and stillbirths in India.

1. Goals and Quantitative Targets:
- **Target 1 (Neonatal Mortality):** Achieve a single-digit Neonatal Mortality Rate (NMR <9 per 1,000 live births) by 2030.
- **Target 2 (Stillbirth Rate):** Achieve a single-digit Stillbirth Rate (SBR <9 per 1,000 total births) by 2030.

2. Guiding Principles:
- **Integration:** Synergistic alignment with RMNCH+A and National Health Mission mechanisms.
- **Equity:** Prioritizing high-burden districts, tribal populations, and disadvantaged socio-demographic strata.
- **Gender Sensitivity:** Eliminating sex differentials in newborn care and protecting the girl child.
- **Quality of Care:** Institutional adherence to standardized evidence-based clinical protocols.
- **Intersectoral Convergence:** Convergence with ICDS, drinking water, sanitation, and rural development.
- **Accountability and Tracking:** Digital tracking via ANMOL and mandatory Maternal and Perinatal Death Surveillance and Response (MPDSR).

3. Strategic Intervention Packages:
- **Package 1 (Pre-conception and Antenatal Care):** Anemia Mukt Bharat supplementation, screening for gestational diabetes, and minimum four antenatal check-ups under PMSMA.
- **Package 2 (Care during Labour and Childbirth):** Respectful maternity care under LaQshya, active management of third stage of labour (AMTSL), and partograph monitoring.
- **Package 3 (Immediate Newborn Care):** Delayed cord clamping, immediate skin-to-skin contact, thermal protection, and initiation of breastfeeding within one hour.
- **Package 4 (Care of the Healthy Newborn):** Exclusive breastfeeding for six months, zero-dose immunization, and routine warmth maintenance.
- **Package 5 (Care of Small and Sick Newborns):** Managed through a 3-tier institutional network:
  - **Newborn Care Corners (NBCC):** Operational at all 24x7 delivery points and PHCs for immediate resuscitation.
  - **Newborn Stabilization Units (NBSU):** Established at First Referral Units (FRUs) and CHCs for managing uncomplicated neonatal illness and stabilizing low birth weight infants.
  - **Special Newborn Care Units (SNCU):** Dedicated 12 to 20 bedded specialized units at District Hospitals with trained pediatricians, phototherapy, and Kangaroo Mother Care (KMC).
- **Package 6 (Care Beyond Newborn Survival):** Screening for 4Ds (Defects, Deficiencies, Diseases, Developmental delays) under Rashtriya Bal Swasthya Karyakram (RBSK) linked with District Early Intervention Centres (DEIC).

4. Community-Based Home Visit Protocols:
- **Home-Based Newborn Care (HBNC):** Scheduled home visits by ASHAs:
  - **Institutional Deliveries:** Six visits on Days 3, 7, 14, 21, 28, and 42.
  - **Home Deliveries:** Seven visits on Days 1, 3, 7, 14, 21, 28, and 42.
- **Home-Based Care for Young Child (HBYC):** Five additional structured home visits at 3, 6, 9, 12, and 15 months to assess growth faltering, nutritional adequacy, and immunization status.

> **EXAM TIP:** Structure as: Launch year (2014) and ENAP alignment -> Single-digit NMR and SBR targets (<9 by 2030) -> 6 guiding principles -> 6 strategic intervention packages along the continuum of care -> 3-tier facility infrastructure (NBCC, NBSU, SNCU) -> HBNC (6/7 visits) and HBYC (5 visits) community protocols.

PM AYUSHMAN BHARAT HEALTH INFRASTRUCTURE MISSION (PM-ABHIM)
- **Strategic Mandate:** Initiated to develop systemic health resilience, preparing public health systems against emerging epidemics.
- **Key Interventions:** Establishes IT-enabled surveillance, district integrated public health laboratories, critical care hospital blocks in all districts, and expands the One Health institutional network.

ENVIRONMENTAL HEALTH POLICY
- **Air Quality Standards:** Ambient air pollution contributes to approximately 18% of aggregate mortality in India. WHO revised Air Quality Guidelines (2021) established strict annual exposure ceilings for PM2.5 (5 ug/m3) and PM10 (15 ug/m3).

KEY POLICY PRINCIPLES
- **Financing Transformation:** Health Sector Reforms under NRHM transitioned financing from rigid vertical programmatic funding to flexible pooled envelopes.
- **Specialist Human Resource Deficits:** High specialist vacancy rates (approaching 80%) at Community Health Centres remain a primary operational bottleneck.
- **Fiscal Health Allocations:** The 15th Finance Commission recommended state governments allocate over 8% of state annual budgets to health.
- **Social Marketing Framework:** Deploys the 6 Ps (Product, Price, Place, Promotion, Partnership, Policy), demonstrated by the Nirodh and Mala-D subsidized public health distribution networks.

[REF]
References:
- **Sunder Lal, Adarsh, Pankaj:** Public Health Management. CBS Publishers; Chapter 2, Evolution of Health Reforms and Health Policy Development in India.
- **Park K:** Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine. 28th ed. Jabalpur: Banarsidas Bhanot; 2025. Chapter 22, Health Care of the Community & Chapter 23, Health Planning and Management.
- **Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (MoHFW):** National Health Policy 2017.
- **Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (MoHFW):** India Newborn Action Plan (INAP) 2014.
[/REF]

subsections.title: Public Health Management Sciences, Organization of Health Services, Health Management Functions and Resources in Health
subsections.content:
OVERVIEW OF THE CHAPTER
This chapter details the fundamental concepts of health management, bridging medical science with management, behavioral, and social sciences. It explores organizational structures, key management functions (POSDCORB-CIR), inventory control techniques (ABC, VED), human resource management, health economics, and various methods of economic evaluation (CMA, CEA, CBA, CUA).

It highlights the critical shift towards decentralized planning and the specific job descriptions of the grassroots health team in primary care delivery.

DEFINITIONS

MANAGEMENT: A systematic process by which human, material, financial, and temporal resources are organized, activated, and optimized to accomplish defined organizational objectives; operationally defined in health services as executing health tasks through coordinated team effort.

ADMINISTRATION VERSUS MANAGEMENT: Administration establishes organizational policies, broad objectives, and structural frameworks (top-level, decisive); management implements and executes those established policies and directives (middle-level, executive).

BEHAVIORAL SCIENCES: The systematic investigation of human and animal behaviors through controlled empirical observation, categorized into Information Processing Sciences (psychology, cognitive science) and Relational Sciences (sociology, social psychology, anthropology).

MEDICAL SOCIOLOGY: The scientific study of social causes and consequences of health, sickness, and healthcare practices, examining societal structures, customs, family dynamics, and community organizations.

HEALTH FINANCING: The cardinal health system function concerned with resource mobilization, risk pooling, and purchasing of healthcare services to secure equitable population health coverage.

OPPORTUNITY COST: The economic value of benefits forgone by allocating finite resources to a chosen intervention rather than to the next best alternative use.

CORE CONCEPTS

[SN]Principles of Health Management and Administrative Functions[/SN]

ORGANIZATIONAL LAWS IN HEALTH ADMINISTRATION
- **1. Parkinson's Law:** Work expands to fill the temporal duration allocated for its completion.
- **2. Pareto's Principle (80/20 Rule):** Approximately 80% of consequences arise from 20% of causes (e.g., 80% of clinical complaints originate from 20% of service bottlenecks).
- **3. Murphy's Law:** If an operational fault can occur, it will occur; approximately 85% of institutional failures trace to system design flaws, while only 15% result from individual employee error.

THEORETICAL APPROACHES TO MANAGEMENT
- **1. Classical Structural Approach (Theory X):** Assumes workers are inherently disinclined toward labor, requiring strict supervision, centralized authority, and formal hierarchy.
- **2. Human Relations Approach (Theory Y):** Assumes workers are self-directed, motivated, and derive intrinsic fulfillment from work, emphasizing democratic decision-making.
- **3. Human Resource Development Approach:** Focuses on team capacity building, delegation of authority, and reciprocal partnership between management and employees.
- **4. Managerial Grid (Blake and Mouton):** Evaluates leadership style along two axes: Concern for People and Concern for Production (scale 1 to 9), establishing the (9,9) team approach as the optimal operational model.

SYSTEMS FRAMEWORK IN PUBLIC HEALTH
A health system functions as a dynamic open system consisting of:
- **Inputs:** Human personnel (men), financial budgets (money), physical facilities, drugs, equipment (materials), and operational time.
- **Processes and Activities:** Workflow execution including planning, clinical diagnosis, epidemiological surveillance, training, and supervision.
- **Outputs:** Immediate, tangible service units generated, including vaccinations administered, deliveries attended, and staff trained.
- **Effects:** Intermediate population shifts, such as improved health literacy, altered practices, and expanded service coverage.
- **Impacts:** Ultimate population health transformations, including reductions in mortality, morbidity, disability, and fertility rates.

ESSENTIAL MANAGEMENT FUNCTIONS (POSDCORB-CIR)
- **Planning (P):** Delineating community health problems, establishing priority goals, and projecting administrative schedules.
- **Organizing (O):** Structuring activities, defining hierarchies, and allocating responsibilities.
- **Staffing (S):** Recruiting, deploying, training, and developing human resources.
- **Directing (D):** Guiding and motivating personnel through effective leadership.
- **Coordinating (Co):** Harmonizing distinct health units and intersectoral stakeholders.
- **Reporting (R):** Maintaining information flow through records, inspection, and surveillance.
- **Budgeting (B):** Fiscal planning, accounting, and financial control.
- **Controlling (C):** Evaluating actual output against pre-established standards.
- **Innovation (I):** Developing creative, context-specific work methodologies.
- **Representation (R):** Interfacing with external administrative bodies and civic leaders.

PRINCIPLES OF HEALTH MANAGEMENT
