Scatter (dot) diagram. Two continuous variables. The vertical axis is usually the outcome. A cloud along a straight line suggests a linear relationship; no cloud suggests none. It shows strong or weak, positive or negative, correlation by eye.

Other plots a protocol or thesis may need: stem-and-leaf; tree diagram of possible outcomes; box-and-whisker (the box holds the middle 50 percent; each whisker 25 percent; marked are minimum, Q1, median, Q3, maximum, and the interquartile range). Tertile, quartile, pentile, decile and centile (percentile) divide the series into 3, 4, 5, 10 or 100 parts. The median is the 50th centile. Percentile Px = (n + 1) × x / 100.

COMPUTERS IN HEALTH RESEARCH
Computers now sit in every stage, from the protocol to dissemination. This is the applied meaning of the undergraduate competency on computers in epidemiology.

During protocol writing, literature is found through Google Scholar and through PubMed. Sample size can be calculated in Epi Info, Statulator, or similar tools. Epi Info can also sketch a structured questionnaire.

During implementation, electronic capture (for example EpiCollect) is used when the ethics committee has approved it and the field can support it. A spreadsheet can generate random numbers for simple random sampling or for a randomised trial.

For management, EpiData is preferred to a bare spreadsheet because of checks and validation. Basic descriptive statistics and a t-test can be done in a spreadsheet. Other tests are run in EpiData, Epi Info, OpenEpi (free) or in licensed packages (SPSS, Stata). Tables and charts for presentation are commonly drawn in a spreadsheet.

For dissemination, journals now receive manuscripts through online systems. Presentation software is used for oral and poster papers.

The protocol should name the packages that will actually be used, and the tests that will be applied, rather than promising “suitable statistical software”.

CONCLUSION
Collection is experiencing, enquiry or examining. The instrument is written, translated and pre-tested. Entry is controlled. Computers are tools at each stage, not a substitute for a codebook and a locked cupboard.

> **EXAM TIP:** Sources → three families of collection → questionnaire rules → processing (edit, code, master chart) → presentation (table rules; bar and pie for qualitative; histogram, line, scatter for quantitative; ogive for median) → computers stage by stage.

subsections.title: Ethics in Health Research
subsections.content:
OVERVIEW OF THE CHAPTER
Ensuring ethical conduct is not an annexure stapled on after the sample size. It is a condition of doing the study. Indian biomedical and health research involving human participants is governed by the Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR) National Ethical Guidelines for Biomedical and Health Research Involving Human Participants, 2017. Clinical trials of new drugs and related products also follow the New Drugs and Clinical Trials Rules, 2019, and are registered on the Clinical Trials Registry - India (CTRI) before enrolment.

DEFINITIONS
RESEARCH ETHICS: The principles and procedures that protect participants, communities and the integrity of the science while knowledge is generated.
INFORMED CONSENT: A process, not a signature, in which a competent person, after adequate information and comprehension, voluntarily agrees to take part.
ETHICS COMMITTEE (EC): An independent multidisciplinary body that reviews scientific and ethical merit before any participant is approached. Also called Institutional Ethics Committee (IEC) or Institutional Review Board (IRB) in many colleges.
VULNERABILITY: Reduced ability to protect one’s own interests because of limited capacity, power or resources.
ASSENT: Affirmative agreement of a child who can understand something of the study, given in addition to permission from a parent or legally acceptable representative (LAR).
BENEFIT–RISK ASSESSMENT: Judging whether the anticipated benefits to participants or to society justify the risks.

[SN]Informed consent[/SN]

[LAQ]Ethics in health research and the ethics committee[/LAQ]

A SHORT HISTORY, THEN THE INDIAN DOCUMENT
The Nuremberg Code (1947) put voluntary consent at the centre after the wartime experiments. The Declaration of Helsinki of the World Medical Association, first adopted in 1964 and revised from time to time (the latest WMA revision is 2024), states the duties of the physician-researcher to the participant. The Belmont Report (1979) named respect for persons, beneficence and justice.

In India the ICMR issued a policy statement in 1980, ethical guidelines in 2000 and 2006, and the expanded national guidelines in 2017 (released 12 October 2017). There is a dedicated 2017 guideline for research involving children. Later addenda cover special topics (systematic reviews, leftover samples, and others). The 2017 document remains the core national reference for health research with human participants.

The 2017 guidelines start from four basic principles (autonomy, beneficence, non-maleficence and justice) and expand them into twelve general principles, to be applied to biomedical, social and behavioural research for health, including biological material and data.

1. Essentiality. After considering alternatives in the light of existing knowledge, the use of human participants is essential, and an ethics committee independent of the work has agreed.
2. Voluntariness. The participant may agree, refuse or withdraw at any time. The consent process is what protects that right.
3. Non-exploitation. Participants are selected fairly, so that benefits and burdens are not placed arbitrarily. Vulnerable groups have extra safeguards.
4. Social responsibility. The work should not deepen social or historic divisions or disturb harmony in a community.
5. Ensuring privacy and confidentiality. Identity and records are restricted to those authorised. Limited exceptions (for example a court order, or a serious risk to life) are handled with the ethics committee. The right to life can supersede the right to privacy.
6. Risk minimization. All stakeholders, at every stage, reduce risk and arrange care and compensation if harm occurs.
7. Professional competence. Those who plan, conduct, evaluate and monitor the work are qualified and trained for it.
8. Maximization of benefit. The design should make a direct or indirect benefit to participants or to society possible.
9. Institutional arrangements. The host institution has policies for research governance and provides infrastructure, staff, funds and training.
10. Transparency and accountability. Plans and outcomes enter the public domain through registries, reports and publications, while privacy is kept. Conflicts of interest are declared and managed. Records are retained for possible audit.
11. Totality of responsibility. Every stakeholder is bound by the ethical guidelines and the law.
12. Environmental protection. Environment and resources are protected at every stage, in line with existing rules.

INFORMED CONSENT
Three pillars, then documentation: information, comprehension, voluntariness.

Essential information includes purpose and methods; duration; procedures; foreseeable risks and discomforts; reasonably expected benefits; alternatives; confidentiality and its limits; compensation and treatment for research-related harm; freedom to refuse or withdraw without loss of entitled care; whom to contact; and any payment or reimbursement.

The information is given in a language the person understands, with time to ask questions. High-risk work may need a test of understanding. Written consent is the default. A person who cannot sign gives a thumb impression before an impartial witness. A child gives assent when able, and a parent or LAR gives permission. Electronic consent is allowed when the ethics committee has approved the method.

Waiver of consent is exceptional (some retrospective reviews of de-identified records) and is granted by the committee, not assumed by the student. Re-consent is needed when the protocol or the risk changes in a material way. Permission from a community leader or a medical superintendent does not replace individual consent.

SAMPLE CONSENT FORM (WORKED)
A form has two declarations. The wording below is the shape examiners expect, to be printed in the local language and adapted to the study.

Declaration by the participant
By signing below, I (name) agree to take part in a research study entitled “(title)”.
I declare that:
- I have read this information and consent form and understand the contents (or it has been read to me).
- I have had a chance to ask questions and they have been answered.
- Taking part is voluntary. I have not been pressured.
- I may leave the study at any time and will not lose any care I am entitled to.
Signed at (place) on (date). Signature, or mark X if the person cannot sign, with an impartial witness.

Declaration by the researcher
I (name) declare that I explained this document; I encouraged questions and took time to answer them; I am satisfied that the person understands the study.
Signed at (place) on (date).

The information sheet that precedes the form carries the essential elements listed above. A signed form without that sheet is not informed consent.

Privacy is kept by unique codes, locked forms, restricted access, and care with photographs and with qualitative quotes. Payment for time and travel is reimbursement. It is not a purchase of risk. Compensation for research-related injury is a duty in interventional work under Indian rules.

ETHICS COMMITTEE
The committee reviews scientific merit and ethical merit before the first participant is approached. It continues to review, and it may monitor a site.

Composition, as used in examination answers: at least seven members; a chairperson from outside the host institution; a member secretary from the institution; a mix that includes a basic medical scientist, clinicians, a legal expert, a social scientist or ethicist or theologian, and a lay person; attention to gender; and no member with a conflict of interest sitting on that protocol.

The file submitted usually contains the protocol, the participant information sheet, consent forms in the local language, the tools, the investigators’ summaries of training, the CTRI number when the study is a trial, and the plan for insurance or compensation in a trial.

Elements of the review (what the committee actually looks at): scientific merit and whether human participants are essential; risk and benefit; the consent process and the language of the sheet; selection of participants and safeguards for the vulnerable; privacy and data security; compensation for research-related harm; conflict of interest; and, for a trial, registration and insurance. A methodologically weak study that cannot answer its question is also ethically weak: people would be used to no purpose.

The member secretary screens incoming work. Three paths are used:

1. Exemption from review: less than minimal risk (some anonymous educational surveys).
2. Expedited review: minimal risk (review of existing records, a minor change to an already approved protocol).
3. Full committee review: more than minimal risk (blood, invasive tests, an intervention).

The meeting may approve, approve with modifications, or reject. Approval is required before the first participant is approached. Multicentre work may use single-review arrangements that are being developed nationally; the local site remains responsible for local context.

Observational dissertations in Indian medical colleges still require committee approval. They are not “only a survey” in the sense that exempts them.

VULNERABLE GROUPS AND PUBLIC HEALTH RESEARCH
The 2017 guidelines treat vulnerability as reduced ability to protect one’s own interests. Groups named there, and expected in an examination answer, include:

- Children: parental or LAR permission plus assent when the child can understand. A dedicated ICMR guideline for children sits beside the 2017 general text.
- Pregnant women and the foetus: extra justification; no convenience sampling of antenatal clinics for an unrelated question.
- Persons with mental illness or cognitive impairment: capacity is assessed; a LAR acts when capacity is lacking.
- Tribal communities: community-level processes as well as individual consent; the work should not deepen historic harm.
- Hierarchical subordinates (students, employees, prisoners, institutionalised persons): they are easy to recruit and hard to refuse. That is the reason not to use them as a default sample.
- The very poor, sex workers, sexual minorities, and the terminally ill: extra safeguards against inducement and against identification.

They are not to be sampled merely because they sit in the next room. Extra justification and extra safeguards are required.

Public health research (cluster trials, use of routine information systems, work in emergencies) has its own section in the 2017 guidelines. Altered or waived consent may be argued for some evaluations, but only with committee approval and with community engagement. Tuskegee and the wartime camp experiments are the reason this machinery exists. They need only a few lines in an answer; the 2017 principles and the consent process need the rest.

CONCLUSION
A Community Medicine dissertation that interviews village women without a local-language information sheet, or that treats an administrator’s letter as consent, fails ethically even if the statistics are faultless. The twelve principles, the consent process, and the committee are the three parts of a complete answer.

**Mnemonic:** ICE (the consent process)
- I: Information
- C: Comprehension
- E: Enrolment that is voluntary

> **EXAM TIP:** Name the 2017 ICMR guidelines → four basic principles and then the twelve general principles (at least name them; expand essentiality, voluntariness, non-exploitation, privacy, risk minimization) → consent as process (information, comprehension, voluntariness, documentation, waiver, re-consent) → committee composition (seven, external chair) → NDCT 2019 and CTRI if the question is a trial. Keep Nuremberg and Helsinki to a few lines.

subsections.title: Protocol, Thesis, Paper, and Critical Appraisal
subsections.content:
OVERVIEW OF THE CHAPTER
Without dissemination the research process is incomplete. The common format for an original report is known by the acronym IMRAD. The same bones appear, with extra academic clothing, in the MD dissertation, and in a shorter form in a journal article. Reading other people’s papers with the same bones in mind is critical appraisal.

DEFINITIONS
PROTOCOL (PROPOSAL): The plan written before data are collected. It is the contract with the guide, the ethics committee, and, if there is one, the sponsor. It is written in the future tense.
THESIS / DISSERTATION: The examined report of the work the resident actually did. Methods are written in the past tense. Copying the protocol into the thesis without changing tense and without inserting the numbers actually achieved is a common failure.
IMRAD: Introduction, Methods, Results, And Discussion.
VANCOUVER STYLE: The citation method of the International Committee of Medical Journal Editors (ICMJE). References are numbered in the order they appear. Journal titles are abbreviated as in MEDLINE.
CRITICAL APPRAISAL: A structured judgement of whether a paper’s methods support its conclusions, and whether those conclusions apply to the reader’s patients or population.

[SN]IMRAD format[/SN]

[LAQ]Steps in writing a research protocol and thesis[/LAQ]

THE PROTOCOL
A typical outline, to be adapted to the college template, is:

Title (population, place, and design when space allows).
Introduction and rationale: why the problem matters, what is known, what gap remains, why this place.
Question, numbered objectives, and a hypothesis where the design needs one.
Review of literature, arranged by theme or by objective, not as a list of papers in date order.
Methods: design, setting, duration, population, inclusion and exclusion, sample size with formula and inputs, sampling, variables and operational definitions, tools, procedure, outcomes, analysis, quality assurance, ethics.
Work plan (a Gantt chart of months against activities). Typical rows: ethics approval, pre-test, recruitment, follow-up, entry, analysis, writing. Typical columns: months 1 to 12. Shading shows when each row is active. Two activities that need the same person in the same week are a planning error, not a software error.

Budget and its justification. Ordinary heads: personnel (investigator time, field worker, data entry); travel; consumables and investigations; equipment (only what the study must buy); contingency (a small stated percentage); overhead if the institution charges it. Each line has a quantity, a unit cost, and a sentence of justification. A budget that hides a laptop “for the study” when the college already has one will be asked about.

Plan for use of the results (who will hear them).
References in Vancouver form.
Annexes: tools, consent forms, ethics undertaking, Clinical Trials Registry - India receipt if the study is a trial.

When a project is later evaluated, the results are compared with these objectives. If the objectives were vague, evaluation is impossible.

IMRAD FORMAT
Introduction. Why did you study this? What is already known? What is still not known? How will this study fill the gap? The section usually ends with the specific objectives.

Methods (materials and methods). How did you study it? The dictum is that another investigator should be able to repeat the work in another setting from this section alone. Usual headings are: study design; setting; duration; study population and sampling; inclusion and exclusion; sample size (calculated and achieved); procedure; data collection and tools; outcome measures; entry and analysis; quality assurance; ethical considerations (committee approval, consent, privacy).

Reporting guidelines help completeness, and should be named only when they fit the design: CONsolidated Standards Of Reporting Trials (CONSORT) for trials, Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology (STROBE) for observational studies, Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) for reviews, Consolidated criteria for reporting qualitative research (COREQ) for interviews and focus groups. A student project that is not a trial should not be dressed in CONSORT language.

Results. What did you find? Findings are given in text, tables and figures, in the order of the objectives. Begin with the flow of participants and a baseline table. Give numbers with percentages. Titles sit above tables and legends below figures. The section does not interpret, and it does not repeat every cell in prose.

Discussion. What does it mean? Important findings are summarised and possible reasons offered. Similarities and contradictions with other studies are discussed with reasoning. Strengths and limitations are stated. Directions for further work may be suggested. The conclusion is aligned with the objectives. This is the one section in which a narrative voice is allowed, provided it does not invent findings that the results section does not contain.

References. Every resource cited in the text appears at the end, in Vancouver style.

INTERPRETING THE STUDY FINDINGS
A statistically significant result is not automatically a clinically useful one. Two teaching examples make the point.

A 2 mm Hg difference in systolic pressure between drug A and drug B may become “significant” when each group grows from 100 to 300. The difference is still 2 mm Hg. The clinician has to say whether that difference matters.

Conversely, a large difference in cure (30 percent versus 60 percent) may fail to reach P less than 0.05 when each group has only 20 patients, and become significant at 30 per group. The size of the effect was always large. The first study was under-powered.

Hence interpretation asks more than “was P below 0.05?”

For a descriptive study: give the point estimate with a confidence interval, not the point alone. The interval is the range in which the reference population value is likely to lie.

For an analytical study, five questions:

1. What is the measure of association (relative risk, odds ratio, difference of means)?
2. What is its confidence interval (precision)?
3. What is the chance of a Type I error (P)?
4. What systematic error remains (selection, measurement, confounding)?
5. What is the utility: is the association likely to be causal (Bradford Hill criteria below); if an intervention, is it acceptable, safe, and affordable?

Criteria of causal association (Bradford Hill), in the same order and sense as in the Epidemiology chapter:
1. Temporal association. The cause precedes the effect. Order and the length of the interval both matter. This is the essential criterion. A concurrent cohort shows it best.
2. Strength of association. Relative risk in a cohort; odds ratio in a case-control study.
3. Specificity. One factor, one disease. The hardest and the weakest criterion.
4. Consistency. The finding repeats in other places and by other hands.
5. Biological plausibility. Anatomy or physiology can credit the link.
6. Coherence. The association sits with other known facts.
7. Dose–response (biological gradient). More exposure, more effect.
8. Reversibility. Removing the cause lowers the risk (ex-smokers versus current smokers for lung cancer).

A randomised trial is the strongest single study for causation. An ecological study is the weakest for testing a risk-factor link. Indirect association (high altitude and goitre, via iodine) must not be sold as direct cause.

P says nothing about the strength of an association. A very small P with a relative risk of 1.05 is not a public health finding. Association is not causation until the causal criteria have been considered. Chance error is handled by the test and the interval. Bias is handled by the design and by an honest discussion.

Results state what was found. Discussion says what it means. Mixing the two is the commonest fault in a first draft.

THE THESIS
Most Indian universities expect, in something like this order. The purpose of each part is what matters.

- Certificates, declaration, acknowledgements: who did the work and that it is the candidate’s.
- Contents, lists of tables and figures, abbreviations: so a examiner can find a table without hunting.
- Introduction: why this problem, here, now. Ends by pointing at the gap.
- Review of literature: what is known, arranged by theme or by objective, including work that disagrees.
- Aims and objectives: the numbered promises against which the rest will be judged.
- Material and methods: enough to repeat the study. Past tense. The numbers actually achieved.
- Results: what was found, in the order of the objectives. No interpretation.
- Discussion: meaning, other studies, strengths, limits.
- Summary and conclusion: a short close that answers the objectives and does not invent a new claim.
- Recommendations: only what the data can support, written so that a programme officer could act.
- References: Vancouver, every in-text number present.
- Annexures: tool, consent, ethics letter, an excerpt of the master chart.

Practical habits that save months: write the methods while the study is running; lock the analysis plan before looking at unexpected P values; keep dated copies of protocol amendments; show tables to the guide and the statistician before drafting the discussion.

THE ARTICLE
A paper is a conversion of the thesis, not a reduction of font size. The target journal’s instructions and word limit govern the draft. A structured abstract and Medical Subject Headings keywords help retrieval. Authorship follows the four ICMJE criteria (substantial contribution; drafting or critical revision; final approval; accountability). Gift authorship is misconduct. The ICMR Policy on Research Integrity and Publication Ethics (RIPE), 2019, is the Indian institutional reference for plagiarism, fabrication and authorship disputes. Journals that charge authors and skip genuine peer review are not a place to send, or to cite as if they were indexed science.

A short checklist before submission:
- Title represents the content and names the design when it helps.
- Abstract covers objectives, design, subjects, setting, outcomes, results and a conclusion that does not outrun the data.
- Introduction states the question or hypothesis and ties the literature to that question.
- Methods describe design, sample, measurements, analysis and ethics in enough detail to repeat the work.
- Results give numbers with the statements; tables are clear; no opinions in this section.
- Discussion covers strengths and limits, brings past findings in, and does not generalise beyond the sample and the tool.
- References are in the journal’s style and were actually read.
- Terminology and units are uniform. The tone is that of a careful worker, not a salesman.

[SN]Critical appraisal of a journal article[/SN]

CRITICAL APPRAISAL
Publication is not proof. The method decides how far the conclusion can be believed. Evaluation can be done by the author before submission, by peer reviewers, or by a reader who must decide whether to change practice. A qualitative impression (“the paper is good”) is weak. Walking the paper under nine headings is stronger.

1. Title: does it represent the content and the breadth of the study?
2. Authors: are affiliations clear?
3. Abstract: does it cover every component, with actual numbers, and without a conclusion larger than the study?
4. Introduction and literature: is the question or hypothesis stated? Are key references present? Are concepts defined? Is the “big picture” given?
5. Materials and methods (the heaviest heading): are variables, design, bias control, procedure, population, sample size, setting, and tests described, and are they appropriate?
6. Results: do numbers accompany the statements? Are tables efficient and accurate? Is this section free of opinion?
7. Discussion and conclusion: are pluses and minuses covered? Is the talk about this study? Do conclusions stay inside the design, the tool and the sample?
8. References: a reasonable number, actually used, in standard form.
9. General considerations: sections labelled, terms uniform, tone rigorous, writing clear.

Then two practical questions. How would you use this paper in your own setting? What two suggestions would you send the author?

A working sequence for a short note can still be the nine reader’s questions: question; design fit; who was studied; measurement and blinding; confounding; effect size and interval, not only P; whether conclusions stay inside the data; funding and conflict; whether practice here should change.

Design-specific checklists (CONSORT, STROBE, CASP) are memory aids. In an examination a structured paragraph is worth more than the sentence “the study is good.”

CONCLUSION
The protocol is the plan. IMRAD is the report. The thesis is the examined form of that report. The article is the public form. Appraisal is how a doctor remains a critical consumer. University work fails more often on muddled objectives, a missing ethics letter and a broken reference list than on the absence of an exotic test.

**Mnemonic:** IMRAD
- I: Introduction (why)
- M: Methods (how)
- R: Results (what)
- D: Discussion (so what)

> **EXAM TIP:** For a protocol or thesis question, write the headings in order (title, rationale, objectives, methods including sample size and ethics, Gantt, budget, IMRAD for the report). For IMRAD, use the four questions: why, how, what, what does it mean. For appraisal, walk the nine points rather than giving a vague opinion.

subsections.title: Framework and How to Answer a Legislation Paper
subsections.content:
OVERVIEW OF THE CHAPTER

Public health legislation operationalizes the State's constitutional responsibility to protect, preserve, and promote the health of its populace. In India, health legislation constitutes the institutional and constitutional backbone of public health administration. Derived from the fundamental right to life and personal liberty under Article 21 and the Directive Principles of State Policy (notably Article 47, which directs the State to improve public health and nutrition), statutes translate broad policy declarations into justiciable duties.

Although Entry 6 of the State List (List II) in the Seventh Schedule vests public health, sanitation, and hospitals primarily in State Legislatures, critical domains including vital statistics, inter-state epidemic containment, drugs, labour welfare, and environmental protection are governed by parliamentary enactments on the Concurrent and Union Lists. Public health law establishes enforceable standards, safeguards reproductive autonomy, regulates clinical establishments, and provides emergency legal mandates for disease containment.

DEFINITIONS

PUBLIC HEALTH LAW: The body of legal rules and statutory provisions enacted by the State to regulate individual, professional, and commercial conduct in order to protect and promote population health, prevent disease and injury, and govern healthcare delivery systems. Public health statutes are enacted by Parliament or State Legislatures and operationalized through notified subordinate rules and regulations.

ACT: Primary legislation enacted by Parliament or a State Legislature and promulgated upon receiving the assent of the President of India or the Governor of the State.

RULES AND REGULATIONS: Subordinate legislation framed by the executive branch (Central or State Government) or a statutory regulatory body to operationalize the substantive provisions of a parent Act.

CODE: A comprehensive consolidating statute that repeals, harmonizes, and replaces multiple pre-existing statutes within a defined domain, exemplified by India's four Labour Codes of 2020.

ORDINANCE: An executive decree with the force of an Act of Parliament or State Legislature, promulgated by the President or Governor when the respective legislature is not in session, subject to subsequent legislative ratification.

INTERNATIONAL HEALTH REGULATIONS (IHR) 2005: A legally binding international agreement under the auspices of the World Health Organization (WHO) that establishes statutory obligations for State Parties to prevent, detect, assess, notify, and respond to public health emergencies of international concern.

[SN]Public health legislation in India[/SN]

[LAQ]Scope and provisions of public health legislations aimed at protecting health of people in India[/LAQ]

CONSTITUTIONAL BASIS
The Constitution of India provides the fundamental legal architecture for health policy and legislation. While the term 'health' is not expressly enumerated as an explicit fundamental right in Part III, progressive judicial interpretation by the Supreme Court has firmly subsumed the right to health and medical care under Article 21 (Right to Life and Personal Liberty). Key constitutional touchstones include:

- **Article 21 (Protection of Life and Personal Liberty):** Encompasses the right to live with human dignity, access to timely emergency medical care, reproductive autonomy, and environmental sanitation.
- **Article 38 (Promotion of Social Welfare):** Mandates the State to secure a social order for the promotion of the welfare of the people and eliminate inequalities in facilities and opportunities.
- **Article 39 (State Policy Directives):** Directs state policy toward securing the health and strength of workers, tender age of children, and protection against exploitation.
- **Article 42 (Maternity Relief and Just Work Conditions):** Mandates provision for just and humane conditions of work and maternity relief.
- **Article 47 (Duty of the State to Raise Nutrition and Public Health):** Establishes the improvement of public health, raising the level of nutrition and standard of living, and prohibition of intoxicating drinks and injurious drugs as primary duties of the State.
- **Articles 14 and 15 (Equality and Non-Discrimination):** Guarantee equality before the law and prohibit discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex, or place of birth in access to public services and healthcare.

SEVENTH SCHEDULE (LEGISLATIVE COMPETENCE)
Legislative jurisdiction over health is divided among the three lists of the Seventh Schedule of the Constitution:

- **Union List (List I):** Covers subjects of national and cross-border importance, including the decennial census (Entry 69), port quarantine and marine hospitals (Entry 28), inter-state migration and quarantine (Entry 81), patents and intellectual property (Entry 49), and central regulatory agencies.
- **State List (List II):** Entry 6 explicitly vests 'Public health and sanitation; hospitals and dispensaries' in State Legislatures. Consequently, several central model laws (such as the Clinical Establishments Act, 2010) require statutory adoption by individual States under Article 252.
- **Concurrent List (List III):** Both Parliament and State Legislatures possess legislative competence. Key entries include vital statistics and registration of births and deaths (Entry 30), population control and family planning (Entry 20A), drugs and poisons (Entry 19), prevention of infectious or contagious diseases spreading across states (Entry 29), labour welfare and social security (Entry 24), and factories (Entry 36). Where conflict arises between Central and State legislation on Concurrent subjects, Central law prevails under Article 254.

TYPES OF LEGISLATIVE INSTRUMENTS

| Instrument | Competent Authority | Illustrative Public Health Example |
|---|---|---|
| Act | Parliament or State Legislature | Mental Healthcare Act, 2017; Epidemic Diseases Act, 1897 |
| Rules | Central or State Government under statutory rule-making powers | Medical Termination of Pregnancy Rules, 2003 (as amended 2021) |
| Regulations | Statutory Autonomous Authorities | Food Safety and Standards Regulations; National Medical Commission Regulations |
| Code | Parliament, consolidating pre-existing statutes | Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020 |
| International Legal Instrument | World Health Assembly / States Parties | International Health Regulations (IHR), 2005 |

SYSTEMATIC EIGHT-DOMAIN CLASSIFICATION OF PUBLIC HEALTH LEGISLATION
Public health enactments in India are classified systematically into eight functional domains:

1. **Reproductive, Maternal, and Sex-Selection Law:** Medical Termination of Pregnancy (MTP) Act, 1971 (amended 2021); Pre-Conception and Pre-Natal Diagnostic Techniques (PCPNDT) Act, 1994; Surrogacy (Regulation) Act, 2021; Assisted Reproductive Technology (ART) (Regulation) Act, 2021.
2. **Child Protection, Feeding, and Education Law:** Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (POCSO) Act, 2012; Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015; Child and Adolescent Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act, 1986 (amended 2016); Prohibition of Child Marriage Act, 2006; Infant Milk Substitutes (IMS) Act, 1992 (amended 2003); Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education (RTE) Act, 2009.
3. **Women's Welfare, Protection, and Dignity:** Maternity Benefit Act, 1961 (amended 2017); Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act (PWDVA), 2005; Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961; Immoral Traffic (Prevention) Act (ITPA), 1956; Commission of Sati (Prevention) Act, 1987.
4. **Mental Health, Disability, HIV, and Vulnerable Populations:** Mental Healthcare Act (MHCA), 2017; Rights of Persons with Disabilities (RPwD) Act, 2016; Human Immunodeficiency Virus and Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndrome (Prevention and Control) Act, 2017; Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act, 2019; National Trust Act, 1999.
5. **Food, Drugs, Tobacco, and Substance Regulation:** Food Safety and Standards Act (FSSA), 2006; National Food Security Act (NFSA), 2013; Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940; Cigarettes and Other Tobacco Products Act (COTPA), 2003; Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances (NDPS) Act, 1985; Drugs and Magic Remedies (Objectionable Advertisements) Act, 1954.
6. **Epidemics, Disasters, and International Health Security:** Epidemic Diseases Act, 1897 (amended 2020); Disaster Management Act (DMA), 2005; International Health Regulations (IHR), 2005.
7. **Occupational Health, Industrial Safety, and Labour Welfare:** Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020; Code on Social Security, 2020 (transitioning from the Factories Act, 1948 and Employees' State Insurance Act, 1948).
8. **Environmental Sanitation, Professional Regulation, and Vital Events:** Environment (Protection) Act, 1986; Bio-Medical Waste Management Rules, 2016; National Medical Commission (NMC) Act, 2019; Clinical Establishments (Registration and Regulation) Act, 2010; Consumer Protection Act, 2019; Registration of Births and Deaths (RBD) Act, 1969 (amended 2023); Transplantation of Human Organs and Tissues Act (THOTA), 1994 (amended 2011).

HISTORICAL FOUNDATIONAL STATUTES AND MODERN SUCCESSORS
Modern public health legislation has systematically reformed colonial and post-independence statutes to establish contemporary, rights-based, and technologically integrated standards:

1. **Food Safety:** The Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954 has been repealed and replaced by the comprehensive Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 (enforced 2011).
2. **Reproductive Rights:** The Medical Termination of Pregnancy Act, 1971 was substantially updated by the 2021 Amendment, expanding gestational thresholds, liberalizing contraceptive failure provisions, and protecting privacy.
3. **Social Security:** The Employees' State Insurance Act, 1948 and Maternity Benefit Act, 1961 are integrated into the Code on Social Security, 2020.
4. **Occupational Safety:** The Factories Act, 1948, Mines Act, 1952, and Plantations Labour Act, 1951 are subsumed under the Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020.
5. **Juvenile Care and Protection:** The Children Act, 1960 and Juvenile Justice Act, 1986 were superseded by the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015.
6. **Civil Registration:** The Registration of Births and Deaths Act, 1969 was reinforced by the 2023 Amendment, establishing an integrated digital national database.
7. **Epidemic Powers:** The Epidemic Diseases Act, 1897 was fortified by the 2020 Amendment, criminalizing acts of violence against healthcare personnel.
8. **Mental Healthcare:** The custodial Mental Health Act, 1987 was repealed and replaced by the rights-based Mental Healthcare Act, 2017.

**Mnemonic:** RCWM FEOX
- **R:** Reproductive, maternal, and sex-selection legislation
- **C:** Child protection and nutrition
- **W:** Women's safety, maternity, and anti-violence
- **M:** Mental health, disability, and vulnerable populations
- **F:** Food safety, drug regulation, and tobacco control
- **E:** Epidemics, disaster management, and global health security
- **O:** Occupational health and industrial safety
- **X:** Cross-cutting statutes (Environment, professional ethics, vital events, organ transplantation)

> **EXAM TIP:** When structuring a comprehensive answer on public health legislation:
> 1. Open with the formal definition and constitutional framework, citing Articles 21 and 47 alongside Seventh Schedule legislative competence (State List Entry 6 versus Concurrent List Entry 29/30).
> 2. Present the systematic eight-domain classification table (RCWM FEOX), specifying at least two landmark Acts per domain with years of enactment and key operative provisions.
> 3. Highlight contemporary transitions: note the repeal of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act 1954 by FSSA 2006, the replacement of the Mental Health Act 1987 by MHCA 2017, and the operationalization of the four Labour Codes (21 November 2025; Central Rules May 2026).
> 4. Emphasize that statutory efficacy depends upon state-level notification of rules, dedicated inspection machinery, and inter-sectoral administrative coordination.

[REF]Reference: Constitution of India, Articles 14, 15, 21, 38, 39, 42, 47 and Seventh Schedule; Ministry of Labour and Employment, Notification on Labour Codes, 21 November 2025; Park K. Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine. 28th ed. Jabalpur: Banarsidas Bhanot; Chapter 12; Kishore J. National Health Programs of India. 12th ed. New Delhi: Century Publications; 2017.[/REF]

subsections.title: Reproductive, Maternal, and Sex-Selection Law
subsections.content:
OVERVIEW OF THE CHAPTER

Reproductive and maternal health legislation provides the statutory architecture for reproductive autonomy, safe pregnancy termination, prohibition of sex selection, and regulation of assisted reproduction in India. Foundational enactments include the Medical Termination of Pregnancy (MTP) Act, 1971 (comprehensively modernized by the 2021 Amendment) and the Pre-Conception and Pre-Natal Diagnostic Techniques (Prohibition of Sex Selection) Act, 1994 (amended in 2003).

Complementary governance of assisted reproductive procedures is established under the Surrogacy (Regulation) Act, 2021 and the Assisted Reproductive Technology (Regulation) Act, 2021. Together, these statutes protect maternal life, uphold bodily autonomy, eliminate gender-biased sex selection, and establish strict ethical oversight over clinical reproductive technologies.

DEFINITIONS

REGISTERED MEDICAL PRACTITIONER (RMP): A medical practitioner possessing a recognized medical qualification under the National Medical Commission Act, 2019, whose name is entered in the State Medical Register or the National Medical Register, and who possesses the prescribed postgraduate training or experience in gynaecology and obstetrics as defined under the MTP Rules.

PRENATAL DIAGNOSTIC TECHNIQUE: Any diagnostic test or procedure, including ultrasonography, foetoscopy, maternal serum sampling, chorionic villus sampling, or amniocentesis, conducted on a pregnant woman to detect chromosomal, genetic, or congenital abnormalities, or to determine foetal sex.

ALTRUISTIC SURROGACY: A surrogacy arrangement in which no financial remuneration, fee, compensation, or monetary incentive is provided to the surrogate mother or her dependents, excluding reimbursement of necessary medical expenses and prescribed health insurance coverage during pregnancy and post-partum recovery.

[SN]MTP Act[/SN]

[LAQ]Medical Termination of Pregnancy Act[/LAQ]

MEDICAL TERMINATION OF PREGNANCY ACT, 1971

The Medical Termination of Pregnancy Act, 1971 liberalized abortion law in India by decriminalizing pregnancy termination under specified medical, eugenic, and humanitarian conditions. The Act came into force on 1 April 1972.

The Medical Termination of Pregnancy (Amendment) Act, 2021 substantially reformed this framework by raising gestational limits, expanding access to unmarried women, establishing State Medical Boards for late-gestation anomalies, and creating statutory penalties for breaches of patient privacy.

OBJECT AND SCOPE
The statutory objective is to reduce preventable maternal mortality and morbidity resulting from unsafe clandestine abortions. The Act guarantees access to safe, legal pregnancy termination by qualified practitioners in certified medical facilities while safeguarding patient confidentiality and reproductive choice.

GROUNDS FOR TERMINATION OF PREGNANCY
A pregnancy may be terminated by a Registered Medical Practitioner when an opinion is formed in good faith that one of the following statutory grounds exists:

1. **Therapeutic Ground:** Continuance of the pregnancy would involve a risk to the life of the pregnant woman or of grave injury to her physical or mental health.
2. **Eugenic Ground:** Substantial risk exists that if the child were born, it would suffer from serious physical or mental abnormalities causing severe handicap.
3. **Humanitarian Ground:** Pregnancy is alleged by the woman to have been caused by rape, where the resultant anguish is statutorily presumed to constitute grave injury to mental health.
4. **Failure of Contraceptive Method:** Pregnancy occurs as a result of failure of any device or method used by any woman or her partner for the purpose of limiting family size or spacing births. The 2021 Amendment extended this statutory presumption of mental anguish to any woman and her partner, removing the earlier restriction to married couples.
5. **Socio-Economic Environment:** In assessing the risk of injury to maternal health, the practitioner may take into account the woman's actual or reasonably foreseeable social and economic environment.

**Mnemonic:** TEHFS
- **T (Therapeutic):** Risk to life or grave injury to physical/mental health
- **E (Eugenic):** Substantial risk of severe physical or mental handicap in the newborn
- **H (Humanitarian):** Alleged rape or sexual assault (anguish presumed grave injury)
- **F (Failure of Contraception):** Failure of contraceptive device/method in any woman or her partner
- **S (Socio-economic):** Account taken of actual or reasonably foreseeable environment

GESTATION LIMITS AND STATUTORY OPINION REQUIREMENTS

| Gestational Age | Practitioner Opinion Required | Eligible Circumstances and Grounds |
|---|---|---|
| Up to 20 weeks | One Registered Medical Practitioner (RMP) | Any statutory ground under the Act (therapeutic, eugenic, humanitarian, contraceptive failure, socio-economic) |
| 20 to 24 weeks | Two Registered Medical Practitioners (RMPs) | Restricted strictly to eligible vulnerable categories specified under Rule 3B of the MTP Rules |
| Beyond 24 weeks | State-level Medical Board | Diagnosis of substantial foetal abnormalities certified by the statutory Medical Board |
| Any gestation | One Registered Medical Practitioner (RMP) | Immediate life-saving emergency under Section 5 to prevent maternal mortality |

CATEGORIES OF WOMEN ELIGIBLE FOR TERMINATION UP TO 24 WEEKS (RULE 3B)
Under Rule 3B of the Medical Termination of Pregnancy (Amendment) Rules, 2021, termination between 20 and 24 weeks requires the concurrent opinion of two RMPs and is restricted to:

- **Survivors of Sexual Assault:** Women who have experienced rape, sexual assault, or incest.
- **Minors:** Pregnant females below eighteen years of age.
- **Change in Marital Status:** Women experiencing a change of marital status during the ongoing pregnancy through widowhood or divorce.
- **Major Physical Disabilities:** Women with permanent physical disability (minimum 40% benchmark disability under the RPwD Act).
- **Mental Illness:** Mentally ill women, including those diagnosed with mental retardation.
- **Substantial Foetal Malformations:** Foetuses with malformations presenting substantial risk of serious handicap.
- **Vulnerable Situations:** Women with pregnancies in disaster, humanitarian crisis, or declared emergency settings.

**Mnemonic:** SM-CPMFH (Survivors of assault, Minors, Change in marital status, Physical disability, Mental illness, Foetal malformation, Humanitarian disaster)

STATE-LEVEL MEDICAL BOARD
For pregnancies exceeding 24 weeks, termination on grounds of substantial foetal malformation requires approval from a State Medical Board. Each State and Union Territory constitutes one or more Medical Boards comprising:

- **Gynaecologist:** One specialist gynaecologist or obstetrician.
- **Paediatrician:** One qualified paediatrician.
- **Radiologist or Sonologist:** One specialist radiologist or sonologist.
- **State-Notified Members:** Other medical specialists notified by the State Government.
- **Mandate:** The Board examines the woman and diagnostic investigations, issuing its decision within three working days.

FACILITY CERTIFICATION AND CONFIDENTIALITY
- **Approved Places:** Termination may only be performed in government-maintained hospitals or facilities approved by the Government or District-Level Committee.
- **Emergency Exception:** Under Section 5, the requirement for approved facility and second opinion does not apply when termination is immediately necessary to save the woman's life.
- **Privacy Protection:** Section 5A strictly prohibits revealing the name or particulars of a woman whose pregnancy was terminated, except to persons authorized by law. Violations carry imprisonment up to one year, a fine, or both.

> **EXAM TIP:** When writing on the MTP Act, emphasize the 2021 Amendment updates: single RMP opinion up to 20 weeks, two RMP opinions for 20-24 weeks restricted to Rule 3B categories, State Medical Board review beyond 24 weeks for severe foetal anomalies, extension of contraceptive failure to unmarried women, and Section 5A statutory privacy protections (imprisonment up to 1 year and/or fine).

[SN]PCPNDT Act[/SN]

PRE-CONCEPTION AND PRE-NATAL DIAGNOSTIC TECHNIQUES ACT, 1994
The Pre-Conception and Pre-Natal Diagnostic Techniques (Prohibition of Sex Selection) Act, 1994 (originally enacted as the PNDT Act and amended in 2003 to include pre-conception techniques and prohibit sex selection) is India's principal statute against female foeticide.

STATUTORY OBJECTIVES
The Act prohibits sex selection before or after conception and regulates prenatal diagnostic techniques exclusively for detecting genetic, metabolic, chromosomal, and congenital anomalies, thereby preventing female foeticide and correcting the skewed Child Sex Ratio (CSR).

OPERATIVE PROVISIONS
- **Section 6 (Absolute Prohibition of Sex Selection):** Prohibits the use of any prenatal diagnostic technique, including ultrasonography, for determining or communicating foetal sex, and bans sex selection prior to or following conception.
- **Mandatory Registration:** Every Genetic Counselling Centre, Genetic Laboratory, and Genetic Clinic (including ultrasound clinics and imaging centres) must obtain registration from the Appropriate Authority.
- **Mandatory Form F:** A comprehensive statutory declaration (Form F) must be completed for every ultrasound or prenatal diagnostic procedure performed on a pregnant woman, documenting clinical indications, written consent, and declarations of non-disclosure.
- **Informed Consent and Non-Disclosure:** Written informed consent must be secured in the patient's language. Communicating foetal sex to the pregnant woman, relatives, or any other person by words, signs, symbols, or documentation is prohibited.
- **Ban on Advertisements (Section 22):** Prohibits advertising facilities or techniques for sex determination or sex selection across print, electronic, and internet media.
- **Enforcement Machinery:** Three-tier Appropriate Authorities (Central, State, and District) assisted by Advisory Committees. The District Appropriate Authority (typically the District Magistrate or Chief Medical Officer) possesses powers of entry, search, seizure of equipment, and cancellation of registration.
- **Maintenance of Records:** All clinical logs, consent forms, and Form F records must be preserved for a minimum period of two years and until final disposal of any related legal proceedings.
- **Penalties:** Stringent criminal penalties apply to practitioners, proprietors, and service providers, including imprisonment up to three years and fines for first offences, with deregistration upon conviction.

PUBLIC HEALTH SIGNIFICANCE
The PCPNDT Act addresses the severe demographic crisis of female foeticide and declining child sex ratios. In public health administration, it complements the MTP Act: while MTP legalizes safe termination for maternal health and autonomy, PCPNDT strictly prevents diagnostic tools from being diverted to female foeticide.

> **EXAM TIP:** Differentiate MTP from PCPNDT clearly: MTP enables legal termination on healthcare grounds, whereas PCPNDT prohibits foetal sex determination and sex selection. Core exam elements include Section 6 prohibition, mandatory Form F documentation, registration of all ultrasound facilities, District Appropriate Authority inspection and seizure powers, and minimum 2-year record retention.

[SN]Surrogacy Regulation Act[/SN]

SURROGACY (REGULATION) ACT, 2021
The Surrogacy (Regulation) Act, 2021 establishes statutory oversight of surrogacy practice across India. The Act prohibits commercial surrogacy and permits exclusively altruistic surrogacy for legally eligible couples with certified medical infertility.

KEY STATUTORY PROVISIONS
- **Prohibition of Commercial Exploitation:** Commercial surrogacy, buying or selling human gametes or embryos, and exploitation or commercial compensation of surrogate mothers are strictly prohibited and penalised.
- **Eligibility for Intending Couple:** The couple must be legally married Indian citizens; the woman must be aged 23 to 50 years and the man aged 26 to 55 years; and they must possess a Certificate of Essentiality indicating proven medical infertility issued by the District Medical Board.
- **Eligibility for Surrogate Mother:** The surrogate mother must be an ever-married woman having a living child of her own, aged 25 to 35 years; she may act as a surrogate only once in her lifetime; and she must be provided comprehensive health insurance coverage for 36 months.
- **Regulatory Boards:** National Assisted Reproductive Technology and Surrogacy Board and State-level Boards formulate policy and oversee implementation.
- **Judicial Clearance:** Parentage and custody of the surrogate child require a formal order from a First Class Judicial Magistrate.

> **EXAM TIP:** Summarize Surrogacy Act with five key anchors: altruistic surrogacy only (commercial banned), intending couple age bands (female 23-50, male 26-55) with certified infertility, surrogate mother criteria (married with living child, 25-35 years, single surrogacy episode), 36-month health insurance, and Magistrate parentage order.

[SN]ART Act[/SN]

ASSISTED REPRODUCTIVE TECHNOLOGY (REGULATION) ACT, 2021
The Assisted Reproductive Technology (Regulation) Act, 2021 regulates clinics and banks providing assisted reproductive technologies, ensuring ethical practice, professional standards, and safety of gamete donors and commissioning individuals.

OPERATIVE PROVISIONS
- **Mandatory Registration:** All ART clinics and gamete banks must register under the National Registry of Assisted Reproductive Technology and Surrogacy.
- **Eligibility of Commissioning Parties:** The commissioning woman must be aged between 21 and 50 years, and the commissioning man between 21 and 55 years.
- **Donor Protection and Screening:** Gamete donors must undergo mandatory medical and genetic screening. A woman may donate oocytes only once in her lifetime, with retrieval capped at a statutory limit, and gametes from a single donor cannot be supplied to multiple commissioning parties.
- **Sex Selection Prohibition:** Absolute prohibition on using ART procedures for sex selection, pre-implantation genetic diagnosis for sex, or sex-selective embryo transfer.
- **Shared Architecture:** Functions in coordination with the Surrogacy (Regulation) Act, 2021 under common National and State Boards.

> **EXAM TIP:** Core points for ART Act: mandatory registration of clinics and banks under the National Registry, commissioning age criteria (woman 21-50, man 21-55), single oocyte donation episode, mandatory genetic screening of donors, absolute ban on sex selection, and oversight by National ART and Surrogacy Boards.

[REF]Reference: Medical Termination of Pregnancy Act, 1971 (amended 2021); MTP Rules, 2003 (amended 2021); Pre-Conception and Pre-Natal Diagnostic Techniques Act, 1994 (amended 2003); Surrogacy (Regulation) Act, 2021; Assisted Reproductive Technology (Regulation) Act, 2021 (India Code / Gazette of India); Park K. Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine. 28th ed. Jabalpur: Banarsidas Bhanot; Chapter 12; Kishore J. National Health Programs of India. 12th ed. New Delhi: Century Publications; 2017.[/REF]

subsections.title: Child Protection, Feeding, and Education Law
subsections.content:
OVERVIEW OF THE CHAPTER

Child health and protection legislation in India establishes a multi-tiered legal framework safeguarding the child across survival, protection, nutrition, development, and education. Medical practitioners and public health administrators encounter these statutes in clinical emergencies, medico-legal assessments, institutional care inspections, and community nutrition programmes.

Foundational statutes include the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (POCSO) Act, 2012, the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015, the Child and Adolescent Labour Act, 1986 (amended 2016), the Prohibition of Child Marriage Act, 2006, the Infant Milk Substitutes Act, 1992, and the Right to Education Act, 2009. Together, these enactments translate constitutional protections under Articles 15, 21, 21A, and 39 into enforceable rights.

DEFINITIONS

CHILD (POCSO ACT, 2012): Any person below the age of eighteen years, irrespective of sex or gender.

CHILD IN CONFLICT WITH LAW: A child who is alleged or found to have committed an offence and has not completed eighteen years of age on the date of commission of such offence.

CHILD IN NEED OF CARE AND PROTECTION: A child defined under the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015 who is orphaned, abandoned, surrendered, destitute, living without subsistence, suffering from abuse or exploitation, or at imminent risk of harm.

ADOLESCENT: A person who has completed fourteen years of age but has not completed eighteen years of age, under the Child and Adolescent Labour Act.

INFANT MILK SUBSTITUTE: Any food product marketed or commercially represented as a partial or total replacement for breast milk, whether or not suitable for that purpose.

[SN]POCSO Act[/SN]

PROTECTION OF CHILDREN FROM SEXUAL OFFENCES ACT, 2012
The Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (POCSO) Act, 2012 is a gender-neutral special criminal statute enacted to protect children from offences of sexual assault, sexual harassment, and pornography, while providing child-friendly judicial and medical procedures.

CLASSIFICATION OF OFFENCES UNDER POCSO ACT
- **Penetrative Sexual Assault:** Penetrative sexual acts committed against a child, attracting stringent minimum statutory sentences.
- **Aggravated Penetrative Sexual Assault:** Penetrative assault committed under aggravating circumstances, including offences by persons in positions of trust or authority (police officers, medical personnel, teachers), in institutional settings, during disasters, or against a child with physical or mental disabilities.
- **Sexual Assault and Aggravated Sexual Assault:** Non-penetrative physical sexual acts committed with sexual intent.
- **Sexual Harassment:** Non-physical conduct involving sexual remarks, gestures, stalking, or exhibitionism.
- **Child Pornography Offences:** Using a child for pornographic representation, recording, facilitating, or possessing child sexual abuse material.

MANDATORY REPORTING (SECTION 19)
- **Statutory Duty to Report:** Any individual, including a treating medical practitioner or hospital administrator, who has knowledge or apprehension that an offence under the Act has been committed, is legally mandated to report the matter to the Special Juvenile Police Unit or the local police station.
- **Criminal Penalty for Non-Reporting:** Failure to report an offence under Section 19 constitutes an independent statutory offence punishable with imprisonment up to six months, a fine, or both.
- **Evidentiary Protection:** Reporting in good faith under Section 19 does not attract civil or criminal liability for breach of professional secrecy.

MEDICAL EXAMINATION AND EMERGENCY TREATMENT
- **Consent Architecture:** Medical examination is conducted with the informed consent of the child, parent, or lawful guardian, and must be performed by a woman doctor if the child is female.
- **Non-Denial of Emergency Care:** Healthcare facilities and practitioners cannot deny, defer, or delay emergency medical treatment pending registration of a police case or legal formalities.
- **Comprehensive Clinical Protocol:** Treatment includes immediate first-aid, injury documentation, collection of forensic evidence, post-exposure prophylaxis for Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV), and emergency contraception where clinically indicated.
- **Minimization of Trauma:** The child must not be subjected to repeated medical examinations; reports are transmitted directly to the Investigating Officer and the Special Court.

CHILD-FRIENDLY SPECIAL COURTS
- **Designated Courts:** Each district establishes a Special Court (or designates a Court of Session) to ensure speedy adjudication.
- **Procedural Safeguards:** Trials are conducted in-camera; aggressive or humiliating cross-examination of the child is prohibited; and children are accompanied by parents, interpreters, or support persons.
- **Confidentiality:** Disclosure of the child's identity, school, residence, or family in print, electronic, or social media is strictly prohibited.

> **EXAM TIP:** POCSO Act high-yield points: universal age definition (under 18 years), gender-neutral character, five offence tiers (penetrative assault, sexual assault, harassment, pornography, aggravated forms), Section 19 mandatory reporting (failure penalised with up to 6 months imprisonment), statutory prohibition against denying emergency care, and Special Courts with identity protection.

[SN]Juvenile Justice Act 2015[/SN]

JUVENILE JUSTICE (CARE AND PROTECTION OF CHILDREN) ACT, 2015
The Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015 consolidates and reforms laws relating to children alleged and found to be in conflict with law, and children in need of care and protection, repealing the earlier Juvenile Justice Acts of 1986 and 2000.

TWO STREAMS AND STATUTORY AUTHORITIES

| Stream | Target Category | Competent Statutory Authority | Composition of Authority |
|---|---|---|---|
| Child in Conflict with Law | Alleged or proven to have committed an offence; aged under 18 years on date of offence | Juvenile Justice Board (JJB) | Principal Magistrate (Judicial Magistrate First Class) and two social workers (at least one woman) |
| Child in Need of Care and Protection | Destitute, orphaned, abandoned, surrendered, abused, or exploited child | Child Welfare Committee (CWC) | Chairperson and four members with child welfare expertise (at least one woman) |

HEINOUS OFFENCES AND THE 16-18 AGE BAND

Under Section 15 of the Act, when a heinous offence (attracting a minimum sentence of seven years or more) is alleged to have been committed by a child who has completed sixteen years of age, the Juvenile Justice Board conducts a mandatory preliminary assessment regarding the child's physical and mental capacity, ability to comprehend consequences, and surrounding circumstances.

Based on this assessment, the Board may transfer the case to the Children's Court for trial as an adult. Transfer is never automatic; preliminary evaluation by the Board is a mandatory statutory prerequisite.

CHILD PROTECTION SAFEGUARDS
- **Observation Homes:** Apprehended children are housed in observation homes or special homes, not regular police lock-ups or adult prisons.
- **Adoption Architecture:** Regulates centralized, legal, and non-exploitative adoption procedures through the Central Adoption Resource Authority (CARA).
- **Rehabilitation Framework:** Mandates institutional and community-based rehabilitation, foster care, sponsorship, and after-care services monitored by the Child Welfare Committee.

> **EXAM TIP:** Present the JJ Act 2015 around its two parallel statutory tracks: Juvenile Justice Board (JJB) for Children in Conflict with Law, and Child Welfare Committee (CWC) for Children in Need of Care and Protection. For 16-18 year-olds accused of heinous crimes, emphasize that adult trial requires a mandatory preliminary assessment under Section 15 and is not automatic.

[SN]Child labour Act[/SN]

CHILD AND ADOLESCENT LABOUR (PROHIBITION AND REGULATION) ACT, 1986
The Child and Adolescent Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act, 1986 (amended substantially in 2016) establishes the statutory legal regime governing employment of young persons in India.

OPERATIVE PROVISIONS
- **Absolute Prohibition for Children (Under 14 Years):** Complete ban on employing children below fourteen years in any occupation or process. Only two narrow statutory exceptions apply: helping family enterprises outside school hours and during vacations, or working as an artist in audio-visual entertainment and sports, provided such work does not affect schooling or involve hazardous processes.
- **Prohibition in Hazardous Occupations for Adolescents (14-18 Years):** Adolescents are prohibited from working in hazardous occupations and processes listed in the Schedule (including mining, inflammable substances, and hazardous industries).
- **Harmonization with RTE Act:** The 2016 Amendment aligned the child labour prohibition floor age with the compulsory school age (14 years) under the Right to Education Act, 2009.
- **Liability and Rehabilitation:** Employers and occupiers face cognizable criminal penalties. Rescued children are rehabilitated through the Child and Adolescent Labour Rehabilitation Fund and reintegrated into formal schooling.

> **EXAM TIP:** Core distinctions under the 2016 Amendment: Children below 14 are banned from all employment (with two conditional exceptions: non-hazardous family enterprises outside school and artistic entertainment); adolescents aged 14-18 are banned from scheduled hazardous occupations and processes.

[SN]Prohibition of Child Marriage Act[/SN]

PROHIBITION OF CHILD MARRIAGE ACT, 2006
The Prohibition of Child Marriage Act, 2006 provides for the prohibition of child marriage, protection of victims, and punishment for perpetrators.

STATUTORY PROVISIONS
- **Prescribed Minimum Age:** Minimum age of marriage is twenty-one years for males and eighteen years for females under current enacted law.
- **Legal Voidability:** Child marriages are voidable at the option of the contracting party who was a child at solemnisation, exercisable by filing a petition within two years of attaining majority.
- **Void Marriages:** Marriages involving trafficking, deceit, kidnapping, or force are void ab initio.
- **Penalties:** Imposes rigorous imprisonment up to two years and fines on any adult male marrying a child, persons who solemnize or direct child marriages, and parents or guardians promoting or permitting child marriage.
- **Child Marriage Prohibition Officers (CMPO):** Executive officers empowered to prevent solemnization, gather evidence, and file injunction petitions.

PUBLIC HEALTH IMPLICATIONS
Early marriage drives adolescent pregnancies, high maternal mortality, severe maternal anaemia, low birth weight, infant malnutrition, and educational discontinuation. Public health strategies link the enforcement of this Act with adolescent reproductive health interventions.

> **EXAM TIP:** Note the statutory ages: 21 for males and 18 for females. Highlight that child marriages are legally voidable rather than automatically void in routine cases, with criminal liability attaching to the adult male spouse, solemnizing priests, and promoting guardians.

[SN]IMS Act[/SN]

INFANT MILK SUBSTITUTES (IMS) ACT, 1992
The Infant Milk Substitutes, Feeding Bottles and Infant Foods (Regulation of Production, Supply and Distribution) Act, 1992 (amended in 2003) operationalizes the World Health Organization International Code of Marketing of Breast-milk Substitutes into Indian domestic law.

STATUTORY PROHIBITIONS
- **Advertising Ban:** Total ban on advertising, promoting, or marketing infant milk substitutes, feeding bottles, or infant foods through print, television, electronic, or institutional channels.
- **Labeling Restrictions:** Containers and packaging must not depict infant pictures, graphics, or idealizing illustrations; packaging must display prominent warnings regarding the unmatched superiority of mother's milk.
- **Prohibition of Inducements:** Prohibits commercial discounts, price inducements, free samples, or promotional gifts to retail customers.
- **Ban on Healthcare Sponsorships:** Healthcare professionals, hospitals, and medical associations are prohibited from accepting gifts, research grants, conference sponsorships, or financial contributions from commercial infant food manufacturers.
- **Educational Materials:** Informational brochures must clearly emphasize the biological benefits of exclusive breastfeeding and the health hazards of unnecessary bottle feeding.

> **EXAM TIP:** Remember the four statutory bans under the IMS Act (1992, amended 2003): no advertising of substitutes; no infant pictures or idealizing images on labels; no commercial incentives or free samples; and absolute ban on gifts, sponsorships, and funds to healthcare workers and medical societies.

[SN]Right to Education Act[/SN]

RIGHT OF CHILDREN TO FREE AND COMPULSORY EDUCATION ACT, 2009
The Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education (RTE) Act, 2009 gives statutory effect to Article 21A of the Constitution, guaranteeing free and compulsory education for all children between six and fourteen years of age.

KEY PROVISIONS
- **Universal Entitlement:** Every child aged 6 to 14 years has a fundamental legal right to free and compulsory elementary education (Classes I to VIII) in a neighbourhood school.
- **Inclusion of Disadvantaged Groups:** Private unaided schools must reserve at least 25% of entry-level seats for children belonging to economically weaker sections and disadvantaged groups, with state reimbursement.
- **Student Welfare Standards:** Prohibits screening procedures for admission, capitation fees, physical punishment, and mental harassment.
- **School Infrastructure and Governance:** Mandates prescribed student-teacher ratios, separate girl-boy sanitation facilities, safe drinking water, and functional School Management Committees (SMCs) comprising predominantly parents.

PUBLIC HEALTH SIGNIFICANCE
Female and maternal literacy represents one of the most powerful social determinants of health, directly correlating with reduced infant and maternal mortality, improved child nutrition, higher immunization uptake, and optimal family planning.

> **EXAM TIP:** Summarize RTE Act: Article 21A operationalization, age band 6-14 years, free and compulsory elementary schooling, mandatory 25% quota in private schools for disadvantaged groups, ban on capitation fees and screening tests, and its role as a fundamental social determinant of public health.

[REF]Reference: Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012; Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015; Child and Adolescent Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act, 1986 (amended 2016); Prohibition of Child Marriage Act, 2006; Infant Milk Substitutes Act, 1992 (amended 2003); Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act, 2009 (India Code); Park K. Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine. 28th ed. Jabalpur: Banarsidas Bhanot; Chapter 12; Kishore J. National Health Programs of India. 12th ed. New Delhi: Century Publications; 2017.[/REF]

subsections.title: Women: Maternity, Violence, Traffic, and Dowry
subsections.content:
OVERVIEW OF THE CHAPTER

Legislation for women's health, social security, and protection against violence forms an interconnected statutory system safeguarding bodily autonomy, maternal recovery, economic stability, and freedom from domestic and commercial exploitation. These enactments operationalize constitutional mandates under Article 15 (protective discrimination), Article 21 (right to live with dignity), and Article 42 (maternity relief).

The principal statutes governing this domain comprise the Maternity Benefit Act, 1961 (amended 2017), the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005, the Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961 (amended 1986), the Immoral Traffic (Prevention) Act, 1956, and the Commission of Sati (Prevention) Act, 1987.

DEFINITIONS

MATERNITY BENEFIT: Statutory payment of average daily wages provided to a woman worker during her period of absence immediately preceding delivery, on the day of delivery, and following childbirth, as prescribed under the Maternity Benefit Act, 1961.

DOMESTIC VIOLENCE: Any act, omission, or conduct of the respondent that harms, injures, or endangers the health, safety, life, limb, or well-being of the aggrieved woman, encompassing physical, sexual, verbal, emotional, and economic abuse, under the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005.

DOWRY: Any property, valuable security, or cash given or agreed to be given directly or indirectly by one party to a marriage to the other party, or by parents, at, before, or any time after the marriage in connection with the marriage, excluding customary gifts, under the Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961.

[SN]Maternity Benefit Act[/SN]

MATERNITY BENEFIT ACT, 1961
The Maternity Benefit Act, 1961 regulates the employment of women in factories, mines, plantations, and commercial establishments with ten or more employees, providing paid leave and health safeguards during perinatal periods. The Maternity Benefit (Amendment) Act, 2017 modernized these protections.

STATUTORY MATERNITY LEAVE ENTITLEMENTS

| Eligibility Category | Statutory Duration of Paid Leave | Maximum Pre-Natal Leave Allocation |
|---|---|---|
| Women with fewer than two surviving children | 26 weeks | Maximum 8 weeks preceding expected delivery date |
| Women with two or more surviving children | 12 weeks | Maximum 6 weeks preceding expected delivery date |
| Adopting mothers (child under three months of age) | 12 weeks | Commences from the date child is handed over |
| Commissioning mothers (biological mothers using surrogacy) | 12 weeks | Commences from the date child is handed over |

OPERATIVE PROVISIONS UNDER THE 2017 AMENDMENT
- **Mandatory Creche Facilities (Section 11A):** Every establishment employing fifty or more employees must provide a functional creche within prescribed distance; female workers are permitted four visits daily, inclusive of rest intervals.
- **Work from Home Provisions:** Employers may permit work from home following completion of maternity leave where the nature of work permits, based on mutual agreement.
- **Nursing Breaks:** Daily nursing breaks are permitted until the child completes fifteen months of age.
- **Code Harmonization:** These maternity entitlements are consolidated into Chapter VI of the Code on Social Security, 2020.

> **EXAM TIP:** Present Maternity Benefit Act with key numerical parameters: 26 weeks paid leave for first two surviving children (up to 8 weeks prenatal), 12 weeks for third child onwards, 12 weeks for adopting and commissioning mothers, mandatory creche for establishments with 50+ employees (4 daily visits), and integration into the Code on Social Security, 2020.

[SN]Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act[/SN]

PROTECTION OF WOMEN FROM DOMESTIC VIOLENCE ACT, 2005
The Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005 (PWDVA) is a specialized civil enactment providing emergency, non-punitive judicial relief to women facing domestic abuse within a shared household.

STATUTORY DEFINITION OF DOMESTIC ABUSE (PS-VEE)
- **Physical Abuse:** Any act causing bodily pain, harm, or danger to life, limb, or physical development, including assault and criminal intimidation.
- **Sexual Abuse:** Conduct of a sexual nature that abuses, humiliates, degrades, or violates the dignity of a woman.
- **Verbal and Emotional Abuse:** Insults, ridicule, humiliation, name-calling, and repetitive threats of physical harm or abandonment.
- **Economic Abuse:** Depriving the woman of economic or financial resources, disposal of household assets, alienation of stridhan, or denial of maintenance.

**Mnemonic:** PS-VEE
- **P:** Physical abuse
- **S:** Sexual abuse
- **V:** Verbal and emotional abuse
- **E:** Economic abuse

STATUTORY ENFORCEMENT MACHINERY AND MEDICAL DUTIES
- **Right to Reside in Shared Household:** Section 17 establishes that every woman in a domestic relationship has the statutory right to reside in the shared household, protecting her against arbitrary eviction.
- **Protection Officers and Service Providers:** State Governments appoint Protection Officers in each district to assist courts, prepare Domestic Incident Reports, and coordinate shelter and medical care.
- **Mandatory Duties of Medical Facilities (Section 7):** When an aggrieved woman approaches a medical facility, the person in charge must provide medical treatment, maintain clinical records, and transmit a medical report to the Protection Officer and Magistrate upon request.
- **Judicial Orders by Magistrate:** The Magistrate may grant Protection Orders (Section 18), Residence Orders (Section 19), Monetary Relief (Section 20), Temporary Child Custody Orders (Section 21), and Compensation Orders (Section 22).

> **EXAM TIP:** Focus on the civil, rights-oriented nature of PWDVA: define the four abuse domains using PS-VEE, emphasize the Section 17 right to shared household, highlight Section 7 duties of medical facilities to document and treat without refusal, and list the five magistrate relief orders (protection, residence, monetary, custody, compensation).

[SN]Dowry Prohibition Act[/SN]

DOWRY PROHIBITION ACT, 1961
The Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961 criminalizes the giving, taking, demanding, or abetting of dowry in connection with marriage.

KEY PROVISIONS
- **Offences and Penalties:** Giving, taking, or abetting the taking of dowry carries a mandatory minimum sentence of five years imprisonment and a fine of not less than Rs 15,000 or the value of the dowry, whichever is higher, under the 1986 Amendment.
- **Demand of Dowry:** Demanding dowry directly or indirectly from parents or guardians is an independent offence punishable with imprisonment from six months to two years and fines.
- **Exemptions:** Customary presents given to the bride or bridegroom at the time of marriage without any demand are permissible, provided they are entered in a formal signed list as prescribed under the Rules.
- **Public Health Intersection:** Dowry harassment is a major upstream determinant of domestic violence, severe physical injuries, severe depression, and suicidal deaths among young women.

> **EXAM TIP:** Key elements of Dowry Prohibition Act: criminalizes giving, taking, demanding, and abetting dowry; 1986 minimum penalty is 5 years imprisonment and Rs 15,000 fine; customary gifts must be recorded in statutory signed lists; connects directly to PWDVA in maternal injury and mental health questions.

[SN]Immoral Traffic Prevention Act[/SN]

IMMORAL TRAFFIC (PREVENTION) ACT, 1956
The Immoral Traffic (Prevention) Act, 1956 (ITPA, amended in 1986) is the principal Central statute suppressing commercial sexual exploitation and trafficking in persons.

STATUTORY FRAMEWORK
- **Scope and Focus:** Covers all persons commercially exploited for prostitution, irrespective of gender. The Act penalizes brothel keeping, living on earnings of prostitution, procuring, trafficking, and detaining individuals in brothels, focusing on exploiters rather than the prostituted individual.
- **Protective Custody and Rehabilitation:** Mandates establishment of Protective Homes and Corrective Institutions by State Governments for rescue, rehabilitation, and medical care of victims.
- **Public Health Linkages:** ITPA interfaces with HIV/AIDS prevention programmes and targeted interventions under the National AIDS Control Programme (NACP), requiring strict adherence to medical confidentiality and voluntary testing.
