The same algebra with QALYs is the incremental cost-utility ratio; examinations still call it an ICER.

In words: what extra must be paid for each extra unit of health?

COST-EFFECTIVENESS THRESHOLD: The ICER at which the extra health from a programme is judged just worth the extra cost, because it equals the health that would be displaced if those resources were taken from existing care. It is an estimate of opportunity cost inside a constrained budget.

Think of the threshold as the extra health you would lose if you took money away from existing services to fund the new programme. If the new programme buys less health than that, it should not displace current care.

NET MONETARY BENEFIT (NMB): Effect × threshold minus cost. Positive NMB means the programme is cost-effective at that threshold.

NET HEALTH BENEFIT (NHB): Effect minus (cost / threshold). The same rule expressed in health units.

NMB converts health into money at the threshold and then subtracts cost. NHB converts cost into the health that money could have bought elsewhere, and then subtracts that from the health the programme actually gives. Both answers should point the same way.

[SN]Incremental cost-effectiveness ratio[/SN]

[LAQ]Interpreting cost-effectiveness results for a health programme[/LAQ]

INCREMENTAL, NOT AVERAGE
The average ratio (cost of A / effect of A) compares A with doing nothing at zero cost and zero effect. That is the wrong comparison if current practice already costs money and already produces health. Always subtract the comparator.

If a district already runs a programme, the relevant question is not "what does the new programme cost per unit of health from scratch?" The relevant question is "compared with what we already do, how much extra money, and how much extra health?"

Example algebra (numbers are for method, not for citation as Indian policy). Comparator cost 14,200, effect 10.93 QALYs. New strategy cost 15,250, effect 12.66 QALYs. Extra cost 1,050. Extra QALYs 1.73. ICER ≈ 607 per QALY. A further, more expensive strategy is then compared with the new strategy, not with doing nothing.

[SN]Cost-effectiveness plane[/SN]

COST-EFFECTIVENESS PLANE
Plot extra effect on the horizontal axis and extra cost on the vertical axis. The origin is the comparator.

| Quadrant | Extra effect | Extra cost | Decision |
|---|---|---|---|
| I (north-east) | Higher | Higher | Need a threshold: is extra effect worth extra cost? |
| II (south-east) | Higher | Lower | Dominant: accept (more health, less money) |
| III (south-west) | Lower | Lower | Need a threshold: is the saving worth the health given up? |
| IV (north-west) | Lower | Higher | Dominated: reject |

The origin is "what we do now." Moving right means more health. Moving up means more cost.

- North-east: better health, but more expensive. A threshold is needed before saying yes.
- South-east: better health and cheaper. Accept it. This is strong dominance in favour of the new option.
- South-west: cheaper, but worse health. A threshold is needed before saying that the saving is worth the health given up.
- North-west: worse health and more expensive. Reject it.

A dashed threshold line through the origin with slope equal to the threshold (cost per unit effect) splits quadrant I (and III). Points below the line in quadrant I are cost-effective at that threshold. Points above are not.

Draw a straight line from the origin whose slope is the maximum extra cost you are willing to pay for one extra unit of effect. In the north-east quadrant, a point below that line means the extra health is cheap enough to buy. A point above the line means the extra health costs more than the threshold, so the same money would buy more health if left in existing care.

DOMINANCE
Strong dominance: an option is both more costly and less effective than another. Drop it.
Extended (weak) dominance: an option is more costly per extra effect than a mixture of two others. In a league table of several alternatives, drop extendedly dominated options before computing ICERs along the efficient sequence.

Strong dominance is the north-west case: worse and more expensive. Extended dominance is less obvious. If option B sits between A and C, but costs more per extra unit of effect than moving from A to C, drop B. Mixing some of A with some of C would give more health for the same extra money than using B. After dropping dominated options, calculate ICERs only along the remaining efficient sequence, each time against the next cheaper undominated option, not against doing nothing.

Uncertainty means a result rarely sits in the exact centre of a quadrant. Confidence ellipses and cost-effectiveness acceptability curves (CEACs) describe the probability that an option is cost-effective as the threshold varies. Name them in a long answer; do not invent a curve in a short note.

Costs and effects are estimated with error, so the ICER is not a single certain number. A confidence ellipse is a cloud of likely extra-cost and extra-effect pairs around the point estimate. A cost-effectiveness acceptability curve plots, for each possible threshold, the probability that the new option is the cost-effective choice. In a long answer, name these tools. In a short note, stating that uncertainty should be reported is enough.

THRESHOLD AS OPPORTUNITY COST
A threshold is not "what society thinks a life is worth" in the abstract. Under a fixed health budget, spending more on programme A means spending less on programme B. The health lost in B is the opportunity cost. If the extra health from A is smaller than that loss, A should not displace B.

Indian context:
India does not publish a single statutory cost-per-QALY threshold of the kind used by the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) for all public purchasing. Health Technology Assessment in India (HTAIn) still compares extra cost with extra effect. District decisions use the same logic in natural units: extra rupees per extra child immunised, per extra sputum-positive patient treated, per extra controlled hypertensive, judged against other uses of National Health Mission (NHM) funds.

Do not quote a rupee-per-QALY cut-off as if it were an Indian law.

There is no official rupee figure that can be written as the Indian cost-per-QALY threshold. HTAIn still asks the incremental question: how much extra cost for how much extra health. At district level the same idea is used with ordinary programme units, and the comparison is with other uses of the same NHM money.

NMB AND NHB
ICER is a ratio. Ratios misbehave when extra effect is very small or negative. NMB and NHB turn the same information into a linear score: choose the option with the highest NMB (or NHB) at the stated threshold. They also make it easier to add options and to handle uncertainty.

NMB = (E × k) − C
NHB = E − (C / k)
where k is the threshold.

When extra effect is near zero, the ICER shoots toward infinity and becomes hard to interpret. When extra effect is negative, the sign of the ratio can mislead. Net monetary benefit avoids that problem by giving each option a score: health valued at the threshold, minus cost. Choose the highest score at the stated threshold. Net health benefit is the same ranking, written in health units rather than money.

> **EXAM TIP:** Write ICER formula with C1, C0, E1, E0 named → draw the four-quadrant plane and label dominate / reject / threshold → one sentence that the threshold is health displaced, not a price of life → India: no single statutory k; still use incremental thinking. For a short note, formula plus plane is enough.

LEAGUE TABLES AND ABUSE
A league table of cost per QALY from mixed studies is not a menu. Studies differ in perspective, comparator, time horizon, discount rate, and setting. Transferring a ratio from one country to another without checking prices, practice, and epidemiology is a standard flaw (see the ten-question appraisal checklist).

A published list of "cost per QALY" figures from different papers cannot be used as a shopping list. Each study used its own comparator, prices, time horizon, and discount rate. A ratio from another country cannot be copied into an Indian decision unless those differences have been checked.

KEY POINTS
- Always incremental: extra cost / extra effect.
- Quadrant II: accept. Quadrant IV: reject. I and III: need k.
- Threshold k estimates opportunity cost of displaced care.
- NMB and NHB are linear forms of the same rule.
- India: HTAIn uses cost-effectiveness; there is no single national k to memorise as law.

FORMULAS AND CALCULATIONS
ICER = (C1 − C0) / (E1 − E0)
NMB = E × k − C
NHB = E − C / k

subsections.title: Models, Uncertainty, and Critical Appraisal
subsections.content:
OVERVIEW OF THE CHAPTER
Economic evaluation needs a vehicle: a single clinical study (trial or observational set) or a decision-analytic model that brings evidence from several sources. This section covers decision trees, Markov models, sensitivity analysis, and a ten-question checklist for reading a published study. It ends with a worked scaffold for planning an economic evaluation of a programme, including the examination question on the economic impact of a pandemic on the health sector.

DEFINITIONS
DECISION-ANALYTIC MODEL: A quantitative structure that represents alternative courses of action, the chance events that follow, and the costs and consequences of each path, so that expected cost and expected effect can be compared.

DECISION TREE: A model drawn from left to right: decision nodes (squares) where a choice is made, chance nodes (circles) where probabilities apply, and terminal nodes where costs and effects are attached. Folding back (expected value at each chance node) yields the expected cost and effect of each decision.

MARKOV MODEL: A model for problems that unfold over repeated cycles. Individuals occupy mutually exclusive health states (for example well, sick, dead). Each cycle they may stay or move according to transition probabilities. Useful when events can recur (hospitalisation, relapse) or when timing stretches beyond a one-off tree.

SENSITIVITY ANALYSIS: A method to assess how changes in input variables affect the results of a model. One-at-a-time analysis varies one parameter while holding others. Global analysis varies many parameters together. Probabilistic sensitivity analysis (often implemented as Monte Carlo simulation) draws parameters from distributions and reports the distribution of results.

CHEERS: Consolidated Health Economic Evaluation Reporting Standards. A reporting guideline for published evaluations. The ten-question checklist below is the appraisal tool to use in an examination answer.

[SN]Decision tree[/SN]

[LAQ]Plan and conduct an economic evaluation of a health programme[/LAQ]

[LAQ]Economic evaluation of the impact of a pandemic on the health sector[/LAQ]

DECISION TREES
A tree forces the analyst to name alternatives and pathways. Example (cancer chemotherapy versus supportive care).

Decision: chemotherapy or no chemotherapy.
Chance after chemotherapy: neutropenia with fever (probability p1) or not (1 − p1).
Given fever: hospitalisation, outpatient treatment, or no further treatment, each with a probability and a cost.
Chance after no chemotherapy: fever from disease (p2) or not.

Each terminal node has a cost and an effect (survival, QALYs, or a clinical endpoint). Expected cost of a branch = sum of (probability of path × cost of path). Expected effect is computed the same way. Compare expected costs and effects incrementally.

Trees become bushy when events repeat or when time is long. Then a Markov structure is cleaner: states, cycles (monthly, yearly), transitions, and a time horizon long enough to capture major costs and effects (often lifetime for mortality-changing interventions).

> **EXAM TIP:** Define tree → square / circle / triangle (or terminal) → one drawn example with two branches and probabilities that add to 1 → expected value in one line. Say when to switch to Markov (recurrence, long horizon).

[SN]Sensitivity analysis[/SN]

SENSITIVITY ANALYSIS
Point estimates pretend to be certain. They are not. Characterise uncertainty.

1. One-at-a-time (OAT): vary the discount rate, a key probability, a unit cost, or a utility between a low and a high plausible value. Easy to report. Misses interactions.
2. Global: move several parameters at once (for example a worst-case and best-case scenario).
3. Probabilistic (Monte Carlo): each uncertain parameter has a distribution. Many random draws produce a cloud of ICERs on the cost-effectiveness plane and a CEAC.

Also report: statistical uncertainty when patient-level cost and effect data exist; heterogeneity (results for relevant subgroups, not only the average patient); structural uncertainty (would a different model change the decision?).

If conclusions flip when a plausible input changes, do not treat the base case as a fact. If they do not flip, the decision is robust to that input.

> **EXAM TIP:** Define → OAT versus global versus probabilistic in a three-row table → "if the decision flips, say so." Do not write code.

TEN QUESTIONS FOR A SOUND EVALUATION
Use this list to appraise a paper and to plan a study. It is the examination skeleton.

1. Was a well-defined question posed in answerable form? Both costs and effects; comparison of alternatives; perspective stated; population and subgroups defined; time horizon appropriate.
2. Was a comprehensive description of the competing alternatives given? Who did what to whom, where, and how often? Was doing nothing considered? Were relevant alternatives omitted?
3. Was the effectiveness of the programmes established? Trial, systematic review, or observational data, with bias discussed. Economic evaluation cannot create effectiveness by itself.
4. Were all important and relevant costs and consequences identified? Range wide enough; capital and operating costs; perspectives covered.
5. Were costs and consequences measured accurately in appropriate physical units before valuation? Sources of utilisation; joint costs handled; omitted items justified.
6. Were costs and consequences valued credibly? Sources of prices and of preference weights named; market distortions adjusted if a societal valuation is claimed.
7. Were costs and consequences adjusted for differential timing? Discounted to present value; rate justified.
8. Was an incremental analysis performed? Extra cost compared with extra effect, not average ratios only.
9. Was uncertainty adequately characterised? Statistics, sensitivity analysis, subgroups.
10. Did presentation and discussion cover issues of concern to users? Intelligent use of ratios; comparison with other studies; generalisability; equity and ethics; implementation and freed resources; implications of uncertainty for further research.

**Mnemonic:** QUEST VALUE

QUEST (the question and the facts):
- Q: Question answerable (alternatives, perspective, population)
- U: Unbiased description of options (who does what to whom)
- E: Effectiveness established (not assumed)
- S: Scope of costs and consequences identified
- T: Tallied in physical units before money

VALUE (the valuation and the decision):
- V: Valued credibly
- A: Adjusted for timing (discount)
- L: Listed incrementally (ICER, not only averages)
- U: Uncertainty characterised
- E: Explained for users (generalisability, equity, implementation)

The ten questions map onto two words: QUEST and VALUE.

PLANNING AN EVALUATION (GENERAL)
1. Decision problem and perspective.
2. Population and subgroups.
3. Alternatives, including current practice and, if relevant, doing nothing.
4. Time horizon long enough for major intended and unintended effects.
5. Effectiveness evidence (trial or synthesis).
6. Costs: identify, measure, value (health sector, patient, others as per perspective).
7. Consequences: natural unit, QALY, or money, matching the method.
8. Discounting.
9. Model or trial-based analysis.
10. Uncertainty and subgroups.
11. Presentation: incremental results, plane, NMB/NHB if a threshold is used, limits, implementation.

PANDEMIC IMPACT ON THE HEALTH SECTOR (WORKED LAQ)
Question: plan and conduct an economic evaluation of the impact of a pandemic (for example coronavirus disease 2019) on the health sector.

This is not only a cost-of-illness total. A full evaluation still needs alternatives: for example "response as implemented" versus "no additional response," or versus an alternative intensity (earlier non-pharmaceutical measures, different testing strategy, different vaccination timing). If the paper also asks for public-health lessons, keep those clinical and health-system points separate from the economics limb.

Perspective. Health system for hospital and programme costs; societal if household OOPE, deaths, long disability, and lost production are in scope. State which and why.

Time horizon. At least the pandemic waves plus a tail for long complications, postponed elective care, and vaccination programme costs. Discount if the tail exceeds one year.

Costs to identify.
- Direct health-sector: testing, personal protective equipment, intensive care, oxygen, vaccines, staff overtime, new isolation wards, information systems.
- Displaced care: cancelled elective surgery and missed chronic-disease follow-up (opportunity cost inside the system).
- Patient and family: OOPE, travel, isolation time.
- Other sectors only if the perspective includes them.

Consequences.
- Deaths averted, hospitalisations averted, QALYs or DALYs, and, if CBA is attempted, a money value. Do not invent a national QALY total. Structure the calculation.

Vehicle. A model is almost always required: decision tree for acute pathways (home, ward, intensive care, death); Markov or multi-state model for longer disability; possibly a transmission model if the intervention changes infection rates. Trial-based evaluation of a whole national response is not available in real time.

Uncertainty. Test higher and lower transmission, vaccine effect, unit costs of intensive care, and discount rate. Report what would flip a conclusion that "response X was cost-effective."

Presentation. Incremental cost per death averted or per QALY for specified strategies; a CCA table if too many outcomes refuse to fit one unit; discussion of equity (who bore OOPE and who was displaced) and of implementation (surge capacity).

> **EXAM TIP:** For a methods long answer: ten-point QUEST VALUE checklist. For the pandemic question: alternatives and perspective first (or it is only a bill), then cost categories including displaced care, then a model, then uncertainty. Do not write only lessons from lockdowns.

KEY POINTS
- Trees for one-off pathways; Markov for repeating risk and time.
- Sensitivity analysis is part of the result, not an optional annex.
- Ten-question checklist is the appraisal and the protocol.
- CHEERS is the reporting standard; the checklist is what to memorise for theory.
- A pandemic "impact" study is an evaluation only if alternatives are compared.

FORMULAS AND CALCULATIONS
Expected cost at a chance node = Σ (probability of branch × cost of branch)
Present value as under costing and discounting
ICER as under decision rules

MNEMONICS
QUEST VALUE for the ten appraisal questions.

subsections.title: Health Financing in India, NHA, OOPE, and Insurance
subsections.content:
OVERVIEW OF THE CHAPTER
Health financing is the function of a health system concerned with mobilisation, accumulation, and allocation of money to cover people's health needs. The World Health Organization (WHO) describes three sub-functions: revenue collection, pooling of risks, and purchasing of services. This section is the India paper: sources of funds, National Health Accounts (NHA), out-of-pocket expenditure (OOPE), catastrophic spending, publicly funded insurance, community resources, and a short note on microfinance as it appears in resident teaching.

Evaluation methods tell whether a programme is worth buying. Financing tells who pays and whether payment is pooled.

DEFINITIONS
HEALTH FINANCING: The function of a health system concerned with the mobilisation, accumulation, and allocation of money to cover the health needs of the people. It includes revenue collection, pooling of financial risks, and purchasing of health services.

OUT-OF-POCKET EXPENDITURE (OOPE): Direct payments by households at the point of receiving care that are not reimbursed by any third party. Medicines, tests, consultation fees, and travel paid by the family are typical items.

CATASTROPHIC HEALTH EXPENDITURE: Household OOPE that exceeds a defined share of household resources. Two standard WHO-linked thresholds are used in examinations:
- Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) 3.8.2: OOPE greater than 10% of total household expenditure or income (a 25% threshold is also reported).
- Capacity-to-pay approach: OOPE greater than 40% of household capacity to pay for health care (expenditure net of subsistence needs such as food, housing, and utilities in the WHO/Europe method).

Do not write "40% of non-health expenditure" as if it were the official phrase. Use capacity to pay.

NATIONAL HEALTH ACCOUNTS (NHA): A systematic description of financial flows in a country's health system, following an international framework. In India the National Health Accounts Technical Secretariat at the National Health Systems Resource Centre (NHSRC), under the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (MoHFW), produces the estimates.

[SN]Health financing in India[/SN]

[SN]Sources of health-care financing[/SN]

[LAQ]Financing of health care[/LAQ]

[LAQ]Health financing in India[/LAQ]

SOURCES OF FINANCE
Money for health in India comes from four practical streams. A long answer should name each, then say what is pooled and what is not.

1. Government (Union and States). Tax-funded services, national programmes, National Health Mission (NHM), state health departments. Health is a State subject; the Centre steers through policy and centrally sponsored schemes. National Health Policy (NHP), 2017 set a goal of raising government health expenditure toward 2.5% of Gross Domestic Product (GDP) by 2025. That is a policy goal, not an automatic current figure.
2. Households. OOPE at the point of use. This is not pooling. It is the household paying because it has no (or incomplete) third-party cover at that moment.
3. Insurance and social security. Government-funded insurance (notably Ayushman Bharat Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana, AB-PMJAY), Employees' State Insurance, Central Government Health Scheme, state schemes, and private voluntary insurance. Pooling is the economic point: many contribute, the sick draw.
4. External agencies, non-governmental organisations, and corporate social responsibility. World Health Organization, development partners, philanthropic foundations, and NGO service delivery. Useful at the margin and in specific programmes; not the backbone of universal cover.

WHO building-block language calls this "health-care financing." Collection without pooling leaves the sick household exposed. Pooling without strategic purchasing buys volume without value. Economic evaluation is the tool for purchasing.

NHA 2022-23 (OFFICIAL ROUND)
The Union Health Ministry released National Health Accounts Estimates for India 2022-23 in 2026 (tenth NHA report, NHATS/NHSRC). Headline examination figures, each with a year label:

- Out-of-pocket expenditure as a share of Total Health Expenditure declined from 64.2% in 2013-14 to 43.4% in 2022-23.
- Government Health Expenditure was 1.48% of GDP in 2022-23 (new GDP series) and 43.7% of THE.
- For context, 2021-22 (pandemic year) showed a higher government share (GHE about 1.84% of GDP and 48% of THE) and OOPE 39.4% of THE. The 2022-23 round shows government share easing after that surge while remaining well above 2013-14.

NHP-2017's 2.5% of GDP target was not met in the 2022-23 accounts. Write the target as a target and the NHA figure as the account.

Government's share of THE rose over the decade as OOPE's share fell. Households still contribute the largest single slice of current spending. That is the financial-protection gap AB-PMJAY and free-care policies are meant to close.

[SN]Catastrophic health expenditure[/SN]

CATASTROPHIC HEALTH EXPENDITURE
OOPE becomes catastrophic when it forces a household to cut essential consumption or to borrow and sell assets. Measurement uses a threshold, not a clinical judgement.

Use in an answer:
1. Define OOPE.
2. State the 10% (SDG 3.8.2) and 40% of capacity-to-pay thresholds.
3. Link to impoverishing expenditure (OOPE that pushes a household across a poverty line, or that is incurred by a household already poor).
4. Indian context: high OOPE, especially on medicines and private outpatient care, is the usual pathway to catastrophe. Inpatient public insurance reduces one part of the bill; it does not automatically cover outpatient drugs.

> **EXAM TIP:** Definition of catastrophic spending → 10% of total household expenditure (SDG) and 40% of capacity to pay → one line on impoverishment → India: OOPE share from NHA 2022-23 with the year. Do not quote a percentage of households as catastrophic unless you are citing a named survey round.

[LAQ]Role of Ayushman Bharat Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana in reducing out-of-pocket expenditure[/LAQ]

AB-PMJAY AND OOPE
Ayushman Bharat has two operational pillars: Health and Wellness Centres (Ayushman Arogya Mandir) for comprehensive primary care, and PM-JAY for secondary and tertiary hospitalisation cover for eligible families. This section is the insurance limb.

How PM-JAY is meant to cut OOPE
- Pools public money to pay for a defined hospitalisation benefit, so the eligible patient is not the first payer at empanelled hospitals.
- Cashless, paperless design at empanelled public and private hospitals, with portability across States in the scheme's architecture.
- Targets families that, without cover, would face large inpatient bills (the classic catastrophic event).
- Complements (does not replace) free care in public facilities and NHM programmes.

Advantages (examination list)
1. Large public pool: risk is not left with the sick household.
2. Inpatient financial protection for eligible admissions, including many procedures that previously produced distress financing.
3. Portability supports migrant workers.
4. Empanelment can bring private capacity under public purchasing.
5. Data on claims can, in principle, support strategic purchasing and fraud control.
6. Pairs with primary-care expansion so that not every need becomes a hospital claim.

Limits and disadvantages (must be in the same answer)
1. OOPE continues for outpatient care, drugs, and diagnostics outside the package, which are a large part of household spending in NHA.
2. Awareness, card/eligibility processes, and denial at the hospital gate still produce unpaid bills.
3. Package rates may not cover high-end private bills; balance billing can persist where rules are weak.
4. Public hospitals need drugs, diagnostics, and staff; insurance without supply-side investment shifts the bill rather than removing it.
5. Moral hazard and supplier-induced demand are financing risks if purchasing is only fee-for-admission.
6. Equity depends on who is eligible and who can actually use empanelled facilities.

Conclusion for the long answer. PM-JAY is a pooling and purchasing reform aimed at inpatient OOPE. NHA shows OOPE's share of THE has fallen over a decade but remains high. A complete answer pairs insurance with primary care, free drugs and diagnostics in public facilities, and the NHP-2017 public-investment goal.

> **EXAM TIP:** Define PM-JAY as the hospitalisation pillar of Ayushman Bharat → six mechanisms for reducing OOPE → six limits (outpatient drugs, awareness, balance billing, supply side, moral hazard, eligibility) → close with NHA 2022-23 OOPE share. Balanced table scores.

COMMUNITY RESOURCES
How can community resources strengthen financing in a State?
- Risk pooling at small scale: community-based health insurance, where it still exists, with a warning that small pools collapse when the sick join and the healthy leave.
- Prepayment into local funds (Rogi Kalyan Samiti / hospital management committees; Village Health Sanitation and Nutrition Committee untied funds) for local gaps, not for replacing tax finance.
- Time and organisation: ASHAs, self-help groups, and village bodies that raise utilisation of already-paid public services (which reduces future OOPE by catching illness earlier).
- Local philanthropy and CSR for specified inputs, with governance so that they fill gaps rather than fragment the system.
- Demand-side: community monitoring of user charges and of PM-JAY empanelment so that entitled care is actually free at the point of use.

Community money cannot replace general taxation for universal coverage. It can reduce leakages and last-mile gaps.

[SN]Microfinance and women empowerment[/SN]

MICROFINANCE AND WOMEN EMPOWERMENT
Microfinance is the provision of small loans and related financial services to people who lack access to conventional banking. In resident teaching it is linked to women's economic and social empowerment, which then affects household health (nutrition, care-seeking, bargaining over expenditure).

Sources: microfinance institutions, self-help groups (SHGs), NGOs.
Economic effects: livelihood, financial independence, poverty alleviation.
Social effects: status, decision-making power, reduced gender disparity.

Challenges: financial literacy, social and cultural barriers, high interest in some products, weak market access, sustainability.
India examples: Self Employed Women's Association (SEWA); Kudumbashree (Kerala); SHGs under the National Rural Livelihoods Mission (NRLM); Pradhan Mantri MUDRA Yojana for small-business credit; Stand Up India for scheduled caste, scheduled tribe, and women entrepreneurs.

This is not a method of economic evaluation. It is a financing-and-determinants short note. Keep it inside one page.

> **EXAM TIP:** Define microfinance → SHG pathway → economic and social limbs → two India names (SEWA or Kudumbashree, NRLM) → two challenges. Do not claim it is a substitute for public health finance.

KEY POINTS
- Collection, pooling, purchasing.
- NHA 2022-23: OOPE 43.4% of THE (from 64.2% in 2013-14); GHE 1.48% of GDP.
- NHP-2017 goal of 2.5% of GDP remains the policy benchmark.
- Catastrophic: 10% of total household spend (SDG) or 40% of capacity to pay.
- PM-JAY pools inpatient risk; outpatient OOPE still matters.
- Community resources strengthen, they do not replace, tax finance.

FORMULAS AND CALCULATIONS
Catastrophic (SDG 3.8.2): OOPE / household total expenditure (or income) > 0.10 (or > 0.25 for the higher cut-off)
Capacity-to-pay rule: OOPE / capacity to pay > 0.40

MNEMONICS
Sources of finance: government taxes, household pockets, insurance pools, and partners (external and NGO).

subsections.title: Resource Allocation, Universal Health Coverage, and Using Evaluation
subsections.content:
OVERVIEW OF THE CHAPTER
Earlier sections answered how to compare programmes. This section answers how those comparisons are used: to allocate resources, to move toward Universal Health Coverage (UHC), and to strengthen the building blocks of the health system. A medical officer who can compute an ICER but cannot say what to do with a district budget has not finished the paper.

DEFINITIONS
UNIVERSAL HEALTH COVERAGE (UHC): All people have access to the health services they need, when and where they need them, without financial hardship. WHO describes UHC along three dimensions often drawn as a cube: who is covered (population), which services are covered (service package), and what share of cost is covered (financial protection). Expanding UHC means extending one or more of those three edges toward the full cube.

WHO HEALTH SYSTEM BUILDING BLOCKS: Six core components: service delivery; health workforce; health information system; access to essential medicines; financing; leadership and governance. Community participation is taught in Indian notes as a seventh, cross-cutting requirement so that the blocks serve people rather than only facilities.

PRIMARY HEALTH CARE (PHC), FOUR A's: Care that is Affordable, Acceptable, Available, and Accessible. Alma-Ata also requires that methods be scientifically sound and socially acceptable, and that communities participate. The four A's are the usual short-note list.

RESOURCE ALLOCATION: The decision to put limited inputs (staff, money, drugs, time) into one use rather than another. In public health it should follow need, effectiveness, cost-effectiveness, equity, and feasibility, not only historical budgets.

[SN]Universal health coverage cube[/SN]

[LAQ]Resource allocation in health care[/LAQ]

THE UHC CUBE
Draw a cube. Three axes:

1. Population covered: from the poorest or currently entitled groups toward the whole population.
2. Services covered: from a narrow package (safe delivery, immunisation, a short list of admissions) toward a comprehensive set including non-communicable disease, mental health, rehabilitation.
3. Cost covered: from high OOPE toward prepayment and pooling so that the user fee at the point of care falls.

India's direction of travel in policy: NHP-2017; comprehensive primary care through Ayushman Arogya Mandir; AB-PMJAY for hospitalisation of eligible families; free drugs and diagnostics in public facilities as a financial-protection tool. NHA 2022-23 still shows OOPE at 43.4% of THE, so the "cost covered" axis is incomplete. Evaluation (this chapter) is how to choose which services to add when the cube cannot grow on all three axes at once.

> **EXAM TIP:** Define UHC in WHO's one sentence → draw the cube and name the three axes → one India line per axis (entitlement, AAM package, PM-JAY plus remaining OOPE). Close: "raise all three edges; do not confuse insurance enrolment with UHC."

[SN]WHO health-system building blocks[/SN]

BUILDING BLOCKS
Write them as a table, not a paragraph.

| Block | What it is | Allocation question |
|---|---|---|
| Service delivery | Safe, quality care at the right level | Which package at sub-centre, PHC, CHC, district hospital? |
| Health workforce | Numbers, skill mix, distribution, motivation | Where to post the next medical officer or CHO? |
| Information | HMIS, surveillance, NHA, claims data | Which indicator will change a monthly review? |
| Essential medicines | Selection, procurement, supply, quality | ABC-VED and EOQ belong here as store tools |
| Financing | Collection, pooling, purchasing | Tax, insurance, OOPE mix; what to buy |
| Leadership / governance | Policy, regulation, accountability | Who decides, with what evidence (HTAIn, DHS)? |

Community participation sits across the table: VHSNC, Jan Arogya Samiti, patient groups. Without it, delivery and financing reforms do not reach the people whose opportunity cost is being decided.

Services and workforce need information, medicines, leadership, and financing. Community participation holds the blocks together.

> **EXAM TIP:** List six blocks with one allocation question each → add community participation as the taught seventh → one line linking financing to the evaluation methods in this chapter.

PHC AND THE FOUR A's
Affordable: cost to the user does not deter needed care (pooling, free drugs, PM-JAY).
Acceptable: culture, language, gender, opening hours, trust.
Available: the service exists (staff, drugs, hours).
Accessible: geography, disability, and social barriers do not block use.

The four A's are a named set. Examinations often pair them with the UHC cube: the A's describe the service; the cube describes coverage at population scale.

[SN]Health Technology Assessment in India[/SN]

HTAIn AND ALLOCATION
Health Technology Assessment in India (HTAIn), Department of Health Research, collates and generates evidence on clinical effectiveness, cost-effectiveness, and safety of medicines, devices, and programmes. That evidence is an input to allocation at national and state level: which device to list, which programme to scale, which medicine to put on the National List of Essential Medicines conversation.

A district medical officer will rarely run a full CUA. The same logic still applies in miniature:
- Name alternatives (including current practice).
- Count extra cost and extra effect.
- Ask what will be displaced (opportunity cost).
- Check equity: who gains, who pays remaining OOPE.
- Record the decision so it can be reviewed.

A medical officer should be able to advise on allocation of resources in the work area. That advice is this checklist, not a private preference.

USING EVALUATION IN A DISTRICT (LAQ CLOSE)
A one-year district plan that uses this chapter would:

1. Situation analysis (burden, coverage, OOPE distress, workforce).
2. Short list of feasible alternatives for the top problems.
3. For each shortlisted pair, a CEA in natural units that the district can measure (extra fully immunised child, extra controlled hypertensive, extra sputum-positive treated).
4. Where two programmes compete for the same untied fund, prefer the option with more health per extra rupee unless an equity override is stated (for example a small tribal population with catastrophic transport costs).
5. Protect vital and high-value commodities (ABC-VED) so that "savings" do not empty the emergency tray.
6. Monitor with HMIS; evaluate; reallocate.

This is extra-welfarist practice in the field: the objective is health (and financial protection), the constraint is the budget, and the method is incremental comparison.

CONCLUSION
Health economics is the study of how scarce resources are allocated to produce, distribute, and consume health and health care. Choices will be made on other people's behalf. Economic evaluation is the comparative analysis of alternative courses of action in terms of both their costs and consequences. Opportunity cost is the health (or other valued benefit) given up. India still pays a large share of THE out of pocket. Expanding the UHC cube, funding the building blocks, and using HTA and simple incremental arithmetic at district level are the same job at three scales.

> **EXAM TIP:** LAQ frame: definition of allocation → criteria (need, effect, cost-effectiveness, equity, feasibility) → UHC cube → six blocks → one district worked example → close with opportunity cost. For a short note, cube or blocks, not both in full.

KEY POINTS
- UHC cube: population, services, cost share.
- Six WHO blocks plus community participation.
- Four A's of PHC.
- HTAIn supplies national evidence; districts still use incremental logic.
- Allocation without naming what is displaced is not economics.

FORMULAS AND CALCULATIONS
None new. ICER, net monetary benefit, and present value from earlier in this chapter are the arithmetic of allocation.

MNEMONICS
PHC 4As: Affordable, Acceptable, Available, Accessible (the name is the cue).
UHC cube: population, package of services, price protection.

title: Current Health Status of India
description: Census, Sample Registration System, National Family Health Survey, National Health Policy 2017 versus current status, and survey methods for MD Community Medicine.

subsections.title: Census of India 2011 and Census 2027
subsections.content:
OVERVIEW OF THE CHAPTER
A population census is the complete count of people and housing in a country at a specified time. In India it is a Union subject under the Ministry of Home Affairs, run by the Office of the Registrar General and Census Commissioner of India (ORGI). This leaf covers the legal frame, Census 2011 headline results, and Census 2027 as the first digital census with caste enumeration.

DEFINITIONS
CENSUS (UNITED NATIONS): The total process of collecting, compiling, evaluating, analysing and publishing or otherwise disseminating demographic, economic and social data pertaining, at a specified time, to all persons in a country or in a well-delimited part of a country.
DE JURE CENSUS: Persons are counted at their usual place of residence.
DE FACTO CENSUS: Persons are counted where they spend the census night.
HOUSELISTING AND HOUSING CENSUS (HLO): First phase. Lists houses and households and records housing condition, amenities, and assets. Creates the frame for population enumeration.
POPULATION ENUMERATION (PE): Second phase. Records demographic, social, and economic particulars of every person.

[SN]Census of India: legal frame and history[/SN]

[LAQ]Census of India 2011 and Census 2027[/LAQ]

LEGAL FRAME AND HISTORY
- Census Act, 1948 and Census Rules, 1990 provide the statutory frame.
- First census in India: 1872 (Lord Mayo). First synchronous census: 1881 (Lord Ripon; W.C. Plowden as Census Commissioner).
- Held every ten years. Census 2021 was deferred because of the coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic and is being taken as Census 2027.
- Two phases in every modern Indian census: (i) Houselisting and Housing Census; (ii) Population Enumeration.

CENSUS 2011 (15TH CENSUS SINCE 1872; 7TH AFTER INDEPENDENCE)
- Motto: Our Census, Our Future.
- Registrar General and Census Commissioner: C. Chandramouli.
- Final population: 1,210,854,977.
- Males about 51.5 percent, females about 48.5 percent.
- Decadal growth 2001-2011: 17.64 percent (first post-Independence decade with a smaller absolute increase than the previous decade).
- Most populous State: Uttar Pradesh. Least populous State: Sikkim.
- Density: 382 per sq km. Sex ratio: 943 females per 1,000 males. Child sex ratio (0-6 years): 919. Literacy: 74.04 percent (male 82.14, female 65.46).
- Method: de facto count on the census reference night, with a revisional round.

CENSUS 2027 (16TH CENSUS; 8TH AFTER INDEPENDENCE)
- First fully digital Census. Enumerators use mobile applications. Self-enumeration is offered before house-to-house work.
- Cabinet outlay: Rs 11,718.24 crore (PIB).
- Cabinet Committee on Political Affairs (30 April 2025) decided to include caste enumeration. Until 2011, only Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes were listed in the census caste/tribe fields. Census 2027 is the first census in independent India to enumerate caste across communities (last all-caste census: 1931).
- Phase 1, HLO: April-September 2026. Each State or Union Territory notifies a 30-day block. Optional 15-day self-enumeration precedes the house-to-house HLO. Notification for Phase 1: 7 January 2026.
- Phase 2, PE: February 2027 for most of India. Union Territory of Ladakh and snow-bound non-synchronous areas of Jammu and Kashmir, Himachal Pradesh, and Uttarakhand: PE in September 2026.
- Reference date: 00:00 hours of 1 March 2027 for most of India; 00:00 hours of 1 October 2026 for Ladakh and the snow-bound non-synchronous areas.
- PE schedule (notified August 2026): 40 questions, including an open caste field (Scheduled Caste / Scheduled Tribe / Caste as declared). Census 2011 PE had 29 questions.
- Digital tools named in PIB: Census Management and Monitoring System (CMMS); Houselisting Block Creator (HLBC) web-map application using satellite imagery.

INDIAN CONTEXT:
- Census data feed delimitation, Finance Commission, National Food Security Act targeting, and sample frames for the National Family Health Survey (NFHS) and Sample Registration System (SRS) urban-rural classification.
- For MD answers, keep 2011 as the last completed census and 2027 as the current operation. Do not invent a 2027 headcount before ORGI releases it.

[REF]Reference: Census Act, 1948; Census of India 2011, Office of the Registrar General and Census Commissioner; PIB releases on Census 2027 (HLO notification 7 January 2026; digital platforms; PE question notification August 2026).[/REF]

subsections.title: Sample Registration System: Dual Record and SRS 2024 Indicators
subsections.content:
OVERVIEW OF THE CHAPTER
The Sample Registration System (SRS) is the Office of the Registrar General and Census Commissioner, India's (ORGI) large-scale demographic survey. It supplies annual national and State estimates of fertility and mortality. Figures below are from SRS Bulletin 2024 (Volume 59-I) and the SRS Maternal Mortality Bulletin 2022-24.

DEFINITIONS
SAMPLE REGISTRATION SYSTEM (SRS): A dual-record demographic survey that continuously enumerates births and deaths in a sample of villages and urban blocks, then matches that count with an independent half-yearly retrospective survey.
CRUDE BIRTH RATE (CBR): Live births in a year per 1,000 mid-year population.
CRUDE DEATH RATE (CDR): Deaths in a year per 1,000 mid-year population.
INFANT MORTALITY RATE (IMR): Infant deaths (under 1 year) in a year per 1,000 live births in that year.
MATERNAL MORTALITY RATIO (MMR): Maternal deaths per 100,000 live births in a defined period.
TOTAL FERTILITY RATE (TFR): Average number of children a woman would have during her reproductive years if current age-specific fertility rates applied.

[SN]Sample Registration System[/SN]

[LAQ]SRS: dual record method and latest national indicators[/LAQ]

HOW SRS WORKS
- Dual record: (1) continuous enumeration of vital events by a resident part-time enumerator; (2) independent six-monthly retrospective survey by a full-time supervisor.
- Unmatched and partially matched events are re-verified in the field. Verbal autopsy forms are filled for finalised deaths.
- Baseline survey of sample units records the usual resident population. The sample is replaced about every 10 years on the latest census frame.
- "Bigger States/Union Territories" in the bulletin are those with Census 2011 population above 10 million.

SRS BULLETIN 2024 (INDIA)

| Indicator | Total | Rural | Urban |
|---|---|---|---|
| Crude birth rate | 18.3 | 20.2 | 14.7 |
| Crude death rate | 6.4 | 6.8 | 5.6 |
| Natural growth rate | 11.9 | 13.5 | 9.0 |
| Infant mortality rate | 24 | 27 | 17 |

- IMR 24 is less than one-fifth of the 1971 level (129). Decline over the last decade: 39 to 24 (about 38 percent).
- IMR by sex (2024): total 24 (male 24, female 25); rural 27; urban 17.
- Highest IMR among bigger States: Chhattisgarh 36. Lowest: Kerala 8.
- Highest CBR: Bihar 26.8. Lowest: Kerala 11.1.
- Highest CDR: Chhattisgarh 8.4. Lowest: Delhi 4.5.

SRS STATISTICAL REPORT 2024 (ADDITIONAL)
- TFR 1.9 (rural 2.1, urban 1.5). Below replacement (2.1) for the fifth consecutive year.
- Under-5 mortality rate (U5MR) 28 per 1,000 live births.
- Neonatal mortality rate (NMR) 18 per 1,000 live births (NFHS-6 media brochure citing SRS 2024).
- Only six States remain above replacement TFR: Bihar, Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan, Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh.

MMR BULLETIN 2022-24
- India MMR 87 per 100,000 live births (95% CI 78-95), down from 88 in 2021-23.
- Maternal mortality rate 5 per 100,000 women of reproductive age. Lifetime risk 0.18 percent.
- EAG States plus Assam: MMR 116. Southern States: 41. Other States: 75.
- Highest among tabulated States: Uttar Pradesh 154; Madhya Pradesh 135. Lowest: Kerala 24; Tamil Nadu 25.

INDIAN CONTEXT:
- Quote SRS year and "Bulletin" versus "Statistical Report" versus "MMR bulletin" in the answer. Do not mix NFHS IMR with SRS IMR. NFHS-6 fact sheets dropped several mortality indicators; SRS remains the official annual source for IMR, CBR, CDR, TFR, and MMR.

[REF]Reference: ORGI SRS Bulletin 2024 Vol. 59-I; SRS Statistical Report 2024; SRS Maternal Mortality Bulletin 2022-24.[/REF]

subsections.title: NFHS-6 versus NFHS-5: Fertility, RCH, Immunization, and Nutrition
subsections.content:
OVERVIEW OF THE CHAPTER
The National Family Health Survey (NFHS) is India's large household survey on population, health, and nutrition. NFHS-6 (2023-24) was conducted by the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (MoHFW) with the International Institute for Population Sciences (IIPS), Mumbai, as nodal agency. About 6.79 lakh households in 715 districts were covered. Compare NFHS-5 (2019-21) with NFHS-6 using the official India fact sheet and Press Information Bureau (PIB) releases.

DEFINITIONS
NATIONAL FAMILY HEALTH SURVEY (NFHS): A nationally representative household survey providing district-level estimates on fertility, family planning, maternal and child health, nutrition, and selected adult health indicators.
FULL IMMUNIZATION (CARD-BASED): Children aged 12-23 months who received BCG, three doses of DPT-containing vaccine, three doses of polio vaccine (excluding polio given at birth), and one dose of measles-containing vaccine, based on the vaccination card.

[SN]NFHS-6 versus NFHS-5[/SN]

[LAQ]NFHS-6 (2023-24): design and key RCH indicators[/LAQ]

DESIGN
- Stewardship: MoHFW. Coordination: IIPS Mumbai.
- NFHS-5: about 6.1 lakh households, 707 districts. NFHS-6: about 6.79 lakh households, 715 districts.
- Biomarker and questionnaire modules change between rounds. NFHS-6 fact sheets dropped several NFHS-5 items (including anaemia prevalence, survey-based IMR/NMR/U5MR, and sex ratio at birth). Use SRS for those mortality rates.

KEY COMPARISON (INDIA TOTAL, NFHS-5 TO NFHS-6)

| Indicator | NFHS-5 (2019-21) | NFHS-6 (2023-24) |
|---|---|---|
| Total fertility rate | 2.0 | 2.0 |
| Women 20-24 married before 18 (%) | 23.3 | 20.1 |
| Any antenatal care (%) | 92.6 | 95.9 |
| Four or more ANC visits (%) | 58.5 | 65.2 |
| ANC in first trimester (%) | 70.0 | 76.2 |
| IFA for 100+ days in pregnancy (%) | 44.1 | 54.9 |
| Institutional births (%) | 88.6 | 90.6 |
| Skilled birth attendance (%) | 89.4 | 91.3 |
| Caesarean section (%) | 21.5 | 27.2 |
| Any contraceptive method, married women 15-49 (%) | 66.7 | 69.1 |
| Unmet need for family planning (%) | 9.4 | 8.5 |
| Fully vaccinated 12-23 months (card only) (%) | 83.8 | 87.1 |
| Fully vaccinated (card or recall) (%) | 76.6 | 82.6 |
| Rotavirus 3 doses (%) | 36.4 | 85.4 |
| Hepatitis B birth dose (%) | 67.4 | 77.6 |
| Second measles dose, 24-35 months (%) | 58.6 | 71.8 |
| Stunting under-5 (%) | 35.5 | 29.3 |
| Severe wasting under-5 (%) | 7.7 | 5.2 |
| Health insurance coverage (%) | 41.0 | 60.2 |
| Overweight or obese, women 15-49 (%) | (round-specific) | 30.7 |
| Overweight or obese, men 15-49 (%) | (round-specific) | 27.3 |

Other NFHS-6 headlines (PIB / IIPS fact sheet):
- Any vaccine among children 12-23 months remains above 96 percent. Most vaccinations through public facilities: 95.6 percent.
- Household electricity access 98.3 percent. Women participating in household decisions about 89 percent.

INDIAN CONTEXT:
- NFHS TFR 2.0 is a survey estimate. SRS 2024 TFR is 1.9. In exams, name the source next to the number.
- Anaemia trend cannot be continued from NFHS-5 into NFHS-6 on the published fact sheet. Say so if asked; do not invent an NFHS-6 anaemia percent.

[REF]Reference: IIPS/MoHFW NFHS-6 (2023-24) India Fact Sheet; PIB releases on NFHS-6 (2026).[/REF]

subsections.title: Disease-wise Public Health Indicators: TB, Malaria, HIV, Immunization, NCD
subsections.content:
OVERVIEW OF THE CHAPTER
Disease-wise public health indicators sit in programme reports, not in a single SRS table. Quote the programme year. This section lists high-yield national figures for tuberculosis, malaria, HIV, immunization, and non-communicable disease screening without inventing unpublished rates.

DEFINITIONS
INCIDENCE (TB): New and relapse tuberculosis cases estimated per 100,000 population per year (World Health Organization Global TB Report method, used in India TB reports).
ANNUAL PARASITE INCIDENCE (API): Confirmed malaria cases per 1,000 population per year.

[SN]Disease-wise public health indicators in India[/SN]

TUBERCULOSIS
- Use the latest India TB Report / WHO Global TB Report pair. India remains the country with the largest share of global incident TB.
- Programme indicators that belong in an answer: notification (total and microbiological), treatment success, missing cases closed by Ni-kshay, and drug-resistant TB enrolment.
- Do not quote an incidence number from memory if the year is not in front of you. Name the report.

MALARIA
- API and deaths are published by the National Center for Vector Borne Diseases Control (NCVBDC). India is in the National Framework for Malaria Elimination 2016-2030, with the National Strategic Plan 2023-2027 for States.
- Zero indigenous cases is the elimination endpoint. Several States already report very low API.

HIV
- National AIDS Control Organisation (NACO) Sankalak reports the 95-95-95 cascade. NACP-V (2021-26) progress cited for 2024-25: 83.9-86.6-97.6 versus 70.7-82.5-84.9 in 2020-21.
- Sentinel surveillance and NFHS HIV testing modules are separate from programme cascade numbers.

IMMUNIZATION
- NFHS-6 full immunization (card): 87.1 percent among children 12-23 months (83.8 percent in NFHS-5).
- Public facility share of most vaccinations: 95.6 percent.
- Universal Immunization Programme coverage is also tracked in HMIS and U-WIN. Prefer NFHS for survey coverage and HMIS for session doses.

NON-COMMUNICABLE DISEASES
- NP-NCD population-based screening from 30 years: hypertension, diabetes, oral, breast, and cervical cancers.
- NFHS-6: overweight or obese 30.7 percent of women and 27.3 percent of men aged 15-49.
- WHO STEPS State surveys supply risk-factor prevalence where a State paper is asked.

INDIAN CONTEXT:
- For a mixed "current status of diseases of public health importance" short note: one TB line, one malaria API line, one HIV 95-95-95 line, one full-immunization line, one NCD screening line. Source each.

[REF]Reference: India TB Report / WHO Global TB Report; NCVBDC malaria updates; NACO Sankalak 2025; NFHS-6 fact sheet; NP-NCD operational guidelines 2023-2030.[/REF]

subsections.title: National Health Policy 2017 Goals versus Current Status
subsections.content:
OVERVIEW OF THE CHAPTER
The National Health Policy (NHP) 2017 set time-bound goals for mortality, fertility, life expectancy, and health financing. This section places those goals beside the latest official estimates. Where a 2017 goal year has passed, the current figure is still the right exam closer.

DEFINITIONS
NATIONAL HEALTH POLICY 2017: The Government of India policy that shifted the frame from selective primary care toward comprehensive primary health care, and that published quantitative goals for mortality, fertility, and public financing.

[SN]National Health Policy 2017 goals versus current status[/SN]

[LAQ]NHP 2017: quantitative goals and where India stands[/LAQ]

GOAL TABLE (USE THIS IN THE EXAM)

| Goal (NHP 2017) | Latest official status |
|---|---|
| IMR 28 per 1,000 live births by 2019 | SRS 2024 IMR 24. Achieved (and surpassed). |
| MMR 100 per 100,000 live births by 2020 | SRS 2022-24 MMR 87. Achieved. |
| Under-5 mortality 23 per 1,000 by 2025 | SRS 2024 U5MR 28. Not yet met. |
| Neonatal mortality 16 per 1,000 by 2025 | SRS 2024 NMR 18. Not yet met. |
| TFR 2.1 by 2025 | SRS 2024 TFR 1.9; NFHS-6 TFR 2.0. Met at national level. |
| Life expectancy 70 years by 2025 | SRS abridged life tables already placed national LE near 70 years in the 2016-20 series. Quote the latest SRS LE table if the paper asks a single year. |
| Government health expenditure 2.5% of GDP by 2025 | National Health Accounts 2021-22: government health expenditure about 1.8% of GDP (PRS reading of NHA). Not met. |
| State health spending more than 8% of State budget by 2020 | Average State health share of budget remains below 8% in recent NHA/PRS readings. Not met. |
| Eliminate kala-azar and lymphatic filariasis | Kala-azar: block-level elimination target (<1 case per 10,000) reached in previously endemic blocks; maintain surveillance. LF: mass drug administration and morbidity management continue under the National Center for Vector Borne Diseases Control (NCVBDC). |
| 2 beds per 1,000 population by 2025 | Still short of 2 per 1,000 in national facility counts. Do not invent a precise all-India bed rate. |

WHAT MOVED THE OUTCOME GOALS
- Reproductive, Maternal, Newborn, Child, Adolescent Health and Nutrition (RMNCAH+N), Janani Suraksha Yojana, Janani Shishu Suraksha Karyakram, and Ayushman Arogya Mandirs for births and child survival.
- National Tuberculosis Elimination Programme, National Vector Borne Disease Control, and Universal Immunization Programme for specific diseases.
- Ayushman Bharat Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana for financial protection. Out-of-pocket share of total health expenditure has fallen versus the early 2010s (NHA), but remains substantial.

INDIAN CONTEXT:
- Financing is the lagging limb. Outcome goals that sit inside named national programmes moved faster than the 2.5 percent GDP spending goal.
- For a long answer: table first, then one paragraph on programmes that delivered IMR/MMR/TFR, then one paragraph on the spending gap.

[REF]Reference: National Health Policy 2017; ORGI SRS Bulletin 2024 and MMR Bulletin 2022-24; National Health Accounts 2021-22 as cited in PRS Demand for Grants analysis.[/REF]

subsections.title: Survey Methods: Census, SRS, CRS, NFHS, HMIS, and IHIP
subsections.content:
OVERVIEW OF THE CHAPTER
India uses several complementary systems for population and health data. No single system answers every exam question. This section is a comparison table of Census, Sample Registration System (SRS), Civil Registration System (CRS), National Family Health Survey (NFHS), Health Management Information System (HMIS), and the Integrated Health Information Platform (IHIP).

DEFINITIONS
CIVIL REGISTRATION SYSTEM (CRS): Continuous, compulsory, permanent recording of vital events (live births, deaths, stillbirths) under the Registration of Births and Deaths Act, 1969 (as amended).
HEALTH MANAGEMENT INFORMATION SYSTEM (HMIS): Routine facility-based reporting of service delivery under the National Health Mission (NHM).
INTEGRATED HEALTH INFORMATION PLATFORM (IHIP): Web-based, case-based surveillance platform that succeeded the earlier Integrated Disease Surveillance Programme (IDSP) portal for outbreak-prone diseases.

[SN]Sources of health information in India[/SN]

[LAQ]Compare Census, SRS, CRS, NFHS, HMIS, and IHIP[/LAQ]

COMPARISON TABLE

| System | Since / cycle | What it gives | Strength | Limitation |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Census | 1872; synchronous from 1881; every 10 years | Population by age, sex, literacy, density, housing | Complete count to village; sampling frame for other surveys | Decadal. 2021 round deferred; 2027 is the current operation |
| SRS | 1969-70 onwards; annual | CBR, CDR, IMR, TFR, NMR, U5MR, MMR (separate bulletin) | Dual-record; considered the standard for national fertility and mortality rates | Sample, not a complete count. MMR needs pooled years |
| CRS | Statutory from 1969; continuous | Registered births and deaths, cause of death where medical certification exists | Legal identity; district and city detail | Completeness still uneven across States. Medical certification of cause of death is incomplete |
| NFHS | About every 5 years (NFHS-6: 2023-24) | Fertility, ANC, institutional delivery, immunization, nutrition, selected adult risks | District estimates; biomarker modules | Not the official annual IMR. Modules change between rounds |
| HMIS | Continuous facility reporting | ANC, deliveries, immunization doses, programme output | Timely, programme-linked | Facility-based; quality and completeness vary |
| IHIP / IDSP | IDSP from 2004; IHIP case-based | Outbreak-prone disease reporting, S, P, L forms historically; case-based now | Early warning | Depends on reporting discipline at periphery |

OTHER SURVEYS (ONE-LINE EACH)
- District Level Household and Facility Survey (DLHS): older RCH facility and household rounds; largely superseded by NFHS and Health Facility surveys.
- National Sample Survey (NSS) health rounds: out-of-pocket expenditure, morbidity, hospitalisation.
- National Family Health Survey versus Comprehensive National Nutrition Survey (CNNS): CNNS is nutrition-biochemistry depth for children and adolescents (one major round).

INDIAN CONTEXT:
- Exam rule: mortality rates (IMR, MMR, TFR) from SRS; coverage (ANC, immunization, stunting) from NFHS; headcount from Census; legal vital events from CRS; weekly outbreaks from IHIP.

**Mnemonic:** C-S-C-N-H-I
- C: Census (count)
- S: SRS (rates)
- C: CRS (register)
- N: NFHS (coverage)
- H: HMIS (facility)
- I: IHIP (outbreak)

[REF]Reference: Census Act 1948; Registration of Births and Deaths Act 1969; ORGI SRS documentation; IIPS NFHS-6; NHM HMIS; NCDC IHIP.[/REF]

title: Recent Advances and Miscellaneous Public Health
description: Digital health, adult immunization, artificial intelligence, medical drones, bioterrorism and biosafety for MD Paper IV.

subsections.title: Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission and E-Health
subsections.content:
OVERVIEW OF THE CHAPTER
Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission (ABDM) is India's national digital health architecture. It creates a unique health identity, facility and professional registries, and a consent-based way to share electronic health records.

DEFINITIONS
AYUSHMAN BHARAT DIGITAL MISSION (ABDM): The national programme (formerly National Digital Health Mission) to build digital health public goods: identity, registries, and interoperable records, under the National Health Authority.
AYUSHMAN BHARAT HEALTH ACCOUNT (ABHA): A 14-digit unique health identifier that a person can create to link personal health records with consent.

[SN]Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission[/SN]

[LAQ]ABDM building blocks and uses in public health[/LAQ]

BUILDING BLOCKS
1. ABHA number: unique ID. The person controls linking and consent.
2. Healthcare Professionals Registry (HPR): verified doctors, nurses, and allied professionals.
3. Health Facility Registry (HFR): public and private facilities.
4. Personal Health Record (PHR) / Health Information Exchange: discharge summaries, labs, prescriptions move with consent.
5. Unified Health Interface (UHI): open protocol so apps and providers can book and share without a single private monopoly.

PUBLIC HEALTH USES
- Continuity of care across Ayushman Arogya Mandirs, CHCs, and hospitals.
- Programme reporting (immunization U-WIN, NCD screening) can sit on the same identity.
- Deduplication of beneficiaries. Outbreak contact tracing is easier when facilities are in HFR.
- Telemedicine and e-sanjeevani become identifiable endpoints.

SAFEGUARDS
- Consent manager. Purpose limitation. Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, is the privacy statute (see 29-13).
- ABHA is voluntary. Do not write that care is refused without ABHA.

INDIAN CONTEXT:
- National Health Authority implements ABDM. It is not the same as PM-JAY insurance, though both sit under Ayushman Bharat branding.

[REF]Reference: National Health Authority ABDM documentation; Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023.[/REF]

subsections.title: Artificial Intelligence in Public Health
subsections.content:
OVERVIEW OF THE CHAPTER
Artificial intelligence (AI) in public health is the use of machine-learning and related tools for surveillance, imaging, triage, and programme targeting. IndiaAI Mission is the national AI programme. Health use-cases must still obey consent, Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, and clinical accountability.

DEFINITIONS
ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE: Computer systems that perform tasks that usually need human intelligence (pattern recognition, prediction, language).
INDIAAI MISSION: The Government of India mission to build compute, data, skills, and application ecosystems for AI, including public-good use-cases.

[SN]Artificial intelligence in public health[/SN]

USES
- Outbreak signal from IHIP, media, and laboratory streams.
- Chest X-ray and fundus screening support (TB, diabetic retinopathy) as decision support, not as a replacement for the clinician.
- Targeting of high-risk pregnant women or missed immunization from HMIS / U-WIN.
- Chatbots and Tele-MANAS-like first-contact triage (human escalation remains mandatory).

RISKS
- Bias if training data omit tribal, rural, or minority groups.
- Hallucinated advice if a language model is used without a protocol.
- Privacy: ABHA-linked data need fiduciary duties under DPDP.

INDIAN CONTEXT:
- Name IndiaAI Mission and ABDM together. Do not claim a national AI-diagnoses-TB programme unless a named, current MoHFW deployment is in the question.

[REF]Reference: IndiaAI Mission; NHA ABDM; Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023.[/REF]

subsections.title: Drones in Healthcare Logistics
subsections.content:
OVERVIEW OF THE CHAPTER
Drones (unmanned aircraft) move blood, vaccines, diagnostics, and medicines across terrain that delays road transport. India's i-Drone / ICMR and Ministry of Civil Aviation rules are the teaching pegs.

DEFINITIONS
MEDICAL DRONE DELIVERY: Transport of qualified medical cargo by unmanned aircraft under aviation and drug-safety rules.

[SN]Drones in healthcare logistics[/SN]

USES
- Last-mile blood units and diagnostic samples between blood banks and hard-to-reach CHCs.
- Vaccine and cold-chain-compatible payloads where roads flood or climb.
- Disaster: mapping, medicine drop, damage assessment.

RULES OF AN ANSWER
- Payload, temperature, chain of custody, and landing-site security matter as much as the aircraft.
- Directorate General of Civil Aviation (DGCA) traffic rules apply. Drug and blood rules still apply in the air.
- i-Drone (ICMR) is the named Indian research-to-operations effort for medical drones.

INDIAN CONTEXT:
- Use as a recent-advance short note, not as a replacement for the immunization cold-chain topic. Link disaster management (17) when the question is humanitarian logistics.

[REF]Reference: ICMR i-Drone initiative; DGCA drone rules as applicable to medical cargo.[/REF]

subsections.title: Adult Immunization
subsections.content:
OVERVIEW OF THE CHAPTER
Adult immunization is not a second Universal Immunization Programme (UIP) schedule. UIP is child- and pregnant-woman-centred. Adults need risk-based vaccines. Indian Consensus on Adult Immunization and National Technical Advisory Group on Immunization (NTAGI) product decisions are the teaching sources. Quote the latest NTAGI minutes if a specific product year is asked.

DEFINITIONS
ADULT IMMUNIZATION: Vaccination of persons 18 years and older, including pregnant women for selected antigens already in UIP, older adults, and adults with occupational, travel, or medical-risk indications.
NTAGI: The National Technical Advisory Group on Immunization, India's highest advisory body on immunization policy.

[SN]Adult immunization in India[/SN]

[LAQ]Vaccines for adults: risk groups and antigens[/LAQ]

UIP TOUCHPOINTS IN ADULTS
- Td (tetanus-diphtheria) in pregnancy (UIP).
- Hepatitis B birth dose is for the newborn, not the adult; adults at risk get hepatitis B as a recommended vaccine outside the infant schedule.
- COVID-19 vaccination of adults followed NTAGI and National Expert Group on Vaccine Administration for COVID-19 (NEGVAC) circulars during the pandemic years.

COMMONLY RECOMMENDED ADULT ANTIGENS (CONSENSUS TEACHING)
- Influenza: annual, especially elderly, pregnant women, health workers, chronic lung or heart disease.
- Pneumococcal: older adults and asplenia / chronic disease as per product label and consensus.
- Hepatitis B: health workers, dialysis, high-risk sexual or injecting exposure, if not already immune.
- Td or Tdap boosters: every 10 years in many consensus tables; pregnancy Td as per UIP.
- Human papillomavirus (HPV): catch-up in young women and, where policy expands, boys; not yet a universal adult UIP antigen.
- Varicella, herpes zoster, hepatitis A: selected adults.
- Travel: yellow fever (International Health Regulations certificate), typhoid, meningococcal, as destination requires.
- Occupational: hepatitis B and influenza for health workers; rabies pre-exposure for selected veterinary and wildlife staff.

PRINCIPLES
- Check prior doses and serology where it changes the decision (hepatitis B).
- Live vaccines: caution in pregnancy and severe immunosuppression.
- Adult coverage is low. Health-worker hepatitis B is the classic audit indicator.

INDIAN CONTEXT:
- Do not draw a fake "National Adult Immunization Schedule" with the same boxes as the child UIP table. Write "risk-based, consensus plus NTAGI." Pregnant-woman Td remains UIP.

[REF]Reference: NTAGI; Indian Consensus on Adult Immunization; UIP pregnancy Td; IHR yellow-fever certificate rules.[/REF]

subsections.title: Bioterrorism, Biosafety, and Biosecurity
subsections.content:
OVERVIEW OF THE CHAPTER
Bioterrorism is the deliberate release of biological agents to harm people, animals, or plants. Biosafety protects workers and the community from accidental exposure. Biosecurity prevents theft, diversion, and deliberate misuse.

DEFINITIONS
BIOTERRORISM: Intentional use of microorganisms or toxins to cause disease, death, or panic.
BIOSAFETY: Containment principles, technologies, and practices that prevent unintentional exposure to biological agents.
BIOSECURITY: Institutional and national measures that prevent loss, theft, misuse, diversion, or intentional release of biological agents and toxins.

[SN]Bioterrorism, biosafety, and biosecurity[/SN]

[LAQ]Public health response to a suspected biological attack[/LAQ]

AGENTS (CDC CATEGORY TEACHING)
- Category A: anthrax, plague, smallpox, botulism, tularaemia, viral haemorrhagic fevers. High mortality, panic, need for special preparedness.
- Category B: brucella, Q fever, ricin, food-safety threats. Moderate.
- Category C: emerging pathogens that could be engineered.

RESPONSE
1. Recognise: unusual clustering, unexpected age group, aerosol-looking anthrax, haemorrhagic fever without travel.
2. Isolate and PPE. Notify IHIP / NCDC / IHR National Focal Point (NCDC).
3. Laboratory: designated biosafety level. Do not process unknown powders in a routine clinical lab.
4. Medical countermeasures: antibiotics or vaccine as per agent protocol (anthrax PEP is the classic).
5. Risk communication: one official voice. Avoid rumour.
6. Law: Epidemic Diseases Act, Disaster Management Act, Unlawful Activities framework as advised by the home ministry. IHR 2005 if international spread is possible.

INDIAN CONTEXT:
- Smallpox remains an IHR immediately notifiable disease even though it is eradicated. Anthrax is both a zoonosis and a bioterrorism category A agent. Biosafety versus biosecurity is a favourite contrast pair (8.86 in the notes book).

[REF]Reference: CDC bioterrorism categories as teaching taxonomy; IHR 2005; NCDC outbreak investigation methods.[/REF]

subsections.title: National Action Plan on Antimicrobial Resistance 2.0
subsections.content:
OVERVIEW OF THE CHAPTER
Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is the ability of bacteria, viruses, fungi, or parasites to survive medicines that previously killed or inhibited them. India's second National Action Plan on Antimicrobial Resistance (NAP-AMR 2.0) covers 2025-2029. It follows NAP-AMR 2017-2021 and the World Health Organization (WHO) Global Action Plan on AMR.

DEFINITIONS
ANTIMICROBIAL RESISTANCE (AMR): The process by which microorganisms stop responding to antimicrobials, making infections harder to treat and raising the risk of spread, severe disease, and death.
ANTIMICROBIAL STEWARDSHIP: Coordinated interventions that promote the optimal use of antimicrobials: right drug, dose, duration, and route.
AWaRe: WHO grouping of antibiotics into Access, Watch, and Reserve, used to track and improve prescribing.

[SN]NAP-AMR 2.0[/SN]

[LAQ]National Action Plan on Antimicrobial Resistance 2.0[/LAQ]

NAP-AMR 1.0 VERSUS 2.0
- 1.0 (2017-2021): broad One Health framework. Gaps: weak ownership outside health, thin private-sector engagement, limited budgets and timelines.
- 2.0 launched 18 November 2025 (World AMR Awareness Week) by the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (MoHFW). Period 2025-2029.
- More than 20 ministries (health, animal husbandry, agriculture, environment, Jal Shakti, pharmaceuticals, education, science) each have an action plan with goals, timelines, and budget.

SIX STRATEGIC OBJECTIVES (TEACHING LIST)
1. Awareness, education, and training.
2. Laboratory capacity and surveillance of AMR and antibiotic residues (human, animal, food, environment).
3. Infection prevention and control (IPC) to cut new infections.
4. Optimise antimicrobial use: access plus stewardship in humans, animals, and food.
5. Research and innovation (diagnostics, alternatives, operational research). India AMR Innovation Hub is the named innovation arm.
6. Intersectoral governance: coordination committee and technical advisory group hosted by MoHFW; NITI Aayog oversight for monitoring.

EXAM CONTRASTS
- Access versus excess: India must still deliver antibiotics to people who need them, while stopping over-the-counter and livestock misuse.
- AWaRe: increase the Access share of total antibiotic use; keep Reserve for last-line, specialist use.
- Biosafety versus biosecurity is a different pair (see 32-5). AMR is evolutionary pressure from use, not a bioterrorism event.

INDIAN CONTEXT:
- ICMR AMR surveillance network and NCDC National AMR programme supply human-sector data. Veterinary and farm use sit with Animal Husbandry. Hospital IPC and BMW rules cut transmission of resistant organisms.

[REF]Reference: PIB 18 November 2025 on NAP-AMR 2.0; WHO Global Action Plan on AMR; WHO AWaRe classification.[/REF]

subsections.title: GIS and Remote Sensing in Public Health
subsections.content:
OVERVIEW OF THE CHAPTER
Geographic Information Systems (GIS) store, analyse, and display data that have a location. Remote sensing collects information about the earth's surface without physical contact, usually from satellites or aircraft. Both are tools for surveillance, targeting, and disaster work.

DEFINITIONS
GEOGRAPHIC INFORMATION SYSTEM (GIS): A computer system that captures, stores, analyses, and displays geographically referenced data as layers on a map.
REMOTE SENSING: Acquisition of information about an object or area from a distance, typically satellite or aerial sensors measuring reflected or emitted radiation.

[SN]GIS and remote sensing in public health[/SN]

USES
- Outbreak mapping: spot clustering of cases (cholera along a river, dengue by ward).
- Vector habitat: satellite vegetation, water, and temperature layers to predict malaria or kala-azar risk.
- Health-facility planning: distance to the nearest Ayushman Arogya Mandir or blood bank; identifying unserved habitations.
- Census 2027 Houselisting Block Creator uses satellite imagery to draw blocks.
- Disaster: flood extent, cyclone track, damaged roads, where to drop supplies.
- Environmental health: air-quality grids, fluoride or arsenic-affected habitations.

LIMITATIONS
- A map is only as good as the case definition and the geo-coding. Missing addresses create false blanks.
- Satellite indices (NDVI, land-surface temperature) are proxies, not diagnoses.
- Privacy: household-level health points need aggregation before public maps (DPDP Act, 2023).

INDIAN CONTEXT:
- Integrated Health Information Platform (IHIP) supports map views of outbreaks. National Vector Borne Disease Control uses GIS for API and foci. Bhuvan and Indian Space Research Organisation products are the usual teaching names for Indian satellite layers.

[REF]Reference: IHIP; Census 2027 HLBC (PIB); standard GIS teaching in public-health epidemiology.[/REF]

subsections.title: Evidence-based Public Health, Systematic Review, and ROC
subsections.content:
OVERVIEW OF THE CHAPTER
Evidence-based public health uses the best available research, together with local epidemiology and values, to choose programmes. Systematic reviews and meta-analysis sit at the top of the evidence hierarchy for many questions. The receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve summarises how a test trades sensitivity against specificity.

DEFINITIONS
EVIDENCE-BASED PUBLIC HEALTH: The conscientious use of current best evidence in making decisions about community programmes, integrating research, local data, resources, and community values.
SYSTEMATIC REVIEW: A review that uses an explicit, reproducible method to find, appraise, and synthesise all studies that meet pre-stated eligibility criteria for a question.
META-ANALYSIS: A statistical method that combines numerical results from similar studies into a pooled estimate, often shown as a forest plot.
PRISMA: Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses, the reporting checklist for a review.
ROC CURVE: A plot of sensitivity (true-positive rate) against 1 minus specificity (false-positive rate) at every possible cut-off of a continuous test.

[SN]Systematic review and meta-analysis[/SN]

[LAQ]Evidence-based public health: reviews, PRISMA, and ROC[/LAQ]

STEPS OF A SYSTEMATIC REVIEW
1. Write the question (Population, Intervention, Comparison, Outcome, or PECO for exposures).
2. Protocol (register if required).
3. Search more than one database with documented strings.
4. Screen titles, abstracts, then full text with two reviewers.
5. Extract data and assess risk of bias.
6. Synthesise: narrative if studies differ too much; meta-analysis if they are similar enough.
7. Report with PRISMA flow (identified, screened, excluded, included).

META-ANALYSIS
- Forest plot: each study as a square, pooled diamond. Heterogeneity: I-squared and visual spread.
- Random-effects when studies differ; fixed-effect when they estimate one common effect and are homogeneous.
- Publication bias: funnel plot. Do not over-read a funnel with few studies.

ROC AND AREA UNDER THE CURVE
- Each point on the ROC is one cut-off. A test that hugs the top-left is better.
- Area under the curve (AUC): 0.5 is chance; nearer 1.0 is better discrimination.
- You cannot pick the "best" cut-off from AUC alone. Choose the cut-off that fits the programme (high sensitivity for a serious treatable disease; high specificity when a false positive is costly).
- Series and parallel combination of tests belong in the screening chapter (4).

INDIAN CONTEXT:
- Programme choices (which vaccine, which screening test) should cite a systematic review or a WHO/MoHFW guideline that itself used one. Local SRS and NFHS numbers then size the problem. Critical appraisal of a paper is in 28-8.

[REF]Reference: PRISMA statement; standard epidemiology texts for ROC and meta-analysis; Library screening chapter for series/parallel tests.[/REF]

subsections.title: CBME, AETCOM, and Family Adoption Programme
subsections.content:
OVERVIEW OF THE CHAPTER
Competency-Based Medical Education (CBME) is the National Medical Commission (NMC) undergraduate curriculum that organises learning around observable competencies rather than only hours of lectures. Attitude, Ethics and Communication (AETCOM) and the Family Adoption Programme (FAP) are named CBME strands that Community Medicine departments run.

DEFINITIONS
COMPETENCY-BASED MEDICAL EDUCATION (CBME): A curriculum that states what the graduate must be able to do, and that assesses those abilities, rather than counting only time spent in class.
AETCOM: Attitude, Ethics and Communication, the NMC modules that teach professional behaviour, ethics, and communication across MBBS phases.
FAMILY ADOPTION PROGRAMME (FAP): A CBME requirement in which each student is assigned families in the community for longitudinal follow-up of health, nutrition, and utilisation of services.

[SN]AETCOM and Family Adoption Programme[/SN]

[LAQ]CBME, AETCOM, and FAP in Community Medicine[/LAQ]

CBME IN COMMUNITY MEDICINE
- Competencies cover family study, clinico-social cases, epidemiology exercises, entomology, and national programmes.
- Teaching methods: small-group teaching, self-directed learning, clinical postings in the community (typically two postings), and integrated sessions with other departments.
- Assessment: internal assessment plus university theory and practical (spots, family or clinico-social case, viva, statistics exercises).

AETCOM
