- Modules run through all professional years. Community Medicine often shares modules on doctor-patient communication, consent, equity, and professionalism.
- Link Mental Healthcare Act (capacity and consent), Consumer Protection, and the NMC code of conduct.

FAMILY ADOPTION PROGRAMME
- Each student follows allotted families over the MBBS years: household survey, antenatal and under-five follow-up, immunization, lifestyle risks, and referral.
- Logbook is mandatory. FAP hours sit in the NMC CBME time table (community visits plus logbook).
- Exam overlap with family-study practical: FAP is longitudinal and community-assigned; the university family case may be a different household on exam day.

RECENT NMC REFORMS (TEACHING LINES)
- Undergraduate CBME regulations (including the 2024 hours notification) change phase-wise teaching hours. Quote the circular year if the question asks for hours.
- Postgraduate eligibility still includes research methodology, ethics, and basic/advanced life-support courses in the first year (NMC PG regulations).

INDIAN CONTEXT:
- Pedagogy as a Practical chapter already covers teaching methods. This section is the theory answer for Paper IV "medical education technology" and "recent reforms."

[REF]Reference: NMC CBME Regulations and AETCOM booklet; NMC PG regulations on research methodology and life-support courses.[/REF]

subsections.title: Medical Tourism, Carbon Footprint, and Genetically Modified Foods
subsections.content:
OVERVIEW OF THE CHAPTER
Three Paper IV miscellaneous topics: medical tourism (medical value travel), carbon footprint of health care, and genetically modified (GM) foods.

DEFINITIONS
MEDICAL TOURISM: Travel across international borders to obtain medical care, usually combining treatment with a stay in the destination country.
CARBON FOOTPRINT: The total greenhouse-gas emissions caused directly and indirectly by an activity, person, organisation, or product, expressed as carbon dioxide equivalent.
GENETICALLY MODIFIED FOOD: Food derived from an organism whose genetic material has been altered by modern biotechnology in a way that does not occur by mating or natural recombination.

[SN]Medical tourism[/SN]

MEDICAL TOURISM
- India attracts patients for elective surgery, oncology, cardiology, transplants, and wellness, citing cost, English-speaking clinicians, and private-hospital capacity.
- Public-health angles: foreign-exchange earnings; pressure on specialist time; need for quality regulation (Clinical Establishments Act, NABH); infection control and antimicrobial stewardship for inbound patients; follow-up after the patient leaves.
- Risks: unethical transplant tourism (Transplantation of Human Organs and Tissues Act), antibiotic-resistant organisms travelling with patients, and neglect of domestic primary care if policy chases only high-end private work.

[SN]Carbon footprint of health care[/SN]

CARBON FOOTPRINT
- Health systems produce a measurable share of national greenhouse-gas emissions (energy, theatres, supply chain, waste, transport).
- Mitigation taught with NPCCHH climate-resilient facilities: efficient buildings, renewable power, rational oxygen and anaesthetic gases, BMW segregation, less unnecessary travel.
- Link the climate and heat-health topic for vectors and heat. This note is the facility carbon line.

[SN]Genetically modified foods[/SN]

GM FOODS
- Examples in global teaching: Bt cotton (India commercial crop, not a staple food); GM soybean and maize in other countries.
- Potential: higher yield, pest resistance, micronutrient biofortification (example: Golden Rice as a teaching case, not an Indian commercial staple).
- Concerns: allergenicity, gene flow to wild relatives, farmer seed dependence, labelling, and public trust.
- Indian regulation: Genetic Engineering Appraisal Committee (GEAC) under the Ministry of Environment; Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) for labelling of GM food. Do not claim a current nationwide commercial GM food staple unless a GEAC approval is named.

INDIAN CONTEXT:
- Medical tourism is a commerce-and-quality question. Carbon footprint is an NPCCHH/green-hospital question. GM food is a regulation-and-nutrition question. Keep the three headings separate in a long answer.

[REF]Reference: Clinical Establishments Act / NABH as quality frame; NPCCHH climate-resilient facilities; GEAC and FSSAI for GM food.[/REF]

subsections.title: Traveler's Health and Yellow Fever IHR Certificate
subsections.content:
OVERVIEW OF THE CHAPTER
Traveler's health is the prevention of illness in people who cross international borders, and the protection of India from imported infection. Yellow fever vaccination under the International Health Regulations (IHR) 2005 is the highest-yield single item.

DEFINITIONS
INTERNATIONAL CERTIFICATE OF VACCINATION OR PROPHYLAXIS: The IHR (2005) model certificate. For yellow fever it becomes valid 10 days after a WHO-approved vaccine given at an authorised centre, and then remains valid for the life of the person.
YELLOW FEVER ENDEMIC COUNTRY: A country on the World Health Organization list of areas with risk of yellow fever transmission. India is not endemic, but Aedes aegypti is present, so import control is strict.

[SN]Yellow fever vaccination certificate and IHR[/SN]

[LAQ]Traveler's health: yellow fever, malaria, and quarantine[/LAQ]

YELLOW FEVER (IHR)
- Only vaccine that IHR currently allows States to require as a condition of entry.
- Dose: live attenuated 17D vaccine, 0.5 ml subcutaneous, at a Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS) authorised centre in India (or equivalent abroad).
- Validity: from day 10 for life (WHO, July 2016 onwards). Older "10-year booster" teaching is outdated for certificate validity.
- India: travellers aged 9 months and above arriving from a yellow-fever risk country (or in transit outside the sterile airport area) must show the original certificate. Missing, photocopied, unstamped, or immature (less than 10 days) certificates lead to quarantine up to 6 days from last possible exposure, or until the certificate becomes valid, whichever is earlier.
- Booking in India: authorised centres listed by DGHS; digital booking exists on the government yellow-fever platform. Original paper/IHR-format certificate is what airport health officers check.

OTHER TRAVEL ITEMS
- Malaria: chemoprophylaxis as per destination (not for ordinary travel inside most of India). Bite prevention (nets, repellent) always.
- Polio: additional IPV/OPV for travel to or from polio-exporting countries as per current International Health Regulations temporary recommendations.
- Meningococcal vaccine for Hajj/Umrah as required by the host country.
- Routine: hepatitis A, typhoid, COVID-19 as per current advice. Adult immunization detail is in 32-4.

QUARANTINE VERSUS ISOLATION
- Isolation: ill or infected person. Quarantine: well person who was exposed. Yellow-fever arrivals without a valid certificate are quarantined, not isolated, unless they become ill.

INDIAN CONTEXT:
- Airport Health Organisation (APHO) and Port Health Organisation enforce IHR at points of entry. NCDC is the IHR National Focal Point. India treats the whole territory of a notifying country as infected when yellow fever is reported.

[REF]Reference: IHR 2005 Annex 6; DGHS/MoHFW yellow-fever vaccination pages; High Commission advisories on YF certificate for travel to India (2025).[/REF]
